_comment: Per-work orientation descriptions shown in Browse Corpus and the Reader. Keyed by language, then by base work id (the .tess filename without language directory, extension, or .part suffix). Two or three plain sentences describing the TEXT itself: its contents, structure, and interest, with author and date kept brief. Every text import should add its entry here.

la.justin.epitome: Justin's Epitome is a Latin prose abridgement of the universal history composed by Pompeius Trogus, who set the histories of Greece and of the whole world in the Latin tongue across forty-four books. In a prefatory address Justin explains that, in leisure spent in the city, he excerpted from Trogus's vast work whatever was most worthy of knowledge, discarded what was neither pleasant to learn nor necessary as an example, and fashioned the remainder into a small 'body of flowers' to remind those who knew Greek and to instruct those who did not. The work is of later imperial date and compresses the deeds of the kings, nations and peoples of every age into a continuous narrative, opening with Ninus of Assyria and the warrior queen Semiramis, passing through the effeminate Sardanapallus and the transfer of empire to the Medes, and reaching the court of Astyages and the exposed Persian infant, suckled by a dog, who was prophesied to deprive him of his kingdom.
la.hyginus.fabulae: A selection of fabulae from the Latin mythological compendium attributed to Hyginus, a prose work of the early imperial period. The entries are short titled narratives recounting Greek myths, including the making of Pandora, Prometheus's theft of fire, Phaethon's fall, Deucalion and Pyrrha after the flood, the rape of Proserpina, Triptolemus and the gifts of Ceres, Io's transformations and wanderings, the Titanomachy, Apollo's slaying of Python, and Apollo's musical contest with Marsyas. Many accounts end with aetiological explanations of names, places, and institutions, such as the Ionian Sea, the Bosporus, the Pythian games, and the Thesmophoria.
la.hyginus.astronomica: The Astronomica is a Latin prose treatise on the celestial sphere and the constellations, attributed to Hyginus and placed in the early imperial period. Its dedicatory preface sets out the scope of the work: the configuration of the sphere and its circles, the names and stories of the constellations and the causes of their placement among the stars, the number of stars in each figure, the rising and setting of the signs, the courses of the sun, moon, and five wandering stars, and the causes of eclipses. The main text proceeds by definition and concise exposition, beginning with the universe, the sphere, its centre, dimension, and poles, and continuing through the circles of the sphere, including the horizon, the parallels, the equinoctial circle, and the zodiac.
la.isidore.etymologiae: An early medieval Latin encyclopedia in prose, written by Isidore, which sets out the vocabulary of knowledge by explaining each term through its etymology. The first book is devoted to grammar and introduces the seven liberal arts, grammar, rhetoric, dialectic, arithmetic, music, geometry, and astronomy, opening with definitions of disciplina and ars. It then treats letters at length, covering the origin of the alphabet among the Hebrews and its transmission through Greek to Latin, the symbolic force of certain Greek letters, and the numerical values the Greeks attached to them. The remaining books carry the same method through the other domains of learning, from language and its parts to the natural world and human institutions.
la.petrarch.africa: Africa is a Renaissance Latin epic in hexameters by Francesco Petrarca. Its subject is the Second Punic War, centring on Scipio Africanus, whose fame the opening lines derive from Africa's defeat beneath Italian arms, and on the Roman resolve to root out the Africans who had devastated Italy. The opening passage invokes the Muses, seeks the favour of a Sicilian royal patron for the poem's passage to posterity, and traces the origin of the war's calamities to envy before the poet vows to sing of Scipio's deeds.
la.pomponius_mela.de_chorographia: De Chorographia is a Latin prose treatise on the geography of the inhabited world by Pomponius Mela, written in the early Imperial period. It opens with an account of the earth's position in the cosmos, its five zones, the encircling ocean and the division of the lands into Asia, Europe and Africa, and then proceeds coast by coast around the three continents. In a rapid and selective manner announced at the outset, it catalogues seas, gulfs, rivers, mountains, peoples and cities, together with whatever in the nature of regions and inhabitants seemed worth recording.
la.varro.de_lingua_latina: De Lingua Latina, a technical prose treatise by Varro written during the Republic, examines the origins and formation of Latin vocabulary. The opening announces a six-book exposition of how words were imposed on things, setting the discipline the Greeks call etymologike against its opponents and ranking explanations in four grades, from popular understanding up to philosophical and recondite origins. The treatise further considers the obscuring of old words by time, the causes of change in letters and syllables, and the division of vocabulary into native, foreign, and forgotten, drawing evidence from both common usage and the poets. Its programme covers names of places and the things found in them, terms of time and what occurs in them, and both subjects as handled by the poets.
la.varro.res_rusticae: Varro's Res Rusticae is a Latin prose treatise on agriculture composed during the Roman Republic. Addressed to Fundania, who has bought an estate, it opens with the author, in his eightieth year, resolving to leave practical farming instructions in three books covering crop cultivation, livestock, and villa-based pasturage, after an invocation of the twelve agricultural deities and a review of earlier Greek and Carthaginian writers on rural matters. The work proceeds in the form of dialogue among Roman landowners such as Fundanius, Agrius, Agrasius, Licinius Stolo, and Tremelius Scrofa, beginning with a discussion of Italy's fertility and suitability for cultivation.
la.velleius_paterculus.historiae_romanae: Historiae Romanae is a Latin prose history by Velleius Paterculus, a writer of the Early Imperial period. Its opening surveys the generations after the Trojan War, recounting the city foundations of the returning Greek heroes, the Heraclid conquest of the Peloponnese, the self-sacrificing death of Codrus at Athens, colonies from Gades and Utica to Cumae and Neapolis, the Greek settlements of Asia Minor, and the life and dates of Homer. From these legendary beginnings the work, a history of Rome, proceeds toward Roman affairs in a compressed, annalistic manner punctuated by moralising judgements on its subjects.
la.frontinus.strategemata: The Strategemata of Frontinus is a Latin prose treatise of the early imperial period that collects brief exempla of the resourcefulness of commanders, a genre the preface distinguishes from strategica, the broader art of generalship. The compilation is arranged in three books by circumstance: examples bearing on war before battle is joined, those concerning battle and the concluding of peace, and those relating to the laying and lifting of sieges. Within each book the anecdotes are classified under headings such as concealing one's plans, discovering the enemy's plans, marching through hostile territory, ambushes, quelling sedition, encouraging an army to fight, and dispelling fear born of unfavorable omens. The entries, drawn from both Greek and Roman history and covering deeds as well as sayings, are narrated in compressed form, ranging from Cato's deception of the Spanish cities to Domitian's concealment of his campaign against the Germans.
la.frontinus.de_aquis: The De Aquis is a Latin prose technical treatise by Frontinus, written in the early Imperial period while its author held the curatorship of Rome's aqueducts, an office he records as having been entrusted to him by the emperor Nerva. The work surveys the nine aqueducts then entering the city, Appia, Anio Vetus, Marcia, Tepula, Iulia, Virgo, Alsietina (also called Augusta), Claudia, and Anio Novus, setting out for each the consular date and circumstances of its construction, the source and point of capture, and the lengths of underground channel, substructure and arched work in Roman paces. It then describes the distribution of the water among public works, imperial purposes and private users, the castella and their quotas, and the legal provisions governing the drawing and upkeep of the supply, together with the penalties fixed by statute, senatus consulta and imperial mandates. The preface presents the compilation as a formula for the administration, drawn up at the outset of the author's tenure for his own instruction and capable of serving any successor in the post.
la.sidonius.carmina: The Carmina of Sidonius form a collection of late antique Latin panegyric and occasional poetry composed in mixed metres. The opening poem, in elegiac couplets, stages a mythological prelude in which gods, demigods and rustic creatures vie in song, before the poet offers his own modest verses to a Caesar hailed as the great hope of the age. A subsequent long poem addresses an Augustus as a former consul entering his second consulship, praising his elevation to the throne, the unanimity of his support, and the Thracian land of his birth.
la.sidonius.epistulae: The Epistulae of Sidonius is a Latin prose letter collection of late antique date, opening with a preface to Constantius in which the author explains his decision to gather his more polished letters into a single volume and names Symmachus and the younger Pliny as his stylistic models. The letters are addressed to named correspondents and combine courtesy, description, and commentary on contemporary affairs. Among them stands a long portrait of Theodoric, king of the Goths, detailing his physique, court routine, hunting, dining, and conduct at the gaming table. The style is elaborate and self-consciously literary throughout.
la.fronto.epistulae: Fronto's Epistulae is a Latin prose correspondence of the later Imperial period, comprising letters exchanged between the orator Fronto and members of the imperial household, above all Caesar, who addresses Fronto as his teacher. The letters combine affectionate greetings, anxious enquiries after health and advice to travel to the waters, and elaborate rhetorical play, including a sustained disquisition arguing that love conceived by chance and impulse surpasses friendship grounded in reasoned services, just as Fortune outdoes Reason in divine honours. Throughout, the correspondents vie in expressions of devotion, addressing each other with tender superlatives and exclamations.
la.nemesianus.eclogae: The Eclogae are a group of Latin pastoral poems in dactylic hexameter by Nemesianus, a poet of the later Roman imperial period. The collection consists of short eclogues in which herdsmen sing and converse amid conventional scenery of pipes, flocks, willows and river banks. The opening poem issues an invitation to song, recalls a contest in which Tityrus defeated Mopsus, and passes into a lament for Meliboeus, an aged poet and arbiter of rural disputes, whose death the singers mourn and whose praises they celebrate before Pan, Apollo, Pales and the other rural deities.
la.nemesianus.cynegetica: A didactic poem on hunting: the breeding, rearing, and ailments of hounds, the choice of horses, and the huntsman's nets and gear, breaking off after 325 lines. Written by Nemesianus about AD 283.
la.nemesianus_pseudo.de_aucupio: A Latin didactic poem in hexameters on fowling, transmitted as a pseudonymous work under the name of Nemesianus and belonging to the later imperial period. The poem gives instruction in the capture of birds, describing their habits, habitats and appearance, the behaviour of species such as the tetrax and the woodcock, and the snares and devices by which they may be taken. An opening passage places the tetrax near Peltinum at the foot of the Apennines and invokes Palamedes as legendary instructor in fowling.
la.symmachus.epistulae: A collection of late antique Latin prose letters attributed to Symmachus, made up in part of an exchange between Symmachus and his father, under the headings 'Symmachus patri suo' and 'Pater Symmacho'. The letters report family news, moves between Campanian villas such as Bauli, and the exchange of literary compositions, and they frequently embed verse, including hexameter descriptions of painted scenes and verse elogia of contemporary Roman aristocrats such as Aradius Rufinus, Anicius Julianus, Petronius Probianus and Verinus. The prose moves between private courtesy, moral reflection on praise and modesty, and accounts of domestic and official affairs, with the poetic insertions woven into the argument of each letter.
la.abelard.historia_calamitatum: The Historia Calamitatum is a medieval Latin prose letter of consolation by Peter Abelard, addressed to an absent friend and framed as an autobiographical account of the author's misfortunes. It narrates his upbringing in Brittany near Nantes, his training in dialectic and his quarrels over universals with his master William of Champeaux, his teaching career at Melun, Corbeil and Paris, his love affair with Heloise and its violent consequences, his entry into monastic life, and the persecutions and ecclesiastical condemnations that attended his theological writing. Each calamity is presented as an example intended to console the recipient, whose own trials are held up against the narrator's as lighter and more bearable.
la.abelard.epistolae: A medieval Latin prose collection of letters transmitted under Abelard's name, comprising the correspondence between Abelard and Heloise. It opens with Heloise's letter to Abelard, answering an epistle of consolation he had addressed to a friend recounting the story of his calamities, including the persecution of rival masters, the treachery within his abbacy, and the founding of the oratory of the Paraclete. The ensuing exchange turns on grief and consolation, on Abelard's obligations to the community of nuns he established, and on the spiritual care and governance of that female congregation, quoting authorities such as Seneca and the Apostle Paul in support of its arguments.
la.gregorius_magnus.dialogi: The Dialogi of Gregory the Great, a work of Latin theological prose from the early medieval period, takes the form of a dialogue between the author and his beloved deacon Peter. It opens with Gregory lamenting the burdens of pastoral office and the loss of contemplative quiet, and then proceeds by question and answer to narratives of holy men and their virtues and miracles in Italy. The tales include, among others, the story of Honoratus, a colonus of the patrician Venantius whose abstinentia was vindicated by a miraculous catch of fish and who founded a monastery with some two hundred monks at Fundi. Gregory repeatedly marks his care for sources, noting for which accounts he preserves only the sense and for which the very words of his informants.
la.gregorius_magnus.regula_pastoralis: The Regula Pastoralis is a Latin prose treatise on spiritual governance by Gregory the Great, addressed in its preface to John, whom the author calls a fellow bishop. Gregory opens by defending his earlier reluctance to undertake pastoral office and announces a fourfold scheme of enquiry: how a man should come to the summit of rule, how he should live once he has reached it, how he should teach, and how he should daily contemplate his own infirmity lest success breed presumption. The work warns at length against the unlearned and the ambitious who seize charge of souls, arguing that the rule of souls is an ars artium that must be preceded by study and upright living, and it supports its arguments with dense citation of Scripture, from the Gospels and Psalms to the prophets and Pauline epistles. Its era of composition is early medieval, though no more precise date is given in the record.
la.lactantius_placidus.in_statii_thebaida_c: A Late Antique prose commentary on Statius's Thebaid, attributed to Lactantius Placidus. It proceeds lemma by lemma through the poem, quoting each phrase of the verse and supplying glosses of difficult words, mythological narratives, and geographical and genealogical details, often retelling the underlying stories at length, as with Cadmus, Semele, Pentheus, and Ino. Alongside the lexical notes it explains figures of speech and paraphrases the poet's statements, such as the proem's declaration that Statius sings of Greek rather than Roman wars because he cannot yet treat Latin themes.
la.aquinas.summa_theologiae_1: The Prima Pars of the Summa theologiae is a Latin work of scholastic theology by Thomas Aquinas, composed in the medieval quaestio format: each article sets out objections (videtur quod), weighs a contrary authority (sed contra), and answers with a reasoned determination (respondeo dicendum). The part opens by examining the nature, necessity, and status of sacred doctrine as a science, asking ten questions about its scope and method before proceeding to its subject matter. The Prima Pars as a whole treats God's existence and attributes, the Trinity, creation, the angels, the work of the six days, and human nature. Its prose is dialectical and heavily citation-laden, adducing Scripture, Aristotle, Augustine, and other authorities as the arguments require.
la.aquinas.hymni: By Thomas Aquinas, a medieval Latin collection of hymns in praise of the Eucharist, opening with 'Pange, lingua, gloriosi' and continuing with 'Lauda, Sion, Salvatorem'. The poems commemorate the institution of the sacrament at the Last Supper and set out the doctrine that the consecrated bread and wine become the true body and blood of Christ, apprehended by faith rather than the senses. The strophic verses exhort veneration of the sacrament and close with doxologies of praise to the Trinity.
la.erasmus.moriae_encomium: Moriae Encomium is a Latin prose satire by the Renaissance humanist Erasmus, prefaced by a letter to Thomas More dated 1508 in which the author anticipates objections that the work is too playful for a theologian and too biting for Christian modesty. The satire proper is an oration spoken by the personified Folly (Stultitia loquitur), who presents herself as the power that gladdens gods and men and proceeds to praise her own sway over human life. The work is arranged in 68 numbered sections.
la.erasmus.colloquia: The Colloquia is a Renaissance Latin prose satire by Erasmus, written as a series of dialogues between named speakers. The opening colloquy presents a conversation in which one speaker recounts a voyage almost lost in a violent storm: the fiery omen the sailors take for Castor and Pollux, the jettisoning of cargo and finally of the masts, and the extravagant vows made by passengers of various nations to the Virgin and to individual saints. Through its brisk question-and-answer exchange the narrative turns into a satire on maritime superstition and popular religious practice.
la.alan_de_insulis.anticlaudianus: The Anticlaudianus is a medieval Latin allegorical epic in hexameters by Alan of Lille (Alanus de Insulis). A prose prologue invites the reader to emend and judge the work, asserts that it embraces grammar, dialectic, rhetoric, arithmetic, music, geometry, astronomy and celestial theology, and warns off readers who follow the senses rather than reason. The verse narrative then opens with Nature resolving to fashion a work surpassing all her earlier creations, weighing the design with the help of personified figures such as Concordia, Copia, Ratio and Prudentia, and summoning counsel from the heavenly court.
la.alan_de_insulis.de_planctu_naturae: De planctu naturae is a medieval Latin prosimetrum in mixed verse and prose, attributed to Alan of Insulis. It opens with an elegiac complaint that men, through magic and unnatural practices, have inverted the sexual order that Venus and nature prescribe. The complaint gives way to a vision in which the personified goddess Nature, radiant and weeping, appears to the narrator, and the work proceeds as an allegorical and philosophical discourse in which she laments humanity's departures from the natural law.
la.bernard_silvestris.cosmographia: The Cosmographia of Bernard Silvestris is a medieval Latin philosophical work in mixed prose and verse, divided into two books entitled Megacosmus and Microcosmus. It opens with a dedicatory epistle and prose summaries of the two books before the narrative proper begins. In the first book Natura laments the confusion of prime matter before Noys, the divine providence, who separates the four elements, arranges the angelic hierarchies, the fixed stars, and the seven planetary spheres, and then orders the world's mountains, rivers, animals, plants, and their kinds. The second book recounts the making of man, in which Noys dispatches Urania and Physis, the latter forming the human body from the remnants of the four elements.
la.cassiodorus.institutiones: Cassiodorus's Institutiones is a Late Antique didactic prose work in two books, framed as an introduction to Christian study for beginners who have mastered the psalms. The first book treats the divine Scriptures, prescribing an order of reading and indicating which Latin expositors should be consulted on each biblical book, while the second offers a brief account of the arts and secular disciplines. In its preface the author recounts his failed attempt, undertaken with Pope Agapitus, to establish public teachers of Scripture in Rome, and presents these books as a substitute for the absent masters.
la.cassiodorus.variae: The Variae is a Late Antique Latin epistolary collection in which Cassiodorus gathered official documents drafted during his tenure in the quaestorship, the mastership of the offices, and the praetorian prefecture, arranged by the author into twelve books. Its preface presents the work as compiled at the urging of friends who maintained that pronouncements issued on behalf of kings merited a written record. Books six and seven assemble formularies for the various public offices, intended as models for future occupants of those posts, while the remaining books contain letters, petitions, and edicts spanning a wide diversity of public business. The title reflects the variety of matters, offices, and styles encompassed in the collection.
la.venantius_fortunatus.carmina: A collection of Latin lyric verse by the Late Antique poet Venantius Fortunatus, composed in a variety of metres. The poems are largely occasional pieces: church dedications and building inscriptions, epigrams and elegies on bishops, saints, and lay patrons, panegyrics of royal and aristocratic figures, and hymns. The opening poem celebrates the church founded by Bishop Vitalis, enumerating the saints whose relics it enshrines, and the collection continues in a similar vein with verse on persons, places, and events of the poet's world.
la.venantius_fortunatus.vita_martini: Vita Martini is a Late Antique Latin epic in hexameters by Venantius Fortunatus, celebrating the life and deeds of Martin, the soldier who became a bishop in Gaul. The poem opens with an account of Christ's triumph over death and the harrowing of hell, followed by a survey of earlier Christian Latin poets, including Juvencus, Sedulius, Prudentius, Paulinus, Arator, and Alcimus, together with the author's professions of his own poetic inadequacy. The narrative then recounts Martin's birth at Sabaria in Pannonia, his sharing of his military cloak with a beggar at Amiens, his renunciation of service under Julian, and further episodes from his career as bishop.
la.walter_de_chatillon.alexandreis: The Alexandreis is a medieval Latin epic in hexameter verse by Walter de Chatillon, recounting the deeds of Alexander of Macedon, including his victories over Darius and Porus and the triumph of Greece over Persia. The work opens with a prose preface in which the author addresses his poem directly, defends it against anticipated critics, and mentions that it was labored over for five years, before turning to an invocation that requests aid in singing the conqueror's exploits. The narrative proper begins with the young Alexander, still beardless, chafing at the dominion that Darius holds over the Greek lands.
la.nigel_wireker.speculum_stultorum: Nigel Wireker's Speculum Stultorum, a twelfth-century Latin beast-fable satire in elegiac verse. Its hero is Burnellus, a donkey dissatisfied with the length of his tail, whose quest to grow a longer one becomes a vehicle for mocking the ambitions and hypocrisies of monks, clerics, and scholars of Wireker's day, and drifts into extended satire of university life and the corruption of the church courts. Wireker, a monk of Christ Church, Canterbury, died around 1198 to 1200.
la.johannes_hanville.architrenius: The Architrenius is a medieval Latin satire composed in hexameter verse and attributed to Johannes Hanville. Its opening denounces sloth (segnities) as the nurse of idleness, marshalling in personified form the crowd of vices that attend her, sleep, luxury, wantonness, torpor, inconstancy and shame, while the speaker disclaims grand poetic ambition and pledges constancy to his undertakings. The poem proceeds in this allegorical and moralising manner, setting the languor of vice against the disciplined pursuit of study and labour.
la.carmina_burana.carmina_burana: A medieval Latin anthology of anonymous goliardic verse, of uncertain date, comprising 228 numbered poems with a supplement and composed in a variety of metres. Its satire opens with an indictment of venal justice, in which money forms pacts, buys counsel and verdicts, and sways prelates and judges, while clerics care for coin rather than conduct, closing with the proclamation that avarice reigns. Alongside such diatribe the collection ranges over moral, devotional, amorous and convivial lyric.
la.tiberianus.carmina: The Carmina attributed to the Late Antique Latin poet Tiberianus consist of four short lyric poems in mixed metres. The first is an ornate description of a spring landscape of running water, flowering banks, laurel and myrtle, and birdsong, culminating in praise of the rose as queen of flowers; the second is a sustained invective against gold, illustrated with mythological exempla such as Danae, Polydorus, and the fall of Troy. The third is a brief fable in which a bird, its wings weighed down by rain, plunges from flight as an admonition against presumptuous ambition, and the fourth is a hymn to an omnipotent, eternal deity who oversees the turning of the ages and the cyclical renewal of the world.
la.pentadius.carmina: Six short poems by Pentadius, a minor Latin poet of the third or fourth century known only from Riese's Anthologia Latina. The best known, De adventu veris, describes the arrival of spring through repeated end-of-line echoes, and it became a model for later medieval spring poems in the locus amoenus tradition.
la.prudentius.cathemerinon: The Cathemerinon is a cycle of twelve Christian lyric poems in Latin by Prudentius, a poet of Late Antiquity. Composed in a variety of lyric meters, the poems follow the course of the day from cockcrow through morning, the hours before and after meals, the lighting of the lamps, and evening, to the onset of sleep. Further hymns address fasting and the burial of the dead, and the collection closes with a hymn for all hours. The opening poem presents the cock's crow as the summons of Christ, rousing the soul from the sleep of sin to vigilance before the coming light.
la.matthew_of_vendome.ars_versificatoria: The Ars Versificatoria is a medieval Latin treatise on the art of composing verse, by Matthew of Vendome. It opens with a prologue in which the author defends his undertaking against imagined detractors, above all a hostile figure named Rufinus, before turning to instruction. The didactic portion discusses the use of epithets, the schemes zeuma and hypozeusis, and the ways a composition may be begun, illustrated with lines from Horace, Ovid, and Statius as well as the author's own examples of praise and invective. Prose exposition is interspersed with Latin verse in a variety of meters.
la.geoffrey_of_vinsauf.poetria_nova: The Poetria Nova of Geoffrey of Vinsauf is a medieval Latin treatise on rhetoric, written in hexameter verse and dedicated in its opening lines to Pope Innocent III, whose name is turned to metrical account in the prologue. After a long encomium of the pope's virtues and liberality, the poem turns to its instructional core, urging that a work be measured out within the mind before it is committed to pen or tongue. The precepts that follow cover the inward planning and ordering of material, the choice of an opening for a composition, techniques of amplification and abbreviation, and the ornamentation of style through figures of thought and diction. The rules are framed for both prose and verse, with the whole argument carried in didactic hexameters.
la.geoffrey_of_vinsauf.documentum: A medieval Latin rhetorical treatise in prose, the Documentum is attributed to Geoffrey of Vinsauf. It treats the making of any work under three heads, beginning, progress, and conclusion, distinguishing natural from artificial openings and enumerating the modes in which an artificial beginning may be taken, whether from the middle, the end, a proverb, or an example. Each mode is illustrated with paired prose and metrical specimens drawn from the story of Minos, Androgeus, and Scylla, with appeal to Tully's teaching on the brevity and clarity of narration. The portion preserved here follows these openings with instructions for continuing the discourse once an artificial beginning has been chosen.
la.eberhard_the_german.laborintus: The Laborintus is a Latin didactic poem on rhetoric, attributed to Eberhard the German and of uncertain medieval date. It opens with an allegory in which Nature relates the birth of a poor schoolmaster whose fate, poverty, toil, and the burden of the teaching chair, is written in the stars, before turning to a versified treatment of rhetorical composition covering invention, arrangement, style, the parts of a discourse, and tropes and figures. The poem ends with an account of the miseries of schoolmasters, and its verse mixes elegiac couplets with other metres.
la.petrus_riga.de_ornatu_mundi: The De Ornatu Mundi is a short medieval Latin religious poem in elegiac couplets by Peter Riga, long circulated and printed under the name of Hildebert of Lavardin. After an invocation to Clio, it unfolds an ornate description of a paradisal grove, cataloguing in paired couplets its fragrant and fruit-bearing trees, the union of vine and elm, its springs and rocks, flowers, birds and beasts. Each feature of the landscape is matched with a counterpart quality, presenting the adorned garden as an earthly rival of paradise.
la.caesar_pseudo.de_bello_africo: De Bello Africo is a Latin prose narrative of Julius Caesar's campaign in Africa, transmitted under Caesar's name but of uncertain authorship and conventionally treated as a continuation of his commentaries. The work belongs to the historiographical prose of the late Republican period and recounts Caesar's embarkation at Lilybaeum in Sicily, his landing on the African coast near Hadrumetum, and his early operations there. Its narrative covers skirmishing with Numidian and Maurian cavalry, encounters with the forces of Scipio and King Juba, dealings with towns such as Leptis and Ruspina, and the logistical difficulties of an army awaiting its scattered fleet and reinforcements.
la.caesar_pseudo.de_bello_alexandrino: Transmitted under Caesar's name but of uncertain authorship, the Bellum Alexandrinum is a Latin historiographical prose account of Caesar's war in Alexandria during the civil wars of the Roman Republic. It opens with Caesar's summoning of fleets from Rhodes, Syria, and Cilicia, archers from Crete, and horsemen from the Nabataean king Malchus while siege works and defenses mount on both sides of the city. The narrative follows the Alexandrians' extensive levies, arms manufacture, and mobile fortifications, the deadly rivalry between the commander Achillas and Arsinoe, daughter of King Ptolemy, whose coup transfers command to the eunuch Ganymedes, and his scheme to flood the Roman quarter with seawater, answered by Caesar's insistence that wells and naval supply render flight unnecessary.
la.caesar_pseudo.de_bello_hispaniensi: The De Bello Hispaniensi is a Latin prose narrative of Caesar's war in Spain, attributed to Caesar but of uncertain authorship, composed during the era of the Republic. After the defeat of Pharnaces and the recovery of Africa, Caesar, holding the dictatorship, crosses into Hispania Ulterior to confront Gnaeus Pompeius the younger and his brother Sextus, who are gathering forces among the towns of the province. The narrative follows the campaign from Caesar's descent on Corduba and the night relief of Ulia to the bridging of the river Baetis and the siege of Ategua, with continual skirmishing between the two armies around the river and the oppida.
la.vegetius.epitoma_rei_militaris: The Epitoma Rei Militaris by Vegetius is a Late Antique Latin treatise on military affairs in four prose books, addressed in its preface to an unnamed emperor. The first book teaches the choice and training of recruits, the second preserves the customs of the old army, the third expounds the arts necessary for land battle, and the fourth enumerates the machines for attacking and defending cities and adds precepts for naval war. The author presents his work as a diligent gathering of material on the military art scattered among historians and teachers, arguing that skill and drill, not mere numbers or untrained courage, bring victory.
la.grattius.cynegetica: The Cynegetica is a Latin didactic poem in hexameters on the arts of hunting, attributed to Grattius and placed in the Augustan period. It opens with an invocation to Diana and a preface contrasting the unarmed violence of early mankind with the later rule of Ratio and the ordered progress of the arts, before turning to technical instruction in hunting equipment. The surviving portion gives detailed directions for weaving hunting nets and for choosing linen from particular regions, including Faliscan, Spanish, and Egyptian supplies, and intersperses mythological exempla of hunters such as Adonis, Ancaeus, and Hercules.
la.germanicus.aratea: The Aratea is a Latin didactic poem in hexameters of the Early Imperial period, attributed to Germanicus and recasting Aratus's Greek Phaenomena on the stars in Latin verse. Its proem acknowledges Aratus as the original singer of the heavens and invokes the emperor, addressed as genitor, before turning to the celestial sphere itself, its unmoved axis and poles and the constellations that wheel about them. The poem then takes up the northern figures in turn, the Bears Helice and Cynosura, the Dragon coiled between them, the kneeling labourer, Ariadne's crown, the serpent-bearer, joining astronomical description to the myths attached to each and presenting the stars as signs by which sailor and ploughman order their labours.
la.solinus.collectanea_rerum_memorabilium: A Latin prose work of the later imperial period by Solinus, the Collectanea Rerum Memorabilium is a compendium of geographical and antiquarian lore arranged as a survey of the inhabited world. The preface presents it as a deliberately condensed compilation drawn from received writers, and the survey begins with Rome as the head of the world before proceeding region by region through its lands and seas. Its material comprises notable sites, the natures of men and other animals, exotic trees, the appearance and rites of remote peoples, and other memorable particulars, treated with an eye to brevity and variety.
la.censorinus.de_die_natali: De Die Natali ('On the Birthday') is a Latin technical prose treatise by Censorinus, an author of the Later Imperial period, presented to his patron Quintus Caerellius as a gift on the latter's birthday. The opening disclaims any intent to write moral precepts or rhetorical praise, describing the book instead as an assortment of scholarly quaestiones drawn from philological and antiquarian sources. After an account of the genius who receives yearly sacrifice at birthdays and a survey of ancient opinions on the origin of humanity, ranging from Pythagorean eternalism to the cosmogonic speculations of Anaximander, Empedocles, Democritus, Epicurus, and Zeno, the preface moves toward matters proper to the day of birth itself.
la.obsequens.liber_de_prodigiis: The Liber de Prodigiis is a Latin prose compilation of portents by the author Obsequens, a writer of late antiquity whose fuller identity and exact dates are uncertain. It arranges reported prodigies year by year under consular dates, recording thunderbolts that struck temples and public buildings, rains of earth, blood, stone, and milk, monstrous and anomalous births, weeping and sweating statues, celestial apparitions, and the expiatory rites, supplications, novendial sacrifices, consultation of the Sibylline books, decreed in response. The entries run consecutively from the consulship of C. Claudius and Ti. Sempronius Gracchus in 177 BC, mixing omens with brief notices of wars, plagues, and political events against which the marvels are set.
la.adamnan.de_locis_santis: An early medieval Latin prose treatise by Adamnan, De Locis Sanctis presents itself as a record of the oral account of the pilgrim Arculf, whom the author repeatedly cites as his informant. The work opens with a chapter list and then describes Jerusalem itself, its walls, towers, and gates, before turning to the principal holy places: the round church built over the Lord's sepulchre, the church on Calvary, Constantine's basilica where the Cross was rediscovered, and the relics kept there, including the chalice, sponge, lance, and sudarium. Further chapters treat sites in and around the city, such as the church of Saint Mary in the valley of Josaphat, the Mount of Olives, and the tomb of Lazarus, along with a house of prayer built by the Saracens that is said to hold three thousand worshippers.
la.aethelwulf.carmen_de_abbatibus: Carmen de Abbatibus is a medieval Latin poem of the Carolingian era by Aethelwulf. It opens with a humble dedication to a bishop, offering rustic verses and asking indulgence for the poet's untutored song, before turning to Northumbrian history: the fall of King Ecgfrith to the Picts and the accession of his brother Aldfrith, under whom a monastery was founded. The poem goes on to recount the community's noble first abbot, Eanmund, who abandoned a military life for monastic service, and the succession of abbots whose deeds and piety form the work's principal subject.
la.agius_of_corvey.epicedium_hathumodae: The Epicedium Hathumodae is a Carolingian Latin funeral lament attributed to Agius of Corvey, mourning the death of Hathumoda, an abbess. The poem explains that its author, present at the abbess's death, had consoled her grieving sisters in speech and now, at their request, casts that consolation into verse so that they might have it continually before their eyes. It mourns a woman praised as sister, mother, nurse, teacher, and lady to her community, while urging the mourners to moderate their tears, since nature permits grief but reason forbids excess.
la.agius_of_corvey.versus_computistici: The Versus Computistici is a short Latin verse treatise on computus, attributed to Agius of Corvey and belonging to the Carolingian period. Addressed to a correspondent named Rimbert, whose name the poet glosses as meaning 'clear in reckoning', it was composed, according to its preface, at the recipient's request and with the needs of learners in mind. The poem sets out the role of number in the ordering of time, explaining the solar and lunar cycles, epacts, concurrents, and the determination of weekdays and the moon's age across the year. A later section describes an alphabetical diagram or table by which these calendar data may be found for any given year.
la.agnellus_ravennatis.liber_pontificalis: A Latin ecclesiastical history of the Carolingian era, the Liber Pontificalis of Agnellus of Ravenna narrates the succession of Ravenna's bishops from apostolic times down to the author's own day. A priest of the Ravennate church who bears the names Agnellus and Andreas, he opens the work with a rhymed hexameter prologue lamenting the long neglect of local episcopal record-keeping and invoking the reigns of the emperors Louis and Lothar. Beyond its importance as a source for early medieval Ravenna, the compilation blends scriptural, classical, and hagiographic diction, and its catalogue of episcopal lives invites comparison with the Roman Liber Pontificalis and other late-antique succession narratives, making it a productive quarry for verbal and structural parallels.
la.aimoin_of_saint_germain.carmen_de_transl: A medieval Latin verse narrative attributed to the Carolingian author Aimoin of Saint Germain, recounting the translation of the relics of Saint Vincent the deacon and martyr. The poem relates how the monk Audaldus, accompanied by a companion and aided by a custodian won over with silver, removes the saint's body from its tomb at Valentia in Spain and carries it home by night. The remainder of the work describes the joyful reception of the relics at his monastery, their placement behind the altar of Saint Benedict, and the miracles worked at the shrine, including the healing of a doubting woman, some of which are noted as having been recorded elsewhere in prose.
la.alcuin.carmina: The Carmina of Alcuin form a corpus of Latin verse by the Carolingian writer, comprising numerous separate poems on devotional, historical, and occasional subjects. The collection opens with a prayer to Christ for poetic eloquence, followed by a long narrative poem on the church of York, tracing the city from its Roman foundation through the coming of the Saxons and the mission of Pope Gregory, with praise of its kings, bishops, and saints. The remaining books contain shorter poems treating varied sacred and secular themes.
la.amalarius.versus_marini: A short Latin poem of the Carolingian period, attributed to Amalarius, cast as a dialogue between a monk and his abbot. It narrates a sea voyage beset by storms, a stay of twenty-eight nights in Constantinople, where the brothers are summoned to the palace of the basileus Leo and prayers are offered for the life of Charles, his sons, and the Frankish people, and a perilous return journey past coasts associated with Moors and Slavs. The travellers reach Italy and are received with tears and joy by the community at a church of a saint. The poem closes with grief at the death of a king named Charles and a prayer that God may reunite the speaker with him and with the brothers forever.
la.ambrose.exameron: The Exameron is a Late Antique Latin prose treatise on the six days of creation by Ambrose. The work opens with a survey of pagan philosophical cosmologies, the principles posited by Plato, Aristotle, Pythagoras, Democritus, and the atomists, and their claims about the eternity and corruptibility of the world, and refutes them from Moses' words in Genesis, 'in principio fecit deus caelum et terram,' presenting God as the creator of matter itself rather than a craftsman working upon it. From there the treatise proceeds to expound the works accomplished on each of the six days.
la.ambrose.explanatio_psalmorum_xii: A Late Antique Latin work of theology by Ambrose, comprising explanations of twelve psalms. The prologue treats delectation as at once the highest incentive to virtue and the devil's chief instrument of deceit, tracing the theme from Adam's fall through the praise of the angels and the canticles of Moses to David's election as psalmist, and commending the Psalter as a medicine for human wounds and a training ground of the virtues. The body of the work then expounds the twelve psalms in succession, quoting each and unfolding its moral and spiritual teaching in continuous prose.
la.ambrosiaster.pseudo_augustini_quaestione: A Late Antique Latin collection of 127 questions on the Old and New Testament, attributed to the anonymous writer known as Ambrosiaster and traditionally transmitted under Augustine's name, as the title Pseudo-Augustine reflects. The work opens with a discussion of the divine nature as simple, invisible and boundless spirit, and proceeds to questions on the origin of evil, defined as a transgression of the good rather than a substance, and on free will as the ground of human merit and guilt. Its remaining questions treat scriptural difficulties and doctrinal points concerning law, sin and the moral life.
la.ammianus.rerum_gestarum: The Res Gestae is a Latin work of historiography in prose, written by Ammianus Marcellinus in the Late Antique period. It chronicles the affairs of the Roman Empire in a classicizing historical manner, and its opening narrative recounts the cruel rule of Gallus Caesar in the East under Constantius, the network of informers and summary condemnations centered on Antioch, and the incursions of the Isaurians. Episodic sections within the narrative are marked by rubrics such as 'Galli Caesaris saevitia' and 'Isaurorum incursiones'.
la.angilbert_carmina: Latin verse by Angilbert, a poet of the Carolingian court. The opening and longest poem addresses Pippin on his return from Italy, dwelling on the joy his coming brings to his father Charlemagne and enumerating by name the brothers Charles and Chlodowih and the royal sisters whose affection for the absent prince suffuses the whole piece. The verse ends in an insistent refrain declaring that 'David', the biblical model of kingship, is the beloved of poets, while the speaker, naming himself Angilbert, calls on his pipe to fashion sweet verses for his lord.
la.angilbert_versus: A short Carolingian Latin poem that serves as a verse preface to Augustine's De doctrina christiana. Its opening section recounts the contents of Augustine's four books: the first on Christ's precepts for the present life, the second and third on signs and things, what they are and how they are to be used and understood, and the fourth summarising the teaching of the earlier books. The poet then names himself as Angilbert, a humble abbot who had the libellus made for King Hloduicus, whom he praises as a lover of divine wisdom, and the poem closes with prayers for the king's prosperity and a doxology to the Trinity.
la.angilbertus_miles.versus_de_fontaneto: Versus de Fontaneto is a short Latin poem of Carolingian date narrating a battle fought at a villa the poem calls Fontaneto, in the war between Lothar and the partisans of Charles and Louis. It opens at dawn with a vision of fratricidal strife, brother against brother and son against father, and reports that God's mighty right hand shielded Lothar as he routed his fleeing enemies, while a king is warned against his own leaders in terms drawn from Judas's betrayal. In the closing lines the speaker names himself Angelbertus, claiming to have fought in the battle and to have survived alone from the front rank. The remainder laments the slaughter of the Franks, curses the battlefield and the day itself, depicts the stripped and unburied dead devoured by vulture, crow, and wolf, and ends with a prayer for the souls of the fallen.
la.anonymi.planctus_de_obitu_Karoli: The Planctus de Obitu Karoli is an anonymous medieval Latin planctus, or lament, of uncertain date, mourning the death of the emperor Charlemagne. Its verses voice the grief of Franks, Romans, and all Christian peoples at the news, hailing the dead ruler as father of orphans, pilgrims, widows, and virgins. Between the recurring refrain 'Heu mihi misero' the poem pronounces woes on Rome and Italy, recalls the emperor's burial at Aachen, and closes with prayers that Christ and the Holy Spirit receive Charles's soul into rest.
la.anonymous.breviarius_de_hierosolyma: The Breviarius de Hierosolyma, an anonymous Latin prose work of uncertain date, is a short guide to the holy places of Jerusalem. In the form of an itinerary it leads from the basilica of Constantine and the sites of Golgotha and the Holy Sepulchre to Mount Sion, the house of Pilate, and the Mount of Olives with the valley of Josaphat. At each stop it records the churches, altars, and relics preserved there, the crosses, the lance, the crown of thorns, and the instruments of the Passion, and connects each place with episodes from the life of Christ and from biblical history.
la.anonymous_pilgrim_of_piacenza.itinerariu: The Itinerarium is a Latin prose itinerary of Late Antique date, an account of pilgrimage to the holy places written by an anonymous traveler who sets out from Piacenza under the guidance of the martyr Antoninus. The route runs from Constantinople by way of Cyprus and the coastal cities of Syria and Phoenicia, including Tripoli, Beirut, Sidon, Sarepta, Tyre, and Ptolemais, and continues through Galilee, Samaria, and Judaea. The author records mileages between stations and describes basilicas, relics, and sites of healing, together with such observations as the destruction of Tripoli by earthquake in the time of the emperor Justinian and the purification customs of Samaritans and Jews.
la.anonymus.carmen_ad_ludovicum_pium: A short medieval Latin poem, anonymous and of uncertain date, addressed in its title to Louis the Pious. The poet presents himself as the maker of the book, composed in dactylic verses, and urges the king, likened to Solomon for his worthy merits, to hold fast to faith in God, love of neighbour, hope of eternal life and the reading of scripture. A long admonitory passage commends mercy, patience, humility, contrition, confession, fasting, almsgiving and chastity, while cataloguing the vices to be shunned: deceit, false witness, envy, pride, wrath, vainglory, gluttony, lust, avarice, sloth, sorrow and vanity. The poem closes by arming the king with the four virtues of justice, prudence, fortitude and temperance, and with the celestial weapons of the breastplate of justice, the helmet of hope, the shield of faith and the sword of the word of the Lord.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_compoti_ratione: An anonymous medieval Latin poem on the computus, of uncertain date, which teaches the reckoning of the calendar in verse. The opening lines tabulate the lengths of the months and the positions of their kalends, nones and ides, and set out rules, keyed to 'regulars' and concurrents and to counting the joints of the fingers, for finding the weekday of any kalends; the age of the moon at the kalends is computed by means of epacts adjusted over the nineteen-year cycle. A concluding section explains how to locate the moon within a given month and to calculate Septuagesima and Quadragesima, with allowances made throughout for leap years.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_conversione_saxonum: An anonymous medieval Latin poem, the Carmen de Conversione Saxonum celebrates Charlemagne's conversion of the pagan Saxons, whom it presents in the ninth year of that king's reign. It opens with a survey of the ages of the world from creation to the Incarnation, then depicts Saxon idolatry and blood sacrifice before recounting Charles's armed conquest of the people in imagery of wolves turned into lambs, ravens into doves, and other ravening beasts into gentle creatures. The poem closes with the defeated Saxons baptised in the name of the Trinity and a prayer that Charles may receive the rewards of the heavenly kingdom at the Last Judgement.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_nynia_episcopo: The Carmen de Nynia Episcopo is an anonymous medieval Latin poem, of uncertain date, on Saint Ninian (Nynia), bishop and evangelist of the Picts. It opens with verses on Christ's incarnation and the spread of divine light through the world before turning to its hero, whose name, the poem states, derives from his native speech. The narrative recounts his sea voyage and journey over the Alps to Rome, his consecration by the pope, his return to preach among the Picts, his conversion of idolaters, his founding of basilicas served by monastic communities, and his passage onward to the Britons. Portions of the poem are addressed directly to the saint as a venerable bishop.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_pippino: The Carmen de Pippino is an anonymous medieval Latin poem, of uncertain date, celebrating a victory of the Frankish king Pippin over the Avars. It opens by recounting the devastation the Avars have inflicted on churches and holy places, then describes how God sends Saint Peter to aid Pippin as he camps with his army on the Danube. An Avar envoy, terrified on the khagan's behalf, urges him to submit with tribute, and the khagan travels to Pippin to surrender his realm, people, and nobles into subjection. The poem closes with thanksgiving for the triumph granted over the pagans and a prayer that Pippin's dynasty may endure.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_temporum_ratione: The Carmen de Temporum Ratione is an anonymous medieval Latin poem on the reckoning of time, of uncertain date and authorship. Its opening distinguishes three grounds for temporal computation, divine authority, human authority, and custom, and the poem then treats the sabbath, the week, olympiads, the length of the month, the circuit of the stars through the zodiac, and a rejection of the pagan personification of Nature as a creatrix. Substantial passages set out the fractional division of the hour in unciae, scripuli, puncti, and related units, and define the day, surveying the differing starting points observed by Hebrews, Chaldaeans, Persians, Egyptians, Romans, Athenians, Umbrians, and Christians. The work belongs to the computistical tradition, combining calendrical, astronomical, and arithmetical material in verse form.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_timone_comite: The Carmen de Timone Comite is an anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date, addressed to the king who dispatched his count Timo to restore the neglected work of law in the Norican land. It holds up biblical rulers, David, Job, Moses, Joshua, Joseph and Gideon, as models of the just king who protects the innocent and curbs the wicked, while Timo hangs robbers, mutilates thieves, and settles quarrels in his court. The poem also records his journey to a wooded hill where new buildings rise around the church of the martyr Stephen under Bishop Alexander, and it closes by rejecting trial by fire and water as a fruitless probe of hidden guilt that falls silent before reasoned judgment.
la.anonymus.carmina_cenomanensia: The Carmina Cenomanensia is an anonymous medieval Latin collection of poems connected with Le Mans (Cenomanum), of uncertain date. The opening verses invoke Christ and the Virgin and commemorate Bishop Aldric's enshrinement of the relics of the martyrs Gervasius, Prothasius and Stephen, with prayers for the bishop and his flock. A long following poem, spoken in the poet's own voice, narrates Aldric's noble birth, his upbringing and religious vocation at Metz, the favour he enjoyed under the peaceful king Louis (Hludowicus pacifer), and his assumption of the bishopric of Le Mans, whose fields he is said to renew by his kindly labours.
la.anonymus.corneli_translationes: Corneli Translationes is an anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date celebrating the translation of the relics of Saint Cornelius to Francia under a king named Charles. It narrates the solemn reception of the body, borne by bishops, clergy, soldiers, and crowds of commoners amid crosses, candles, incense, and song, into the king's palace church, which Charles then enriches with gold, silver, vestments, and gifts. The poem further records miracles at the shrine, including healings of the sick, the confession and flight of demons, and a divine deliverance in which fire kindled by barbarian raiders consumes the surrounding buildings while sparing the church and its defenders.
la.anonymus.hymnus_nynie_episcopi: The Hymnus Nynie Episcopi is an anonymous medieval Latin hymn of uncertain date in honour of Saint Ninian (Nynia), bishop. Its verses proceed through the alphabet, and each couplet repeats its opening phrase as a refrain at the close of the line. The poem opens with God as creator and with Christ's birth from a virgin mother and redeeming death, then turns to Ninian himself, recounting his miracles, the cleansing of leprosy at his tomb, his burial beneath the temple roof, and the bearing of his soul to heaven by angels. It ends with the faithful companies in the celestial court singing perpetual praise to the king.
la.anonymus.karolus_magnus_et_leo_papa: Karolus Magnus et Leo Papa is an anonymous medieval Latin epic of 536 lines, of uncertain date, celebrating Charlemagne and his dealings with Pope Leo. The opening verses deploy the seafaring imagery of an epic prologue before moving into panegyric: Charlemagne, 'victor pius' and mightier than all kings in justice, is set against King David and the sun-god Phoebus, outshining the biblical king as the constant sun outshines the waning moon, while his rule joins piety, clemency, and divinely sanctioned discipline. Readers hunting textual parallels will find in the poem a Carolingian fusion of classical epic diction with biblical typology and the Latin panegyric tradition.
la.anonymus.laudes_mediolanensis_civitatis: Laudes Mediolanensis Civitatis is an anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date, comprising 72 lines in praise of Milan. It celebrates the city's lofty situation, its twelve-foot walls, nine iron-bound gates, water supply, and splendid churches, then enumerates the saints buried there, Ambrose, Protasius, Gervase, Nazarius, Celsus, Benedict, and others, hailing Milan as queen of cities and metropolis toward which the bishops of Ausonia converge. As a specimen of the medieval urban encomium, it offers readers of intertexts parallels for topoi of city praise, relic catalogues, and the literary promotion of a see city through its sacred dead.
la.anonymus.laudes_veronensis_civitatis: An anonymous medieval Latin encomium in praise of the city of Verona, of uncertain date. The poem extols Verona's situation in Venetia, its square plan, forty-eight towers, labyrinth, paved forum, and pagan temples, then turns to the coming of Christianity and the succession of Veronese bishops from Euprepus down to the martyr Zeno, whose preaching, miracles, and destruction of idols it recounts at length. The latter part catalogues the saints and martyrs whose relics guard the city on every side, recalling the renewal of the church under Bishop Anno in the time of the Lombard kings Desiderius and Adelchis, and closes with a description of a richly scented and gilded tomb.
la.anonymus.tituli_metrici_saeculi_viii: A collection of medieval Latin metrical inscriptions, transmitted anonymously and ascribed by its title to the eighth century. The opening and longest piece is a funerary inscription spoken in the first person by Peter, bishop of Pavia, who recounts his upbringing in the church of Ticinum, his exile from his homeland, and his restoration in the days of Charles the Great, closing with an appeal to readers for prayers for his soul. Subsequent verses eulogise the same bishop, praising his lineage, his charity toward pilgrims, captives and the sick of many peoples, and lamenting his death, in the epigraphic manner of verses composed for carved marble.
la.anonymus.versus_ad_ebonem_remensem: Versus ad Ebonem Remensem is an anonymous medieval Latin poem addressed to Ebbo, bishop of Reims, whom it greets with a long series of honorific epithets as pastor, luminary, doctor, and friend of Christ. The body of the poem recounts how the humble abbot Peter produced a Gospel book containing Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, adorned it with gold within and ivory without, and dedicated it to the apostolic lord Peter. Later lines present the book as the four-horsed chariot of Christ and as medicine for the ailing, urging all the sick to hasten to it for healing and salvation. The poem closes with a prayer that Christ reward Ebbo and Peter for the work; its date of composition is unknown.
la.anonymus.versus_de_eversione_monasterii_: An anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date, the Versus de Eversione Monasterii Glonnensis opens with an invocation to the lyre and Orpheus before turning to the burning of the basilica of Saint Florentius at Glonna by savage Bretons. The narrative recalls a devout foundation of the place by King Charles, continued under his son Hludovicus, before the realm fragments amid rebellion. Nemenoius, a poor ploughman enriched by a buried treasure, rises against Charles, ravages the lands of the Redonenses, Nannetenses and Pictavenses, and has the monastery put to the flames; the poem then recounts the apparition of Saint Florentius, the chastened invader's restitution, Abbot Dido's appeal to the king, and the abbey's re-endowment and restoration. It closes with a prayer asking Saint Florentius to be present from heaven.
la.apuleius.de_deo_socratis: De Deo Socratis is a Latin philosophical treatise in prose by Apuleius, a writer of the later imperial period. Following Plato's threefold division of the nature of things, the work distinguishes the orders of divinity, from the celestial gods perceived by sight, such as the sun, moon and stars, to the incorporeal gods grasped only by the intellect, before turning to the human condition, endowed with reason and immortal souls yet bound to mortal and troubled bodies. The argument then presses the question of what bond joins gods and men, preparing the discussion of Socrates' guardian deity from which the treatise takes its title.
la.apuleius.metamorphoses: The Metamorphoses, also known in English as The Golden Ass, is a Latin prose work in eleven books by Apuleius, a writer of the later Imperial period. Its prologue presents the narrator Lucius, who announces a series of 'stories in the Milesian manner' and claims Greek origins together with a self-taught command of Latin. The narrative follows Lucius's journey to Thessaly, where the tales of witchcraft he hears from fellow travelers, beginning with the story of Socrates and the innkeeper Meroe, feed the curiosity about magic that leads to his transformation into an ass. The work also incorporates the long embedded tale of Cupid and Psyche and closes with Lucius's restoration to human form through the goddess Isis.
la.audradus_modicus.carmina: The Carmina of Audradus Modicus constitute a collection of Latin verse by a poet of the Carolingian period. The opening poem is framed as an allegorical vision in which the poet, urged on by his friend Hincmar, is led to a sacred fountain of miraculous size and, after a night of fruitless waiting, receives from a celestial voice both an interpretation of the seven-spouted vessel he must procure and instructions for obtaining it. The visionary narrative, with its riddling symbolism and dialogue between the poet and the guardian of the living fountain, opens a corpus of further Latin poems in a predominantly devotional register.
la.audradus_modicus.de_sancta_trinitate: De Sancta Trinitate is a Carolingian Latin verse treatise on the doctrine of the Trinity by Audradus Modicus, who presents himself in the opening lines as a chorepiscopus of Sens drawn from the flock of Saint Martin of Tours. The poem begins with a prayer in which Audradus enumerates the twelve books he has composed and begs Christ for mercy and an eternal reward. The remainder expounds Trinitarian teaching, affirming that the Son is generated from and equal to the Father, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, and that three distinct persons share one simple and eternal substance.
la.augustine.confessiones: Augustine's Confessions is a late antique Latin prose work of theology, cast throughout as a direct address to God. It opens with a hymn of praise and a series of questions about how a finite creature can invoke, know, and contain its maker. The work blends autobiographical narrative of infancy, schooling, rhetorical career, and religious searching ending in conversion with extended reflection on memory, time, and creation, and its final books offer a running commentary on the opening chapters of Genesis.
la.augustine.contra_adimantum: A short Latin prose treatise of Late Antique theology by Augustine, written against the Manichaean Adimantus, who held that certain passages of Genesis contradict the New Testament. Taking the disputed verses in turn, the creation of heaven and earth in the beginning, God's rest on the seventh day, and the formation of Eve from Adam, Augustine argues that each coheres with the Gospel, reading the Trinity in the work of creation, distinguishing God's rest from his continued governance of the world, and interpreting the Sabbath as a figure spiritually fulfilled in Christ. The work closes with the observation that passages in the two testaments which seem to conflict should be understood rather than rashly condemned.
la.augustine.contra_duas_epistulas_pelegian: A Late Antique Latin prose treatise by Augustine, cast in epistolary form and addressed to Pope Boniface, directed against two letters of the Pelagians: one sent to Rome by Julian, the other to Thessalonica by eighteen bishops who shared his error. The opening is a courteous dedication in which Augustine thanks Boniface for forwarding the Pelagian documents, one of which had cited his own name maliciously, before turning to the refutation of Julian's letter. Julian's arguments are quoted and answered point by point as Augustine defends the necessity of divine grace for faith and righteous living, maintaining that free will persists in sinners but can be restored only by the grace of the Saviour. Scriptural authority, above all the Pauline letters and the Gospel of John, is invoked throughout against the Pelagian claim that unaided human will suffices for goodness.
la.augustine.contra_epistulam_fundamenti: Contra Epistulam Fundamenti is a Latin prose polemic by Augustine, cast in the form of a letter addressed to the Manichaeans and directed against a Manichaean writing known as the Epistula Fundamenti. The author opens with a prayer for a calm and peaceable mind in refuting the sect, urges his addressees to lay aside all arrogance so that truth may be sought jointly, and sets terms for a disputation, declining to assume the Manichaean name. He then contrasts the ties that bind him to the Catholic church, the consent of peoples and nations, an authority begun in miracles, antiquity, and the priestly succession from the see of Peter, with the Manichaeans' mere promise of manifest truth, undertaking to weigh their teaching only if it can be shown without obscurity.
la.augustine.contra_epistulam_parmeniani: Contra Epistulam Parmeniani is a late-antique Latin polemical treatise by Augustine, written in reply to a letter in which Parmenian, a Donatist bishop, had reproached Tychonius for proclaiming a church diffused throughout the whole world. Composed at the request of fellow Christians, it refutes Parmenian's charge that the African traditores had cut the churches of Gaul, Spain and Italy off from true communion, and adduces the scriptural promises made to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob to argue that God's pledge of blessing for all nations in the seed of Christ is fulfilled in the church spread over the entire earth. The short work forms part of Augustine's writings against the Donatists and defends the unity and catholicity of the universal church against separatist claims.
la.augustine.contra_felicem: Contra Felicem is a prose record of a disputation between Augustine, bishop of the Catholic church at Hippo, and Felix, a Manichaean, held at Hippo in the sixth consulship of the emperor Honorius. It opens with Felix undertaking to defend Manichaean scriptures, whereupon Augustine challenges him to show that Mani can rightly be called an apostle of Jesus Christ and questions him on the Manichaean Epistle called 'Fundamenti'. Augustine's side of the debate rests on extended citation of the Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles, especially the promise of the Paraclete, which he argues was fulfilled within the church rather than in Manichaean writings. A late-antique work of polemical theology, it belongs among Augustine's writings against the Manichaeans.
la.augustine.contra_litteras_petiliani: The Contra Litteras Petiliani is a Latin prose treatise of Late Antiquity in which Augustine replies to a letter by Petilian, a Donatist bishop. Addressed to the brothers entrusted to Augustine's pastoral care, it quotes Petilian's letter piecemeal and refutes its claims, concentrating on the Donatist teaching that baptism administered by an unworthy minister is invalid and must be repeated. Augustine argues from scripture that the efficacy of baptism rests on Christ rather than on the moral condition of the baptizer, and that the Donatist position makes salvation depend on human merit instead of God. The work belongs to Augustine's wider polemic against the Donatist schism.
la.augustine.contra_partem_donati_post_gest: A short Latin polemical treatise by Augustine, composed in prose during late antiquity as part of his writings against the Donatists, and addressed to them after a public conference held at Carthage. The author confronts his defeated opponents with the record of the official acts, rebutting their claim to be the progeny of the martyrs rather than of traditores and pressing against them their own maxim, recorded in the acts, that neither one cause nor one person prejudices another. Scriptural testimonies from the prophets, the Gospels, and the letters of Peter, John, and Paul are then marshalled to show that the church was foretold to spread from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth, with the eastern churches founded by the apostles called as witnesses against the Donatists' refusal of communion with Africa.
la.augustine.de_beata_vita: De Beata Vita is a Latin prose dialogue by Augustine, a late-antique work of theology addressed to a correspondent named Theodorus. It opens with an elaborate nautical allegory in which philosophy is a harbour reached after shipwreck, while a shining but hollow mountain before the port figures the perilous lure of vainglory. The work then turns to autobiography: Augustine recounts how a reading of Cicero's Hortensius kindled his love of wisdom, how a youthful sect that worshipped visible light and a later adherence to the Academic sceptics delayed his course, and how the books of Plotinus urged him toward the voyage's end. The discussion among the assembled company proceeds to define the happy life, concluding that beatitude consists in the perfect knowledge of God.
la.augustine.de_bono_coniugali: De Bono Coniugali is a Latin prose theological treatise by Augustine, belonging to the Late Antique period. Taking the creation of man and woman as the first bond of human society, it defends marriage as a natural good and considers whether the first parents would have had offspring had they not sinned. Augustine then sets out the goods of marriage in the present human condition: the mutual fidelity owed by husband and wife, the chastity of older couples who abstain by consent, and the way even incontinent intercourse is directed toward the honest raising of children, closing with a discussion of adultery as the violation of conjugal faith.
la.augustine.de_civitate_dei: A late antique Latin theological prose treatise by Augustine, addressed to Marcellinus, in which the author undertakes to defend the city of God against those who set their own gods above its founder. The opening responds to pagans who blame Christian times for the calamities of Rome, pointing to the recent devastation of the city, in which barbarians spared those who took refuge in the basilicas of the martyrs and apostles. Augustine opposes the earthly city, governed by the love of dominion, to the heavenly city founded in humility by its king Christ, and cites Roman poets such as Virgil and Horace as evidence of the weakness of the gods whom Rome trusted. The argument announces as its governing theme the contrast between these two cities, one wandering in faith through the present age, the other awaiting eternal peace in its heavenly seat.
la.augustine.de_continentia: De continentia is a late-antique Latin prose treatise on the virtue of continence by Augustine. It argues that continence is a gift of God, without which no one can restrain desire, and supports the claim from the book of Wisdom, the Psalms, the Gospel, and the apostle Paul. Its central move is to extend continence beyond the lusts of the flesh to the interior 'mouth of the heart', so that the consent given to unspoken evil thoughts counts as sin even when no outward act follows. The closing section expounds Christ's saying that what proceeds from the mouth, rather than what enters it, is what defiles a man.
la.augustine.de_doctrina_christiana: De Doctrina Christiana is a late-antique Latin prose treatise on theology in which Augustine lays down precepts for interpreting and expounding the Christian Scriptures. The prologue answers three classes of would-be critics and argues that God ordinarily teaches human beings through other human beings, citing Antony, the apostle Paul, and the eunuch reading Isaiah as examples. Divided across several books, the work proceeds from the distinction between things and signs to guidance on resolving scriptural obscurity and, in its closing book, on the eloquence suited to preaching.
la.augustine.de_fide_et_symbolo: A Latin theological treatise in prose by Augustine, De Fide et Symbolo belongs to the late antique era and sets out an exposition of the creed. It argues that faith, held in the heart, must also be professed by the mouth, and that the creed's brief formula, committed to memory by those newly reborn in Christ, demands fuller explanation lest heretical distortions corrupt it. The exposition proceeds article by article, opening with God the Father's omnipotence and creation from nothing, then treating the divine Word, whose generation from the Father is contrasted at length with human speech.
la.augustine.de_genesi_ad_litteram: De Genesi ad Litteram is a prose work of Latin theology by Augustine, composed in Late Antiquity, expounding the opening chapters of Genesis according to the literal sense. It begins with a programmatic account of how divine scripture is to be read, dividing it into the Old and New Testaments and asking whether narrated events are to be taken only figuratively or also as historical fact. The exposition then proceeds through the creation narrative by way of successive questions, considering what is meant by 'in principio', how an unchangeable God can produce mutable and temporal things, what is signified by 'heaven and earth' and by unformed matter, and whether the light made at God's word 'fiat lux' is spiritual or corporeal.
la.augustine.de_gratia_christi: A Latin theological treatise by Augustine, cast in the form of a letter addressed to Albina, Pinianus and Melania. Written amid the controversy over Pelagius, it takes up the correspondents' report that they had pressed Pelagius to condemn in writing the view that grace is not necessary for every human act. Augustine quotes and examines Pelagius's division of the capacity for good into possibility, will and action, assigning the first to God's creative gift and the latter two to man, and argues that will and act, no less than possibility, require the aid of divine grace. The work is continuous prose of Late Antique date.
la.augustine.de_nuptiis_et_concupiscentia: The De nuptiis et concupiscentia is a Latin theological treatise in two books by Augustine, addressed to Valerius, a count, and written amid the Late Antique controversy over original sin. A prefatory letter praises Valerius's orthodox faith and conjugal chastity before the work proper opens against recent heretics who accuse Augustine of condemning marriage and the divine work of human generation. The argument distinguishes the goodness of marriage from the evil of carnal concupiscence, holds that children born of such union nevertheless contract original sin, and defends the necessity of infant baptism for its cleansing.
la.augustine.de_peccato_originali: A short Latin prose treatise by Augustine on original sin and the baptism of infants, written against the teaching of Pelagius and Caelestius. It examines the claims that Adam's sin injured him alone rather than the human race and that newborn children stand in the state Adam occupied before his transgression. Augustine cites the ecclesiastical proceedings against Caelestius at Carthage and the libellus Caelestius presented to Pope Zosimus at Rome, arguing from these documents that both men deny the transmission of original sin while still permitting infant baptism. He contrasts Caelestius's open statements with the more guarded answers given by Pelagius at the apostolic see.
la.augustine.de_peccatorum_meritis_et_remis: A Latin theological treatise in prose by Augustine of Hippo, addressed to Marcellinus, on the merits and remission of sins and on the baptism of infants. The work opens by refuting the claim that Adam was created mortal by natural necessity rather than as a penalty for sin, arguing from Genesis and from the Pauline epistles that bodily death entered the world through transgression. Augustine treats at length the condition of humanity before the Fall, the wages of sin, and the renewal of the body promised in the resurrection.
la.augustine.de_perfectione_iustitiae_homin: A short Late Antique theological treatise in Latin by Augustine, cast as a letter to the bishops Eutropius and Paulus. It answers, point by point, a set of brief 'definitions' said to come from Celestius, taking up questions such as what sin is, whether it is voluntary or necessary, natural or accidental, an act or a thing, and whether a human being ought to be, is commanded to be, and is willed by God to be without sin. Augustine's replies hold that sin can be avoided only where corrupted nature is healed by the grace of God through Jesus Christ, an argument he illustrates throughout with the analogy of a lame man who cannot escape his limping until his foot is cured.
la.augustine.de_trinitate: The De Trinitate is a Latin theological treatise in prose by Augustine, a major doctrinal work of Late Antiquity on the nature of the triune God. It opens with a dedicatory letter to Aurelius in which Augustine recounts that he began the books in youth and published them in old age, having been compelled to finish and correct a work that had been taken from him before he could revise it to his satisfaction. The opening argument warns against three kinds of error in thinking about God, those who reason from bodily things, from the soul, and from false suppositions found in neither, and explains how scriptural language accommodates human weakness through bodily and spiritual figures. From this Augustine proceeds to the purification of the mind, nourished by faith, as the necessary path toward understanding the incomprehensible and unchangeable divine substance.
