la.augustine.epistula_ad_catholicos_de_sect: A late-antique Latin epistolary work by Augustine, who writes as a bishop to the brothers entrusted to the care of his ministry. The letter answers the full text of an epistle by Petilian, a Donatist bishop of Constantine, a small portion of which had earlier reached Augustine, and it undertakes the reply from the beginning, as though the disputants were present and contentiousness set aside. The question at issue is where the church is to be found, with the Catholics or with the Donatists, and Augustine argues that the one church, called catholic because it exists 'according to the whole', is the body of Christ present throughout the world. After weighing the accusations each side levels at the other concerning traditio, purification, and persecution, he holds that the Donatists cannot escape the crime of schism incurred by their separation from the unity of the whole world.
la.augustine.liber_qui_appellatur_speculum: A Latin prose treatise on theology of Late Antique date, attributed to Augustine and known as the Speculum ('Mirror'). Its opening preface explains the plan of the work: to gather from the canonical scriptures the commandments concerning morals that remain binding in the time of the new testament, collecting them 'as in a mirror' in which the already-believing reader may observe his progress in good conduct and perceive what he still lacks, while precepts that appear mutually contrary are to be posed as questions and resolved. The body of the work then assembles long sequences of quoted preceptive material arranged by source book, distinguishing these enduring moral commands from the sacramental observances of the old testament, which Christians must now understand rather than perform; it begins with the Decalogue and the moral and judicial statutes of the book of Exodus and continues with the corresponding precepts of Leviticus.
la.augustine.locutiones_in_heptateuchum: The Locutiones in Heptateuchum is a Late Antique Latin work of biblical exegesis by Augustine, examining phrases in the Heptateuch, the first seven books of the Bible, that appear anomalous in Latin because they are idioms of the Hebrew or Greek original. Arranged as a series of short notes, the treatise quotes a Latin wording, sets it against Greek equivalents or variant Latin renderings, and explains the idiom of the source language that accounts for the construction. The notes begin with Genesis, addressing word order, case usage, and the sense of particular verbs and phrases.
la.augustine.psalmus_contra_partem_donati: A Latin work by Augustine, written in the Late Antique period, composed in the manner of a psalm against 'the part of Donatus,' the party that separated from the church in the Donatist controversy. Each stanza closes with the refrain 'Omnes qui gaudetis de pace, modo uerum iudicate,' and the opening exposition reads the gospel parable of the net drawn from the sea as an image of the mixed Church until the end of the age. The argument answers the accusation of traditio, the surrender of the holy books in persecution, contending that those who broke the nets of peace and set up 'an altar against an altar' were guilty of the crime they imputed to others. The later sections recall the disputed ordination at Carthage, where Caecilian had already been consecrated, and the role of Botrus and Caelestius in fabricating the charge, insisting that no judges, accusers, witnesses, or documents ever established it.
la.augustine.quaestiones_in_heptateuchum: The Quaestiones in Heptateuchum is a Latin prose work of biblical theology by Augustine, written in the late antique period. It gathers questions arising from the reading of the seven books of the Heptateuch, together with brief discussions or tentative solutions, based on a comparison of scriptural codices including the Septuagint and Hebrew texts. Its material consists largely of problems in Genesis, such as Cain's founding of a city, the lifespan of Mathusala, the union of the sons of God with the daughters of men, and the construction, capacity, and provisioning of Noah's ark, treated in a deliberately rapid, notebook-like style.
la.augustine.retractationum: The Retractationes of Augustine is a Late Antique Latin prose work of theology in which the author surveys his own writings in order. It opens with a numbered catalogue of his books, running from the early dialogues De Academicis and De beata uita through anti-Manichaean, anti-Donatist, and anti-Pelagian treatises, exegetical and moral works, and major texts such as the Confessiones and De ciuitate dei. Each entry in the catalogue is followed by a summary of the work's subject and by corrections or clarifications that Augustine supplies on reconsideration.
la.ausonius.cupido_cruciatus: Cupido cruciatus, a short late-antique Latin poem in lyric metre by Ausonius, imagines the heroines of myth who died for love, Semele, Caenis, Procris, Sappho, Pasiphae, Ariadne, Phaedra, Laodamia, Thisbe, Canace and Dido among them, gathered in a shadowy myrtle grove in the plains of the air, where each re-enacts the manner of her death. Around them bloom the flowers sprung from doomed lovers such as Narcissus, Hyacinthus, Crocus and Adonis. Cupid, straying into their midst on a careless nocturnal flight, is recognized as their common tormentor, seized and bound to a myrtle tree, where each woman punishes him with the noose, sword, flame or other instrument of her own death. The tumult closes with the arrival of Venus herself, who moves unafraid through the scene because she too shares the guilt.
la.ausonius.de_bissula: A short Latin collection by the late antique poet Ausonius, consisting of a prose preface addressed to his friend Paulus followed by a group of brief lyric poems. The poems centre on Bissula, a Suebian girl of stock from beyond the Rhine who was captured in war and now holds sway over the household of her master; they dwell on her name, her blue eyes and golden hair, her mingled Germanic and Latin character, and the impossibility of imitating her natural beauty with paint. One prefatory epigram urges the reader to drink before reading, framing the verses as the playful product of leisure and wine.
la.ausonius.de_herediolo: A short lyric poem in Latin by the Late Antique poet Ausonius, introduced by a prose note explaining that it was composed in a Lucilian style when the author, by then a consul, returned to his native place and entered the small villa left by his father. The verses address the herediolum itself, greeting it as the realm of the poet's ancestors and lamenting the father's hurried death, before turning to reflections on the boundlessness of desire, illustrated by Croesus, Diogenes, Aristippus and Midas. A later passage inventories the property in detail: two hundred iugera of land, a hundred under vines, meadows, woodland, a well, spring and tidal stream bearing boats, and fruits stored for two years. The estate is situated neither far from the city nor at it, allowing the poet to alternate his residence between country and town.
la.ausonius.eclogarum_liber: The Eclogarum Liber is a book of short poems in lyric metres by the Late Antique poet Ausonius. It opens with a dedicatory piece presenting the author's humble book of verse to a patron, followed by miscellaneous eclogues on moral and practical subjects. Among its principal pieces is a survey of the cares attending every age and condition of life, from the burdens of the forum, the household, trade, farming, and soldiering to the infirmities of old age, which leads into the Pythagorean maxim that it is best never to be born, cited in a Greek distich. A closing poem answers that doctrine in Christian terms, arguing that a further life must be earned after the present one.
la.ausonius.ephemeris_id_est_totius_diei_ne: The Ephemeris, subtitled Totius diei negotium ('the business of a whole day'), is a Late Antique Latin poem by Ausonius that traces the occupations of a single day from dawn to nightfall in a sequence of lyric meters. It opens with a comic waking scene in which the speaker, still abed, scolds himself and his sluggish servant Parmeno, whose gluttony and drinking hold him fast asleep, with stanzas in Sapphic and iambic measures. The day then proceeds through rising, ablution, and private prayer, including a solemn hymn invoking God the Father and Christ his Son as creator and redeemer, before continuing through the further offices of the day toward evening.
la.ausonius.epicedion_in_patrem: A short funerary poem by the late antique poet Ausonius, the Epicedion in Patrem commemorates the poet's father. It opens with a prose preface explaining the Greek title and the work's devout rather than ambitious purpose, addressed to any reader who is himself a son or a father, and asking for love rather than praise. The verse lament that follows is voiced in the person of the dead father, who recounts his life as a physician of Vasates with a home at Burdigala (Bordeaux): his moderate means and unstained conduct, a marriage of forty-five years that produced four children, the early deaths of two of them, the prefecture of his son over Gaul, Libya and Italy, his own prefecture of Illyricum, and his death at ninety, sound of body and without a staff.
la.ausonius.epigrammata_ausonii_de_diversis: Epigrammata de Diversis Rebus ('Epigrams on Various Matters') is a collection of short Latin epigrams by Ausonius, a poet of the Late Antique period. A prefatory piece addressed to the book itself debates whether the damage done by moths is preferable to the wear of being read, and the poems that follow treat an assortment of subjects: a Sicilian king sprung from a potter, a jealous wife whose doubled poison inadvertently saves her husband, a charlatan physician, teachers and men who mistake purchased books for learning, and a running series of jokes at the expense of the silent statue of the rhetor Rufus of Pictavis. The individual pieces are brief, pointed exercises in the satirical and moralizing epigram tradition, and at least one is marked as translated from Greek.
la.ausonius.epistularum: The Epistulae of the late-antique author Ausonius form a collection of prose letters addressed to learned friends and fellow writers, among them Symmachus. The letters combine warm personal greetings with elaborate discussion of literary composition, praising a correspondent's eloquence, weighing the propriety of publishing versus keeping verse private, and invoking orators and poets such as Cicero, Demosthenes, Isocrates and Vergil as standards of style. Recollections of shared service in the imperial comitatus and playful conceits about honeyed speech and jealous readers give the correspondence its urbane, rhetorical character.
la.ausonius.epitaphia_heroum_qui_bello_troi: A late-antique Latin collection of lyric epitaphs for the heroes who fought in the Trojan War, by the poet Ausonius. In a prose preface addressed to his reader, Ausonius explains that he attached these sepulchral titles of the heroes to a libellus commemorating teachers of Bordeaux, having found the ancient epitaphs with a philologist and rendered them into Latin. The epitaphs that follow are voiced by the heroes themselves, Agamemnon, Menelaus, Ajax, Achilles, Ulysses, Diomedes, Nestor, Antilochus, Pyrrhus, Protesilaus, Deiphobus, Hector, Astyanax, Sarpedon, and Troilus among them, each speaking of a death and burial bound up with the war at Troy.
la.ausonius.griphus_ternarii_numeri: The Griphus ternarii numeri ('Riddle of the Ternary Number') is a short Latin poem in lyric metre by the late antique poet Ausonius. Cast as a riddle on the number three, it assembles a dense catalogue of triads drawn from mythology, natural history, mathematics, law, rhetoric, medicine and music: the three Fates and three Graces, Hecate's triple form, Cerberus and the trident, the three parts of philosophy, the threefold law, the three styles of oratory, and the three branches of medicine. The verse continually multiplies its governing conceit, nesting ternary divisions within one another until it closes on the tripartite ordering of Roman society.
la.ausonius.ludus_septem_sapientum: The Ludus Septem Sapientum ('Game of the Seven Sages') is a short late-antique Latin poem by Ausonius, composed in lyric metres and cast in the form of a stage performance. A prologue addressed to Pacatus Drepanius debates whether the verses deserve publication and discusses Roman theatrical buildings and conventions before the sages are summoned onto the stage. Thereafter Solon, Chilon, Pittacus, Bias, Periander, Cleobulus and Thales appear in turn, each delivering a famous maxim given in the Greek original alongside a Latin rendering, with remarks on disputed attributions of individual sayings. The whole proceeds as a sequence of sententiae within a light dramatic frame.
la.ausonius.mosella: The Mosella is a Latin poem in hexameters by Ausonius, a poet of Late Antiquity, working in the epic genre. It opens with the poet's journey overland past Dumnissus and Tabernae to the country of the Belgae, where he greets the Moselle and its vine-clad banks near Neomagus. The poem proceeds largely as description, dwelling on the river's transparent depths, its pebbled bed and varied fish, its smooth currents and navigable waters. Further passages extend the encomium to the vines and villas lining the river and to the settled landscape of the region.
la.ausonius.oratio_consulis_ausonii_versibu: A short Latin prayer by the Late Antique consular poet Ausonius, composed in rhopalic verses in which each successive word adds a syllable. Addressed to Christ and the Father as sources of eternal hope, it asks for purification and pardon of sins, recalls baptism in the Jordan, the redemptive cross, and the examples of Stephen and Paul, and closes by pleading that the speaker, a late servant instructed under a bishop of religion, may be received into the heavenly fellowship. The invocation 'Spes, deus, aeternae stationis conciliator' both opens the poem and returns, in capitals, at its end.
la.ausonius.ordo_urbium_nobilium: A late antique Latin poem in lyric metre attributed to Ausonius, the Ordo Urbium Nobilium ranks the principal cities of the Roman empire in order of precedence. Beginning with Rome and Constantinople, it passes in review Carthage, Antioch, Alexandria, Trier, Milan, Capua, Aquileia, and Arles, among others, devoting a few lines to each. The sketches dwell on founders, geographic situation, monuments, commercial wealth, and episodes from civic history, and they often set older and newer foundations, or rival cities, against one another.
la.ausonius.parentalia: The Parentalia is a Latin collection of commemorative verses by the late antique poet Ausonius, taking its name from the ancient Roman festival of offerings to deceased kindred which its prose preface traces back to Numa. A prose introduction concedes the unadorned nature of the subject, the mournful remembrance of the author's departed dear ones, before the poems begin. The verses that follow give short notices recording the names, lineage, characters and careers of dead members of Ausonius' family, beginning with his father Ausonius and his mother Aeonia and continuing with his uncle Arborius and his maternal grandfather Arborius.
la.ausonius.praefatiunculae: A cycle of short prefatory poems in lyric metres by the late-antique poet Ausonius, originally composed as prefaces to his individual works. The opening preface is autobiographical: Ausonius names his father, traces his family's origins in Bordeaux and other Gallic cities, and recounts his education in grammar and rhetoric, his three decades of teaching, his summons to the imperial court as tutor to the emperor's children, and his advancement through high office to the consulship. The remaining pieces comprise a complimentary preface addressed to Syagrius, an autograph letter from the emperor Theodosius soliciting a copy of Ausonius's writings, and prefaces in which the poet complies with imperial commands to compose verse.
la.ausonius.technopaegnion: The Technopaegnion is a late antique Latin verse collection by Ausonius, dedicated to the proconsul Pacatus. Its short poems are built of lines that both begin and end with monosyllables, and the closing monosyllable of each line serves as the opening word of the line that follows, so that the verses run together in a continuous chain. The pieces include prefaces in prose and verse explaining the game, moral and proverbial sententiae, a poem on the parts of the human body, and a catalogue of gods whose names are monosyllables, among them Fas, Rea, Dis, Vis, Sol, Mars, and Pax. The author presents the work as a playful opusculum in which labour and ludus are joined.
la.avitus_of_vienne.de_consolatoria_laude_c: De Consolatoria Laude Castitatis is a late antique Latin Christian poem by Avitus of Vienne. Its opening sends verses from a brother to a virgin dedicated to Christ, renouncing the trappings of classical song, Pegasus, the Pierian sisters, and Phoebus, in favor of a truth-telling Christian lyre. The poem then recounts the girl's presentation to God as an infant, contrasts the costly ornaments described by Isaiah with the adornment given by grace, and passes into a mother's speech as her daughter's vow of chastity is affirmed.
la.avitus_of_vienne.de_spiritalis_historiae: De Spiritalis Historiae Gestis is a Late Antique Latin epic in hexameter verse by Avitus of Vienne, composed in five books. The poem retells the opening narrative of Genesis in classical epic style, beginning with the six days of creation and the fashioning of Adam, whose first disobedience brought mortality and inherited sin upon his descendants. Its later books carry the sacred story through the fall and the sentence on the serpent, the deluge, and the crossing of the Red Sea to the baptism and temptation of Christ, who in the prologue is said to have paid in himself the debt incurred by the race. The whole is framed as an account of the labours and brief span of human life under the stain of primal transgression.
la.bede.historiam_ecclesiasticam_gentis_ang: Bede's Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum is an early medieval Latin prose history of the church and people of the English. It is divided into five books and opens with a dedicatory epistle to King Ceolwulf, in which the author, styling himself a servant of Christ and priest, sets out his informants and method of compilation. The narrative begins with a description of the situation, resources, and earliest inhabitants of Britain and Ireland, the Britons, Picts, and Scots, before proceeding to the conversion of the English to Christianity and ecclesiastical affairs in the various Anglo-Saxon provinces up to the author's own day.
la.bernowinus.carmina: A short collection of 388 lines of medieval Latin verse attributed to Bernowinus, an otherwise unidentified poet of the Carolingian period, printed by E. Dümmler in 1881. The poems move through the chief events of Christ's life, Gabriel's salutation of Mary, Joseph's presence, the nativity, passion, resurrection, and ascension, in short declarative couplets introduced by 'Hic', in the manner of tituli labelling scenes at a sacred site. The closing lines name Bernowinus as the maker of the work, refer to a saint's body resting within the building and to miracles worked there, and invite visitors to pray. For readers of intertexts, the sequence offers parallels with Carolingian ecclesiastical inscription verse and devotional treatments of the life of Christ.
la.bertharius_of_monte_cassino.carmen_de_sa: The Carmen de Sancto Benedicto is a medieval Latin poem of the Carolingian period, attributed to Bertharius of Monte Cassino. Addressed throughout to the saint in apostrophe, it gives a verse account of the life of Benedict of Nursia, following him from his boyhood and schooling at Rome through a sequence of miracles: the restoration of a broken sieve, poisoned bread carried off by a raven, the rescue of the drowning Placidus by his fellow monk Maurus, the fall of a persecuting priest, the destruction of temples of false gods, and the healing of a boy crushed by a collapsing wall. The poem closes with the tyrant's servant Riggo and with King Totila, who prostrates himself before the saint and receives knowledge of the things to come in his life.
la.boethius.commentaria_in_porphyrium_a_se_: Latin prose commentary by the late-antique philosopher Boethius on Porphyry's Isagoge, the introductory treatise to Aristotle's Categories. Cast as a dialogue between Boethius and Fabius, begun during a winter retreat in the Aurelian mountains, it works through the six standard preliminary questions about a philosophical work, aim, utility, order, authenticity, title, and the part of philosophy to which it belongs, and identifies Porphyry's subject as genus, species, difference, property, and accident. The dialogue also refers to the Latin version said to have been made by the orator Victorinus, and divides philosophy into theoretical and practical parts, distinguishing within the theoretical the intellectible, the intelligible, and the natural.
la.boethius.liber_de_persona_et_duabus_natu: A late-antique Latin prose treatise by Boethius, cast as a letter to John the deacon, opening with an account of a dispute at a council over whether Christ is to be confessed as consisting from two natures or in two natures. The work examines and rejects the opposed errors of Eutyches and Nestorius, and undertakes a systematic analysis of the terms natura, substantia, and persona, giving multiple definitions of each. It concludes that in Christ the divine and human natures subsist united in a single person, holding a middle course between the positions it refutes.
la.boethius.utrum_pater: Utrum Pater is a short Latin prose treatise on Trinitarian predication, presented under the name of Manlius Severinus Boethius, the Late Antique philosopher and patrician, and addressed to John the Deacon. Working from the foundations of the catholic faith, it asks whether the terms Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are predicated of the divinity substantially or in some other manner. The argument distinguishes predicates that are substantial and common to the three persons, such as deity, truth, goodness, justice, and omnipotence, from relational names like Father, Son, Spirit, and even Trinity, which are shown to be said ad aliquid rather than of the divine substance. It closes with a request that the recipient either accept the reasoning or examine it more closely and join faith to reason.
la.caesar.de_bello_gallico: De Bello Gallico is a Latin prose historiographical work, in eight books, by Julius Caesar, written during the Roman Republic. It opens with an ethnographic and geographical survey dividing Gaul among the Belgae, the Aquitani, and the Gauls or Celts, before turning to the Helvetian migration planned by Orgetorix and Caesar's response at Geneva. The narrative proceeds in the third person through Caesar's campaigns against the peoples of Gaul and Germany, including expeditions across the Rhine and to Britain. Its account of the war is interspersed with digressions on the geography, customs, and institutions of the peoples encountered.
la.calpurnius_siculus.eclogae: A collection of pastoral eclogues in hexameter verse by Calpurnius Siculus, a poet of the early Imperial period. The opening poem presents the shepherds Ornytus and Corydon entering a grove sacred to Faunus, where verses newly carved on a beech tree are read aloud: a prophecy foretelling the end of civil strife, the return of a golden age of peace, and a new era under a ruler of the Julian line. The remaining poems continue in the same bucolic mode, with dialogues, songs, and scenes of shepherd life set among groves, springs, and rural shrines.
la.candidus_of_fulda.epitaphia_aegili: Attributed to Candidus of Fulda, a short Carolingian Latin composition of nineteen lines preserving two epitaphs for Eigil, abbot of Fulda. The first, a twelve-line titulus, summons the passing reader to read the inscription and recounts the abbot's deeds, his happy governance of the monastery, his translation of a martyr's relics with the bishop, the dedication of two churches, closing with a signature by his successor Hrabanus, who calls himself unworthy. The second gives Eigil a speaking voice from the tomb: he rests in the small sepulchre he built while alive and awaits the Lord who will loose the bonds of death and raise him. Readers hunting intertexts will find here the classic address to the passerby, the speaking-deceased inscription, and stock formulas of Carolingian memorial verse that reach back to late antique epitaph and epigram.
la.candidus_of_fulda.vita_aegili: A Latin verse life composed during the Carolingian period by Candidus of Fulda, commemorating the deeds and death of Aegil, abbot of the monastery of Fulda. The poem opens with an address to the author's brother Modestus, urging him to read the work carefully and to guard it against destructive readers, before turning to its subject: Aegil's noble birth in Noricum, his journey as a boy to Fulda, a place named for the river amid the beechwood of Buchonia, and his welcome there by the abbot Sturmi near the shrine of Boniface. The narrative then recounts his schooling in the monastery's school, his assumption of the monastic habit, and his service as a faithful companion and minister to the abbot.
la.cato_the_elder.de_agricultura: Cato the Elder's De Agricultura, a Latin prose treatise of technical character dating from the Roman Republic, offers practical instructions for the acquisition and management of a rural estate. A preface ranks farming above trade and moneylending, after which the work gives advice on inspecting and choosing a property, on the relative worth of vineyards, gardens, olive groves, arable land, and woodland, and on the pater familias' supervision of the vilicus, the scheduling of seasonal labour, and the keeping of accounts. Its prescriptive chapters cover planting, livestock, equipment and buildings, together with household provisions and the buying and selling of surpluses, in the terse style of a working farmer's handbook.
la.catullus.carmina: The Carmina of Catullus, a Republican collection of lyric poetry in mixed metres, comprises some 113 poems totalling about 2,300 lines in Merrill's edition. The book opens with a dedication to Cornelius and the famous passer poems for the beloved puella, and ranges from personal lyrics of love, friendship, and invective to learned mythological narratives such as the epyllion on the marriage of Peleus and Thetis and the Attis. Its compressed diction, Hellenistic models, and dense allusiveness made it a touchstone for later Latin poets, and it remains a prime hunting ground for readers tracing echoes, phraseology, and mythological material across classical and later literature.
la.celsus.de_medicina: De Medicina, by A. Cornelius Celsus, a Roman writer of the early Imperial period, is the surviving medical portion of an encyclopedic work, arranged in eight books of technical Latin prose. The long preface surveys the history of medicine from Aesculapius and Hippocrates through Herophilus, Erasistratus, Asclepiades, and Themison, and weighs the claims of the rationalist and empiric sects against the Methodists before adopting a middle position grounded in evident causes, experience, and dissection of cadavers. The books that follow treat regimen for the healthy, the causes and dietetic cure of diseases, the preparation and use of drugs, and surgical operations.
la.cicero.de_divinatione: De Divinatione is a Latin philosophical dialogue in two books by Cicero, written during the era of the Roman Republic, in which Cicero and his brother Quintus debate whether divination is real. The work surveys divinatory practice among Assyrians, Chaldaeans, Egyptians, Greeks, and Romans, including augury, oracles, dreams, astrology, haruspicy, and the Sibylline books, and reviews philosophical positions from Xenophanes and Epicurus to the Stoics Chrysippus, Diogenes, Antipater, and Posidonius, with the doubts of Panaetius and the arguments of Carneades also weighed. Framed as a conversation between the brothers at Cicero's Tusculan villa and explicitly continuing the discussion of his three books De Natura Deorum, it sets the Stoic case for divination against Academic skepticism about how far omens, religion, and superstition deserve assent.
la.cicero.de_domo_sua: De Domo Sua is a Latin oration by Cicero of the Roman Republic, delivered before the college of pontiffs in a claim for the restitution of the speaker's house on the Palatine, which had been confiscated and consecrated to Liberty by the tribune Clodius while Cicero was in exile. The speech answers the tribune's charges point by point, defending Cicero's conduct at the time of his recall and arguing from pontifical law, precedent, and religious antiquity that the consecration was invalid. It alternates between technical argument about sacred places and sustained invective against the opponent and his followers, ending with a plea for the restoration of both the property and the orator's public standing.
la.cicero.de_haruspicum_responso: A prose oration of the Roman Republic, delivered before the senate and preserved among the speeches of Cicero. The speaker recounts how he checked the insolence of Publius Clodius while Clodius was impeding the cause of the publicani with frivolous interrogations, and defends the measured conduct that some had thought excessive. Much of the speech is invective: Clodius is attacked for his shamelessness, for a contio in which he professed concern for neglected rites, and for the profanation of the sacred rites of the Bona Dea, an act hidden even from men's eyes, while Cicero justifies his own enmity and leaves Clodius's prosecution to Titus Annius Milo. The oration takes its theme from a response of the haruspices, which Clodius had exploited to complain that religion, sacrifices, and ceremonies were being neglected and violated, and it closes in anticipation of a further contio by Clodius on pudicitia.
la.cicero.de_imperio_cn_pompei: A Latin prose oration of the Roman Republic, delivered to the Roman people by Cicero in support of conferring an extraordinary military command on Gnaeus Pompeius. The speech considers the nature, magnitude and conduct of the war against Mithridates and Tigranes, laments the danger to Asia and the public revenues, and argues from Pompey's singular virtus and record that he alone is fit to be appointed commander. Cicero also dwells on Rome's duty to avenge the killing of Roman citizens and the outrages done to envoys and allies, framing the war as a matter of Roman dignitas and glory.
la.cicero.de_natura_deorum: Cicero's De Natura Deorum is a Latin philosophical prose work of the Roman Republic, dedicated to Brutus and devoted to the difficult and obscure question of the nature of the gods. Its opening surveys the irreconcilable disagreement among philosophers over whether the gods exist, what their forms and abodes are, and whether they govern the world and provide for human affairs, ranging from the doubt of Protagoras to the outright denial of Diagoras and Theodorus, and it defends the Academic practice of withholding assent where knowledge is uncertain. Cicero also explains his late turn to writing philosophy, attributing it to grief and to the state of public affairs, and argues that such weighty subjects deserve to be treated in Latin as well as Greek letters. The discussion is carried forward across three books.
la.cicero.de_oratore: De Oratore is a Latin rhetorical treatise in three books, written by Cicero during the Roman Republican era. A prefatory address to Cicero's brother Quintus leads into a recollection of discussions in which the most eloquent and distinguished Roman orators set out their views on the whole art of speaking. The work considers whether eloquence rests on systematic art or on natural talent and practice, compares oratory with the other liberal disciplines and with philosophy, and examines the training and qualities of the ideal orator.
la.cicero.de_republica: Cicero's De re publica, a Latin prose philosophical dialogue on the best constitution of a state, composed during the Roman Republic and here edited from C. F. W. Mueller's Teubner edition of 1889, survives only in fragments, of which the present record preserves some 257 lines. Its dramatic frame gathers Scipio Aemilianus, Laelius, Furius Philus, Manilius, Tubero, and their circle during the Latin holidays, and its preface argues that the wise man owes service to the state rather than retreat into learned otium. The surviving discussion defines the res publica as res populi, a people joined by consent of law and community of advantage, in conscious rivalry with Plato's Republic, while quoting Ennius and Pacuvius and invoking Archimedes' sphere, eclipses, and Roman exempla from Camillus and Cato to the aftermath of Tiberius Gracchus. Readers of intertexts will find here a dense meeting of Greek philosophy and Roman political idiom, with named citations of Greek and Roman poets woven into Cicero's defense of active civic life.
la.cicero.de_senectute: De Senectute is a prose philosophical dialogue by Cicero of the Roman Republic, framed as words addressed to his friend Titus (Atticus) on the burden of approaching old age. The argument is placed in the mouth of the aged Marcus Cato, who, questioned by Scipio and Laelius about his equanimity, contends that the complaints commonly laid to old age, loss of pleasure, neglect, bodily decline, arise from character rather than from age itself. The discussion is illustrated with exempla from Roman history, notably Fabius Maximus, and includes a quotation of Ennius in his praise.
la.cicero.divinatio_in_q_caecilium: A Latin forensic oration by Cicero of the Roman Republic, delivered before the judges in the preliminary hearing to decide who should hold the right to prosecute Gaius Verres, former governor of Sicily, on a charge of extortion. In it Cicero contests the rival claim of Quintus Caecilius Niger, explaining his long reluctance to act as an accuser and arguing that the wronged Sicilian communities have chosen him as their advocate. He reviews the alleged crimes of Verres, including the plundering of provinces and the spoliation of temples and cities, and maintains that the wishes of the injured parties and the resistance of the accused should govern the choice of prosecutor.
la.cicero.in_catilinam: Cicero's In Catilinam comprises the orations he delivered as consul in the late Roman Republic against the conspirator Catiline. The first speech, addressed to the senate, confronts Catiline with the evidence of his plot, nocturnal gatherings, an armed camp in Etruria, and designs of arson and assassination, and invokes earlier precedents for the execution of enemies of the state, famously opening with the challenge 'quo usque tandem abutere, Catilina, patientia nostra?'. The prose is highly wrought public oratory, marked by sustained rhetorical questions, apostrophe, and pointed epigram.
la.cicero.in_vatinium: A specimen of Republican forensic oratory in Latin prose, In Vatinium records Cicero's cross-examination of Publius Vatinius, a witness arrayed against Sestius at his trial. The speaker sets out his reasons for interrogating a man of disreputable life and then presses him over contradictions in his testimony, notably concerning his dealings with Albinovanus and the suborning of Sestius's accusers. The latter part passes into invective and self-defence, as Cicero justifies his conduct as consul, his withdrawal, and his recall, contrasting his service to the state with Vatinius's destructiveness.
la.cicero.letters_to_atticus: Letters to Atticus is a collection of Latin prose letters written by Cicero to his friend Atticus during the Roman Republic, arranged in sixteen books. The correspondence mixes public and private business: reports on elections and political manoeuvring at Rome, lawsuits and the conduct of friends and rivals, alongside family news, financial dealings, and requests between the two correspondents. Its style is familiar and conversational, with occasional Greek phrases, rather than the polished manner of formal oratory.
la.cicero.pro_a_caecina: A prose oration of the Roman Republic, delivered by Cicero as advocate for Aulus Caecina in his action against Sextus Aebutius before a court of recuperatores. The dispute concerns force committed by armed men and the retention of possession under the interdict, with Cicero contending that the opposing witnesses effectively confess the violence of which Caecina accuses Aebutius. Against objections that Caecina's chosen action is dishonourable or that the case hinges on obscure points of civil law, Cicero argues that such delays defeat the purpose for which courts were established.
la.cicero.pro_a_cluentio: A forensic defence speech in Latin prose by Cicero of the Roman Republic, delivered in court on behalf of Aulus Cluentius, who stood trial on a charge of poisoning (veneficium). The exordium divides the case into two parts: the long-standing invidia attached to the earlier trial before Iunianus, in which Cluentius was said to have corrupted the jury with money so that Statius Albius, his innocent enemy, was condemned, and the poisoning charges proper to the standing court constituted under that statute. Cicero undertakes to show that Albius was condemned on the gravest charges and weightiest testimony, that the alleged bribery of that jury was attempted against rather than by Cluentius, and that the judges should lay aside preconceptions and hear the defence as if the case were being argued for the first time.
la.cicero.pro_archia: Cicero's Pro Archia is a prose oration of the Roman Republic, delivered in defence of the Greek poet A. Licinius Archias against a challenge to his Roman citizenship. The speech opens by acknowledging Archias's part in the orator's own training and argues at length for the worth of literature and the liberal studies, before rehearsing Archias's career from Antioch through Greece and Italy and his patronage by leading Roman nobles such as the Luculli, the Metelli and Catulus. Its later sections defend his enrolment as a citizen of Heraclea and his registration before the praetor under the lex Silvani et Carbonis, addressing the loss of the town's public records in the Italian War.
la.cicero.pro_balbo: A Latin forensic oration by Cicero of the Roman Republic, spoken in defence of Lucius Cornelius Balbus of Gades in a Roman court. The speech counters a prosecution challenging the Roman citizenship that Cn. Pompey had granted Balbus, arguing that the grant was lawful and honourable and that Balbus, far from fraudulently assuming citizenship, had served Rome with distinction in the Spanish wars under Metellus and Memmius. Cicero opens by acknowledging the earlier advocacy on Balbus's behalf, above all Pompey's own appearance for the defence, and repeatedly grounds his case in Pompey's authority, achievements, and right to reward his associate.
la.cicero.pro_c_rabirio_perduellionis_reo: A Latin forensic oration by Cicero, spoken during the Roman Republic in defence of Gaius Rabirius, who stood charged with perduellio (treason) before the Roman people. The speech answers accusations brought by the tribune Titus Labienus, most prominently the killing of Saturninus, which Cicero reframes as a consular act taken to preserve the state. Its exordium sets out his reasons for taking the case, protests the half-hour limit imposed on the defence, and argues that a conviction would undermine the authority of the consuls, the senate, and the consensus of loyal citizens.
la.cicero.pro_fonteio: A prose forensic oration of the Roman Republic, delivered by Cicero in defence of Marcus Fonteius, accused of misappropriating money during his quaestorship in the province of Gaul. The speech presses the absence of witnesses and of any trace of theft in the public accounts, examining at length the tabulae instituted by Hirtuleius to show that no deduction from the aerarium can be established against the defendant. Cicero dismisses the accusations of the Gallic provincials in favour of Roman witnesses, invoking the citizens of Narbo Martius, the loyal Massiliots, and the numerous negotiatores through whose hands no coin in Gaul moved without record. The extant material closes with an inventory of Fonteius's services to the province, including his levies of cavalry, grain, and money for Rome's wars.
la.cicero.pro_ligario: Pro Ligario is a forensic speech in Latin prose by Cicero of the late Republic, addressed to Caesar as presiding judge in defence of Quintus Ligarius, who stood accused by Quintus Tubero of bearing arms against Caesar in Africa during the civil war. The oration reviews Ligarius's service as legate and administrator of the province, his refusal to join the opposing side there, and a comparison between his conduct and that of his accuser, and it contains Cicero's open confession of his own adherence to that side, framed as an appeal to Caesar's clemency. The closing argument holds that condemnation would amount not merely to punishment but to the killing of a Roman citizen, since it would bar the accused from Italy, family and homeland alike.
la.cicero.pro_milone: Pro Milone is a Latin forensic oration by Cicero, written in the era of the Roman Republic as a defence speech for Titus Annius Milo, who stood trial for the killing of Publius Clodius. The speech opens with an acknowledgment of the armed guard surrounding the courtroom and the altered conditions of the hearing, then argues that Milo acted in self-defence against an ambush laid by Clodius. Cicero develops the case through appeals to natural law, the Twelve Tables, and historical precedents for the justified killing of seditious citizens, while portraying Milo as a guardian of the state and Clodius as a destructive agitator.
la.cicero.pro_plancio: A Latin forensic speech by Cicero, delivered during the Roman Republic, in defence of Gnaeus Plancius against a prosecution brought by Marcus Laterensis arising from Plancius' candidature for public office. Cicero opens by acknowledging Plancius' decisive services to his own safety and argues that such gratitude should not weigh against the defendant. The argument contests Laterensis' claim that his dignity was unfairly passed over at the elections, discussing whether the Roman people can be relied upon as a judge of merit in conferring magistracies.
la.cicero.pro_publio_quinctio: Pro Publio Quinctio is a Latin forensic oration by Cicero of the Republican era, written in prose on behalf of Publius Quinctius, whose entire fortune is at stake in a civil suit brought by Sextus Naevius. The exordium, addressed to the judge Gaius Aquilius, laments the speaker's difficult position against the eloquence of Quintus Hortensius, who appears for the opposing side, and against the influence of Naevius' wealthy backers. The narrative portion then recounts how Quinctius' brother Gaius entered a partnership with Naevius in property acquired in Gallia, a business arrangement whose disputes gave rise to the present litigation. The work survives as a single continuous speech without division into books.
la.claudian.carmina_minora: The Carmina Minora is a collection of shorter Latin poems by Claudian, a poet of Late Antiquity, composed for the most part in hexameter. Its contents mix panegyric and nuptial verse in honour of Stilicho and the imperial house with epigrams, brief mythological narratives, and descriptive pieces on subjects such as a bull of the Clitumnus, the lodestone, and the porcupine. The poems are occasional in character, ranging from formal court poetry to playful treatments of marvels of nature and art.
la.claudian.de_bello_gothico: The De Bello Gothico is a Latin panegyric in hexameters by the late antique poet Claudian, addressed to and celebrating the general Stilicho for his wars against the Goths. Its proem invokes the Muse and compares the poet's daunting task with the Argo's passage through the Symplegades, before turning to praise of Stilicho as the saviour who rescued Rome from barbarian menace and restored law, order, and confidence to a people lately in fear of invasion. The poem then proceeds to an account of the Gothic campaigns, magnifying Stilicho's achievements in the elevated style of Claudian's court verse.
la.claudian.de_consulatu_stilichonis: Claudian's De Consulatu Stilichonis is a Late Antique Latin panegyric in three books of hexameters celebrating the consulship of the general Stilicho. The poem joins conventional encomium, justice, martial valour, and other blessings elsewhere divided among different men but combined in Stilicho, with a narrative of his career: a youthful embassy to the Parthian court to conclude peace, his marriage to the emperor's daughter, and his victories, above all the defeat of Gildo in Africa and the subjugation of the East. The opening sets the praise amid the festivities of an imperial wedding, and the nuptial celebrations frame the account of Stilicho's rise.
la.claudian.de_raptu_proserpinae: De Raptu Proserpinae is a Latin epic in hexameters by Claudian, a poet of the late antique period, preserved in three books. After a preface on the first navigator who ventured upon the deep and an invocation to the gods of the underworld, the poem relates how Dis, denied a spouse and on the point of waging war against the gods, is promised Proserpina as a bride by the Fates. The narrative then proceeds through the abduction of Proserpina in Sicily, Ceres' anguished search for her daughter, and the divine confrontations that follow, breaking off unfinished in the third book.
la.claudian.epithalamium_de_nuptiis_honorii: Claudian's Epithalamium de Nuptiis Honorii Augusti is a Late Antique Latin panegyric in hexameters composed for the marriage of the emperor Honorius to Maria, daughter of Stilicho. The poem opens with the mythological wedding feast of Peleus and Thetis on Pelion, where Phoebus foretells the deeds of Achilles, before turning to the imperial bridegroom, depicted as a youth smitten with love for his bride and ignorant of his own feelings. A lament addressed to Stilicho over the delayed wedding, Cupid's flight across the sea to carry a message to Venus, and the description of the goddess's golden palace lead into the nuptial celebration and the praise of the imperial house.
la.claudian.in_consulatum_olybrii_et_probin: A Latin panegyric in hexameter verse by the Late Antique poet Claudian, celebrating the joint consulship of the brothers Olybrius and Probinus, sons of Probus. The poem opens with an address to the Sun and praise of the Auchenian family, in which consular office is treated as a hereditary distinction, before extolling the generosity and virtue of the father, Probus. It then turns to the two young brothers, whose attainment of the consulship together far outstrips even their father's career. The surviving portion ends as Rome, resolved to repay Probus with due gratitude for his sons, sets out on an allegorical journey to petition the emperor.
la.claudian.in_eutropium: Claudian's In Eutropium ('Against Eutropius') is a Late Antique Latin poem in two books of hexameters, an invective directed at Eutropius, a eunuch elevated to the consulship. The opening gathers prodigies and oracular warnings over his appointment, and the verse goes on to rehearse his servile birth, his castration, and his passage from owner to owner, presenting his rise as a disgrace afflicting the Roman state. Composed within the court panegyric tradition, the work proceeds by formal blame, heaping vituperation on the consul whose title is said to effeminate the year.
la.claudian.in_rufinum: In Rufinum is a two-book Latin invective in hexameters by the Late Antique poet Claudian, denouncing Rufinus, the powerful minister in the eastern empire under the emperor Theodosius and his sons. The proem weighs whether human affairs are governed by providence or by chance and presents Rufinus's punishment as proof of divine order, framed through an allegory in which Invidia and Allecto convene the personified vices to subvert the peace maintained by the August brothers. Book 1 traces Rufinus's origins, avarice, and rise to political dominance, while Book 2 recounts his downfall and violent death before the young Arcadius, closing with the elevation of Eutropius in his place.
la.claudian.panegyricus_de_quarto_consulatu: A late antique Latin panegyric in hexameter verse by Claudian, celebrating the fourth consulship of the emperor Honorius in a single continuous poem of 656 lines. The opening casts the consular year as a fusion of war and civic ritual, returning fasces, a soldiery grown togate, Bellona herself laying aside helmet and shield, before a genealogical encomium traces the imperial line and its conquests from the frozen north, where the Orcades ran with Saxon blood and ice-bound Hibernia mourned her dead, to the deserts of Libya, the Mauretanian strongholds, and the burning reaches of Ethiopia. Readers of intertexts will find the poem dense with epic diction, mythological exempla, and recycled Augustan and Silver Latin material, and it stands as a principal witness to the rhetoric and political imagery of late Roman court panegyric.
la.claudian.panegyricus_de_sexto_consulatu_: A Latin panegyric in hexameters by the late antique poet Claudian, celebrating the sixth consulship of the emperor Honorius. The poem opens with a nocturnal dream vision in which the Muses summon the speaker to recite verses before Jupiter's throne, an omen fulfilled in the figure of a prince likened to the gods of the Palatine. Further sections treat the auspices surrounding the consular year, drawing on astrological and Apolline imagery, together with the temple of Fortuna Redux and the temples and marvels crowning the imperial palace in Rome.
la.claudian.panegyricus_de_tertio_consulatu: A Latin panegyric in hexameters by the late antique poet Claudian, celebrating the third consulship of the emperor Honorius. The poem opens with the allegory of the eagle that tests its fledglings against the sun's fire as an image of imperial election, before turning to the poet's own summons to the palace, where his lyre sounds before an Augustan judge. Its narrative traces Honorius' birth amid portents of conquest, his boyhood among the spoils and standards of triumph, and his father's stern schooling of him in endurance and arms, with the grandfather's campaigns against the Moors, Picts and Scots set before the boy as examples of valour.
la.claudius_mamertinus.panegyricus: A later imperial Latin panegyric in prose, Claudius Mamertinus' speech of thanks for the consulship conferred on him by the emperor Julian. The oration opens with an apology for beginning his gratitude only at the consulship and with reflections on that honor, then praises Julian's reconquest of the Gallic provinces in a single campaign and his correction of provincial administration and the courts. It also rebuts hostile slanders that pitted Julian's glory against that of his co-ruler Constantius, whose partisans had stirred jealousy by celebrating the Caesar's deeds in Gaul.
la.columella.de_re_rustica: The De Re Rustica of Columella is a Latin prose treatise on agriculture of the early Imperial period. In a preface addressed to P. Silvinus, the author rejects claims that the soil has grown exhausted or the climate deteriorated, attributing instead the decline of farming to the negligence of landowners and invoking exempla such as Cincinnatus, Fabricius, and Curius Dentatus, who combined husbandry with public service. The work proceeds to systematic instruction in estate management and rural economy, covering the choice and cultivation of land, crops, viticulture and arboriculture, the keeping of livestock, and the organization of the household and its slaves.
la.commodian.carmen_apologeticum: The Carmen Apologeticum is a lengthy Christian apologetic and didactic work attributed to Commodian, a Latin author of the later imperial period whose precise dates are uncertain. It is composed in a loose, prose-like verse form and opens with an autobiographical account of the speaker's former wandering in pagan error, his conversion upon reading the scriptures, and exhortations to rich and poor alike to study the law. The work then surveys sacred history from Moses and Abraham onward, presents teaching about Christ drawn from the prophets, and intersperses its argument with warnings of coming calamity and calls to prudent preparation.
la.commodian.instructiones: The Instructiones is a Latin Christian theological work in two books by Commodian, of the later Roman imperial period. It opens with a preface in which the author declares his aim of showing the errant the way to eternal life and recounts his own abandonment of pagan cults after reading the law. The opening portion then mounts a polemic against pagan religion, arguing that deities such as Saturn and Jupiter were mortal men, rehearsing and refuting the myths told of them, and urging their worshippers to forsake vain idols.
la.corippus.johannis: The Iohannis is a late antique Latin epic in eight books of hexameter verse by Corippus. Its invocation announces a theme of wars, famine, and slaughter in Libya, praising the emperor Justinian before turning to the general John, earlier distinguished in campaigns against the Persians, as the commander chosen to restore Roman rule in Africa. The poem proceeds to narrate the devastation wrought by barbarian enemies in the province and John's campaigns, battles, and leadership against them.
la.cyprian.ad_donatum: Ad Donatum is a short Late Antique Latin treatise in prose, addressed by Cyprian to a friend named Donatus. Framed as a conversation in the seclusion of a garden at vintage time, it opens with a disclaimer of eloquence and then recounts the author's own conversion: entangled in the vices of his former life, he is reborn through the saving water of baptism into a new, spiritual existence. The closing pages dwell on the boundless and unmeasured gift of divine grace and on the authority over unclean and hostile spirits granted to the renewed soul.
la.cyprian.de_lapsis: De Lapsis ('On the Fallen') is a Latin prose treatise on church discipline by the Christian writer Cyprian, composed in the aftermath of a persecution. The opening rejoices at the restoration of peace and celebrates the confessors who endured imprisonment and torture rather than deny Christ. The greater part of the work mourns the lapsi, Christians who had sacrificed to idols or denied their faith, and indicts the greed, vanity and clerical worldliness that, in Cyprian's view, had provoked divine chastisement. It goes on to weigh the terms on which the fallen may be received back into communion through penance.
la.cyprian.de_mortalitate: De mortalitate is a late-antique Latin prose treatise, transmitted under the name of Cyprian, written to console Christians confronting a lethal pestilence. It argues that the present mortality is not a common ruin but a testing and a deliverance, since death for the believer is a passage to immortality, the reward of intended martyrdom, and the true homeland of paradise. Its argument rests on dense citation and paraphrase of scripture, Simeon's Nunc dimittis, Job, Tobias, Abraham, Paul, and John among others, woven together with similes drawn from shipwreck, agriculture, and military discipline. For readers of intertexts, the work offers a rich witness to the scriptural texture of early Christian consolation and a source for images of death, exile, and pilgrimage that echo throughout later Latin literature.
la.cyprian.epistulae: The Epistulae of Cyprian, composed in Late Antique Latin prose, consist of correspondence dealing with church order and clerical conduct. The letters collected here take up questions of ecclesiastical discipline, including a ruling that clergy may not be named as guardians or curators in wills, the exclusion from communion of a stage performer who persists in his trade, and the reproof of a deacon who insulted his bishop. Biblical precedent is cited throughout in support of the decisions, and each letter closes with a formulaic wish for the recipient's continued health.
la.cyprian_pseudo.ad_senatorem_ex_christian: A Latin tract transmitted under the name of Cyprian of Carthage and of later imperial date, addressed to a senator who has abandoned Christianity for the service of the pagan gods. The author professes astonishment at the apostate's return to idolatry, satirising the rites of the Great Mother and of Isis, whose priests and devotees are described in scornful detail, and arguing that every excess turns against itself and brings its own harm. The closing appeal exhorts the senator to acknowledge God before old age calls him back and to repent of his errors, warning that a lapse committed in ignorance is a light fault, whereas to abandon known truth is grave.
la.cyprian_pseudo.de_pascha: De Pascha is a short Latin poem of 69 lines, transmitted under the name of Cyprian and assigned to the later imperial period, that presents an allegorical vision of Easter centred on Golgotha. In the opening hexameters a tree cut from barren wood and planted on the site of the Crucifixion bears salutary fruit, grows to heaven in forty days, puts forth twelve branches spread through the whole world for the sustenance of all peoples, and after fifty days distils the nectar of the divine Spirit, while nations of every age, sex, and rank gather at a fountain beneath its shade to wash away the stains of their former life. Readers hunting textual parallels will find here a compact example of later imperial Christian allegory, reworking Passover typology through the imagery of the cross as life-giving tree, baptismal washing, and Pentecostal outpouring in a diction close to that of biblical epic.
la.cyprianus_cordubensis.cypriani_et_samson: The Cypriani et Samsonis Carmina is a short collection of Latin verse attributed to Cyprian of Córdoba and Samson, rooted in the medieval church of Córdoba. The opening poem praises a comes Adulfus who provided a book chest for the books of the Old and New Testament, addresses his son Fredenandus with instructions for its keeping, and invokes the martyr Acisclus; later pieces include verses on a flabellum inscribed for Guifredus and Guisinda and lines on Samson, a most illustrious abbot whose remains rest in an urn. The collection closes with a series of brief epitaphs and tomb inscriptions, among them one dated 918 and a final inscription for a Valentinian.
la.cyprianus_gallus.heptateuchos: A Late Antique Latin epic in dactylic hexameters, the Heptateuchos is attributed to Cyprianus Gallus and versifies the first seven books of the Old Testament. Its opening book retells Genesis, from the six days of creation and the formation of Adam and Eve to the serpent's temptation, the Fall, and the naming of the rivers of Paradise. The seven books correspond to the biblical Heptateuch, carrying the verse narrative from Genesis onward.
la.descartes.meditations: The Meditations (Meditationes de prima philosophia) is a prose philosophical work in Latin by René Descartes, belonging to the modern era and cast as a sequence of reflective meditations. It undertakes to demolish all previously accepted beliefs and rebuild knowledge on firm foundations, holding that assent must be withheld from whatever is not clearly and indubitably perceived. The opening meditation calls the senses into question, argues that waking and dreaming cannot be securely distinguished, and raises the possibility that even mathematics might be falsified by a deceiving God or some malevolent deceiver. The subsequent meditations seek certainty in the existence of the thinking self, proceed to proofs of God's existence, and treat the distinction between mind and body.
la.dhuoda.rhythmy_ex_manuali_dhuodanae: The Rhythmy ex Manuali Dhuodanae gathers the Latin verses transmitted with Dhuoda's Carolingian Manual, a didactic work of uncertain date addressed by a mother to her son William. Across 289 lines the pieces open with a hymn-like invocation of God as maker of light and eternal king, confess the speaker's frailty and exile, and commend young Willelmus to divine protection, grace, and peace of body and mind. Verse by a named Carolingian woman is rare, and the hymnic formulas, biblical diction, and language of parental solicitude here give readers of intertexts abundant points of comparison.
la.dicuil.versus: A brief Carolingian Latin poem attributed to Dicuil, addressed to the son of Charles and greeting Louis, Charles's successor. The poet announces that he composed it beginning from April, eight hundred and fourteen years after the Lord's conception, and names himself as Dicuil. He presents his verses as humble offerings, likening them to the widow's two small coins which outweighed the lavish gifts of the mighty. The poem closes with a vignette of herds and flocks driven to their stalls and a weary ploughman unyoking his slow-footed oxen.
la.dracontius.de_laudibus_dei: The De Laudibus Dei ('On the Praises of God') is a Latin Christian epic in hexameters by the late antique poet Dracontius. Composed in three books, the poem announces its aim of making known the nature of the supreme deity, at once wrathful and merciful, beginning with God as the cause of all things and the ordering of the cosmos out of chaos. It catalogues the rewards and calamities that descend from God's seat according to human deserts, and dwells at length on the portents by which a disordered nature, afflicted by sin, warns of coming dangers. A further movement introduces the advent of Christ and the redemption of the human race.
la.dracontius.romulea: The Romulea of Dracontius, a Late Antique poet, is a compact collection of short mythological poems in lyric measures, preserved in some 2,350 lines and edited by Vollmer in 1905. Its preface invokes a revered teacher credited with restoring letters to the African city and joining Romulean youths with barbarian pupils in his lecture room, before the collection turns to mythological narrative, opening with the tale of Hylas borne off by the nymphs to the grief of Hercules. The poems gather familiar figures, Orpheus, Venus, Hercules and their peers, retold in polished miniature, and offer rich hunting ground for readers tracing reworkings of classical myth and allusion to earlier Latin narrative poetry.
la.engelmodus.carmina: A collection of Latin poems attributed to Engelmodus, a poet of the Carolingian period, of otherwise uncertain date. The opening piece is an amatory verse epistle in elegiac couplets, in which a small letter is instructed to seek out a friend and deliver the poet's greetings, and which then turns to a lament over unrequited passion for a beloved named Agi, whose favour is said to have passed to another, Alexis. The poems treat love, friendship, and complaint in the manner of medieval Latin lyric.
la.ennius.annales: The Annales is a Republican epic in dactylic hexameters by Ennius, transmitted only in fragments. Its opening lines invoke the Muses and recount the poet's dream of Homer, before turning to early Roman legend: Aeneas's arrival in Hesperia, the wanderings by the Tiber, Ilia's dream and the suckling of her twins by a she-wolf, and the augury contest by which Romulus and Remus settle the founding and naming of Rome. The surviving portions carry the narrative forward in a continuous annalistic sequence through the legends and historical episodes of Rome's past.
la.ennodius.carmina: The Carmina of Ennodius are a collection of Latin verse by a poet of the Late Antique period, comprising short poems on varied occasions rather than a single sustained composition. The opening piece describes a journey across the Alps in conditions of extreme cold and heat, and then turns to an invocation of the martyrs Saturninus, Crispinus, Daria, Maurus, Eusebius, Quintus, Octavius, Adventor and Solutor. A second poem praises a distinguished contemporary addressed as the glory of Italy, and the collection as a whole combines devotional, encomiastic and occasional material.
la.ermenricus_elwagensis.epistola_ad_grimal: A Carolingian Latin verse epistle by Ermenricus Elwagensis, addressed to Grimald. It opens with an invocation of the triune God and a prayer for divine aid in composing song, and then calls upon Saint Gall, whose life and merits the poet proposes to celebrate. The verses weave Greek words into the Latin and include direct addresses to God, to the saint, and to the reader.
la.ermoldus_nigellus.carmen_in_honorem_Ludo: The Carmen in Honorem Ludowici Pii is a Latin panegyric epic in hexameter verse by Ermoldus Nigellus, a poet of the Carolingian period who presents himself as an exile seeking the favor of Emperor Louis the Pious, the work's dedicatee. It opens with a Christian invocation that deliberately rejects the pagan muses, and goes on to narrate Louis's deeds, beginning with Charlemagne's partition of his realm, Louis's kingship in Aquitaine, and his subsequent rule as emperor. Woven through the celebration of the emperor's arms and piety are repeated autobiographical appeals in which the poet asks Louis to lift his banishment, framing the poem itself as the gift that may win his restoration.
la.ermoldus_nigellus.carmen_in_laudem_pippi: The Carmen in Laudem Pippini Regis is a Carolingian Latin epic in hexameters by Ermoldus Nigellus, composed in praise of King Pippin. The poem opens with an invocation to the muse Thalia, sent as the speaker's envoy to a royal palace standing amid fertile riverside lands, and sets out her instructions for the journey. It depicts the king's radiant arrival, likened to Phoebus dispelling the clouds, the queen's procession to the church with her attendant maidens, and the greetings the muse is to offer the assembled clergy, nobles, and courtiers. Woven into the panegyric is the speaker's own exile: the muse is told to report his banishment and plead his cause, while the king in turn asks after the exile's fortunes.
la.ermoldus_nigellus.carminum_appendix: A short appendix of Latin hexameter verse by the Carolingian poet Ermoldus Nigellus, transmitted alongside his carmina. Its opening section is a song addressed to King Pippin, in which the pipe is bidden to sound for the boy and rare wares from India, Saba, Arabia, and the Jordan are listed alongside exhortations to learn what Maro, Cato, and the psalms teach. The remaining lines take the form of an epitaph spoken by Himiltrudis, mother of Bishop Ebbo, recounting the renewal of a church's foundations under Emperor Louis at his coronation by Pope Stephen, the rivers that nursed her son, their shared labours on the holy see, her death and burial beneath the tomb, and a closing prayer that God pardon sinners.
la.eucherius_of_lyon.formulae_spiritalis_in: A late-antique Latin theological treatise by Eucherius of Lyon, cast as a letter of instruction to his son Veranus. It opens with a preface defending the allegorical reading of scripture, outlining the historical, tropological, allegorical, and anagogical senses, and comparing the study of the divine books to worldly philosophy. The bulk of the work is a compact lexicon of figurative meanings for biblical names and words, arranged in ten chapters that move from the members of the Lord and supernal creatures through animals, the inner man, and Jerusalem to numerical symbolism, each entry furnished with a scriptural reference.
la.eucherius_of_lyon.instructiones: The Instructiones of Eucherius of Lyon is a Late Antique prose manual of scriptural explanation cast in the form of questions and answers. In a prologue addressed to Salonius, the author undertakes to answer queries about matters in the divine books, drawing not on his own ingenuity but on the judgement of illustrious doctors. The work is arranged in two books, one collecting the meanings of terms such as alleluia, diapsalma, amen and ephod, which recur in the sacred volumes or in ecclesiastical usage, and the other resolving difficulties raised by the biblical narrative, beginning with proofs of the Trinity and questions on Genesis, among them the tree of knowledge, paradise and Eden.
la.eutropius.breviarium: The Breviarium of Eutropius is a Latin prose work of historiography from the late imperial period, dedicated to the emperor Valens, whom the author addresses in his capacity as magister memoriae. It offers a concise chronological account of Roman affairs from the founding of the city down to the author's own time, gathering the events notable in war and civil life and adding brief notices of the distinguished deeds of the emperors. The narrative opens with Romulus and the seven kings, covering the foundations of Roman institutions and religion under Numa Pompilius, the expansions of Tullus Hostilius, Ancus Marcius, and Tarquinius Priscus, the census of Servius Tullius, and the rape of Lucretia and expulsion of Tarquinius Superbus, before proceeding to the establishment of the consulship under Brutus and Collatinus.
la.fardulfus.carmina: A Latin poem of the Carolingian period by Fardulfus, who names himself as abbot in its closing lines. In the poet's own voice it recounts his earlier exile, the fidelity he kept toward his lords in adversity, and his restoration through the victorious campaigns of Charlemagne, whose rewards included his appointment as head of the church of Saint-Denis; the poem records a vow, made in the first days of exile, to raise a church in honor of the saint. The verses describe the completed basilica as a place of grace and salvation where God dwells and the bodies of saints rest, pray for the growth of Charlemagne's friendship and lasting memory, and end with a petition for the abbot's eternal reward, adding that Fardulf also made the ciborium.
la.faustus_of_riez.de_gratia_libri_duo: A Late Antique prose treatise on grace in two books by Faustus of Riez, opening with an address to a Pope Leontius concerning a council convened to condemn the error of predestination. The work refutes the Pelagian claim that human labour can suffice without grace while likewise opposing the contrary position that would abolish free will altogether, and its chapters proceed through disputed points in sequence: infant baptism, the works of the law, the meaning of 'by grace you have been saved', the survival of free choice, the union of divine grace with the human will, the fall of the angel, Christ's death for all, and the claim that no one perishes by God's will. Biblical testimony is adduced throughout, and the author presents the pairing of grace with obedient effort as the mean between two opposing errors, figured in the opening as the strait between Scylla and Charybdis.
la.faustus_of_riez.sermones: A Latin prose sermon of Late Antique date ascribed to Faustus of Riez, belonging to the homiletic corpus transmitted as the Sermones. The sermon urges its hearers to prepare in purity for the approaching feast of the Lord's nativity, so as to receive the eucharist worthily rather than to their own judgment, developing the theme through scriptural citation and the image of a household cleaned and adorned for an earthly birthday. Further sections press moral exhortation, calling for chastity, charity, and almsgiving, for abstinence from marital relations, drunkenness, anger, and hatred before the feasts, and for prompt recourse to penitence, and they close with the promise of eternal reward for those who persevere in good works.
la.florus.epitome_bellorum_omnium_annorum: The Epitome Bellorum Omnium Annorum, attributed to the early imperial writer Florus, is a Latin prose epitome of Roman history from the founding of the city under Romulus to the author's own day, reaching at least the reign of Trajan, who is named in the prologue. Its preface models Roman history on the ages of a single human life, likening the city under the kings, the conquest of Italy, and the world empire of Augustus to infancy, youth, and maturity, before turning to the emperors who follow. The narrative that follows recounts the reigns of the kings and the wars of the Roman people in compressed, rhetorical prose, arranged largely by campaigns and adversaries rather than by strict annalistic sequence.
la.gerwardus.versus: A brief Latin poem of uncertain date within the Carolingian period, attributed to Gerwardus, who in the opening lines presents himself as a suppliant famulus. The verses are dedicated to a prince for his praise and everlasting memory, with the prayer that his renowned name be raised to the stars. The closing couplet instructs the reader to recognize as the poem's subject 'Einhard, magnifier of great Charles,' that is, Einhard, the celebrated biographer of Charlemagne.
la.giovanni_aurelio_augurelli.chrysopoeia: Chrysopoeia ('Gold-Making') is a Latin poem by the Renaissance author Giovanni Aurelio Augurelli on the art of transmuting metals into gold. The opening prologue dedicates the work to a pope, asks his leave and protection for publishing it, and explains that where the poem names pagan divinities these stand for figures of the Christian faith, so that the aurific art may be pursued without offence to true religion. The four books that follow set out the origins of an art the poet claims was unknown to earlier writers, the hidden means by which gold is made and metals changed, the ordered method and constant labours it demands, and the part played by experience in bringing it to perfection.
la.godescalcus_saxus.carminum_appendix: A brief appendix of medieval Latin verse attributed to Godescalcus Saxus, a poet of Carolingian date. It opens with a penitential prayer to Christ, asking pardon and deliverance from sin, and continues with a hymnic address to Christ as creator of the heavens, stars, and earth, born of the ever-virgin Mary, who conquered death and redeemed mankind. The closing section bestows a blessing on a dear friend, granting him the gifts of wisdom, keen understanding, ready eloquence, and abundance in both prose and metrical song. The whole is composed in short lines throughout.
la.hegesippus_pseudo.de_excidio_hierosolymi: A late-antique Latin historiographical work in prose, transmitted under the name of Hegesippus and hence conventionally cited as Pseudo-Hegesippus, of uncertain date. The preface criticises Josephus for partiality to the Jewish cause and presents the work as a continuation of sacred history beyond the biblical books, composed in the manner of secular historiography. The narrative begins with the Maccabean revolt and the fortunes of the Hasmonean rulers, then recounts the Jewish war with Rome down to the siege of Jerusalem, the burning of the temple, and the spoils carried off by Titus. Throughout, the account of the war follows Josephus while casting the Jews as the authors of their own destruction.
la.hibernicus_exul.carmina: A collection of Carolingian Latin verse attributed to the poet known as Hibernicus Exul ('the exiled Irishman'), composed in praise of Charlemagne. The work opens with a prayer that God will preserve Caesar Charles, prolong his life, and grant him victory over his enemies and enduring peace. Short complimentary verses to a girl named Gundrada follow, and the main portion takes the form of a dialogue between the poet and the Muse over what gift a king most deserves, treasure or song, which passes into an account of one who tried to break the established peace and plunge the realm into arms. The author is known only by the designation Hibernicus Exul, and his dates are uncertain.
la.hilary_of_poitiers.fragmenta_historica: A Late Antique Latin prose work transmitted under the name of Hilary of Poitiers, the Fragmenta historica preserves fragmentary documents from the ecclesiastical conflicts surrounding the councils of Nicaea and Ariminum. Its contents are chiefly episcopal correspondence, opening with a synodal letter of the Gallican bishops to their Eastern counterparts that upholds the confession of homoousios, denounces the silencing of the term ousia at Ariminum, and excommunicates Auxentius, Ursacius, Valens, Gaius, Megasius, Justinus and Saturninus. A further letter from Eusebius to Gregory reports Ossius' resistance to the Rimini settlement and laments the exile of orthodox bishops, attributing the Arian cause to dependence on secular power. The collection as a whole records the anti-Arian position of Western bishops through professions of faith, doctrinal argument and notices of condemnation.
la.hilary_of_poitiers.tractatus_mysteriorum: The Tractatus Mysteriorum is a Latin prose treatise of Late Antique theology by Hilary of Poitiers. It sets out to show that everything contained in the sacred books announces and prefigures the advent of Christ, his birth, preaching, passion, and resurrection, together with the gathering of the church. Reading the biblical narrative in sequence from Adam, it treats figures and events of Genesis and early sacred history, Adam's sleep, Eve's formation from his side, Noah's flood, the blessing of Melchisedech, Abraham's justification, the birth of Isaac, Jacob's servitude, as types fulfilled in Christ and the church. The opening chapters expound Adam and Eve at length, taking Eve's creation from Adam's side as an image of the church born from the water and blood of Christ, and supporting the interpretation with apostolic teaching.
la.hilary_of_poitiers_pseudo.de_evangelico: A short Latin poem on the gospel, ascribed to Hilary of Poitiers though the attribution is uncertain, and belonging to the later imperial period. The poem opens with an account of the nativity, the virgin birth, the rejoicing of sea and sky, the serpent's dismay, and the Magi who follow the star and offer myrrh and frankincense, before addressing the infant Christ in a long catalogue of his names, natures and offices. The closing section describes the four living creatures about the heavenly throne, man, lion, calf and eagle, and reads them allegorically as an image of Christ, together with the twenty-four elders who cast down their golden crowns in praise.
la.hilary_of_poitiers_pseudo.hymni: The Hymni transmitted under the name of Hilary of Poitiers form a small Latin collection of Christian hymns from the later imperial period, attributed to Hilary though of uncertain authorship. The opening piece, 'Lucis largitor splendidi', is a morning hymn addressing Christ as the true light of the world, the dispenser of inward illumination, and closes with a doxology to the Trinity. A second, penitential hymn, 'Ad caeli clara non sum dignus', unfolds in an alphabetical series of stanzas in which the sinner confesses his guilt and catalogues the personified vices that assail him, lust, pride, envy, discord, vainglory and gluttony, before pleading with Christ for mercy and tears.
la.hilary_saint_archbishop_of_arles.epistul: A late antique Latin prose letter from Hilary, Archbishop of Arles, addressed to Eucherius and classed among works of theology. Hilary explains that, having announced in a previous letter that he would carry copies of Eucherius's books with him, he sent the works on despite anxiety over their freshly made transcription, and records his admiration after reading them through.
