He begs not to be long deprived of Eucherius's instruction, asking to be counted among his pupils on the ground that his old age and lack of youthful training press upon him the more, and closes by commending Eucherius, as blessed father, to the Lord for the progress of his church.
la.hilary_saint_bishop_of_poitiers.collecta: A Late Antique Latin prose compilation of documents from the anti-Arian church controversy, associated with Hilary, bishop of Poitiers. It gathers letters exchanged between Eastern and Gallican bishops, including a creed expounded at Paris that upholds the homoousion and condemns and excommunicates Ursacius, Valens, Auxentius and their associates, together with material concerning the councils of Nicaea and Ariminum and the disputed term ousia. The compilation also contains a letter congratulating Ossius on his resistance to the Arian party at Ariminum and urging perseverance in the faith of the Nicene fathers.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.carmen_in_libros_r: Carmen in Libros Regum is a medieval Latin verse paraphrase in four books, totalling 1,350 lines, attributed to Hildebert of Lavardin. It recasts the biblical Books of Samuel and Kings in continuous verse, opening with Elkana, the rivalry of Hannah and Phenenna, and the birth and calling of Samuel at Shiloh, before proceeding through the loss of the ark to the Philistines and the fortunes of the Israelite monarchy. For readers of intertexts the poem is a substantial specimen of biblical epic, showing how scriptural narrative was refashioned in classical Latin diction, and it affords abundant verbal and thematic material traceable in later literary treatments of the same stories.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.carmina_minora: The Carmina Minora is a collection of short medieval Latin poems by Hildebert of Lavardin. Its pieces are chiefly brief occasional verses addressed to named individuals, bishops, noblemen and noblewomen, kinsmen and friends, alongside epigrammatic and moralising poems on subjects such as death, the cross, the Virgin Mary, avarice and the origin of evil. Several poems take the form of advice or admonition, offering maxims on conduct, prudence and worldly success, while others are lighter satirical pieces, including verses on the merchant Milo and an abbott Odo. The collection consists of compact poems of a few lines each rather than extended sustained compositions.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.carminum_supplemen: A medieval Latin poem of uncertain date, attributed to Hildebert of Lavardin and transmitted as a supplement to his Carmina. It opens with a typological reading of the sun, crystal, water, and stone as figures of the Virgin Birth, then proceeds hour by hour through the day, assigning each hour a scriptural event, Adam's formation and fall, the Deluge, Moses' crossing of the Red Sea, the Crucifixion, along with corresponding prayers and moral exhortation. The poem closes with meditations on vespers and the night hours, binding the course of the liturgical day to salvation history.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.de_machabaeis: De Machabaeis is a medieval Latin poem attributed to Hildebert of Lavardin, retelling the Maccabean history in verse. It opens with Alexander the Great's conquest of Persia, his death at Babylon, and the partition of his empire among Ptolemy, Lysimachus, Cassander, Seleucus, and the other successors, before turning to the rise of the persecuting Antiochus, who burns the books of the Jewish law and moves against the Jews. The narrative then follows the machinations of Simon against the high priest Onias and the mission of Heliodorus, sent by Seleucus to seize the treasury of the temple at Jerusalem.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.de_mysterio_missae: A medieval Latin poem attributed to Hildebert of Lavardin, the De Mysterio Missae expounds the mystical significance of the Mass rite in verse. After a prologue in which the poet pleads indulgence for the faults of his work, the poem moves through the liturgy in order, explaining the introit, Kyrie eleison, Gloria, epistle, gradual, alleluia, and gospel reading as figures of events in salvation history, from the utterances of the prophets to the advent of Christ. The celebrant's approach to the altar, his vestments, and his words at the sacrifice are likewise interpreted, each element of the Mass being matched with an antecedent in Old Testament prophecy or the life of Christ.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.de_ordine_mundi: The De Ordine Mundi is a medieval Latin poem attributed to Hildebert of Lavardin. It opens with a prayer entreating Christ to come in judgment and bring the present age to its appointed end, framing the work as a metrical retelling of sacred history. The poem then surveys the order of the world from the fall of Adam onward, dwelling on the spread of sin among his descendants, Cain's murder of Abel, Noah's deliverance through the Flood, the confusion of tongues at Babel, and the destruction of Sodom, before turning to the faith of Abraham and the birth of Isaac.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.de_querimonia_et_c: A medieval Latin poem attributed to Hildebert of Lavardin, dramatizing the conflict of flesh and spirit as a lament voiced by a personified soul. The soul, figured as a woman held in servile condition within a narrow and crumbling house, recalls her spotless bridal union with Christ, mourns the seduction that robbed her of purity, and longs for release from her bodily prison. A companion answers her with a promise of help, and the poem proceeds through reflections on the vanity of worldly care, the contempt into which virtue falls, and the soul's anxious prospect of returning to her abode.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.in_primum_caput_ec: In Primum Caput Ecclesiastes is a medieval Latin verse exposition of the first chapter of Ecclesiastes, attributed to Hildebert of Lavardin. Short quotations from the biblical text serve as lemmata, which the poem expands in sequence, dwelling on the vanity of all things, the transience of successive generations, the sun's ceaseless course, and the rivers that flow without ever filling the sea. Later passages turn to human mortality, the body consumed like wood by rot, and the purging of the elements by fire at the end of the world, when the earth will be cleansed and stand renewed.
la.hincmar.carmina: A collection of medieval Latin verse attributed to Hincmar, a bishop of the Carolingian period. Its opening pieces concern an altar dedicated to the Mother of God that Bishop Hincmar adorned with gifts, and include an epitaph for Bishop Tilpinus, sent as a watchful pastor to the people of Reims by the martyr Dionysius. The bulk of the work is a poem addressed to the Virgin Mary expounding the incarnation, the two natures of Christ united in one person, baptism in the trine name, and the Eucharistic sacrifice.
la.horace.ars_poetica: Horace's Ars Poetica is a hexameter poem of 476 lines from the Augustan age, a didactic and satirical verse treatment of literary craft in which the poet offers counsel on writing to the Pisones. Its argument ranges over artistic unity and decorum, the choice and handling of subject matter, diction and meter, the training and office of the poet, and the conventions of Roman drama, rejecting the 'purple patch' and urging matter matched to the writer's strength. Because its maxims and turns of phrase were quoted, translated, and reworked by later writers across antiquity and the vernacular traditions, it stands among the most consequential Latin sources of poetic theory and a dense node for readers tracing classical commonplaces into subsequent literature.
la.horace.carmen_saeculare: A choral lyric in Latin by the Augustan poet Horace, the Carmen Saeculare is a solemn prayer addressed to Apollo and Diana on behalf of the Roman people. Speaking as a trained chorus of boys and maidens in obedience, as the poem says, to the Sibylline verses, it asks the gods for fruitful land, lawful marriages and offspring, and the continued security of Roman power. Its invocations recall Aeneas, Ilia, and Romulus, and the closing stanzas have the chorus promise to report the good hope and sure fortune granted by Jupiter and all the gods, singing the praises of Phoebus and Diana.
la.horace.epistles: Horace's Epistles, an Augustan sequence of moral verse letters in hexameters closely allied to the satiric tradition, comprises two books totalling 1,513 lines and is presented here in H. Rushton Fairclough's 1929 edition. The first book opens with a programmatic letter to Maecenas renouncing the poet's earlier ludus and professing allegiance to no single philosophical master, and the epistles proceed to treat friendship, wealth, contentment, and the art of living in a style rich in memorable sententiae. The second book turns largely to literary questions, and the collection as a whole became one of the most quarried reservoirs of moral and critical commonplaces in Latin, making it a natural point of comparison for later epistolary, satiric, and didactic verse.
la.horace.epodes: A book of short Augustan lyric poems in Latin by Horace, running to 641 lines and printed here in Vollmer's Teubner edition of 1912. The opening poem addresses Maecenas, vowing to share the perils of Caesar's campaigns as a companion in arms, while the second begins with the celebrated praise of rural retirement, 'Beatus ille qui procul negotiis.' The collection moves between friendship, politics, invective, love, and pastoral idealisation in compact stanzas. Its memorable phrasing and motifs recur throughout later Latin and vernacular poetry, making the Epodes a productive source for readers tracing textual parallels.
la.horace.odes: The Carmina is a collection of Latin lyric odes in four books by the poet Horace, writing in the Augustan age. The opening poem addresses Maecenas, Horace's patron, and the collection proceeds through hymns to the gods, political odes concerned with Augustus and the Roman state, invitations to wine and song, love poems, and pieces on friendship, country life, and mortality. Its poems vary in length and are composed in a set of lyric meters, chiefly Alcaic and Sapphic stanzas, with lines of varying length within fixed stanza patterns.
la.horace.satires: The Satires of Horace, written in the Augustan age, form a two-book collection of hexameter verse in the genre of satire. The opening poem, addressed to Maecenas, asks why no one is content with the lot that reason or fortune has assigned him and turns from that question to a running attack on avarice and false notions of sufficiency. The poems proceed in a conversational manner, blending comic anecdote and parody with serious moral criticism of human folly, in keeping with the speaker's avowed aim of telling truth amid laughter.
la.hrabanus.carmen_evangeliorum: A Latin poem by the Carolingian author Hrabanus, the Carmen Evangeliorum takes the four Evangelists as its subject, naming Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John and associating each with his field of preaching, from Judaea and Achaia to Egypt after Mark's departure from Italy. It pairs the Evangelists with their symbolic figures of man, calf, lion, and eagle, and expounds the mystical meaning of the four forms through a tropological reading. The closing lines gather the symbols together in Christ and celebrate the concord of the four Evangelists in proclaiming his name.
la.hrabanus.carmina: A Carolingian Latin verse collection of 3,237 lines transmitted under the name of Hrabanus. The opening poem, a dedicatory prayer to a saintly bishop, recounts how a Frankish boy was sent by his abbot, rector of the Fulda fold, from the forest of Bochonia to learn at the saint's church the art of metre and sacred scripture, and how, once thirty years had passed ('sex lustra'), he offered a book in praise of Christ, instilled with typological numbers and tropological figures to display the gifts of God and the glory of Christ's passion foretold by prophets and by the letter of the law. Its self-conscious account of figured and typological verse-making, together with dense biblical diction throughout the collection, makes it rewarding terrain for readers tracing Carolingian engagement with earlier poetic and scriptural models.
la.hrabanus.carminum_appendix: The Carminum Appendix is a Latin collection of medieval verse preserved under the name of Hrabanus, belonging to the Carolingian period. Its opening poem, arranged in four-line stanzas, celebrates charity (caritas) as the supreme gift of the Creator, tracing its work from the making of the world through the Incarnation, Passion, and Pentecost to the union of the Church as Christ's body. The collection proceeds through shorter poems, including a Christmas hymn carried by the refrain 'Christo nato rege magno, totus orbis gaudeat,' which recounts the prophecy of the ruler from Judah, the birth at Bethlehem, and the announcement to the shepherds.
la.hrabanus.laudes_crucis: The Laudes Crucis is a medieval Latin verse encomium of the cross attributed to Hrabanus and composed in the Carolingian period. The opening frames the work as a humble gift: the speaker, calling himself a poor and needy servant, likens his verse to the widow's mite and to the varied offerings brought to the temple under the old law, asking that his small tribute not be despised by the wealthy. The poem then extols the cross as the holy trophy of the crucified king and unfolds an extensive sequence of scriptural names and titles for Christ, from Emmanuel, light, word and cornerstone to lion, lamb, shepherd, priest and sacrifice.
la.iulius_firmicus_maternus.liber_de_errore: The De errore profanarum religionum is a Latin prose treatise on theology of the later imperial period by Iulius Firmicus Maternus, written as a polemic against pagan religion. It opens by arguing that divination was an invention of the devil, then takes up in turn the errors of particular peoples, including the Egyptian cult of Isis and Osiris with its annual laments for the dismembered god, and the Phrygian rites at Pessinus, which mourn and then celebrate the revival of a young man beloved by a queen. Throughout, the myths and mourning rites of each cult are contrasted with the worship of the one supreme God, to whom the author urges their adherents to turn.
la.jerome.epistulae: The Epistulae attributed to Jerome form a large corpus of late-antique Latin prose letters. The collection opens with a dedicatory epistle to one Innocentius, in which the author protests the difficulty of recording a miracle of his own age, likening himself to a raw passenger set at the helm on the Euxine, and illustrates divine mercy with the story of a woman at Vercellae who, falsely accused of adultery, survives torture and three strokes of the executioner's sword, alongside biblical exempla such as the three youths in the furnace, Daniel, and Susanna. The corpus is transmitted as a single sequence of letters without book divisions.
la.jerome.in_hieremiam_prophetam: The In Hieremiam Prophetam is a Late Antique Latin prose commentary on the Book of Jeremiah in six books, composed by Jerome and dedicated to a correspondent whom he addresses as brother Eusebius, presented as the sequel to his commentaries on Isaiah, Daniel, Ezekiel and the Twelve Prophets. Its preface announces a concise exposition that will restore the order of Jeremiah's words, which scribal error has confused, and supply what is missing from Hebrew sources, while expressly excluding Baruch and the pseudonymous Epistle of Jeremiah as absent from the Hebrew canon. The work then proceeds through the prophet's text in sequence, beginning with Jeremiah's priestly lineage at Anathoth and the dating of his prophecy from Josiah to the fall of Jerusalem, and throughout contrasts the Septuagint rendering with the Hebrew, interspersing philological notes with moral and allegorical interpretation.
la.jerome.vulgate: The Vulgate is the Latin Bible in the version attributed to Jerome, a work of Late Antique prose belonging to the genre of scripture. It contains the books of both the Old and the New Testament, opening with the first chapter of Genesis. The initial lines recount the creation of heaven and earth in six days, the forming of Adam and Eve and their placement in the garden of paradise, and the serpent's temptation that leads to the fall of the first parents.
la.johannes_hymonides.versiculi_de_cena_cyp: A Carolingian Latin poem by Johannes Hymonides that recasts the Cena Cypriani in verse, its prologue invoking Cyprian as the rhetor and pope of Libyan Carthage and playfully imagining performance at the banquets of Emperor Charles. The poem assembles a vast company of biblical figures, patriarchs, kings, prophets, apostles and notorious sinners alike, as guests at a wedding feast, assigning each a fitting seat, dish and garment drawn from scriptural incident. The narrative proceeds from the arrivals and seating arrangements to the serving of the meal and the king's distribution of vestments to his guests.
la.john_scotus_eriugena.carmina: A collection of medieval Latin verse attributed to John Scotus Eriugena, of Carolingian date, comprising some 845 lines. The opening poem is programmatic, setting the pagan epic tradition, Homer's songs of Hellas and Troy and Virgil's Romulean progeny, against Christian hymnody on Christ's Passion, the wood of the cross, the two thieves, and the darkness and earthquake at the Crucifixion. Classical allusion and biblical paraphrase are interwoven throughout, and the explicit staging of Homer and Virgil as foils makes the collection valuable for tracing how Carolingian Latin poets refashioned inherited classical models for Christian themes.
la.juvenal.satires: The Satires of Juvenal are a collection of sixteen poems in dactylic hexameter, written in the early imperial period and constituting the largest surviving body of Latin verse satire. The opening poem sets out the speaker's program with the claim that indignation itself compels verse, and the collection proceeds to survey the vices and follies of contemporary Rome, including hypocrisy, greed, legacy-hunting, sexual misconduct, luxury, the miseries of clientage and patronage, and the pretensions of the rich and upwardly mobile. The poems range from crowded city streets to country villas and provincial courts, voiced throughout by an angry and hyperbolic observer of morals who mixes savage caricature with moral earnestness.
la.juvencus.historia_evangelica: The Historia Evangelica is a Latin biblical epic in four books of hexameter verse by Juvencus, a Christian poet of the Later Imperial period. The poem retells the gospel narrative in epic form, opening with the angel's announcement to Zacharias of the birth of John the Baptist and the annunciation to the Virgin Mary. Its books carry the story forward in continuous verse through the life, teaching, death, and resurrection of Christ.
la.lactantius.carmen_de_passione_domini: The Carmen de Passione Domini, a short Latin verse Passion narrative of Late Antique date attributed to Lactantius, presents an account of Christ's suffering spoken largely in Christ's own voice. It recounts the incarnation and virgin birth, the poverty of the nativity and the flight into Egypt, Christ's ministry of teaching and healing, and the plotting of Jerusalem that leads to scourging and crucifixion. A closing address summons the reader to contemplate the wounds of the crucified body, venerate the cross, and endure adversity in hope of reigning with Christ in eternal life.
la.lactantius.de_ave_phoenice: A Late Antique Latin poem attributed to Lactantius, De Ave Phoenice treats the myth of the phoenix. Its opening depicts a remote eastern paradise, the grove of the Sun, exempt from age, disease, and death, where the solitary phoenix dwells in the sun's service, greeting his rising with song and marking the hours with its cries. The remainder narrates the bird's thousand-year lifespan, its flight to Syria, and its building of a nest of spices and aromatic woods in which it perishes so as to live again, an account of death and self-renewal that gives the poem its theological character.
la.lactantius.epitome_divinarum_institution: The Epitome Divinarum Institutionum is a Latin prose work in which the late antique Christian author Lactantius condenses his seven-book apologetic treatise, the Divinae Institutiones, at the request of his correspondent Pentadius. It defends the truth of the Christian religion against pagan philosophy, opening with arguments for divine providence and for the unity and nature of God, and adducing testimony from Greek and Roman poets and philosophers, from Hermes Trismegistus, and from the Sibylline books. The author acknowledges that the abbreviated form omits many arguments and examples found in the larger treatise, while aiming to preserve both substance and clarity.
la.lios_monocus.libellus_sacerdotalis: The Libellus Sacerdotalis is a medieval Latin poem of the Carolingian period, attributed in the source record to one Lios Monocus, an otherwise unidentified author. Its proem announces a 'little book' on the priestly art set in truthful verse, and the work unfolds as a moral exhortation addressed to clerics, urging the 'ministers' of the altar to cultivate upright conduct, peace, and fear of God. A central episode dramatizes the deceitful devil tempting a young man into sin with false assurances of divine leniency, casting his victim into infernal darkness, and this is followed by a prayer and an extended passage of praise for a blessed virgin servant of God, figured as temple, precious pillar, and ark of the law. The poem closes by directing its audience toward humble attention to sacred scripture and the things of God.
la.livy.ab_urbe_condita: Livy's Ab Urbe Condita is an Augustan prose history narrating the fortunes of the Roman people from the city's origins onward. Its preface weighs the difficulties of the undertaking and presents Roman history as a record of conduct to be imitated or avoided, before the narrative opens with the Trojan settlement of Latium under Aeneas, the founding of the city, and the reigns of the early kings. Composed in annalistic Latin prose, the work proceeds year by year, recounting wars, domestic politics, and the leading figures and institutions of the Republic.
la.lucan.bellum_civile: Lucan's Bellum Civile, commonly known as the Pharsalia, is an Early Imperial Latin epic in ten books of hexameter verse. The proem laments wars 'more than civil' and addresses a panegyric to Nero before the poet announces his theme: the causes of the struggle between Caesar and Pompey, which set Roman arms against Roman and shook the entire world. The narrative traces the conflict from its outbreak through the campaigns and battles of the war, including the confrontation at Pharsalia that gives the poem its alternative title, dwelling throughout on the horror of citizens taking up arms against citizens.
la.lucretius.de_rerum_natura: De Rerum Natura is a didactic epic in six books of Latin hexameters by Lucretius, composed during the Roman Republic. The poem opens with a hymn to Venus and is addressed in part to Memmius, and it expounds Epicurean philosophy in verse, covering the nature of matter and void, the mortality of the soul, and the explanation of natural phenomena without divine intervention. Later books treat sense perception, celestial and meteorological events, the origins of life, and the development of human civilisation and religion, closing with the account of the Athenian plague.
la.lupus_servatus.versus: A short Latin poem by Lupus Servatus of the Carolingian period, addressed to Evrardus, who is said to have caused a book of laws to be written. Its lines survey that compilation, moving through the codes of the Salic Franks, Ripuarians, Lombards, Alamanni and Bavarians, each accompanied by depicted figures of the peoples concerned, and then celebrate the radiance of Carolingian rulers named as Charles, Pippin, Louis and Lothar. It closes with the poet signing himself Lupus and a prayer that the Father, the Son and the nurturing Spirit protect, exalt and honor the dedicatee.
la.macrobius.fragment: A short Latin prose fragment attributed to Macrobius, an author of late antiquity. The passage offers a satirical sketch of indolent aristocrats who play dice, anoint themselves with unguents and keep company with courtesans, sending a boy to the comitium to learn the day's business in the forum while they drain wine from every amphora along the way. It closes in the council chamber, where the presiding figure, scarcely able to keep his eyelids open from drink, muses on mulsum mixed with Greek wine and on rich fish and fowl, rendering the parody of civic life in colloquial prose.
la.macrobius.in_somnium_Scipionis_commentar: Macrobius's Commentarii in Somnium Scipionis is a late antique prose philosophical commentary on the Dream of Scipio, the closing episode of Cicero's De re publica, addressed in its prologue to the author's son Eustathius. The opening book defends the philosopher's use of fable against Epicurean objections, comparing Cicero's dream narrative with Plato's myth of Er at the end of the Republic. The commentary then follows Cicero's account of a dream vision in which the younger Scipio is shown the celestial spheres, the smallness of Earth, and the fate of souls after death, and expands it with discussions of the immortal soul, cosmic order, number and harmony, astronomy, and the rewards of the just life.
la.macrobius.saturnalia: The Saturnalia is a seven-book Latin prose work of Late Antiquity by Macrobius, cast as the record of learned conversation held during the Saturnalian festival at the house of Vettius Praetextatus in Rome. Its speakers are members of the Roman senatorial aristocracy and other educated men, including Praetextatus, Flavianus, Albinus, Symmachus and Eustathius, who devote the mornings to serious disputation and the dinner table to lighter, more playful talk. The conversations range widely over Greek and Roman literature, history, religious antiquities and philosophical questions, drawing extensively on earlier authors in both languages. A prefatory dedication to Macrobius's son Eustachius sets out the work's design, explaining that material gathered from diverse readings has been digested and arranged into a single ordered whole.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.benedictio_cerei_i: The Benedictio Cerei I is a Latin prose blessing of the paschal candle, composed in late antiquity and transmitted under the name of Magnus Felix Ennodius. The prayer opens by arguing that human speech owes God a return for the gift of language, surveys the creation of the world from nothing and the ordered alternation of day and night, and then hails the night of deliverance in which the candle is offered as a figure of Christ, the lamb slain not by but for humankind. Its imagery encompasses the virgin bee that yields wax without mating, the column of fire leading across the sea with the Egyptian drowned and the Hebrew saved, and closing petitions that the blessed light protect against winds and storms and that the reviving spring bring increase of fruits.

The Benedictio Cerei II of Magnus Felix Ennodius is a late antique Latin prose blessing of the paschal candle for the Easter Vigil, opening with the liturgical acclamation 'Dignum et iustum est'. The prayer rehearses the creation of humankind from the earth, the fall into voluntary error and exile, and the regeneration of the fallen through baptism, in which water and flame, otherwise discordant elements, are reconciled. It unfolds the symbolism of the candle itself, wax from the untainted fecundity of bees and fire infused from heaven, alongside the type of the burning bush that burned without being consumed. The blessing closes with petitions that the consecrated candle withstand storms and incursions and that the officiating priest, his clergy, and the lands be granted abundance together with innocence of conduct.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.carmina_1_praefati: Prose prefaces by Magnus Felix Ennodius, a Latin author of the Late Antique period, standing at the head of his collection of Carmina. Composed in ornate, rhythmical prose rather than verse, the two pieces justify the act of writing after a safe homecoming, defend the author's eloquence against detractors and slanderers, and give thanks to patrons whose favour has nourished his talent. Their language mingles classical exempla, such as the playing of homecoming swans celebrated by the Mantuan, with Christian sentiment and recollection of the prophets who shaped their longings and vows into song.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.petitorium_quo_abs: The Petitorium for Gerontius is a short prose petition by the late antique author Magnus Felix Ennodius, composed as a formal plea on behalf of a man seeking restoration to free status. An opening meditation on divine recompense for the faithful gives way to the case of Gerontius, whose faith, integrity, and character the speaker attests, declaring that the obedience once owed to him is now freely remitted. The petition asks the Roman see to admit Gerontius to its fellowship, to record his absolution in the ecclesiastical acts, and to secure his entire property without diminution.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.vita_epiphanii: A late-antique Latin prose life of Epiphanius, bishop of Pavia (Ticinum), composed by Magnus Felix Ennodius. The preface meditates on the double pitfall of praise-writing, the invention that falsifies and the silence that withholds due honour, before the narrative begins with the saint's birth at Pavia to Maurus and Focaria and the heavenly light said to have shone over his cradle. It follows his entry as a boy into ecclesiastical service under the bishop Crispinus, his humility and charity within the clerical order, and a defence of his bodily beauty as the outward index of the soul. The opening closes with an account of his gifts in doctrine, intercession, exhortation, and correction.
la.manilius.astronomica: The Astronomica is a didactic poem in Latin hexameters by Manilius, a poet of the Augustan age, transmitted in five books. It opens with an invocation of the emperor and an account of how knowledge of the stars arose among the first sages and priests, and then sets out the mechanics of the heavens: the circles of the celestial sphere, the constellations with their risings and settings, and the character and subdivisions of the twelve zodiacal signs. The later books expound the doctrine of nativities, explaining how the positions of the stars and the degrees of the signs at birth determine human fortunes, while the fifth book treats the constellations that rise in conjunction with each degree. Digressions on the creation and progress of civilisation, on the child Erechtheus reared by Athena, and on the persecution of learned men are woven through the astrological instruction.
la.marbodus_redonensis.certamina_septem_fra: The Certamina Septem Fratrum Machabaeorum is a brief medieval Latin poem attributed to Marbodus Redonensis (Marbod of Rennes). It narrates the martyrdom of the seven Maccabean brothers and their mother, who defy King Antiochus's edict compelling the Israelites to eat pork and abandon the law of their fathers. Brother after brother refuses the offered reprieve, endures torture and death, and denounces the tyrant in speeches asserting resurrection and divine judgment, while the mother encourages her sons and receives the highest crown of virtue among them.
la.martial.epigrams: The Epigrams of Martial, a Latin poet of the early Imperial period, are a collection of short satirical poems in fourteen books, written in a variety of metres. The collection ranges from formal tributes to the emperor and his spectacles, through witty portraits of patrons, rivals, parasites, and dinner guests, to openly obscene invective and epitaphs. Prefatory poems in the first book address the reader directly and defend the poet's playful, licentious verses, announcing the persona of a sharp observer of everyday life in Rome. Individual poems are frequently addressed to named contemporaries, grounding the satire in the social world of early Imperial city life.
la.martialis.de_spectaculis: The De Spectaculis of Martial is a sequence of short hexameter poems, classified as satire, from the Early Imperial period. Its verses celebrate the games held in Rome's newly dedicated amphitheatre, addressing an emperor as Caesar and ranking the arena above the pyramids of Memphis, Babylon, Delos, and the Mausoleum of the Carians, and noting that it rises on ground that had been Nero's lake. The poems catalogue the spectators summoned from the farthest peoples of the empire, the punishment of delatores, and the displays staged in the arena, from beast hunts with lions, bears, boars, bulls, and a rhinoceros to mythologically framed executions such as that of Laureolus. Recurring passages present the spectacles as outdoing ancient myth, so that Orpheus, Daedalus, Prometheus, Hercules, and Pasiphae serve as figures for what the sand now offers to the emperor.
la.micon_of_saint_riquier.opus_prosodiacum: The Opus Prosodiacum is a brief Latin poem transmitted under the name of Micon of Saint Riquier, a figure of the Carolingian period. Its verses accompany a gift of soap: they open with an invocation of cleansing by living water and fire and a prayer that heavenly warmth may dissolve the heaps of sin, then commend the soap both as a token of virtue and as a remedy that drives off the fluid humour of phlegm and cleanses sharp gnawings of the belly. The poem breaks off incomplete in its final line.
la.micon_of_saint_riquier.prologus_in_tract: A Latin verse prologue by the Carolingian author Micon of Saint Riquier, written to introduce a treatise on the quantity of initial syllables. The poet announces a six-part treatment of long first syllables and surveys the matters the work will cover: the interjection, the prefix pro, tense and derivation in verbs, defective impersonals, the gerund, and the elision or retention of s in hexameter. Addressed to young learners, it promises rules that will spare pupils the labour of hunting quantities in words that lack metrically fixed form, and it closes with the announcement that verse now gives way to prose for the instruction that follows.
la.minucius_felix.octavius: Minucius Felix's Octavius is a Latin apologetic dialogue of the late antique period, framed as the narrator Marcus's recollection of a debate held on the shore at Ostia between his two friends, the pagan Caecilius and the Christian Octavius. Caecilius first argues from the antiquity of custom and the obscurity of first causes that allegiance to the traditional gods is the safer course, and attacks Christian beliefs and rites as monstrous. Octavius replies with a sustained defence of Christianity, arguing from the order of nature to a single divine providence, cataloguing the absurdities of pagan myth and cult, and rebutting the slanders levelled at the Christian community. The dialogue closes with Caecilius conceding the argument and acknowledging the truth of his opponent's case.
la.moduin.carminum_appendix: A short Carolingian Latin poem by Moduin, preserved as an appendix to his Carmina. Writing as an aged poet now 'broken in body', the speaker addresses a young 'fratercule' and urges him to turn his muse away from Virgil toward Arator, whose verse on the acts of the apostles offers grain where Virgil supplies only chaff. The poem contrasts the two poets throughout, Virgil as singer of pastoral causes, Venus, and Aeneas, whose eloquence the speaker dreads and whose fate is torment in hell, against Arator, who narrates apostolic virtues and the sweet words of the Lord, and closes by exhorting the youth to follow the better writings, which drive impurity from the heart and keep the mind on God.
la.moduin.eclogae: The Eclogae are a group of Latin pastoral poems attributed to Moduin, a poet of the Carolingian period. Cast in the dialogue form of ancient bucolic verse, the poems stage exchanges between shepherd-speakers who dispute their poetic reputations, defend themselves against charges of crude or borrowed song, and appeal to the judgement of an elder poet. Carolus, addressed as Caesar and figured as David, appears as patron and judge, while one passage proclaims the rebirth of a golden Rome in the line 'Aurea Roma iterum renovata renascitur orbi'. The collection couples pastoral convention with praise of the Carolingian ruler and the theme of imperial renewal.
la.nithardus.historiae: A Latin prose history of the Carolingian era by Nithard, cast as a first-person account of recent political affairs. The opening is a dedicatory preface addressed to an unnamed lord, in which the author explains his commission to commit the deeds of the lord's own times to writing and justifies beginning with a summary of earlier reigns. The narrative then recounts the death of Charlemagne, the succession and partition of the empire under Louis, and the ensuing conflict between the emperor and his sons, covering the revolt of Lothar, the veiling of the empress Judith, the downfall of Duke Bernard, and the emperor's restoration. Annalistic in manner, the account traces a sequence of oaths, reconciliations, and renewed discord within the royal house.
la.optatian.epistula: A Latin prose letter by Optatian, a poet of the later imperial period, addressed to the emperor Constantine and panegyric in character. Writing as one whose slight talent has been honoured beyond its merit, the author gives thanks for the imperial testimony bestowed on a carmen he had tied 'with the tighter bonds of the Muses', and dwells on Constantine's favour toward the Muses amid his triumphs, laws and victories. The letter arrays the traditional apparatus of poetic inspiration, Helicon, the Castalian spring, Apollo's lyre, Virgil as Mantuan priest of the Roman Muses and his patron Maecenas, before closing with a plea for indulgence toward the boldness of the new work it commends to the emperor.
la.optatus_saint_bishop_of_mileve.s_optati_: Seven books of Latin theological prose by Saint Optatus, bishop of Mileve, written in late antiquity. The work is a sustained rejoinder to Parmenian, a bishop of the schismatic party whose treatises against the catholic church had been spread widely, and it opens from the position that the peace which Christ left to all Christians has been broken by the authors of the schism. Optatus answers Parmenian's charges point by point, defends the unity of the one church, and takes up disputed questions such as the rebaptism of the faithful and the accusation that the leaders of the schism were traditores.
la.ovid.ars_amatoria: The Ars Amatoria is a didactic elegy in three books by the Augustan poet Ovid, composed in elegiac couplets. Opening with the claim that love, like chariot-driving or seamanship, is governed by art, the poem undertakes to teach its pupils how to find a partner, win affection, and keep an affair alive. The first two books address male readers, while the third offers comparable instruction to women, and throughout Ovid supports his precepts on dress, conversation, and seduction with mythological exempla and playful wit. The poet presents himself as praeceptor Amoris, the tutor of Love, speaking in the persona of a seasoned practitioner rather than a recipient of divine inspiration.
la.ovid.ex_ponto: Ovid's Ex Ponto is a collection of four books of verse letters in elegiac couplets, written during the poet's exile at Tomis on the Black Sea coast and addressed to friends in Rome and to the emperor. Continuing the themes of his earlier exile poetry, the poems mingle pleas for clemency and recall with accounts of life among the Getic peoples, defenses of his poetry, and recommendations of acquaintances. The opening elegy presents the new work as the successor to the poet's earlier book of sad verses, asking that a poem shorn of its author's name no longer be barred from public shelves.
la.ovid.fasti: Ovid's Fasti is an Augustan Latin poem in elegiac couplets that moves through the Roman calendar month by month, giving the causes and origins of its festivals, ritual observances, and days. It is arranged in six books covering January to June, and weaves together aetiological myth, religious practice, notices of the rising and setting constellations, and episodes from Roman legend and history. The opening lines dedicate the work to Germanicus Caesar, and the poem breaks off, incomplete, partway through the sixth book.
la.ovid.heroides: The Heroides is a collection of Latin elegies by Ovid, an Augustan poet, composed in elegiac couplets and cast as letters in the voices of mythological women, Penelope, Dido, Phyllis and others, addressed to their absent or faithless lovers. The opening epistle, in which Penelope writes to Ulysses, establishes the recurring pattern of anxious complaint, recollection and entreaty. The work is arranged in two books, the second consisting of paired exchanges in which the male lovers reply.
la.ovid.ibis: The Ibis of Ovid is a curse poem in elegiac couplets, written during the poet's exile on the Black Sea, directed against an unnamed adversary who has attacked him even in banishment. In the proem the speaker recounts his grievances, declares that he will withhold his enemy's name, and announces that he takes both his title and his method of veiled attack from Callimachus's lost Ibis, threatening harsher iambics if the provocation continues. The greater part of the work consists of a long catalogue of mythological exempla, in which the enemy is assigned the sufferings and deaths of figures drawn from Greek and Roman legend, framed by solemn prayers and imprecations.
la.ovid.medicamina_faciei_femineae: A didactic elegy by Ovid of the Augustan period, the Medicamina Faciei Femineae offers instruction to Roman women on the care and embellishment of the face, written in elegiac couplets. Its opening section argues in favour of cultus, or personal adornment, against old-fashioned ideals of rustic simplicity, while insisting that the guardianship of character must precede attention to beauty. The remainder consists of practical recipes, including a barley face-pack ground with narcissus bulbs, gum, and honey, and compounds of lupines, beans, cerussa, and iris for clearing the complexion. The work survives incomplete, ending amid its cosmetic recipes.
la.ovid.metamorphoses: An epic in fifteen books of dactylic hexameter, composed by Ovid in the Augustan period. The poem presents a continuous mythological history of the world, beginning with the creation of the cosmos and of mankind and moving in roughly chronological order through the legends of gods, heroes, and Roman figures. Its episodes are linked by the recurring theme of metamorphosis, in which bodies change shape, and the narrative runs from primordial chaos down to the poet's own day.
la.ovid.remedia_amoris: The Remedia Amoris ('Cures for Love') is a didactic elegy in elegiac couplets by the Augustan poet Ovid, addressed to lovers seeking release from unhappy passion. The speaker opens with an apologia to Cupid, then sets out precepts for extinguishing desire, shunning the beloved, stopping at the threshold, keeping away from the haunts of love, illustrated by mythological exempla including Phyllis, Dido, Pasiphaë, Phaedra, and Scylla. The poem frames itself as an antidote to the poet's own earlier instruction in how love is won, and closes by invoking Apollo as patron alike of poetry and of healing.
la.ovid.tristia: The Tristia is a collection of five books of elegiac poetry by Ovid, an elegist of the Augustan age, written in the voice of a poet living in exile and unable to return to Rome. The first book opens with an address to the book itself, dispatched to the city in place of its banished master and instructed to appear in the unkempt guise befitting an exile's misfortune. Across the five books Ovid laments his fate, refers to the earlier work that brought the emperor's punishment upon him, pleads with Augustus for the lifting of his sentence and permission to die in his homeland, and writes to friends and readers in Rome of his fortunes amid sea, storm, and separation.
la.paschasius_radbertus.carmina: A Carolingian Latin poem attributed to Paschasius Radbertus, taking the form of a lament for a deceased abbot and spiritual father. The verse calls on men, women, clergy, and monastics alike to join in weeping, and recalls the dead man's care for his flock, his earlier charge at Ambianense, and his founding of a monastery at Corbeia, where a pagan cult site had been supplanted by Christian worship. Later passages meditate on death's indiscriminate seizure of patrons and give voice to a grieving sister-figure who addresses the departed as a gentle master, mingling mourning with prayers for his soul.
la.paul_the_apostle_saint.epigramma: A brief Latin item attributed in the source record to Paul the Apostle under the title Epigramma, its six lines being the edition's prefatory prose rather than verse: a note on transmission followed by an argumentum. The note reports that the piece survives in Parisinus 7558 appended to Claudius Marius Victor's Alethia under the inscription 'S. Paulini epigramma', that Gagneius first printed it as Victor's work, and that Wernsdorf judged it a sermon rather than an epistle, so that its authorship remains disputed; the accompanying summary relates how Salmon, a priest revisiting the city of his upbringing after long absence, discusses with the aged monk Thesbo the vices of its men and, more severely still, of its women despite the blow of barbarian ravages. Dated in the record to the Early Imperial era and classed as theology, the item serves readers of intertexts chiefly as evidence for the attribution history of a Christian moral dialogue and for themes of civic corruption in Christian Latin poetry.
la.paulinus_of_aquileia.carmina: The Carmina of Paulinus of Aquileia form a collection of Carolingian Latin verse, of uncertain date within the poet's career. The work opens with a long doctrinal poem in which the speaker confesses one God in three persons, rejecting any suspicion of three gods, before rehearsing the creation of the world, Christ's baptism in the Jordan, and the transfiguration, and concluding with Peter's reception of the keys and his charge to feed the flock. The closing section of this poem dwells on pastoral and paradisal imagery of meadows, four rivers, and evergreen groves. The collection is divided across several books, gathering further poems in the same religious and doctrinal vein.
la.paulinus_of_aquileia.versus_de_destructi: The Versus de Destructione Aquilegiae is a Carolingian Latin lament, attributed to Paulinus of Aquileia, on the destruction of the city of Aquileia by Attila. Opening as a tearful address to the city's ashes, the poem recalls Aquileia's former splendour in walls, riches, churches, and its rank as metropolis of Venetia, and ascribes its fall to divine wrath provoked by civic pride. It then recounts Attila's siege, the massacre and burning of the population, the enslavement of survivors, the looting of sacred vessels, and the destruction of the books of divine law, closing with the tyrant himself tormented in hell.
la.paulinus_of_nola.carmina: The Carmina of Paulinus of Nola gather the Latin verse of a Late Antique Christian poet. The collection opens with a verse epistle, introduced by a short prose note, in which the poet sends a friend a modest gift of songbirds in return for a present of fish, and the poems that follow include further occasional pieces, catalogues of legendary kings and magi, prayers for domestic peace and prosperity, and hymnic invocations of God the Father and Christ the Word. The poems move between playful amicable exchange and solemn devotional address, all cast in Latin verse.
la.paulinus_of_nola.epistulae: The Epistulae of Paulinus of Nola are a late-antique collection of Christian letters in Latin prose. Written to fellow believers and ascetics, they combine personal address with moral and spiritual instruction: the opening passages console a correspondent who has sold his property for the sake of heaven, urging him to disregard the taunts of worldly acquaintances, to refuse disputation with unbelievers, and to accept insult as the price of the reward promised in the gospels. Scriptural citation runs throughout, and the letters press themes of perseverance on the narrow way, separation from the unfaithful, and almsgiving done to Christ himself in the poor.
la.paulinus_of_pella.eucharisticus: A Latin work of Late Antiquity by Paulinus of Pella, an aristocratic Christian of Aquitaine writing in his old age. After a prose preface, the poem, whose title denotes a thanksgiving, recounts the author's whole life as an offering of gratitude to God: his birth near Thessalonica, childhood and education at Bordeaux, youthful wealth and worldly pursuits, the losses and perils brought by the Gothic invasions of Gaul and his dealings with Gothic and Alan leaders, and his eventual poverty and exile at Marseille. Reflections on sin, divine providence, and the author's late turn to religious devotion run through the narrative.
la.paulus_albarus.carmina: A collection of medieval Latin verse attributed to Paulus Albarus and assigned to the Carolingian era. The opening poem is an address to the nightingale, bidden to sing and ranked above organs, citharas and the Muses, while the cries of cock, wolf, ass, swine, dog, fox and goat are made to yield before her, and swans and peacocks are summoned to lead her measured song. The same poem closes with praise of God, who loosens the tongues of infants, and denounces the monstrous rhythms whose wayward bellowing disgraces the songs of the church's people. Its Latin is characterised by numerous non-classical spellings and forms.
la.paulus_diaconus.carmina: A collection of Latin poems by Paul the Deacon, a writer of the Carolingian period. The opening piece is a versified reckoning of sacred and world chronology, counting the years from creation through the Flood, Abraham, Moses, the Law, the temple and the Babylonian captivity down to the incarnation and thence to the reigns of Desiderius and Adelchis in Italy and of Arichis of Benevento with his consort Adelperga, ending with a warning of the Last Judgment. A further substantial poem celebrates Saint Benedict, recounting episodes from his youth in Nursia through the trials and miracles of his monastic career. Shorter pieces in the collection likewise centre on religious and courtly subjects.
la.persius.saturae: Six satires in hexameters by the Roman poet Persius, writing in the Early Imperial period. The work opens with a prologue in which the poet dismisses popular approval and defends his literary independence, and the poems that follow attack the literary affectations and moral failings of contemporary Rome while treating themes of prayer, self-knowledge, spiritual freedom, and the right use of wealth. The style is highly compressed throughout, marked by abrupt dialogues and dense, often obscure diction.
la.petronius.satyricon: The Satyricon, a Latin satire of the Early Imperial period attributed to Petronius, is represented here by 315 lines of verse in mixed metres. The opening sequence sets a programmatic poem on poetic discipline and the assimilation of Greek and Roman models from Homer and Demosthenes to Cicero beside satiric epigrams on the rule of money in the lawcourts, the tyranny of desire, a scornful summons to effeminate dancers, and a bleak reflection on human mortality. With its generic variety and densely allusive engagement with canonical literature, the work serves as a central point of reference for studies of satire, parody, and intertextuality in early imperial Latin poetry.
la.petrus_riga.aurora: Aurora is a lengthy Latin poem of medieval date attributed to Petrus Riga, divided into twenty-three books. Its prefatory verses praise the work as nourishment drawn from both testaments, contrasting the letter of the old law with its revelation in Christ, and a passage on the author's name gives the poet's identity in a play on his own. Further verses by Aegidius of Paris, included in the preface, describe him as the corrector who brought order and polish to Petrus's original composition. The poem offers a versified treatment of scriptural material with mystical and typological interpretation running alongside the biblical narrative.
la.phaedrus.fabulae_aesopiae: The Fabulae Aesopiae is a collection of Latin verse fables by Phaedrus, a fabulist of the early Imperial period, who states in his prologue that he has polished the material found by Aesop into senarii. The work opens programmatically with a declaration of its double purpose, to move laughter and to offer prudent counsel for life, and proceeds through animal and human exempla such as the wolf and the lamb at the stream, the frogs who ask Jupiter for a king, the jackdaw in borrowed plumage, and the dog carrying meat across the river. Many pieces close with an explicit moral, and the collection also includes fables embedded in historical settings, such as the tale Aesop told the Athenians groaning under the tyranny of Pisistratus.
la.philastrius.diversarum_hereseon_liber: A Late Antique Latin prose treatise by Philastrius, the Diversarum Hereseon Liber catalogues the heresies that have emerged from the beginning of the world, first among the Jews and then since the coming of Christ in the flesh. Its preface compares the devil, the enemy of mankind, to the partridge of Jeremiah's prophecy, a bird that hatches and fosters the young of others as its own. The work then enumerates the sects in succession, beginning with the Ophites or Serpentines, the Cainians and the Sethians, and passing through the followers of Dositheus and the Sadducees, Pharisees, Samaritans, Nazoreans and Essenes to the sun-worshipping Heliognostes, giving for each a short account of its doctrines and the errors attributed to it.
la.plautus.amphitruo: Amphitruo is a comedy in Latin dramatic verse by the Republican playwright Plautus, the only one of his surviving plays to draw on mythological material. Its plot turns on Jupiter, who assumes the appearance of the Theban general Amphitruo so that he may spend a night with Amphitruo's wife Alcmena, while Mercury impersonates the slave Sosia. The play opens with a prologue spoken by Mercury, who conveys Jupiter's command, solicits the audience's goodwill, and declares that because gods and kings share the stage with slaves, the drama must be neither pure tragedy nor pure comedy but, in his coinage, a 'tragicomoedia'.
la.plautus.bacchides: The Bacchides is a comedy in Latin by Titus Maccius Plautus, written for the Roman stage of the Republican period in dramatic metre. Its action turns on two sisters, courtesans who bear the same name, Bacchis, and the entanglements that follow when young men in love with them must contend with a soldier who expects one of the women to be kept for him alone. The opening scenes pass between lovers' banter, including a jest that a young man who wanders only within the city walls outdoes Ulixes in wandering, and the women's scheming, as they plan to flatter and deceive the soldier while pursuing their love affairs.
la.plautus.cistellaria: The Cistellaria is a Latin comedy of the Roman Republican period by Titus Maccius Plautus, composed in dramatic metres within the palliata tradition of Roman plays adapted from Greek models. The work survives only in part, and the 680 lines preserved in Leo's 1895 edition centre on the world of the courtesans: the opening scene follows Selenium and her companions as they weigh friendship, freedwoman status, and the raising of daughters against the hazards of their trade, while the plot as a whole turns on recognition and a young woman's recovered parentage, as the title 'The Casket' suggests. For readers hunting intertexts, the play offers parallels with Greek New Comedy and with other Plautine and Roman comic treatments of recognition tokens, stock lovers, and courtesan diction.
la.plautus.curculio: The Curculio is a Latin comedy by Plautus of the Roman Republic, named for the parasite Curculio whose errand sets the plot in motion. The action centers on the young Phaedromus, in love with Planesium, a slave girl held by the pimp Cappadox, and on the trickery by which money is procured to ransom her, ending in a recognition scene that restores the heroine to free birth. Composed in dramatic meters for the Roman stage, the play includes the celebrated fourth-act monologue in which a speaker surveys the trades and characters gathered in the Roman Forum.
la.plautus.epidicus: The Epidicus is a Latin comedy by Plautus, a playwright of the Roman Republic, composed in dramatic verse within the palliata tradition. The action is set at Athens and turns on the young Stratippocles, who has bought a captive girl from the spoils of war with money borrowed at interest in Thebes, and on the resourceful slave Epidicus, who must contend with the moneylender's demands while concealing the affair from the young man's father. As in other Plautine comedies, the plot advances through brisk repartee, servile scheming, and the threat of punishment, with the talkative but anxious title character at the center of the intrigue.
la.plautus.menaechmi: A Latin comedy by Titus Maccius Plautus of the Roman Republican period, written in dramatic verse for the stage. Its spoken prologue lays out the premise: twin brothers, both named Menaechmus, separated in childhood when one is carried off from Tarentum and raised in Epidamnus, and the confusion that ensues when the other twin arrives there with his slave to search for him. The action turns on mistaken identity among stock comic figures, including the Epidamnian twin's wife and the parasite Peniculus, and the prologue jokes that although the plot is Greek in manner it 'plays Sicilian' after the twins' Syracusan home.
la.plautus.miles_gloriosus: A Latin comedy of the Roman Republic by Plautus, the Miles Gloriosus ('The Braggart Warrior') takes its name from its central figure, Pyrgopolynices, a vainglorious soldier whose tall tales of battlefield prowess are punctured over the course of the play. Set in Ephesus, the action opens with the parasite Artotrogus flattering the soldier, then follows the resourceful slave Palaestrio as he contrives to smuggle the courtesan Philocomasium out of the soldier's house to her lover, ultimately tricking Pyrgopolynices into surrendering her and enduring a beating. Written for the Roman stage in dramatic metres, the play deploys the stock figures of the braggart soldier, the flattering parasite and the scheming slave that characterise Plautine comedy.
la.plautus.stichus: Stichus is a Latin comedy by the Republican-era dramatist Plautus, written for the stage in dramatic metres. The plot centres on two sisters whose merchant husbands have been away for three years; their father urges them to remarry, and the husbands, on their return, test the wives' fidelity before revealing themselves. A comic subplot follows the parasite Gelasimus's unsuccessful attempts to secure a dinner invitation, and the play closes with the banquet and carousing of the slaves Stichus and Sangarinus, from whom it takes its title.
la.plautus.truculentus: The Truculentus is a Latin comedy by Plautus of the Roman Republican period, composed in dramatic metres and set, as its prologue announces in the voice of the city of Athens itself, before the house of the courtesan Phronesium. The prologue offers a satirical survey of the ways lovers are drained of money and reputation by courtesans' demands, and introduces a plot in which Phronesium feigns the birth of a child to extort gifts from a soldier. The play takes its title from Truculentus, a churlish rustic whose rough manners are tamed in the course of the action, and the comedy unfolds among the suitors, slaves, and hangers-on of the courtesan's household.
la.pliny_the_younger.letters: The Letters (Epistulae) of Pliny the Younger, a Latin prose epistolary work of the Early Imperial period, comprise a collection of polished letters addressed to named friends and correspondents, arranged in ten books. Pliny explains in the opening letter that he gathered them not in chronological order, since he was not composing history, but as each had come to hand. The contents range across private and public life, including villa life near Comum, literary activity and publication, courtroom advocacy before the centumviri, and the conduct of contemporaries such as Regulus, with the aftermath of Domitian's death forming a backdrop in the opening books.
la.poeta_saxo.annales_de_gestis_karoli_magn: The Annales de gestis Karoli magni is a Latin epic in hexameter verse attributed to the poet known as Poeta Saxo, of the Carolingian period. Cast in annalistic form across five books, it narrates the deeds of Charlemagne, beginning with his accession to sole rule after the death of his brother Carloman, the Christmas and Easter celebrations at Attigny, and the general council at Worms, and continuing with his campaigns against the Saxons, including the capture of the Eresburg and the destruction of their idol the Irminsul. Chronicle-style annal entries, marked by regnal computations and notices of papal successions, are woven into continuous epic verse.
la.polignac.antilucretius: The Antilucretius is a lengthy Latin philosophical poem by Polignac, a writer of the modern era, cast as an address to a young addressee named Quintus. Its opening lines announce a defence of the supreme Deity and divine providence, declaring war on the Epicurean sect and its celebrated poet, whose teaching that the world is governed by chance and that the fear of a future life may be scorned the author vows to refute. Invoking the eternal Wisdom and Reason of God as his guide, the poem contrasts its austere doctrine of truth with the pleasures and fables sung in Greek verse, and urges Quintus to weigh the case with an unprejudiced mind.
la.pontius_diaconus.acta_proconsularia: The Acta Proconsularia, attributed to Pontius Diaconus, is a short Latin prose narrative in the genre of martyr acts, transmitted with the collected works of Cyprian of Carthage. It records the proceedings against Bishop Cyprian at Carthage during the persecution under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus: his interrogation by the proconsul Paternus, his refusal to abandon the Christian faith, and his banishment to Curubis, followed by his recall, his second examination before the proconsul Galerius Maximus, his condemnation to beheading, and his execution on 14 September, after which his body was buried by night in the gardens of Macrobius Candidianus. The account closes with a note of the date of his martyrdom under Valerian and Gallienus.
la.priscian.perihegesis: The Perihegesis is a Late Antique Latin geographical work by Priscian. Opening with an invocation to the creator of nature for aid in singing worthily, it announces a survey of the lands, sea-routes, rivers, cities and peoples of the inhabited world, beginning with the encircling Ocean, its manifold local names, and the great gulfs cut into its expanse. The earth is then divided into the three continents of Libya, Europe and Asia, with attention to the boundaries variously drawn at Gades, the mouths of the Nile, the Tanais and the Hellespont, before the account proceeds to the western Mediterranean from the Pillars of Hercules along the coasts of Spain, Gaul and Liguria.
la.propertius.elegies: The Elegies of Sextus Propertius, an Augustan poet, constitute a collection of Latin elegy in four books, composed in elegiac couplets. The opening book centres on Cynthia, the poet's mistress, and the collection as a whole treats the servitudes, jealousies, and raptures of love, supported by mythological exempla and poems of recantation and advice to friends. A final book turns toward aetiological subjects, setting poems on Roman legend, origins, and ritual beside continued erotic verse.
la.prudentius.apotheosis: The Apotheosis is a Latin Christian didactic poem by the late antique poet Prudentius, written in defence of orthodox teaching on the Trinity and the full divinity of Christ. It opens with an affirmation of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as one God without difference of age or dignity, and a warning against the many deceitful paths by which heretical sects draw believers from the narrow way of salvation. The poem then refutes doctrines that deny or diminish Christ's godhead, opposing those who would confine the divine nature to a human body and expose it to death, and it appeals to scriptural authority, notably the testimony of the Gospel of John that God has never been seen.
la.prudentius.contra_symmachum: Contra Symmachum is a two-book Latin Christian poem of the Late Antique period by Prudentius, cast as a polemic against Symmachus and the pagan religion he championed. Its prefatory allegory shows Paul, shipwrecked on Malta, casting off a viper whose concealed venom figures the latent resurgence of paganism, an episode the poet applies to the renewed conflict of his own age. The main poem begins with an invocation to Christ as 'Salvator generis Romulei' and unfolds as a sustained verse defense of Christianity against pagan cult and tradition.
la.prudentius.dittochaeon: A late antique Christian poem by Prudentius, the Dittochaeon consists of a sequence of four-line stanzas, each a compressed verse epitome of a biblical episode. The opening stanzas run through the Old Testament, from Adam and Eve, Cain and Abel, and Noah through Abraham, Joseph, Moses, Samson, and David, regularly adding an allegorical or typological gloss to the narrative. New Testament scenes follow in the later portion of the work.
la.prudentius.epilogus: The Epilogus is a brief Latin Christian poem by the Late Antique poet Prudentius, cast as a closing offering to God the Father. The speaker surveys gifts of differing worth, money given for the relief of the poor, and the varied vessels of a wealthy household, from gold and silver to common earthenware and wood, and sets against them his own humble iambic and trochaic verses. He figures himself as an obsolete little pot set in a corner of the Father's house, which Christ nonetheless fits to his uses, and concludes that even the lowliest service profits God, since whatever befalls it is a joy to proclaim Christ aloud.
la.prudentius.hamartigenia: The Hamartigenia is a Late Antique Latin Christian poem by Prudentius, a polemical didactic work directed against Marcionite dualism. Its opening allegorizes Cain and Abel, whose rival offerings end in the first murder, as figures of heretical and true worship, with Cain standing for Marcion. The poem then attacks the division of the godhead into a good and an evil deity, arguing that evil possesses no substance of its own but arises from the perversion of good, and reads the fratricide as a type fulfilled in Christ's death. Its precise date of composition is uncertain.
la.prudentius.peristephanon: Peristephanon ('Crowns of Martyrdom') is a Late Antique Latin collection of fourteen Christian poems by Prudentius in honour of the martyrs. The pieces commemorate the trials, torments and deaths of individual martyrs, the shrines and relics that house their remains, and the intercession and healing sought there by visitors from near and far. The opening poem celebrates two martyrs venerated in Spain, whose names are written in heaven and whose cult site draws suppliants from across the world. Across the collection, narrative accounts of passion and execution alternate with invocations and hymnic praise of the victorious dead.
la.prudentius.psychomachia: The Psychomachia is a late-antique Latin allegorical poem by the Christian poet Prudentius that depicts the struggle for the human soul as an armed conflict between personified virtues and vices. An allegorical preface reads Abraham's armed rescue of Lot, his tithe to Melchizedek, and the promise of Isaac as figures of the soul's inner warfare, before an invocation to Christ asks how an armed mind may drive sin from the heart. The main narrative then stages successive duels between virtues such as Faith, Chastity, and Patience and their vices, ending with the soul in which they dwell consecrated as a temple of Wisdom.
la.pseudo_cyprian.adversus_judaeos: The Adversus Judaeos transmitted under the name of Cyprian (Pseudo-Cyprian) is a Latin theological treatise of uncertain authorship and date, belonging to the Later Imperial period. Composed in prose, it opens by urging its audience to apprehend the divine sacrament of Christ with the eyes of faith rather than by hearing alone, so as to understand the testament of which Christians stand as heirs. It then surveys sacred history from Adam through Noah, Abraham, and Moses, and passes into a sustained indictment of Israel for abandoning God, persecuting the prophets who preached Christ, and clamouring for his crucifixion, closing with a contrast between the people's rejoicing at the Passion, Pilate's protest of innocence, and the grief of the apostles.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_duplici_martyrio: De Duplici Martyrio is a Latin prose treatise of Christian theology from the later imperial period, transmitted under Cyprian's name but of uncertain authorship and date. Framed as a reply to a correspondent named Fortunatus and written as a sequel to an earlier short work on martyrdom, it takes up the two kinds of martyrdom the author had promised to discuss: one endured openly under the cruelty of torturers, the other of a more hidden kind that likewise demands a steadfast spirit. The surviving portion reflects on the meaning of 'martyr' as witness, argues that the whole life of the pious bears testimony to God, and draws on passages from Deuteronomy, Leviticus, Ezekiel, and the apostolic writings to show how the faithful glorify or defame God's name by their conduct, closing with an exposition of the three witnesses of spirit, water, and blood.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_singularitate_clericor: A Latin prose treatise of the later Roman imperial period, of uncertain date, transmitted among the works of Cyprian of Carthage and hence attributed to a pseudo-Cyprianic author. Addressed to the clergy as 'dear sons', it explains that a promised letter on general clerical discipline has been overtaken by the scandal of clerics who live together with women, and it argues from Solomon and the apostle Paul that such cohabitation cannot be reconciled with chastity. The argument moves from rebuke of negligence and warnings against presumption, through scriptural proofs of divine punishment for the unwatchful, to a closing exhortation to 'separate from the pestilential contagion', in which fear of another's fall is presented as the means of victory over temptation.
la.quintilian_pseudo.major_declamations: The Major Declamations are a collection of extended Latin judicial declamations transmitted under Quintilian's name, of uncertain authorship and assigned to the early Imperial period. Each declamation is a complete prose speech arguing one side of a fictitious lawsuit, and the themes centre on sensational domestic crime: parricide, disputed wills, and the machinations of stepmothers against stepchildren. The opening declamation defends a blind young man accused of stabbing his father, whose stepmother cites as evidence the son's sword left in the wound and bloodstains along the wall; the speaker contends that the physical proofs were staged and that the charge serves the stepmother's interest in the dead man's testament. Throughout, argument over evidence and motive is combined with characterisation of the parties and direct appeals to the judges.
la.rufinus_of_aquileia.interpretatio_oratio: The work is Rufinus of Aquileia's Latin translation of nine orations of Gregory of Nazianzus, produced in late antiquity. It opens with a preface addressed to Apronianus, in which Rufinus recounts the circumstances of the commission, gives a lengthy account of Gregory's life and character, and remarks on the difficulty of conveying Gregory's Greek eloquence in Latin. The translated orations follow in prose, beginning with Gregory's apologetic discourse on his withdrawal from his congregation and his defence of the conduct that led to it.
la.rusticus_presbyter.epistula_ad_eucherium: A late-antique Latin prose letter of thanks from a presbyter named Rusticus to Eucherius of Lyon, classified as theology. Rusticus announces that the volumes which Eucherius had sent to be transcribed at his entreaty have been hastened back to the addressee, and he praises Eucherius's teaching, which resolves the questions of the great enigmas of both Testaments and, the veil being lifted, pours the true light of spiritual understanding into the eyes of the heart. The letter also recalls an epigram beneath a portrait of Virgil in a library of secular letters, declaring that the poet's own songs praise him best, before closing with a request that Eucherius pray for the writer.
la.rutilius.de_reditu: De Reditu is a Late Antique Latin elegy by Rutilius, composed in elegiac couplets. The opening lines pair an address to the reader with a hymn to Rome as mother of men and gods, 'urbem fecisti, quod prius orbis erat,' before turning to the speaker's reluctant departure from the city. The poem then recounts a sea voyage from Rome toward the speaker's native Gallic estates, a route taken because 'Getic' devastation has wrecked the Tuscan countryside and the Via Aurelia. Its contents combine first-person travel narrative, topographical description, patriotic panegyric, and lament for a war-torn Italy.
la.sallust.catilina: Catilina is a Latin historiographical monograph by Sallust, composed during the Roman Republic, devoted to the conspiracy of L. Sergius Catilina. The work opens with a preface on the pursuit of lasting glory through deed and the writing of history, followed by a character sketch of Catiline as a man of great energy of mind and body but of corrupt and twisted character. A digression then traces the growth of Rome from its foundation by Trojan settlers under Aeneas and the discipline of the ancestors down to the moral corruption brought by luxury and avarice. From there the narrative proceeds to the conspiracy itself, which the author undertakes to set out as truthfully as he can.
la.sallust.jugurtha: A Latin historiographical monograph by Sallust, composed during the Roman Republic, recounting the war waged by the Roman people against Jugurtha, king of Numidia. The work opens with a preface on human nature, ambition and the moral condition of the state, in which the author justifies his withdrawal from political life and his turn to writing history. The narrative then reaches back to the Second Punic War and the reigns of Masinissa and Micipsa, tracing Jugurtha's rise within the Numidian royal house before turning to the war itself, which the author frames as the moment when the arrogance of the Roman nobility was first confronted.
la.salvianus.ad_ecclesiam: Ad Ecclesiam is a Late Antique prose treatise of theology attributed to Salvian, a presbyter of Marseille. Cast as a letter from one 'Timotheus minimus' to the catholic Church spread throughout the world, it laments the decline of Christian charity and denounces avarice as a servitude akin to idolatry. The work censures believers who hoard earthly wealth rather than give alms, reads the gospel contrast between treasures on earth and treasures in heaven in a spiritual sense, and rebuts the excuses, such as care for children and family obligations, by which Christians claim to be hindered from renouncing riches.
la.scriptores_historiae_augustae.historia_a: The Historia Augusta is a late antique Latin prose collection of biographies of Roman emperors, transmitted under the collective title Scriptores Historiae Augustae and ascribed to several named biographers, of whom Aelius Spartianus opens the work with the life of Hadrian. The opening life recounts Hadrian's origins in Picenum and Spain, his family and Greek-leaning education, his military and civil career under Trajan, and the contested adoption that brought him to power. It continues with his conduct as emperor, including the abandonment of Trajan's eastern conquests, acts of clemency and largesse, and the suppression of unrest in Mauretania, Judaea, and elsewhere. The precise date of composition and the identity of the author or authors remain uncertain.
la.secundinus.epistula_secundini_ad_augusti: A late-antique Latin theological letter in prose, the Epistula Secundini ad Augustinum is addressed by Secundinus to Augustine. Writing from a Manichaean standpoint, the author gives thanks for Augustine's sanctity, expounds the struggle between the spirits of good and evil over the human soul with appeal to Paul's Epistle to the Ephesians, and traces the devil's assaults on figures from Peter and Thomas to the crucifixion and the early church. The letter then reproaches Augustine for his abandonment of Manichaeus' teaching, ridicules episodes from the Hebrew scriptures such as the stories of the patriarchs, and urges him to renounce a conversion made out of fear and return to his former allegiance.
la.sedulius.a_solis_ortus_cardine: A late antique Latin Christian poem by Sedulius, 'A solis ortus cardine' is an alphabetic hymn whose stanzas on the birth and infancy of Christ begin in sequence with the letters of the alphabet. Its 92 lines rehearse the gospel Nativity episodes one by one: the Word made flesh of the Virgin, the annunciation and the leaping of John in the womb, the manger and the angels' song to the shepherds, Herod's alarm, the adoration of the magi, and the slaughter of the Innocents. The poem belongs to the same corpus as the Paschale carmen with which the CSEL edition presents it, and stanzas such as 'Hostis Herodes impie' had a long independent life in the Latin liturgy, making the hymn a recurrent reservoir of phrases and motifs for later writers of gospel verse.
la.sedulius.carmen_paschale: The Carmen Paschale is a Late Antique Latin Christian epic by Sedulius, composed in hexameters and introduced by an elegiac preface that invites the guest at a paschal banquet to set aside the grandiose fictions of pagan poets in favour of the saving miracles of Christ. After an invocation of God as Creator and Redeemer, the poem unfolds the history of salvation, presenting Old Testament events such as the Flood as figures fulfilled in Christ and in the sacrament of baptism. Its narrative proceeds through the Gospel story of Christ's teaching, miracles, passion and resurrection, told in the dress of classical epic.
la.sedulius.carmina_ad_sedulium_spectantia: A small late antique Latin collection of poems connected with the name of Sedulius, transmitted with the works of the minor Christian poets. It contains a dedicatory piece by Turcius Rufius Asterius praising Sedulius as a truthful poet of Christ, two poems by the scholastic Bellesabius shaped by acrostic and telestich letter-play that celebrate Sedulius's verses on Christ's miracles and invite a guest to a modest meal, and an anonymous poem on the Incarnation, built from Virgilian hexameters, which narrates the Father's decree, the annunciation to a virgin, the birth of Christ, and the appearance of the star, closing with a promise of blessings to those who keep the feast. The individual pieces are of uncertain date beyond their late antique setting.
