la.sedulius.epistola_ad_macedonium: A Latin prose dedicatory letter by the Late Antique Christian poet Sedulius, addressed to the priest Macedonius as preface to his Paschale carmen. Sedulius sets out the reasons for composing that work, defends the use of verse for expounding divine things, and recounts his turn from secular learning to Christian writing. The letter also considers other possible dedicatees, among them Ursinus, Laurentius, Gallianus, Felix, and the virgin Syncletica with her sister Perpetua, before commending to Macedonius the four books that gather matter from the four Gospels as far as the Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension of Christ.
la.sedulius.hymnus_i: A Latin hymn beginning 'Cantemus, socii, Domino', by the Late Antique Christian poet Sedulius. Its short couplets move through salvation history: each first line recalls an episode from the Old Testament or the life of Christ, while the second restates it as its fulfilment, so that Adam's fall, Cain's murder of Abel, the Flood, the Exodus, the manna and the deeds of David are read against the coming of Christ. Later couplets treat the Virgin birth, Christ's miracles, the hardening of the Jews, the conversion of the Gentiles, the Passion, resurrection and enthronement, closing with a doxology to Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
la.sedulius_scotus.carmen_pastorale: A Latin didactic poem by Sedulius Scotus, a poet of the Carolingian period. Written as an exhortation to priests, it takes the pastoral office as its governing image and proceeds through short titled sections on the priest's honour, the study of reading, the sevenfold daily recitation of praise, attendance at synods, fraternal charity, and holy baptism. The priest is addressed throughout as a shepherd charged with guarding his flock, and the instruction is delivered in compressed, aphoristic verse.
la.seneca.agamemnon: Agamemnon is a Latin tragedy of the Early Imperial period by Seneca, taking its material from the doomed house of Atreus. After a prologue in which the ghost of Thyestes rejoices at the vengeance to come, the play stages Agamemnon's return from the Trojan War, his murder by Clytemnestra and Aegisthus, and the prophecies of Cassandra, while Electra and Orestes escape the fallen palace. Choral odes on the deceitfulness of fortune, the peril of exalted kingship, and the crimes that attend power alternate with the dramatic dialogue.
la.seneca.apocolocyntosis: The Apocolocyntosis is a brief Latin satire of the early Imperial period, attributed to Seneca, that burlesques the death and deification of the emperor Claudius. It opens with the Fates spinning a golden thread and Apollo prophesying the coming reign of Nero, laments the dead emperor in a mock dirge, and then follows Claudius to heaven, where the gods debate and finally refuse his claim to divine honors. Written largely in hexameters with lyric interludes, the work takes its title from a grotesque pun that replaces apotheosis with 'pumpkinification.'
la.seneca.de_consolatione_ad_helviam: The De Consolatione ad Helviam is an Early Imperial Latin prose consolation in which Seneca addresses his mother Helvia, writing as an exile who resolves to cure her grief by proving that his banishment is no true evil. The speaker first recounts the calamities fortune has already dealt her, then argues that the wise man stands secure against fortune and dismantles the conventional terrors of exile as a mere change of place, illustrated through exempla of peoples' migrations, foundation legends from Antenor to the Roman colonists, and the repeatedly resettled island of his own exile. Readers hunting parallels will find a compact repository of consolatory topoi, virtue as the only secure good, the devaluation of popular opinion, and the catalogue of wandering nations, that echo throughout the consolatio tradition and Senecan philosophical prose.
la.seneca.medea: A Latin tragedy of the Early Imperial period by Lucius Annaeus Seneca, the Medea dramatises the revenge of the Colchian sorceress on Jason after he abandons her for a new bride in Corinth. The play opens with Medea's prayer invoking the gods of marriage and of the underworld as she vows ruin upon Jason's wedding, and moves through her confrontation with her former husband to the killing of their children. Choral odes, including an epithalamium sung by Corinthian women for the impending nuptials, divide and comment on the action, which is composed in dramatic metres throughout.
la.seneca.octavia: The Octavia is a Latin drama of the early imperial period transmitted among the tragedies of Seneca but generally regarded as the work of a later imitator of uncertain date. It is the sole surviving fabula praetexta, a tragedy drawn from recent Roman history rather than myth, dramatizing Nero's repudiation of his wife Octavia in favor of Poppaea and Octavia's banishment to her death. The play opens with Octavia lamenting the ruined house of Claudius and the deaths of Agrippina and Britannicus in conversation with her nurse, and proceeds through dialogue and lyric chorus to depict Nero's fury, the counsel of the philosopher Seneca, and the princess's final condemnation.
la.seneca.oedipus: Oedipus is a Latin tragedy in dramatic verse by Seneca, a dramatist of the Early Imperial period. The play takes the Theban king's confrontation with his fate as its subject, opening with Oedipus in flight from Corinth under the Delphic oracle's threat of parricide and incest with his mother, alongside a long description of the plague devastating Thebes. Its action passes through the ghost of Laius, Tiresias's divinatory rites, and the Corinthian messenger's revelations to the catastrophe of Jocasta's suicide and Oedipus's self-blinding before his departure into renewed exile.
la.seneca.phoenissae: The Phoenissae is a Latin tragedy of Early Imperial date by Lucius Annaeus Seneca, preserved in roughly 672 lines of dramatic verse. Bearing the traditional title of dramas on the Theban legend, the play opens with the blind Oedipus, guided by his daughter Antigone toward Cithaeron, and belongs to the cycle of stories surrounding Oedipus' cursed house and the strife of his sons. Even its opening speech displays the compressed mythological texture typical of Senecan tragedy, piling up exempla of Actaeon, Pentheus, and Ino in rapid rhetorical succession. For readers of intertexts, the play stands as a major Latin reworking of Greek tragic material on Thebes and a rich source of verbal and thematic echoes for later European drama.
la.seneca.quaestiones_naturales: Quaestiones Naturales is a Latin prose treatise on natural philosophy by Seneca of the early imperial period, framed as an address to Lucilius. Its opening preface contrasts the part of philosophy that concerns human affairs with the loftier part that concerns the gods, urging the mind's ascent from earthly ambitions toward knowledge of the divine as the mind of the universe. Across its seven books the work examines physical and meteorological phenomena, including celestial lights, thunder and lightning, clouds and precipitation, winds, earthquakes, and comets, while its prefaces repeatedly turn from physics to moral reflection.
la.seneca.thyestes: An early Imperial Latin tragedy by L. Annaeus Seneca in about 1,166 lines, Thyestes dramatises the culmination of the house of Pelops' curse: Atreus lures his exiled brother back to Argos, slays his sons, and serves them to him at a banquet, closing with Atreus' exultant revenge speech and the ghost of Tantalus framing the action. The play opens with Tantalus summoned from the underworld and unfolds through five acts with choral odes, including a well-known meditation on kingship and power after the second act. Because Seneca's treatment of the myth gathers nearly every earlier Greek and Roman version of the Atreus-Thyestes feud, it stands as a hub for intertextual study of the story and, in turn, exercised wide influence on later European revenge drama.
la.seneca.troades: A Latin tragedy by Seneca of Early Imperial date, composed in dramatic meter. Its subject is the aftermath of Troy's capture: Hecuba and the captive Trojan women lament the fallen city and Priam's death, while the Greeks decree the sacrifice of Polyxena at Achilles' tomb and the killing of Astyanax, the young son of Hector. Choral odes alternate with the dialogue, and the play opens with a song on the fragility of proud fortune, illustrated by Troy's burning.
la.seneca_the_elder.controversiae: The Controversiae is a Latin prose work of the early Imperial period by Seneca the Elder, framed as an address to his three sons, Novatus, Seneca, and Mela. It gathers declamatory exercises built on fictional legal cases, recording the sententiae, divisiones, and colores that leading orators and rhetors of the late Republican and Augustan age contributed to each theme. Prefatory discussions treat declamation, the workings and failures of memory, and the decline of eloquence since the generation of Cicero. Under each case the remarks of several declaimers are set side by side, without a fixed overall order.
la.seneca_the_elder.fragmenta: The Fragmenta of Seneca the Elder preserve a small group of quotations attributed to the early imperial rhetor Seneca the Elder. Taken from Quintilian's Institutio oratoria and from Donatus' Life of Virgil, they concern the diction of tragedy, the bold imagery of declaimers, the impropriety of unnecessary oaths in court, and Julius Montanus' remark that he would steal from Virgil if he could also possess his voice, mouth, and delivery. All are prose remarks falling within the field of oratory and rhetorical criticism.
la.sigloardus_remensis.rhytmi: Latin rhythmic verse attributed to Sigloardus of Reims, a lament for Fulco, archbishop of Reims, who was killed in 900. The poem opens with acclamations of the bishop's virtue and eloquence, curses the noble Guinemar, who with armed men attacked and treacherously brought about Fulco's death, and then narrates the clergy's recovery of the body, its solemn translation vested in episcopal vestments before the altar, the excommunication of the murderer and his abettors, and the honourable burial, closing with a dating clause that places the burial at Reims in the year 900.
la.smaragdus.carmen_in_psalterio: Carmen in Psalterio is a brief Latin poem of the Carolingian period attributed to Smaragdus, whose speaker names himself in the closing lines. Framed as a prologue to a work on the Psalter, the poem describes a little book set in a beautiful golden case with ivory, plain in outward appearance yet bearing mystical words within. It recalls that David sang hidden songs beneath the covering of the letter and that the holy proclamation of the ancient prophets has now been set forth more clearly by the new fathers. The speaker closes by announcing his intention to gather gems from the book so that its pages may shine.
la.smaragdus.carmina: A Latin verse work of the Carolingian period attributed to Smaragdus, the Carmina opens with a direct address to a candid reader, presenting the booklet as the product of a humble pen and promising both sacred and worldly coin within its pages. The poem announces a programme that interweaves scriptural matter, including the deeds of the patriarchs and prophets, the ten commandments of Sinai, the Psalms, Solomon's three books, and the evangelic quadriga, with grammatical instruction, dwelling at length on the forms and species of nouns and the degrees of comparison from bonus to optimus. The author frames the whole as a cleared and smoothed path, or a calm sea, over which the novice's little boat may pass safely through the waters of letters.
la.smaragdus.epitaphium: A brief Carolingian Latin epitaph, attributed in the source record to Smaragdus, though the verses commemorate him in the third person. The poem relates that Smaragdus, abbot of the place, flourished while the pious Louis held the reins of empire, and that he moved his seat a short distance away because the original site was ill suited to human uses. It adds that, when called to the heavenly kingdom, he returned his body to be tended in the old place, and closes by marking the hour of his death, when the scorpion pressed Phoebus in the twelfth part and the heavens opened to the theologian.
la.smaragdus.versus_ad_filium_ludovici_pii: Versus ad Filium Ludovici Pii is a Carolingian Latin verse address ascribed to Smaragdus and directed to a son of the emperor Louis the Pious. In the manner of an admonitory instruction to a young king, it urges constant love of God and obedience to his precepts, commending wisdom, prudence, patience, and simplicity of heart. Its counsel extends to the conduct of rule: just judgement, lawful dealing, relief of the hungry and needy, payment of tithes, and protection of widows and orphans, with the promise of heavenly treasure and an eternal crown for the ruler who governs rightly.
la.statius.achilleid: The Achilleid is a Latin epic in hexameters by the early Imperial poet Statius, conceived in two books but left incomplete early in the second. Its opening invokes the Muse and Apollo to sing the life of Achilles beyond the events treated by earlier poets, beginning with Thetis' alarm at prophecies of her son's fate at Troy. The first book recounts how Thetis conceals the youthful Achilles on Scyros among the daughters of Lycomedes, his liaison with Deidamia, and his discovery by the Greek envoys, and the surviving portion breaks off as the fleet sets out for Troy.
la.statius.silvae: The Silvae of Statius, a Latin poet of the Early Imperial period, is a collection of occasional poems in five books, composed for the most part in hexameters. The pieces range from imperial panegyric, the opening poem describes an equestrian statue of the emperor in the Roman forum, celebrating his victories on the Rhine and against the Dacians, to consolations, epithalamia, birthday verses, and descriptions of villas, baths, trees, and works of art. Most of the poems address individual patrons or friends and commemorate both public events and private occasions.
la.statius.thebaid: A Latin epic in twelve books of dactylic hexameters by the Early Imperial poet Statius, the Thebaid treats the fraternal strife between Eteocles and Polynices, the sons of Oedipus, and the resulting war of the Seven against Thebes. The proem invokes the Muse and ranges over the whole Theban past, from Cadmus's wanderings and Amphion's raising of the walls to the disasters of the royal house, while Oedipus's prayer to Tisiphone for vengeance on his sons sets the conflict in motion. The later books follow the assembling and march of the Seven, the fighting before the city, and the mutual slaughter of the brothers.
la.sulpicius_severus.chronica: Sulpicius Severus's Chronica is a late antique Latin work of sacred history in prose, which the preface describes as a compression of many volumes into two books, written at the urging of readers who wished to grasp the contents of Scripture through compendious reading. The narrative opens with the creation of the world and proceeds through the patriarchs, the flood, the Tower of Babel, and the succession of generations down to Abraham, setting biblical events within a counted scheme of years. It then runs on through the life of Christ and the acts of the Apostles, and continues, as the preface announces, with the fall of Jerusalem, the persecutions of the Christian people, the times of peace that followed, and the internal troubles that later disturbed the churches. The author also states that, wherever the chronology required it, he used secular histories to distinguish the epochs and maintain a continuous series.
la.sulpicius_severus.vita_martini: A late antique prose hagiography by Sulpicius Severus, the Vita Martini recounts the life of Martin, the Pannonian-born soldier who converted to Christianity, embraced the monastic life, and was later made a bishop. It opens with a preface contrasting the pagan commemoration of warriors and philosophers with the writing of a saint's life, and then narrates Martin's childhood piety, his enforced military service under Constantius and Julian, his baptism, and his ascetic career, including the episode in which he divides his cloak to clothe a beggar and receives a vision of Christ. The author states that the account records only tested and attested material, omitting lesser matters to avoid wearying the reader.
la.tacitus.agricola: The Agricola, a Latin prose biography by the historian Tacitus, was composed early in the reign of Trajan and honours the author's father-in-law, Gnaeus Iulius Agricola, whose life it traces from birth through a series of magistracies and military posts to his governorship of Britain and his death. The preface reflects on the suppression of free speech under Domitian and its renewal under Nerva and Trajan, framing the work as an act of pietas toward the dead man. The narrative of Agricola's British command is accompanied by a digression on the island's geography and inhabitants, and culminates in the battle at Mons Graupius, with speeches assigned to the Caledonian leader Calgacus and to Agricola himself. Closing chapters offer an assessment of the general's character and conduct in retirement.
la.tacitus.annales: The Annales of Tacitus is a Latin historiographical work of the Early Imperial period, narrating Roman history from the end of Augustus' reign through the principates of Tiberius, Gaius, Claudius and Nero. Its opening chapters survey the development of the Roman constitution from the kings to the principate and announce the author's intention to write 'sine ira et studio', without anger or partiality. The narrative then proceeds from Augustus' last days and the death of Agrippa Postumus to the accession of Tiberius, treating court intrigue, the fortunes of the imperial family, and the consolidation of one-man rule at Rome.
la.tacitus.de_origine_et_situ_germanorum_li: The De Origine et Situ Germanorum, commonly known as the Germania, is a Latin prose ethnographic treatise by Tacitus of the early imperial period. It opens with the geography of Germany, bounded by the Rhine, the Danube and the Ocean, and discusses the origins, physical appearance, and legendary past of the Germani, including their ancient songs and deities. Subsequent sections treat the land and its resources, arms and methods of fighting, the powers of kings and war-leaders, priesthoods, assemblies, and other social and religious institutions. A closing survey describes the individual tribes of Germania in turn, moving region by region beyond the Rhine and Danube.
la.tacitus.dialogus_de_oratoribus: The Dialogus de Oratoribus is a Latin prose dialogue on rhetoric from the early Imperial period, attributed to Tacitus. Cast as a narrator's report to Fabius Iustus of a conversation he once overheard as a young man, it stages an exchange among the advocates Marcus Aper, Julius Secundus, and Curiatius Maternus, beginning with Maternus's tragedy on Cato and the question whether poetry or forensic oratory is the worthier pursuit. The speakers then take up the problem announced in the opening address, why the present age produces no orators to match those of earlier generations, weighing the training of advocates, the vogue for declamation, and the changed conditions of public speech under the principate.
la.tacitus.historiae: The Historiae is a prose work of historiography in Latin by Tacitus, belonging to the Early Imperial era. Its preface reflects on the corruption of historical writing since the battle of Actium and announces a narrative of the civil wars following Nero's death, in which Galba, Otho, and Vitellius successively seized and lost power and Vespasian rose to the principate. The work is divided into five books and treats the state of the city, the temper of the armies and provinces, the savagery of the age, and the prodigies and omens attending these upheavals.
la.terence.adelphi: The Adelphi is a Latin comedy by the dramatist Terence, written for the Roman stage during the Republic in dramatic verse. A prologue spoken in the poet's own voice answers his critics before the action begins, which then turns on two elderly brothers with opposite views on raising sons: Micio, an indulgent city-dweller who has adopted and brought up his brother's elder boy Aeschinus with leniency, and Demea, a harsh and frugal countryman. Micio's opening monologue argues for governing children by affection and example rather than fear, and the plot follows the young men's romantic entanglements and the collision of the brothers' contrasting methods.
la.terence.andria: The Andria is a comedy in Latin by Terence, a playwright of the Roman Republic, and one of the six comedies transmitted under his name. Its prologue answers critics of the poet's practice of blending Greek material, acknowledging that passages from Menander's Perinthia have been transferred into an adaptation of Menander's Andria. The action opens in Athens, where the elderly Simo confides to his freedman Sosia the predicament that drives the plot: his son Pamphilus's attachment to Glycerium, a young woman who has migrated from Andros, and the marriage negotiations that this attachment unsettles.
la.terence.heautontimorumenos: Terence's Heautontimorumenos ('The Self-Tormentor') is a Latin comedy of the Roman Republican period, preserved in some 1,112 lines of dramatic verse. Its opening prologue, delivered by an actor at the poet's request, defends Terence's habit of combining material from several Greek plays in single Latin works and explains why an old man has been given parts conventionally assigned to the young. The play's Greek title and its open engagement with Greek models make it a key witness to the adaptation of Greek comedy on the Roman stage, and a natural point of comparison for readers tracing such transpositions between traditions.
la.tertullian.adversus_hermogenem: A short Late Antique Latin treatise in which the theologian Tertullian attacks the teaching of Hermogenes, who set matter beside God as eternal, unbegotten, and without beginning or end. After an opening invective that portrays Hermogenes as a painter turned heretic, converted from the church to the academy and drawing his matter doctrine from the Stoics, the work refutes his arguments that God could have made all things neither from himself nor from nothing. Tertullian then argues from scripture that God was not always 'Lord', since lordship presupposes something over which it is exercised, and that eternity cannot be shared with matter, since what is proper to God belongs to God alone; to make matter eternal is, he concludes, to introduce a second god.
la.tertullian.adversus_marcionem: Tertullian's Adversus Marcionem is a late-antique Latin prose treatise of Christian polemical theology directed against the teacher Marcion. The opening preface recounts the loss of an earlier, hastily composed version of the work through faulty transcription and its subsequent rewriting on a fuller scale. Invective against Marcion's Pontic origins and character, with Cerdon noted as an early exponent of the same doctrine, gives way to doctrinal argument over whether two gods may be admitted. The treatise contends that God, defined as the highest and greatest being, can have no equal and must therefore be one, opposing Marcion's distinction between the creator and a good god.
la.tertullian.de_anima: De Anima is a Latin prose treatise on the soul by the Christian author Tertullian, a work of theology composed in late antiquity. It opens by attacking Hermogenes for supposing the soul to be constituted from matter rather than from the breathing of God, and sets the wisdom of Socrates in his prison against the certainty that comes through Christ and the Holy Spirit. Passing from there to the remaining questions concerning the soul, the work surveys the doctrines of philosophers and of medicine and argues that the soul is best known from its author, God, whose revelation settles what human speculation cannot.
la.tertullian.de_idololatria: De Idololatria is a Latin prose theological treatise by Tertullian that argues idolatry is the principal crime and all-encompassing sin of humankind, subsuming homicide, adultery, fraud, lust, and every other offence against God. The work expands the definition of idolatry beyond overt sacrifice and worship to include hidden and habitual forms, asserting that any sin directed against God belongs to the realm of demons and idols. It then examines the making of images itself as culpable, tracing the origins of idol-making to craftsmen of statues and simulacra, and forbids the fashioning of idols on the authority of the divine law. Scriptural authorities including Enoch, Isaiah, and David are cited in condemnation of both the makers and the worshippers of idols.
la.tertullian.de_pudicitia: De Pudicitia is a Late Antique Latin prose treatise on chastity and modesty attributed to Tertullian, belonging to the genre of Christian theology and polemic. It opens with an encomium of pudicitia as the flower of morals and foundation of sanctity, before denouncing an episcopal edict, issued by a bishop styled pontifex maximus, that grants remission of adultery and fornication to those who have performed penance. Drawing on prophetic and apostolic passages, the author contends that divine justice accompanies divine mercy, upholds the church's right to judge grave sinners, and divides offences into remissible and irremissible classes. The argument turns on the question whether adultery and fornication must be reckoned among the sins that cannot be forgiven.
la.tertullian.scorpiace: A Latin theological treatise in prose by Tertullian, belonging to the Late Antique period. It opens with a prolonged image of the scorpion and its venom, applied to persecution and to heretical teachers, Gnostics and Valentinians in particular, who deter believers from martyrdom by arguing that Christ died once for all. Tertullian then turns from the obligation of martyrdom to its necessity and benefit, adducing the Old Testament commandments and other scriptural authority to show that God wills confession of the faith unto death.
la.theodulf_of_orleans.carmina: A collection of Latin verse attributed to Theodulf of Orleans, a poet of the Carolingian era. The Carmina gather poems of varied subject and form, much of it didactic in cast. The work opens with a long moral poem on the passions, portraying tristitia and ira as sicknesses of the mind that cloud reason, and setting against them the remedies of prayer, sacred reading, and fraternal conversation.
la.theodulf_of_orleans.epitaphia: A short Carolingian Latin epitaph by Theodulf of Orleans, composed in the first person as the speaker's own tomb inscription. The verse traces a life in outline: birth abroad, arrival in Frankish territory under the emperor Charlemagne, service as bishop and abbot with Orleans named as the speaker's see, and a fall under Louis, his successor, after the false words of accusers led to confinement and loss of office. The closing lines ask passers-by to pray for Theodulf the servant and express hope of rising from the dust before the face of the coming judge.
la.unknown.corpus_scriptorum_ecclesiasticor: A brief Latin prose excerpt of uncertain date, attributed to Augustine, which argues that the law serves as a pedagogue driving transgressors toward the grace of God. It takes up the question whether any human being can be without sin, finding that Scripture names no one so except Christ, and answers objections drawn from the Letter of James, above all the saying that no one among men can tame the tongue. Such sayings are read as showing that command of the tongue and fulfilment of the precepts rest not on natural strength but on divine aid, for which the soul must pray, and the discussion closes with an examination of the 'wisdom of the flesh' that is enmity against God. The author also refers to books he had written on the same question to Marcellinus.
la.valerius_flaccus.argonautica: An Early Imperial Latin epic in eight books of hexameter by Valerius Flaccus, retelling the expedition of Jason and the Argonauts to Colchis in quest of the Golden Fleece. The poem opens with a double proem invoking Phoebus and the god of the open sea, before turning to Pelias, who, frightened by oracles and by Jason's fame, sends the young man to fetch the fleece from Aeetes' Scythian realm. Subsequent books recount the muster of the Greek heroes, the Argo's voyage and its successive adventures, and the arrival in Colchis, where Medea is drawn into love for Jason through the machinations of the gods.
la.vergil.aeneid: The Aeneid is a Latin epic in twelve books of dactylic hexameter, composed by Vergil in the Augustan period. It follows the Trojan hero Aeneas, who, a fugitive by fate and harried by the wrath of Juno, wanders from Troy toward Italy, where he is destined to found a city, bring his gods to Latium, and become the ancestor of the Latin people, the Alban fathers, and the walls of Rome. The narrative recounts his sea wanderings, including the storm Aeolus raises at Juno's prompting, his arrival among the peoples of Italy, and the warfare through which his fated settlement is secured.
la.vergil.eclogues: The Eclogues, also known as the Bucolics, are a collection of ten short pastoral poems in Latin hexameter by Vergil, written in the Augustan age. Set among idealized herdsmen such as Tityrus and Meliboeus, the poems take the form of songs, dialogues, and laments dealing with love, rivalry in music, and the loss of ancestral land. The opening exchange contrasts Tityrus's ease in the shade of a beech tree with Meliboeus's exile from confiscated fields, introducing the figure of a beneficent patron the shepherds call a god.
la.vergil.georgics: Vergil's Georgics is a didactic poem in Latin hexameters, composed in the Augustan period. The prologue invokes the agricultural deities and addresses Maecenas and Caesar before announcing the poem's subject, the arts of husbandry. Four books treat, in turn, the cultivation of field crops, the growing of vines and fruit trees, the care of cattle and other livestock, and the keeping of bees. Practical instruction is interspersed with weather lore, mythological episodes, and reflections on rural life.
la.vergil_pseudo.aetna: The Aetna is a Latin didactic poem in hexameters of uncertain authorship, transmitted under Vergil's name and assigned to the Augustan period. Its subject is Mount Etna and the origins of its eruptions: the opening invokes Apollo and surveys legendary material before dismissing the mythological explanations of earlier poets, among them Vulcan's forge and the giant Enceladus buried beneath the mountain. The greater part of the poem is devoted to physical inquiry into the causes of volcanic fire, weighing subterranean winds and other natural agencies against the fabulous tales of the mythographers, and the closing lines return to the poet's own undertaking in preference to traditional song.
la.vergil_pseudo.ciris: The Ciris is a Latin narrative poem in hexameters, of uncertain authorship but transmitted under Vergil's name and generally assigned to the Augustan period. It retells the story of Scylla, daughter of King Nisus of Megara, who betrayed her father to Minos by cutting the purple lock of hair on which his life depended and was transformed into the sea bird called the ciris. A substantial prologue sets out the poet's artistic aspirations, dedicates the finished work to Messalla, and argues that its Scylla must be distinguished from the monster encountered by Odysseus in the Homeric account.
la.vergil_pseudo.dirae: The Dirae is a Latin poem of imprecation in dactylic hexameters, handed down under Virgil's name but of uncertain authorship and assigned to the Augustan era. Its speaker, addressing a companion named Battare, pronounces a series of elaborate curses against the impious men who have divided and seized his fields, praying that crops, meadows, fruit and a beloved grove may wither or burn, that the order of nature be inverted, and that fire, drought, the sea and flooding rivers ravage the estate. The refrain 'rura, quibus diras indiximus, impia vota' recurs throughout to bind the successive maledictions together, and the poem alternates harsher and gentler curses as Battare is twice said to have recalled them in altered form.
la.vergil_pseudo.moretum: The Moretum is a brief Latin poem of uncertain authorship transmitted under Virgil's name and assigned to the Augustan era. It depicts a single winter morning in the life of Simylus, a poor smallholder, who rises before dawn, kindles his fire, and grinds grain into flour with the help of his African serving-woman Scybale. While his loaf bakes, he gathers garlic, herbs, and cheese from his cramped kitchen garden and pounds them into the pungent relish that gives the poem its title. The work includes a detailed catalogue of garden vegetables and extended descriptive passages on its rustic figures.
la.vergil_pseudo.priapea: The Priapea is a short collection of Latin poems in lyric metres, of the Augustan era and transmitted under the name of Pseudo-Vergil. Its pieces are set in a modest country garden, where Priapus, installed as the garden's guardian, enumerates the offerings each season brings, spring roses, summer grain, autumn fruit, and menaces would-be thieves with crude threats of phallic punishment. Other poems give voice to the dry poplar and the oak of a poor man's homestead, which describe their own fashioning and their watch over the little plot, the hovel's household, and the nearby shrine.
la.victor_vitensis.historia_persecutionis_a: Victor, bishop of Vita, composed in Late Antique Latin a prose account of the persecution of the church in the African province after its conquest by the Vandals. A prologue, addressed to an enquirer who had studied under the bishop Diadocus, presents the undertaking as performed in obedience to a command, after which the narrative opens in the sixtieth year since the Vandals under their leader Geiseric crossed from Spain into Africa. The work records the ravaging of cities and countryside, the torture, enslavement and killing of clergy and laity, and the seizure or destruction of churches, monasteries and martyrs' shrines, including the basilica of Perpetua and Felicity at Carthage.
la.victorinus_saint_bishop_of_poetovio.comm: A Latin prose commentary on the Book of Revelation composed by Victorinus, bishop of Poetovio, a theological work of the Later Imperial period. A preface addressed to Anatolius explains the circumstances of the enterprise, appeals to the agreement of Papias of Hierapolis and Nepos on the thousand-year reign, and notes both corrections of passages corrupted by scribes and material added toward the end of the volume. The body of the work follows the Apocalypse in sequence, expounding the opening visions image by image: the seven spirits as the gifts of the Holy Spirit, the golden candlesticks as the churches, the two-edged sword as the word by which humanity will be judged, and comparable figurative readings throughout.
la.vitruvius.de_architectura: Vitruvius' De Architectura is a Latin technical treatise on architecture in ten books, composed in the Augustan period and dedicated to the emperor Caesar, whose building activity the preface gives as the occasion for writing. The opening book defines architecture as a science grounded in both craftsmanship and reasoning, and catalogues the disciplines a trained architect must master, including drawing, geometry, history, philosophy, music, medicine, law and astronomy. The work as a whole sets out practical prescriptions for temple design and the orders, public and private construction, building materials, aqueducts and water supply, and machines of civil and military use, interspersed with explanatory digressions such as the account of the caryatids and the Persian portico.
la.vulfinus_diensis.vita_marcelli_metrica: The Vita Marcelli metrica is a Carolingian Latin verse life of Marcellus, bishop of Die, attributed to Vulfinus of Die. It opens with praise of Marcellus's episcopal dignity at Die and then recounts his ascetic youth: his renunciation of his father's estates, servants, and riches, his spare diet and rough clothing, and his ceaseless devotion to the law of God. It introduces his brother Petronius, bishop of the city formerly called Essa and now Die, and describes how Marcellus, though a dweller in the desert, was summoned by his brother to share the episcopal honor and took upon himself the care of the clergy and people of the see.
la.walafrid_strabo.de_cultu_hortorum_carmen: The De cultu hortorum, a Latin didactic poem by the Carolingian author Walafrid Strabo, describes the making and tending of a small kitchen garden. Its opening sections follow the speaker through the seasonal round of clearing weeds, digging, manuring, sowing, and watering, before turning to a verse catalogue of the plants grown there. Each plant is treated in turn, with its name, growth, character, and usefulness against human ailments, the practical instruction framed by the speaker's account of his own plot and labour.
la.walafrid_strabo.de_vita_et_fine_mammae: De Vita et Fine Mammae is a Latin hagiographic poem by the Carolingian writer Walafrid Strabo on the life and death of Saint Mammes of Caesarea in Cappadocia. A preface in short verses, addressed to the poet's companions Anshelm, Wulfing, and Lantwine, asks for their prayers before the narrative begins. The poem then recounts the saint's Cappadocian homeland, his pious upbringing as a child, and his conduct under the persecution ordered by Aurelian, closing with an account of his end.
la.walafrid_strabo.in_natalem_s_mammetis_hy: A Latin hymn in honour of Saint Mammes, composed for the saint's natale or feast day and attributed to the Carolingian writer Walafrid Strabo. In four-line stanzas it praises the martyr's charity, virtue and contempt for worldly riches, recounts his endurance of adversity, his life among wild beasts and his victory over princes and the dragon, and petitions him for protection for those who pray to him. The hymn closes with a doxology to the Trinity, invoked through the intercession of the martyrs.
la.walafrid_strabo.visio_wettini: The Visio Wettini is a Latin epic in hexameters, some 1000 lines long, by the Carolingian poet Walafrid Strabo, recounting a vision of the afterlife granted to Wettin, a monk of the island monastery of Reichenau (Augia). After a proem in which the young poet offers his first fruits to Christ, the poem sketches Reichenau's foundation by Pirmin and the line of its early abbots before narrating the vision, in which the dreamer is conducted through scenes of punishment and reward among the dead and shown the lot of souls famous and obscure. As a Carolingian reworking of the otherworld vision, the poem blends Virgilian epic diction with Christian eschatology and stands near the head of the medieval visionary tradition, making it fertile ground for tracing classical, biblical, and later medieval parallels.
la.walahfrid_strabo.carmina: Carmina is a collection of Latin poems by Walahfrid Strabo, a writer of the Carolingian period. The assembled pieces are predominantly religious and occasional in character, comprising formal addresses and admonitions to bishops and other churchmen on pastoral conduct and the reform of clerical life, together with shorter devotional, didactic, and personal poems, including playful verses connected with his pupils. The collection ranges from extended exhortatory compositions to brief epigrammatic pieces, and is transmitted without division into books.
la.walahfrid_strabo.carminum_appendix: An appendix of Latin verse transmitted under the name of the Carolingian writer Walahfrid Strabo, made up of epitaphic, inscriptional and dedicatory poems. It opens with an elegiac epitaph and lament for Walahfrid himself, who died while crossing the Loire, followed by an appeal to passing travellers for their prayers. The remaining pieces include verses on the rebuilding of the monastery of Auua by its abbot Haito and on gifts offered there under the Frankish ruler Louis, an inscription recording an altar given by one Geroltus, and a versified invitation to communion. The epitaph itself closes with an adjuration by the scribe Reginbert, who had charge of the burial, that the book be lent out only against a pledge.
la.walahfrid_strabo.versus_de_Blaithmaic: A Latin poem of the Carolingian period attributed to Walahfrid Strabo, the Versus de Blaithmaic recounts the life and death of the Irish saint Blaithmaic, born of royal stock, who renounced his father's wealth for the monastic life and, as the prologue's promise of his 'finis' indicates, ultimately received the crown of martyrdom. Composed at the request of a Felix whom the poet addresses as a revered father, it opens by contrasting the fame that poets of old won for wicked men with the narrator's stated aim of singing the deeds of the saints. The verse celebrates Blaithmaic's virtues of humility, chastity, and learning, and his progress from princely heir to monk and spiritual leader of a community of brothers.
la.wandalbert.de_creatione_mundi: The De Creatione Mundi is a Latin verse account of the creation of the world by the Carolingian author Wandalbert. It opens with praise of the eternal and triune God as the fountain of all goodness and recounts the making of the angels, part of whom fall through pride into night and shadow. The poem then follows the Genesis narrative through the successive days of creation, describing the ordering of the elements, the separation of the waters and the firmament, the seas, springs and rivers, the earth clothed in vegetation, and the fashioning of the sun and moon.
la.wandalbert.horarium: A short Latin didactic poem by the Carolingian author Wandalbert, the Horarium explains how to tell the hours of the day from the length of a shadow cast by a vertical line. It works through the year month by month, pairing months of equal daylight, January with December, February with November, March with October, and so on to June with July, and gives the shadow's extent in feet at each successive hour. A closing rule instructs the reader to observe the same method of reckoning throughout the calendar.
la.wandalbert.horologium: The Horologium is a short Latin didactic poem attributed to Wandalbert and belonging to the Carolingian period. Addressed throughout to a reader, it sets out how the hours are paired with the months of the year and how shadows lengthen and diminish with the sun's course, giving a versified scheme for reckoning time by a sundial. It further observes that shadow measurements vary from region to region, contrasting lands scorched beneath the south with those lying cold under the northern pole, and closes by fixing its instructions to the region stretching from the Danube toward Gaul, marked by Lugdunum and the Rhone and facing the Britons across the ocean.
la.wandalbertus.martyrologium: A Latin verse martyrology by the Carolingian poet Wandalbert, presenting commemorations of the saints day by day across the annual cycle. The poem opens with an invocation to God as creator and fount of light, followed by an exhortation to imitate the deeds of the martyrs, confessors and virgins whose feasts it records. In the body of the work each successive day or feast brings an account in verse of a saint's passion, miracles or teaching, ordering hagiographic narrative according to the liturgical calendar.
la.william_of_tyre.historia_rerum_in_partib: A Latin prose chronicle of twenty-three books attributed to William of Tyre, twelfth-century archbishop of Tyre and chancellor of the kingdom of Jerusalem, recounting the history of the Latin East from the First Crusade down to the reign of Baldwin IV. Opening with a lengthy prologue on the duties and dangers of the historian, the work surveys the condition of Christians under Muslim rule, the rise of the Turks, Peter the Hermit and the preaching of Urban II at Clermont, and the deeds of the crusading princes through the capture of Jerusalem and its aftermath, drawing on Greek and Arabic sources as well as oral testimony. The opening books circulated widely, and the chronicle's mixture of royal biography, character sketches, and episodic narrative made it a staple source for later retellings of crusading history; its rare vocabulary and idiosyncratic diction have also furnished frequent parallels for readers tracing the Latinity of medieval historiography.
la.ambrose.apologia_altera_prophetae_david: Apologia Altera Prophetae David, a Latin prose treatise of late antiquity by Ambrose, forms a second apology for King David. It opens from the difficulty raised by the title of the psalm in which Nathan comes to David over Bathsheba and by the gospel passage in which Christ dismisses the adulteress without condemnation, asking whether David's unhidden sin and Christ's sparing judgment give licence to wrongdoing. The answer distinguishes David's acknowledged fault and public repentance in sackcloth from the concealed crimes of other kings, and the work announces a tripartite treatment directed in turn against pagans, Jews, and Christians, beginning with the reply to gentile objections.
la.ambrose.apologia_prophetae_david_ad_theo: The Apologia Prophetae David ad Theodosium Augustum is a Latin prose treatise by Ambrose, addressed to the emperor Theodosius, defending the prophet David against readers troubled that so great a figure fell into adultery with Bethsabee and the murder of her husband Uriah. Drawing on the books of Kings and on Pauline passages, the author argues that God permitted the lapses of holy men so that later believers might learn humility, the danger of judging others, and the practice of penance. The work dwells on David's prompt confession and grief when rebuked by Nathan, treats his numbering of the people as a second fall, and holds up the repentant sinner as a model for those running the course of this life.
la.ambrose.de_benedictionibus_patriarcharum: The De benedictionibus patriarcharum ('On the Blessings of the Patriarchs'), a single-book Latin exegetical treatise by Ambrose, expounds the blessings pronounced by the dying Jacob over his sons and grandsons in Genesis. It opens with a meditation on the sanctity of paternal benediction and an allegorical treatment of Jacob's adoption and blessing of Ephraim and Manasseh, then takes up the patriarchs one by one, beginning with Reuben, Simeon, and Levi. Ambrose reads each pronouncement as prophecy concerning the later history of the tribes and, figuratively, Christ and the Church, frequently citing and rebutting Jewish interpretations and deriving meanings from the Hebrew names. The prose moves between literal exposition, moral exhortation, and allegorical application throughout.
la.ambrose.de_cain_et_abel: A Late Antique Latin prose work of theology by Ambrose, De Cain et Abel expounds the biblical narrative of Cain and Abel as an allegory of two opposed dispositions within the soul, one ascribing all achievement to human ingenuity and the other referring everything to God as creator. The treatise presents itself as a sequel to Ambrose's discussion of paradise and the fall of Adam and Eve, and develops the contrast between the brothers through etymology, arithmetic illustration, and scriptural commentary. Extended typological readings identify Cain with the unbelieving people and Abel with those who adhere to God, while Rebecca's twins, Isaac, and Moses are drawn into the same interpretive scheme as figures of divine election.
la.ambrose.de_fuga_saeculi: De Fuga Saeculi is a short late-antique Latin prose treatise by Ambrose on escaping from the world. It opens by observing that detachment from worldly desires is easier to wish for than to achieve, since the allurements of sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch continually draw the soul toward vanity, with the circus and the theatre named among the spectacles to be shunned. Biblical figures support the argument: Lot's wife, the apostle pressing toward the prize, David, and Ecclesiastes' verdict that all things under the sun are vanity. The main exposition allegorizes the six cities of refuge of the Mosaic law, reading the Levites as those who forsake country, parents, and kin for God, and the manslayer's flight as the sinner's renunciation of the world; it ends by describing the priestly ministry itself as a flight from domestic ties, patterned on Christ's words concerning his mother and brethren and on Elijah's claim to have been left alone.
la.ambrose.de_helia_et_ieiunio: De Helia et Ieiunio is a late-antique Latin prose treatise on fasting by Ambrose. It frames the ascetic life as spiritual warfare announced by the trumpet of solemnity, presenting Christ's fast and temptation as the model contest in which the cross is victory and fasting is the Christian's battle. Its central exemplar is the prophet Elijah, whose fasting shuts and opens the heavens, withholds and restores rain, raises the widow's son, calls down fire, crosses the Jordan dryshod, and wins divine presence through forty days of abstinence. Further sections present John the Baptist as heir to Elijah's spirit, define fasting as the food of the mind and the life of angels, and trace abstinence from the six days of creation to the command laid on Adam in paradise, whose transgression through food brought the fall.
la.ambrose.de_iacob: A Latin prose treatise on theology by Ambrose, composed in late antiquity, De Iacob takes the patriarch Jacob as its central exemplar in an argument on temperance and the governance of the passions by right reason. The opening exposition holds that bare exhortation must be completed by rational reflection, since persuasion rather than servile necessity leads to virtue, and that concupiscence can be repressed but not eradicated, the mind being a controller of its passions rather than their master. Biblical examples carry the argument: David pouring out the water of Bethlehem he had coveted, Joseph resisting his master's wife, and Jacob, together with Joseph, as figures of temperantia, which is called the herald of correction and mistress of discipline. A catalogue of the passions, with delight and sorrow as their leaders and concupiscence, fear, sadness, and gratulation among the rest, frames the psychological analysis.
la.ambrose.de_joseph: De Joseph is a Latin prose work of theology by Ambrose, a late-antique Christian author, expounding the biblical story of the patriarch Joseph. It presents Joseph as a mirror of chastity and a figure of Christ, treating the envy of his brothers, Jacob's partiality and the variegated tunic, and Joseph's dreams as prophecies of Christ's resurrection and of the adoration paid him by father, mother and brethren. Moral instruction on patience under injury, forgiveness of enemies, and due measure in parental affection is drawn from the narrative as it proceeds through the opening of the Joseph story in Genesis.
la.ambrose.de_mysteriis: A late-antique Latin prose treatise of theology attributed to Ambrose, composed as instruction for the newly baptized on the rites they have just undergone. It recalls earlier addresses on morals drawn from the deeds of the patriarchs and the precepts of Proverbs, and explains why the mystery of the sacraments was withheld until after initiation. The work then reviews what the neophytes saw and answered at the font, the renunciation of the devil and his works, the turning toward the east, the ministers and consecration of the waters, and argues for the divine presence and operation in baptism. Old Testament prefigurations support the argument: the Spirit moving over the waters at creation, the wood, raven, and dove of Noah's flood, and the Israelites' passage beneath the cloud and through the sea, where the Egyptian perished and the Hebrew escaped.
la.ambrose.de_nabuthae: De Nabuthae is a Late Antique Latin prose treatise by Ambrose, taking its subject from the biblical story of Naboth's vineyard and King Ahab's violent attempt to seize it. The opening universalises the episode, declaring that Ahab daily is born and Naboth daily is killed as the wealthy covet the land and goods of the poor, before turning to a running exposition of the scriptural narrative. Throughout the work Ambrose attacks avarice, defends the earth as the common endowment of rich and poor alike, and meditates on poverty, inheritance and the insatiable nature of greed.
la.ambrose.de_noe: De Noe is a Latin prose treatise of biblical exposition by Ambrose, belonging to the Late Antique period. The work sets out to describe the life, character, and deeds of the biblical Noah and the depth of his mind, explaining his name as signifying justice or rest. It offers an allegorical reading of his three sons Sem, Cham, and Iapheth as the good, the evil, and the indifferent, arranged like ranks in battle, and reflects on the fecundity of the generation before the flood and on the spirit that does not remain in human beings because they are flesh. The exposition closes on Christ as the one just man, born of a virgin and free from the sin that reigns over all the descendants of Adam.
la.ambrose.de_paradiso: De Paradiso is a Late Antique theological treatise in Latin prose by Ambrose. Taking its start from the Genesis account of God planting a garden in Eden, the work investigates what and where paradise is, offering an allegorical reading in which the garden figures the soul and its virtues, while treating the tree of life, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and the serpent as manifestations of the devil. Invoking Paul's rapture to the third heaven and examples such as Job, Joseph, and Abraham, Ambrose defends the presence of temptation and evil in paradise as serving the common good and the proving of the just.
la.ambrose.epistula_ad_sororem: A late-antique Latin prose letter by Ambrose, the Epistula ad Sororem is addressed to the author's sister and gives a first-person account of the struggle over the basilicas of Milan. It narrates the demand of the imperial court that the extramural Porcian basilica be surrendered for Arian use, the assembly of the people in the new intramural basilica, the imprisonment of merchants and the levying of gold from the citizens, and Ambrose's refusal to hand over the temple of God to imperial authority. The closing portion records a sermon on the book of Job, delivered to the congregation during the occupation, in which the people's endurance under persecution is presented as a renewal of Job's patience.
la.ambrose.epistulae_variae: Epistulae Variae preserves a group of Latin prose letters attributed to Ambrose, the Late Antique writer who signs the opening epistle as a bishop. The first letter is addressed to the emperor Gratian, commends his handwritten confession that Christ is not a creature, and urges that the same faith be extended to the eternal divinity of the Holy Spirit; it closes with an allegory of divine Scripture as a sea into which prophetic rivers, fountains, and streams pour. The correspondence combines courteous address to imperial power with episcopal teaching on faith, the church's steadfastness, and the reading of Scripture.
la.ambrose.expositio_evangelii_secundum_luc: A Latin prose exposition of the Gospel according to Luke by Ambrose, a Christian writer of Late Antiquity. The work comments on the Gospel in sequence and opens with a long treatment of Luke's prologue, discussing the many who attempted to order an account of the things brought to fulfilment, the rejection of apocryphal gospels attributed to Basilides, Thomas and Matthias, and the apostolic witness to the divine Word, whom the faithful see in spirit where the unbelieving see only the body. The exposition that follows combines literal explanation of the Gospel narrative with allegorical and moral interpretation.
la.ambrose.expositio_psalmi_cxviii: A Latin prose exposition of Psalm 118 by Ambrose, a Christian author of the Late Antique era. The work proceeds verse by verse through a long psalm arranged under the letters of the Hebrew alphabet, with eight verses to each letter, attending above all to the moral sense of the verses while also unfolding mystical and sacramental meanings, including baptismal purification. A substantial prologue sets out the relation of moral to mystical teaching, the symbolism of the number eight, and an allegory of the Church as the bride longing for her bridegroom.
la.anonymous.laudes_domini: The Laudes Domini is an anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date. It opens by rebuking those who complain that divine rewards come slowly, and cites as proof the miracle of a married couple of the Aeduan land by the river Arar, whose shared tomb became the scene of a sign of enduring conjugal love. The greater part of the poem addresses Christ as creator and governor of the world, crediting him with the bounds of sea and land, the fertility of fields, vines and trees, the subjection of animals to humankind, the fashioning of islands, hills, woods and birds, and the ordered alternation of the seasons.
la.anonymus.carmen_ad_agobardum: An anonymous medieval Latin prayer-poem of uncertain date, addressed to a certain Agobard and written in four-line stanzas. The opening stanzas invoke God as the measureless creator of earth and heaven and as an omnipresent witness and judge, pleading for mercy under sin and for deliverance from death, with imagery of prison bonds and the gaping furnace. The poet appeals to Christ for strength and a share in eternity, and remarks that the addressee's name may be read in the first letters of the verses. The closing stanzas petition for the welfare of the poet's brothers, commend the writer to fellow Christians, and end with a trinitarian formula and amen.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_exordio_francorum: A medieval Latin poem, anonymous and of uncertain date, addressed to a Charles of renowned ancestry and composed to recount in verse the origins of the Frankish gens. The poet explains that a prose account had already celebrated Charles's lineage and now sets it out in verse, beginning with Rome's dominion over a trembling Gaul and the Roman senate. It then relates the marriage of Blithild, daughter of the Frankish king Hlotharius, to the nobleman Ansbertus, and follows their offspring: Arnold, the bishop and martyr Feriolus, the confessor-bishop Modericus, and Tharsicia, a virgin credited with reviving a dead body. The genealogy continues through Harnulfus, raised to the episcopate, and his son Flodulfus, tracing a line of holy and regal forebears down to its dedicatee.
la.anonymus.carmina_augiensia: The Carmina Augiensia is a short anonymous collection of medieval Latin devotional verse associated with the monastery of Reichenau (Augia), of uncertain date. It comprises an address to Saint Valentine, verses on an altar dedicated in honour of Saint Mary by a priest-monk with the aid of fellow devotees, invocations of Peter, Paul, John the Baptist, Sebastian and other saints, and poems venerating the sign of the cross, which name the four evangelists and recall the raising of Lazarus. Several passages survive in fragmentary form, with words and whole lines missing from the transmitted text.
la.anonymus.carmina_bibliothecarum_et_psalt: The Carmina Bibliothecarum et Psalteriorum is an anonymous medieval Latin verse composition of uncertain date, evidently connected with a library of scriptural books associated with a King Charles, whom the opening couplets compare to Josiah and Theodosius. Its opening lines invoke the psalm-singers David, Asaph, Eman, Ethan and Idithun, praise Jerome's work on the 'laws of David', and interleave devotional and moral exhortation with verses on the virtues of reading. The poem then proceeds to a versified survey of the books of the two Testaments, beginning with the five books of Moses and continuing through the historical books of Joshua and Judges, describing the deeds, lineage and wars each book records.
la.anonymus.carmina_de_ludovico_ii: An anonymous medieval Latin poem in two parts on Emperor Louis II and events at Benevento, of uncertain date. The longer first part, in rhythmic verse, recounts how the Beneventans under Adelferius conspire to kill the emperor, seize him from his palace, and confront the troops coming to his aid, whereupon the usurper who crowns himself is struck down by God and Saracen forces invade Calabria and threaten Salerno. The second part, in elegiac couplets, is an epitaph and lament for the dead Caesar, praising his government of Italy, his piety, and the mourning of Rome, Latium and Gaul.
la.anonymus.carmina_libris_saec_viii_adiect: An anonymous collection of medieval Latin verse, so titled as pieces appended to books of the eighth century. The opening poem calls on Christ to protect one Ragnardus, names a youthful scribe Hieronymus of noble birth, and passes into praise of King Charles as defender of the church, victor over the Lombards and their king Desiderius, and benefactor of the Roman see. A later section is addressed to Pope Hadrian, celebrating the king's triumphal entry into Pavia, his gifts of cities and strongholds to the church, and an organ, likened to David's lyre, dedicated in honour of Christ.
la.anonymus.translatio_sancti_mercurii: The Translatio Sancti Mercurii is an anonymous medieval Latin verse narrative of the transfer of the relics of Saint Mercurius. It recounts how the emperor Constans, seeking to subdue Apulia, destroyed the wealthy city of Quintodecimum near Benevento, carried off the martyr's body with monks assigned to bear it, and came to a violent death at the hands of his own attendants while bathing in Sicily. The poem then relates the body's burial and concealment, its near oblivion over ninety-five years, and its recovery through the devotion of Prince Arechis, who had built the basilica of Sancta Sophia at Benevento and gathered the remains of the twelve holy brothers there. It concludes with the prince and the Beneventan bishop digging at the half-ruined shrine where nuns kept vigil, a nocturnal appearance of the martyr urging the work on, and the joyful removal of the body on a bier.
la.anonymus.translatio_xii_martyrum: A medieval Latin poem of uncertain date, transmitted anonymously, recounting the translation of the relics of twelve martyrs to Benevento. The narrative credits Prince Arechis with securing the remains from Apulia and installing them in the city amid popular celebration, donations of land and treasure, and a solemn procession of clergy and people, before their enshrinement in a marble church he built near the princely palace. The closing lines supply internal chronological indications, noting the month of May, the thirteenth indiction, and a regnal-year formula for the event.
la.apuleius.apologia: The Apologia, also transmitted under the title Pro se de magia, is a Latin prose defence speech by Apuleius of later imperial date. Delivered in court against a charge of magic brought by Sicinius Aemilianus, it turns on the author's marriage to the widow Pudentilla and is addressed to the judge Claudius Maximus. The opening portion recounts the accusers' shifting charges, from the alleged death of a stepson to the calumny of magic, and protests that philosophy itself stands accused before the ignorant. Apuleius answers the slanders point by point, beginning with the jibes at a philosopher's good looks and eloquence, and undertakes to vindicate both his own innocence and the reputation of philosophy.
la.apuleius.florida: The Florida is a collection of prose extracts from the public speeches and declamations of Apuleius of Madaura, the Platonist writer of the later imperial period. The excerpts are brief and episodic, ranging over diverse subjects: the religious observance owed to sacred places encountered on a journey, an anecdote of Socrates on judging men by the mind rather than the eyes, the myth of the piping contest between Marsyas and Apollo, remarks on the tibicen Antigenidas, and reflections on the varied pleasures of the theatre. The pieces preserve the ornate, rhythmically polished Latin characteristic of Apuleius' oratory.
la.arnobius.adversus_nationes: Adversus Nationes is a seven-book Latin prose apology for Christianity by the late antique author Arnobius. The work opens from the pagan accusation that crop failures, plagues, earthquakes and other calamities have beset the world since the Christian religion appeared, and answers it by surveying such misfortunes as attested long before the Christian name was known. The remaining books turn to the attack, assailing the myths, images, temples, cults and sacrifices of the traditional gods and arguing over the nature of the supreme God, the origin and destiny of the human soul, and the role of Christ.
la.augustine.adnotationes_in_iob: The Adnotationes in Iob is a late antique Latin prose work of biblical theology in which Augustine supplies short exegetical notes on the Book of Job. Each annotation quotes a lemma from the biblical text and appends an interpretive gloss, working phrase by phrase through the narrative of Job and the speeches of his friends. The readings are predominantly moral and allegorical: the devil, the earthly city, sinners, and the faithful soul are identified behind individual phrases, with frequent appeal to the Passion of Christ and to the teaching of the apostle Paul.
la.augustine.breviculus_collationis_cum_don: A short Latin prose epitome by Augustine of the official record of the conference between Catholic and Donatist bishops, convoked by imperial command and held at Carthage before the tribune and notary Marcellinus. Because the full transcript of the disputation had grown so prolix that it was hard to read, Augustine compressed the whole proceedings into a breviarium arranged as a numbered sequence keyed to the acts, so that any point in them could be found without difficulty. The work runs from the imperial rescript and the commissioner's edicts through the petitions, notoriae, and letters exchanged by the two parties, including the Donatist objections to the appointed disputants and their procedural claims that the allotted time for the hearing had lapsed.
la.augustine.contra_academicos: A Latin prose dialogue by Augustine, of Late Antique date, cast as a letter of consolation and exhortation addressed to Romanianus. The opening reflects on fortune, providence and the author's own recent retreat to philosophy after worldly setbacks, and introduces Licentius, Trygetius, Navigius and Alypius as participants in a disputation set at a country estate. The debate, taken down by a notary, turns on whether a happy life is possible without the possession of truth, and the title announces the work's polemic against the Academic sceptics' denial that anything can be known.
la.augustine.contra_cresconium_grammaticum_: A Late Antique Latin prose treatise of polemical theology by Augustine, Contra Cresconium Grammaticum et Donatistam replies to Cresconius, a lay grammarian of the Donatist communion who had written against Augustine's response to Petilian, bishop of Cirta, on the Donatist insistence on rebaptism. Augustine answers Cresconius point by point, defending the catholic communion against charges of arrogance and insisting that the dispute over the true church rests on the weight of scriptural documents rather than on abuse. A substantial portion addresses Cresconius's attack on eloquence, arguing that skill in speaking is in itself neither good nor bad but takes its worth from the content it expresses, and that Cresconius condemns in Augustine a facility he praises in Donatist writers.
la.augustine.contra_faustum: The Contra Faustum is a Latin prose work of late antique theology by Augustine, written against the Manichaean Faustus of Milevis, whom Augustine introduces as an African by race, eloquent in speech and astute in intellect, who had published a treatise against the Catholic faith; Augustine notes that he had known Faustus personally and had mentioned him in his Confessions. At the request of the brethren who had read Faustus's work, the treatise answers it point by point, setting out Faustus's words under his name and Augustine's reply under his own. The exchanges cover the Manichaean charge that Catholics are mere 'semi-Christians', the question of what properly constitutes a gospel, and the relation between the genealogy of Christ and his birth, with appeal to Pauline testimony that Christ rose from the seed of David.
la.augustine.contra_gaudentium_donatistarum: A Latin prose polemic by Augustine, bishop of Hippo, aimed against Gaudentius, the Donatist bishop of Thamugadi, who had threatened to burn himself in his church along with followers rather than submit to imperial laws enforcing religious unity. The work is structured as a point-by-point rebuttal: Augustine quotes successive passages from the two letters Gaudentius wrote to the tribune and notary Dulcitius, each quotation followed by a reply defending the Catholic position and attacking the Donatist claims to innocence and persecution. In the preface Augustine explains his method, noting that he cites the words as those of the letter rather than naming their author directly, so as to forestall objections of the kind raised over his earlier reply to Petilian.
la.augustine.contra_mendacium: Contra Mendacium is a Latin theological treatise by Augustine, written in the late antique period and framed as a reply to his correspondent Consentius. It argues that lying is never permissible, even as a stratagem for unmasking heretics, and attacks the Priscillianist teaching, described in the opening as licensing falsehood to conceal doctrine. Augustine supports the case with scriptural condemnations of lying, the steadfast confession of the martyrs, the biblical example of Jehu, and a survey of the kinds of falsehood. The treatise also distinguishes deliberate lying from unwitting error and asks whether believing a lie can ever harm the believer rather than the teller.
la.augustine.contra_secundinum: A short late-antique Latin theological treatise by Augustine, written in prose against Secundinus, a Manichaean correspondent who had suggested that Augustine abandoned Manichaeism out of fear or ambition. The work opens with a reply to Secundinus's letter, in which Augustine defends the motives behind his departure from the Manichaean community and his embrace of the catholic faith. It then turns to doctrinal argument, using Secundinus's own phrasing to show that Christ cannot be the 'king of lights' as Manichaean teaching claims, since a king necessarily rules subjects inferior to himself. Augustine concludes that the lights over which Christ reigns must be created rather than begotten, and that this exposes the incoherence of the Manichaean division between the kingdom of light and the kingdom of darkness.
la.augustine.de_agone_christiano: De Agone Christiano is a late-antique Latin prose treatise on theology by Augustine, of uncertain date. Taking the victor's crown promised to those who contend as its governing image, it identifies the Christian adversary as the devil, who rules through cupidity, and teaches that the invisible hostile powers are defeated within the soul when its own cupidities are overcome. The argument expounds scriptural passages such as the 'prince of this world' and the 'rulers of darkness and spiritual wickedness' of Ephesians, and closes with sustained polemic against the Manichaeans and their myth of a pre-mundane race of darkness mingled with the divine substance.
la.augustine.de_baptismo: De Baptismo, a late-antique Latin prose treatise by Augustine, fulfils a promise made in his earlier books against the letter of Parmenian to treat the question of baptism more closely, refuting the objections customary among the Donatists and confronting their appeal to the authority of the martyr Cyprian. Augustine argues that baptism conferred outside the Catholic communion remains a true sacrament, though it profits the recipient only within Catholic unity, and he parallels the baptized who lapse with the ordained who depart, neither losing the sacrament they hold. The work condemns rebaptism as an impious act against the unity of the whole world and sets out four propositions concerning where baptism exists and where it is rightly received, urging those in the party of Donatus to weigh what the two sides jointly affirm against what Catholics alone maintain. It belongs among Augustine's writings against the Donatists.
la.augustine.de_bono_viduitatis: A short Latin treatise by Augustine, who writes in the salutation as a bishop, defending the goodness of widowhood as a Christian profession. Addressed to the widow Juliana, it exhorts her to persevere in her consecrated state, expounding the apostle Paul's counsels in 1 Corinthians 7 on marriage, virginity, and widowhood, and arguing that second marriages, though licit, are ranked below the continence of the widow. Augustine criticises those, naming Tertullian and the Cataphrygian and Novatian sects, who condemned second marriage outright, and closes by distinguishing between condemning and merely ranking lower the good that Juliana has chosen.
la.augustine.de_conjugiis_adulterinis: De coniugiis adulterinis (On Adulterous Marriages) is a short Latin theological treatise by Augustine, of the late antique period, framed as a reply to questions submitted in writing by a correspondent named Pollentius. Interpreting Paul's precepts on marriage in the first letter to the Corinthians alongside the Gospel's sole exception for fornication, Augustine argues that no spouse may separate without that cause, that one who departs must remain unmarried or return to the former partner, and that union with another after divorce amounts to adultery. He also takes up the question of continence within marriage, holding that neither husband nor wife may abstain from the marital debt without the other's consent.
la.augustine.de_consensu_evangelistarum: A late antique Latin theological treatise in prose by Augustine on the mutual agreement of the four evangelists. The opening argues that the gospel excels all other divine authorities, that Matthew and John, who followed the Lord in the flesh, and Mark and Luke, who followed the apostles, alone merit canonical standing, and that writings falsely inserted under other names were rightly rejected by the church on the rule of catholic and apostolic faith. The discussion then takes up the order in which the evangelists wrote, the distinctive emphases of each account, including Matthew's attention to the royal line and Luke's to the priestly line and person of Christ, and the relations of abbreviation and supplementation among the four narratives.
la.augustine.de_cura_pro_mortuis_gerenda: De Cura pro Mortuis Gerenda ('On the Care to be Taken for the Dead') is a short Latin prose treatise by the late antique theologian Augustine, cast as a reply to a letter from the bishop Paulinus, who passed on a widow's question about whether burial near the memorial of a saint benefits the deceased. Taking as its occasion the burial of her son in the basilica of the confessor Felix, the work asks whether the place and manner of burial avail the soul at all. Augustine argues that funeral care and sepulture are solace for the living rather than help to the dead, since any posthumous benefit rests on merit acquired during life, and he defends this position from the scriptural precedent of sacrifice for the dead in the books of Maccabees and the universal practice of the church. He rejects the poetic notion that unburied corpses are barred from crossing the infernal river, insisting that whatever enemies do to the bodies of the slain cannot harm the faithful, whose bodies are promised resurrection.
la.augustine.de_fide_et_operibus: De Fide et Operibus is a Latin theological treatise in prose by Augustine, dating to the Late Antique period. It takes issue with the practice of admitting candidates to the baptismal regeneration without requiring any amendment of life, and it concentrates on cases of men and women who persist in adulterous unions. Arguing that instruction in Christian conduct should precede the sacrament, Augustine cites scriptural passages on the coexistence of good and evil within the church and sets out a discipline of correction, excommunication and restoration, maintaining that faith retained without corresponding works cannot secure salvation.
la.augustine.de_genesi_ad_litteram_imperfec: A Late Antique prose work of theology by Augustine, an incomplete literal commentary on the opening chapters of Genesis. The treatise begins with a summary of Catholic faith concerning creation ex nihilo, the consubstantial Trinity, evil as sin or the punishment of sin, and redemption through Christ, before turning to the scriptural verse 'in principio fecit deus caelum et terram'. It sets out four traditional modes of scriptural exposition, named in Greek as history, allegory, analogy, and aetiology, and then pursues questions on the meaning of 'in principio', the order and timing of the creation of the angels, and whether time can exist apart from the motion of bodies. The discussion ends abruptly, in keeping with the work's unfinished state.
la.augustine.de_mendacio: De mendacio (On Lying) is a late-antique Latin prose treatise by Augustine on the moral question of lying, which he presents as one that troubles everyday conduct. The argument sets out to define what a lie is, holding that the liar has one thing in the heart and another in speech, and distinguishing error or rash belief, speaking what one takes to be true, from falsehood uttered with the desire to deceive. Excluding jokes, it weighs subtle cases, such as the speaker who says something false precisely to prevent deception and the speaker who tells the truth in order to deceive, and it tests competing definitions before arriving at its final judgment, prefaced by the caution that a reader should not censure what has not been read in full.
la.augustine.de_natura_boni: A short Late Antique theological treatise in Latin prose by Augustine, arguing that God, the supreme and unchangeable good, is the source of every nature and that all things made from nothing are therefore good insofar as they exist. Against those who would posit a malignant nature that God did not create, it defines evil not as a substance but as the corruption of the measure, species, and order natural to a thing. The argument moves from the goodness of mutable and corruptible natures to the standing of rational spirits, whose willing disobedience brings corruption in sin and punishment, and closes on the ordered hierarchy of lesser creatures within a harmonious creation.
la.augustine.de_natura_et_gratia: De Natura et Gratia is a late antique theological treatise in Latin prose, written by Augustine and addressed to Timasius and Jacobus, who had sent him a book attacking those who blame nature rather than the will for human sin. The work maintains that human nature, though created good, is wounded by original sin and cannot attain righteousness without the grace of Christ. It treats the guilt inherited from Adam, the need of infants and adults alike for baptismal regeneration, and the wholly unmerited character of grace, which justifies the sinner freely rather than as a reward for merit.
