The argument rests throughout on scriptural authority, quoting the apostle Paul extensively.
la.augustine.de_natura_et_origine_animae: A short Latin theological treatise by Augustine, composed in prose in the late antique period and framed as a letter to his friend Renatus. It responds to two books sent by Vincentius Victor, a young writer unknown to Augustine, who had taken issue with positions Augustine had stated in earlier works on the soul. Augustine defends the doctrine that each soul is created by God out of nothing, rejecting Victor's apparent implication that the soul is made from God's own substance, and argues against Victor's claim that the soul is a body rather than a spirit. The opening also remarks on Victor's recent conversion from Donatist or Rogatist error and on his eloquent but undisciplined style, which Augustine judges in need of correction.
la.augustine.de_opere_monachorum: De Opere Monachorum is a short Latin prose treatise by Augustine, cast as a reply to a request from Aurelius concerning monks who decline manual labour. It first sets out the monks' case: that Paul's precept 'qui non uult operari, non manducet' refers to spiritual work, and that the Gospel's injunction against anxiety over food and clothing exempts them from bodily toil. Augustine then argues from Paul's own practice and letters that bodily work is commanded, and that the Gospel precepts invoked by the monks are not opposed to the apostolic teaching. The work belongs to the theological literature of the late antique period.
la.augustine.de_ordine: De Ordine is a Latin prose work by Augustine, addressed to a certain Zenobius, that examines the order governing the universe and the difficulty of reconciling divine providence with the apparent disorder and perversity of human affairs. The opening argues that only a mind withdrawn from the senses and cultivated through the liberal disciplines can grasp the unity and beauty of the whole, ignorance of which stems chiefly from man's ignorance of himself. A narrative section then recounts how Augustine, compelled by a stomach ailment to leave his school, withdrew to the villa of his friend Verecundus, where conversations with Alypius, Navigius, Licentius and Trygetius were recorded in writing. The work belongs to the theological and philosophical prose of late antiquity.
la.augustine.de_patientia: De patientia is a short Latin prose treatise on patience by Augustine, the late-antique theologian, of uncertain date. It opens with the paradox of divine patience, asking how God, who cannot suffer, may yet be called patient, and defines human patience as a God-given virtue of bearing evils with an even mind so as not to abandon greater goods. Augustine distinguishes this true patience from the endurance shown by misers, the ambitious, and criminals, whose perseverance in wicked ends deserves reproach rather than praise. The work closes with an exhortation to endure temporal hardships for the sake of eternal life, reinforced by the Lord's saying that in patience the faithful possess their souls.
la.augustine.de_sancta_virginitate: A Late Antique Latin treatise in prose on holy virginity by Augustine, composed as a companion to his De Bono Coniugali, which its opening lines announce as recently published. Augustine argues that virginity is the higher gift and merits exhortation, but must be guarded against pride, while the married deserve consolation rather than reproach; the treatise dwells on Mary, mother and virgin alike in body and in spirit, and on the Church as at once virgin and mother of Christ's members. Spiritual kinship with Christ, shown in obedience to the will of the Father, is ranked above ties of blood, and Mary's bodily motherhood is held of less account than her faith. Closing chapters consider the voluntary vow of virginity, its preservation from violence, and the dignity of consecrated virgins within the ecclesial body.
la.augustine.de_spiritu_et_littera: A Late Antique Latin prose treatise of Augustine, written in reply to Marcellinus, who had objected to the claim, made in an earlier book on the perfection of justice, that a human being can be without sin when the will does not fail of divine assistance. The work argues that no one in this life, apart from the one mediator, has been or will be entirely without sin, and opposes those who hold that unaided human will can achieve or advance toward righteousness, showing that even the good commandment provokes concupiscence and so becomes the letter that kills unless the spirit gives life. It maintains that the human will is divinely aided above all by the gift of the Holy Spirit, who awakens delight and love of the unchangeable good and pours charity into the heart, so that justice is wrought through grace rather than free will alone.
la.augustine.de_utilitate_credendi: A late-antique Latin theological treatise by Augustine, framed as a letter addressed to Honoratus, arguing that belief rightly precedes understanding and that faith in the Catholic religion is not irrational. Against the Manichaeans, who attacked the Old Testament and ridiculed those who believe before they can see truth directly, the work distinguishes the heretic from the sincere but deceived believer and defends the necessity of credendo praeuenire. Augustine draws on his own experience, recalling the nearly nine years he spent among the Manichaeans as an Auditor before returning to the Catholic faith, and discusses how the difficult passages of Scripture are to be received. The argument is carried in continuous prose, moving from personal recollection to a general account of the relation between authority and reason.
la.augustine.epistulae: A collection of letters in Latin prose composed by Augustine, a writer of the late antique period. The correspondence treats philosophical and religious questions arising from Augustine's earlier writings, including the arguments of the Academic sceptics about the attainability of truth, the nature of the blessed life, and the pull of bodily and sensory existence, set within affectionate exchanges with correspondents such as Nebridius and Alypius. The letters combine doctrinal and philosophical argument with intimate self-examination in the polished prose characteristic of late antique epistolography.
la.augustine.gesta_cum_emerito_donatistarum: A brief Latin acta preserving a verbatim disputation between Augustine of Hippo and Emeritus, a Donatist bishop, held at Caesarea in the greater church before bishops including Deuterius, Alypius, and Possidius, with the consuls Honorius and Theodosius named in its heading. Late Antique theological prose, the record belongs to the aftermath of the celebrated conference at Carthage: Augustine presses Emeritus, who has come of his own accord, to state what he would still argue in defense of the party of Donatus, while Emeritus refuses to speak except through the official proceedings, which will show whether he was defeated by truth or overborne by power. Though very short, the exchange cites Pauline verses on again travailing in birth until Christ be formed in converts and on the troubler who shall bear his own judgment, and its phrasing echoes the formulae of Augustine's wider anti-Donatist polemic, making it a compact witness to that controversy's argumentative repertoire.
la.augustine.liber_de_divinis_scripturis_si: A Late Antique Latin prose treatise of theological and moral content attributed to Augustine, the Liber de divinis scripturis sive Speculum consists of a long numbered sequence of short chapters, each headed by a single doctrinal or ethical topic. It opens with chapters on the one God and the distinction of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and proceeds through precepts on charity and peace, almsgiving, prayer and penance, humility, patience and obedience, truthful speech and the renouncing of oaths, and the avoidance of idolatry, fornication, drunkenness and false prophecy. Further chapters take up the honour due to priests, parents and the poor, widows and orphans, the creation of the world by God from nothing, tithes and first fruits, the rearing of children, and the praise of virgins.
la.augustine.liber_de_unico_baptismo: A short Latin treatise of Augustine arguing against the Donatist practice of rebaptism, addressed to a brother named Constantine. The work responds to a Donatist composition on the uniqueness of baptism, which Augustine says was given to him while he was staying in the countryside, and defends the position that baptism is a sacrament of Christ rather than of the minister, so that converts from schism or heresy are not to be baptized again. Its discussion ranges over the treatment of Jews, pagans, and heretics, drawing chiefly on the Apostle's words to the Romans to argue that whatever is true in them must be preserved while their error is corrected.
la.augustine.sermo_ad_caesariensis_ecclesia: A brief Latin sermon by Augustine, addressed to the people of the church of Caesarea and preserved among his writings against the Donatists. The speaker gives thanks that Emeritus, the Donatist bishop of the city, has shown himself willing to contemplate unity with the catholic church, and weighs the objection that schismatics returning to communion should not be received as brothers. The greater part of the address argues that baptism belongs to Christ rather than to Donatus, likening the baptismal character to the mark of a soldier under his emperor rather than of a deserter, and closes with exhortations to prayer for unity.
la.aurelius_victor.de_caesaribus: De Caesaribus is a Late Antique Latin work of historiography by Aurelius Victor, composed in prose and consisting of a sequence of brief biographies of the Roman emperors. The narrative opens with Augustus, describing his rise to sole power and his death at Nola some seven hundred and twenty years after the founding of the city, and proceeds reign by reign through rulers such as Tiberius, Caligula, and Claudius. Each emperor receives a compact account of his accession, deeds, and character, with pointed assessments of virtues and failings, as in the depiction of Tiberius's dissimulation and retreat to Capri and of Caligula's extravagance and assassination.
la.aurelius_victor.epitome_de_caesaribus: Attributed to Aurelius Victor, the Epitome de Caesaribus is a Late Antique Latin prose work of historiography consisting of short biographical notices of the Roman emperors, beginning with Augustus. Each notice records the emperor's family background, wars and provincial administration, building works, personal character, and death, often with anecdotal detail and moral judgement. The opening account of Augustus, for example, moves from his conquests and reorganisation of Egypt and Rome to his friendships, vices, and the disputed circumstances of his end at Nola.
la.ausonius.de_xii_caesaribus: De XII Caesaribus is a Latin poem-cycle by the Late Antique poet Ausonius, made up of a short prose preface and several verse sequences devoted to the Roman emperors. The preface announces single-line epigrams (monosticha) for the twelve Caesars whose names, deeds, lives and deaths Suetonius had formerly treated at length. The verses characterise rulers from Julius Caesar to Domitian, noting the length of each reign and the manner of each death, and then continue with further epigrams on later emperors from Nerva through the Antonines and the early Severan house, ending with a ruler who falsely bore the Antonine name.
la.ausonius.gratiarum_actio: Gratiarum Actio is a Latin prose oration by Ausonius of the late antique period, cast as a formal speech of thanks addressed to the emperor Gratian. The speaker gives gratitude for his elevation to the consulship, an honour he insists was conferred without canvassing, purchase, or solicitation, and rehearses the emperor's clemency, liberality, and military success on the Danube and Rhine frontiers. The oration dwells on the omnipresence of thanksgiving in every place and hour, catalogues the emperor's titles and merits, and closes by weighing his benefactor's words against the eloquence of Menelaus, Ulysses, and Nestor.
la.ausonius.libri_de_fastis_conclusio: A short lyric epilogue in Latin by Ausonius, closing his books of Fasti, which traced Rome's magistrates from the age of the kings onward through names scattered across Latin history. The poem recapitulates the work's chronological scheme, giving a numerical formula for reckoning the years from the city's foundation down to the poet's own consulship. Addressed to Proculus, it anticipates the completion of an Olympiad cycle and invites the reader to carry the record further if fortune permits.
la.ausonius.precationes: A short lyric prayer for the New Year by the Late Antique poet Ausonius, addressed to the two-faced god Janus under the recurring refrain 'Iane, veni'. The poem petitions the god for an orderly round of seasons, fair winds, timely solstices, gentle autumn and winter, for the benign influence of the planets, and for peace and victory over foreign peoples. It culminates in the celebration of Ausonius's own consulship and the prospect of the emperor's in the following year, and closes with an astronomical account of the sun's annual course through the signs of the zodiac.
la.ausonius.versus_paschales_pro_augusto_di: A short Easter poem in lyric metre by the Late Antique poet Ausonius, spoken in honour of an emperor. It opens on the returning festival of Christ the Saviour and the fasts of the devout, then turns to a prayer addressed to God the Father, describing the Son as his true and living Word, the pity shown to deceived Adam, and the threefold faith of a single author sealed in the washing of baptism. The closing section praises the Augustus as father of two emperors, a brother and son who share an undivided rule while all things remain his alone, and ends with a plea that Christ present these gentle rulers, ministers of earth and heaven, to his eternal Father.
la.bede_the_venerable.de_locis_santis: De locis sanctis is a brief Latin prose treatise by Bede the Venerable describing the holy places of Jerusalem in the early medieval period. The work opens with the site and circuit of the city, its walls, towers and gates, and surveys in detail the Constantinian complex of the Martyrium, Golgotha and the rotunda of the Anastasis, including the tomb of Christ and the relics of the lance and the cup preserved there. Further notices cover the Temple site, where Saracens gather for prayer, the pool of Bethsaida, the fountain of Siloe, and the churches, monastic cells and sacred spots of Mount Sion, together with the place of Saint Stephen's martyrdom outside the walls. Bede notes that he had the churches and their ground plans drawn to accompany the account, and the closing lines quote Victorinus of Pettau on Golgotha as the centre of the earth.
la.bertharius_of_monte_cassino.carmen_de_sa: A Carolingian Latin poem on Saint Benedict, attributed to Bertharius of Monte Cassino and transmitted in a form whose title marks it as interpolated. Opening with an invocation of Benedict as a confessor celebrated in all the world, the verse narrative recounts the principal episodes of his legend: the mended sieve, the poisoned bread carried off by the raven, the rescue of Placidus from the flood and Maurus's walk upon the waters, the collapse of a building and the raising of a crushed boy, the prophecy to Totila, and predictions concerning the fate of Rome. The poem closes with injunctions to a cleric and to the city of Rome, ending on the promise that no enemy shall breach its walls.
la.boethius.consolatio_philosophiae: The Consolatio Philosophiae is a Late Antique Latin work by Boethius, arranged in five books that alternate prose dialogue with lyric verse. It opens on a narrator facing exile on false charges and mourning his fall from fortune, who is visited by the personified figure of Philosophy; she dismisses the poetic Muses from his bedside and begins his cure by restoring his memory of his former vigour. From this account of grief and Fortune's instability the dialogue moves to larger questions, treating in its course the nature of true happiness, the order of the cosmos, and the relation of divine providence to human freedom.
la.boethius.de_fide_catholica: A short Late Antique Latin prose treatise attributed to Boethius and transmitted with his theological tractates. It presents an account of the Catholic faith grounded in the authority of the Old and New Testaments, setting out the unity of God in three persons and defending the coeternal generation of the Son and the procession of the Holy Spirit against the positions of Arius, the Sabellians and the Manichaeans. It then summarises sacred history: God's making of the world when it did not exist, neither from his own substance nor from pre-existing matter, the fall of the angels, the formation of Adam and Eve and their disobedience, the modes of scriptural meaning (historical, allegorical, or both together), the transmission of Adam's penalty to his posterity, and Pelagius' denial of that transmission. The work breaks off before completing its exposition.
la.boethius.quomodo_substantiae_in_eo_quod_: A short Latin prose treatise on metaphysics by Boethius, written in the late antique period and framed as a reply to a correspondent asking for a clearer exposition of a problem treated in the author's Hebdomads: how substances can be good insofar as they exist without being substantial goods. After a brief dialogue-preface, the work sets out numbered axioms on being, essence, and participation, described as common conceptions of the mind. It then formulates the paradox that, if all existing things tend toward the good and are therefore good, they might seem to be good by substance, which would entail that all things are God. The proposed solution distinguishes ipsum esse from id quod est and argues that things other than the first good are good because they flow from it, while that first good alone is good by its very substance.
la.boethius.quomodo_trinitas: A short Latin prose treatise of Late Antiquity by Boethius, addressed to his father-in-law Q. Aurelius Memmius Symmachus, on how the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God and not three. After a preface on the difficulty of the question and on the seeds of its argument found in the writings of Augustine, the work opposes Arian diversification of the Trinity by analysing difference according to genus, species, number, and accidents. It then distinguishes the three parts of speculative philosophy, natural, mathematical, and theological, and argues that divine substance, being form without matter, is truly one and identical with its own essence.
la.caesar.de_bello_civili: De Bello Civili is a Latin prose historiographical narrative by Julius Caesar, composed in the late Roman Republic and transmitted in three books. It recounts the civil war between Caesar and Pompey, opening with the senatorial debates at Rome over Caesar's command, the senate's ultimatum, and the flight of the tribunes of the plebs to Caesar's camp, before following the outbreak of hostilities and the campaigns in Italy, Spain, and Greece. The narrative breaks off abruptly in Alexandria, without a formal conclusion.
la.caesar_augustus.res_gestae_divi_augusti: The Res Gestae Divi Augusti is a Latin prose account in which the emperor Augustus, writing in the first person, sets out the deeds of his reign and the sums he expended on the Roman state. The opening presents the work as a copy of an inscription engraved on two bronze pillars erected at Rome. Its paragraphs catalogue his youthful raising of a private army and vindication of the republic's liberty, his civil and foreign wars and his sparing of defeated citizens, his triumphs and acclamations, his refusal of the dictatorship, his priesthoods and other honours, the census lustra conducted with Agrippa and Tiberius, his legislative and moral reforms, and the altars, temples and ritual observances decreed in his honour. It ends with the public dignities conferred on his sons Gaius and Lucius Caesar.
la.cicero.brutus: The Brutus is a Latin prose dialogue on rhetoric by Cicero, a work of the Roman Republican era. It opens with Cicero mourning the death of the orator Quintus Hortensius, whose passing he takes both as a personal and a public loss, before a visit from Marcus Brutus and Titus Pomponius Atticus turns his thoughts to study and writing. From grief for Hortensius and the troubled condition of the state the conversation moves to eloquence itself, surveying the history of Roman oratory down to Hortensius and Cicero's own place in it.
la.cicero.cum_populo_gratias_egit: A brief Latin prose oration of thanks addressed by Cicero to the Roman people, belonging to the oratory of the Republican period. The speaker recounts the vow he made to Jupiter Optimus Maximus and the other immortal gods before his wretched departure, and catalogues the goods restored to him by popular favour: his brother, his children, his property, his friendships, his revived honours and dignities, and the homeland itself, all rendered sweeter by their loss. He contrasts his recall, obtained through the intercessions of his mourning kin, his brother Quintus, his son-in-law C. Piso, his wife and daughter, with the armed return of Gaius Marius, and concludes that no eloquence could adequately enumerate or repay so vast a debt of gratitude.
la.cicero.de_fato: De Fato is a Latin prose treatise on fate and human freedom by Cicero, composed in the last years of the Roman Republic and framed as a dialogue with Hirtius, the consul designate, at Puteoli in the aftermath of Caesar's death. Cicero takes up a question he identifies with the Greek peri dynaton, concerning what is possible, and asks what force statements about the future possess and whether events are bound by fate. The discussion weighs the Stoic doctrines of Chrysippus and Posidonius on antecedent causes, environmental and inherited influences on character, and the alleged necessity of all that happens, against the position that human actions and choices originate in the agent's own will. Cicero notes that, unlike in his other philosophical works, an interruption prevented him from setting out both sides of the question in a single unbroken exposition.
la.cicero.de_finibus_bonorum_et_malorum: De Finibus Bonorum et Malorum is a philosophical dialogue in five books by Cicero, written in Latin prose during the Roman Republic. Its preface, addressed to Brutus, defends the treatment of Greek philosophy in Latin before the work turns to its central question, the highest good and the greatest evil. Successive books set out and examine the Epicurean, Stoic, and Academic answers to that question, with figures such as Torquatus, Cato, Piso, and Brutus among the speakers. The closing book weighs whether virtue alone or virtue combined with other goods suffices for the happy life.
la.cicero.de_inventione: De Inventione is a two-book Latin prose treatise on rhetoric by Cicero, belonging to the era of the Roman Republic. The work takes its name from inventio, the discovery of arguments, which it treats as the first of the orator's tasks; a preface debates whether eloquence has benefited humankind more than it has harmed it and recounts rhetoric's civilizing origins before turning to precepts. The first book defines the art, its office, end, material and parts, and sets out the doctrine of the issues of a case, while the second develops the treatment of proofs, the topics from which arguments are drawn, and the parts of the speech through the peroration.
la.cicero.de_officiis: De Officiis is a Latin philosophical treatise on moral duty, written by Cicero during the Roman Republic and cast as a letter of paternal counsel to his son Marcus, then studying philosophy under Cratippus at Athens. Composed in three books of continuous prose, it follows Stoic doctrine, and Panaetius above all, though avowedly with independent judgement, to define what an officium is and to distinguish ordinary from perfect duties. Cicero organises deliberation around three questions: whether an act is honourable, whether it is expedient, and how to decide when the honourable and the useful appear to conflict, offering precepts meant to govern conduct in public, private, forensic and domestic life.
la.cicero.de_optimo_genere_oratorum: De Optimo Genere Oratorum is a short Latin rhetorical treatise by Cicero of the Republican era. It argues that, unlike poetry, oratory admits no plurality of genera: there is a single perfect kind of orator, who instructs, delights, and moves his hearers, and differences among speakers are of degree rather than of kind. Cicero rejects the view that Attic style is confined to a plain manner, maintaining that grand, ornate, and copious speaking is equally Attic, and holds up Demosthenes as the supreme model. The treatise closes by announcing his Latin versions of the opposed speeches of Aeschines and Demosthenes, rendered, as he says, not as an interpreter but as an orator, preserving force and sense rather than translating word for word.
la.cicero.de_provinciis_consularibus: A prose oration by Cicero, addressed to the senate and dating from the Roman Republic, De Provinciis Consularibus takes up the question of which provinces the consular governors should hold. Cicero argues that Syria and Macedonia, occupied by Gabinius and Piso, are the provinces that must be reassigned, while the two Gallic provinces remain united under a single command. Much of the speech catalogues the misrule of the two governors in Macedonia, Greece and Byzantium, including ruined armies, extortion and the stripping of temples, all framed by Cicero's insistence that public advantage, not private grievance, guides his judgement.
la.cicero.epistulae_ad_familiares: Epistulae ad Familiares is a collection of Latin prose letters written by Marcus Tullius Cicero during the Roman Republic. It gathers correspondence addressed to a wide circle of friends, family members, and political associates, much of it reporting on public business such as senatorial debates, provincial commands, and the manoeuvres of figures like Pompey, alongside letters of recommendation and personal news. The letters are arranged in sixteen books.
la.cicero.letters_to_brutus: Latin prose letters by Cicero, the Roman orator and statesman of the late Republic, addressed to Marcus Junius Brutus. The correspondence belongs to the period of civil conflict after Caesar's death, and the surviving pieces discuss the war against Mark Antony and his kin, the campaigns of Dolabella, the deaths of the consuls Hirtius and Pansa, and the rising fortunes of the young Caesar. Alongside news of military and political events, the letters weigh senatorial decrees against open enemies and debate whether clemency or severity better serves the state.
la.cicero.letters_to_quintus: A collection of letters in Latin prose from Marcus Tullius Cicero to his brother Quintus, written during the Roman Republic. The opening letter, sent in Quintus's third year governing the province of Asia, offers fraternal counsel on provincial administration, urging personal incorruptibility amid the province's wealth, even-handed dealing between allied communities and Roman publicani, and careful oversight of legates and the quaestor. The remaining letters carry on the brothers' correspondence in the same direct epistolary manner.
la.cicero.lucullus: The Lucullus is the second book of Cicero's Academica, a Latin philosophical dialogue of the Roman Republic named for its principal speaker, L. Licinius Lucullus. It opens with a preface in Cicero's own voice praising Lucullus's military and civic career and defending the pursuit of philosophy by leading Romans, before turning to a debate on whether truth can be known: Lucullus expounds the teaching of Antiochus of Ascalon, who had broken with the skeptical Academy, while Cicero replies on behalf of the Academic practice of withholding assent. The discussion ranges over the criteria of truth, the reliability of the senses, and the nature of assent, with the disputation conducted on both sides of each question in the Academic manner.
la.cicero.orator: The Orator is a prose treatise on rhetoric by Cicero, written in Latin during the Roman Republic and addressed to Brutus, who had repeatedly asked its author which kind of eloquence he judged best and most perfect. It undertakes to fashion the figure of the ideal orator, a form that no single speaker may ever have fully embodied but that shines forth in parts among many, and it weighs the differing styles of the great Greek orators, above all Demosthenes. Drawing expressly on Plato's doctrine of ideas, it argues that copious and elevated speech cannot be achieved without philosophy, which aids the orator as the palaestra aids the performer.
la.cicero.paradoxa_stoicorum_ad_m_brutum: Paradoxa Stoicorum is a short prose philosophical treatise by Cicero of the late Roman Republic, addressed to Marcus Brutus and prompted by his admiration for Cato of Utica as a model Stoic. Writing in an ornate oratorical style rather than a technical one, Cicero sets out six Stoic doctrines counter to popular opinion, the so-called paradoxes, in order to show that they can be argued persuasively before a general audience: that virtue alone is good, that the virtuous man possesses all that is needed for a happy life, that all offences are equal, that all fools are mad, that only the wise man is free, and that only the wise man is truly rich. The section on the madness of fools survives only in part, with fragments of another paradox on the wise man as the sole true citizen, aimed at Clodius.
la.cicero.post_reditum_in_senatu: The Post Reditum in Senatu is a prose oration in which Cicero addresses the Roman senate upon his return from exile, offering formal thanks for the decrees and concerted efforts by which he, his brother, and his children were restored to their former standing. The speech celebrates the senate's constancy during his absence, singles out the consul P. Lentulus as the chief author of his recall, and praises figures such as Q. Metellus and Cn. Pompeius, while denouncing the tribunician obstruction and political violence that had sought to bar his return. Composed in the elaborate, highly balanced manner of a senatorial address of thanks, it belongs to the oratory of the late Republic.
la.cicero.pro_c_rabirio_postumo: A forensic oration by Cicero in defense of Gaius Rabirius Postumus, a wealthy Roman eques prosecuted under the Julian law on extortion after the condemnation of Aulus Gabinius, on the charge that money traced from Gabinius's conviction had reached him. Cicero recounts the family's tradition of public contracting and Rabirius's vast loans to the exiled Ptolemy of Alexandria, made in reliance on the king's expected restoration by the senate and Roman people. The speech then separates the defendant's affairs from the alleged corruption of the senate, disputes the novelty of the procedure 'quo ea pecunia pervenerit' against the prosecutor Memmius, and pleads that a man already ruined by fortune should not be crushed further.
la.cicero.pro_m_caelio: The Pro M. Caelio is a Latin forensic speech by Cicero of the Republican period, delivered in defence of Marcus Caelius Rufus, a young Roman of good standing accused by Atratinus. The speaker argues that the prosecution rests on slander rather than defined charges, defends Caelius' character, upbringing, and standing among his family and municipality, and answers the objection of familiarity with Catiline. Written in the prose of Republican oratory, the speech moves from an attack on the accusers' motives and methods to a sustained vindication of the defendant's conduct.
la.cicero.pro_marcello: A short Latin senatorial oration in which Cicero breaks a long public silence to thank Julius Caesar for pardoning and restoring Marcus Claudius Marcellus, the exiled former consul. Delivered evidently after Caesar's victory in the civil war, the speech first surveys and extols Caesar's military achievements, then argues that his clemency and moderation toward the defeated constitute a still greater title to glory. Cicero dwells on Caesar's victory over his own anger, the restoration of the noble Marcellus family, and the claim that Caesar, by sparing the vanquished, has in effect conquered victory itself.
la.cicero.pro_murena: Pro Murena is a forensic oration in Latin prose from the Roman Republic, in which Cicero, speaking as consul, defends Lucius Murena against a charge of electoral bribery. Murena had been declared consul at the comitia centuriata presided over by Cicero, and the speech opens with a formal prayer before turning to the objections of the prosecutors, among them Marcus Cato and Servius Sulpicius Rufus. Cicero, himself the author of the anti-bribery law, answers the charge that undertaking the defence is inconsistent with his office, addresses Cato's complaint that the man who expelled Catiline now pleads for leniency, and replies to Sulpicius's grievance at a friendship apparently slighted.
la.cicero.pro_rege_deiotaro: A forensic oration by Cicero of the late Roman Republic, addressed to Julius Caesar in defence of King Deiotarus, who stood accused of a capital offence, an alleged plot against Caesar's own life, tried before Caesar alone within his private house rather than in a public court. The speech opens with an exordium dwelling on the difficulties of the case: the novelty of a king facing a capital charge, accusers comprising the king's own grandson Castor and an enslaved informer, and the burden of pleading before the very man whose life the charge concerns. Cicero then appeals to Caesar's recorded clemency and hospitality towards Deiotarus and reviews the king's conduct in the civil war, his standing with the senate and Roman people, and his adherence to Pompey.
la.cicero.pro_s_roscio: An oration in Latin prose from the Roman Republic, delivered in court by Cicero in defence of Sextus Roscius, who stood accused of murdering his father. The exordium explains why Cicero, then young and new to public life, took up the cause when other distinguished orators present dared not speak, since any word about public affairs in such times would be reported as more than was said. The speech contends that the charge was contrived so that Lucius Cornelius Chrysogonus, who had bought the murdered man's vast estate from Sulla for a trifling sum, could keep it once the son was condemned and driven out. Cicero appeals to the judges to withstand the criminals' audacity, relieve the innocent man's peril, and treat the danger as one directed against them all.
la.cicero.pro_sestio: Pro Sestio is a forensic oration in Latin prose by Cicero, of the Roman Republic, defending Publius Sestius, a former tribune of the plebs who stands trial on charges touching his life, reputation, citizenship, and fortunes. The speaker takes over the case after the peroration of Quintus Hortensius, declaring that he pleads from piety and grief rather than eloquence, and surveys Sestius' parentage, marriage, domestic virtues, quaestorship under Gaius Antonius, and decisive action against an armed conspiracy at Capua. Throughout, the defence casts Sestius as one of the citizens who, together with the senate and all good men, raised the afflicted republic and freed it from domestic brigandage, while his enemies now seek through the courts and the judges' verdicts to destroy those whom violence and arson could not.
la.cicero.pro_sulla: A Latin prose oration by Cicero, dating from the era of the Roman Republic, in which the speaker pleads the defence of Publius Sulla on charges connected with the conspiracy. Addressing the judges, Cicero answers the objection of the prosecutor Lucius Torquatus that it was inconsistent for him, having given testimony against Autronius, now to defend Sulla, arguing that his appearance for the accused accords both with the severity he had shown in exposing the conspiracy and with the clemency long ascribed to him. He invokes the precedent of Hortensius and other leading citizens who likewise appeared for Sulla, and makes his own conduct, reputation, and sense of duty central to the plea.
la.cicero.pro_tullio: A Latin prose oration of the Roman Republic, attributed to Cicero, delivered before recuperatores on behalf of Marcus Tullius, a kinsman and namesake of the advocate, in an action for quadruple damages under the judicium de vi coactis armatisque hominibus. The opposing party is Publius Fabius, whose armed slave household is alleged to have inflicted damage on the plaintiff's farm in the territory of Thurii. The surviving portion opens with a reply to the admissions of the opposing advocate Lucius Quinctius and remarks on Fabius' character, then recounts the institution of the damages action by Manius Lucullus and begins a narrative of the disputed estate, its centuria Populiana, and the neighbouring property acquired by Fabius. The speech breaks off before its conclusion.
la.cicero.timaeus: A short Latin prose work of philosophy by Cicero, dating from the era of the Roman Republic, offering a version of the cosmogony expounded in Plato's Timaeus. A brief preface recalls learned discussions with P. Nigidius and the Peripatetic Cratippus before the discourse proper begins, treating the distinction between what is eternal and what comes to be, the divine craftsman who fashions the world upon an eternal exemplar, and the cosmos as a single intelligent animal. The account of the world's unity and generation proceeds only partway, and the work ends there incomplete.
la.cicero.tusculanae_disputationes: A Latin philosophical work by Cicero, written during the Roman Republic and framed as five books of disputations held at his Tusculan villa. The preface, addressed to Brutus, defends the exposition of Greek philosophy in Latin letters and recounts Cicero's return to study after release from forensic and senatorial labours. Each book poses a question and proceeds by question and answer in what the author calls the old Socratic method of arguing against an interlocutor's opinion. The successive books treat whether death is an evil, the bearing of pain, grief, the other disturbances of the soul, and whether virtue alone suffices for the happy life.
la.cicero_pseudo.in_sallustium: A short Latin prose invective directed against C. Sallustius Crispus, attributed to Cicero but of uncertain authorship and date, transmitted among the pseudo-Ciceronian works. Cast as a speech to the senate, it puts in Cicero's mouth a reply to Sallust's attacks on his character and career, answering charges about his age, eloquence, wealth, and withdrawal into exile, which the speaker justifies as yielding to a tribune's fury before a honored return. He defends his public conduct, cites his own verses 'cedant arma togae' and 'fortunatam me consule Romam', and throughout turns the accusations back upon Sallust's alleged depravity and servile way of life.
la.cicero_pseudo.pridie_quam_in_exilium_ire: A Latin prose oration transmitted under Cicero's name but of uncertain authorship, presenting itself as a speech delivered to the Roman people on the day before the speaker's departure into exile. Speaking as M. Tullius, the orator recounts how he crushed a conspiracy and saved his fellow citizens from fire and slaughter, and urges them to repay those benefactions by defending him, insisting that he is prosecuted not for wrongdoing but for the envy his virtue has aroused. He laments that no ally or city can now offer him refuge, asks to be allowed to remain in the state he preserved, and closes with reflections on the insecurity of all good men when one innocent citizen is brought down. The work is grouped with the oratory of the Republican era; its actual date and author are unknown.
la.claudian.de_bello_gildonico: A Late Antique Latin panegyric in hexameters by Claudian, celebrating the suppression of the revolt of Gildo, the African magnate whose seizure of the grain supply reduced Rome to famine. The opening depicts the empire reunited under a single ruler and the restored concord of the imperial brothers after the tyrant's defeat, followed by a supplication in which personified Roma pleads with Jupiter, lamenting her dependence on African grain now that Egypt's produce has been diverted to her eastern counterpart. The poem then moves toward an account of the war against Gildo, combining praise of the imperial house with rhetorical laments and epic description.
la.claudian.panegyricus_dictus_manlio_theod: A late antique Latin panegyric in hexameters by Claudian, composed in honour of Manlius Theodorus on his consulate. The poem opens with an address to the poet's muse Thalia amid an assembly of the Roman nobility, and an image of two eagles sent by Jupiter from east and west meeting on Parnassus. It then recounts Theodorus's precocious eloquence in the forum and his career as a judge and administrator, with service in Libya and Macedonia and authority extending over Spain, Germany and Britain, so that the empire's affairs are portrayed as directed by a single man. The consulship is presented as the crowning of honours earned by virtue rather than fortune.
la.claudianus_mamertus.de_statu_animae: De Statu Animae ('On the State of the Soul') is a Late Antique Latin prose treatise by Claudianus Mamertus. It is cast as answers to questions posed by a revered priest, chief among them how to reply to Arians who assert that the Son, as begotten, must be junior to the unbegotten Father. Against this it argues that genitus and ingenitus are appellations of relation rather than names of substance, so that the Son's generation entails neither temporal posteriority nor inferiority, since the divine majesty is distinguished by names but not ordered by degrees. The discussion then turns to whether God can be said to feel or suffer, contrasting human affections with what in God is virtue and nature, and reading scriptural passages that ascribe anger, repentance, eyes, ears, or hunger to God as accommodations of divine speech to human understanding.
la.claudianus_mamertus.epistolae: A late-antique Latin letter collection attributed to Claudianus Mamertus, prose in form and epistolary in genre. The surviving epistles deal with the obligations of learned friendship: the first reproaches a correspondent for long silence and for sharing his writings with others while withholding a promised rescript on the writer's own little books, and the second apologises for such delay in self-deprecating terms about its author's Latin style. The reply then celebrates the addressee's treatise on the state of the soul and his hymn, praising both through catalogues of Greek, Roman, and Christian authors.
la.commodianus.instructiones: The Instructiones of Commodianus, a Christian author of the later imperial period writing in Latin, consist of a long series of short theological chapters, preceded in the file by sigla for the manuscripts and early editions and by a list of contents. The chapters attack the classical gods one by one, Saturn, Jupiter, Mercury, Apollo, Bacchus, Hercules and the rest, then address pagans, judges, the wealthy and Jews, before turning to instruction for catechumens, the faithful, penitents, apostates, infants and soldiers, and closing with chapters on the Antichrist, the day of judgement and the resurrection. The work offers readers of intertexts a compact repertory of classical myth handled polemically and of biblical phrasing in later imperial Christian idiom.
la.couplet_et_alii.confucius_sinarum_philos: Confucius Sinarum Philosophus is a Latin prose work of uncertain date, ascribed to Couplet and other authors. It opens with a lengthy dedicatory epistle to Louis XIV of France, in which a speaker recently arrived from the far shores of China presents Confucius as the supreme sage of the Chinese, a master of moral and political philosophy whose words still govern their laws, magistracies and customs. The epistle imagines Confucius kneeling at the king's feet, acknowledging in Louis the perfect ruler whom his own books had portrayed in advance, and extols the king's piety, clemency and equity, above all his triumph over heresy in a France made thoroughly Christian.
la.cyprian.ad_quirinum_aut_testimoniorum_li: A Late Antique Latin prose treatise on theology attributed to Cyprian, known as Ad Quirinum or the three books of Testimonia, sets out an anthology of scriptural testimonies framed as an address to a correspondent named Quirinus. The preface explains the plan of the work: one book assembles evidence that the Jews fell from God's favour and forfeited the promises given and promised to them, their place being taken by Christians from all nations and the whole world who believe in the Lord, while another presents the mystery of Christ, who came as foretold in the scriptures and accomplished all things by which he was foreannounced. The material is arranged under numbered chapter headings, among them Jewish idolatry, unbelief in and killing of the prophets, blindness to the scriptures, and the supersession of the old circumcision, law, baptism, temple, sacrifice and priesthood, each followed by passages cited chiefly from the Old Testament, including Exodus, Deuteronomy, Judges, Jeremiah, Kings, Ezra and Malachi.
la.cyprian.de_bono_patientiae: A Late Antique Latin prose treatise on the virtue of patience, De Bono Patientiae is transmitted among the works of Cyprian. Addressed to 'fratres dilectissimi', it opens by observing that even the hearing of saving discourse requires patience, and argues that patience takes its origin and dignity from God, who endures human impiety and makes the sun rise and the rain fall on just and unjust alike. Against the philosophers, who profess a patience without knowledge of the patience of God, the treatise sets a Christian patience grounded in scripture, notably the gospel precept to love one's enemies and Pauline teaching on divine forbearance, and presents patience as the means by which believers imitate God the Father and manifest the divine likeness lost through Adam's sin.
la.cyprian.de_dominica_oratione: De dominica oratione is a late-antique Latin treatise on prayer by Cyprian. Opening from the premise that the gospel precepts are divine teachings and that the prayer taught by Christ himself is the truest and most spiritual form of petition, the work first treats the manner of prayer, urging modesty, quiet, and humility before God and illustrating the point with the silent prayer of Anna and the confession of the publican in the temple. It then expounds the Lord's Prayer petition by petition, laying particular stress on the prayer as a common and public act in which the whole people pray as one, since God is a teacher of peace and unity.
la.cyprian.de_habitu_virginum: A Latin prose treatise attributed to Cyprian, opening with a meditation on disciplina as the guardian of faith and the foundation of religion, supported by quotations from the Psalms, Solomon, Jeremiah, and Paul. Its principal concern, announced partway through, is the conduct of the virgins of the church, whom the author addresses with affection rather than authority. He urges those dedicated to Christ to perfect their vow of continence in spirit as well as body, arguing that virginity is compromised by elaborate dress, ornaments, and any desire to please others, and that a virgin should be recognisable as such in her whole manner of life.
la.cyprian.de_opere_et_eleemosynis: De Opere et Eleemosynis is a short Latin prose treatise of Late Antique theology transmitted under the name of Cyprian. Its argument is that although baptism grants forgiveness of sins once, God in his continued mercy has appointed almsgiving as a further remedy, so that the impurities contracted after the font may be washed away by works of mercy. In support of this teaching the author gathers authorities from both Old and New Testaments: Isaiah's command to break bread with the hungry, Solomon on alms lodged in the heart of the poor, the Psalms, Daniel's counsel to Nebuchadnezzar to redeem his sins by almsgiving, the angel Raphael's declaration that almsgiving delivers from death and purges sin, and Christ's saying in the Gospel that almsgiving makes all things clean. The treatise is framed as an exhortation addressed to the 'fratres dilectissimi', opening with an account of the divine benefits wrought through the Son's humiliation and death.
la.cyprian.de_unitate_ecclesiae_catholicae: A Latin prose treatise by Cyprian on the unity of the Catholic Church, framed as an exhortation addressed to the 'fratres dilectissimi'. It warns that the devil's most dangerous assault comes not through open persecution but through heresy and schism creeping under the very name of Christianity. Biblical proofs are then gathered for the Church's singleness, Christ's commission to Peter as the rock and holder of the keys, the Song of Songs' 'una est columba mea', and Paul's 'one body and one spirit', culminating in the declaration that the episcopate is one and indivisible, of which each bishop holds a part in its entirety. Figures of the sun's rays, a tree's branches, and streams flowing from a single fountain illustrate how a Church spread across the world yet preserves unity in its one origin.
la.cyprian.de_zelo_et_livore: A short Latin prose treatise on zeal and envy (De Zelo et Livore), attributed to Cyprian and belonging to the Christian theological literature of Late Antiquity. Cast as an exhortation to the 'fratres dilectissimi', it argues that envy is a hidden and deadly peril, since the devil, who first fell through envy, exploits it to assault chastity, honesty, and faith through both covert temptation and open persecution. The argument traces the vice from the devil's own fall through the biblical examples of Cain and Abel, Esau and Jacob, Joseph's brothers, Saul's persecution of David, and the Jews' rejection of Christ, before cataloguing the manifold evils that flow from envy, including hatred, avarice, ambition, pride, discord, and the resentment of bishops that leads to heresy and schism.
la.cyprian.quod_idola_dii_non_sint: Quod idola dii non sint is a short Latin prose treatise on theology, transmitted under the name of Cyprian and belonging to the late antique period. It argues that the gods whom the populace worships were once mortal men, kings and heroes deified after death, and it catalogues Greek and Roman divinities from Saturn, Jupiter and Hercules to the tutelary gods of Rome in order to trace their cults to human origins, contending further that empires rise and fall by chance rather than by religious observance. The closing chapters identify the pagan gods as unclean spirits lurking beneath statues and images, who inspire oracles, disturb bodies and minds, yet confess and depart when adjured by the true God.
la.cyprian_pseudo.de_iona: A short Latin work on the prophet Jonah, of uncertain date within the later imperial period, handed down under the name of Cyprian. It opens by recalling the fiery destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah and then turns to God's resolve to warn Nineveh through a prophet rather than destroy it at once. The narrative follows Jonah's flight by ship from Joppa toward Tarshish, the sudden storm, the sailors' labours and prayers to their gods, the casting of lots that identifies Jonah as the cause, and his confession that he flees from the God who made heaven and earth. It retells the biblical book of Jonah throughout, proceeding as far as the sailors' failed attempt to bring the ship back to land.
la.cyprian_pseudo.orationes: A short collection of Latin Christian prayers transmitted under the name of Cyprian, of uncertain authorship and date, composed in prose. The prayers address God through long strings of biblical epithets, God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, of the prophets, apostles, martyrs and virgins, and petition for purity of heart, integrity of conscience and protection from the snares of the devil. Their petitions are supported by a catalogue of deliverances from scripture, including Jonah, the three youths in the furnace, Daniel in the lions' den, Tobit and Sarah, Susanna and Hezekiah, alongside apostolic rescues such as Thecla in the flames and Peter on the waves, and they close with doxologies to Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
la.cyprian_saint.de_exhortatione_martyrii: A short Latin prose treatise by Cyprian, of the later Roman imperial period, addressed to a beloved correspondent named Fortunatus. Written as persecution looms with the approach of antichrist's time, it gathers scriptural testimony to prepare and strengthen believers for confession and martyrdom, casting the Christian life as spiritual combat against an ancient adversary, the devil. The material is arranged under numbered headings, beginning with the claim that idols are not gods and moving through God's threats against idolaters to the rewards promised to those who persevere in faith and persecution. The author explains that he deliberately provides the raw scriptural material, like wool and purple from the lamb, rather than a finished treatise, so that readers may fashion their own exhortation.
la.dracontius.orestes: A late antique Latin tragedy by Dracontius on the revenge of Orestes. After an invocation to Melpomene to sing the pious crime of Agamemnon's son, the poem recounts the king's homecoming from Troy, his unexpected reunion with Iphigenia serving as priestess of Diana among the Tauri, and his murder at Mycenae by Clytemnestra and Aegisthus. It then follows Orestes' vengeance on his mother and her lover, casting the matricide as both an impious deed and an act of filial piety.
la.ennodius.epigrammata: The Epigrammata of Ennodius is a Late Antique Latin collection of short poems on funerary, devotional, and encomiastic subjects. The pieces include epitaphs, notably for a young man cut down in his prime, verses of praise addressed to figures such as a Faustus and to bishops, and epigrams on death, chastity, and the Christian soul. A substantial sequence commemorates the rebuilding of a church of Lawrence after destruction by fire, treating the flames as a passage to a nobler structure. The poems move between classical epigrammatic forms and explicitly Christian themes.
la.eucherius_of_lyon.de_laude_heremi: De Laude Heremi is a brief Latin prose treatise on the merits of the desert and the eremitical life, written in Late Antiquity by Eucherius of Lyon. Cast as a letter, it opens by praising an addressee who renounced home, kindred, wealth, and even a beloved brother for the solitude of the wilderness, later returning to it despite elevation to episcopal rank. The body of the work celebrates the desert as a temple of God where divinity is found and revealed, arguing from scriptural exempla such as Moses at the burning bush, Elijah veiling his face, and the Israelites led through the wilderness by the pillar of cloud and fire and across the parted sea. The piece belongs to the genre of ascetic theology in prose.
la.eucherius_of_lyon.unknown: The Passio Agaunensium martyrum is a Late Antique Latin prose martyrological narrative by Eucherius of Lyon. It recounts the passion of the Theban Legion, six thousand six hundred soldiers summoned from the East to aid the emperor Maximian, colleague of Diocletian, who refused his command to persecute Christians and were decimated and put to death at Agaunum in the Alpine valley of the Rhone. The narrative describes the site of Agaunum, some sixty miles from Geneva and fourteen from Lake Geneva, names Maurice, Exuperius and Candidus as officers who encouraged the soldiers' constancy, and reproduces the legion's answer to Maximian declaring that they owed the emperor their military service but God their faith, and would rather die than kill the innocent.
la.eugippius.epistula_ad_probam_virginem: A short Latin prose letter of Late Antique date by Eugippius, addressed to the virgin Proba and written as the preface to his Excerpta, a collection of passages drawn from the works of Augustine. Eugippius explains that the collection was made at the prompting of Abbot Marinus and his fellow monks, defends the undertaking against possible charges of presumption, and praises Augustine as an eminent doctor of the catholic church. The letter also outlines the arrangement of the excerpts, which open and close with treatments of charity, and notes that each chapter identifies the Augustinian work from which its material is taken.
la.eugippius.exerpta_ex_operibus_augustini: A Late Antique prose florilegium of Latin theology, the Excerpta ex operibus Augustini assembles passages drawn from the works of Augustine under the name of Eugippius. The portion preserved here is a letter addressed to Jerome, in which Augustine asks how the apostle James's saying that whoever keeps the whole law but offends in one point becomes guilty of all is to be understood. The discussion ranges over the origin of the soul and the bond of sin from which even infants must be freed by the grace of Christ, and argues against the Stoic tenet that all sins are equal, distinguishing the inseparability of the virtues from an equality of sins, with Catiline's counterfeit fortitude among the examples weighed. The argument proceeds through the definition of virtue as caritas, the degrees of guilt attaching to lighter and graver offences, and the mercy that superabounds over judgment.
la.eugippius.vita_sancti_severini: The Vita Sancti Severini is a Latin prose hagiography of Late Antique date, by Eugippius, recounting the life and miracles of Saint Severinus. The narrative opens amid the confusion in Pannonia and the Danubian provinces after the death of Attila, and follows Severinus, a holy man from the East, as he settles at Asturis and moves among the towns of Noricum Ripense. Its episodes include his prophecy of the destruction of the contemptuous town of Asturis, the delivery of grain-bearing barges freed from the frozen Danube to relieve famine at Favianis, his rebuke of a widow hoarding stores, and the capture of brigands by unarmed soldiers emboldened by his prayers. Throughout, the work depicts Severinus as an ascetic and wonderworker whose fasting, almsgiving and intercession protect the Christian communities of a threatened frontier.
la.evagrius_monachus.altercatio_legis_inter: A late-antique Latin theological dialogue attributed to Evagrius Monachus, framed as a letter to the author's brother Valerius reporting a disputation on the Law held between Simon, a Jew, and Theophilus, a Christian. The debate turns chiefly on the divinity of Christ: Simon presses his objections from scripture, and Theophilus answers with a chain of biblical citations drawn from Deuteronomy, Isaiah, the Psalms, Genesis and the book of Joshua, interpreting them against Jewish objections and defending Christ as God and son of God. The exchange proceeds in rapid question-and-answer form and closes with the episode of the armed figure who appears to Joshua son of Nun by the Jordan.
la.evodius.de_fide_contra_manicheos: A short Latin theological treatise in prose, attributed to Evodius and of Late Antique date. It opens with a doxology confessing the one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and then argues that the Manichaean race of darkness cannot be ingenerate and coeternal with God, since scripture declares that God alone has immortality. Quoting from Mani's own 'Thesaurus' and 'Epistula Fundamenti', the work contends that evil is not a nature or substance but sin committed by the voluntary choice of the rational soul, concluding in defence of the free will of the soul against the Manichaeans.
la.faustus_of_riez.de_ratione_fidei: De Ratione Fidei is a short Latin theological treatise in prose by Faustus of Riez, a Late Antique author. Framed as a series of objections followed by responses, it answers those who read the Gospel saying 'the Father is greater than I' as proof that the Son is inferior in divinity. The argument distinguishes Christ's two nativities, eternal from the Father and temporal from the Virgin Mary, and gathers scriptural testimonies to his single person in two substances, divine and human, showing how he speaks now as man and now as God. A closing section defends the divinity of the Holy Spirit against those who pronounce him a creature or a ministerial being rather than God.
la.faustus_of_riez.de_spiritu_sancto_libri_: A two-book Latin prose treatise on the Holy Spirit by Faustus of Riez, a theological writer of late antiquity. Defending the Spirit's full divinity against the Macedonians, Faustus expounds the text of the creed and argues from prophetic and apostolic scripture that the Holy Spirit is God and creator, coequal with the Father and the Son, rather than a created being. His chapters treat, among other questions, the sense of believing 'in the Holy Spirit' as opposed to 'in the holy catholic church', the Spirit's part in Christ's conception, the Spirit as the finger of God and giver of the charisms of the perfect, and the fate of those who blaspheme against him.
la.faustus_of_riez.epistulae: A late antique Latin collection of prose letters under the name of Faustus of Riez. The opening letter, written to correct the error of an incautious brother, treats the relation between divine grace and human obedience and sets out a series of anathemas against positions attributed to Pelagius, including claims concerning predestination to death and the universality of Christ's death. It ends with the subscriptions of numerous bishops, followed by a reply in which the recipient makes a formal recantation, condemning a catalogue of doctrines on grace, free will, predestination, and the salvation of those who fall away after baptism.
la.favonius.disputatio_de_somnio_scipionis: A short Latin prose treatise of the later imperial period, the Disputatio de somnio Scipionis is a philosophical exposition of Cicero's Dream of Scipio by Favonius Eulogius, addressed to a correspondent styled a man of clarissimus rank. After arguing that Cicero composed the dream not as fabulous fiction, in the manner of Plato's tale of Er, but as a rational account of the soul's immortality and its celestial reward, the work turns to Pythagorean number doctrine, explaining the span of Scipio's life through arithmetical proportions. Its surviving portion defines number and then expounds the monad, dyad, and triad, illustrating the powers of each with cosmological, theological, metrical, and grammatical examples.
la.flavius_josephus.de_iudaeorum_vetustate_: An early Imperial prose treatise of historiographical and apologetic character by Flavius Josephus, addressed to Epaphroditus and presented as a sequel to his written account of Jewish antiquity. It defends the great age of the Jewish people against those who dismiss them as a nation of recent origin, answering the slanders of Apion and other detractors and citing Greek authors of repute as witnesses. The argument contrasts the longstanding records of the Egyptians, Chaldaeans and Phoenicians with the late and mutually contradictory historiography of the Greeks, whose writers from Cadmus of Miletus and Acusilaus of Argos down to Herodotus and Thucydides are shown to disagree among themselves.
la.fulcher_of_chartres.historia_hierosolymi: A medieval Latin prose chronicle by Fulcher of Chartres, the Historia Hierosolymitana records the deeds of the Franks who journeyed armed to Jerusalem in the years 1095 to 1127. It opens with the Council of Clermont and the appeal of Pope Urban II, then narrates the First Crusade and the subsequent fortunes of the Franks in Jerusalem, drawing on what the author saw with his own eyes on the expedition. The work continues with affairs of the Latin settlement and church of Jerusalem down to 1127, written throughout in historiographical prose.
la.gellius.attic_nights: The Attic Nights (Noctes Atticae) of Gellius is a Latin prose miscellany of the later imperial period, named in its preface for the long winter nights in the Attic countryside during which the author says he began composing it. Arranged without systematic order, it collects short notes and essays on grammar, rhetoric, philosophy, law, antiquities, and literary questions, excerpted promiscuously from Greek and Latin reading as an aid to the author's memory. The preface distinguishes the work from other miscellanies by both title and method, presenting its contents as brief admonitions for the already cultivated rather than thorough instruction, and excludes readers without leisure for learned reading.
la.giraldus_floriacensis.carmina: Carmina is a medieval Latin verse work of 754 lines attributed to Giraldus Floriacensis, whose byname points to the monastery of Fleury (Floriacum) on the Loire. The opening section recounts in verse the Lombard devastation of Italy and of Benedict's monastery at Monte Cassino, expressly referring readers to Gregory the Great's Dialogues for fuller details, before turning to the Frankish king Clovis son of Dagobert and Abbot Leodebodus, whose exchange of the royal estate of Floriacus enabled the founding of the abbey there. Blending hagiographic episode drawn from Gregory with an institutional foundation narrative centered on Fleury, the poem offers useful material for readers tracing the reception of the Dialogues and the motifs of monastic foundation poetry in medieval Latin verse.
la.godescalcus_saxus.carmina: The Carmina of Godescalcus Saxus constitute a modest corpus of medieval Latin verse, some 1,068 lines transmitted in two books, by a poet of the Carolingian period. The collection opens with an extended prayer to Christ for pardon, cleansing, and firmness of purpose, composed in rhymed, rhythmical lines whose diction is steeped in biblical and liturgical language. Readers of intertexts will find the poems useful as a witness to the shared vocabulary of Carolingian devotional poetry and hymnody, where scriptural phrasing and rhymed rhythms converge.
la.hilary_of_poitiers.fragmenta_minora: A brief collection of Latin prose fragments attributed to Hilary of Poitiers, the Late Antique Gallic bishop. The excerpts, introduced as quotations from his writings, deal chiefly with the incarnation, the Son of God made man and the man Christ exalted in glory, and include a passage said to come from a letter written to the emperor Constantius on the incarnation of the Lord. Further items expound the book of Job as an account of the devil's unceasing war against humanity, through which the faithful are purged, and explain the petition for daily bread in the Lord's Prayer as a request that Christ, the bread of life, dwell daily in the faithful. The remaining fragments are drawn from an exposition of the Gospel according to Matthew, from a comment on the Epistle to Timothy concerning Christ's twofold nature as mediator, and from a discussion of Christ's coming in the likeness of sinful flesh, in which the likeness of sin is distinguished from sin itself.
la.hilary_of_poitiers.hymni: A compact Latin collection of hymnic verse transmitted under the name of Hilary of Poitiers, the late-antique bishop whose Opera Feder printed at Vienna in 1916; it runs to only 141 lines. The hymns speak in the voice of a congregation at prayer, rehearsing Christ's eternal generation from the Father before the ages, his birth from the Virgin, his agency in creation, and his triumph on the cross. Their blend of Trinitarian doctrine, scriptural allusion (David as the first to proclaim Christ in song), and formulas such as light from light makes them a natural point of comparison for readers tracing Christological hymnody and credal phrasing in late-antique Latin.
la.hilary_of_poitiers.oratio_synodi_sardice: A short Latin prose oration attributed to Hilary of Poitiers and presented under the title of the address of the Council of Sardica to the emperor Constantius. The petition implores Constantius to relieve the persecutions afflicting the catholic church, to bar provincial judges from adjudicating clerical causes, and to recall bishops held in exile, denouncing the disseminators of Arian doctrine, among them the two Eusebii, Narcissus, Stephen, Acacius, Ursacius and Valens, and recalling Athanasius's absolution by the council. Its governing argument is that faith must be voluntary, since God desires willing confession rather than coerced worship, illustrated with scenes of imprisoned priests, chained congregations and consecrated virgins exposed to public view.
la.hilary_of_poitiers.tractatus_super_psalm: The Tractatus super Psalmos is a Latin prose work of theology from late antiquity by Hilary of Poitiers. Its opening section surveys divergent earlier opinions on the division of the psalter into five books and on the ascription of individual psalms to David, Solomon, Asaph, Idithun, the sons of Core and Moses, arguing from the Acts of the Apostles that the collection should be called the book of psalms rather than the psalms of David. The author likewise reports the tradition that Ezra gathered the psalms into a single volume after the captivity, and maintains that the prophecies of the psalms, sealed and closed to worldly understanding, must be interpreted of Christ's advent, incarnation, passion, kingdom and resurrection, as the seven-sealed book of the Apocalypse is opened by the key of David.
la.hilary_saint_bishop_of_poitiers.libri_tr: A Late Antique Latin prose compilation in three books against Valens and Ursacius, ascribed to Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers, gathering documents and narrative concerning the fourth-century controversies over the Nicene faith. Its contents include synodal letters and acts associated with the councils of Arles, Sardica, Milan, Ariminum and Seleucia, the creed of Nicaea and other credal formulas, letters of the emperor Constantius, of Liberius of Rome, of Valens, Ursacius and Germinius, and connecting narrative passages. The editorial tradition dates the composition in stages to 356, the winter of 359/360 and 367, and several sections survive in abbreviated form or with portions lost.
la.hilary_saint_bishop_of_poitiers.spuria: A Latin prose piece preserved among the spuria of Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, of uncertain date, its actual author unknown. It takes the form of a letter from a father to his daughter, recounting his long and difficult journey to a beautiful young man from whom he seeks an imperishable garment and a pearl of matchless worth to bring back to her. The young man grants the gifts on condition that the daughter refuse dyed, silk, and gilded clothing and all ordinary jewels, describing the garment as never consumed, worn, soiled, or torn, and the pearl as granting freedom from sickness, age, and death. The letter closes with the father's exhortation, together with scripted replies, whereby the daughter is to reject silk, purple, and gold and any pearl offered for neck or finger while awaiting these heavenly gifts.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.vita_mariae_aegypt: A medieval Latin verse life of Saint Mary of Egypt, attributed to Hildebert of Lavardin. The opening lines trace the ascetic career of the monk Zosimas, whose growing renown draws crowds of admirers until a mysterious voice warns him that no victory can be presumed before the end and sends him to a community of monks by the Jordan. The poem then follows the traditional legend of Mary the Egyptian, recounting her repentance and long penance as a solitary in the desert beyond the river, and her encounter with Zosimas, through whom her hidden sanctity is revealed.
la.italicus.ilias_latina: The Ilias Latina is a Latin epic in hexameters from the early imperial period, attributed to Italicus. It presents a compact Latin retelling of Homer's Iliad, opening with an invocation of the Muse for the wrath of the proud son of Peleus. The narrative runs from the quarrel between Agamemnon and Achilles and the plague sent by Apollo through the principal events of the war at Troy, closing with the death and funeral of Hector.
la.john_cassian.conlationes: The Conlationes of John Cassian is a Late Antique Latin work of monastic theology. Its preface, addressed to Leontius and Helladius, explains that the ten conferences were promised to Bishop Castor as a sequel to the twelve books on cenobitic institutions and the remedies for the eight principal vices, and were dedicated to Leontius and Helladius after Castor's death. The work then reports, largely in dialogue form, the teaching of the elders of the desert of Scetis, beginning with Abba Moses on the goal and end (scopos and telos) of the monastic life, as transmitted by Cassian and his companion Germanus, moving from outward discipline to the inward purity and unceasing prayer of the 'inner man'.
la.john_cassian.de_incarnatione_domini_cont: De Incarnatione Domini contra Nestorium is a Latin prose treatise of Late Antique date by John Cassian, composed at the entreaty of Leo, a deacon of the Roman church whose praise and importunity fill the preface. The work is a polemic against the recently arisen Nestorian heresy, which the author introduces under an extended image of heresy as a hydra whose severed heads regrow. It first catalogues earlier Christological errors, those of the Ebionites, Sabellians, Arians, Eunomians, Macedonians, Photinians and Apollinarians, before turning to the contemporary error, of uncertain name but sprung from the old Ebionite stock, that the title identifies with Nestorius.
la.john_cassian.institutiones: The Institutiones of John Cassian is a Late Antique Latin prose treatise on monastic theology, framed as a dedicatory address to Castor, whom the author urges to found monasteries in Gaul on the pattern of Eastern practice. Cassian sets out the customary observances of the monasteries of Egypt and Palestine as handed on by the elder monks, deliberately passing over accounts of marvels in favour of instruction in the perfected life. The work proceeds to an examination of the eight principal vices as designated by the Egyptian fathers, treating their origins, causes, and methods of cure.
la.lactantius.de_ira_dei: De Ira Dei is a Latin prose treatise on theology by Lactantius, a Christian writer of the Late Antique era, framed as an address to one Donatus. It takes issue with the philosophers who deny that the supreme god can be angry, arguing that divine beneficence and divine wrath must stand or fall together. The opening criticises the pretensions of human wisdom, invoking Socrates' professed ignorance, and presents the work as a supplement to the author's Divinae Institutiones, whose second and fourth books it cites. Lactantius then lays out a fourfold partition of possible positions on whether anger and favour may be ascribed to God, and proceeds to test each in turn.
la.lactantius.de_mortibus_persecutorum: De Mortibus Persecutorum is a Late Antique Latin prose work of Christian theology attributed to Lactantius, cast as a letter of consolation and instruction to a correspondent named Donatus. It sets out to record how divine justice punished the persecutors of the church from its foundation onward, opening with Nero's crucifixion of Peter and killing of Paul and proceeding through Domitian, Decius, and Valerian, each of whom meets ruin or disgrace as recompense for hostility to God. The preface celebrates the recent collapse of tyrannical rulers and the restoration of the church after a period of violent persecution, and announces the work's purpose of documenting the penalties heaven's judgment has inflicted upon the enemies of the Christian name.
la.lactantius.de_opificio_dei: De Opificio Dei ('On the Workmanship of God') is a Latin prose treatise on theology by the Late Antique Christian author Lactantius, addressed to a correspondent named Demetrianus. It opens with an admonition to the addressee to treat worldly prosperity as fleeting and deceptive, before the author undertakes to set out the make-up of body and soul, a subject he judges to have been handled too summarily in Cicero's philosophical writings. The main argument reads the structure and functions of the human body, from the senses and organs to speech and upright bearing, together with the rational soul, as evidence of the providence and skill of the divine maker, contrasting man's naked and unarmed condition with the natural defences granted to other animals.
la.lactantius.divinarum_institutionum: Lactantius's Divinarum Institutionum is a Late Antique Latin prose treatise of Christian apologetic theology, arguing that true religion and divine wisdom are attainable through God's revelation rather than through human philosophy. Its prologue announces seven books devoted to religion and divine matters, intended to direct the learned to true wisdom and the unlearned to true religion, against pagan superstition and the discordant schools of philosophy. The author, who records a long career teaching rhetoric, presents the work as a worthier successor to that profession, turning eloquence to the defence of truth on questions of God, worship, salvation and immortality.
la.lucifer_bishop_of_cagliari.de_non_conven: De non conveniendo cum haereticis is a short Latin prose treatise of Late Antique date, attributed to Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, and belonging to the genre of polemical theology. Cast as a reply to an opponent who had accused the author and his sympathisers of being enemies of peace, unity and brotherly love, it argues that Christians must refuse all communion and peaceful dealings with heretics, in particular with Arians and their pseudo-bishops. The case is built almost entirely from scriptural exempla: Moses pitching the tabernacle outside the camp, the rebellion of Core, Dathan and Abiron, the Deuteronomic bans on covenant and intermarriage with foreign peoples, and the fall of Jericho, where only Rahab and her household were spared.
la.lucifer_bishop_of_cagliari.de_non_parcen: A late-antique Latin theological polemic by Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, De non parcendo in deum delinquentibus ('On not sparing those who sin against God') is addressed to the emperor Constantius, who has accused the author of insolence and contumacy for rebuking him. Lucifer defends his censure by assembling scriptural precedents for severity toward idolatry: Moses' slaughter of the worshippers of the golden calf, Phinehas' killing of the idolater in the assembly, and the Deuteronomic command that a prophet, kinsman, or friend who entices others to serve foreign gods must be put to death. These exempla are turned against the emperor's acceptance of Arian doctrine, which the treatise terms idolatry, and it closes on the Johannine dictum that whoever denies the Son does not have the Father.
la.lucifer_bishop_of_cagliari.epistulae: A brief Latin correspondence associated with Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, a late-antique opponent of Arianism. It gathers letters written both to and from Lucifer, including exchanges with the bishops Eusebius and Liberius, with Florentius, and with Athanasius. The letters concern the Arian controversy under the emperor Constantius, treating the persecution and exile of orthodox clergy, steadfast confession of the catholic faith against Arian doctrine, and requests for news and mutual support among the confessors.
la.lucifer_bishop_of_cagliari.moriendum_ess: A Latin prose invective by Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, addressed to the emperor Constantius in the heat of the fourth-century Arian controversy.
