The work upbraids the emperor as a persecutor and heretic for his alliance with the Arians and for the torture and killing of Christians who refuse to deny the Son of God, recalling his victims in Alexandria and elsewhere as martyrs. In direct second-person address it urges the faithful to stand firm in the confession of faith, arguing from scriptural authorities, among them the Hebrew youths in the fiery furnace, the Psalmist on the death of the saints, and the apostolic writings, that death endured for Christ brings not destruction but eternal reward.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.ennodius_ambrosio_: A late antique Latin paraenetic treatise by Magnus Felix Ennodius, composed in prose with interspersed verse and addressed to an Ambrose, who is said to have repeatedly begged for a page of didascalic instruction. The work urges devotion to God, love of neighbour, and cultivation of the virtues, presenting Verecundia (Modesty), Pudicitia (Chastity), and Fides (Faith) as personified speakers who each admonish the addressee. It then turns to the liberal studies, assigning speeches to Grammar and to Rhetoric and alternating exhortatory prose with short verses uttered by the personified figures.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.libellus_adversus_: A short Latin prose treatise by the late-antique author Magnus Felix Ennodius, written against unnamed opponents who had attacked the decisions of a synod. The work defends the Roman pontiff and his bishops, rebutting objections that not all priests had been summoned to the council and that a royal command could not oblige the pope to convoke one. It opens with an elaborate apology for the necessity of speaking before turning to point-by-point invective against the accused schismatics.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.panegyricus_theodo: A late-antique Latin prose panegyric addressed to King Theodoric, composed by Magnus Felix Ennodius. The speaker begins with disclaimers about the inadequacy of human praise before celebrating an unbroken series of victories, in which no enemy or terrain resisted the king, and conquests reaching from the cold of Scythia to Meroe and the heat of the tropics. A further section recounts the king's upbringing in Greek lands and his youth, when he confronted a usurper who had seized the palace and restored the sceptre to a fugitive ruler whose safety was in doubt.
la.maximianus.elegiae: The Elegiae is a collection of Latin elegies in elegiac couplets from the late antique period, attributed to the poet Maximianus. The poems are spoken in the first person by an old man who opens by begging senescence to hasten his end and pronouncing death a rest after life has become a punishment. The speaker contrasts his present bodily decay with recollections of youthful attainment as orator, poet, athlete, and lover, and recalls how he dwelt among the maidens of Rome while refusing all marriage. The collection dwells throughout on the failing body, the loss of youthful powers, and the persistence of desire in old age.
la.milo_of_saint_amand.carminum_appendix: A Carolingian Latin collection of 221 lines attributed to Milo of Saint-Amand, the 'Carminum Appendix' gathers dedicatory and colophon verses, an account of the shrine of Saint Amandus, epitaphs for the abbey's sacristan Lotharius, its abbots, and an epitaph of the poet Milo himself, closing with a rhythmic hymn to the saint. The opening lines record that Lotharius had the book written for the honour and praise of the Lord, and the poems commemorate those who enriched the church's structures, relics, and library. The verses combine inscriptional and funerary forms with scriptural and hagiographic diction in varied patterns of verse. Readers hunting intertexts will find here the conventional formulas of the Carolingian scribe's colophon and tomb poetry, echoes of the Psalms and classical idiom, and hagiographic praise diction characteristic of the Saint-Amand milieu.
la.optatus_saint_bishop_of_mileve.appendix_: The Appendix of Ten Ancient Documents is a dossier of official records and letters transmitted with the seven anti-Donatist books of Optatus, bishop of Mileve in Late Antique North Africa. It collects, as its heading enumerates, the proceedings held before the consularis Zenophilus concerning the traditor Silvanus, the acta of the purgation of bishop Felix under the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian, several letters of Constantine addressed to African officials and to the Catholic and Donatist bishops, the letter of the Council of Arles to Pope Sylvester, and a letter of the praetorian prefect Petronius. The records describe the seizure of scriptural codices and church plate, the requisitioning of church buildings, and the imperial attempts to adjudicate the dispute dividing the African church.
la.ovid.amores: The Amores is a collection of love elegies in elegiac couplets by the Augustan poet Ovid, preserved in three books. The poems follow a male speaker through the progress of an erotic affair, from its involuntary onset under Cupid's arrows to scenes of seduction, reproach, jealousy and separation, together with mythological and aetiological set pieces. A programmatic poem declares that the work once ran to five books before the author reduced it to three, and recounts how Cupid stole a foot from the poet's hexameter, announcing the mock-epic wit that runs through the collection.
la.paulus_orosius.historiae_adversum_pagano: The Historiae adversum paganos of Paulus Orosius is a Latin prose universal history in seven books, written in Late Antiquity at the prompting of Augustine, to whom the opening letter is addressed. Composed to answer pagans who blamed the miseries of the present age on the abandonment of the old gods, it gathers from the surviving historians and annalists an account of wars, plagues, famines, earthquakes, floods, fires, and other calamities, arguing that such sufferings were at least as grave before the coming of Christianity. The narrative runs from Adam and the reign of Ninus through the empires of the ancient world to the birth of Christ under Augustus and onward to the author's own times.
la.petronius.fragmenta: The Fragmenta attributed to Petronius, an early Imperial writer associated with satire, collect short poems in mixed meters that survive outside the author's main works. Their subjects include the vulture as an image of envy, nature's varied means of producing offspring, the origin of the gods in human fear, the impossibility of keeping secrets, the unreliability of the senses, dreams as self-made fictions, and an Indian bird that has exchanged barbarian speech for Latin. The pieces are brief and fragmentary, and their original settings within Petronius' satirical output cannot be recovered.
la.plautus.aulularia: A Latin comedy of the Roman Republic by Plautus, composed in dramatic meter, whose prologue is spoken by the Lar familiaris, the household god of Euclio's family. The Lar explains that a hoard of gold was buried beneath the hearth by Euclio's grandfather and entrusted to his keeping, and that he has now arranged for the miser Euclio to find it, so that his daughter, seduced by a young man of high standing during the nocturnal rites of Ceres, may be dowered and married. The opening scenes show Euclio driving his old serving-woman from the house so that he can inspect the treasure unseen, while she laments his nightly vigils, seclusion, and violent temper.
la.plautus.captivi: Captivi (The Captives) is a comedy in dramatic verse by Plautus, the Latin playwright of the Roman Republican period. Its prologue lays out the plot: Hegio of Aetolia, whose younger son was kidnapped and sold into slavery in Elis and whose elder son has been taken prisoner in the war between the Aetolians and the Eleians, buys captives in the hope of arranging an exchange, whereupon the Eleian prisoner Philocrates and his slave Tyndarus swap names and clothing so that master and servant may each serve the other's hidden designs. The prologue also notes that the play departs from comic convention by omitting such stock figures as the brothel-keeper, the wicked courtesan, and the boastful soldier, and by keeping its battles offstage.
la.plautus.casina: Casina is a comedy in Latin by Plautus, composed for the Roman stage during the Republican period and written in dramatic metres. The prologue states that the play reworks a Greek comedy by Diphilus, called Clerumenoe in Greek and Sortientes in Latin, and sets out the situation: Casina, a girl exposed as an infant and raised as a slave in the household, is desired by both the old master and his son, while the wife, siding with her son, guards against her husband's designs. The action turns on the rival marriage schemes, the father betroths Casina to his bailiff, the son to his own attendant, and culminates in the farce surrounding the wedding preparations.
la.plautus.mercator: Mercator is a Latin comedy by Plautus, a fabula palliata of the Roman Republican period written in dramatic metres. Its prologue identifies the play as the Latin Mercator, adapted from Philemon's Greek Emporos, and dwells at length on the miseries that attend lovers before turning to the story. The opening exposition recounts a young man sent by his father to trade at Rhodes, where he has fallen in love with a woman of exceptional beauty, and the conflict with his father provoked by his spendthrift passion; the play then develops the complications of the affair.
la.plautus.persa: Persa is a Latin comedy by Plautus, a playwright of the Roman Republic, composed in dramatic meters in the tradition of the fabula palliata. The play opens with a monologue weighing a poor lover's torments against the labors of Hercules, then follows the slave Toxilus and the parasite Sagaristio as they scheme to raise money to free the woman Toxilus loves. The plot turns on an elaborate deception involving a disguise as a Persian envoy, from which the play takes its title, and draws on the stock figures of slave, parasite, and pimp that populate Plautine comedy.
la.plautus.poenulus: Poenulus is a Latin comedy of the Roman Republic by Titus Maccius Plautus, written in dramatic meter. Its prologue, spoken by an actor styled imperator histricus, parodies a general's edict in a set of comic regulations for the spectators before sketching the plot's background: two wealthy Carthaginian cousins, the death of one, and the abduction of his seven-year-old son, who is carried off to Calydon, sold to a rich old man eager for heirs and hostile to women, and adopted as that man's heir. The main action follows the elderly Carthaginian merchant Hanno, who arrives in Calydon searching for his lost children and comes to recognize the stolen son as his own. The prologue gives the play the alternative title Carchedonius, 'the Carthaginian,' by which it is also known.
la.plautus.pseudolus: A Latin comedy by Plautus of the Roman Republican period, written in dramatic meter and named for its leading figure, the slave Pseudolus. The opening scene presents Pseudolus promising his young master Calidorus aid by deed, effort, or good counsel as Calidorus laments over a letter from his beloved, the courtesan Phoenicium. In the letter Phoenicium reports that her owner has sold her to a Macedonian soldier for twenty minae, fifteen already paid, and that she is to be delivered when a token matching the soldier's ring-seal is presented, the day having been set for the Dionysia. The action proceeds from Pseudolus's efforts to defeat the transaction before that deadline.
la.plautus.rudens: The Rudens ('The Rope') is a Latin comedy by Plautus, a dramatist of the Roman Republic, surviving in some 1,428 lines of dramatic verse and printed here from F. Leo's 1895 edition. Its prologue, spoken by the star Arcturus, opens a tale set on the coast of Cyrene: a pimp carries off a kidnapped Athenian girl by sea, but a storm wrecks the ship and washes her and her companion ashore near the villa of the exile Daemones, leading to rescue and recognition. The prologue names the Greek poet Diphilus as the source of the plot. Readers of intertexts will find here a compact assembly of comic stock types, a shipwreck-and-recognition sequence of lasting influence, and meditations on perjury and divine justice that later comedy repeatedly echoes.
la.plautus.trinummus: Trinummus is a Latin comedy by Plautus of the Republican period, written in dramatic meter. Its prologue is delivered by the personified figure Luxuria, who announces that the play adapts Philemon's Greek Thēsauros under a new Latin title, and who introduces her daughter Inopia and the young man who, with Luxuria's aid, has squandered his father's estate. The prologue leaves the full argument to the old men who arrive in the opening scene, where two friends, Megaronides and Callicles, begin the action with a reproachful exchange.
la.pliny_the_elder.naturalis_historia: The Naturalis Historia of Pliny the Elder is a Latin prose encyclopaedia of the natural world, composed in the Early Imperial period. Its thirty-seven books proceed from cosmology, astronomy and geography through animals, plants and trees to medicine, agriculture, metals, minerals and works of art, drawing together material from a large body of earlier Greek and Roman writers. The work opens with a dedicatory preface to the emperor, in which the author sets out his sources, method and purpose before the technical exposition begins.
la.pontius_diaconus.vita_caecilii_cypriani: A Later Imperial Latin prose composition by Pontius, a deacon, presenting the life of Caecilius Cyprianus, bishop and martyr. The author, protesting his own inadequacy before so grand a subject, recounts Cyprian's conversion and heavenly birth of faith, his immediate ordination despite the apostolic rule against advancing neophytes, his renunciation of wealth and lavish almsgiving, and the charity of his household, leading toward the account of his passion. Written in a highly rhetorical style, the work frames the bishop's deeds as an enduring example of faith handed on to posterity.
la.priscian.carmen_in_laudem_Anastasii_impe: A Late Antique Latin panegyric by Priscian, the Carmen in Laudem Anastasii Imperatoris praises the emperor Anastasius. The speaker opens by renouncing the flattery customary in poems in praise of rulers and promises to say nothing false, before celebrating Anastasius's justice, wisdom, clemency, and piety. The poem credits the emperor with the defeat of the Isaurians, whose tyrants had spread violence and overturned the laws, and measures him against earlier rulers including Nerva, Titus, Trajan, Antoninus, and Marcus, as well as against Pompey. Divine providence, the restoration of justice after a period of oppression, and the emperor's devotion to God run throughout the work.
la.priscillian.tractatus_undecim: A Late Antique Latin prose work of theology attributed to Priscillian, the Tractatus Undecim ('Eleven Tractates') survives in a critical edition of the surviving corpus. The opening tractate is a confession of faith addressed to 'beatissimi sacerdotes', in which the author affirms belief in one God and in Christ as God, recounts his conversion from a secular past to baptism, and proceeds to anathematize a long catalogue of heresies, including Patripassian, Novatian, Nicolaitan, Ophite, and Manichaean teachings. The argument rests on dense quotation of the Law, prophets, Gospels, Apocalypse, and apostolic writings, which the author reads parabolically, treating figures of beasts, idols, dragons, and celestial bodies as symbols of vices and demonic error rather than as literal claims. The work closes with a plea that the bishops who receive this account of his faith judge him by his confession and absolve him from slander.
la.priscillian_bishop_of_avila.canones_in_p: The Canones in Pauli Apostoli Epistulas is a Latin prose theological treatise of Late Antique date attributed to Priscillian, bishop of Avila. It opens with a covering letter explaining its design: to furnish compact scriptural proofs against heretics by extracting brief doctrinal statements (canones) from the fourteen Pauline epistles and marking each testimony in the epistle text with a system of numbers. There follow some ninety numbered canons, each setting out a doctrinal position, on the veracity of God, the two spirits, the two wisdoms, the works of darkness, the incarnation and person of Christ, and the foundation of apostolic faith, under which verse references are listed from Romans, the two Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Thessalonians, Timothy, Titus, and Hebrews.
la.proba_active_4th_century.cento: A Late Antique Latin epic cento by Proba, a Christian poetess active in the fourth century, prefaced by a dedicatory address to one Arcadius that asks him to preserve the poem and hand it on to his descendants. Composed of lines and phrases drawn from the poems of Vergil, as the author's own preface declares, the work renounces war, triumph, and pagan fable in order to sing the gifts of Christ. Its narrative runs from the creation of the world and the fall of man through the murder of Abel, the spread of wickedness, and the flood, before turning to the prophecies, birth, baptism, temptation, miracles, passion, resurrection, and ascension of Christ. It closes with an injunction to celebrate the risen Lord in an annual observance.
la.pseudo_cyprian.ad_novatianum: Ad Novatianum is a short Latin prose treatise transmitted under Cyprian's name and attributed to an anonymous author of uncertain date. It is a polemic against Novatian and his followers, attacking their denial of penance and reconciliation to the lapsed, whom the author defends as brothers wounded by the devil rather than by their own will. The argument insists on the unity of the church as the sole ark of salvation and closes with an allegorical reading of Noah's raven and dove as figures, respectively, of apostates beyond return and of the church's sacrament of baptism. The style is impassioned and densely scriptural, stringing together proof texts from the gospels, the prophets, and the Apocalypse.
la.pseudo_cyprian.ad_vigilium_de_iudaica_in: Ad Vigilium de Iudaica Incredulitate is a brief Latin prose treatise of later imperial date, transmitted under Cyprian's name but of uncertain authorship, addressed to a correspondent named Vigilius on the subject of Jewish unbelief. The author dwells on the hardness of heart by which the Jewish people persist in rejecting Christ, arguing that his coming was openly foretold by the prophets and manifested in the Gospel episodes of the magi, Simeon in the temple, and the lament over Jerusalem, and that such continued incredulity is therefore without excuse. The work belongs to the genre of Christian anti-Jewish apologetic theology written in the rhetorical manner associated with Cyprian's circle.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_disciplina_et_bono_pud: De Disciplina et Bono Pudicitiae is a later-imperial Latin prose treatise on discipline and the good of chastity, transmitted under the name of Cyprian though of uncertain authorship. Written in the voice of a bishop exhorting his flock, it opens by weighing the duties of episcopal teaching and prayer before urging the faithful to hold fast the strongholds of pudicitia. The work ranks chastity among virgins, the continent, and the married, sets forth its praises in a cascade of definitions, and argues from scripture that husband and wife owe each other mutual love and fidelity. A final invective portrays impudicitia as the enemy of continence, corrupting bodies, households, and lineage alike.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_laude_martyrii: The De laude martyrii is a short Latin prose treatise in praise of martyrdom, transmitted under the name of Pseudo-Cyprian among works attributed to Cyprian of Carthage and of uncertain date in the later imperial period. It opens with an apology for the inadequacy of human eloquence before so great a subject, then proposes to treat three questions: what martyrdom is, how great it is, and of what benefit. Martyrdom is defined as the end of sin, the termination of peril, and the guide of salvation, while the tract dwells on the confessor who stands unmoved under torture, sustained by the thought that Christ himself suffers in him. It closes by celebrating the passion and death of Christ as the model by which mortal human beings are made immortal and the martyr's crown is won.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_rebaptismate: The De Rebaptismate is a short Latin prose treatise on a question of church discipline, transmitted under Cyprian's name and of uncertain authorship, belonging to the later imperial period. It asks whether persons baptized among heretics in the name of Christ, on returning penitently to the church, ought to be baptized again, or whether imposition of the bishop's hands for the receiving of the Holy Spirit suffices, and it defends the oldest ecclesiastical custom against innovation and controversy. The remainder gathers the relevant passages of scripture bearing on baptism, beginning with the preaching of John the Baptist and the apostolic testimony in Acts, in order to set out the salutary and pacific form of practice in the church.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_spectaculis_liber: A short Latin prose treatise of uncertain date, transmitted under the name of Cyprian and cast in the form of an exhortatory letter to fellow Christians. It argues that the games of the circus, theatre and arena are inseparable from idolatry, since every spectacle originates in sacrifice to a deity, and that the silence of Scripture on such entertainments amounts to prohibition rather than permission. Apparent biblical precedents for music, dancing and athletic imagery are answered one by one, and the obscenity of the stage, the cruelty of beast-hunts and the vanity of partisan enthusiasm for charioteers are catalogued as inventions of the devil.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_xii_abusionibus_saecul: The De XII Abusionibus Saeculi is a short Latin prose treatise on Christian morality, transmitted under the name of Cyprian of Carthage but of uncertain authorship, and belonging to the later imperial era. An opening catalogue lists the twelve abuses of the world, the wise man without works, the old man without religion, the youth without obedience, the rich man without almsgiving, the woman without chastity, the master without virtue, the contentious Christian, the proud pauper, the unjust king, the negligent bishop, the people without discipline, and the people without law, through which, it declares, the wheel of the world is turned towards the darkness of hell. Each abuse is then expounded in turn with moral exhortation and scriptural argument, citing Gospel sayings and Old Testament examples such as Solomon's transgression and Moses' fourfold account of the kinds of fathers.
la.pseudo_cyprian.epistulae: A Latin collection of four epistolary pieces transmitted under the name of Cyprian and of uncertain date, classed among the pseudo-Cyprianic works of the later imperial period. The letters concern scriptural reading and ecclesiastical discipline: one urges a correspondent to strengthen himself in the divine reading, another condemns writings against the catholic faith that impugn true baptism in the rebaptism controversy, a third reports conciliar rulings on traditores who had surrendered the scriptures, and the longest consoles a bereaved father for his daughter's death, drawing on Job and the raising of Lazarus to argue that Christian hope excludes immoderate grief.
la.pseudo_cyprian.liber_de_aleatoribus: The Liber de Aleatoribus is a Latin prose treatise of the later imperial period, transmitted under Cyprian's name though of uncertain authorship. Writing in the voice of a bishop addressing the faithful, the author invokes the episcopal power to bind and to loose, gathers scriptural injunctions to pastoral vigilance, and argues that shepherds who persistently pardon delinquent brothers incur guilt themselves. The greater part of the work is an invective against dice-playing, portrayed as a snare of the devil that breeds perjury, discord, and the squandering of inherited wealth, and ends with an account of gamblers' nocturnal revels, where the sin of gaming is joined to sexual transgression.
la.pseudo_eucherius.de_situ_hierusolimitana: A brief late antique Latin prose work, attributed to Eucherius, describing the situation of Jerusalem and of Judaea itself, framed as a letter from the bishop Eucherius to a priest named Faustus. It surveys the site and circuit of the city under its name Aelia, its gates and hills, and the principal holy places, including the Martyrium built by Constantine, Golgotha and the Anastasis, together with Mount Sion, the ruins of the Temple, the pool of Bethsaida, the spring of Siloa and the valley of Josaphat. It then records the position and distances of surrounding places such as Bethlehem, Jericho, the Jordan, Chebron and Joppa, gives the dimensions of Judaea from Dan to Bersabee, and closes with a lengthy quotation from a letter of Jerome to Dardanus on the extent of the promised land.
la.pseudo_severus_sulpicius.epistolae_septe: Seven Latin prose letters transmitted under the name of Sulpicius Severus and of uncertain date, belonging to late antique theological and ascetic literature. Addressed to a female correspondent, the letters exhort perseverance in the Christian life, warning against relapse into sin, the ambushes of the devil, and any turning back once the hand is set to the plough. One passage envisages the last judgement, in which Noah, Abraham, Moses, David and Isaiah refute the excuses of the damned, who plead that they received no law, prophets or preachers.
la.pseudo_tertullian.adversus_omnes_haerese: Adversus Omnes Haereses is a short Latin treatise on heresies transmitted among the works of Tertullian but attributed to an anonymous author, whose date and identity are uncertain. In compressed prose it runs from the Jewish sects, Dositheus, the Sadducees, the Pharisees, the Herodians, through Simon Magus, Menander, Saturninus, Basilides, the Nicolaitans, the Ophites, the Cainites, and the Sethians, summarizing each group's doctrines of God, creation, Christ, and the resurrection of the flesh. The treatment is chiefly expository, setting out the teachings under survey rather than refuting them at length, and it closes with the Sethian account of the pure seed of Seth preserved through the flood.
la.pseudo_victor_vitensis.passio_septem_mon: A short late-antique Latin passio in prose, preserved under the name of Victor of Vita (Pseudo-Victor Vitensis), narrating the martyrdom of seven monks during the persecution of African Catholics under the Vandal king Huneric, which the narrative sets in the seventh year of his reign. After a prologue appealing for divine aid, it recounts Huneric's edicts against the catholic population of Africa, including the exile of clergy, the closing of churches and monasteries, and forced rebaptism urged by the Arian bishop Cyrila, before introducing seven brothers of a monastery in the territory of Capsa, named Bonifatius, Servus, Rusticus, Liberatus, Rogatus, Septimus and Maximus. Brought to Carthage, the seven refuse bribes and threats to accept rebaptism, proclaiming one Lord, one faith and one baptism, and are imprisoned and loaded with chains before being condemned to be burned at sea on a ship laden with dry brushwood, the youngest, the boy Maximus, insisting on sharing the fate of his brethren.
la.q_cicero.on_running_for_consul: A Latin prose letter of the Roman Republican era, attributed to Quintus Tullius Cicero, giving advice to its addressee on his campaign for the consulship. It opens with the maxim a new man should rehearse daily on descending to the forum, I am a new man, I seek the consulship, this is Rome, and surveys the resources a candidate should marshal: forensic distinction, the support of the publicani and much of the equestrian order, municipal connections, collegia, cultivated young nobles, and the goodwill of consular senators. Further counsel on canvassing and on framing one's political record leads into a long invective against the rival candidates, cataloguing the vices and crimes ascribed to Antonius and Catiline.
la.quintilian.institutio_oratoria: The Institutio Oratoria of Quintilian is an early Imperial Latin prose treatise on oratory, arranged in twelve books. It sets out the full education of the ideal orator, from upbringing and elementary schooling through the technical parts of rhetoric, invention, arrangement, style, memory, and delivery, to a closing book on the orator's character and duties. The opening lines given here form the preface to that final book, which reflects on the magnitude of the task remaining and, invoking Cato's definition, argues that no one can become an orator without being a good man, since eloquence joined to a corrupt character is a weapon against society rather than an instrument of justice.
la.remigius_of_auxerre.expositione_in_pasch: An early medieval Latin prose exposition by Remigius of Auxerre on Sedulius's Paschale Carmen. It opens with an account of Sedulius's life taken from the catalogue of illustrious men begun by Jerome and completed by his disciple Paterius, then proceeds lemma by lemma through the poet's dedicatory letter to the presbyter Macedonius and the preface of the poem. The glosses explain individual words, supply Latin and Greek etymologies, note grammatical points and figures of speech, cite scripture, and unfold the allegorical sense of the poet's nautical imagery, including the depths of the paschal mystery, the small boat of the poet's modest talent, and the anchor of firmness.
la.rufius_festus.breviarium: The Breviarium of Rufius Festus is a short Latin prose epitome of Roman history, composed in the Late Antique period and addressed to the reigning emperor, whose command that the work be brief the author announces in the opening lines. Festus explains that he will mark down the res gestae rather than narrate them at length, and he tallies the years elapsed from the foundation of the city under its kings, its consuls and its emperors alike, a total reckoned at 1,117 years. The surviving survey then traces, under each of those three constitutional orders, the outward growth of Roman power and proceeds province by province, describing how Sicily, Sardinia and Corsica, Africa, Numidia and Mauretania, the Spains, Gaul and Britain were conquered and later organised into provinces, with the number and administrative rank of each enumerated.
la.ruricius_i_bishop_of_limoges.epistulae: The Epistulae of Ruricius I, bishop of Limoges, constitute a short late-antique Latin letter collection in prose. The letters are addressed to bishops and priests and are framed in a rhetoric of humility, in which the author presents himself as a sinner seeking correction, prayer, and spiritual guidance from his correspondents. Their language is densely scriptural and ornate, dwelling on themes of confession, penitence, and pastoral authority.
la.sallust.histories: Sallust's Histories, a Latin prose work of historiography belonging to the Roman Republic, survives only in fragments, the preserved material consisting chiefly of speeches that once stood within a continuous historical narrative. The opening piece is an address to the Roman people denouncing the tyranny and proscriptions of L. Sulla, the loss of tribunician and legal rights, and the corruption of public life, and urging the citizens to follow the consul Marcus Aemilius in recovering their liberty. A second oration, opening a speech to the senate on the disorders of the commonwealth, follows.
la.salutati.de_laboribus_herculis: De Laboribus Herculis ('On the Labours of Hercules') is a Renaissance Latin prose work by Salutati, cast in epistolary form. Its opening section, announced as a compendious defence of poetry against its detractors, prefaces a treatment of the labours of Hercules as the poets sang of them. It rebukes self-styled Aristotelians who disparage the poets and answers Plato's expulsion of poets from his ideal city by recalling the honours Greek states bestowed on Tyrtaeus, Sophocles, and Euripides. Poetry is then traced to the earliest peoples' praise of divinity and virtue, the figurative diction of Scripture is presented as sharing the poets' veiled manner of speech, and Moses, Orpheus, Musaeus, and Linus are named among its earliest practitioners.
la.salutati.de_tyranno: De Tyranno is a Latin prose letter by Coluccio Salutati, chancellor of Florence, addressed to Master Antonio de Aquila, a student of arts at Padua, written in the Renaissance as a reply to questions about tyranny. Salutati first defines the tyrant, treating both the meaning of the name and the essence of the thing and distinguishing its several kinds, before asking whether it is ever lawful to kill a tyrant. The main body of the work examines whether Julius Caesar can justly be reckoned among the tyrants, whether his killing by his assailants was just or unjust, and whether Dante erred in consigning Caesar's murderers to the deepest hell. A closing section records what the ancients report concerning Antenor and Aeneas as traitors to their fatherlands.
la.salvianus.de_gubernatione_dei: Salvian's De Gubernatione Dei is a late-antique Latin prose treatise of theology, written by the author whom the tradition identifies as a presbyter of Marseille. It opens by contrasting the vain eloquence of secular writers with writing intended as remedy rather than ornament, and takes as its theme the charge that God is careless of human affairs, allowing the good to suffer and the wicked to prosper. The opening chapters marshal testimonia from pagan philosophers and poets, including Pythagoras, Plato, the Stoics, Cicero, and Virgil, to show that even non-Christian antiquity affirmed divine providence, before turning to the moral state of professed Christians and the apparent prosperity of the wicked.
la.saxo_grammaticus.gesta_danorum: A Latin history of the Danes, the Gesta Danorum was composed by Saxo Grammaticus at the urging of Archbishop Absalon and is of uncertain date. Its prologue, addressed to Absalon, to the canon Andrew, and to King Valdemar, announces an account of Danish deeds beginning with a description of the homeland and extending from legendary antiquity to the author's own day. The work draws on old Danish songs, whose matter is rendered in Latin metres, on the reports of Icelandic informants versed in antiquity, and on Absalon's own testimony of deeds he performed or learned of. Written in elaborate prose interspersed with verse, it traces the deeds of Danish kings across their whole recorded past.
la.sedulius.epistola_ad_macedonium_altera: A short Latin dedicatory epistle by the Late Antique Christian poet Sedulius, addressed to the priest Macedonius and transmitted as the prose preface to the Paschale Opus, the prose counterpart of his verse Paschale Carmen. Sedulius explains that, at Macedonius's prompting, he has recast the Paschal poem into rhetoricised prose, defends the doubled edition against prospective critics by citing the multiple recensions of Hermogenianus and Origen, and distinguishes genuine completion from illegitimate alteration. The letter offers a rare ancient rationale for verse-to-prose conversion and for authorial self-revision, making it valuable for readers tracing the relation between the Carmen and the Opus, the mechanics of biblical paraphrase, and Late Christian conventions of preface and dedication.
la.sedulius.hymnus_ii_a_solis_ortus_cardine: A Late Antique Latin Christian hymn by Sedulius, 'A solis ortus cardine' is an abecedarian poem whose quatrains begin successively with the letters of the Latin alphabet from A to Z. The hymn sings the life of Christ, moving from the annunciation and nativity through Herod's persecution, the adoration of the magi, and the massacre of the innocents to Christ's baptism, miracles, passion, and triumph over death. Its stanzas treat such episodes as Peter walking on the waves, the raising of Lazarus, the healing of the paralytic, Judas's betrayal, the women at the tomb, and Christ's harrowing of hell.
la.sedulius.opus_paschale: The Opus Paschale is a Late Antique Latin prose work by Sedulius, the prose counterpart of the author's verse account of Christ's miracles and passion. It opens with a preface contrasting the embellished trifles of gentile poetry with the duty of proclaiming the saving works of Christ, followed by a long invocation asking divine guidance on the way toward the heavenly Jerusalem. The narrative then proceeds through scriptural history, beginning with Enoch and the Old Testament prefigurations, toward the paschal mystery of Christ's passion.
la.seneca.ad_lucilium_epistulae_morales: Seneca's Ad Lucilium Epistulae Morales is a collection of Latin prose letters on moral philosophy from the Early Imperial period, addressed to Lucilius, each opening with the salutation 'Seneca Lucilio suo salutem'. The letters treat the conduct of life, beginning with reflections on the scarcity and proper use of time, the disciplined choice of reading, and the demands of genuine friendship, with recurring attention to poverty and death. The collection is arranged in thirteen books.
la.seneca.carminum_fragmenta: The Carminum Fragmenta are a small collection of Latin lyric fragments in mixed meters attributed to Seneca, an author of the Early Imperial period. The opening piece invokes a supreme parent and ruler of the lofty heavens, begging to be led wherever he pleases, and closes with the maxim that fate leads the willing and drags the unwilling. Subsequent fragments weigh wealth against virtue, style money a great good of humankind, declare that the speech of truth is simple, and touch on luxurious dress. The lines are sententious and aphoristic throughout, preserving detached moral reflections rather than continuous poems.
la.seneca.de_beneficiis: De Beneficiis is a Latin philosophical treatise in seven books by Lucius Annaeus Seneca, written in prose in the early Imperial period. Addressed to Liberalis, it examines how benefits should be given, received, and repaid, treating at length the virtues of the grateful giver and recipient and the vices of the ungrateful. The opening book deplores that people neither know how to bestow nor to accept benefits properly, and argues for perseverance in generosity even in the face of ingratitude, with later books pursuing questions of motive, obligation, and repayment through examples drawn from daily life and Roman society.
la.seneca.de_clementia: De Clementia, a Latin prose treatise by Seneca of the Early Imperial period, is addressed to the young emperor Nero. The work opens by casting the treatise as a mirror in which Nero may see himself, voicing an imagined speech in which the emperor boasts that his mercy alone restrains the swords of a vast empire. Seneca then argues that clemency is the most humane of virtues and the one most fitting to a ruler, answering the objection that sparing the guilty breeds lawlessness and insisting that forgiveness must be guided by moderation rather than granted indiscriminately. He announces a division of the subject into three parts, the practice of pardoning, the nature and distinguishing marks of clemency, and the training of the soul in the virtue, and proceeds to show that the prince who holds power of life and death over all is stable in his greatness only when that power is exercised for salvation rather than harm.
la.seneca.de_consolatione_ad_marciam: De Consolatione ad Marciam is a Latin prose consolation addressed by Seneca to Marcia, who for three years had grieved unremittingly for her dead son. The essay argues that such prolonged mourning is a bondage to be actively broken rather than indulged, and it opens by praising Marcia's devotion to her father, the historian Cremutius Cordus, whose writings she had restored to public circulation after his condemnation in the time of Sejanus. Extended exempla set before her the contrasting figures of Octavia, who never rose from the loss of her son Marcellus, and Livia, who bore a comparable bereavement with self-command. The work belongs to the early Imperial period and to Seneca's philosophical writings in prose.
la.seneca.de_consolatione_ad_polybium: A Latin prose consolation of the Early Imperial period, attributed to Seneca and addressed to Polybius on the death of his brother. It opens with reflections on the perishability of cities, monuments, and the world itself, arguing that awareness of the universal necessity of death should temper grief, since fortune strikes the great and humble alike. A personified indictment of Fortune laments the blow dealt to a household favoured by the emperor, praises the dead brother's innocence, modesty, and literary gifts, and closes by urging that tears be curtailed where they accomplish nothing, as every human life supplies abundant matter for mourning.
la.seneca.de_constantia: A Latin prose philosophical treatise by Seneca, written in the Early Imperial period and addressed to Serenus. From a Stoic standpoint it argues that the wise man stands beyond the reach of injury and insult, however many wrongs are attempted against him, and that the appearance of hardship on the path to wisdom is less forbidding than it seems. Cato serves as the chief exemplar of the sage, ranked by the author above the Ulysses and Hercules of earlier ages, while Serenus is made to voice the objections that Seneca then answers, illustrating his case with comparisons to stone, flame, and cliff.
la.seneca.de_ira: De Ira is a Latin prose treatise on anger by L. Annaeus Seneca, a philosopher of the early imperial period. Written at the request of Novatus, who asked how anger might be calmed, it characterises anger as the foulest and most frenzied of the passions, a 'brief madness' whose ravages run from private murders to the destruction of cities and whole peoples. The work sets out definitions of anger, weighed against among others Aristotle's account of it as a desire to repay pain, distinguishes human anger from the mere impulses of animals, and describes its bodily signs and its harms before turning to how the emotion may be checked and soothed.
la.seneca.de_providentia: De Providentia is a brief Latin prose dialogue of the early imperial period by L. Annaeus Seneca, framed as a reply to Lucilius's question why, if a providence governs the world, many misfortunes fall to the lot of good men. Seneca argues that adversity cannot harm the good man, who stands superior to externals, and that the deity treats the virtuous with paternal severity, exposing them to suffering as discipline and proof of their strength. The argument is carried through analogies of the athlete and the stern father and culminates in the figure of Cato, upright amid the collapse of the republic, whose chosen death is presented as an assertion of liberty beyond the reach of fortune.
la.seneca.de_tranquillitate_animi: De Tranquillitate Animi is a Latin philosophical essay by Seneca the Younger, composed in prose during the Early Imperial period and cast as a dialogue with Annaeus Serenus. Serenus opens by confessing a persistent restlessness of mind, describing how his commitment to frugality, withdrawal, and Stoic teaching is repeatedly unsettled by the attractions of luxury, public life, and literary ambition. Seneca replies with an extended diagnosis of such mental fluctuation and a series of remedies for attaining tranquillitas animi, a steadiness of spirit unshaken by circumstance. Drawing on Stoic authorities named in the dialogue, such as Zeno, Cleanthes, and Chrysippus, the discussion ranges over frugality, ambition, public service, leisure, friendship, and the disciplined ordering of daily life.
la.seneca.de_vita_beata: A Latin prose treatise of the early Imperial period by Lucius Annaeus Seneca, addressed to his brother Gallio, on the question of what constitutes the happy life. It opens by diagnosing the human tendency to follow the crowd and the discordant clamour of common opinion rather than reason, insisting that the goal of life must first be defined before any path towards it can be chosen. Adopting broadly Stoic doctrine, it defines the happy life as one in agreement with nature, grounded in a sound, brave and self-possessed mind that uses the gifts of fortune without serving them. The work proceeds through a series of alternative formulations of the supreme good, variously expressed as a spirit that despises the fortuitous and delights in virtue.
la.seneca.hercules_furens: Seneca's Hercules Furens is a Latin tragedy of the early imperial period dramatizing the madness of Hercules. The play opens with a prologue in which Juno, displaced from heaven by Alcmene's son and enraged that he has subdued the monsters of earth, sea, and even the underworld, vows unending war against him. The dramatis personae include Hercules, Lycus, Amphitryon, Iuno, Megara, Theseus, and a chorus of Thebans, and the action moves from Lycus' usurpation at Thebes toward Hercules' divinely inflicted frenzy and the slaughter within his own house.
la.seneca.hercules_oetaeus: Hercules Oetaeus is a Latin tragedy of early imperial date attributed to Seneca and composed in dramatic verse. It treats the closing episode of Hercules' life: Deianira, displaced by Iole, sends her husband a robe steeped in what she takes to be a love charm but which is in fact the blood of the centaur Nessus, and the hero, consumed by its poison, mounts a funeral pyre on Mount Oeta before being received into heaven. Speaking parts fall to Hercules, Deianira, Iole, Alcmene, Hyllus, Lichas, Philoctetes and a messenger, with choruses of maidens and of Aetolian women, and the opening scene presents Hercules appealing to Jupiter for admission to the heavens now that his labours are complete.
la.seneca.phaedra: Seneca's Phaedra is a Latin tragedy of the early imperial period dramatizing the destructive passion of Phaedra, wife of Theseus, for her stepson Hippolytus. The action opens with a hymn to Diana sung over the hunting grounds of Attica, then proceeds through the Nurse's mediation and Phaedra's confession, Theseus' return from the underworld, his curse upon his son, and Hippolytus' death by a bull from the sea, to the final recognition, Phaedra's suicide, and the lament over Hippolytus' mangled remains. Spoken dialogue alternates with lyric choral odes throughout the five-act structure.
la.seneca_the_elder.excerpta_controversiae: A Latin collection of excerpts from the Controversiae of Seneca the Elder, dating from the early Imperial period. Its entries set out declamation themes cast as legal cases, the disinheritance of sons who failed in duties of support, a captured and prostituted woman seeking a priesthood, a Vestal condemned for incest to be cast from the rock, and a maimed father's dispute with the son who refused to kill an adulterer, together with the sententiae, divisiones, and colores of the orators and rhetors who argued each case. Brief remarks designated as spoken outside the controversy and named declaimers such as Alfius Flavus are interspersed among the excerpts.
la.seneca_the_elder.suasoriae: A collection of suasoriae in Latin prose, compiled in the Early Imperial period by Seneca the Elder to preserve the arguments, divisions and striking sayings of Roman orators and rhetoricians. Each suasoria presents excerpts from speeches by named declaimers on a historical theme requiring deliberation, followed by a divisio setting out how the case ought to be argued. The collection opens with counsel urging Alexander the Great not to sail beyond the Ocean, delivered by rhetoricians including Argentarius, Pompeius Silo, Albucius Silus and Fabianus, and continues with Cestius's discussion of the adulation and caution owed when speaking before kings, illustrated by anecdotes concerning Antonius at Athens.
la.servius_honoratus.in_virgilii_georgicon_: A Late Antique prose commentary by Servius Honoratus on Virgil's Georgics, arranged in four books corresponding to those of the poem. The work moves through Virgil's verses line by line, glossing individual words, paraphrasing difficult constructions, and deriving the etymologies of proper names. Longer digressions supply mythological narrative, agricultural and antiquarian lore, and allegorical interpretations, and the opening discussion sets out the poem's title, subject matter, and fourfold division before the exegesis begins.
la.silius_italicus.punica: The Punica, a Latin epic in dactylic hexameters by Silius Italicus of the early Imperial period, recounts the Second Punic War between Rome and Carthage in seventeen books. Its opening invokes the Muse and ascribes the origins of the conflict to Dido's foundation of Carthage and to Juno's enduring hostility toward the descendants of Aeneas, before turning to Hannibal and his oath of enmity against Rome. The narrative follows his campaigns in Italy, including the battles at the Ticinus, the Trebia, Lake Trasimene, and Cannae, alongside the divine machinations and human ambitions that sustain the war.
la.suetonius.de_vita_caesarum: De Vita Caesarum is a Latin prose work of historiography by Suetonius, written in the early imperial period. The work comprises a series of biographies of the Roman emperors, opening with the life of Julius Caesar. That life follows Caesar from his youth, priesthood, and marriage to Cornelia, through his defiance of Sulla, early military service in Asia, capture by pirates, and ascent through the Roman magistracies, mixing public achievement with rumours of scandal, alleged conspiracies, dreams, and omens.
la.sulpicius_severus.epistula_ad_Bassulae_p: A short late-antique Latin letter in prose, addressed by Sulpicius Severus to Bassula, the venerable parent whom he playfully accuses at the outset of purloining and circulating his letters, drafts, and jottings. He protests that he had resolved not to publicise anything about Martin, then relents and gives an account of the death of Martin, bishop of Tours: his foreknowledge of his end, his journey to reconcile quarrelling clerics, his command over the birds preying on fish in the river, his deathbed sayings and prayers, and the angelic brightness of his body at the moment of death. The piece thus moves from a facetious complaint of literary theft to a narrative of the saint's passing, framed as a favour granted to the recipient.
la.sulpicius_severus.epistula_ad_aurelium: A short Latin prose letter of late antiquity by Sulpicius Severus, addressed to his friend Aurelius to report the death of Martin, bishop of Tours. It opens with a dream in which Martin, radiant and as the author had known him in life, appears, blesses him, and is borne up to heaven, an ascent soon followed by the priest Clarus; on waking, the author learns from a messenger from Tours that Martin has died. The remainder of the letter pours out grief shared with the addressee while arguing that Martin, though denied a bloody martyrdom, won a martyr's crown through ascetic endurance, fasting, vigils, and charity toward the suffering. It closes with the hope that Martin will remain present with those who mourn him, tempered by the author's sense that the burden of his own sins may bar him from following along that same path to heaven.
la.terence.eunuchus: Eunuchus is a Roman Republican comedy in dramatic verse by Terence, adapted from the Greek of Menander. Its action turns on the young Chaerea, who disguises himself as a eunuch to enter the house of the courtesan Thais and reach the girl he loves, while his brother Phaedria and the bragging soldier Thraso compete for the same woman's favours. The prologue defends the poet against accusers who charged him with taking the parasite and the soldier from an older Latin play of Naevius and Plautus, and closes with an appeal for the audience's silent attention.
la.terence.phormio: Phormio is a Latin comedy by Terence, a playwright of the Roman Republic, composed in dramatic verse for the stage. Its prologue replies to an older poet's attacks on Terence's manner of writing and announces the Greek original, the Epidicazomenon, whose Latin title derives from the parasite Phormio through whom the action chiefly proceeds. The opening scene introduces Geta, slave in the household of the brothers Chremes and Demipho, whose absent masters leave their sons' affairs of secret marriage and money to set the plot in motion; the play runs to 1,079 lines. Readers hunting textual parallels value the work as a Republican reworking of Greek New Comedy, whose stock figures, the parasite, the clever slave, the deceived senex, invite comparison with Plautine comedy and with Terence's other plays.
la.tertullian.ad_martyres: Ad Martyres is a short prose exhortation by Tertullian, addressed to Christians imprisoned while awaiting trial and martyrdom. The work counsels the prisoners against despair, arguing that the world is itself a darker prison and that confinement offers seclusion for the spirit, freedom from worldly corruption, and opportunity for prayer. Military and athletic imagery runs throughout, presenting the prisoners' hardships as training for the contest in which God presides as judge and an eternal crown awaits the victor.
la.tertullian.adversus_valentinianos: Tertullian's Adversus Valentinianos is a Late Antique Latin prose treatise of anti-heretical theology directed against the Valentinian sect. It attacks the group's secretive habits, likening their initiatory discipline to the Eleusinian mysteries, and defends Christian simplicity against their claimed prudence, arguing that what is hidden so elaborately can be destroyed merely by being exposed. A later section traces the movement's origins to Valentinus, who is said to have broken with the church after failing to obtain a bishopric, and enumerates his successors, Ptolemy, Heracleon, Secundus, Marcus, and Theotimus, and their modifications of his system. The work closes by observing that the sect's adherents, though divided on individual points, remain known by Valentinus's name.
la.tertullian.de_carnis_resurrectione: De Carnis Resurrectione ('On the Resurrection of the Flesh') is a Latin prose treatise on theology by the Christian author Tertullian, belonging to the late antique period. The opening argument mocks the inconsistency of a crowd that denies survival after death yet lavishes funeral rites upon the dead, and reviews philosophical verdicts on the soul's fate from Epicurus, Seneca, Pythagoras, Empedocles and Plato. Against heretics such as Marcion, Basilides, Valentinus and Apelles, who allow salvation to the soul while despising the flesh, the work insists that the body too is raised, framing the question after the author's earlier volume on the flesh of Christ. Its case rests on divine reason and scripture as well as on common human sentiment, which the opening contrasts with the wisdom of the age.
la.tertullian.de_ieiunio_adversus_psychicos: De Ieiunio Adversus Psychicos is a Latin theological treatise by Tertullian, a Christian author of the late antique period, composed in prose. The work defends frequent and rigorous fasting, including the practices of stations and xerophagies, against opponents whom Tertullian calls the 'psychici' and charges with gluttony and frequent remarriage. He upholds the authority of Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla and the new prophecy, answers scriptural objections drawn from Leviticus, the Gospels, Isaiah, and the apostle Paul, and grounds the discipline of abstinence in Adam's fall through the appetite of the belly.
la.tertullian.de_patientia: De Patientia is a Latin prose treatise on patience by Tertullian, a work of Late Antique Christian theology. The author opens by confessing his own impatient temperament and invoking divine grace as the source of a virtue he cannot claim for himself. The argument presents God himself as the exemplar of patience, sustaining the undeserving in creation and supremely in Christ's acceptance of teaching, betrayal, and crucifixion, while noting that even the philosophical sects, for all their disputes, made patience the common goal of their study. It closes with an exhortation to believers to render to God the obedience and patience that his lordship demands.
la.tertullian.de_spectaculis: De Spectaculis is a Latin prose treatise on Christian discipline by Tertullian, a work of theology belonging to the late antique period. The author addresses converts to Christianity, arguing that the faith requires them to renounce the public spectacles of pagan life, including the circus, the theatre, the games, and the gladiatorial shows. The treatise answers pagan objections that everything created by God is good and therefore fit for enjoyment, and responds to fellow Christians who ask for an explicit scriptural prohibition, appealing to Psalm 1 and to the principle that God's works are corrupted when turned to forbidden uses.
la.tertullian.de_testimonio_animae: A short Latin theological treatise of the Late Antique period, attributed to Tertullian. The work summons the human soul as a witness to Christian truth, insisting that the simple and unlettered soul of ordinary people, rather than the one formed in schools, academies and libraries, spontaneously confesses such doctrines as the existence and goodness of a single God, his judgement, the reality of demons and the malice of Satan. Addressed to the soul in the second person, the argument sets this innate testimony against the authority of pagan philosophers and poets, whose writings the author pronounces superfluous and unreliable for the defence of the faith.
la.thedulf_of_orleans.carmina_appendix: A short appendix of Latin verse transmitted with the carmina attributed to Theodulf of Orleans, a poet of the Carolingian period. The opening piece speaks in an enigmatic first-person voice, cataloging wonders such as eyes beyond number, sweet song, and bolted thresholds, in the manner of the Latin riddle tradition. The remaining lines move into devotional territory, closing with a prayer that what is rooted in earthly soil be transplanted to the fields of heaven. No meter is specified, and the collection is dated only by its Carolingian setting.
la.theodosius.de_situ_terrae_sanctae: The De Situ Terrae Sanctae is a short late antique Latin itinerary of Palestine, attributed to a certain Theodosius and of uncertain date. Organised as a sequence of measured routes, it records the distances in miles and paces between Jerusalem and sites across the region, including Jericho, Galilee, Samaria, the coastal cities and Hebron, noting churches, martyria, tombs and wells linked to biblical figures and saints. A closing section moves through Jerusalem itself, describing the Holy Sepulchre, Calvary, Golgotha, holy Sion and other stations of the city, together with the traditions attached to them.
la.valerius_maximus.facta_et_dicta_memorabi: Valerius Maximus's Facta et Dicta Memorabilia, a Latin prose work of the early Imperial period, gathers noteworthy deeds and sayings of Romans and of foreign peoples in nine books. The material is arranged thematically rather than chronologically, moving from religious rites, augury, and priestly discipline through anecdotes about magistrates, generals, and private citizens, with the preface addressed to the reigning Caesar. Short narrative exempla, often drawn from earlier historians and orators, illustrate each topic, and the opening preface states the compilation's aim of relieving readers of a long search through scattered authors.
la.vergil_pseudo.catalepton: The Catalepton is a small collection of short Latin lyric poems of the Augustan period, transmitted under the name Pseudo-Vergil, the attribution to Vergil himself being uncertain, and edited by R. Ellis (Oxford, 1907). Its 222 lines gather occasional verse in the Catullan manner: an exchange with a Tucca, an attack on a rhetorician who mangles Greek and Gallic words, a renunciation of rhetoric upon leaving the school of Siro, letters to friends such as Varius, and a greeting to a young victor in his triumph. Its dense verbal play on Catullus and its diction standing close to Vergil's youthful manner make it a fertile source for readers tracing Augustan intertexts.
la.ambrose.de_interpellatione_iob_et_david: A short late-antique Latin prose treatise by Ambrose, the De interpellatione Iob et David takes the complaints of Job and David as acts of intercession with God that set forth both the perturbations of human life and the consolations that answer them. After recalling Paul's teaching on the sufferings of this present time and the endurance shown by Elijah and Peter, it dwells on Job's protest under his losses and disease and on the forty-first psalm, in which David pleads that God has seemingly forgotten and forsaken the man he made. From these laments the work draws out the hireling's servitude of human existence, the vain hope of hiding sin in darkness from God's all-seeing eye, and the conscience wounded even in sleep and dreams.
la.ambrose.de_tobia: A late-antique Latin prose treatise by Ambrose expounding the biblical Book of Tobit. It rehearses the virtues of the prophet Tobit, justice, mercy, hospitality, patient endurance of captivity and blindness, and the burial of the dead, before passing into a sustained denunciation of usury, contrasting the charity of lending without gain with the rapacity of wealthy creditors who exploit borrowers. The argument is reinforced throughout with quotations from Job, Ecclesiastes, the Psalms and other scriptural authorities.
la.anonymous.s_silviae_peregrinatio: The Peregrinatio attributed to Silvia is a Latin first-person account of a pilgrimage to the holy places of the Near East, of uncertain date and transmitted under an otherwise unattested author's name. The narrative follows the pilgrim through the Sinai region, describing the vast valley below the mountain, its association with the sojourn of the Israelites and the ascent of Moses, and the local guides who identify each site from scripture. Monastic communities along the way receive the travellers with hospitality, lead them to the church on the summit and to the cave where Moses is said to have stood, and give them eulogiae from the orchards at the mountain's foot. Readings from the book of Moses, prayer, and communion are recorded at each halting place.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_aquilegia: The Carmen de Aquilegia is an anonymous medieval Latin poem, of uncertain date, opening with a lament for Aquileia, once a glorious and warlike capital of the Veneti until its utter destruction by Attila. It recounts the city's evangelization through Mark the Evangelist, who sends Hermagoras to be its bishop, together with the companions Fortunatus, Helarus, and Tatianus, whose martyrdoms are said to have begotten a great people of God. The poem then relates the city's divinely warranted ruin at the hands of the Avars, with priests trampled, nobles slain, and women and virgins carried captive, while the faith survives among the Veneti. A polemical closing section condemns the Aquileian church for heresy, likening the schism of the patriarch John of Forum Iulii under the Lombards to Jeroboam's idolatry in Israel, before narrating Italy's passage to the Catholic Franks and the deposition of the patriarch Maxentius under Charlemagne, Louis, and Lothar, ending in a prayer to the Trinity for victory over the deceitful Aquileians.
la.aristotle.economics_book_3: The third book of the Economics, a prose treatise on household management transmitted under Aristotle's name, is presented here in a Latin version. Its concern is the well-ordered household and the reciprocal duties of wife and husband: the wife is to govern the interior of the house under written ordinances, keep modest in dress and expenditure, and take her husband's character as her law, while the husband is charged with fidelity, restraint from other women, and care in begetting and rearing legitimate children. Alcestis, Penelope, Admetus, and Odysseus are cited as exemplars of conjugal faithfulness, and the procreation of children is set forth as the means by which mortal nature attains a share in immortality and divine favour.
la.augustine.commonitorium: The Commonitorium is a brief Latin prose treatise on Church procedure, ascribed to Augustine and of Late Antique date, dealing with Manichaeans who renounce their heresy and seek readmission to the catholic church. It prescribes that each convert anathematise the sect according to a set formula, submit a written confession of repentance, and receive from the bishop a letter securing him against further civil or ecclesiastical penalty; the formula itself pronounces anathemas on a series of Manichaean doctrines, including the two principles, the captivity and purgation of particles of God in food, the shadowy generation of Adam, the denial of Christ's true flesh, and the claim that Manes was the Paraclete. A concluding section regulates the treatment of former Manichaean elect, who are to remain under supervision among clergy or in a monastery before baptism or reconciliation.
la.augustine.contra_duas_epistulas_pelagian: Augustine's Contra Duas Epistulas Pelagianorum is a Latin prose treatise of the Late Antique period, framed as a letter addressed to Pope Boniface. It answers two documents put forward in the Pelagian cause: a letter said to have been sent to Rome by Julian, and another sent to the bishop of Thessalonica in the name of eighteen bishops who shared his error. Augustine argues against their teaching on grace and free will, holding that free will was not destroyed by Adam's sin but that the liberty to live justly is recovered only through the grace given in Christ. In the course of the refutation he treats of merit, of faith as a divine gift, and of the freedom that remains in sinners yet must be healed by the Saviour.
la.augustine.contra_fortunatum: The Contra Fortunatum records a public disputation held at Hippo, in the baths of Sossius before the assembled people, under the consulship of Arcadius and Rufinus, between Augustine and Fortunatus, a Manichaean presbyter. Augustine conducts the questioning, obliging his opponent to spell out the Manichaean account of a revolt by the race of darkness against God's kingdom and of the power sent to resist it, from whose mixture with evil the world and the suffering of good souls arise. Fortunatus answers with his side's profession of faith in an incorruptible and impassible God, in a Saviour like himself, and in the return of chosen souls through Christ, while resisting Augustine's attempts to turn the discussion toward Manichaean morals. The exchange closes on Augustine's dilemma that a God who could suffer harm from the race of darkness is not inviolable, and a God truly inviolable would have had no cause to expose souls to earthly misery.
la.augustine.de_divinatione_daemonum: A short Latin theological dialogue by Augustine, of late-antique date, on the question whether pagan divination and the foreknowledge of demons can be reconciled with the worship of the Christian God. Its first part recounts a conversation held with lay Christian brothers during the octave of a feast, in which objections are raised over the destruction of the temple of Serapis at Alexandria and over how events permitted by an omnipotent and just God should be judged. The remainder argues that demons foretell the future and work marvels through the sharpness and swiftness of their aerial bodies and their long accumulated experience, yet on that account deserve no honour from those who seek blessedness in what endures.
la.augustine.de_duabus_animabus: A short anti-Manichaean treatise in Latin prose by Augustine, a work of late-antique theology. Writing as one who has escaped the snares of the Manichaeans and been restored to the bosom of the Catholic Church, the author deplores his past misery and sets out to refute the sect's teaching that there are two souls, one of the substance of God and one evil. He argues that every soul, precisely insofar as it lives, derives from God as from the sole fountain and principle of life, so that even the souls the Manichaeans call evil live, and live immortally; and he imagines how he might have reasoned with his former coreligionists to show that the soul, apprehended by intellect rather than by the five bodily senses, is superior to the visible light of sun and moon that they worship.
la.augustine.de_gestis_pelagii: A Latin prose treatise of theology by Augustine, belonging to the Late Antique period and addressed to the bishop Aurelius, De Gestis Pelagii takes its occasion from the ecclesiastical proceedings in which fourteen bishops of the province of Palestine pronounced Pelagius Catholic. Augustine gives thanks that the judges' verdict matched his expectation, and then examines the answers Pelagius returned at the synod, distinguishing between an unsound faith and a merely incautious manner of expression. He contrasts what Pelagius stated orally in Greek before judges unacquainted with Latin with what his books actually say, treating at length the claim that no one can be without sin without knowledge of the law. Illustrations such as threshing without tribula, boys reaching school without paedagogi, and recovery without physicians support his division of aids into those without which an end cannot be achieved and those which merely assist, within the broader argument that no one lives rightly without the grace of God.
la.augustine.sermo_de_rusticiano_subdiacono: A late-antique Latin sermon ascribed to Augustine and transmitted with his writings against the Donatists. The speaker opens in grief for a recently deceased pastor, assuring his flock that their love will pass to his successor, before turning to a second sorrow: Rusticianus, a deacon of the church at Mutigena who had served under Valerius at Hippo, has deserted to the Donatists, been rebaptised, and made a deacon by their bishop Macrobius. The closing portion recounts the author's letter urging Macrobius not to rebaptise the fugitive, its rebuff, and the public reading of that correspondence before the congregation, together with a defence of the once-given baptism of Christ against the Donatist practice.
la.ausonius.cento_nuptialis: The Cento Nuptialis of the late antique poet Ausonius is a wedding poem in hexameters composed entirely from lines and half-lines of Virgil, cut and joined at the permitted caesuras so that borrowed fragments run together as continuous narrative. It is preceded by a prose preface addressed to Paulus in which Ausonius defines the cento form, acknowledges its playful inferiority to the Virgilian original, and explains that he undertook the piece at the command of the emperor Valentinian, who had written a nuptial cento of his own and wished to test Ausonius in rivalry. The verse cento that follows, itself framed by an invocation to two young men of promise, describes a marriage feast, the singing and dancing that accompany it, the processional entry of bride and groom, and the exchange of wedding gifts, all rendered in the diction and metre of epic.
la.cicero.de_lege_agraria_contra_rullum: A Latin prose oration of the Roman Republic, transmitted among Cicero's speeches and directed against an agrarian bill brought by the tribune Rullus. Speaking as consul, Cicero attacks the sweeping powers the bill would grant to a board of commissioners (the xviri), who would be empowered to sell public land, dispose of tax revenues, and alienate territories from Capua and Sicily to Asia Minor, Egypt, and the eastern settlements associated with Pompey. He depicts the measure as an auction of the Roman people's possessions for private gain, weaving point-by-point rebuttal of the law's clauses into invective against its author.
la.cicero.de_partitione_oratoria: A Republican-era Latin prose dialogue on rhetoric, cast as a conversation in which Cicero as a young man asks his father to set out in Latin the theory of oratory he had previously received in Greek. The father divides the whole teaching of speaking into three parts, the orator's faculty, the speech, and the question, and treats the invention and arrangement of arguments, the loci from which proofs are drawn, the appeal to the emotions, and the four divisions of a speech: exordium, narration, confirmation and peroration. He then distinguishes the indefinite question from the definite cause, surveys the judicial, deliberative and epideictic genres, and closes with contrasting tactical advice for accuser and defendant in the courts.
la.cicero.divinatio_in_c_verrem: A prose oration of the Roman Republic, the Divinatio in C. Verrem is the speech in which Cicero sought to be appointed prosecutor of Gaius Verres, the former governor of Sicily, in preference to a rival claimant, Quintus Caecilius. Addressing the judges, Cicero argues that he alone has gathered sufficient evidence, having travelled through Sicily to collect testimony from communities and private individuals, and that the standing of the courts depends on Verres's conviction. The speech consists largely of invective, recounting Verres's alleged depredations as quaestor, as legate in Asia and Pamphylia, and as governor of Sicily, and alleging that he intends to escape judgement by bribing the judges.
la.cicero.in_l_pisonem: Cicero's In L. Pisonem is a prose invective of the Republican era, addressed to the senators against Lucius Piso, whose origins at Placentia, ancestry, appearance, and character come under sustained abuse. The speech contrasts Piso's passage through the quaestorship, aedileship, praetorship, and consulship with the speaker's own record of service to the state, above all his suppression of the Catilinarian conspiracy, and recalls a marriage alliance between the two families. Cicero's case rests less on argument than on a catalogue of vituperation, portraying Piso as a man of servile looks, dulness of mind, and concealed vice who won office by deceiving the Roman people.
la.cicero.philippicae: The Philippicae are a cycle of fourteen speeches by Cicero, written in Latin prose during the Roman Republic and directed against Marcus Antonius in the aftermath of Caesar's assassination. The opening oration, cast as an address to the senate, recounts the speaker's departure from and return to Italy and reviews the collapse of the concord that had seemed to follow the Idus Martias, from the abolition of the dictatorship to Antony's growing dominance. The remaining speeches carry on the attack, alternating deliberative argument before senate and people with sustained invective, and defend the authority of the senate and the cause of Brutus and Cassius against Antony's measures.
la.cicero.pro_q_roscio_comoedo: Pro Q. Roscio Comoedo is a forensic speech in Latin prose by Cicero, belonging to the Republican era, in which he defended the comic actor Quintus Roscius in a private lawsuit over money. The surviving text is fragmentary and begins mid-argument; the preserved portion presses the opposing claimant Fannius Chaerea to produce his formal account books (codex accepti et expensi) rather than rough memoranda, and includes direct appeals to the judge, C. Piso. The argument turns on the evidential authority of written accounts as against personal notes and on the legal distinction between a judgment for a fixed sum and an arbitrator's assessment of what is fair.
la.curtius_rufus.historiae_alexandri_magni: The Historiae Alexandri Magni is a Latin prose history by Curtius Rufus, a Roman author of the early Imperial period, recounting the campaigns of Alexander the Great of Macedon against the Persian king Darius III. Its surviving books begin with Alexander's operations in Asia Minor, including the occupation of Celaenae, the severing of the Gordian knot at Gordium, and the muster of Darius's vast forces near Babylon, and go on to follow the Macedonian advance deeper into the Persian Empire. Composed in rhetorical historiographical prose, the narrative interweaves accounts of battles and sieges with descriptions of the geography, peoples, and courts encountered on the march.
la.cyprian.ad_demetrianum: Ad Demetrianum is a late-antique Latin prose treatise by Cyprian, framed as an apologetic answer to a certain Demetrianus who had accused Christians of bringing wars, pestilence, famine and drought upon the world by neglecting the traditional gods. Cyprian replies that these calamities are not the work of offended deities but signs that the world itself has grown old and is hastening toward its appointed end, as scripture foretold for the last times. He develops the point through an extended analogy between the waning vigour of nature and the senescence of the human body, and enforces it with a series of biblical citations warning that divine indignation falls upon those who abandon the one true God, not upon those who worship him.
la.cyprian.sententiae_episcoporum: The Sententiae Episcoporum is a short Latin record transmitted under Cyprian's name, preserving the declarations of bishops assembled at Carthage on the kalends of September to settle the dispute over the baptism of heretics. The opening narrates the gathering of many bishops from the African province, Numidia, and Mauretania, with presbyters and deacons and a large part of the laity, the reading of the correspondence between Cyprian and Jubaianus on the question, and Cyprian's own address to his colleagues. The remainder consists of the individual opinions delivered in turn, each maintaining that there is one baptism only in the church, that baptism among heretics and schismatics is void, and that those coming over from them must be baptised before admission to communion.
la.cyprian_pseudo.ad_flavium_felicem_de_res: A Latin theological work of the later imperial period, transmitted under the name of Cyprian but of uncertain authorship and date, addressed to Flavius Felix on the resurrection of the dead. Its opening invokes the Muses for a song on eternal things and catalogues God's works in creating light, sea, earth, animals, and humankind, whom he formed and endowed with dominion over the world. It then recounts the command given to Adam, the transgression of Eve and Adam at the serpent's prompting, and the spread of sin and death through their offspring, laying the ground for the promised treatment of the resurrection and the rewards of eternal life.
la.dante.divina_comedia: A Latin version of Dante's Divina Commedia, composed in dactylic hexameters and arranged in three books corresponding to the poem's three realms of the afterlife. An epic of the medieval era, it opens with its protagonist lost in a dark wood, menaced by a panther, a lion, and a gaunt she-wolf, and there confronted by the shade of Virgil, who undertakes to lead him through the eternal places. The translator and the date of the Latin rendering are uncertain.
la.dracontius.satisfactio: The Satisfactio is a Late Antique Latin poem in lyric metre by Dracontius, framed as an apology in which the poet begs pardon from God and from his sovereign for an unnamed offence. It opens with a hymnic address to the eternal, unchanging creator and argues that every human fortune, good and bad alike, proceeds from the anger or favour of God, illustrating the theme through Nebuchadnezzar's transformation into an ox and later restoration, and through the muteness inflicted on the father of John the Baptist.
