The poet laments that his guilt has left him more wretched than a wounded hound, recalls that he might otherwise have narrated the triumph-bringing wars of the Asding line, and urges that, since the creator mingled good with evil throughout creation, even a grievous fault may deserve forgiveness. He promises, if restored to favour, to sing the praises of the king's grandfather, his fatherland, and the royal house.
la.ennodius.epistulae: The Epistulae of Ennodius form a collection of prose letters from Late Antiquity, composed in ornate and highly rhetorical Latin. The letters are addressed to friends and clerical correspondents and open with elaborate compliments on eloquence, including a mock-invective challenge to a correspondent named Faustus. Other items give thanks for consolation in distress, lament the threatened loss of a friend's conversation, and touch on the calamities Rome endures at barbarian hands, setting rhetorical display alongside Christian sentiment.
la.eobanus.iliad: A Renaissance Latin version of Homer's Iliad by Eobanus, arranged in 24 books. The opening invocation calls on the Muse to sing the wrath of the son of Peleus, and the narrative proceeds through the quarrel between Agamemnon and Achilles, the plague Apollo sends upon the Greek camp at the prayer of his priest Chryses, and the suffering of the Achaeans before Troy. The 24-book division follows the structure of the Homeric epic, retelling its action in Latin verse.
la.florus_of_lyon.carminum_appendix: A short appendix of Latin verse attributed to Florus of Lyon, a Carolingian author. Its principal piece is an elegiac epistle in which the poet welcomes songs sent by a dear friend, extols a faithful love that rises above hills, valleys, rivers and winds, and prays that grace, strong in the seven virtues, may fill both hearts; the friend's gift of fourteen odes is recalled along the way. The appendix closes with fragmentary lines, among them verses on a feast day of Florus and a broken invocation of Christ as witness to the writer's affection.
la.glass.washingtonii_vita: Washingtonii Vita is a Latin prose life of George Washington by Francis Glass, an American schoolmaster educated in Philadelphia who taught the classical languages in rural Ohio. Glass composed the work at Dayton with a view to its use in schools, and it appeared in print in 1842, after his death. The opening of the record is occupied by a long English preface in which the editor recounts Glass's career and obscurity, the circumstances in which the manuscript was obtained, and the work's rendering of modern military and political terminology into classical Latin idiom.
la.hilary_of_poitiers.liber_ad_constantium_: The Liber ad Constantium imperatorem is a late antique Latin prose treatise in which Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, addresses the emperor Constantius. Writing in exile and protesting that he was banished through faction and false accusation rather than any crime, Hilary appeals to the emperor's piety, cites the religiously observant Caesar Julian as a witness to his case, and declares his intention to expose those who contrived his banishment. The argument then turns against the multiplication of new creeds after the Council of Nicaea, tracing the disputes over homoousion and ousia that have produced as many faiths as there are wills, and insisting that the apostolic faith confessed at baptism be retained unchanged.
la.hilary_of_poitiers_pseudo.ad_leonem_papa: The Ad Leonem Papam is a Latin hexameter poem of later imperial date transmitted under the name of Hilary of Poitiers, though the attribution is uncertain. After a preface addressed to Pope Leo, in which the speaker apologises for the roughness of his verse and offers thanks to God, the poem unfolds a versified account of creation: the emergence of the world from dark chaos, the settling of the elements, the formation of the heavens, earth, and seas, and the establishment of light, day, and night. Later passages name the constellations and the twelve signs of the zodiac and exalt the sun as chief of the heavenly bodies, presenting the whole ordered universe as the work of an eternal and ungenerated creator.
la.hilary_of_poitiers_pseudo.de_martyrio_ma: A short Latin work of the later imperial period, transmitted under the name of Hilary of Poitiers (Pseudo-Hilary) and of uncertain authorship and date. It narrates the martyrdom of the seven Maccabean brothers and their mother under King Antiochus of Syria, who seeks by promises of gold and by torture to make them abandon the law of their fathers. The mother, unmoved by the king's offers, exhorts each son in turn to endure the flames and torments steadfastly, and the account dwells on their constancy and their trust in the reward promised by God.
la.hilary_of_poitiers_pseudo.epistula_ad_ab: The Epistula ad Abram filiam is a short Latin prose letter of uncertain date, transmitted under the name of Hilary of Poitiers and addressed to Abra, the writer's beloved daughter. In it the father recounts a long pilgrimage to a resplendent young man from whom, after tearful supplication, he obtains a garment that never stains, wears out, or tears, and a pearl whose beauty surpasses sky, light, sea, and earth and whose possessor neither sickens, ages, nor dies. The letter closes with instructions that Abra refuse silk, dyed and gilded clothing, and ordinary pearls worn at the neck or on the finger, awaiting instead these heavenly gifts. The allegory amounts to a father's plea for ascetic renunciation and dedication to the life it figures.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.de_operibus_sex_di: De Operibus Sex Dierum is a medieval Latin poem attributed to Hildebert of Lavardin. It retells the Genesis account of the six days of creation and, moving day by day, supplies an allegorical interpretation of each divine act. Light and darkness are read as faith and the sinful heart, the firmament as Scripture, the division of the waters as the separation of men and angels, and the sun and moon as Christ and the Church, with the stars standing for the just. The poem proceeds from the initial making of heaven and earth through the appearance of plants, luminaries, and living creatures, interweaving reflections on the good and evil impulses found in human hearts.
la.hrabanus.de_imagine_caesaris: De Imagine Caesaris is a short Carolingian Latin poem attributed to Hrabanus. It opens with an invocation to Christ as king of kings who redeemed the sins of mankind on the cross, and turns to praise of a Christian emperor styled Caesar and Augustus, whose divinely guarded rule draws tribute from Greeks and Persians and keeps peace over the Christian flock. The closing lines disclose the work's occasional purpose: the author reports that he has composed a little book in verse and prose and offers it to the emperor, whose image, standing armed in faith, precedes the book and everywhere points to the victor.
la.john_scotus_eriugena.carminum_appendix: A short Latin poem of the Carolingian era, preserved as an appendix to the Carmina attributed to John Scotus Eriugena. The opening lines describe a shroud or cloth wrought with wondrous skill by the needle, embroidered with gems and incense, and bearing the image of Christ together with the torments of his passion, blows, bonds, hunger, prison and wild beasts, which the beholder who views it will not suffer. The poem then turns to a lament over the fallen state of Rome: her kings and nobles have deserted her, her name and honour have passed to the Greeks, Constantinople flourishes as the new Rome while old Rome decays in morals and walls, and slaves of slaves now stand as her masters. The closing lines denounce the city's avarice and its traffic in the bodies of the saints and in false relics.
la.lactantius.fragmenta: A gathering of fragments and testimonia for works of Lactantius, also called Firmianus, that do not survive intact. The excerpts, drawn from Jerome, Rufinus, Victorinus and an anonymous Greek preface to the Sibylline oracles, together with a marginal note from an Ambrosian, formerly Bobbian, codex, attest to letters to Probus, Demetrianus and Severus, a discussion of the metres of Roman comedy, Greek Sibylline verses, and a short account of the motions of the soul as divinely implanted in human nature. The collection also preserves Jerome's biographical notice, which records that Lactantius, a pupil of Arnobius, taught rhetoric at Nicomedia under Diocletian and in old age served as teacher of the Caesar Crispus in Gaul. The material is late-antique prose belonging to the field of theology.
la.lucifer_bishop_of_cagliari.de_regibus_ap: A short polemical treatise in Latin prose by Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, of late antique date, addressed to the emperor Constantius and accusing him of apostasy for persecuting the catholic faith in favour of Arianism. The work confines itself to kings of Israel who had known God and then fell away, retelling at length the story of Gideon (Jerobaal), who after delivering Israel from the Midianites lapsed into idolatry through the making of the ephod. From such biblical examples the author argues that rulers who turn against God after receiving his favours incur divine judgment, and warns Constantius that God will in due course rescue the Christians from his hands.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.carmina_2: Carmina 2 is a book of Latin verse by the late-antique poet Magnus Felix Ennodius. It opens with an epitaph for a young man of twenty whose sudden death is framed as a passage from life to life, and continues with short occasional poems on varied subjects. Among them are a laudatory piece for a learned friend named Faustus, verses mourning the death of a virgin, and a poem on the offering and consecration of a basilica of Saint Lawrence in connection with Xystus. Christian themes of merit, salvation, and the soul's survival of the grave recur throughout the collection.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.eucharisticum_de_v: The Eucharisticum de Vita Sua is a late-antique Latin prose work by Magnus Felix Ennodius, cast as a thanksgiving to God for recovery from grave illness. The opening section meditates on bodily weakness as a path to spiritual strength, then the narrator recounts his former immersion in secular poetry and rhetoric and the pride that accompanied it. A violent fever follows as divine correction, and when human medicine fails, he turns to the shrine of the martyr Victor, where he vows to abandon worldly composition and devote his eloquence wholly to sacred writing.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.praeceptum_quando_: A short Latin prose precept of late antique date, attributed to Magnus Felix Ennodius, whose title refers to an occasion when all bishops were commanded to act. The work opens with an elaborate prologue contrasting the brilliance of a blameless life with the darkness of slander, citing a recent uprising against the bishop of the apostolic see as an example of malicious accusation. Its prescriptive core requires that priests, deacons and religious of older and newer rules live with a well-approved companion, conduct all their affairs publicly before witnesses, and keep no women in their households beyond those the canons allow. Penalties of loss of office and honour are pronounced on transgressors, upheld by the authority of blessed Peter of the apostolic see and his papal successor and reinforced by a quotation from Ambrose on the sin of suspicion.
la.nepos.vitae: A Latin prose work of the Republican period by Nepos, the Vitae is a collection of short biographies of eminent commanders, announced in its preface as a book 'de vita excellentium imperatorum.' The preface, addressed to Atticus, defends the genre against those who judge it lightweight and contrasts Greek and Roman customs to account for differing standards of honorable conduct. The narrative opens with Miltiades, recounting his leadership of the Athenian colony to the Chersonese, his counsel at the bridge over the Ister during Darius's Scythian campaign, and the outbreak of Persian hostilities against Greece, and continues with further lives of celebrated Greek generals.
la.orientius_saint.carmina: A collection of short Latin Christian poems attributed to the late-antique poet Orientius. It opens with De Nativitate Domini on the birth of Christ, followed by De Epithetis Salvatoris Nostri, a catalogue of the many names and titles given to the Saviour, and De Trinitate, a doctrinal poem on the Trinity that also dwells at length on the Passion, the cross and its Greek-letter symbolism. A concluding Explanatio Nominum Domini glosses the catalogue title by title, explaining why Christ is called door, lion, shepherd, stone, fish and the rest.
la.orientius_saint.commonitorium: The Commonitorium is a didactic Christian poem in Latin by Saint Orientius, a poet of late antiquity. Framed as an admonition on the path that leads to eternal life, it opens with a prayer to Christ for understanding and eloquence, recalling the ass that spoke to Balaam. The first book expounds the two lives granted to humankind, the double precept of loving God and neighbour, and the golden rule, before warning at length against sexual temptation, envy, and avarice, each illustrated with biblical exempla such as Dinah, Tamar, Solomon, Samson, and Ananias. The book closes with injunctions to almsgiving and to peace for the reader who would attain everlasting life.
la.paschasius_radbertus.epitaphium_arsenii: The Epitaphium Arsenii is a Latin prose dialogue of the Carolingian period by Paschasius Radbertus. It stages a conversation among three speakers, Adeodatus, Paschasius, and Theophrastus, who resolve to complete a lament for the dead Arsenius that they had long before begun to commit to writing, electing one of his former companions as a witness so that the truth may be commended, as they put it, as if under three testimonies. Their recollections tell how Arsenius, reading divine displeasure in the calamities visiting the empire, laid before the emperor, the bishops, and the senators a written schedule of the realm's vices, and how the misfortunes of the age, including pestilences, famines, and terrors of visions, together with new miracles at the resting places of the saints, mark a moment demanding correction. The dialogue frames the whole as a threnos composed so that, if not for the speakers themselves, at least for posterity it may stand as an example of amendment.
la.paulinus_petricordiae.de_vita_sancti_mar: De vita sancti Martini is a verse life of St Martin by the Late Antique poet Paulinus of Périgueux. It opens with a prose preface in which Paulinus accepts a correspondent's request to recast in verse a prose history of the saint's merits and virtues. The verse narrative then recounts Martin's origins in Pannonia, his career as a soldier, his renunciation of arms, the division of his cloak with a beggar and the ensuing vision of Christ, his baptism, and his association with Hilary of Poitiers. Further episodes include his journey to convert his parents, his conflicts with Arian error, the raising of a dead catechumen, and the restoration of a hanged servant to life.
la.paulus_orosius.commonitorium_de_errore_p: A short Latin theological treatise of Late Antique date, attributed to Paulus Orosius and cast as a consultative memorial (commonitorium) addressed to Augustine. It opens with an apology for its hasty composition and then reports the doctrines of Priscillian, including the soul's descent through celestial circles, its bondage to a written decree of fate, the mapping of patriarchs and zodiac signs onto the body, and an unorthodox Trinitarian formula. It next sets out the Origenist teachings said to have been brought back by the two Aviti and the Greek Basil, among them the pre-existence of souls, the material world as a place of purgation, a merely figurative and non-eternal punitive fire, and a subordinate view of Christ's body. The memorial closes by begging Augustine to root out these malignant plantings and supply an orthodox refutation.
la.petrus_of_pisa.carmina: A short Carolingian collection of Latin verse by Petrus of Pisa. It opens with a hymn in praise of Christ as creator and redeemer, followed by an elaborate encomium to a Paulus praised as the peer of Homer, Virgil, Philo, Horace and Tibullus, who is credited with teaching Greek grammar to court clerics and consulted about undertaking Hebrew studies. Later poems exchange courteous verses with the same Paulus, mention a king's daughter crossing the sea with a Michael as escort to take up a kingdom's sceptre, and pose three enigmatic questions, ending with riddling instructions about head, ear, belly and a letter with three branches. The collection closes with a pastoral dialogue in which a beautiful youth discloses a hidden saying about what the Father gives the Son.
la.plautus.asinaria: The Asinaria is a Latin comedy by Plautus of the Roman Republic, written in dramatic verse. Its prologue announces the Greek model, the Onagos of Demophilus, rendered into Latin by 'Maccus', and gives the work its title, 'the comedy of asses', before the dialogue opens between the old man Demaenetus and his slave Libanus. The plot follows Demaenetus' effort to help his lovesick son Argyrippus secure the courtesan Philaenium from her pimp, as he and the slaves Libanus and Leonida raise the necessary money while concealing the scheme from Demaenetus' harsh wife.
la.plautus.mostellaria: A Latin comedy by Plautus, dating to the Roman Republic and composed in dramatic verse. The opening scene stages a fierce quarrel between the slaves Tranio and Grumio over the disorder of the household during its master's three-year absence abroad, and over the young heir's lapse from thrift into drinking, love affairs, and the lavish keeping of parasites. The action, set in an Athenian milieu with references to the Piraeus, follows the scheming Tranio's efforts to conceal the squandered estate from the returning father, and the title points to the pretended haunting of the house that figures in his deceptions.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_montibus_sina_et_sion_: De montibus Sina et Sion (adversus Iudaeos) is a short Latin prose treatise of later imperial date, transmitted under the name of Cyprian and printed among the works attributed to him. It sets Mount Sinai against Mount Zion, interpreting the two Hebrew names to show that Sinai, where the Mosaic law was given to a carnal people, is an earthly mountain, while Zion, where Christ the son of God reigns, is heavenly and spiritual. Old Testament figures, including Rebecca as a type of the church and the name and number of Adam, are read as foreshadowings fulfilled through Christ, and earthly Jerusalem is condemned in contrast with the celestial mountain. The work belongs to the adversus Iudaeos tradition of Christian polemical theology.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_pascha_computus: A short Latin treatise on the computation of Easter, transmitted under the name of Cyprian and belonging to the later imperial period. The author describes a search of the divine scriptures for the true first day of the lunar month in which the Jews in Egypt were commanded to sacrifice the Passover on the fourteenth moon, arguing from the institution of the Paschal lamb in Exodus and the separation of light from darkness in Genesis that this day falls on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. Computations that instead begin the month at the Ides of March are shown to be mistaken, and the work closes with the announcement of a table (pinax) by which the future dates of Passover for Jews and of Easter for Christians can be determined without error.
la.pseudo_victor_vitensis.notitia_provincia: A late-antique Latin notitia transmitted under the name of Victor Vitensis, listing the Catholic bishops of the African provinces who came to Carthage by royal command in the sixth year of the Vandal king Huneric to render an account of their faith. The bishops are recorded name by name with their sees, arranged by province, proconsular Africa, Mauretania Caesariensis, Mauretania Sitifensis and Tripolitana, followed by a separate list of bishops exiled to Sardinia, with priests noted among them. The register closes with numerical tallies of the clergy overall, distinguishing those who perished, those banished to Corsica or remained in exile, those who fled, and those who suffered.
la.salvian_of_marseilles.epistulae: A short collection of Late Antique Latin prose letters attributed to Salvian of Marseilles, addressed to named recipients including Bishop Eucherius, Ursicinus, Bishop Agrycius, and the author's parents Hypatius and Quieta together with Palladia and Auspiciola. The opening letter commends to Eucherius a young kinsman taken captive at Agrippina, whose widowed mother remains in poverty among the captors, and asks that the young man be received, instructed and formed in spiritual life. A second letter reproves Ursicinus for conveying a greeting through a servant rather than writing himself, and a third apologises to Bishop Agrycius for a lapse in dutiful correspondence. A further letter, addressed to his family, opens with a discussion of the apostle Paul's practice of joining other names to his own in the headings of his epistles.
la.sedulius_scotus.carminum_appendix: An appendix to the verse of the Carolingian Latin poet Sedulius Scotus, consisting of a dream vision. The poem opens with an allegory of two laws, evil and good, contending within the soul; the narrator then falls asleep and beholds a radiant maiden of towering stature who names herself Sophia, wisdom known to Greeks and Latins alike, and sends him to the house of one Guntarius. The poem closes in praise of Guntarius as a venerable, peace-bringing bishop of noble Frankish lineage, learned, devoted to sacred song, and generous to the poor, the blind, and the lame.
la.seneca.de_brevitate_vitae: A Latin prose treatise on philosophy by Seneca, written in the early imperial period and addressed to Paulinus. Opening from the common complaint that nature allots too short a span of life, the work argues that time is squandered rather than scarce, cataloguing the pursuits, avarice, ambition, luxury, restless busyness, servile attendance on others, through which people lose their years without ever possessing themselves. Seneca urges an exact accounting of how time has been spent, rebukes those who defer living to old age, and presents devotion to wisdom as the way to make life genuinely long.
la.seneca.de_otio: De Otio is a Latin philosophical prose essay by Seneca of the early Imperial period. It defends otium, the withdrawal of the wise man from public affairs into study and contemplation, and answers the objection that Stoic teaching binds him to public service until the end of life. Setting the precepts of Zeno against those of Epicurus, it argues that leisure can itself benefit mankind, that the sage serves a greater commonwealth embracing gods and men, and that the contemplation of virtue, divinity, and the natural world is a worthy use of retirement.
la.severus_sulpicius.epistulae_tres: The Epistulae Tres are three letters in Latin prose by Sulpicius Severus, a late antique writer. The letters center on Martin, bishop of Tours, whose life the author had previously recorded in a separate book: they respond to a critic who mocked Martin for having nearly perished in a fire, defend him through comparisons with Peter and Paul, and then narrate the incident itself, in which Martin was trapped among flames while sleeping in a church and escaped unharmed. The closing portion turns to a dream vision arising from the writer's reflections on sin, judgment, and the fear of punishment.
la.sulpicius_severus.dialogi: The Dialogi of Sulpicius Severus is a Late Antique Latin prose work of theology composed as a conversation among three speakers: the author, his friend Gallus, and Postumianus, newly returned from several years of travel in the East. The opening exchange, set during a reunion at a secluded retreat in Gaul, records Postumianus's promise to recount his pilgrimage, which carried him from Carthage and the shrine of Cyprian to Alexandria and the desert regions of Egypt. The dialogue proceeds through his narrative and the companions' questions about the state of the Christian faith in the East, the institutions of monks, and the miracles and rest of the saints, framed throughout by the speakers' devotion to the memory of Martin, whose disciple Gallus had been.
la.terence.hecyra: The Hecyra is a Latin comedy in dramatic verse by Terence, a playwright of the Roman Republic. Its prologue recounts that earlier performances were wrecked when audiences deserted the play for a rope-dancer and, on another occasion, for gladiators, and it pleads for an undisturbed hearing now that the crowd is absent. The action centres on the young husband Pamphilus, his lingering ties to the courtesan Bacchis, and the revelation that the child borne by his estranged wife was fathered by Pamphilus himself before the wedding, a discovery that reconciles the two households.
la.tertullian.ad_nationes_libri_duo: Ad Nationes Libri Duo is a Latin prose treatise of theology by Tertullian, a late-antique author, written in two books against the pagan nations. The opening argues that hatred of Christians springs from ignorance, since those who come to know them cease to hate and often join them, and it rebukes Roman courts for treating confessed Christians differently from other accused persons, pressing them under torture to deny rather than to confess. The argument then turns to the charge against the name itself, maintaining that no crime attaches to the word 'Christian', whose meaning, even in the mispronounced form 'Chrestian', derives from unction and pleasantness.
la.tertullian.adversus_praxean: Adversus Praxean is a Latin prose treatise on theology by Tertullian, a work of the late antique period directed against the teaching of Praxeas. The opening chapters charge Praxeas with claiming that the Father himself descended into the virgin, was born, and suffered, and recount his opposition in Rome to the new prophecy of Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla. The treatise then argues for one God whose unity of substance is administered through the oikonomia of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, three not in status but in grade, form, and species. It further contends that the divine monarchia is not divided by this ordering, and grounds its case in a rule of faith held from the beginning of the gospel.
la.tertullian.apologeticum: The Apologeticum is a Latin prose treatise of Christian apologetic theology by Tertullian, a writer of late antiquity. It addresses the magistrates of the Roman Empire on behalf of the Christians, arguing that it is unjust to condemn the name without examining the deeds behind it, and it rebuts popular accusations such as infanticide, incest, and disloyalty to the state. The work contrasts the fear and shame shown by ordinary wrongdoers with the Christian's open confession even under sentence, and it cites Pliny the Younger's consultation of Trajan to expose the contradiction of an imperial policy that forbade searching out Christians yet punished those who were found.
la.tertullian.de_baptismo: De Baptismo is a Latin prose treatise by Tertullian, a Christian writer of the Late Antique period, defending the necessity of water baptism against a teacher of the Cainite heresy who had lately won followers by abolishing the rite. The argument proceeds from the dignity of water in the creation narrative, where the Spirit of God moved upon the waters, to the claim that baptismal waters are sanctified by the Spirit wherever they are used. The treatise maintains that baptism is equally valid in sea, pool, river, spring, lake, or bath, citing John in the Jordan, Peter in the Tiber, and Philip's baptism of the eunuch, and it frames Christians as little fish who survive only by remaining in water after their fish, Jesus Christ.
la.tertullian.de_oratione: De Oratione is a Latin theological treatise by Tertullian on the discipline of Christian prayer. It opens by presenting the Lord's Prayer as the new form of prayer established by Christ for the disciples of the new covenant, contrasting it with the teaching of John the Baptist and describing prayer as constituted from word, spirit, and reason. The work then proceeds through the petitions of the prayer individually, offering expositions of the address to God as Father, the sanctification of the divine name, and the petition that God's will be done on earth as in heaven.
la.tertullian_pseudo.de_iona_propheta: De Iona Propheta is a short Latin work of the later imperial period attributed to Tertullian, though the ascription is doubtful. It retells the biblical story of the prophet Jonah, opening with the fate of Sodom and Gomorrah and God's patient mercy toward penitent sinners before turning to Jonah's commission to preach destruction against Nineveh. The narrative follows his embarkation at Joppa, the storm that batters the ship and its desperate crew, the casting of lots that exposes the fugitive prophet, and his confession of the God who made heaven, earth, and the seas.
la.tibullus.elegies: The Elegies of Tibullus, an Augustan Latin poet, form a collection of love elegies in elegiac couplets transmitted in three books. The opening poem sets the tone, contrasting wealth and military glory with contentment in rural poverty and with prayers to Ceres, Priapus, and the Lares, before turning to the poet's devotion to his beloved Delia. Throughout the collection, poems on love and loss are woven together with country festivals and rituals and with verses honouring the poet's patron Messalla; the later books introduce a second mistress, Nemesis. The range of subjects extends from harvest rites and rustic gods to sickness, dreams, and the approach of death.
la.vergil_pseudo.copa: The Copa is a short Latin poem in lyric metre, attributed to Vergil but of disputed authorship and placed in the Augustan period. It opens with a Syrian tavern-girl, her head bound in a Greek headband, dancing lasciviously in a smoky inn, and passes into her invitation to a weary traveller to trade the summer's dust for wine, shade, music and love. A catalogue of the establishment's rustic pleasures, including cheap wine, roses, lilies, cheese, chestnuts and plums, a cicada-filled orchard and a watchman armed with a willow sickle, leads to a closing exhortation to seize the day, as death tugs the ear and declares 'Vivite: venio.'
la.vergil_pseudo.culex: The Culex ('The Gnat') is a Latin poem in hexameters of Augustan date, attributed to Vergil and transmitted among his works under a pseudonymous heading. It opens with a prologue dedicating its light verses to the young Octavi, invoking Phoebus, the Muses and the pastoral goddess Pales, and disclaiming the grand subjects of war, gigantomachy and epic travel in favour of humble song. The narrative that follows tells how a shepherd sleeping at noon is saved from a serpent by the bite of a gnat, and how the gnat's ghost later visits him in a dream to lament its unnoticed death and to demand burial.
la.vergil_pseudo.lydia: Lydia is a Latin lyric poem of the Augustan period, transmitted among the pseudonymous works ascribed to Vergil. Composed in lyric metre, it takes the form of an amatory complaint: the speaker apostrophises fields, meadows, and woods, envying the landscape that now enjoys the presence of his mistress Lydia, and laments the wasting sickness of unfulfilled love. He contrasts his frustrated state with the contented pairing of animals and with the love affairs of gods and heroes, including Jupiter, Mars and Venus, and Aurora, before closing with a curse upon his birth and a picture of his bodily ruin.
la.victor_claudius_marius.alethia: The Alethia is a Late Antique Latin Christian epic by Claudius Marius Victor, retelling the opening chapters of Genesis. A prefatory invocation addresses the Trinity, dwells on God's goodness as the cause of creation, and treats free will and the problem of evil; the first book then narrates the six days of creation, the making of Adam and Eve, the delights and four rivers of Paradise, the serpent's temptation, the fall, God's sentencing of the transgressors, and the expulsion from Eden. Throughout, the poet interweaves reflection on providence, mortality, and redemption through Christ.
la.victor_claudius_marius.commentariorum_in: A three-book Latin poem in epic verse by Claudius Marius Victor, an orator of Massilia (Marseille) in late antiquity, presenting a verse commentary on the book of Genesis. The work opens with a preface addressed to God, invoking the Trinity and asking for aid in the task of writing, and bears a notice that the preface has been interpolated by Joannes Gagneius. Book one recounts the creation of the world in six days, the formation of Adam from dust and of Eve from his rib, paradise and its four rivers, the temptation by the serpent, the fall, and the sentence pronounced on the serpent, Eve, and Adam, ending with the couple's expulsion from Eden.
la.victorinus.de_machabeis: De Machabeis is a Latin narrative poem of the later Roman imperial period, transmitted under the name of Victorinus, though the attribution is uncertain. In hexameter verse it retells the biblical account of the Maccabean martyrs: Antiochus, king of Syria, seeks by promises, torments, and fire to compel a devout mother and her seven sons to abandon the law of their God. The poem proceeds through the sons' deaths one by one, giving extended direct speech to the defiant mother and the enraged king, and dwelling on the mother's exhortations to each son as he is led to execution.
la.walafrid_strabo.vita_sancti_galli_confes: A Latin verse life of Saint Gall, the Irish missionary and companion of Columbanus, composed in the Carolingian period and attributed to Walafrid Strabo. Addressed to Gotzbert, the poem presents itself as a metrical treatment of an account of the saint written some sixteen years earlier. It narrates Gall's departure from Ireland in Columbanus's company, the expulsion of the missionaries from Frankish territory, their reception in the Thurgau, Gall's preaching and destruction of pagan shrines among the Alemanni, and his settlement at Arbona on Lake Constance, together with his miracles and death.
la.wandalbert.de_mensium_nominibus: De Mensium Nominibus ('On the Names of the Months') is a medieval Latin poem by the Carolingian writer Wandalbert on the origins of the names of the twelve months. It undertakes to explain why the months bear their names, which signs of the zodiac preside over each, and what tasks cultivation and husbandry demand through the year. Proceeding month by month, the poem derives the names from Roman deities and rulers such as Janus, Februus, Mars, Venus, Romulus, and Pompilius, and pairs each month with its constellation and seasonal character. Alongside these astronomical and etymological matters it sets out the rural occupations proper to each season, including ploughing, sowing, vine-pruning, beekeeping, fishing, and the hunting of hare, deer, and boar.
la.alcuin.carmina_rhytmica: A series of short Latin religious poems attributed to the Carolingian scholar Alcuin. The pieces are arranged alphabetically by their opening words, from 'Altus auctor omnium' to 'Xristo in cruce', and take doctrinal themes: the Trinity and its unity, the procession of the Holy Spirit, the Incarnation and Christ's single person in two natures, the motherhood of the Virgin Mary, and Christ's Passion and Resurrection. Most items occupy a few lines of rhythmic verse, frequently built on paired or antithetical statements of a single theological proposition.
la.anonymous.itinerarium_hierosolymitanum: An anonymous Latin prose itinerary, of uncertain date, presented under the title Itinerarium Hierosolymitanum as an account of a journey to Jerusalem. It opens at Burdigala (Bordeaux) and proceeds in the tabular manner of a Roman road itinerary, naming cities, mutationes, mansiones, and other stations with distances given in Gallic leagues (leugae) and Roman miles. The opening sections trace the route from Bordeaux through Aquitaine and Narbonensis, across the Alpine passes, and into Italy.
la.augustine.de_dialectica: A Late Antique Latin prose treatise on dialectic by Augustine, the De Dialectica, which defines dialectic as the science of disputing well (bene disputandi scientia). The opening exposition distinguishes simple from conjoined words and sentences, separating statements capable of truth or falsity from imperatives, wishes, and execrations that affirm nothing, and explains how a summa is reached from conceded propositions. It then sets out the fourfold distinction of verbum, dicibile, dictio, and res, illustrated from Vergil's 'arma', and sketches the divisions of the discipline from the treatment of single words (de loquendo) to the judgment on the combination of sentences (de proloquiorum summa).
la.augustine.libellus_adversus_fulgentium_d: A short Latin polemical treatise attributed to Augustine, of uncertain date in the late antique period, directed against a Donatist named Fulgentius. Written in prose, it is framed as a reply to a libellus sent by Fulgentius, and its structure pairs Donatist assertions with rebuttals introduced as the responses of a Catholic speaker. The argument centres on the validity of baptism performed outside the church: the respondent denies that heretical baptism must be repeated, affirms a single true baptism in the name of the Trinity, and draws on scriptural proof-texts, notably an extended comparison of the Donatists with the Samaritans of the biblical narrative.
la.cicero.academica: The Academica of Cicero, a philosophical dialogue in prose from the Roman Republican era, survives only in part, the corpus preserving the work's opening exchange. Set at Cumae, the dialogue brings together Cicero, Atticus, and Marcus Terentius Varro, with Varro explaining his long hesitation to expound Greek philosophy in Latin, on the grounds that Greek technical doctrine can be neither conveyed to the unlearned nor made attractive to the learned. Cicero replies that Latin treatments of the Old Academy and its controversies with the Stoics would nevertheless find an audience, and he praises Varro's antiquarian and literary writings while urging a philosophical literature in Latin to stand beside the Greek.
la.cicero.pro_l_flacco: The Pro L. Flacco is a forensic oration by Cicero, composed in the Roman Republic in defence of Lucius Valerius Flaccus, who stood accused of extortion arising from his administration of the province of Asia. Delivered in the aftermath of the Catilinarian conspiracy, the speech frames the prosecution as an assault on the men who preserved the state, and Cicero seeks to discredit the testimony of the Lydian, Mysian and Phrygian witnesses who have brought the charge. He also reviews Flaccus's career, citing his service as military tribune under Publius Servilius, as quaestor in Hispania under Marcus Piso, and as praetor presiding over the courts, and argues that the province itself was neither willing nor lawful in joining the accusation.
la.cicero.pro_scauro: Pro Scauro is a Latin forensic oration by Cicero of the Roman Republic, composed in prose for delivery before a jury. It defends Marcus Scaurus against prosecution, recalling earlier charges brought against him under the lex Servilia and the lex Varia and answering accusations arising from his conduct in Sardinia. The surviving portions rebut an allegation of poisoning centered on the death of a Sardinian woman, attack the credibility of hostile witnesses, notably Triarius, and include a digression on voluntary death illustrated by Greek examples such as Socrates, Themistocles, and Cleombrotus. The oration is preserved only in fragments.
la.cyprian_pseudo.sodoma: The Sodoma is a Latin poem on the destruction of Sodom, transmitted under the name of Cyprian in the later imperial period, though the attribution and precise date are uncertain. It opens with God's postdiluvian covenant of the rainbow, then recounts the depravity of Sodom, the arrival of the two angelic visitors, Lot's hospitality and his offer of his daughters to the mob, and the assault on his house. The work treats the city's punishment by fire as divine judgement upon sexual vice and as a sign of a final conflagration to come.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.de_vita_beati_anto: Magnus Felix Ennodius's De Vita Beati Antoni Monachi is a late antique prose vita recounting the life of Anthony, a monk born at Valeria on the Danube in Pannonia to a father named Secundinus. Addressed to Abbot Leontius at whose request the work was undertaken, it opens with a preface on the preservation of the deeds of the virtuous before invoking the Holy Spirit. The narrative follows Anthony's early years under the renowned Severinus and his uncle Bishop Constantius, the devastation of Pannonia by the incursions of Franks, Heruli and Saxones, and his journey to Italy, where he settles in the Tellina valley and is joined to the priest Marius.
la.milo_of_saint_amand.carmina_figurata: A short Carolingian Latin collection of figure poems, the Carmina Figurata is attributed to Milo of Saint-Amand and consists of verses composed to form visual shapes, with explicit reference to cross-shaped schemata and circular ornament. The poems address a ruler named Charles in panegyric terms, extolling his justice, piety, and dominion extending even to Thule. A closing passage declares that the author has written the blessed deeds of a beloved bishop, whose virtue and honour are said to endure beyond the stars. Throughout, grand praise of the king is interwoven with the poet's self-deprecating pleas for his ruler's clement reception.
la.paulus_orosius.liber_apologeticus: The Liber Apologeticus of Paulus Orosius is a late-antique Latin prose treatise of Christian polemical theology, composed as a defence of its author against suspicion of Priscillianism and as an exposure of heresy within the church. Addressed to a gathering of bishops, it invokes the authority of Cyprian, Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, and Jerome against the doctrines of Origen, Priscillian, Jovinian, Pelagius, and Caelestius, which it depicts as poisons revived among the living. Its narrative portions report what Orosius had witnessed of Caelestius's condemnation at Carthage and of the proceedings against Pelagius in Jerusalem, casting the controversy in the scriptural figures of Goliath, Absalom, and the serpent.
la.petrus_diaconus.de_locis_santis: De locis sanctis is a medieval Latin prose treatise on the holy places of Jerusalem, composed by Peter the Deacon of Monte Cassino and addressed to Guibald, abbot of Monte Cassino and Stablo. In the prologue Peter states that he has collected the material from various books and from the oral accounts of those who had travelled to the Holy Sepulchre, and he asks the abbot to confirm and endorse the work. The body of the treatise describes the church of the Holy Sepulchre, Golgotha and Calvary, the Temple of the Lord with its associated traditions, Solomon's temple, the church of Saint Anne, the probatic pool, and other sites of Jerusalem and its vicinity.
la.salvian_of_marseilles.epistulae_selectio: A Latin prose letter by Salvian of Marseilles, a Christian writer of the Late Antique period. The letter congratulates its addressee on books he has composed, praising them as brief in style, rich in doctrine, and written chiefly for the instruction of the addressee's sons, whose holy upbringing the author commends. Salvian prays that God may make the young men equal to the works composed for them, so that their teaching may bear fruit for the churches, and closes with an affectionate farewell asking that the addressees, once his pupils, now become his daily intercessors before God.
la.tertullian_pseudo.de_sodoma: De Sodoma is a short Latin poem in hexameters on the sin and punishment of Sodom, transmitted under Tertullian's name but of uncertain authorship, belonging to the later imperial period. Opening with the flood by which God destroyed the first age of mankind and set the rainbow in the clouds as a pledge, it turns to the renewed impiety of a second race of men and to Sodom, whose lusts against nature mark the city out for destruction by fire rather than water. The poem then follows the arrival of two angelic youths at the gate, the hospitality of the righteous Lot, the assault threatened by the Sodomite mob, Lot's offer of his daughters in his guests' stead, and the divine decree of the city's coming annihilation, to which his sons-in-law respond only with incredulous laughter.
la.vergil_pseudo.elegiae_in_maecenatem: The Elegiae in Maecenatem is a short group of Latin elegiac poems transmitted under Vergil's name and assigned to the Augustan era. The opening declares that, having lately bewailed the death of a young man in song, the poet must now give verses to the aged Maecenas, and the poems go on to mourn and praise him: sprung from Etruscan kings, he appears as Augustus' comrade in arms and watchful guardian of Rome, dear to the emperor yet so unthreatening that no one feared his power. His single alleged fault, a loosely worn tunic matched by an easy simplicity of character, is defended at length through mythological exempla, above all the figure of Hercules spinning among the Lydian women, while his steadfastness is traced from Philippi through Actium to the Egyptian war. The poems close by asserting that Maecenas' little books will surpass monuments of marble, since genius alone lives on and all else belongs to death.

grc.septuaginta.genesis: The opening book of the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures rendered by Jewish translators in the Hellenistic period and transmitted anonymously. Written in biblical prose, it narrates the creation of heaven and earth, Adam and Eve in the garden of Eden, the flood, and the generations of the patriarchs, concluding with the descent of Jacob's family into Egypt under Joseph. Its Greek is the versional idiom of the Alexandrian translation rather than classical Attic, and the wording served as the Old Testament of Greek-speaking Judaism and later of the early church.
grc.septuaginta.exodus: The Greek version of the biblical book of Exodus, a prose rendering produced in the Hellenistic period as part of the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures, by translators of uncertain identity. The book opens with the names of the sons of Israel who entered Egypt with Jacob, and recounts the Israelites' multiplication and enslavement under a new pharaoh, the rescue of the infant Moses from the Nile, his upbringing at the Egyptian court, his flight to Midian and marriage to Sephora, and his call from the burning bush. The narrative then proceeds to the plagues upon Egypt, the Israelites' departure from the land, and the giving of the law at Sinai.
grc.septuaginta.levitikon: The priestly law code at the center of the Pentateuch, covering sacrifice, ritual purity, the priesthood, and the annual festivals, including the Day of Atonement. It is organized as instructions delivered to Moses at Sinai rather than as narrative, and its vocabulary for sacrifice and purity later shaped Christian theological language. Traditionally ascribed to Moses, like the rest of the Pentateuch, and translated into Greek in the third century BC.
grc.septuaginta.arithmoi: Arithmoi (Numbers) is the Greek version of the fourth book of the Pentateuch, preserved in the Septuagint, the Greek rendering of the Hebrew scriptures produced in the Hellenistic period; the individual translators are unnamed. The book opens with the muster of the Israelite fighting men, tribe by tribe and household by household, which Moses and Aaron carry out in the wilderness of Sinai in the second year after the departure from Egypt. Its prose narrative and legislation go on to cover the ordering of the camp and march around the tent of testimony, the duties assigned to the Levites, and the journey of the Israelites under Moses from Sinai toward the borders of the promised land, including episodes of rebellion, the mission of the scouts, and the encounter with Balaam.
grc.septuaginta.deuteronomion: The Deuteronomion is the Septuagint's Greek version of Deuteronomy, the fifth book of the Mosaic Pentateuch, rendered into Greek prose during the Hellenistic period by an anonymous translator. The book presents itself as the words Moses spoke to all Israel beyond the Jordan in Moab, opening with a retrospective narrative of events from Horeb onward, including the appointment of judges, the mission of the spies from Kadesh Barnea, and the people's refusal to enter the promised land. Its remainder consists of Mosaic exhortation and legislation, covenant stipulations, statutes, blessings and curses, concluding with the transfer of leadership to Joshua and an account of Moses' death.
grc.septuaginta.basileion_a: The First Book of Kingdoms (Basileion A) is the Greek counterpart of 1 Samuel, transmitted as part of the Septuagint, the Greek version of the Old Testament produced in the Hellenistic period. Rendered in biblical prose, it opens with Hannah's vow, the birth and dedication of Samuel at Shiloh, and her hymn of praise, and proceeds through the corruption of Eli's sons, the loss and return of the ark, and Samuel's career as prophet and judge. The remaining chapters recount the anointing and reign of Saul, his rejection, and the rise of David, ending with Saul's death.
grc.septuaginta.basileion_b: The Second Book of Kingdoms (Basileion B), corresponding to 2 Samuel, preserved in the Septuagint, the Greek version of the Hebrew scriptures produced by anonymous translators of the Hellenistic period. Written in prose, the book opens with the Amalekite's report of Saul's death on Mount Gilboa and David's lament over Saul and Jonathan. It then narrates David's anointing as king at Hebron over Judah, the war between the house of David and that of Saul under Iebosthe, and the continuing account of David's reign over Israel, its wars and court conflicts.
grc.septuaginta.basileion_g: The third Book of Kingdoms, corresponding to 1 Kings, opening with the succession struggle in David's final days and Solomon's accession. It covers Solomon's wisdom, wealth, and construction of the Jerusalem temple, the kingdom's split after his death into Israel and Judah, and the early kings of both, including the prophet Elijah's confrontations with King Ahab and Jezebel.
grc.septuaginta.basileion_d: The fourth and final Book of Kingdoms, corresponding to 2 Kings, continuing the parallel histories of Israel and Judah through the ministry of Elisha and other prophets. It narrates the Assyrian conquest of Israel in 722 BC, the reforms and failures of Judah's later kings, and ends with the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem and the temple in 586 BC.
grc.anthologia_graeca: The Anthologia Graeca is a large anthology of Greek epigrams transmitted in sixteen books, the work of many poets spanning several centuries, from the Hellenistic period into late antiquity. The books are arranged largely by subject, gathering dedicatory, sepulchral, amatory, epideictic, and epigrammatic verse on art and literature, composed in a mixture of meters. Book 1 collects Christian epigrams, and the opening lines here record the founding and adornment of churches in Constantinople by imperial and aristocratic patrons, among them Justinian, Eudocia, and Juliana.
grc.achilles_tatius.leucippe_et_clitophon: The Leucippe et Clitophon is a Greek prose romance by Achilles Tatius, a work of uncertain date. It opens with a frame narrative in which a traveller at Sidon, viewing a painting of the abduction of Europa, listens to the hero Clitophon recount the story of his love for Leucippe. The tale then follows the lovers through elopement by sea, shipwreck, capture by pirates and brigands, and a series of separations and apparent deaths across Tyre, Byzantium, Alexandria, and Egypt, before ending in reunion and marriage.
grc.acta_joannis.acta_joannis: The Acta Joannis is an anonymous Greek apocryphal narrative about the apostle John, of uncertain date, transmitted with the apocryphal acts of the apostles. It opens with an account of Vespasian's siege of Jerusalem and the persecution of Christians ordered by Domitian, who summons John from Ephesus to Rome to answer for his preaching that a heavenly king will one day supplant all earthly rule. The narrative follows the apostle's austere journey under military escort and his dialogue with the emperor, in which he proves his teaching by drinking deadly poison unharmed.
grc.aelian.de_natura_animalium: Aelian's De Natura Animalium is a Greek prose miscellany in seventeen books on the natures and habits of animals. A preface defends the claim that irrational creatures share in virtue by nature, after which the work proceeds through short, self-contained notices on beasts, birds, fishes, and insects. Its entries range from the fishing of the scarus and the mutual rescue behaviour of shoals to marvellous tales such as the herons of Diomedes' island, said to be the hero's transformed companions.
grc.aelian.varia_historia: Aelian's Varia Historia is a Greek miscellany of short anecdotes and notices on animal behaviour, human customs, historical episodes, and memorable sayings, compiled from earlier writers. The collection, given here in Rudolf Hercher's Teubner edition of 1866, runs to nearly two thousand lines and opens with accounts of the cunning of octopuses, the weaving of spiders, and the resourcefulness of Egyptian frogs, dogs, and foxes, before proceeding to further stories of animals and men. Aelian names and paraphrases earlier authorities such as Aristotle and preserves versions of many anecdotes otherwise lost, making the work a rich quarry for readers tracing parallels in ancient natural lore and moralising narrative.
grc.aelius_aristides.orationes: The Orationes is a collection of Greek prose speeches by Aelius Aristides. The work opens with a hymn to Zeus, framed as thank-offerings made in fulfilment of a vow after escape from a storm at sea, in which the speaker laments the belatedness of his sacrifice and calls upon the Muses for aid. The hymn proceeds to celebrate Zeus as self-generated and eternal, first cause and craftsman of the cosmos, recounting his creation and ordering of earth, sea, air and aether, his adornment of the heavens with stars, and his allotment of proper dwellings to gods, humankind and the other races of living creatures. Further orations follow in the collection.
grc.aeschines.against_ctesiphon: A forensic oration by the Athenian orator Aeschines, prosecuting Ctesiphon for proposing an illegal decree that granted Demosthenes a golden crown in the name of the people. Addressed to the Athenian judges, the speech presents the indictment for unlawful legislation as the chief safeguard of democracy, contrasting rule by law with tyranny and oligarchy and lamenting the corruption of assemblies, council business, and the public audit of officials. Aeschines argues that the decree is unlawful, false, and harmful to the city, and urges the jury to void it and so uphold the laws.
grc.aeschines.on_the_embassy: A forensic defence speech in Greek, delivered before an Athenian jury by the orator Aeschines in answer to a prosecution brought by Demosthenes on a charge of bribery connected with the embassy to Philip of Macedon and the peace concluded with him. The proem asks the jurors for a fair and benevolent hearing, weighs the danger confronting the defendant, and attacks the prosecutor's rhetorical manoeuvres before turning to the accusations concerning Philocrates, Phrynon, and the other ambassadors. The argument then proceeds into a narrative of the peace negotiations, taking up the Euboean envoys, Phrynon's capture and ransom, Ctesiphon's report of Philip's goodwill, and the decree of Philocrates permitting embassies concerning peace.
grc.aeschylus.agamemnon: The Agamemnon is a Greek tragedy by the fifth-century BC Athenian poet Aeschylus, the first play of his Oresteia trilogy. It opens with a watchman on the roof of the palace at Argos who sighted the beacon fire announcing the fall of Troy, after which a chorus of Argive elders recounts the expedition of Menelaus and Agamemnon against Priam's city. The play goes on to follow Agamemnon's homecoming with the captive Cassandra, his murder at the hands of Clytemnestra and her lover Aegisthus, and the queen's defence of the deed as vengeance for Iphigenia and the curses upon the house of Atreus.
grc.aeschylus.agamemnon_hypothesis: An ancient prose hypothesis, or plot summary, transmitted with Aeschylus's tragedy Agamemnon and composed in antiquity by an anonymous author of uncertain date. It recounts the drama's action: the beacon signal of Troy's fall, Clytemnestra's posting of a watchman, Agamemnon's return with the captive Cassandra, her prophecy of the murders to come, and the killing of the king, concluding with the argument between Clytemnestra and Aegisthus over responsibility for the deed, and it adds a remark on Aeschylus's handling of the deaths off stage. The summary is followed by a didascalic notice recording production under the archon Philocles in the second year of the 80th Olympiad (458 BC), when Aeschylus won first prize with Agamemnon, the Choephoroi, the Eumenides, and the satyr play Proteus, together with a list of the drama's characters.
grc.aeschylus.eumenides: A Greek tragedy by Aeschylus in which Orestes, pursued by the Erinyes after the murder of his mother, seeks purification. The opening scene at Delphi presents the Pythia's prayer to the succession of oracular deities and her terrified discovery of Orestes as suppliant beside the sleeping chorus of Furies. The action then moves to Athens, where Athena institutes a court to try the case, and the play closes with the Furies appeased and transformed into the benevolent Eumenides, honored as guardian goddesses of the city.
grc.aeschylus.eumenides_hypothesis: A prose hypothesis, or plot summary, to the Eumenides of Aeschylus, transmitted in Greek with the hypothesis material accompanying the plays. It relates how Orestes, harried by the Erinyes at Delphi, is directed by Apollo to Athens, where through the counsel of Athena he is acquitted and returns to Argos, the appeased Erinyes thereafter being addressed as Eumenides. The summary closes with the note that the story was treated by neither of the other two tragedians.
grc.aeschylus.persians: A Greek tragedy by Aeschylus, set in the Persian capital of Susa. The chorus of Persian elders waits for news of Xerxes' expedition against Greece; a messenger arrives with an account of the naval defeat at Salamis, and the ghost of Darius, summoned at the bidding of the queen mother Atossa, reflects on the ruin of the campaign. The play closes with the return of Xerxes himself and the lament of the elders over the lost host.
grc.aeschylus.persians_hypothesis: An ancient prose hypothesis, or argument, to Aeschylus's tragedy the Persians, transmitted with the play and of uncertain authorship. It sets out the dramatic situation: Xerxes' invasion of Greece with a vast army and a fleet of over a thousand ships, his defeat by land at Plataea and by sea at Salamis, and his retreat through Thessaly back to Asia, while the scene of the drama is placed at the tomb of Darius and the prologue assigned to a chorus of Persian elders. The hypothesis cites the notice in Glaucus's work on the myths of Aeschylus that the Persians was modeled on Phrynichus's Phoenissae, observing differences in the two openings, and appends the didascalic record of Aeschylus's victory under the archon Menon with the Phineus, Persians, Glaucus of Potniae, and Prometheus. A closing note distinguishes the two Persian expeditions against Greece, the first under Darius ending in failure at Marathon and the second under Xerxes at Salamis and Plataea.
grc.aeschylus.seven_against_thebes: Seven Against Thebes is a Greek tragedy by Aeschylus on the expedition of the Seven against Thebes, in which the brothers Eteocles and Polyneices contend for rule of the city. The play opens with Eteocles rallying the citizens as a scout reports that seven Argive champions have sworn over a sacrificed bull either to raze the city or to die upon its ground. The action proceeds through the assignment of defenders to each of the seven gates, the scout's descriptions of the attackers and their blazoned shields, the battle itself, and the deaths of the two brothers at each other's hands, closing with laments and a decree concerning their burial.
grc.aeschylus.suppliant_women: Suppliant Women (Hiketides) is a Greek tragedy by Aeschylus, composed in a mixture of lyric choral odes and iambic trimeters. The play opens with the chorus of Danaid maidens, who have fled Egypt by ship with their father Danaus and landed at Argos, where they grasp suppliant boughs, invoke Zeus, and recount their descent from Io through Epaphus. The action turns on their petition for asylum from forced marriage to the sons of Aegyptus, their cousins, and on the response of the Argive king and people to their appeal. The drama stages themes of supplication, sanctuary, and kinship obligations within the mythic genealogy of Argos.
grc.andocides.on_the_mysteries: An Attic forensic speech by the Athenian orator Andocides, On the Mysteries gives the defence he offers before an Athenian jury against charges of impiety concerning the Mysteries. The speaker opens by asking for a fair hearing against enemies who have long conspired to ruin him, and then undertakes to narrate from the beginning the events that led to the prosecution, including the assembly that dispatched Nicias, Lamachus and Alcibiades on the Sicilian expedition and the accusations of celebrating the Mysteries that followed. The oration combines a detailed account of those events with arguments that the denunciations against him were false and that he acted lawfully in returning to the city to stand trial.
grc.anonymous.stadiasmus_magni_maris: The Stadiasmus Magni Maris ('Coastal Survey of the Great Sea') is an anonymous Greek periplous, or coastal sailing guide, of uncertain date and authorship. Framed as a communication to an honored brother, it sets out the Mediterranean coastline in numbered stages, beginning at Alexandria and running along the North African shore toward Paraitonion, and covering the route from the hieron opposite Chalcedon to the Pillars of Heracles and Gades, together with the Pontic coast as far as Dioscurias. Each entry gives the distance in stades between landfalls and notes on harbors, summer anchorages, reefs, headlands, watering places, sanctuaries, and islands, including the intervals between the islands and the winds used in sailing to them.
grc.apollodorus.library: The Library is a prose compendium of Greek mythology attributed to Apollodorus and of uncertain date. It arranges the myths in genealogical sequence, beginning with the reign of Uranus, the birth of the Hecatoncheires, Cyclopes, and Titans, and Cronus' overthrow of his father. The opening narrative covers the rearing of Zeus in Crete, the Titanomachy, the partition of heaven, sea, and underworld among Zeus, Poseidon, and Hades, the offspring of the Titans, and the marriages and children of Zeus, down to the story of Orpheus and Eurydice. The work as a whole carries the account onward through the lineages and exploits of the gods and heroes of Greek myth.
grc.apollonius_of_perga.conica: The Conica is a Greek mathematical treatise on conic sections by Apollonius of Perga, a geometer of the Hellenistic period. The preserved lines set out propositions in the Euclidean manner, each consisting of a general enunciation followed by a demonstration, and deal with tangents and secants drawn from external points to sections of a cone and to circumferences of circles. The hyperbola receives particular attention, with propositions involving its asymptotes and its opposite sections, and ratios of divided straight lines are used to determine where lines drawn from points of contact meet or touch the curve.
grc.apollonius_rhodius.argonautica: The Argonautica of Apollonius Rhodius is a Greek epic in four books, totalling 5,834 lines, opening with an invocation to Phoebus Apollo. It recounts Pelias' charge to Jason, the building of the Argo under Athena's guidance, and the muster of heroes beginning with Orpheus, then follows the voyage through the Cyanean Rocks toward Colchis in quest of the Golden Fleece, with Medea's passion for Jason at its centre. As the fullest surviving treatment of the Argonautic saga, it offers rich material for readers tracing epic diction, heroic catalogues, and the Jason–Medea story across later Greek and Latin literature.
grc.archimedes.arenarius: The Arenarius (Psammites, or Sand-Reckoner) is a short treatise by Archimedes, written in Doric Greek and addressed to King Gelon of Syracuse. Against those who hold the number of grains of sand to be infinite, Archimedes argues that a number can be named large enough to exceed the sand that would fill a sphere the size of the cosmos, and devises a nomenclature for very large numbers built on powers of the myriad. The opening section sets out his assumptions about the earth's perimeter and the relative sizes of earth, moon, and sun, reports the hypothesis of Aristarchus of Samos that the earth revolves about the sun, and describes an instrumental measurement of the sun's apparent diameter. Geometric demonstrations follow, establishing that certain named numbers surpass the quantity of sand contained in the sphere just defined.
grc.archimedes.de_corporibus_fluitantibus: A short Greek treatise on hydrostatics by the mathematician Archimedes, transmitted under the Latin title De Corporibus Fluitantibus, 'On Floating Bodies', with parts of the argument supplied in Latin alongside the Greek. It opens with postulates defining the behaviour of a fluid, in which parts lying equally and continuously are pushed outward by those more strongly compressed, and each part is pressed vertically by the fluid above it. The demonstrations that follow establish that the surface of a fluid at rest has the figure of a sphere with the same centre as the earth, that solids of equal weight with the fluid descend until they no longer project above its surface, and that solids lighter than the fluid, when released into it, are not wholly submerged but partly stand above the surface.
grc.archimedes.de_lineis_spiralibus: A Greek mathematical treatise by Archimedes, known by the Latin title De Lineis Spiralibus ('On Spirals'). The prefatory letter reviews the geometric problems circulated in Conon's lifetime, several of which Archimedes brands false, and then defines the spiral traced by a point moving uniformly along a straight line that revolves uniformly about a fixed end. The theorems announced there concern the areas enclosed by the spiral in its successive turns and the tangent drawn at the spiral's terminal point.
grc.archimedes.de_planorum_aequilibriis: A treatise on statics by Archimedes, the De Planorum Aequilibriis (On the Equilibrium of Planes) derives, from seven postulates on weights suspended from a balance, the law of the lever and the properties of the centre of gravity of plane figures, with propositions on commensurable and incommensurable magnitudes, composite bodies, and the parallelogram. It is written in the Doric dialect characteristic of ancient Greek mathematical prose, with forms such as τᾶς for τῆς, μακέων for the beam of the balance, and σαμεῖον for σημεῖον, which distinguish it sharply from Attic literary Greek. For readers tracing intertexts it offers the canonical formulation of mechanical vocabulary, κέντρον τοῦ βάρεος (centre of gravity), ἰσορροπέω (to balance), ῥέπω (to incline), on which later discussions of the lever and the balance in Greek technical and literary authors draw.
grc.archimedes.problema_bovinum: A Greek arithmetical epigram attributed to Archimedes, presented as the problem he sent to scholars at Alexandria in a letter to Eratosthenes of Cyrene. The poem challenges the solver, in epicizing hexameters, to reckon the numbers of white, dark, yellow, and dappled bulls and cows grazing in the Sun's herds on Trinacria (Sicily) from a series of fractional relations among the herds, and adds the harder requirements that the white and dark bulls together form a square number and the yellow and dappled together a triangular one. A prose summary follows, restating the conditions and recording the total of each herd and of all the cattle together in Greek numerals.
grc.archimedes.quadratura_parabolae: A Greek geometrical treatise by Archimedes, edited in the second volume of Mugler's Budé Archimède (Paris, 1971) and running to some fifty-four lines, the Quadratura Parabolae takes the form of a letter to Dositheus that opens by mourning the death of the geometer Conon. It establishes that every segment bounded by a straight line and a section of a right-angled cone, the parabola of the title, is four-thirds of the triangle on the same base and of equal height, first by mechanical balancing arguments on a lever and then by purely geometrical demonstration, with preliminary lemmas drawn from conic elements. For readers of intertexts, the work preserves Archimedes' explicit engagement with the quadrature attempts of earlier geometers, appeals to results from his Mechanics, and the formulaic propositional and reductio style of Greek mathematical prose that later technical writers perpetuate.
grc.aretaeus.curatione_acutorum_morbum: A Greek medical treatise ascribed to Aretaeus of Cappadocia, a physician of uncertain date, transmitted under the Latin title De curatione acutorum morborum (On the Cure of Acute Diseases). The material gathered here gives a detailed clinical account of acute convulsive disorders, describing the warning signs, the seizure itself, and the aftermath of epilepsy, and the spasms of tetanus in its rigid, backward-arching (opisthotonic) and forward-curving forms. Further sections discuss the causes of these spasms, their incidence by season, age, and sex, and the physician's limited prospects of aiding those they strike.
grc.aristophanes.clouds: Clouds (Nephelae) is a Greek comedy by Aristophanes, preserved complete in 1,481 lines and edited by F. W. Hall and W. M. Geldart in the second volume of their Oxford Clarendon edition of 1907. The plot opens with the elderly Strepsiades lying awake over debts run up through his son Pheidippides' passion for horses, and follows his attempt to enrol in the thinking-house of Socrates to master specious argument and evade his creditors, an education that rebounds when the son turns his new skills against his own father. The comedy's caricature of Socrates, its satire of sophistic instruction, and its debate between Just and Unjust Argument made it a touchstone for ancient and later portrayals of philosophy, and its scenes, characters, and phrases supply plentiful parallels for readers tracing intertexts.
grc.aristophanes.ecclesiazusae: A Greek comedy by Aristophanes, of uncertain date, in which the women of Athens disguise themselves as men to seize control of the assembly and enact a scheme of common property, shared meals, and communal households. The opening scene shows the conspirators gathering before dawn by lamplight, exchanging accounts of their preparations, false beards, men's cloaks, Laconian shoes and staffs, in accordance with the plan resolved at the festival of the Scira. The action proceeds from the capture of the assembly to scenes in which citizens surrender their private goods to the new order, with choral interludes and episodic encounters interspersed among the dialogue.
grc.aristophanes.frogs: The Frogs (Batrachoi) is a Greek comedy by Aristophanes in which Dionysus, disguised as Heracles and attended by his slave Xanthias, travels to the underworld to bring back the recently deceased tragedian Euripides. The opening exchange between master and slave before the house of Heracles leads on to the famous chorus of frogs, the procession of the initiated, and encounters with Aeacus and the inhabitants of Hades. The central episode is an agon in which Aeschylus and Euripides compete for the chair of tragedy, their verses weighed on scales and their arguments tested, until Dionysus awards victory to Aeschylus and prepares to lead him back to Athens. Alongside its sustained criticism of tragic poetry, the play touches on the political condition of the city, including a parabasis addressed to the citizens.
grc.aristophanes.knights: A comedy by Aristophanes, in which the slaves of the irascible old man Demos of the Pnyx, a figure for the Athenian people, conspire against the Paphlagonian, the flattering, thieving leather-seller who has gained complete sway over their master. A vulgar sausage-seller proves the only rival capable of outdoing the Paphlagonian in pandering, and their contest for Demos' favour drives the action until the old man, restored to his senses, renders judgment. The chorus takes the part of the Athenian knights from whom the play takes its title, with parabatic passages among its interludes.
grc.aristophanes.lysistrata: The Lysistrata of Aristophanes is an Athenian comedy of the late fifth century BC, written in Greek in the alternating spoken and lyric metres of Old Comedy. Its heroine convenes women from Athens, Sparta, Boeotia, and elsewhere to a secret assembly, where she unveils a scheme, sealed with an oath, by which the women will withhold themselves from their husbands and occupy the Acropolis until the men make peace and end the war between Athens and the Peloponnesians. The action draws its humour from the women's struggle to keep the vow, the escalating frustration of the men, and the quarrels and eventual reconciliation of choruses of old men and old women, closing with a peace negotiated amid celebration.
grc.aristophanes.peace: Peace is an Attic comedy by Aristophanes in which the farmer Trygaeus, weary of wartime hardship, flies to heaven on an enormous dung beetle to confront Zeus and to rescue the goddess Peace from the pit into which she has been cast. Once she is restored to earth, the play stages celebrations among farmers and craftsmen, the abandonment of the arms trade, and the protagonist's marriage to the personified Harvest. Throughout, Aristophanes' satire falls on profiteers, sycophants, and oracles that prolong the fighting, while the chorus of farmers voices the miseries of war in song.
grc.aristophanes.wasps: The Wasps (Vespae) is an Athenian comedy in Attic Greek by Aristophanes, a dramatist of the late fifth century BC. It opens with two slaves keeping watch over Philocleon, an old man addicted to jury service, whom his son Bdelycleon tries to confine indoors, and the chorus of wasps embodies the sting of the Athenian jurymen. The play's satire strikes at the demagogue Cleon and the popular law courts, and its later scenes follow Philocleon's riotous conduct at a symposium.
grc.aristotle.analytica_priora: A Greek philosophical treatise by Aristotle on the theory of the syllogism, the form of argument in which certain things being laid down, something other than the premises follows of necessity through them. Opening by announcing that its inquiry concerns demonstration and demonstrative science, it defines proposition, term, and syllogism, distinguishes perfect from imperfect syllogisms, and states the rules for converting universal, particular, and indeterminate premises, whether assertoric, necessary, or possible. The treatise proceeds through syllogisms in the three figures and gives a sustained treatment of modal propositions concerning necessity, possibility, and contingency.
grc.aristotle.de_caelo: A Greek treatise by Aristotle on the heavens, opening with the claim that natural science concerns bodies and magnitudes, their affections and movements, and the principles of such substance. Early chapters define the continuous, the divisible, and dimension, citing Pythagorean doctrine that the all and completeness are delimited by the number three, so that body, bounded in three dimensions, alone counts as perfect magnitude. Further argument distinguishes simple local motions as circular, upward, and downward, and holds that circular motion cannot belong by nature to fire or any of the elemental bodies, from which it follows that there exists another simple body, more divine and prior to the perceptible elements, whose proper motion is circular. The opening defers the question whether the universe as a whole is infinite in magnitude in order to treat first of its parts in kind.
grc.aristotle.de_generatione_animalium: A Greek zoological treatise on the generation of animals by Aristotle, the fourth-century BC philosopher, transmitted in five books. The work treats the male as the principle of motion and form in generation and the female as matter, and discusses the nature and origin of seed, the generative organs such as testes and uteri, and sexual differentiation among blooded and bloodless animals. It also considers modes of reproduction across the various animal kinds, including creatures said to arise spontaneously from putrefying matter rather than from paired parents.
grc.aristotle.de_interpretatione: De Interpretatione (Peri Hermeneias) is a Greek prose treatise by Aristotle on language and judgment. It defines the name, the verb and the sentence as units of signification, holding that spoken words are symbols of affections of the soul and that names signify by convention rather than by nature. The discussion then turns to affirmation and negation, distinguishing contradictory from contrary pairs of propositions and asking when such opposed statements can be simultaneously true. Part of the Aristotelian logical corpus, the work treats the declarative proposition as the bearer of truth and falsity, as in its example of the goat-stag, which signifies something yet says nothing true or false until existence is predicated of it.
grc.aristotle.de_sophisticis_elenchis: A Greek prose treatise by Aristotle, the De Sophisticis Elenchis (On Sophistical Refutations) examines arguments that appear to be genuine refutations but are in fact fallacious reasonings. It defines syllogism and elenchus, distinguishes didactic, dialectical, peirastic and eristic kinds of reasoning, and surveys the aims of contentious disputants before classifying the fallacies on which sophistical arguments rely, dividing those dependent on language, such as homonymy, amphiboly, composition, division, pronunciation and form of expression, from those independent of it. The treatise proceeds to consider how such fallacies are produced, how they may be detected, and how they are to be resolved in question and answer.
grc.aristotle.divisiones_aristoteleae: A short ancient Greek collection of division (diairesis) passages transmitted under Aristotle's name, of uncertain date and authorship. Its chapters classify individual subjects into their species: goods of the soul, of the body, and external; the natural, companionable, and hospitable kinds of friendship, to which some add the erotic; the five forms of constitution; justice towards gods, towards humans, and towards the dead; the theoretical, productive, and practical sciences; and the five branches of medicine.
