Several topics are treated twice, first in the wording that Diogenes Laertius cites from Aristotle (III 80 ff.), then in a fuller parallel version, so that related reports of the same divisions stand side by side.
grc.aristotle.epistulae: A short collection of Greek letters transmitted under Aristotle's name, of uncertain date and authenticity. The letters are hortatory and moral-philosophical in character: one counsels a new ruler against tyranny and in favour of benefaction, while others dwell on the inconstancy of fortune, gratitude owed to benefactors, the endurance of friendship, and the keeping of lecture notes from wider circulation. Their polished, sententious prose belongs to the Greek epistolographic tradition in which the collection has been handed down.
grc.aristotle.magna_moralia: The Magna Moralia is a Greek ethical treatise transmitted under Aristotle's name and traditionally attributed to him, of uncertain date and disputed authorship. It opens by situating the study of character within politics, arguing that good action in civic life requires an account of what virtue is and from what it arises. The opening discussion reviews earlier treatments of virtue by Pythagoras, Socrates, and Plato, each judged deficient in its handling of the soul and of the virtues. The inquiry then distinguishes the human good from the good simply and from the Platonic Idea of the good, in preparation for an account of virtue that aims at becoming good rather than at mere knowledge.
grc.aristotle.meteorologica: The Meteorologica is a Greek philosophical treatise by Aristotle on natural phenomena in the region below the moon, presented as the remaining part of natural inquiry after the study of first causes, the heavens, the elements, and coming-to-be and passing-away. It examines the nature of the space between the earth and the stars, the constitution of the four bodies, and such celestial appearances as the Milky Way, comets, and fiery apparitions. Its account further covers clouds, winds, earthquakes, thunderbolts, and related atmospheric occurrences, explained through exhalations from the earth and the heating action of the sun's motion.
grc.aristotle.nicomachean_ethics: A Greek ethical treatise by Aristotle, the Nicomachean Ethics inquires into the supreme human good and identifies it with happiness (eudaimonia), framing the study of that good as the business of politics. Its successive books examine virtue of character as a mean between excess and deficiency, voluntary choice and responsibility, individual virtues such as courage, temperance and justice, intellectual virtue and contemplation, and the roles of pleasure and friendship in the good life. The opening book also lays down methodological ground rules, holding that exactness should be sought only so far as the subject matter allows and that the young, whose lives are governed by feeling, are unsuited audiences for ethical argument.
grc.aristotle.physica: Aristotle's Physica, a Greek prose treatise of the fourth century BCE, is the work of the Aristotelian corpus devoted to natural philosophy. It opens with a methodological account of scientific knowledge and a review of earlier thinkers' positions on first principles, including an extended critique of the monism of Parmenides and Melissus. The eight books then treat the causes and principles of natural bodies, nature itself, motion, the infinite, place, void, and time, together with the continuity and divisibility of magnitudes and the kinds of change and their causes.
grc.aristotle.politics: A Greek prose treatise in political philosophy, the Politics of Aristotle opens by defining the polis as a community directed toward the highest good and argues that the city exists by nature, that man is by nature a political animal, and that rule over slaves differs in kind from political and royal rule. From an analysis of the household, the village and the city it proceeds to questions of slavery, property and citizenship, and to a classification of constitutions, including democracy, oligarchy, kingship and tyranny. Later portions examine the causes of constitutional change, the conditions under which regimes are preserved or destroyed, and the best constitution together with the education proper to its citizens.
grc.aristotle.αριστοτέλους_φυσικά_προβλήματα: A Greek collection of natural and medical problems attributed to Aristotle and of uncertain date, transmitted under the title 'Physical Problems: a collection by kind'. It is arranged as a sequence of short question-and-answer units, each opening with a 'Why...?' question and followed by a proposed explanation. The opening problems ask why excess and deficiency cause disease, why changes of season, winds and climate aggravate, settle or provoke illness, and why particular weather patterns bring fevers, eye inflammations and other ailments. The explanations appeal to balance and imbalance among bodily qualities and humours such as bile and phlegm, and to the effects of heat, cold, moisture and dryness on the body.
grc.aristotle.φυσιογνωμονικά: The Physiognomonica is a Greek treatise on physiognomy attributed to Aristotle and of uncertain date. Its opening argument holds that body and soul undergo their affections together, so that a given disposition necessarily accompanies a given bodily form, and that character can accordingly be read from outward signs. The work surveys and criticises earlier physiognomical methods, drawing on animal kinds, bodily resemblance, ethnic types, and visible emotions, before setting out its own procedure and cataloguing the signs taken from movements, shapes, colours, facial expression, hair, skin, voice, flesh, individual body parts, and the overall frame of the body.
grc.arrian.cynegeticus: A short Greek prose treatise on hunting by Arrian, the Cynegeticus presents itself as a supplement to Xenophon's treatise of the same name, whose author it judges to have been unacquainted with Celtic dogs and with Scythian and Libyan horses. After an opening table of chapters, the work describes the appearance, speed, and temperament of the Celtic hound, the selection, feeding, exercise, tethering, and breeding of dogs, and the pursuit and capture of hares without nets, as the Celts hunt. Later chapters treat the hunting of deer and other large game, the Libyan practice of taking big quarry with horses, and the ages at which dogs should be brought into the field. The treatise closes with injunctions that hunters sacrifice to Artemis, followed by Homeric passages adduced in support of honoring the discoverers of useful arts.
grc.bacchylides.dithyrambs: The Dithyrambs of Bacchylides are choral lyric poems in ancient Greek that survive in fragmentary condition, many pieces beginning or breaking off mid-line with lacunae supplied in brackets and metrical scansion recorded above the verses. Their subjects are drawn from heroic myth, including Menelaus and Odysseus among the Trojans at an assembly summoned before Priam, the burning of Oechalia and the fate of Deianira upon learning that Iole is to enter her house, and hymnic passages celebrating Apollo and Urania at Delos and Pytho. Alongside the narrative sections stand gnomic passages on Zeus, Dike, Eunomia and the destructive power of Hybris, and the collection also gathers shorter remains too incomplete to yield continuous sense.
grc.bacchylides.epinicians: The Epinicians gather the victory odes of the Greek lyric poet Bacchylides, songs in lyric metre composed for choruses in honour of victors at athletic contests. Each poem typically pairs praise of the victor, his family and his city with an extended mythological narrative drawn from heroic legend, as in an ode that opens with an address to the Pierian maidens and goes on to recount Minos' arrival with fifty ships and the Cretan host. Many of the odes are preserved only in fragmentary form, with long lacunae interrupting both metre and sense, while others survive as short excerpts.
grc.basil_of_caesarea.epistulae: A Greek collection of letters by Basil of Caesarea, the fourth-century bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia. The correspondence opens with letters to Gregory of Nazianzus that recall their studies at Athens, question whether fortune and necessity rather than human choice govern events, and recount the writer's travels after leaving the city. A following letter defends withdrawal from the world, setting out the discipline of the solitary life in terms of silence, scriptural reading, prayer, fasting, simple diet, and night vigils as the means of purifying the soul. Elsewhere the collection ranges more widely, addressing friends, clergy, and civic officials on personal consolation, ascetic counsel, and the affairs of the church.
grc.bion_of_phlossa.epitaphius: A Greek lament for the dying Adonis ascribed to Bion of Phlossa, built on the ritual refrain 'Woe for Adonis, the beautiful Adonis is dead.' The poem describes the hunter's mortal thigh wound, Aphrodite's frantic grief as she abandons her toys and her guise as a goddess, her farewell address to the dying youth, her appeal to Persephone in the underworld, and the transformation of his blood into roses and her tears into anemones. Nymphs, rivers, springs, oaks and the Erotes join the mourning, and the closing lines give instructions for the dead youth's funeral, ordering perfumes, garlands and the ceremonial laying-out of his body in the purple robes in which he once slept.
grc.bion_of_phlossa.epithalamium: A short fragmentary Greek poem attributed to Bion of Phlossa and preserved under the title Epithalamium. Written in Doric literary hexameters, it opens as a bucolic dialogue in which a speaker asks what song he should perform, then takes up the story of Achilles concealed among the daughters of Lycomedes on Skyros, disguised as a girl and secretly joined to Deidameia. The surviving lines also recall Paris' abduction of Helen and the gathering of the Achaeans, and the poem breaks off in the middle of a speech to Deidameia.
grc.callimachus.epigrams: The Epigrams of Callimachus gather short Greek poems, most in elegiac couplets, on sepulchral, dedicatory, erotic, and literary themes. Among them are epitaphs for individuals such as Saon of Acanthus, dedications including a shell offered to Arsinoe, and verses on poets, books, and brevity, with many pieces cast as the direct speech of the dead, of dedicators, or of the poet himself. The collection is transmitted as a single sequence of epigrams without book division.
grc.callimachus.hecala: The Hecale is a short Greek epic poem (epyllion) by the Hellenistic poet Callimachus, surviving only in fragments quoted by ancient scholiasts, lexicographers, epigrammatists, and miscellanists. Its narrative told how the old Athenian woman Hecale received Theseus with hospitality on the eve of his contest with the Marathonian bull, and how Theseus honoured her after her death. The fragments combine narrative hexameters, including scenes of omens, birds, weather, and rustic fare, with quotations and comments from later sources that identify lines and explain rare words.
grc.callimachus.hymns: A collection of six hymns in Greek dactylic hexameter by the poet Callimachus. The poems address Zeus, Apollo, Artemis, the island of Delos, Athena at her bath, and Demeter, combining praise of the gods with divine biography, aetiological episodes, and scenes of cult. The collection opens with a hymn to Zeus that weighs rival traditions of his birth on Crete and in Arcadia before recounting his rise to kingship among the gods.
grc.claudius_ptolemaeus.μαθηματικὴ_σύνταξις: The Μαθηματικὴ Σύνταξις is a comprehensive treatise on mathematical astronomy in Greek by Claudius Ptolemy, better known in the later tradition as the Almagest. Its preface, addressed to a certain Syrus, follows Aristotle in dividing theoretical philosophy into the physical, the mathematical and the theological, and argues that mathematics alone yields secure knowledge of the heavens. The work treats in turn the relation of the earth to the heavens, the motions of the sun and moon, the sphere of the fixed stars and the five planets, each part resting on observations and geometrical demonstrations. Book 1 opens with proofs that the heavens revolve spherically and that the earth, spherical and without translatory motion at the centre, bears the ratio of a point to the stellar sphere, and supplies tables of chords and of the obliquity of the ecliptic.
grc.clement.exhortation: A Greek Christian exhortatory discourse attributed to Clement and of uncertain date, written as direct second-person counsel on the ordered life of the believer. It instructs the hearer to cultivate quietness in word and deed, to speak gently and measure his speech, to honor elders, and to guard against anger, pride, gluttony, and drunkenness. All works and words are to be referred to God and to Christ, accompanied by prayer and hymns by day and night, while sickness and hardship are to be borne with trust in divine providence.
grc.clement_of_alexandria.protrepticus: The Protrepticus of Clement of Alexandria, a Greek Christian exhortation urging conversion away from Greek religion. Its opening chapter rehearses the myths of Amphion, Arion, Orpheus and Eunomus, treating Greek music and myth as bewitching fictions, and opposes to them the 'new song' of the divine Logos, which alone tames humanity and harmonises the cosmos. The argument sets quotations from Greek poets and mythic lore against biblical and apostolic citations, attacks the mysteries of Cithaeron and Helicon as rites of error, and directs the hearer from those mountains toward Zion and the prophetic word.
grc.demetrius.elocutione: A Greek treatise on prose composition, transmitted under the Latin title De elocutione (On Style) and attributed to Demetrius; its date is uncertain. The work analyses how prose discourse is divided into kōla and commata, the fitting length of clauses, and the construction of periodic sentences, illustrating its points with quotations from Hecataeus, Xenophon, Plato, Homer, Archilochus and Anacreon. Its opening chapters treat short and long clauses, the aphoristic brevity exemplified by sayings such as 'know thyself', and the effect produced by concise, abrupt composition, termed the komma. The treatise goes on to distinguish and characterise different styles of prose, including the plain, the grand, the elegant and the forceful.
grc.demosthenes.against_aphobus_3: An Athenian forensic speech of Demosthenes, the third of his orations arising from the disputes with his guardians Aphobus, Demophon, and Therippides over his father's estate. Written for a suit for false witness brought against Aphobus after the earlier guardianship trials, it opens in answer to Aphobus's defence, rehearses the stripping of the patrimony, the house, the farm, the furniture, and the slaves, and then concentrates on a single deposition concerning a slave whom Aphobus had acknowledged to be a free man of Miletus. The speaker challenges that testimony, recalls the examinations and the seizure of the property, and argues that the verdict must turn on whether he or Aphobus is deceiving the judges.
grc.demosthenes.against_boeotus_2: An Athenian forensic speech in Greek, transmitted in the Demosthenic corpus as the second oration Against Boeotus. The speaker, contesting a claim on his deceased father's estate, argues that Boeotus and his brother Pamphilus were fraudulently passed off as the old man's sons through the machinations and perjury of their mother Plangon. He recounts his mother's first marriage and its dowry arrangements, the deceptive oath sworn at the Delphinium, his father's refusal to acknowledge the pair, and their forced introduction to the phrateres, presenting the whole inheritance dispute as the consequence of that deception.
grc.demosthenes.against_midias: A forensic oration by Demosthenes, composed for delivery before an Athenian jury in a prosecution of Meidias for hubris. The speaker, who had served as choregos at the Dionysia, recounts the blows and other violent outrages he suffered from Meidias during the festival, together with the assembly's vote by which the people sanctioned his prosecution. The speech cites the laws governing probolai arising from offences at the Dionysia and other festivals, and argues that the case concerns not the speaker's private injuries alone but the protection of all citizens from unpunished outrage.
grc.demosthenes.against_onetor_30: A short forensic speech in the Demosthenic corpus, written in Attic Greek for delivery before an Athenian jury in a private suit against Onetor, brother-in-law of Aphobus and son of Timocrates. The speaker, engaged in prolonged litigation to recover the estate of which Aphobus had been guardian, argues that Onetor never paid the dowry promised with his sister, that her reported abandonment and the assessment of a farm in lieu of it were a sham to shield Aphobus' property, and he supports the claim with witnesses, challenges, and the threat of torture evidence for slaves. Readers of intertexts will find it valuable for its legal vocabulary (apoleipsis, apotimēma, basanos), its rhetoric of character and shamelessness, and its place within the Demosthenic sequence of orations arising from the guardianship dispute.
grc.demosthenes.against_phormio: An Athenian forensic speech of Demosthenes, composed for a maritime commercial suit before the dikasts in the fourth century BC. The speaker, Chrysippus, argues against a paragraphe entered to bar his claim, holding that the case is admissible under the laws governing written contracts. The underlying dispute concerns a loan of twenty minas advanced to Phormio for a trading voyage to the Bosporus, the wreck of the ship belonging to Lampis, and Phormio's assertion that he repaid the money to Lampis there; the speech narrates the contract, the clandestine sub-loan at the Peiraieus, and the supporting testimony.
grc.demosthenes.against_polycles: Against Polycles is a forensic speech transmitted in the Demosthenic corpus, addressed to an Athenian jury in a dispute between the speaker and Polycles over the exchange of a trierarchy. The speaker recounts how the assembly, amid a naval crisis involving events in the Pontus and the northern Aegean, ordered the launching of the fleet, and how he fitted out a trireme at his own expense, serving for five months and six days beyond his term and making an advance payment of the war tax. He prosecutes Polycles for refusing to take over the ship when his own turn came, contesting the opposing arguments about whether the laws governing trierarchic service are binding. The speech cites decrees of the council and assembly and supports its narrative with witness testimony.
grc.demosthenes.against_stephanus_2: A short Attic forensic speech attributed to Demosthenes, the second of two speeches against Stephanus in the litigation over the estate of Pasion. The speaker prosecutes Stephanus for false testimony given in the case against Phormion, arguing that the witnesses' statements about the sealed chest and the wills were fabricated, heard at second hand, and contrary to the laws on evidence, several of which are quoted. The oration repeatedly takes up the defense claim that the evidence amounted to a challenge rather than testimony, and seeks to prove from documents and statutes that the testimony was perjured.
grc.demosthenes.against_timocrates: A forensic speech attributed to Demosthenes, of uncertain date, delivered in an Athenian prosecution against a law proposed by Timocrates. The speaker, an associate of Euctemon, seeks the annulment of a measure under which debtors to the state could evade imprisonment and the penalties fixed for their offences by offering security. The argument recounts the earlier denunciation of Androtion and his colleagues for retaining sacred and public monies, and contends that Timocrates' law would nullify the judgments of the council, the assembly, and the courts and leave the common funds open to plunder.
grc.demosthenes.exordia: The Exordia (Prooimia) form a collection of prefatory openings for deliberative speeches, transmitted among the orations of the Athenian orator Demosthenes of the fourth century BC. Each entry is a self-contained proem rather than a complete oration: the speaker claims the floor in the assembly, asks for an unprejudiced hearing, defends plain and disinterested counsel, or urges the Athenians to weigh advice before acting. The proems are addressed throughout to the assembly as 'men of Athens' and vary in theme, though all serve to introduce civic deliberation.
grc.demosthenes.for_phormio: A forensic oration of Demosthenes in Attic Greek, delivered in an Athenian court on behalf of Phormion, the freedman and former manager of the banker Pasion, against a twenty-talent suit brought by Pasion's son Apollodoros. Because Phormion is presented as unpractised in speaking, the case is argued by supporters, who maintain that the action is inadmissible under a preliminary plea (paragraphē). The argument rehearses the lease of Pasion's bank and shield factory, the terms of his will, the marriage of Phormion to Pasion's widow and his guardianship of the younger son, the subsequent division of the estate, and the conduct of the bank's business under Phormion's management.
grc.demosthenes.olynthiac_2: The Second Olynthiac is a deliberative oration in Ancient Greek addressed to the Athenian assembly, transmitted among the public speeches of Demosthenes. The speaker takes the Olynthians' willingness to fight Philip of Macedon as a sign of divine favour toward Athens and an opportunity not to be squandered. Reviewing how Philip grew great by deceiving the Olynthians, the Athenians, the Thessalians, and the Phocians in turn, he argues that power built on perjury and injustice must eventually collapse, and closes by urging prompt aid for Olynthus and the sending of an embassy to the Thessalians.
grc.demosthenes.on_organization: A short deliberative oration in Attic Greek, transmitted under the name of Demosthenes with the title 'On Organization' (Peri syntaxeōs) and of uncertain date. Addressed to the Athenian assembly, it sets aside the quarrel over the two obols of assembly pay, on which the speaker says the citizens fix all their attention, arguing that the money matters less than the habit it fosters. The speaker proposes instead that the city organize itself for war, drawing hoplites, cavalry, and the rest of the citizen body into a single standing arrangement under its own generals, supported by its own revenues and those of its allies rather than by mercenaries. He closes with the charge that the Athenians' ears have been corrupted by pleasant talk, and that the city must first be trained to hear what is best for it.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_chersonese: A Greek deliberative oration addressed to the Athenian assembly and handed down among the speeches of Demosthenes. The speaker reports that Philip of Macedon has now spent eleven months campaigning in Thrace and may soon move against Byzantium, and he defends the general Diopeithes, whose conduct in the Chersonese had drawn accusations in Athens. Against opponents who counsel peace so long as Philip refrains from Attica, he argues that Philip's seizures of Greek and barbarian lands alike have already made defence necessary, and he warns that delay will leave the city powerless to protect the Hellespont. The opening plea that counsellors speak from the city's advantage rather than from private enmity or favour frames the speech's sustained attack on its critics.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_crown: A forensic oration in Attic Greek by the Athenian orator and statesman Demosthenes, composed for the public suit in which Aeschines prosecuted Ctesiphon for proposing an honorary crown for Demosthenes. Speaking as Ctesiphon's advocate, Demosthenes treats the trial as a shared contest and uses his defence of the decree as an occasion for a full answer to Aeschines' accusations and an account of his own life and political conduct. The speech opens with a prayer to the gods, an appeal for impartial hearing under the laws of Solon, and reflections on the disadvantages of answering a personal enemy before proceeding to rebut the charges concerning his citizenship and public career.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_false_embassy: A forensic speech in Greek by the Athenian orator Demosthenes, delivered in prosecution of Aeschines for his conduct on an embassy to Philip of Macedon. The speaker charges that Aeschines gave the assembly false reports of Philip's intentions, gave corrupt counsel, neglected his instructions, and took bribes together with Philocrates, and he frames the case around what the envoy reported, what he persuaded, what he was ordered to do, and whether he acted without payment. The proem stresses the danger that lapse of time and familiarity with the alleged wrongs may have dulled the jurors' sense of them, and the speech goes on to review Aeschines' earlier political career and his dealings with Philip.
grc.demosthenes.philippic_1: An assembly speech by the Athenian orator Demosthenes, the first of the speeches known as the Philippics, directed against Philip II of Macedon. Addressing the citizens as 'men of Athens', the speaker argues that the city's misfortunes stem from its own inaction rather than from Philip's strength, citing the earlier Spartan hegemony as proof that vigilance determines success and recalling the loss of Amphipolis, Pydna, Potidaea and Methone. He calls on each citizen, whether wealthy or of military age, to serve the city in person and to abandon the delays and apathy that have allowed Philip's power to grow.
grc.demosthenes.philippic_3: Philippic 3 is the third of the Philippic orations of the Athenian orator Demosthenes, a deliberative speech delivered before the Athenian assembly. The speaker reviews Philip of Macedon's conduct since the peace was made, arguing that his actions against the Olynthians, the Phocians, the people of Pherae in Thessaly and the Oreians amount to open war, whatever the nominal settlement may be. He traces the city's difficulties to its own negligence and to the flatterers who fill the assembly, and urges frank counsel and vigorous preparation while the situation can still be set right.
grc.demosthenes.philippic_4: A Greek deliberative oration by Demosthenes, cast as an address to the Athenian Assembly, arguing that Philip II of Macedon has broken the peace and is effectively at war with Athens. The speaker reviews a series of Philip's aggressions in Thrace, Euboea, Megara, and central Greece, and blames Athenian inattention and ease for his successive gains. The closing section contends that Philip's hostility is aimed above all at the Athenian democracy itself, which stands as the one obstacle to his secure rule, and urges the city to prepare accordingly.
grc.diogenianus_of_heraclea.παροιμίαι_δημώδε: A Greek prose collection of popular proverbs transmitted under the heading 'Diogenianus on proverbs' and drawn from the compilation of Diogenianus of Heraclea, an author of uncertain date. An opening treatise discusses how the word paroimia arose and distinguishes proverbs from the various kinds of ainos or fable, including the Aesopic, Carian, Sybaritic, Cyprian, and Libyan forms, with illustrative passages from poets such as Archilochus, Homer, and Aristophanes. The main body arranges proverbs alphabetically, each entry followed by a brief explanation of its meaning and, in many cases, an anecdote or myth accounting for its origin.
grc.dionysius_calliphontis.dionysii_callipho: A description of Greece in Greek prose, transmitted under the title Anagraphe tes Hellados and attributed to Dionysius son of Calliphon, an author of uncertain date. The work is cast as an address to one Theophrastus and promises a rapid but comprehensive survey of the cities, sanctuaries, mountains, rivers, islands, harbours and coastal voyages of the Greek world. Beginning at Ambracia, it proceeds region by region through Acarnania, Aetolia, Locris, Phocis, Boeotia and Megaris toward the Peloponnese, giving distances in stadia and noting landmarks such as Delphi with its oracle, the Euripus, and the sanctuary of Trophonius at Lebadeia. The account continues with Crete and further island material, with lacunae marked in the course of the survey.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_isocrate: Dionysius of Halicarnassus' short Greek treatise De Isocrate combines a biographical notice of Isocrates with a critical appraisal of his prose style. The biography records Isocrates' Athenian birth in the 86th Olympiad, his schooling under Prodicus, Gorgias and Tisias, his abandonment of public speaking for written political discourse, the wealth and fame of his school, and his death by voluntary abstinence a few days after the battle of Chaeronea at nearly a hundred years of age, drawing in part on Isocrates' own remarks in the Panathenaicus. The stylistic survey compares his diction, periodic composition and figures with those of Lysias, judging his language to fall short of Lysias' in charm and purity while surpassing it in elevation and grandeur, and closes by likening Isocrates' rhetoric to the monumental art of Polycleitus and Phidias and Lysias' to that of Calamis and Callimachus.
grc.epictetus.discourses: The Discourses of Epictetus, preserved in Greek prose and written down by his pupil Arrian, who explains in an opening letter to Lucius Gellius that he recorded what he heard in his master's own words as notes for later use rather than as polished composition. The individual discourses take the form of exhortations and dialogues examining the rational faculty's power to test impressions, the distinction between what lies within one's control and what does not, and equanimity in the face of death, exile, and imprisonment. Examples drawn from Roman contemporary life, including figures such as Nero, Agrippinus, and Thrasea, illustrate the arguments throughout.
grc.epictetus.enchiridion: The Enchiridion, or 'Handbook', is a compact Greek manual of Stoic ethical instruction drawn from the teaching of the philosopher Epictetus and traditionally credited to his pupil Arrian. It consists of a sequence of brief chapters of precepts and maxims, opening with the division of things into those that are and are not 'up to us', judgment, impulse, desire, and aversion on one side; the body, possessions, and reputation on the other. Later chapters treat the disciplined handling of impressions, the proper management of desire and aversion, equanimity toward illness, loss, and death, and the conduct of ordinary tasks and relationships.
grc.epicurus.epistula_ad_herodotum: A Greek prose letter from Epicurus to Herodotus, preserved among the Epicurean works transmitted by Diogenes Laertius. In it the author offers, as the opening states, a compact and memorisable epitome of his larger writings on nature for those unable to work through the longer books. The contents set out the fundamentals of Epicurean physics: bodies and void, the indestructible atoms and their motion, the infinity of the universe and of worlds, sense perception and preconceptions as criteria of judgement, and the films of images (eidola) given off from solid objects.
grc.epicurus.gnomologium_vaticanum_epicureum: A short Greek collection of Epicurean aphorisms, transmitted as the Gnomologium Vaticanum Epicureum or Vatican Sayings and attributed to Epicurus. The maxims give compressed formulations on the blessedness and impassivity of the gods, the irrelevance of death, pleasure and pain, the classification of desires, friendship, justice, fate, dreams, and the place of natural philosophy in the undisturbed life. Among the sayings stands a first-person address to Fortune renouncing subjection to circumstance.
grc.euclid.elements: Euclid's Elements is a Greek mathematical treatise that sets out geometry as a deductive system. It begins with definitions of the point, line, straight line, surface, plane, angle, circle, and rectilineal figures, together with five postulates and five common notions. The body of the work consists of propositions, each stated as a construction or theorem and accompanied by a formal proof; the opening propositions give elementary constructions, such as the equilateral triangle erected on a given straight line and the transfer of a length to a given point.
grc.euripides.alcestis: A Greek tragedy by Euripides of the classical period, the Alcestis dramatizes the story of Alcestis, wife of Admetus of Pherae, who consents to die in her husband's stead when the Fates require a substitute for his death. The opening scene sets Apollo, who once served Admetus as a herdsman and tricked the Fates into sparing him, against Thanatos, who arrives to escort Alcestis to the house of Hades. The action proceeds through the household's mourning and Admetus' quarrel with his father Pheres to the arrival of Heracles, who wrestles with Death and restores Alcestis, still silent, to her home.
grc.euripides.andromache: Andromache is a Greek tragedy by Euripides, its date of first production uncertain. The play takes its name from Hector's widow, who as a slave of Neoptolemus has borne him a son and now, threatened with death by his Spartan wife Hermione and by Menelaus, takes refuge at the altar of Thetis in Pharsalia. Peleus arrives to rescue Andromache and her child, while a messenger later reports Neoptolemus' death at Delphi, and Thetis appears as dea ex machina to ordain marriages and a cult for Peleus. The action thus moves from a household intrigue in Thessaly to the demise of Achilles' son and the divine settlement that closes the play.
grc.euripides.bacchae: The Bacchae is a Greek tragedy by Euripides dramatizing the arrival of the god Dionysus in Thebes. Disguised in mortal form, Dionysus comes to establish his rites and to vindicate his birth from Semele and Zeus, punishing the royal house of Cadmus for denying his divinity. King Pentheus refuses to acknowledge the new cult, and the god leads him to Mount Cithaeron, where the maddened Theban women, including his own mother Agave, tear him apart. A chorus of Asiatic Bacchants brought from Lydia and Phrygia accompanies the action with lyric odes in praise of Dionysiac worship.
grc.euripides.cyclops: Euripides' Cyclops, the only complete satyr play to survive from Greek tragedy, recasts the Cyclops episode of Odyssey 9 as burlesque: Odysseus and his crew, blown off course to Aetna, find Silenus and his satyrs enslaved to the man-eating Polyphemus and eventually engineer the giant's blinding with wine and a stake. The opening speech of Silenus recounts Dionysus' wanderings and his punishment of the Tyrrhenian pirates before turning to the satyrs' servile life in the Cyclops' cave. Readers of intertexts will find a comic counterpoint to Homer's narrative with sustained verbal engagement with the epic, as well as a rare witness to satyr-drama conventions and to Dionysiac myth on the tragic stage.
grc.euripides.fragmenta: Fragments of Greek tragedy by Euripides, comprising single lines, gnomic sayings, and longer passages of dialogue drawn from plays that do not survive complete. The material is arranged under titles of individual lost plays, among them the Πάνακτος, the Ἄκρατες, and the Ἄρρητος κόρη, and touches on themes such as wealth and poverty, noble birth, slavery, old age, and the power of Aphrodite. Among the longer excerpts are speeches and exchanges involving Priam and Hecuba and scenes connected with the house of Oedipus.
grc.euripides.hecuba: Hecuba is a Greek tragedy by the Athenian dramatist Euripides, composed in the fifth century BC, dramatising the fate of Priam's widow after the fall of Troy. The prologue is spoken by the ghost of her son Polydorus, murdered on the Thracian shore by the king Polymestor, to whom he had been sent with treasure for safekeeping. The action follows Hecuba, now a slave among the Greek victors, as she mourns the sacrifice of her daughter Polyxena demanded at Achilles' tomb and then takes vengeance on Polymestor, so that the deaths of her two children frame the play's twin movements of grief and retribution.
grc.euripides.helen: Euripides' Helen is a Greek tragedy of the fifth century BC that dramatizes the tradition in which the Helen taken to Troy was only a phantom, while the real woman waited in Egypt. The opening prologue, spoken by Helen herself, recounts the judgment of the goddesses, Hermes' concealment of her at the house of Proteus, and the great war fought over her counterfeit likeness. The ensuing action centres on her reunion with the shipwrecked Menelaus and their attempt to escape Egypt before King Theoclymenus can compel her into marriage.
grc.euripides.heracleidae: A classical Greek tragedy by Euripides, the Heracleidae dramatizes the flight of Heracles' children to Attica and their reception there as suppliants. The aged Iolaus and Heracles' mother Alcmena protect the fugitives, whom Eurystheus of Argos demands back by herald, and Demophon, son of Theseus, takes up their defense in war. The conflict turns on the voluntary sacrifice of one of Heracles' daughters, and the play closes with Eurystheus captured and condemned by Alcmena, his burial at Athens accompanied by a prophecy that his tomb will guard the city. The date of first production is uncertain.
grc.euripides.hippolytus: A Greek tragedy by Euripides dramatizing the destruction of Hippolytus, the chaste son of Theseus who honors Artemis and scorns Aphrodite. Aphrodite's prologue announces her revenge: Phaedra, Theseus' wife, conceives a hopeless passion for her stepson, and after the nurse betrays the secret Phaedra hangs herself, leaving a tablet that falsely accuses Hippolytus of assault. Theseus curses his son with one of the three boons granted him by Poseidon, and Hippolytus is mortally injured when a bull from the sea panics his horses, dying just before Artemis appears to reveal the truth. The action is set at Troezen and includes a hymn to Artemis sung by Hippolytus' hunting retinue and a closing scene of reconciliation between father and dying son.
grc.euripides.iphigenia_tauris: A Greek tragedy of uncertain date by the fifth-century BC Athenian poet Euripides. The play takes its name from the land of the Taurians, where Iphigenia, rescued by Artemis from sacrifice at Aulis, serves as priestess in the goddess's temple and must offer any Greek who lands there as a human victim. The opening scene gives Iphigenia's account of her family's history and her own deliverance, and introduces Orestes and Pylades, who have come by sea to carry off the statue of Artemis and are seized on arrival. The drama proceeds through the brother and sister's recognition of one another and their flight from the Taurian king Thoas with the goddess's image.
grc.euripides.orestes: Orestes, a Greek tragedy by Euripides, is presented here in Gilbert Murray's Oxford text of the Euripidis Fabulae (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1913) and runs to 1,705 lines. The play opens on the sixth day after Orestes, urged on by Apollo and aided by his sister Electra and his friend Pylades, has killed their mother Clytemnestra, and follows his collapse into madness, the Argive assembly's vote of death, the plot against Helen and the seizure of Hermione as a hostage, and the concluding settlement imposed by Apollo, who deifies Helen and ordains Orestes' marriage to Hermione and trial at Athens. Its prologue recapitulates the whole cursed genealogy of the house, Tantalus, Pelops, Atreus, Thyestes, Agamemnon, and the drama recasts the matricide legend treated in Aeschylus' Oresteia with pointedly revisionist emphases. The result is a fertile source of verbal and thematic parallels for readers tracing the Orestes myth, the rhetoric of guilt and madness, and the representation of divine justice across Greek literature.
grc.euripides.phoenissae: A Greek tragedy by Euripides on the house of Thebes, tracing the fortunes of the line of Cadmus from the marriage of Laius and Jocasta to the war of the Seven against Thebes. The prologue is spoken by Jocasta, who recounts the oracle warning Laius against fathering a child, the exposure of the infant Oedipus, his unwitting killing of his father and marriage to his mother, and the birth of Eteocles, Polyneices, Antigone and Ismene. The main action dramatises the brothers' broken agreement to alternate rule, Polyneices' return at the head of an Argive army, and the ruin that overtakes the city and its royal house.
grc.euripides.rhesus: Rhesus is a Greek tragedy of uncertain date, transmitted among the plays of Euripides. Set in the Trojan camp during the war with the Achaeans, it follows the alarm raised by a night raid, Hector's preparations for battle, and the exploits of Odysseus and Diomedes, who infiltrate the enemy lines and kill the newly arrived Thracian king Rhesus, carrying off his horses. The closing scenes bring Athena's intervention and the lament of the Muse over her dead son.
grc.euripides.trojan_women: A Greek tragedy by Euripides, the Trojan Women stages the morning after the sack of Troy: Poseidon opens the play above the ruined city, and Hecuba, Cassandra, Andromache, and Helen learn their allotment to Greek masters while Polyxena lies sacrificed on Achilles' tomb and the boy Astyanax is brought in for burial. The drama unfolds as a chain of laments and formal speeches rather than a continuous plot, with the captive women's dirges over Priam, Hector, and the fallen city forming its structural spine. Its laments for Troy's women, its judgement of Helen, and its catalogue of Trojan suffering draw on the epic tradition of the city's fall and became a recurrent source of verbal and thematic echoes for later ancient drama and for post-classical retellings of the Trojan story.
grc.flavius_josephus.antiquitates_judaicae: Antiquitates Judaicae ('Jewish Antiquities') is a twenty-book historical work in Greek prose by Flavius Josephus, written after the author had separately composed his account of the Jewish war against Rome. In its preface Josephus explains that the work sets out the whole ancient history and constitution of the Jewish people, rendered from the Hebrew writings into Greek, and that its completion was urged by his patron Epaphroditus. The narrative runs from the creation of the world and the laws attributed to Moses through the biblical and later periods, carrying the account down to the final years before the war with Rome.
grc.flavius_josephus.josephi_vita: The Vita is a short Greek autobiography by Flavius Josephus, composed largely as a defence of his conduct during the Jewish revolt against Rome. Josephus traces his ancestry to the priestly aristocracy of Jerusalem and, through his mother, to the Hasmonean royal house, then describes his education, his survey of the Pharisee, Sadducee, and Essene sects, and his three years spent with the desert ascetic Bannus. He recounts his voyage to Rome to secure the release of imprisoned priests, surviving a shipwreck in the Adriatic, and his return to find Judaea sliding into rebellion. The greater part of the work defends his command in Galilee against unnamed accusers, setting out his dealings with the Jerusalem authorities, the revolutionary factions, and the Roman forces.
grc.gaius_romanus.fragmenta: Greek fragments ascribed to Gaius, an ecclesiastical writer of Rome, preserved through quotation in Eusebius's Ecclesiastical History (books ii, iii, v and vi). The principal piece derives from a dialogue conducted at Rome during the episcopate of Zephyrinus against Proclus, an adherent of the Phrygian heresy; in it Gaius points to the trophies of the apostles Peter and Paul at the Vatican and on the Ostian road, and reckons thirteen epistles of the apostle Paul, not counting that to the Hebrews. The shorter excerpts recount the delusion and penance of the confessor Natalius, who accepted a heretical bishopric for a monthly stipend, and attack sectaries who emended the divine scriptures, practised syllogistic logic, and admired Aristotle, Theophrastus and Galen.
grc.galen.de_atra_bile: A brief Greek treatise by the second-century AD physician Galen on black bile, the humour that ancient medicine regarded as a cause of melancholy and other disorders. The opening surveys earlier accounts of the humour, crediting Hippocrates with the first useful remarks, censuring Erasistratus for omitting the subject altogether, and noting the discussions by Pleistonicus, Praxagoras, Philitimus and Rufus of Ephesus. The body of the work distinguishes the humours by colour, taste and coagulation, blood, phlegm, and yellow bile in its watery, yolk-like and leek-green varieties, before turning to black bile proper, its generation from the burnt residue of blood and yellow bile, and the diagnostic marks separating its harmful evacuations from harmless dark discharges.
grc.galen.de_dignoscendis_pulsibus: De Dignoscendis Pulsibus ('On the Diagnosis of Pulses') is a Greek medical treatise by the physician Galen dealing with how the pulse is to be recognised and distinguished by touch. The work presents itself as the second of four parts of a complete account of pulse theory, the first part covering the genera and species of pulses, the third their causes, and the fourth their significance for practice, a division it argues has left diagnosis comparatively neglected by both philosophers and physicians. It maintains that accurate diagnosis of diastole, systole, and the differing qualities, rhythms, and uniformity of the arterial beat demands many years of disciplined practice, and it illustrates this claim from Galen's own experience as a young student of medicine and his slow attainment of certainty in distinguishing the movements of the artery.
grc.galen.de_dignotione_ex_insomniis: A short Greek treatise on diagnosis from dreams by the physician Galen. It holds that dreams reveal the prevailing disposition of the body: visions of fire signal excess of yellow bile, of smoke, mist or darkness black bile, of rain an abundance of cold moisture, and of snow, ice or hail cold phlegm. Interpretation must take account of the timing of the dream and of food recently eaten, and must distinguish bodily indications from dreams arising from daily activities, from waking preoccupations, and from genuinely prophetic dreams. Illustrative cases include a man who dreamt his leg had turned to stone shortly before it was paralysed, and a wrestler seen standing in a pool of blood, taken to indicate a plethora requiring evacuation.
grc.galen.de_methodo_medendi: De Methodo Medendi ('On the Method of Healing') is a Greek treatise on therapeutics by Galen. Its opening section takes the form of a preface addressed to Hiero, in which the author explains his long hesitation to write on the therapeutic method, complains of an age in which patients favour obsequious and flattering physicians over the truly skilful, and delivers an extended invective against Thessalus, who professed to teach medicine in six months and vilified Hippocrates and the ancient Asclepiads. The preface also recalls the old rivalry among the medical schools of Cos, Cnidus and Italy, illustrating its argument with quotations from Hesiod on the two kinds of strife.
grc.galen.de_optima_doctrina: De Optima Doctrina ('On the Best Teaching') is a short Greek essay by the physician and philosopher Galen, directed against the Academic scepticism of Favorinus. It surveys the Academic doctrine of suspension of judgement (epochē) and the dispute over the 'cataleptic' impression, citing Favorinus's works and Carn­eades' arguments. Against the claim that nothing can be securely known, Galen defends sense perception and intellect as reliable criteria of truth and argues that a teacher must train pupils' judgement and correct their errors, in the manner of trainers, grammarians, geometers and other craftsmen, rather than unsettling their trust in the senses.
grc.galen.de_ossibus_ad_tirones: De Ossibus ad Tirones ('On Bones, for Beginners') is a short Greek treatise on osteology by Galen. It opens by arguing that a physician must know each bone in itself and in its arrangement with the others if he is to treat fractures and dislocations correctly, then defines the skeleton and the technical vocabulary of its connections: arthrosis and symphysis, the kinds and subdivisions of each, the forms of synarthrosis (suture, gomphosis, harmonia), and the unions made through cartilage, sinew or flesh, with a corresponding distinction among nerves, tendons and ligaments. The preliminary definitions concluded, the treatise proceeds to the bones individually, beginning with the skull.
grc.galen.de_rebus_boni_malique_suci: A short Greek medical treatise by Galen, known under the Latin title De rebus boni malique suci ('On the Good and Bad Juices'). It opens with an account of successive famines in provinces subject to Rome, describing the diseases, skin sores of many kinds, fevers, dysentery and mental disturbance, that arose when people were driven to eat unwholesome foods, and argues from such observations for the Hippocratic doctrine that diseased bodily humours are the cause of illness. It closes with an autobiographical passage in which Galen recounts his father's supervision of his diet in childhood, the recurring autumnal illnesses of his youth, and the regimen of moderation and exercise that he holds responsible for his continued good health.
grc.galen.de_semine: De Semine is a Greek medical treatise by Galen on the nature of seed. Its opening question asks what the use and power of semen are, and whether, as Hippocrates held, it possesses both a material and an active principle, or only the formative principle, as Aristotle maintained. To determine whether semen remains in the womb of a woman due to conceive, Galen reports observations of horses, dogs, donkeys, cattle, goats and sheep after mating, inquiries of women about sensations at conception, and dissections of pregnant animals, describing the uterus in Platonic terms as a creature that craves childbearing. He also rebuts self-styled Aristotelians and Peripatetics who, in his view, misread On the Generation of Animals, arguing that male semen contributes bodily substance to the embryo rather than mere motion and form.
grc.galen.de_typis: A short Greek medical treatise by the physician Galen, active in the second century CE, on fever types (typoi). The opening states Galen's aim of setting out the theory of periodicity more succinctly and definitively after the fuller treatments of others, and the work proceeds to define a typos as a recurrent pattern of tension and relaxation in disease. It classifies fevers as first or second, stationary or moving, simple or compound, and describes the quotidian, tertian, quartan, and semitertian fevers together with their symptoms, pulses, seasonal incidence, and dangers. The closing sections discuss rival explanations of the semitertian fever's name and duration, reporting the differing views of Hippocrates and Agathinus.
grc.galen.de_venereis_ap_oribasium: A short Greek treatise by Galen on sexual intercourse (aphrodisia) as part of the medical regimen, preserved under the title De Venereis in the excerpts of Oribasius. Against the Epicurean position that no use of intercourse is ever healthful, it holds that intercourse at suitably long intervals benefits the body when the constitution is in balance, neither overfull nor depleted, overheated nor chilled. It then distinguishes the effects of intercourse on strong and weak temperaments, notes the harm caused by retaining semen in certain bodily conditions, and prescribes corrective measures, including preparatory exercise, cold bathing in season, and moist, moderately warming foods taken afterwards.
grc.galen.quos_quibus_catharticis_medicament: A Greek treatise by the physician Galen (second century CE) on the purging of patients with cathartic drugs, addressing which persons should be purged, with which drugs, and at what season. Its argument is that the humour requiring evacuation, phlegm, yellow or black bile, or a serous excess, must be judged from the nature of the disease, with conditions such as podagra, apoplexy, epilepsy, melancholy, cancerous affections of the breast, and elephantiasis given as examples requiring catharsis, often at the onset of spring. The discussion goes on to cover preparation of the body through rest and moistening foods, preliminary trials with mild emetics before administering hellebore, the choice of upward or downward evacuation, the timing of doses in relation to paroxysms and critical days, the admixture of fragrant and cutting simples to blunt a drug's harshness, and the reasons for which a cathartic may fail to act.
grc.galen.thrasybulus_sive_utrum_medicinae_s: A short Greek treatise by Galen, cast as a discourse addressed to a certain Thrasybulus, on the question whether the healthful (to hygieinon) belongs to medicine or to gymnastics. The opening chapters record the speaker's reluctance to commit the argument to writing and insist that such problems be settled by logical method, starting from precise definitions of medicine, gymnastics, and the healthful, and distinguishing a thing's mere concept from its essence. The remaining chapters weigh rival definitions and analogies drawn from the crafts, such as building, weaving, and shoemaking, to show why the healthful cannot be assigned to either art without proof.
grc.galen.περὶ_τῶν_ἐν_ταῖς_τροφαῖς_δυνάμεων: A Greek medical treatise by Galen, On the Powers of Foods sets out the properties of foodstuffs and their effects on digestion and health, insisting that knowledge of a food's faculty rests on disciplined experience rather than on speculative causal argument. The opening chapters examine and correct earlier dietary writers, quoting Diocles and invoking Erasistratus and Mnesitheus, and the argument turns repeatedly to Hippocratic writings, above all the Epidemics and the book On Diet, whose attribution Galen weighs. Sustained discussion of digestibility, binding and purging foods, the humours, and the differing temperaments of individual bodies gives the work a dense web of verbal parallels with earlier Greek medicine. Readers of intertexts accordingly gain substantial quotation and adaptation of dietary writers otherwise preserved only in fragments.
grc.gorgias_of_leontini.ὑπέρ_παλαμήδους_ἀπολ: A Greek defense speech attributed to the rhetorician Gorgias of Leontini and of uncertain date. Cast as the apology of the mythological hero Palamedes at his trial, it answers the charge brought by Odysseus that he betrayed Greece to the barbarians, arguing that the alleged treason was impossible in its means, no meeting, interpreter, pledge, payment, or admission of the enemy into the camp could have escaped notice, and that neither tyranny, wealth, nor honor could have supplied a motive. The argument proceeds by systematically refuting each conceivable circumstance of the supposed crime and closes with an appeal to the speaker's past life and standing as witness to his character.
grc.gregory_of_nazianzus.christus_patiens: Christus Patiens is a Greek drama in tragic form on the passion of Christ, attributed to Gregory of Nazianzus and of uncertain date. Its prologue announces verses on the saving passion of Christ and on the disciple Judas, who betrayed the Lord with a treacherous kiss, and it places the Virgin Mary at the centre of the action as its chief mourner and first speaker. The dramatis personae also include Christ, John the theologian, Joseph, Nicodemus, Mary Magdalene, an angel, a chorus of maidens, the guard at the tomb, the synagogue of chief priests, and Pilate. The action runs from the betrayal and condemnation before Pilate through the crucifixion and the mother's lament to the burial and the events at the tomb.
grc.heraclitus_of_ephesus.fragmenta: The Fragmenta collect the surviving remains of Heraclitus of Ephesus, an early Greek philosopher whose sayings survive only as quotations embedded in later ancient authors. The fragments include the opening of his book on the logos, sayings on the ever-living fire and its transformations into sea and earth, on the harmony and strife of opposites, on the soul, on knowledge and human folly, and on ritual practices. Each fragment is accompanied by the source that transmits it, among them Sextus Empiricus, Aristotle, Plutarch, and Clement of Alexandria, together with numeration from earlier collections.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.catoptrica: The Catoptrica of Hero of Alexandria is a Greek treatise on mirrors and the reflection of sight. Its opening argument proceeds from the axiom that nature does nothing in vain to the conclusion that vision striking a mirror is reflected at equal angles. A geometrical proof then shows, by reductio with congruent triangles, that any path of vision making unequal angles at the mirror is longer than the path through equal angles. The work belongs to the ancient genre of catoptrics and treats the behaviour of reflected vision before plane and curved surfaces.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.dioptra: A Greek technical treatise in prose by Hero of Alexandria on the dioptra, a sighting instrument used in surveying. The opening chapters set out the practical uses of dioptrics for aqueducts, city walls, harbours, building, siege operations, astronomy, and geography, before describing in detail the construction of the instrument itself, with its screws, toothed drums, water levels, and auxiliary sighting rules and disks. Hero represents the work as an improvement on earlier treatments of the subject, offering corrected and simplified accounts where his predecessors had erred.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.geodaesia_sp: The Geodaesia is a short Greek treatise on land-measurement attributed to Hero of Alexandria and of uncertain date. It opens with definitions of elementary geometric terms, point, line, plane surface, angle, circle, diameter and the like, and then recounts that the invention of measurement arose among the Egyptians, whose field boundaries were effaced by the flooding of the Nile. The body of the work sets out the divisions and terminology of plane geometry, classifies the figures of measurement (triangles, squares, rhombi, trapezia, circles) together with their theorems, adds the corresponding solid figures such as the sphere, cone, cylinder and pyramid, and closes with rules of mensuration, including the triangle inequality and the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter as three and a seventh.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.pneumatica: The Pneumatica of Hero of Alexandria is a Greek technical treatise on devices and effects produced by the interplay of air, water, fire and earth, by an author of uncertain date. Its preface presents the work as a sequel to Hero's earlier four-book account of water clocks, gathering what the ancients handed down and adding the author's own discoveries, some devices serving the necessities of life and others displaying astonishing marvels. The opening section is devoted to physical theory, arguing from vessels, siphons, cupping glasses and a compressed-air sphere that void exists only as minute interspersed spaces within bodies rather than as continuous vacuum, and it appeals to the demonstrations of Archimedes on bodies in liquids.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.stereometrica: Stereometrica is a Greek handbook of solid mensuration attributed to Hero of Alexandria. It consists of rules and worked examples, expressed in Greek arithmetical notation, for finding the volumes and surface areas of spheres, cones, cylinders, and other figures, together with definitions of terms such as the axis of a sphere and the horizon circle. Several procedures rest on results drawn from Archimedes' On the Sphere and Cylinder, notably the relations of a circumscribing cylinder and of cubes on the diameter to the volume of a sphere, and the fourfold ratio of a sphere's surface to its greatest circle. The problems are phrased as step-by-step instructions to take, multiply, and divide concrete dimensions given in feet and fingers, each yielding a numerical answer.
grc.herodianus.συμπόσιον: A short collection of etymological and grammatical notes ascribed to the grammarian Herodian and transmitted under the title Symposium. The entries, most of them a single sentence, explain the derivation of individual Greek words, chiefly terms for foods, condiments, and vessels used at table, such as βολβός, ὄξος, τάριχος, and φιάλη, through phonetic change and analogy, occasionally citing Homer or the grammarian Philoxenus. Herodian is referred to by name throughout, and the work survives only in the form of these brief excerpts.
grc.herodotus.histories: The Histories of Herodotus of Halicarnassus, a prose work in Ionic Greek divided into nine books, opens with a programmatic statement that its purpose is to preserve the memory of the great deeds of Greeks and barbarians and to set out the cause of the war between them. The first book begins with Persian and Phoenician accounts of the mutual abductions of Io, Europa, Medea and Helen, before turning to Croesus of Lydia, the first ruler to subject Greeks to tribute. The narrative proceeds through ethnographic and geographical digressions to the rise of Persia and the great conflict between Greece and Persia.
grc.hesiod.theogony: The Theogony is a Greek poem in dactylic hexameters ascribed to the poet Hesiod, of uncertain date. Its proem describes the Muses of Mount Helicon appearing to Hesiod as he shepherded on the mountain, granting him a scepter of flowering laurel and the power to sing of things that were, are, and are to come. The poem then unfolds the origins of the cosmos and the genealogy of the gods, tracing the succession from Chaos, Gaia, and Uranus through Cronus to the supreme rule of Zeus, and incorporates extensive catalogues of Titans, sea deities, monsters, and the offspring of Night. It closes with an account of the goddesses who joined with mortal men and bore them children.
grc.hippocrates.aphorismi: Aphorismi is a collection of concise medical maxims in Greek, traditionally attributed to Hippocrates and counted among the works of the Hippocratic Corpus, of uncertain date. Its numbered sections give terse practical guidance on diagnosis, prognosis and treatment, with particular attention to regimen and diet, purging, the influence of age, season and bodily constitution upon disease, and the interpretation of crises, paroxysms and other critical signs. The opening maxim, Ὁ βίος βραχὺς ('Life is short, the art long'), states the difficulties that attend the physician's judgement and practice. Later maxims consider, among other things, sleep, fasting, the nourishment of the sick, and the signs by which the course and outcome of illness may be judged.
grc.hippocrates.de_aere_aquis_et_locis: De Aere Aquis et Locis (On Airs, Waters, and Places), transmitted under the name of Hippocrates in the Hippocratic Corpus and of uncertain date, is a treatise on environmental medicine addressed to the travelling physician. It opens with instructions for assessing an unfamiliar city's exposure to winds, waters, and the sun's course, then classifies waters by their effects on health and correlates seasonal changes with epidemic disease. Its latter part compares Asia and Europe, arguing that climate and terrain shape the bodies and characters of their inhabitants, with ethnographic excursuses on the Macrocephali, the people of Phasis, the Sauromatae, and the nomad Scythians. Its naturalistic explanations of conditions customarily deemed divine, together with an Asia–Europe contrast closely akin to Herodotean ethnography, make the treatise a key intertext for the study of ancient environmental determinism.
grc.hippocrates.de_aere_aquis_locis: A Greek medical treatise of the Hippocratic Corpus, attributed to Hippocrates and of uncertain date. The work instructs the physician arriving in an unfamiliar city to examine its exposure to the winds, the character of its waters and terrain, the course of its seasons, and the manner of life of its inhabitants. It then sets out how a city's situation relative to warm and cold winds shapes the bodily condition and endemic diseases of its men, women, and children, treating in turn cities exposed to the warm winds and those exposed to the cold.
grc.hippocrates.de_capitis_vulneribus: De Capitis Vulneribus (On Wounds of the Head) is a Greek medical treatise of the Hippocratic Corpus, attributed to Hippocrates in the manuscript tradition and of uncertain date. It opens with a description of the sutures of the skull, whose patterns vary with the shape of the head and are likened to the Greek letters tau, eta and chi, before discussing the varying thickness, hardness and vulnerability of cranial bone in different regions, including the especial danger of wounds at the bregma. The surviving opening portion then sets out the ways in which head wounds may occur, distinguishing forms of fracture and of contusion and noting that some injuries are not immediately visible to the eye.
grc.hippocrates.de_diaeta_in_morbis_acutis: A Greek medical treatise of uncertain date, attributed to Hippocrates. It opens with a polemic against the compilers of the so-called Cnidian opinions and their reliance on purgative drugs, then sets out principles for the treatment of acute diseases such as pleurisy, pneumonia, phrenitis and other continuous fevers. Most of the discussion concerns diet and drink, especially the administration of ptisan (barley gruel), its quantity and timing, the choice of wine or honeyed water, and the use of purges, arguing that changes in a patient's regimen should be gradual rather than abrupt.
grc.hippocrates.de_flatibus: A prose treatise of the Hippocratic Corpus, transmitted under the name of Hippocrates and of uncertain date. It opens with general reflections on the art of medicine, the burdens it places on its practitioners and the relief it brings to the sick, before advancing its central thesis that all diseases share one cause: air, or breath, which the body draws in continually and with every meal. The argument distinguishes common epidemic fevers, ascribed to corrupted air shared by all who breathe it, from fevers arising from faulty regimen, and traces how breath trapped in the body chills the blood and produces shivering.
grc.hippocrates.de_fracturis: De Fracturis (On Fractures), a Greek surgical treatise in Ionic prose attributed to Hippocrates and of uncertain date, sets out the treatment of broken bones, chiefly their extension, coaptation, and bandaging. The opening chapters criticise physicians who force an injured forearm into postures borrowed from archery or other manual crafts, arguing from the natural structure of the bones, tendons, and flesh that the injured hand must be dressed in its proper position. The work then gives detailed instructions for extension, the application of wax plaster, linen rollers, and splints, distinguishing cases by the site and number of the fractured bones, and its teaching extends to other bones of the body besides the forearm.
grc.hippocrates.de_prisca_medicina: De Prisca Medicina (On Ancient Medicine) is a Greek medical treatise of uncertain date, attributed to Hippocrates. It argues that the art of medicine was discovered long ago and rests on an accumulated body of knowledge, so that it needs no speculative hypothesis, and it attacks those who postulate one or two elemental causes, hot, cold, moist, or dry, as the origin of all disease and death. The speaker further traces the origins of medicine to the human need to adapt diet and food preparation to the body's constitution, showing how the discovery and refinement of suitable nourishment arose from the sufferings caused by a raw and powerful diet.
grc.hippocrates.jusjurandum: The Jusjurandum, or Oath, is a short Greek prose work attributed to Hippocrates and of uncertain date. It takes the form of a physician's sworn pledge, invoking Apollo the healer, Asclepius, Hygieia, Panakeia and all gods and goddesses as witnesses. The speaker undertakes to honour the teacher of the medical art as a parent, to teach the art without fee to the teacher's sons and to sworn pupils, and to use diet and treatment for the benefit of the sick while abstaining from harm and injustice. Further clauses forbid giving deadly drugs or abortive remedies, leave cutting for stone to male practitioners of that craft, and impose lifelong silence on what the physician learns of patients' private affairs.
grc.homer.hymns: The Homeric Hymns are a collection of thirty-three anonymous Greek hymns in dactylic hexameter, transmitted under the name of Homer and of uncertain date. Each poem addresses an individual deity, recounting the god's birth, deeds, or institution of cult, and most close with a greeting and farewell to the god honoured. The collection opens with a hymn to Dionysus that rehearses conflicting accounts of his birthplace before hailing him as son of Zeus and Semele; other substantial hymns narrate Demeter's search for Persephone, Apollo's foundations at Delos and Delphi, Hermes' theft of Apollo's cattle, and Aphrodite's union with Anchises. The pieces range in length from a few lines to several hundred.
grc.homer.iliad: The Iliad is a Greek epic poem in dactylic hexameter, attributed to Homer and of uncertain date, arranged in twenty-four books. It opens with an invocation of the wrath of Achilles, son of Peleus, and of the quarrel between Agamemnon and Achilles that brought death to many Achaeans. The poem recounts Apollo's plague sent upon the Greek army after Agamemnon dishonoured the priest Chryses, the ensuing strife between the two leaders, and the fighting before Priam's city of Troy.
grc.homer.odyssey: The Odyssey is an epic poem in twenty-four books of dactylic hexameter, traditionally attributed to Homer and of uncertain date. It opens with an invocation to the Muse to sing of the resourceful man who wandered long after sacking Troy's holy citadel, seeing the cities and learning the minds of many peoples. The narrative encompasses the wanderings and sufferings of Odysseus at sea, his detention on the island of Calypso, the divine council in which Zeus and Athena plan his homecoming despite Poseidon's anger, and the parallel story of his son Telemachus and wife Penelope awaiting his return in Ithaca.
grc.isaeus.speeches: Speeches attributed to Isaeus, an Attic logographer of uncertain date who composed courtroom orations for litigants pleading before Athenian courts. The surviving speeches deal almost entirely with inheritance disputes: claimants argue rival rights to estates through wills, adoption, and degrees of kinship, as in the opening oration, where relatives of the deceased Cleonymus contest a will he was said to have sought to revoke before his death. The prose is terse and argumentative, weighing testimony and the dead man's intentions in close legal detail.
grc.isocrates.speeches: The Speeches of Isocrates gather twenty-one separate Greek prose discourses of the Athenian rhetorician Isocrates. The opening speech is an address to the young Demonicus, son of Hipponicus, sending him paternal counsel on piety toward the gods, honour for his parents, disciplined care of body and soul, and the company he should keep. The collection ranges from such protreptic and advisory pieces to public and forensic orations, all cast in the long, carefully balanced periods characteristic of Isocrates' prose.
grc.libanius.declamations_13-30: Greek declamations 13 to 30 of Libanius, rhetorical exercises in which imagined speakers adopt historical personae and argue set cases before assembled audiences. The opening speech is delivered in the person of the Corinthians, who address the Greeks in a deliberative oration on the wrongs done to Potidaea, recounting the Athenian siege of the city, the grievances of its allies, and the question whether the Athenians should be called to account. The speeches that follow likewise stage forensic or deliberative arguments on invented historical situations of the kind used in ancient schools of rhetoric.
grc.libanius.declamations_31-51: A set of twenty-one Greek declamations, numbered 31 to 51 within the corpus of the rhetorician Libanius. Such declamations are fictitious display speeches composed for rhetorical training, delivered in the persons of imagined speakers before courts or councils. The first speech in the collection, addressed to a city council, is spoken by a man whose property has been repeatedly confiscated; he recounts his father's teaching on frugality and argues that death is preferable to living on after the loss of his estate.
grc.libanius.orations_26-50: Greek prose orations numbered 26 to 50 in the collected corpus of Libanius, the fourth-century CE rhetorician of Antioch. The opening speech counsels a newly appointed governor whom, on the speaker's account, the citizens resent in favour of his predecessor Proclus: it attributes the disturbances in the theatres and baths to a small circle of wrongdoers rather than to the population of Antioch, and urges punishment that is measured and falls on the guilty. The remaining speeches in the range continue this public oratory on civic affairs and the conduct of officials.
grc.lucian.alexander: Alexander is a satirical prose narrative by the Greek satirist Lucian of Samosata, writing in the second century AD, addressed to a correspondent named Celsus. It recounts the career of Alexander of Abonoteichus, whom Lucian depicts as a charlatan and oracle-monger, framing the task of recording his schemes as a cleansing akin to the stables of Augeas. The narrative describes Alexander's striking appearance and quick intelligence, his apprenticeship to a magician and physician of Tyana, his partnership with the Byzantine Cocconas, and his rise through fraud and manufactured miracles, culminating in the oracle of the serpent Glycon at Abonoteichus.
grc.lucian.contemplantes: A short comic dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, of uncertain date, printed from Jacobitz's 1896 Teubner edition. Charon abandons his ferry to find out what human life is worth, and Hermes guides him to a lookout raised by piling Pelion on Ossa in imitation of Homer's Aloeidae, from which the pair survey cities and rulers, the threads the Fates spin for each person, tomb cults and funerary offerings, and the ruin of once-great cities such as Nineveh, Babylon, and Troy. Saturated with Homeric quotation and reworking historical episodes from the tradition of Herodotus, above all the exchange of Solon and Croesus on happiness, the dialogue's memento mori satire offers readers of intertexts a compact repertory of epic and historical allusion.
grc.lucian.dearum_iudicium: The Dearum Iudicium is a short Greek comic dialogue by Lucian of Samosata retelling the judgment of Paris. Zeus sends Hermes with the apple of discord to Mount Ida, where Hera, Athena and Aphrodite must submit to the verdict of the Phrygian herdsman Paris; on the way the goddesses banter about their rustic judge, and Paris in turn protests that so remarkable a spectacle and so delicate a task lie far beyond a simple cowherd's competence. The conversation is carried entirely by the alternating speeches of Hermes, the three goddesses, and Paris himself.
grc.lucian.dialogi_meretricii: The Dialogi Meretricii, or Dialogues of the Courtesans, is a collection of short dramatic dialogues in Greek by Lucian of Samosata. Its scenes are set in the world of the hetaerae, who converse with lovers, mothers, madams, and one another about seduction, jealousy, deception, marriage, and pregnancy. The exchanges are brief and mimetic, with named speakers such as Thais, Glycerion, Myrtion, Doris, and Philinna carrying on the conversations.
grc.lucian.icaromenippus: Icaromenippus is a satirical Greek dialogue by Lucian of Samosata in which Menippus recounts to a friend how he flew to heaven on wings taken from an eagle and a vulture. Frustrated by the philosophers' contradictory teachings about the origin and ordering of the cosmos, he ascends past the moon to Zeus's citadel in order to observe the heavens and human affairs from above. The opening exchange covers the distances of the journey, joking comparisons with Icarus, and Menippus's account of the large fee he paid to astronomers and philosophers who proved unable to answer his questions.
grc.lucian.patriae_encomium: Patriae Encomium is a short Greek prose encomium, or speech in praise of the fatherland, by Lucian of Samosata. The speaker begins from the commonplace that nothing is sweeter than one's patria and argues further that it is more revered and quasi-divine, since the homeland stands to each person as parent, nurse and teacher, giving birth, speech, laws and education. The piece observes that the gods themselves favor their native places, that travelers and the aged yearn for their patria and wish to end their days and be buried in ancestral soil, and that genuine citizens praise their land even when it is small, rough or poor.
grc.lucian.podagra: Lucian's Podagra ('Gout') is a short Greek dramatic satire that travesties the diction and metres of tragedy, attributed to Lucian of Samosata. A speaker invokes Gout as a hateful child of Cocytus nursed by an Erinys, cataloguing the disease's fire and bitterness in the joints and veins, and contrasts the springtime processions of Phrygian, Lydian, and Cretan worshippers with the mock-rites of gout sufferers, whose 'hymns' are laments over their staff-supported steps. The monody closes as the speaker, summoned out of doors toward the sunlight, asks whether approaching garlanded staff-bearers are celebrating Apollo Paian or dancing in honour of Bacchus.
grc.lucian.rhetorum_praeceptor: A short Greek dialogue by Lucian of Samosata in which an older speaker instructs a young man who asks how he may become a rhetorician and win the prestige of a sophist. The teacher promises an easy and agreeable shortcut to rhetorical success, in contrast with the long and toilsome path of conventional training, and illustrates the incredulity that such promises encounter through the anecdote of a Sidonian merchant who offers to show Alexander a three-day route from Persia to Egypt. The work closes by setting out two roads to Rhetoric, a steep and laborious ascent and a broad one leading through flowering meadows and shade, the latter associated with flattery and the praise of the powerful.
grc.lucian.toxaris_vel_amicitia: A Greek prose dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, conducted between Mnesippus, a Greek, and Toxaris, a Scythian, and concerned with friendship, as its alternative title indicates. The opening exchange turns on the Scythian cult of Orestes and Pylades: Mnesippus questions the worship of foreigners who had plundered the country and slain its king, while Toxaris defends his people's honours to men they judge good and beneficent. Toxaris goes on to describe the bronze stele in the Oresteion recording the friends' deeds and the painted scenes in the temple enclosure, showing the shipwreck, the sacrifice to Artemis averted, and the fight during their escape. The remainder of the work is devoted to stories of devoted friendship told on the Greek and the Scythian side in turn.
grc.lucian.verae_historiae: Lucian of Samosata's Verae Historiae ('True Histories') is a Greek prose narrative whose preface declares that it describes things the narrator neither saw nor suffered nor learned from others, things that do not exist and could never have existed, and that readers should believe none of it.
