The work is offered openly as fiction, written in ridicule of earlier poets and prose writers, Ctesias, Iambulus and Homer's Odysseus among them, who recorded marvellous voyages and fabulous peoples. The narrative then follows the narrator and his fifty companions beyond the Pillars of Heracles into the western ocean, where, after seventy-nine days adrift in a storm, they land on an island bearing an inscription of Heracles and Dionysus, a flowing river of wine, and fish that taste and colour of it.
grc.lycurgus.against_leocrates: Against Leocrates is a forensic speech in Ancient Greek by Lycurgus, written for the prosecution of Leocrates before an Athenian court in the aftermath of the disaster at Chaeronea, when the Athenian people had decreed that no one should leave the city or abandon wives and children. The prosecutor argues that Leocrates, who left Athens and travelled to Rhodes and then Megara, was guilty of treason rather than, as the defence claimed, absence for trade. The speech opens with a summary of the case and an analysis of the issue at stake, followed by an appeal to Athena and the other gods, and proceeds through arguments that the defendant deserted his fatherland, its temples and his fellow citizens, that death is too slight a penalty for such a crime, and that the jurors' verdict will serve as a precedent and an encouragement to the young.
grc.novum_testamentum.actus_apostolorum: The Actus Apostolorum, or Acts of the Apostles, is a book of the Greek New Testament written in Koine prose during the Imperial period; its author is not named within the work. Addressed to a certain Theophilus as a sequel to a former account of Jesus' ministry, it opens with the ascension of the risen Jesus and the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles at Pentecost in Jerusalem. The narrative then follows the growth of the first Christian community, the preaching and miracles of Peter, the conversion and missionary journeys of Paul, and his arrest, trials, and voyage to Rome, tracing the spread of the message from Jerusalem toward the ends of the earth.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_colossenses: An epistle of the Greek New Testament, written in koine prose and addressed to the saints and faithful brethren in Colossae under the name of Paul the apostle together with Timothy his brother; the work is attributed to Paul, and its date within the Imperial period is uncertain. After a thanksgiving and prayer for the recipients' knowledge of God's will, the letter sets out a hymnic christology in which Christ is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation, and the head of the body, the church, through whom all things are reconciled by the blood of his cross. It then warns the Colossians against philosophy, empty deceit, and human tradition governing food, drink, festivals, and ascetic practice, and moves into ethical exhortation, urging them to seek the things above and to put to death what is earthly.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_corinthios_i: The First Letter to the Corinthians is an early Christian epistle in Greek prose, composed during the Imperial era and forming part of the New Testament. It opens with a salutation from Paul, called to be an apostle, together with Sosthenes, addressed to the church of God at Corinth, and takes up reports of quarrels and factions among the believers, who claim allegiance to Paul, Apollos, Cephas, or Christ. The letter sets the message of the crucified Christ against the wisdom and eloquence prized in the world, presenting Paul and Apollos as mere servants through whom the Corinthians came to faith. It further describes the community as God's field, building, and temple, in which each person's work will be tested by fire.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_corinthios_ii: Ad Corinthios II, the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, is a letter in Koine Greek belonging to the New Testament, addressed to the church of God at Corinth and to the saints throughout Achaia; its salutation names Paul, styled an apostle of Christ Jesus, together with Timothy as co-sender. The work is a prose composition of the Roman Imperial period within the early Christian biblical corpus. Its opening chapters give thanks for consolation amid affliction, recount Paul's distress in Asia, discuss a tearful letter and the forgiveness of an offender who has caused grief, and defend the change in Paul's travel plans. The letter then characterizes Paul's service as a ministry of a new covenant, in which the spirit gives life where the letter kills, illustrated by the contrast between the veiled glory of Moses' face and the open boldness of the Christian proclamation.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_ephesios: The Epistle to the Ephesians is a Greek Christian letter preserved in the New Testament, composed in prose during the Imperial era and attributed to the apostle Paul, who presents himself as a prisoner writing to the saints at Ephesus. Its opening chapters offer a blessing and thanksgiving followed by doctrinal exposition on salvation by grace through faith, the reconciliation of Jews and Gentiles into one body, and the disclosure of the mystery of Christ once hidden but now revealed. The later chapters turn to exhortation, urging unity and right conduct, setting out rules for households, and describing the armor of God against spiritual powers.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_hebraeos: The Epistle to the Hebrews (Pros Hebraious) is an early Christian letter in Greek prose, preserved in the New Testament and composed at some point in the Roman Imperial period; its author is not named. It opens by presenting the Son as God's definitive word to humanity, the radiance of his glory and heir of all things, exalted above the angels and ranked higher than Moses as a son over God's house. The exposition then turns to exhortation, warning against the unbelief of the wilderness generation through an extended quotation of the psalm on hardening the heart and holding out the promise of entering God's rest. Jesus is portrayed throughout as a merciful and faithful high priest who, having shared in flesh and blood and been tested through suffering, aids those who are tempted.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_philemonem: The Epistle to Philemon (Ad Philemonem) is a brief Greek letter of the New Testament, composed in the Imperial era, opening with Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, together with Timothy addressing Philemon, Apphia, Archippus, and the church that meets in Philemon's house. After a thanksgiving for Philemon's faith and love, the body of the letter is a personal appeal on behalf of Onesimus, whom Paul calls his child begotten in bonds, asking that he be received no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother, while Paul offers to repay any wrong or debt on Onesimus's behalf. The letter closes with greetings from Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, together with a final benediction.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_romanos: The Epistle to the Romans is a Greek prose letter of the New Testament, attributed to the apostle Paul and addressed to the believers at Rome in the Imperial era. It opens with Paul's self-designation as a called apostle set apart for the gospel and a thanksgiving for the recipients' widely known faith, before launching an extended argument on sin, divine judgment, and the righteousness of God revealed to Jew and Greek alike. The letter weighs the place of law, circumcision, and faith in determining standing before God, and goes on to develop themes of justification, reconciliation, and the new life made possible apart from the law.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_timotheum_i: The First Epistle to Timothy is a Greek epistle of the New Testament, presented as a letter from the apostle Paul to Timothy and attributed to him, of uncertain date within the Imperial era. Opening with a salutation naming Paul as sender, it urges Timothy to suppress divergent teaching at Ephesus and sets out qualifications for overseers and deacons, instructions on prayer and the conduct of women, and rules for behaviour within the church as the household of God. The letter also warns against ascetic teachers who forbid marriage and certain foods, and closes with personal advice to Timothy on teaching, conduct, and the gift entrusted to him.
grc.novum_testamentum.apocalypsis: The Apocalypse (Revelation), the final book of the New Testament, is a Greek prose apocalypse of the Imperial era. It presents itself as a revelation given by God to Jesus Christ and relayed through an angel to John, who writes from the island of Patmos to seven churches in the province of Asia. After an opening vision of the glorified Christ, the work contains dictated letters to those seven churches, followed by visions of heavenly worship, seals, trumpets and bowls, the fall of Babylon, the final judgement, and the new Jerusalem. The book closes with promises of Christ's coming and a concluding benediction.
grc.novum_testamentum.iacobi: The Epistle of James is a New Testament letter written in Greek prose during the Imperial period; its opening verse names the sender as James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, who addresses the twelve tribes in the dispersion, while the precise date of composition is uncertain. The letter consists of paraenetic instruction on trials and temptation, wisdom, hearing and doing the word, partiality toward the rich, faith and works illustrated by Abraham and Rahab, restraint of the tongue, and the dangers of envy and worldliness, closing with teaching on patience, oath-taking, prayer for the sick, and the recovery of those who wander from the truth. Its argument proceeds in short, loosely connected discourses in the manner of wisdom literature, with frequent appeals to the law, to scripture, and to the sayings of Jesus.
grc.novum_testamentum.ioannes: The Gospel of John (Ioannes), a Koine Greek prose narrative forming the fourth book of the New Testament, belongs to the Imperial period. It opens with the Prologue on the Logos made flesh, then recounts John the Baptist's testimony, the calling of the first disciples, and Jesus' first sign at the wedding at Cana. The work comprises twenty-one chapters narrating Jesus' public ministry in Galilee and Judea, his signs and discourses, the cleansing of the temple, and his passion and resurrection, in a manner of telling distinct from the Synoptic Gospels.
grc.novum_testamentum.ioannis_ii: The Second Epistle of John is a brief New Testament letter in Greek prose, written during the Roman Imperial period and addressed to 'the elect lady and her children' by an author who identifies himself only as 'the elder.' The letter urges its recipients to walk in love and in the commandments received from the beginning, warns against deceivers who do not confess Jesus Christ as come in the flesh, and instructs the community to withhold welcome and greeting from anyone who does not bring the teaching of Christ. It ends with the author's preference to speak face to face rather than write further, followed by greetings from the children of the recipient's elect sister.
grc.novum_testamentum.ioannis_iii: The Third Letter of John is one of the shortest writings of the New Testament, a Greek prose composition of the Imperial era that opens in the voice of 'the Elder' writing to the beloved Gaius. The author commends Gaius for supporting itinerant missionaries sent out for the sake of the name, sharply censures Diotrephes, who refuses to receive the brothers and expels their supporters from the congregation, and adds a testimony on behalf of Demetrius. The letter closes with the writer's intention to visit soon and speak face to face, a wish of peace, and mutual greetings among the friends.
grc.novum_testamentum.iudae: A Greek epistle belonging to the New Testament, attributed to Judas (Jude), who identifies himself in the opening verse as a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James. Written in prose during the Imperial period, the letter addresses an audience of called and beloved believers and denounces intruders who pervert the grace of God and deny Christ. Its warning is supported by a chain of examples of divine judgement, including the Israelites saved from Egypt, the fallen angels, Sodom and Gomorrah, Cain, Balaam, and Korah, together with Michael's dispute with the devil over the body of Moses and a prophecy attributed to Enoch. It closes with exhortations to build oneself up in the faith, keep within the love of God, and rescue others from judgement, followed by a doxology.
grc.novum_testamentum.marcus: The Gospel according to Mark, the second of the four canonical gospels of the New Testament, is an anonymous prose narrative in Koine Greek recounting the ministry, death, and resurrection of Jesus; its date is uncertain, and it is traditionally attributed to a certain Mark. It opens with the preaching and baptism of John the Baptist, Jesus' baptism and temptation in the wilderness, and his proclamation of the kingdom of God in Galilee, followed by the calling of the first disciples and a succession of healings, exorcisms, and disputes with scribes and Pharisees. Later sections include parables and miracles around the Sea of Galilee, the journey to Jerusalem, the Last Supper, the passion and crucifixion, and the women's discovery of the empty tomb. The narrative moves rapidly, marked throughout by the recurring adverb euthys, 'immediately'.
grc.novum_testamentum.matthaeus: The Gospel of Matthew is a Greek prose narrative of the Imperial period, attributed to Matthew and preserved as the first book of the New Testament. It opens with a genealogy of Jesus traced from Abraham through David to Joseph, followed by accounts of the virginal conception, the birth at Bethlehem, the visit of the magi, the flight into Egypt and the preaching of John the Baptist in the wilderness of Judaea. The work as a whole narrates the ministry, teaching, death and resurrection of Jesus in Galilee and Judaea.
grc.novum_testamentum.petri_i: The First Epistle of Peter is a New Testament letter written in Greek prose during the Roman Imperial period and attributed in its opening lines to the apostle Peter. Addressed to the 'elect sojourners of the Dispersion' in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, it opens with a benediction on rebirth through the resurrection of Christ and proceeds through exhortations to holiness, mutual love, submission to human authority, and endurance of innocent suffering after the example of Christ. Its later sections extend to household duties, conduct before outsiders, and counsel for the ordering of the Christian community.
grc.oppian.halieutica: The Halieutica is a Greek didactic poem in hexameters by Oppian, addressed to an emperor named Antoninus, of uncertain date. In five books it surveys the tribes of fish of the sea, their kinds, haunts, breeding and feeding, and the craft and toil by which fishers take them. The proem contrasts the hardships and perils of fishermen at sea with the comparative ease of hunters and fowlers, and invokes Thetis and the other marine powers before proceeding to its catalogue of sea creatures.
grc.oppian_of_apamea.cynegetica: A Greek didactic poem on hunting in four books of hexameter verse, attributed to Oppian of Apamea and of uncertain date. The proem invokes a young imperial prince named Antoninus, son of Severus and Domna, as patron, while Calliope and Artemis turn the poet from other subjects towards the chase. The poem describes the nature and habits of wild animals, the breeding and training of dogs and horses, and the practice of hunting on land, including the use of nets, snares, spears, and mounted pursuit.
grc.pausanias.description_of_greece: Pausanias' Description of Greece is a Greek prose periegesis in ten books that surveys the regions of the Greek mainland site by site, beginning with Attica. The opening book starts at Sounion and moves through the Piraeus and the city of Athens, recording temples, cult statues, tombs, harbours and notable works of art. At each place the account accompanies the monuments with local history, myth and anecdote, touching on figures such as Themistocles, Conon, Menander and Euripides.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_mutatione_nominum: De Mutatione Nominum is a Greek allegorical exegetical treatise by Philo Judaeus, taking as its starting point Genesis 17:1, in which Abraham, aged ninety-nine, is visited by the Lord. Opening with the symbolic value of the number ninety-nine as a figure of perfection, the work argues that God's appearance to the patriarch comes not through the bodily eyes but through the mind's own light, and that the truly Existent is unnameable and incomprehensible, the title kyrios being applied to him only by catachresis. On this basis it distinguishes the names kyrios and theos as assigned to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, read as symbols of ascetic discipline, teaching, and perfection, and draws on further episodes such as Moses' entry into the darkness of Exodus 20:21, his request to behold God in Exodus 33, and Jacob's wrestling with the unnamed divine antagonist in Genesis 32.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_posteritate_caini: De Posteritate Caini is a Greek allegorical commentary by the Jewish exegete Philo Judaeus, taking its start from the scriptural account of Cain's departure 'from the face of God' (Genesis 4:16). Arguing that scripture should be heard figuratively rather than literally, it rejects any bodily or anthropomorphic conception of deity, contending that the incorporeal God has no face or parts and fills the whole cosmos so that nothing can flee his presence. The work contrasts Cain's voluntary exile, visited with incurable loss, with Adam's involuntary expulsion and with the birth of Seth as the grace-bestowed gift of a god-taught soul, and follows Moses' prayer to behold the divine nature into a meditation on the incomprehensibility of God's essence, which withdraws forever beyond the seeker's reach.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_sobrietate: De Sobrietate is a Greek exegetical treatise by Philo Judaeus that takes up Genesis 9:24, where Noah wakes from his wine and knows what his younger son has done to him, continuing a prior discussion of drunkenness and the nakedness that follows it. Its central argument is that scripture's terms 'younger' and 'older' mark not bodily age but the condition of the soul: Ishmael is called a child beside Isaac, the Israelites are 'children' in the song of Deuteronomy, Rachel is 'younger' than Leah as bodily beauty is inferior to the beauty of the soul, Joseph remains 'youngest' while serving the body, and Abraham, the youngest of the patriarchs in years, is named 'old' as the man worthy of honour. The discussion proceeds in Philo's allegorical manner, reading the patriarchal narratives as figures for the powers and dispositions of the soul.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_specialibus_legibus_lib: De Specialibus Legibus is a Greek treatise in four books by Philo Judaeus on the particular statutes of the Mosaic law. Having dealt with the ten commandments in a preceding work, the author takes up the individual decrees in the order of scripture, opening with a lengthy inquiry into the reasons for circumcision and proceeding to laws on monarchy, the worship of the heavenly bodies, and the making of images, quoting passages from Deuteronomy and Exodus as he goes. The exposition combines scriptural commentary with philosophical argument about God, creation, and the order of the cosmos.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_virtutibus: De Virtutibus ('On the Virtues') is a Greek philosophical treatise by Philo Judaeus, the Jewish philosopher who wrote in Greek, presenting the individual virtues as inculcated by the Mosaic law. It opens by turning from the preceding treatment of justice to courage, defining true courage not as the rage that accompanies warfare but as knowledge, and contrasting the discipline of the wise with the savagery of those who kill through bodily strength. Poverty, disrepute, disability and disease are then treated as trials that fortitude and sound judgment enable one to withstand, with sophrosyne identified as the health of the soul that holds the passions in check. The closing passage cites concrete provisions of the law, such as the prohibition of a man's wearing a woman's garment, as exercises by which the legislator trains the soul toward courage.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_vita_mosis_lib_iii: De Vita Mosis Lib III carries the third book of Philo Judaeus' Greek treatise on the life of Moses, edited in Cohn's Berlin edition of 1902 and running to 627 lines. Philo, a Jewish author writing in Greek, ranks Moses above Greek sages as lawgiver and interpreter of sacred laws and recasts the biblical narrative in the idiom of Greek biography, following him from his Chaldaean lineage and Egyptian birth through exposure on the Nile, adoption by the king's daughter, a royal education in mathematics and philosophy, and the enslavement of his people. The opening prologue defends Moses against the mockery of Greek men of letters and announces an account drawn from the sacred books and from elders of the nation. For readers of intertexts, the work stands among the fullest ancient Greek treatments of Moses, bridging scriptural narrative and the conventions of Greek paideia, biography, and encomium.
grc.philo_judaeus.legatio_ad_gaium: A Greek historical treatise by Philo of Alexandria, the first-century Jewish philosopher, giving an account of the embassy sent by the Jews of Alexandria to the emperor Gaius Caligula. The work opens with a meditation on fortune and divine providence and on the name Israel, 'one who sees God', before turning to the rejoicing that greeted Gaius's accession after the death of Tiberius and the consternation caused by his grave illness. The narrative then traces the emperor's conduct toward the Jews, culminating in the mission to Rome, on which Philo himself served as an envoy, to plead the cause of the Alexandrian community.
grc.philostratus_the_athenian.heroicus: Heroicus, a Greek dialogue by Philostratus the Athenian, is cast as a conversation between a Phoenician traveller engaged in trade and a vinedresser living on the Thracian Chersonese, who keeps a vineyard belonging to the hero Protesilaus. Protesilaus, who died at Troy for Helen and was restored to life in Phthia through his love for Laodamia, now dwells with the vinedresser and instructs him, and the talk moves from farming and the character of the place to the hero's own fortunes. Further on, the vinedresser reports the hero's accounts of the Trojan War and describes heroes still appearing in the plain before Troy, in terms that depart from the epic tradition.
grc.philostratus_the_athenian.vitae_sophista: The Vitae Sophistarum ('Lives of the Sophists') is a Greek prose work by Philostratus the Athenian, presented in its opening letter as a record, in two books, of celebrated sophists, dedicated to Antonius Gordianus. The selection preserved here comprises the dedicatory letter and the opening of the first book. In it Philostratus surveys the history of sophistic rhetoric, distinguishing an older sophistic founded by Gorgias of Leontini from a second sophistic associated with Aeschines, and illustrates its character with anecdotes about Prodicus, Chaerephon, Demosthenes, and other figures.
grc.pindar.odes: The Carmina collects the epinician odes of Pindar, an ancient Greek lyric poet, arranged in four books named for the Olympian, Pythian, Nemean, and Isthmian games at which the honored victors competed. Each ode celebrates an athletic or equestrian winner, sometimes a ruler of the Greek West such as Hieron of Syracuse, and is composed in triadic choral lyric in a literary Doric idiom. The poems interweave mythological narratives, including the stories of Pelops and Tantalus in the opening Olympian, with praise of the victor and gnomic reflection on human excellence, wealth, and divine favor. The odes address patrons and audiences across the Greek world, from mainland sanctuaries to the courts of Sicily.
grc.plato.cleitophon: A short Greek dialogue transmitted among the works of Plato, in which Cleitophon, son of Aristonymus, answers a report that he has belittled Socrates while praising the company of Thrasymachus. Cleitophon concedes that Socrates' exhortations to care for virtue are the finest he has heard, but complains that neither Socrates nor his associates would say what justice is or how it is to be learned, and he presses Socrates to complete what his protreptic has begun. The conversation ends just as Socrates begins his reply, so the exchange breaks off almost as soon as it is joined.
grc.plato.cratylus: A dialogue of Plato in which Socrates, Cratylus and Hermogenes debate whether names are correct by nature or by convention. Cratylus maintains that each thing has a name naturally suited to it, the same for Greeks and barbarians alike, while Hermogenes argues that a name is only what people agree to call a thing. Socrates examines both positions, surveys a long series of etymologies of Greek names, divine and human, and then asks whether names are images of reality and whether things can be known through them or only through themselves. The conversation closes with the suggestion that things be investigated directly rather than by way of their names.
grc.plato.crito: Plato's Crito is a short Socratic dialogue set in Socrates' prison cell in Athens on the eve of his execution. Crito arrives before dawn with news that the ship from Delos is expected, and urges Socrates to escape, offering money, willing friends, and refuge in Thessaly, while appealing to his reputation and to his duty toward his children. Socrates replies that the opinion of the many must not govern conduct, and the dialogue culminates in the speech of the personified Laws of Athens, who argue that escape would be an act of injustice against the city and its laws.
grc.plato.euthydemus: Euthydemus is a dialogue in Attic Greek prose by Plato, the Athenian philosopher of the fourth century BCE, cast as a report Socrates delivers to Crito about a meeting in the Lyceum with the brothers Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, sophists originally of Chios and later of Thurii who profess to teach virtue and the art of fighting arguments to a standstill. The brothers display their eristic method by entangling the young Cleinias and Ctesippus in contradictory conclusions through punning and fallacious reasoning, while Socrates interposes protreptic speeches urging that wisdom is the source of virtue and must be sought through philosophy. The dialogue closes with Socrates' criticism of mere verbal combat and his insistence that dialectic, rightly practised, is the instrument of moral education.
grc.plato.gorgias: A dialogue by Plato, of uncertain date, in which Socrates questions the rhetorician Gorgias about the nature of rhetoric and whether it is a genuine art, having arrived with Chaerephon just after one of Gorgias's public displays. The conversation draws in Polus and Callicles, moving through debates over power, whether doing injustice is worse than suffering it, and the place of pleasure in the good life, before turning to the philosophical life itself. The dialogue ends with a myth of the judgement of souls after death.
grc.plato.hippias_minor: A Greek prose dialogue of Plato in which Socrates questions Hippias of Elis, a sophist from that city. The conversation begins with Hippias's claim that Homer made Achilles the best of the Greeks who went to Troy and Odysseus the most versatile, and moves on to ask whether the truthful man or the deceiver is the better. Quoting the exchange between Achilles and Odysseus in Iliad 9, Socrates argues that the power to deceive belongs to those with knowledge and ability, and the dialogue closes with the paradox that the voluntary wrongdoer is better than the involuntary one.
grc.plato.laches: The Laches is a Socratic dialogue by Plato in which two elderly Athenians, Lysimachus and Melesias, ask the generals Nicias and Laches whether instruction in fighting in armour would benefit their sons. Under Socrates' prompting the discussion shifts from the merits of such training to a search for the definition of courage, examining whether it is a kind of endurance, a wise endurance, or knowledge of what is to be feared and dared. The inquiry ends without a settled answer, Socrates proposing that the companions continue their examination together on another day.
grc.plato.leges: Plato's Leges (Laws), a dialogue in twelve books, opens with three speakers, an unnamed Athenian, a Cretan, and a Spartan, walking from Cnossos toward the cave and sanctuary of Zeus on Mount Ida. Their conversation begins by asking whether god or man gave the laws to their cities, citing Zeus for the Cretans and Apollo for the Spartans and the traditional accounts of Minos and Rhadamanthys. The speakers then examine the claim that the Cretan and Spartan institutions of common messes, training, and arms are directed wholly toward war, holding that peace is for most people only a name and that an undeclared war exists between every city and every other. The dialogue goes on from there to its larger inquiry into the constitution and the code of laws appropriate to a well-ordered city.
grc.plato.lysis: The Lysis is a Greek philosophical dialogue by Plato, dramatizing a conversation of Socrates with the young Hippothales, Ctesippus, Lysis and Menexenus in a newly built palaestra outside the walls of Athens. After an opening exchange about Hippothales' infatuation with Lysis, Socrates questions Lysis and Menexenus on the nature of friendship, testing successive accounts of who or what can be a friend. The discussion closes aporetically, with the participants left unable to define what a friend is.
grc.plato.menexenus: Plato's Menexenus is a short Socratic dialogue of uncertain date, framed as a conversation between Socrates and the young Menexenus about the speeches delivered over Athens' war dead. At Socrates' insistence, the greater part of the work consists of a funeral oration which he recites, claiming to have learned it from Aspasia, the teacher of rhetoric whom he names as the consort of Pericles; the speech praises the fallen and their forebears and recounts Athenian history from the earliest times down to recent campaigns. A closing exchange between the two speakers rounds off the recitation.
grc.plato.meno: A Socratic dialogue of Plato in Attic Greek, the Meno opens with the Thessalian aristocrat Meno asking Socrates whether virtue can be taught, is gained by practice, or comes by nature. The conversation weighs successive definitions of virtue, presents the doctrine that learning is recollection through Socrates' questioning of one of Meno's slave boys over a geometrical problem, and confronts the paradox that inquiry is impossible either for those who know or for those who do not. The dialogue closes by distinguishing true opinion from knowledge and asking whether statesmen lead cities by the former or the latter.
grc.plato.parmenides: Plato's Parmenides is a philosophical dialogue in Greek. Its dramatic frame has Cephalus of Clazomenae, on arriving in Athens, ask Glaucon and Adimantus to have their half-brother Antiphon recite the account of a conversation once witnessed by Pythodorus at the Great Panathenaea between the aged Parmenides of Elea, Zeno, and the young Socrates. In the first part Socrates questions Zeno's arguments against plurality and asks how sensible things can participate in Forms such as likeness and justice, drawing criticism from Parmenides; the second part is the exercise Parmenides then demonstrates, a long dialectical survey of the consequences of a series of hypotheses about the existence, unity, and non-existence of the One, both for the One itself and for the others.
grc.plato.phaedo: The Phaedo is a Socratic dialogue by Plato, written in Greek, in which Phaedo of Elis recounts to Echecrates the events of the day on which Socrates drank the hemlock in his Athenian prison cell. Framed as a report of the last hours after the trial, whose execution was delayed by the sacred ship sent to Delos, the dialogue gathers companions such as Simmias, Cebes, and Crito around the philosopher. Its central portion presents a sequence of arguments for the immortality of the soul, Socrates' account of philosophy as preparation for death, and a myth describing the earth and the destiny of souls after it. The work closes with the death scene, in which Socrates calmly drinks the poison among his friends.
grc.plato.phaedrus: Plato's Phaedrus is a dialogue set on a walk outside the walls of Athens along the Ilissus, where Socrates and Phaedrus discuss a speech by Lysias arguing that favours should be granted to the non-lover rather than the lover. Socrates twice answers with speeches of his own, the second a palinode that defends erotic madness as divine and depicts the soul as a winged chariot that once beheld the Forms. The dialogue then turns to rhetoric proper, treating the definition of the art, the requirements of truth, collection and division as instruments of dialectic, and the speechwriting of the statesman, before closing with the myth of Theuth and a critique of writing as weaker than living discourse. Plato composed the work in the fourth century BC.
grc.plato.protagoras: Plato's Protagoras is a Socratic dialogue in Greek prose in which Socrates recounts to an unnamed companion how Hippocrates roused him before dawn, eager to pay the visiting sophist Protagoras of Abdera for instruction. The opening exchange follows the two to the house of Callias, where Protagoras is lodging, as Socrates questions what such paid teaching would make of a pupil. The dialogue as a whole takes up whether virtue can be taught, leading into debate between Socrates and Protagoras over the nature and unity of virtue.
grc.plato.respublica: Plato's Respublica (Politeia) is a Greek prose dialogue in ten books, narrated by Socrates, who recounts how he went down to the Piraeus to attend a festival and was persuaded to remain at the house of Cephalus. His interlocutors include Cephalus, Polemarchus, Thrasymachus, Glaucon and Adeimantus, and the conversation moves from the definition of justice to the construction in speech of an ideal city, the education of its guardians, the parts of the soul and the rule of philosophers. The later books take up imitation and the standing of the poets, the allegory of the cave, and the myth of Er concerning the fate of the soul after death.
grc.plato.sophista: A philosophical dialogue by Plato in which Socrates, Theodorus, and an unnamed Eleatic Stranger, described as a companion of Parmenides and Zeno, come together to inquire what the sophist is. The Stranger, cross-examining the young Theaetetus, employs the method of division (diaeresis), first defining the angler as a small-scale example and then pursuing the sophist through successive classifications. The inquiry broadens into a discussion of non-being, image-making, and the possibility of false statement, including an account of the interweaving of the greatest kinds such as being, sameness, difference, motion, and rest.
grc.plato.statesman: A dialogue of Plato in which the Eleatic Stranger, interrogating a younger Socrates before Socrates and Theodorus, attempts to define the true statesman by the method of division. Continuing the inquiry begun in the Sophist, whose cast it shares and to which it promises a forthcoming account of the philosopher, the work separates the royal art from kindred sciences and rival claims to rule, weighs the expert ruler against the rule of law across the standard constitutions, and embeds its argument in the myth of an age of Cronos when the cosmos moved in reverse. Composed in Plato's later period, it affords fertile ground for readers of intertexts through its shepherding imagery, its diaeretic technique, and its continuities with the Theaetetus, the Sophist, and later political philosophy.
grc.plato.theages: A short Socratic dialogue in Greek, transmitted among the works of Plato. Demodocus approaches Socrates in the stoa of Zeus Eleutherius, anxious about his son Theages, who has been stirred by young men in the city and longs to become wise. Socrates questions father and son about what sort of wisdom the boy wants, distinguishing arts such as piloting and chariot-driving from the political wisdom that would let him govern, and asks who could properly teach him. The conversation ends with Socrates suggesting that his companions benefit from him not through any art of teaching but through a divine sign.
grc.plato.timaeus: Plato's Timaeus is a philosophical dialogue in Ancient Greek. It opens with Socrates recapitulating the previous day's discussion of an ideal city, covering its classes, the education and communal life of its guardians, and its marriage and eugenic arrangements, before Timaeus is called upon to give an account of the universe from its beginning, with Critias and Hermocrates among those present. The work consists chiefly of Timaeus' cosmological discourse, treating the divine craftsman, the ordering of the world soul, the four elements, the heavens, and the construction and workings of the human body.
grc.plutarch.aemilius_paulus: A Greek prose biography by Plutarch, composed under the Roman empire, paired in the parallel Lives with the account of Timoleon of Corinth. It opens with a programmatic prologue on the writing of biography, comparing history to a mirror by which the reader may shape his own life, before turning to its subject, Lucius Aemilius Paullus. The narrative traces the antiquity of the Aemilian house in Rome and his father's death at Cannae, then follows Aemilius's rejection of courtroom oratory and popular flattery, his scrupulous conduct of the augurate, his guardianship of traditional military discipline, and his commands in the war against Antiochus and in Iberia.
grc.plutarch.amatorius: A Greek dialogue from Plutarch's Moralia, in prose, in which Flavianus asks Autoboulus to repeat the speeches on Eros that his father once delivered on Mount Helicon at the festival of Eros celebrated there by the Thespians beside the Muses. The narrative recalled in the dialogue turns on the marriage of the wealthy widow Ismenodora to the young Bacchon, opposed by jealous rivals and settled by the intervention of their friends. It also stages a sustained debate between Protogenes and Daphnaeus over whether true Eros belongs to boys or to women, conducted in a Platonic vein with discussion of pleasure, friendship, and the discipline of desire.
grc.plutarch.an_seni_respublica_gerenda_sit: A Greek philosophical dialogue by Plutarch on the question of whether an old man should engage in public affairs, framed as an address to Euphanes. The speaker rejects the claim that old age furnishes a respectable excuse for withdrawing from politics, arguing that civic energy and the desire for honourable action persist into old age. The case is made through historical exempla, chiefly Cato, Pericles and Agesilaus, together with the counter-example of Dionysius of Syracuse and remarks attributed to Diogenes, and is supported by quotations from poets and historians. The essay forms part of Plutarch's Moralia.
grc.plutarch.animine_an_corporis_affectiones: A short Greek ethical treatise by Plutarch, preserved in the Moralia under a Latin title conventionally rendered 'Whether the affections of the soul are worse than those of the body.' The argument maintains that psychic passions are more grievous than bodily diseases because they escape their bearer's notice, so that the sufferer mistakes his worst states for virtues or blessings and shuns the philosophical remedy while readily summoning physicians for bodily ills. Illustrations drawn from medicine, from Aesop's fable of the fox and the leopard, and from the spectacle of a litigious crowd thronging the marketplace support the diagnosis, which opens from Homer's verdict that nothing that breathes and creeps upon the earth is more wretched than man.
grc.plutarch.antony: A Greek prose biography of Marcus Antonius by Plutarch. The narrative opens with Antony's ancestry, his grandfather, the orator Antony, killed in Marius's purge, and his father surnamed Creticus, and recounts his upbringing by his mother Julia, his profligate youth under the influence of Curio and Clodius, and his first campaigns with Gabinius in Judaea and Egypt. Anecdotes throughout present his character: heavy debts and lavish spending, a consciously Heraclean self-image in dress and bearing, and the strong affection he inspired among his soldiers.
grc.plutarch.bruta_animalia_ratione_uti: A Greek prose dialogue transmitted among the Moralia of Plutarch, taking its premise from Circe's transformation of Odysseus's companions into beasts. Odysseus asks the sorceress to restore his men to human form, but she produces instead Gryllus, one of the swine, who refuses and undertakes to defend the animal way of life. The ensuing debate measures the reason and virtue of beasts against those of humanity, Gryllus contending that animals possess courage, justice, and the other virtues untaught and according to nature, while human reasoning serves appetite and ambition. From the name of its principal animal speaker the work is also known as the Gryllus.
grc.plutarch.caesar: Written in Greek by Plutarch, the Life of Caesar is a biographical account of the Roman general and statesman, forming part of the author's Parallel Lives. The narrative follows Caesar from his youth, when his kinship with Marius drew Sulla's hostility, through his capture by Cilician pirates and his studies in rhetoric at Rhodes, into his rise in Roman politics, the conquest of Gaul, the civil war against Pompey, the dictatorship, and his assassination. In Plutarch's manner, political and military narrative is interspersed with anecdote and character portraiture, as in the early episode of Cicero's remarks on Caesar's concealed ambition.
grc.plutarch.caius_gracchus: A Greek biographical account by Plutarch of the Roman tribune and reformer Gaius Sempronius Gracchus, younger brother of Tiberius Gracchus, preserved among his Parallel Lives. The narrative opens with Caius's cautious withdrawal from public life after his brother's death, follows him through his quaestorship in Sardinia under the consul Orestes, and recounts his contested election to the tribuneship, his powerful oratory, and his rallying of popular feeling against the senatorial nobility. Anecdote, reported speech, omens, and moral judgement characterize the telling, as throughout Plutarch's biographical writing.
grc.plutarch.camillus: A Greek life of the Roman statesman and general Marcus Furius Camillus, forming part of Plutarch's collection of biographies of Greek and Roman figures. The opening notes that Camillus, though chosen dictator five times, awarded four triumphs, and recorded as a second founder of Rome, never held the consulship, an outcome the work explains by the political arrangements of his day; the narrative then follows his rise from distinction in battle against the Aequi and Volscians, through his censorship, to his command in the prolonged siege of Veii. Later sections recount the portents attending that war, above all the unseasonable and unexplained rise of the Alban Lake, which the Romans took as a sign demanding public religious response.
grc.plutarch.cicero: A Greek biography of the Roman statesman and orator Marcus Tullius Cicero by Plutarch. The work opens with Cicero's family origins, the mock etymology of his name, and his precocious boyhood, then follows his education in rhetoric and philosophy under Philon and Antiochus of Ascalon, his defense of Roscius in the time of Sulla, and his withdrawal to Athens for study and voice training. The narrative continues through his re-entry into public life and his political career in the late Roman Republic.
grc.plutarch.cleomenes: Plutarch's Cleomenes is a Greek biography of the Spartan king Cleomenes, son of Leonidas II, written as part of his collection of parallel lives. The narrative opens with Cleomenes' marriage to Agiatis, the widow of the reformer king Agis, and portrays his ambitious and forceful temperament alongside the influence of the Stoic philosopher Sphaerus of Borysthenes. It then follows his accession to the throne, his plans to revive Agis' reforms in a city grown lax, and his campaigns against the Achaean League and its leader Aratus. The life closes with Cleomenes' downfall and death after his flight from Sparta.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_pericles_and_fabi: A short Greek comparison (synkrisis) by Plutarch, forming the formal epilogue to his paired Lives of Pericles and Fabius Maximus. It weighs the two statesmen against each other in generalship and political virtue: Pericles leading an Athens at the height of her prosperity and Fabius steering Rome through the disasters of the war against Hannibal. The discussion covers their conduct toward the demos and the senate, their successes and failures as commanders, their treatment of rivals such as Cimon, Thucydides, and Minucius, their disinterestedness in money, and Pericles' monumental building programme at Athens, concluding that each man's greatness is shown by the different circumstances in which he governed.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_sertorius_and_eum: The Comparison of Sertorius and Eumenes is the short formal synkrisis with which Plutarch concludes his paired biographies of the Roman general Sertorius and Eumenes of Cardia. Both men are described as foreign-born exiles who commanded large and warlike armies of diverse peoples, though they won and held their commands in different ways and differed in temperament, Eumenes being combative and contentious, Sertorius given to mildness and quiet. The piece weighs their conduct in war and closes with their deaths, one taken unawares at the hands of friends and the other captured while trying to flee, pleading in vain for his body after his enemy already held his soul.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_solon_and_publico: A short Greek comparison by Plutarch weighing the Athenian lawgiver Solon against the Roman statesman Publicola, forming the concluding assessment of their paired lives. The discussion moves point by point through Solon's pronouncement to Croesus on happiness, his refusal of tyranny, his cancellation of debts, and his constitution for Athens, matched against Publicola's generosity, his overthrow of the kingship at Rome, his enlargement of the senate and extension of appeals to the people, and his dealings with the Tarquins and Porsena. The verdict is divided, granting Solon the more brilliant founding of a polity and Publicola the greater fortune and success in seeing it endure.
grc.plutarch.conjugalia_praecepta: A short Greek treatise by Plutarch, transmitted among the Moralia under the Latin title Conjugalia Praecepta, on the conduct of married life. It is framed as a wedding gift sent to a newly married couple after the bridal rites performed by the priestess of Demeter, with a prayer that the Muses assist Aphrodite in the household. The body of the work consists of brief, aphoristic precepts on harmony between husband and wife: spouses should win one another by reason and persuasion rather than force, the temperate wife should practise modesty and reserve her presence for her husband, and early quarrels and love-potions alike blight a marriage at its beginning. Historical and mythological exempla, from Solon's quince and the Boeotian asphodel crowns to the fable of the sun and the north wind and Cato's strictness about public displays of affection, serve throughout as illustrations of the counsels.
grc.plutarch.de_animae_procreatione_in_timae: A Greek philosophical treatise by Plutarch, preserved among the Moralia, devoted to the passage of Plato's Timaeus on the generation and composition of the world-soul. It rehearses earlier interpretations of Plato's account of the blending of indivisible and divisible being with sameness and difference, reporting the doctrines of Xenocrates, Crantor, and Eudoxus and criticising those who identify the soul with number or with a mixture of intellectual and sensible nature. Plutarch argues that Plato's account of the soul's becoming in time is adopted for the sake of intelligibility rather than literally, while maintaining that the soul is self-moving, the source of all motion, and prior in time to the body. The closing section turns to the difficulties arising from the soul's precedence over the body and from the question of the cosmos's eternity.
grc.plutarch.de_cohibenda_ira: Plutarch's De Cohibenda Ira (On Restraining Anger) is a short Greek dialogue in which Fundanus and Sulla discuss the control of temper. Fundanus recounts how he tamed his own quick anger, and the speakers compare anger to a disease requiring continuous treatment rather than a single remedy, arguing that reason must be cultivated within the soul in advance, since a person in rage admits no outside counsel. The exchange draws on sayings of Musonius, medical and nautical imagery, and anecdotes and verses illustrating how slight provocations kindle wrath. The dialogue is preserved among Plutarch's moral essays (Moralia).
grc.plutarch.de_herodoti_malignitate: De Herodoti Malignitate ('On the Malice of Herodotus') is a short Greek essay by Plutarch, preserved among the Moralia and addressed to a certain Alexander. It argues that Herodotus' apparently simple and agreeable narrative style conceals deliberate bias, directed in particular against the Boeotians and Corinthians. The bulk of the essay sets out a series of signs by which malice may be recognised in historical writing, hostile word choice, the gratuitous insertion of misfortunes, omission of noble deeds, preference for the worse of competing accounts, and the imputation of base motives, drawing illustrations from Herodotus himself alongside Thucydides, Ephorus, Philistus and other historians.
grc.plutarch.de_liberis_educandis: A Greek prose treatise attributed to Plutarch and preserved among the Moralia, De Liberis Educandis ('On the Education of Children') addresses the rearing of freeborn children and the formation of good character. It opens with advice on marriage, birth, and procreation, stressing the claims of noble lineage, before turning to the interplay of nature, instruction, and habit in producing virtue. The argument is enlivened by anecdotes and exempla drawn from figures such as Themistocles, Diogenes, and the Spartan lawgiver Lycurgus.
grc.plutarch.de_stoicorum_repugnantis: De Stoicorum repugnantiis (On the Contradictions of the Stoics) is a short Greek polemical essay by Plutarch, transmitted among the Moralia. It charges the Stoic philosophers with failing to achieve the agreement between doctrine and conduct that their own principles require, observing that Zeno, Cleanthes, and Chrysippus wrote at length on politics, lawgiving, judging, and rhetoric yet lived as withdrawn scholars, declined Athenian citizenship, and never held public office. Further inconsistencies are gathered from Stoic writings, including Zeno's doctrine that temples ought not to be built although Stoics frequent and honour them, his differing definitions of the individual virtues, and his argument that both parties to a dispute must be heard, which he contravenes in answering Plato's Republic.
grc.plutarch.epitome_libri_de_animae_procrea: A very brief Greek epitome, of uncertain date and transmitted in the Bernardakis edition of the Moralia under Plutarch's name, condensing Plutarch's treatise On the Generation of the Soul in the Timaeus. It reproduces the treatise's account of the world-soul's composition from the indivisible and divisible essences bound by harmonic and numerical intervals, its criticism of the Posidonian claim that soul is a geometrically constituted idea, and the doctrines that matter is eternal, that evil springs from matter, and that the divine shapes matter through soul. The summary further touches on sensation, opinion, phantasia and memory, on a sketch of the ten categories, and on the Timaeus' 'receptacle' (chōra) as the intermediary seat of becoming. Readers of intertexts will find here a compressed paraphrase in which Platonic wording and Plutarch's psychological and cosmological arguments can be traced in close conjunction.
grc.plutarch.fabius_maximus: A Greek life of the Roman statesman Fabius Maximus by Plutarch, which opens by announcing a turn in the narrative from Pericles to Fabius and recounts a legendary genealogy tracing the Fabian house to Heracles and a nymph by the Tiber. The account characterizes Fabius as slow and taciturn, marked by the childhood nicknames Verrucosus and Ovicula, with a steadiness of mind that outsiders mistook for dullness. It then follows his public career through his consulships, a triumph over the Ligurians, and the early years of Hannibal's invasion of Italy, including the Roman defeats at the Trebia and Lake Trasimene and Fabius's policy of refusing battle in order to wear down the invader.
grc.plutarch.instituta_laconica: A brief Greek collection of notices on Spartan institutions and customs transmitted among the Moralia of Plutarch. Its entries describe the common messes and their austere fare, including the much-praised black broth, the hardening regimen of boys and youths, sleeping on reed beds, moving about in darkness, enduring hunger and licensed stealing, and the strict deference owed to elders. Later entries turn to Spartan music and poetry, covering the three choruses of the age-classes, the martial marching rhythms ascribed to Lycurgus, and punitive episodes involving Terpander and Timotheus. The whole is arranged as a loose antiquarian compilation rather than a connected narrative.
grc.plutarch.lacaenarum_apophthegmata: A collection of apophthegms attributed to Spartan women, transmitted among the works of Plutarch as part of his Moralia and of uncertain date. It preserves brief anecdotes in which mothers, wives, and daughters of Lacedaemon deliver terse remarks on courage, childbearing, and loyalty to Sparta, with figures such as Gorgo daughter of Cleomenes and Argileonis the mother of Brasidas among the speakers. Many entries turn on a mother's reply to news of a son's death or flight from battle, and several close with short epitaphs on cowardly sons.
grc.plutarch.lucullus: Plutarch's Lucullus is a Greek biographical account of the Roman statesman and general Lucius Licinius Lucullus, whose career belongs to the late Republic and was bound up with Sulla, Pompey, and the Mithridatic War. The narrative opens with Lucullus' ancestry and his youthful prosecution of Servilius the augur, then follows his cultivated eloquence, his service under Sulla, and his missions by sea to Crete, Cyrene, and Alexandria. The life proceeds through his command against Mithridates in the East and closes with his withdrawal from public affairs into a retirement of great wealth.
grc.plutarch.maxime_cum_princibus_philsopho_: A short Greek essay by Plutarch, known by its Latin title Maxime cum principibus philosopho esse disserendum, 'that a philosopher should discourse especially with men in power'. The argument urges that philosophy benefits the many when its practitioners cultivate the friendship of rulers, citing Anaxagoras with Pericles, Plato with Dion, Pythagoras with the leading men of Italy, and Cato's voyage to Athenodorus and Scipio's summons of Panaetius as examples. The opening discussion also distinguishes inward thought from spoken discourse, makes friendship the end of both, and contrasts the retired, private philosopher with one engaged in politics and public action.
grc.plutarch.nicias: Plutarch's Life of Nicias belongs to his series of paired biographies and is presented alongside the Life of Crassus, the opening preface defending the comparison of the Sicilian calamities of Athens with the Parthian disasters of Rome. The work treats the career of the Athenian statesman and general Nicias, son of Niceratus, drawing on Aristotle's judgement of him as one of the three most patriotic citizens of his day. It follows his rise to leadership after the death of Pericles, his rivalry with Cleon, his great wealth and lavish public benefactions, his pronounced piety and timidity, and finally his command of the Athenian expedition to Sicily and its destruction before Syracuse.
grc.plutarch.non_posse_suaviter_vivi_secundu: A Greek dialogue by Plutarch, transmitted among the Moralia, whose title may be rendered 'That a Pleasant Life Is Impossible According to Epicurus'. The work answers the pamphlet of Colotes, an associate of Epicurus, who had claimed that under the doctrines of the other philosophers no one could even live; Plutarch reverses the charge and contends that a pleasant life is impossible on Epicurean principles. Cast as a conversation among the narrator, Zeuxippus, Theon and Aristodemus after the breaking-up of a school session, it argues that bodily pleasures are brief, unstable and inseparable from pain, and that Epicurus and Metrodorus themselves concede how slight the pleasure of the flesh is.
grc.plutarch.otho: A Greek biographical narrative by Plutarch, one of the Lives, devoted to the Roman emperor Otho. It opens with Otho's accession after Galba, his overtures to the Senate and people, his treatment of Tigellinus, and his efforts to conciliate the soldiery, whose restlessness repeatedly threatens his authority. News then arrives that Vitellius has taken on the dignity and power of emperor, and letters come from Mucianus in Syria and Vespasian in Judaea, as the account moves towards war between the rivals.
grc.plutarch.philopoemen: A Greek Life of Philopoemen of Megalopolis, the statesman and general of the Achaeans, preserved among the biographies of Plutarch. The account opens with the circumstances of his birth and upbringing, his orphaned childhood, and a philosophical education under teachers associated with the Academy, before characterizing his temperament in the mould of Epaminondas. Subsequent narrative treats his rejection of athletic training in favour of military preparation, his frugal country life and farming, and his spending on horses, arms, and the ransoming of captives. Anecdotes about his appearance and manners, including a jest attributed to Titus Flamininus, round out the portrait of the man.
grc.plutarch.platonicae_quaestiones: Platonicae Quaestiones is a Greek prose work by Plutarch, transmitted in the Moralia, comprising a sequence of philosophical questions on puzzles arising from Plato's dialogues. The opening question asks why the god instructed Socrates to act as midwife for others while forbidding him to father doctrines of his own, citing the Theaetetus and discussing the elenchus, the dangers of partiality in judging one's own teachings, and the maieutic method; a subsequent question considers why the supreme god is addressed as both father and maker of the cosmos. The discussion proceeds dialectically, weighing rival answers in the manner of Platonic interpretation.
grc.plutarch.publicola: Plutarch's Greek biography of Publicola, one of the Parallel Lives and expressly paired with the Life of Solon, concerns Publius Valerius, who later received the surname Publicola from the Roman people. The narrative follows his prominence in speech and wealth under the kings, his part alongside Brutus in the expulsion of Tarquinius Superbus after the outrage upon Lucretia, and his disappointment when Collatinus, not he, was chosen as Brutus's colleague in the consulship. It then recounts Publicola's oath never to yield to the Tarquins, the embassy seeking the return of the exiles' property, and the discovery of the conspiracy of the Aquillii and Vitellii, in which members of Brutus's own household were implicated.
grc.plutarch.quaestiones_convivales: Quaestiones Convivales ('Table Talk') is a Greek dialogue by Plutarch, framed as a letter to Sossius Senecio collecting problems raised at banquets the author attended in Rome and Greece. The work is arranged as a series of symposium questions, whether philosophy belongs at a drinking party, what conduct and conversation suit the table, and related matters of ethics, custom, and natural inquiry, resolved through reported dinner-table discussion. In the opening section the speakers debate whether philosophy may properly be pursued over wine, adducing the symposium writings of Plato, Xenophon, Aristotle, Epicurus, and other philosophers as precedent.
grc.plutarch.quomodo_adulator_ab_amico_inter: A Greek moral essay by Plutarch, preserved among the Moralia, framed as a discourse addressed to Antiochus Philopappus on how to distinguish the flatterer from the true friend. Opening from Plato's remark that excessive self-love blinds judgement, the speaker argues that everyone is his own first flatterer and that flattery fastens most readily on the ambitious and the great, sometimes overturning kingships and empires. The essay explores why the agreeable friend is so hard to tell from the parasite, since both offer pleasure and timely praise, and illustrates the danger with anecdotes about notorious flatterers, including Melanthion, the parasite of Alexander of Pherae.
grc.plutarch.regum_et_imperatorum_apophthegm: The Regum et Imperatorum Apophthegmata, a Greek collection of sayings of kings and commanders preserved among Plutarch's Moralia, is dedicated to the emperor Trajan. Its preface argues that offhand remarks and spoken judgments reveal a ruler's character and disposition more clearly than deeds, which are mingled with fortune. The body of the work assembles brief anecdotes and pointed utterances arranged by individual, beginning with Persian monarchs such as Cyrus, Darius, Xerxes, and Artaxerxes, and continuing with Semiramis and other figures from Greek and Roman history. Each entry typically offers a single apophthegm or short episode illustrating the speaker's wit, generosity, or exercise of power.
grc.plutarch.solon: Plutarch's Life of Solon, one of the Greek biographies collected in the work known as Plutarch's Lives, recounts the career of the Athenian statesman, lawgiver and poet. The account opens with the question of Solon's parentage and his family ties to Peisistratus, then treats his youth in trade, the moral and political maxims of his poetry, his place among the Seven Sages, and the story of the disputed tripod. The Life goes on to follow Solon's travels, his legislation and reforms at Athens, and his meeting with Croesus, quoting extensively from his elegiac and iambic verse throughout.
grc.plutarch.theseus: The Life of Theseus is a Greek biographical work by Plutarch, paired with the life of Romulus in the Parallel Lives. It opens with a preface addressed to Sossius Senecio on the remotest age of myth, in which the writer proposes to sift away the fabulous element by reasoned argument and to follow credible history where it is attainable. The narrative traces Theseus's descent from Erechtheus and Pelops, the wisdom of his grandfather Pittheus at Troezen, the Delphic oracle given to Aegeus, his union with Aethra, and the hiding of sword and sandals beneath a rock, before turning to the hero's birth, upbringing, and dedication of his hair at Delphi. Theseus is set against Romulus throughout as a child of obscure birth ascribed to the gods, a founder and unifier of Athens, with the two compared in their abductions of women and their misfortunes with their fellow citizens.
grc.plutarch.tiberius_gracchus: Plutarch's Life of Tiberius Gracchus, a Greek prose biography from the Plutarchan Lives as printed in Perrin's Loeb edition, presents the elder Gracchan brother within the 'Roman pairing' with Gaius announced at its opening. It sets out the family's standing through the elder Tiberius Gracchus and Cornelia, daughter of Scipio Africanus, contrasts the brothers' looks, speech, and habits, and then follows Tiberius through service under Scipio at Carthage, the quaestorship under Mancinus and the negotiated surrender to the Numantines, and his tribunate with its agrarian law, whose defence against the propertied class ends the preserved portion. The 97 lines break off in the conflict with the tribune Marcus Octavius, so the Life's later course is unrepresented. Readers hunting parallels will find Polybius, Fannius, and Gaius Gracchus's memoir invoked as authorities, allusive touches such as the Dioscuri comparison of the brothers' oratory, and the celebrated passage likening landless Italians to beasts that have dens and lairs but no share in the land they fight for.
grc.plutarch.vitae_decem_oratorum: The Vitae decem oratorum ('Lives of the Ten Orators'), a Greek prose work preserved among the Moralia attributed to Plutarch, consists of short biographies of the ten canonical Attic orators, beginning with Antiphon. The opening life recounts Antiphon's family and pupils, his association with Socrates, his role as the first to write courtroom speeches for citizens, the decree passed against him at the fall of the Four Hundred, and the conflicting ancient reports of his death. Each notice covers ancestry, teachers, careers, writings and death, citing earlier authorities such as Xenophon, Theopompus and Caecilius, and occasionally quoting public documents, including the condemnation decree against Antiphon in full.
grc.plutarch_pseudo.placita_philosophorum: The Placita Philosophorum ('Opinions of the Philosophers'), a Greek doxographic treatise attributed to Plutarch but pseudepigraphic and of uncertain date, assembles the doctrines of Greek philosophers on natural philosophy. It opens by dividing philosophy into its physical, ethical, and logical parts and by defining nature, then proceeds through successive thinkers and schools, Thales and the Ionian succession, Pythagoras and the Italians, Heraclitus, Empedocles, Epicurus, Socrates and Plato, Aristotle, and Zeno, reporting each one's teaching on first principles, elements, and the cosmos. Entries typically identify a philosopher by patronymic and city, state his position on the principle of things, and often append criticism of it.
grc.polyaenus.strategemata: The Strategemata of Polyaenus is a Greek collection of military stratagems dedicated to the emperors Antoninus and Verus, placing it in the mid-second century CE. Its author, who presents himself as a Macedonian too old for active service, offers instead an account of the ruses by which commanders have won victories with minimal risk, prefaced by a long discussion of cunning and trickery in Homer. By its own account the work comprises eight books and nine hundred stratagems, arranged commander by commander, beginning with the mythological Dionysus and Pan and continuing through the generals of Greek and barbarian history, each entry recording a brief anecdote of a successful trick.
grc.pseudoaristotle.de_mundo: The De Mundo is a Greek philosophical treatise addressed to Alexander and transmitted under Aristotle's name, though of uncertain authorship and date. Its opening proem praises philosophy as a divine endowment by which the soul beholds the whole of things, after which the cosmos is defined as an ordered system of heaven and earth, its arrangement maintained by gods. The work then surveys the structure of the universe: the spherical heavens with their fixed stars and seven planetary circles, the aether as a fifth element, the fiery and airy regions with their comets, winds and storms, and the motionless earth at the centre. It closes with the five elements laid out in concentric spherical layers and a description of the inhabited world as a single island amid the encircling Atlantic, itself one of many such islands beyond human sight.
grc.pseudoarrianus.anonymi_arriani_ut_fertur: A short Greek periplus of the Euxine or Black Sea, transmitted under Arrian's name (pseudo-Arrian) but of uncertain authorship and date. The account begins at the Hieron of Zeus Ourios on the Bithynian coast by the mouth of the Pontus and follows the southern shore eastwards through Bithynia and Paphlagonia, listing rivers, harbours, promontories, towns and trading-places with the distances between them given in stadia and converted into Roman miles. The coastal measurements are interspersed with brief notes on anchorages and sailing conditions and on colonial foundations, including Heracleia, a Dorian foundation of the Megarians and Boeotians, and Amastris, named after Amastris, the Persian wife of Dionysius, tyrant of Heracleia.
grc.pseudogalen.de_theriaca_ad_pamphilianum: A Greek medical treatise on theriac, the compound antidote, spuriously attributed to Galen and of uncertain date. Cast as a letter to a certain Pamphilianus, it sets out when and how theriac is to be taken: against venomous bites and poisonous draughts, as a prophylactic administered in health and during travel, and for a range of acute and chronic ailments, with dosages and diluents specified case by case. The closing sections give instructions for preparing the remedies involved, including the formulations of Hedyochrus and of Andromachus's theriac as later arranged by Crito, along with their long lists of ingredients.
grc.pseudolucian.χαρίδημος_ἢ_περὶ_κάλλους: A brief Greek dialogue transmitted in the Lucianic corpus, attributed to Lucian but of uncertain authorship and date. The opening conversation between Hermippus and Charidemus gives way to Charidemus' account of a symposium held in the Piraeus at the house of Androcles, where the beauty of the youth Cleonymus prompted the guests to deliver speeches in praise of beauty. The reported speeches hold that beauty alone wins the favour of gods and men, drawing exempla from Pelops, Ganymede, Helen, Heracles and the Dioscuri, with much made of Zeus's pursuit of beautiful youths.
grc.pseudomenander.sententiae_corresponds_to: A Greek collection of moral maxims transmitted under the name of the comic poet Menander, their actual authorship and date being uncertain. The sayings, mostly single-line iambic trimeters with a few longer pieces, are arranged in rough alphabetical order and give gnomic advice on friendship, wealth, marriage and women, old age, self-control, and the workings of fortune. The version given here is the Greek counterpart of an Arabic transmission of the so-called Sentences of Menander.

A short Greek collection of monostich moral maxims transmitted under the name of the comic poet Menander, of uncertain date, preserved in the form corresponding to the second Arabic version of the so-called Menander Sentences. Its one-line precepts counsel piety toward God, honour to parents and elders, mastery of tongue and temper, constancy in friendship, moderation in wealth and poverty, and wariness of pleasure, women, and old age. A few verses also circulate in other authors, among them one maxim taken from Gregory of Nazianzus's Carmen morale.
grc.pseudoplutarch.de_fluviis: A short Greek prose treatise on rivers and mountains, transmitted under Plutarch's name (hence the conventional designation Pseudo-Plutarch) but generally treated as the work of an unknown later author of uncertain date. Each numbered entry takes a river or mountain, chiefly in Boeotia, Thrace, and the eastern lands reached by Alexander, and recounts an aetiological myth, usually a suicide, metamorphosis, or divine act, that explains a change of name, often adding notices of marvellous stones, plants, and local customs. Named authorities, many otherwise unknown, are cited throughout in support of the individual stories.
grc.pseudoscymnus.scymni_chii_ut_fertur_peri: A Greek geographical periegesis of uncertain date, transmitted under the name of Scymnus of Chios but preserved as the work of Pseudo-Scymnus, an attribution its own title marks as reported tradition rather than secure. Composed in iambic trimeter and addressed in its proem to a king Nicomedes, it opens with a defence of the comic metre as a vehicle for a brief, clear, and memorable digest of history and geography, and names its chief authorities, among them Eratosthenes, Ephorus, Timaeus, and Demetrius of Callatis. The survey then sets out from the Atlantic strait and the Pillars of Heracles and follows the coasts of Iberia, Liguria, Italy, Sicily, the Adriatic, mainland Greece, the Aegean islands, Thrace, and the Black Sea, recording city foundations, colonial settlements, peoples, rivers, and local customs.
grc.quintus_smyrnaeus.fall_of_troy: A Greek epic in fourteen books by Quintus Smyrnaeus, of uncertain date, narrating the Trojan War from the death and cremation of Hector to the fall of the city. The poem opens with the arrival of the Amazon queen Penthesilea and her company at Priam's Troy, and proceeds through the coming of Memnon, the death of Achilles, the contest for his arms, and the stratagem by which the Greeks at last enter and sack the town. Composed in Homeric hexameters, it is conventionally known as the Posthomerica.
grc.sappho.fragments: Surviving fragments of the lyric poetry of Sappho, composed in the Aeolic Greek dialect of Lesbos and preserved in a fragmentary state, with many poems broken at beginning, middle, or end. The more complete pieces include a prayer to Aphrodite for release from the pains of love, a song praying to Hera for the safe return of the speaker's brother Charaxos with a fully laden ship, and an invitation to Aphrodite to enter a fragrant garden grove. Shorter remains touch on love and desire, the appearances and power of the gods, voyages, and festive occasions, across a variety of lyric metres.
grc.septuaginta.aggaeus: Aggaeus (Haggai) is the Greek version of one of the twelve Minor Prophets, transmitted in the Septuagint, the Hellenistic-era Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures. The work comprises four dated oracles attributed to the prophet Haggai, set in the second year of the reign of King Darius, in which the prophet summons Zerubbabel son of Salathiel and Joshua son of Josedek the high priest to rebuild the house of the Lord, warning of drought, blight, and hardship on the people's labors and promising that the glory of the new temple will exceed that of the former one. A closing oracle addresses Zerubbabel directly, declaring that the Lord will make him as a signet.
grc.septuaginta.amos: The Greek version of the biblical book of Amos contained in the Septuagint, a rendering of the Hebrew prophetic corpus produced in the Hellenistic period. The book presents the words of Amos of Thecue, who is set in the days of Uzziah king of Judah and Jeroboam son of Joash king of Israel, two years before the earthquake. It opens with a series of oracles pronouncing judgment on Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, Ammon, Moab, Judah, and finally Israel for their transgressions, followed by extended denunciations of Israelite injustice, idolatry, and complacency, with punishments announced by fire, sword, and exile. Later chapters bring visions of destruction, the overthrow of the sanctuary at Bethel, and closing promises of restoration.
grc.septuaginta.canticum: The Canticum is the Greek Septuagint version of the Song of Songs, a biblical love poem whose opening superscription names Solomon as its author. The Greek rendering belongs to the Hellenistic period and casts the work as a dialogue between a bride and her bridegroom, with interjections from the daughters of Jerusalem, in prose form and richly stocked with imagery of gardens, vineyards, spices, and perfumes. The poem traces the lovers through scenes of seeking and reunion, mutual praise, the king's bridal procession from the wilderness, and the enclosed garden where the couple's love is celebrated.
grc.septuaginta.daniel_theodotionis: The Book of Daniel in the Greek version attributed to Theodotion, preserved within the Septuagint corpus under that name. A prose biblical work of Hellenistic date, it follows Daniel and his companions Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah into exile at the Babylonian court of Nebuchadnezzar, recounting the interpretation of the king's dreams and of the writing on the wall at Belshazzar's feast, the deliverance from the lions' den, and a series of apocalyptic visions. The version also carries the deuterocanonical additions to Daniel, namely the Prayer and Song of the Three Young Men, the story of Susanna, and the tale of Bel and the Dragon.
grc.septuaginta.daniel_translatio_graeca: The Septuagint Greek translation of the biblical book of Daniel, written in Hellenistic prose as part of the Greek Old Testament. It opens with Nebuchadnezzar's siege of Jerusalem and the deportation of Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah to the Babylonian court, where the youths refuse the king's rations and surpass the Chaldean sages. The book proceeds through Daniel's interpretations of royal dreams, the deliverance of his companions from the fiery furnace, and the writing on the wall under Belshazzar, to visions culminating in the first year of Cyrus. In its Greek form it also carries stories additional to the Hebrew-Aramaic Daniel, such as those of Susanna and of Bel and the Dragon.
grc.septuaginta.ecclesiasticus: Ecclesiasticus, or the Wisdom of Jesus son of Sirach, is a Hellenistic Jewish wisdom book preserved in Greek in the Septuagint. Its prologue presents the work as sayings gathered by Jesus son of Sirach, a follower of Solomon, and arranged in Greek by his grandson. The book consists of aphorisms and longer instructional discourses on the fear of the Lord, piety, family duties, friendship, wealth, and speech, together with prayers, hymns, and accounts of men of earlier generations who pleased God.
grc.septuaginta.epistula_jeremiae: The Epistle of Jeremiah is a short Greek prose work preserved in the Septuagint, cast as a letter from the prophet Jeremiah to the exiles whom Nebuchadnezzar is about to carry off to Babylon for seven generations. Its argument is a sustained polemic against idolatry: it mocks gods of silver, gold and wood as man-made objects that cannot speak, walk, save or benefit their worshippers, and repeatedly urges the deportees not to fear them. Of uncertain authorship, the work belongs to the Hellenistic period and is counted among the biblical books of the Greek Old Testament.
grc.septuaginta.esdras_a: Esdras A, conventionally known in English as 1 Esdras, is an anonymous Greek prose work of uncertain Hellenistic date, preserved in the Septuagint and printed in Swete's Cambridge edition of 1896. It retells the history of Judah from Josiah's celebration of the Passover at Jerusalem and his defeat and death before Pharaoh Necho, through the Babylonian conquest of the city and temple and the exile, in a form closely related to the narrative of Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah. For readers of intertexts its interest lies in the close verbal parallels it offers with those Hebrew-based accounts, since the divergences between the Greek and Hebrew forms of the same episodes illuminate translation practice, source arrangement, and the reception of the biblical story in the Hellenistic world.
grc.septuaginta.ezechiel: The Greek version of the biblical book of Ezekiel as preserved in the Septuagint, the Hellenistic-era Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures. The book presents itself as the visions and oracles of Ezekiel son of Buzi, a priest set among the exiles by the river Chebar in the land of the Chaldeans. Its opening chapters recount the prophet's inaugural vision of four living creatures and whirling wheels beneath the divine throne, together with his commission to speak a hard word to the house of Israel; the remainder consists of oracles of judgment and restoration directed at Israel and the surrounding nations.
