grc.septuaginta.isaias: The Book of Isaiah in Greek, forming part of the Septuagint, the Greek version of the Hebrew scriptures, and given here in the form witnessed by Codex Alexandrinus. The translation belongs to the Hellenistic period and its makers are unrecorded, while the prophecies themselves are attributed to Isaiah son of Amoz and are set, by the opening verse, in the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah of Judah. The book consists of prose oracles and visions of judgment and salvation directed against Judah, Jerusalem, and the foreign nations, together with denunciations of corrupt worship and injustice, oracles on the day of the Lord, and promises of the restoration of Zion.
grc.septuaginta.jeremias: The Book of Jeremiah in its Greek form as preserved in the Septuagint, the Hellenistic-era Greek version of the Hebrew scriptures. The book opens with a superscription dating the prophet's activity from the thirteenth year of Josiah to the captivity of Jerusalem under Zedekiah, followed by an account of Jeremiah's call and visions. The remainder consists largely of oracles of judgment against Judah and Israel for idolatry and apostasy, together with narratives and prophetic discourses; the Greek version is shorter than the Hebrew and arranges much of the material in a different order.
grc.septuaginta.joel: The Greek Joel, preserved in Swete's Cambridge Septuagint as the second book of the Twelve Prophets, renders into Hellenistic Greek a Hebrew prophecy attributed to Joel son of Bathuel and of uncertain date. In roughly seventy lines the book moves from a devastating locust plague, lamented in oracles and calls to fasting and weeping, to the promise that God's spirit will be poured out on all flesh and that the nations will be judged on the great day of the Lord. Its apocalyptic imagery, the trumpet alarm in Zion, a darkened sun and blood-red moon, the approach of an irresistible army, was widely echoed in later Jewish and Christian apocalyptic writing, most famously in the Pentecost speech of Acts, and the Septuagint wording supplies the Greek forms in which those echoes circulated.
grc.septuaginta.jonas: The Book of Jonah in its Greek Septuagint version, a biblical prose narrative rendered into Greek in the Hellenistic period. It recounts how the word of the Lord commissions Jonah son of Amathi to preach against Nineveh, how the prophet flees by ship toward Tharsis, is cast into the sea to calm a divinely raised storm, and passes three days and nights in the belly of a great sea-monster, praying for deliverance. The latter chapters follow his renewed mission to Nineveh, the fast and repentance decreed by its king, Jonah's anger at the city's pardon, and the episode of the gourd that shades him and then withers, through which the divine mercy is set against the prophet's displeasure.
grc.septuaginta.josue: The book of Joshua in its Greek Septuagint version, a translation of the Hebrew original into koinē prose made by an unnamed translator at some point in the Hellenistic period. The narrative continues the story of the Pentateuch after the death of Moses: Joshua son of Nun leads the Israelites across the Jordan into Canaan, beginning with the spies sent from Shittim who are sheltered by Rahab in Jericho. The work recounts the crossing of the river, the fall of Jericho, the campaigns against the kings of the land, and the allotment of the conquered territory among the tribes of Israel.
grc.septuaginta.judith: Judith, preserved in Greek as part of the Septuagint, is a prose biblical narrative of Hellenistic date by an unknown author. It recounts how Nebuchadnezzar, portrayed as king of the Assyrians at Nineveh, defeats Arphaxad of the Medes and despatches his general Holofernes to punish the western nations that refused to aid him. The story moves to the siege of the Judean town of Bethulia, which is resolved when the widow Judith enters the enemy camp, gains Holofernes' confidence, and kills him, whereupon the Assyrian army is routed and her people delivered.
grc.septuaginta.kritai: The Book of Judges (Kritai) in its ancient Greek form, one of the historical books of the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures undertaken in the Hellenistic period by translators of unknown identity. Opening after the death of Joshua, it recounts the Israelite tribes' campaigns against the Canaanites and Amorites and then the recurring cycle of apostasy, foreign oppression, and deliverance by leaders known as judges. Its narratives include the exploits of figures such as Othniel, Gideon, Jephthah, and Samson, and it closes with episodes of tribal warfare and the migration of the Danites.
grc.septuaginta.machabaeorum_b: The second of the Maccabean books in the Greek Old Testament, a prose work of the Hellenistic period by an unknown author. It opens with two letters sent from Jerusalem to the Jewish communities of Egypt, urging observance of the feast of the purification of the temple and relating how the sacred fire, hidden by priests at the time of the exile, was recovered in the days of Nehemiah, and how Jeremiah concealed the tabernacle, the ark, and the altar of incense. The remainder recounts the Maccabean uprising: the persecution under Antiochus IV, the martyrdoms, the campaigns of Judas Maccabaeus, and the cleansing and rededication of the temple in Jerusalem. Prayers, speeches, and visions are woven into the narrative.
grc.septuaginta.machabaeorum_d: Fourth Maccabees is a Greek prose work transmitted with the Septuagint, of uncertain date and authorship. Writing in a philosophical register, the author argues that pious reason is sovereign over the passions, defining reason, wisdom, temperance, courage, and justice before illustrating the thesis from the Jewish law. The central narratives recount the martyrdoms of the aged scribe Eleazar and of seven brothers with their mother under Antiochus IV, presenting their endurance of torture as proof that reason strengthened by piety masters pain and death. Though biblical in setting and long circulated among Old Testament texts, it stands as an appendix rather than a canonical book.
grc.septuaginta.machabaeorum_i: First Maccabees is a Hellenistic prose narrative of biblical character, preserved in Greek within the Septuagint and of uncertain authorship and date. It opens with the conquests of Alexander the Great and goes on to recount the rise of Antiochus Epiphanes, his plundering of the temple in Jerusalem, and the royal decree compelling all peoples to abandon their ancestral laws, culminating in the erection of the abomination of desolation upon the altar. The narrative then follows the persecution of observant Jews and the outbreak of the Maccabean revolt against Seleucid rule in Judea.
grc.septuaginta.nahum: The Book of Nahum in its Greek form as transmitted in the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures made during the Hellenistic period. The book presents itself as an oracle of vision concerning Nineveh delivered by Nahum the Elkoshite, and opens with oracles on the zeal, vengeance, and long-suffering of the Lord, who is good to those who take refuge in him in the day of affliction. The remaining oracles proclaim the deliverance of Judah, the siege and plunder of Nineveh, and the city's denunciation as a deceitful harlot, closing with a lament over the incurable wound of Assyria and the applause of all who hear of its ruin.
grc.septuaginta.odae: The Odae, or Odes, form a collection of biblical canticles transmitted as an appendix in manuscripts of the Septuagint and printed as such in Swete's Cambridge edition of the Greek Old Testament (1905). The songs are prose canticles in Septuagintal Greek attributed to biblical figures, opening with the Song of Moses at the Red Sea ('Let us sing to the Lord, for gloriously has he been glorified') and continuing with the song of Deuteronomy 32 and related pieces; the constituent songs belong to the Hellenistic-era Greek Bible, though the compilation itself is of uncertain date. Because these canticles circulated liturgically and supplied a shared stock of phrasing for Greek-speaking readers, their language echoes throughout later hymnody, prayer, and poetry, making the collection a rich source of parallels for hunters of intertexts.
grc.septuaginta.proverbia: The Paroimiai is the Greek version of the biblical Book of Proverbs, preserved as part of the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament, and belongs to the Hellenistic period. Its opening ascribes the collection to Solomon, son of David, who reigned over Israel. Written in prose, it comprises paternal instructions to a son, speeches of personified Wisdom crying out in streets and gates, longer discourses on discipline, justice, and the fear of God, and collections of short moral maxims.
grc.septuaginta.psalmi: The Psalms (Psalmi) form the Greek Psalter of the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament, translated in the Hellenistic period. The collection consists of prayers, laments, hymns of praise, and royal psalms, most of them introduced by superscriptions that ascribe them to David or connect them with episodes in his life, such as his flight before Absalom. The verses are punctuated by the recurring refrain διάψαλμα, and the Greek throughout is prose rather than verse.
grc.septuaginta.ruth: The Book of Ruth in its Greek form, part of the Septuagint, the Hellenistic-era Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible made by anonymous translators whose individual identities and precise dates are unrecorded. The book is a short prose narrative recounting how Naomi, bereft of her husband and sons in the land of Moab, returns to Bethlehem with her Moabite daughter-in-law Ruth; Ruth gleans in the fields of the kinsman Boaz, is married to him after a nearer kinsman declines, and bears Obed, grandfather of David. The Greek rendering, presented in four chapters, follows the Hebrew storyline while exhibiting the word choices and occasional expansions characteristic of Septuagint translation style.
grc.septuaginta.susanna_theodotionis: A Greek prose narrative of Hellenistic origin, Susanna is transmitted in the Septuagint in the version attributed to Theodotion and is traditionally counted among the Greek additions to the Book of Daniel. It tells how Susanna, the beautiful and God-fearing wife of Joakim in Babylon, is accosted by two elders who, when she refuses them, bring a false charge of adultery against her, and how the assembly condemns her on their testimony. The young Daniel intervenes, separates the two witnesses and exposes their contradictions under questioning, so that Susanna is vindicated and the elders themselves face judgment.
grc.septuaginta.threni_seu_lamentationes: The Greek version of the biblical book of Lamentations, transmitted in the Septuagint under the title Threni. The work consists of five laments over the fall of Jerusalem, the desolation of Judah, and the exile of their people, arranged in short stanzas headed by the letters of the Hebrew alphabet as an acrostic scheme. The Hebrew original mourns the destruction of the city and temple and pleads with God for compassion upon a chastened Sion; the Hellenistic-era Greek translation renders it in prose and is transmitted anonymously as part of the Septuagint corpus.
grc.septuaginta.tobias: The Book of Tobias (Tobit) is a biblical narrative preserved in Greek in the Septuagint, of Hellenistic date and anonymous authorship. Told in the first person, it recounts how Tobit, a devout Israelite of the tribe of Naphtali deported to Nineveh, loses his sight after burying fellow Israelites killed by the Assyrian king, while in Media his kinswoman Sarah loses seven husbands to the demon Asmodeus. God sends the angel Raphael, who in human guise guides Tobit's son Tobias to Media, where he marries Sarah, drives out the demon with the smoke of a fish's heart and liver, and returns to cure his father's blindness with the fish's gall. The book closes with Tobit's hymn of praise and deathbed instructions to his son and with Tobias's witnessing of the fall of Nineveh.
grc.septuaginta.zacharias: The Book of Zechariah as preserved in the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament, a Hellenistic-era translation of Hebrew prophetic writings. The prophecies are ascribed to Zechariah, son of Berechiah and of the line of Iddo, and are set in the early Persian period, dated within the book by the regnal years of Darius. The book opens with calls to repentance and proceeds through a series of night visions, riders among the myrtle trees, four horns and four smiths, a man with a measuring line, the cleansing of the high priest Joshua (rendered Jesus in Greek), and the golden lampstand, followed by oracles on the restoration of Jerusalem, its king, and the nations.
grc.sophocles.ajax: A Greek tragedy by Sophocles, dramatizing the fate of Ajax after the arms of Achilles are awarded to Odysseus. In the prologue Athena shows Odysseus that she has turned Ajax's murderous rage upon the army's flocks and herds, which he has slaughtered in the belief that they were the Atreidae and their followers, and she holds him deluded inside his tent. The play goes on to depict Ajax's recognition of his disgrace and his suicide, the laments of Tecmessa and the chorus, the quarrel between Teucer, Agamemnon and Menelaus over his burial, and its settlement through Odysseus's intervention.
grc.sophocles.antigone: A Greek tragedy by Sophocles, of uncertain date, dramatizing the conflict between Antigone and Creon over the burial of her brother Polynices. The opening scene presents Antigone telling her sister Ismene of Creon's edict that Polynices be left unburied on pain of death, and of her resolve to bury him regardless. The action follows her arrest and condemnation, the debate over divine versus civic law, and the deaths that befall Creon's household in consequence.
grc.sophocles.ichneutae: The Ichneutae ('Trackers'), a satyr drama by the Greek tragedian Sophocles, survives in fragmentary form on a papyrus from Oxyrhynchus, with substantial lacunae throughout. The plot concerns the theft of Apollo's cattle: Silenus and the satyrs, promised a reward, track the stolen herd from Thessaly and Boeotia to Cyllene, where the trail leads to the infant Hermes and his invention of the lyre. The preserved portions include a herald's proclamation announcing the search and its terms, tracking scenes in which the satyrs pursue the thieves, dialogue with the child Hermes, and choral passages.
grc.sophocles.oedipus_at_colonus: Oedipus at Colonus is a Greek tragedy by Sophocles, written in iambic trimeter with lyric portions for the chorus of elders of Colonus. The play opens with the blind Oedipus, led by his daughter Antigone, arriving at a sacred grove near Athens, which he comes to recognise as the seat of the Eumenides and the appointed place of his death. The action turns on his reception by Theseus, Creon's attempt to seize him and carry him back to Thebes, his meeting with his son Polynices, and his final withdrawal from mortal sight. The drama closes with Antigone and Ismene mourning their father and Antigone preparing to return to Thebes.
grc.sophocles.oedipus_tyrannus: Sophocles' Oedipus Tyrannus is a Greek tragedy in which Oedipus, king of Thebes, undertakes to discover the cause of the plague devastating his city and learns that he himself is the source of the pollution, having killed his father and married his mother. The opening scene shows Oedipus addressing the priest and the suppliants gathered before the palace and announcing that Creon has been sent to Delphi for an oracle; later episodes bring the confrontation with Tiresias, the quarrel with Creon, and the successive revelations that end in Jocasta's death and Oedipus' self-blinding. Spoken dialogue in the episodes alternates throughout with songs of the chorus of Theban elders.
grc.sophocles.philoctetes: Philoctetes is a Greek tragedy by Sophocles, written in verse. The action is set on the deserted island of Lemnos, where Odysseus and Neoptolemus, son of Achilles, come to obtain the bow of Heracles held by Philoctetes, a Greek hero left behind years earlier because of a festering, noisome wound. Odysseus instructs the young Neoptolemus to win Philoctetes' confidence by lying about the quarrel over Achilles' arms and to secure the weapon by stealth, since the fall of Troy depends upon it. The drama hinges on Neoptolemus' growing conflict between the deceit demanded of him and his sense of honour toward the suffering archer.
grc.sophocles.trachiniae: Trachiniae, a Greek tragedy by Sophocles and of uncertain date, takes its name from Trachis, where Deianira awaits news of her long-absent husband Heracles. The play opens with Deianira's account of her wooing by the river-god Achelous and her rescue by Heracles, and moves through the revelation that he labours in Lydia and campaigns against Eurytus in Euboea. The action turns on Deianira's unwitting gift of a robe steeped in the blood of the centaur Nessus, which destroys Heracles and leads to his death on the pyre of Mount Oeta, while their son Hyllus is directed to take Heracles' captive Iole as his bride.
grc.soranus.de_signis_fracturarum: De Signis Fracturarum is a short Greek medical treatise by Soranus on the diagnostic signs of fractures. It opens by defining the cranial fracture (katagma) and distinguishing its named varieties, including the fissure, the depressed fracture, the bending of one bone against another, the impaction and the axe-like severance, before proceeding region by region over the rest of the body, from nose, jaw, clavicle and scapula through spine, sternum and ribs to hips, upper arm and thigh. Throughout, fractures are identified by sight and by palpation, through deformity, crepitus, swelling and accompanying symptoms such as sharp pain, difficulty in breathing, coughing of blood and numbness of the neighbouring limb.
grc.soranus.gynaeciorum_libri_iv: A Greek treatise on women's medicine in four books, attributed to Soranus and transmitted under the Latin title Gynaeciorum Libri IV. The opening passage sets out a programmatic division of the art into the part concerning the midwife and the part concerning the conditions that fall to her, and then characterizes the ideal midwife, enumerating her intellectual, physical, and moral qualifications. The announced plan proceeds from the female anatomy, beginning with the womb and the etymologies of its names, through hygiene and disorders of women, including suppressed menstruation, hysterical suffocation, difficult labor, and prolapse of the uterus, as well as the care of the newborn.
grc.themistocles.epistulae: A collection of Greek letters attributed to the Athenian statesman Themistocles, of uncertain date. Composed in the statesman's voice after his ostracism, the letters recount his intended settlement at Delphi and his removal to Argos, the welcome he received from the Argives, and his fear of pursuit by Athenians and Lacedaemonians. Addressed to correspondents that include Aeschylus, Pausanias, Polygnotus, and Habronichus, they warn Pausanias against the perils of prosperity and power, report a hurried departure by sea toward Corcyra, and dwell on the envy and injustice that have followed the writer at Athens.
grc.theocritus.epigrams: The Epigrams are a collection of short Greek poems transmitted under the name of Theocritus, composed in literary dialects with marked use of Doric. The pieces include dedications to gods such as Pan, Priapus, and Aphrodite, epitaphs for figures ranging from herdsmen to physicians and sophists, and verses on statues, votive offerings, and choregic victories. Varied in subject and scale, they stand as a brief epigrammatic complement to the bucolic poetry of the Theocritean corpus.
grc.theocritus.idylls: The Idylls are a collection of thirty short Greek poems by Theocritus, composed largely in hexameters and written in a literary Doric dialect. Most are bucolic pieces in which herdsmen and country folk sing, compete, court, and mourn in idealised rural settings, chiefly in Sicily, while other poems take up mythological subjects, urban scenes, and the praise of rulers. The collection opens with the song of Thyrsis lamenting the death of the herdsman Daphnis.
grc.theophrastus.characters: The Characters of Theophrastus is a Greek prose work consisting of short sketches of moral types, each introduced by a definition and illustrated through typical conduct, speech habits, and social behaviour. A prologue addressed to Polycles sets out the plan of cataloguing the varieties of human disposition so that the young, guided by such examples, may choose the most reputable companions and conversation. The sketches follow type by type, beginning with the ironical man, the flatterer, and the garrulous man, and portray each figure through characteristic utterances and everyday situations.
grc.tryphiodorus.the_taking_of_ilios: The Taking of Ilios (Iliou Halosis) is a short Greek epic poem attributed to Tryphiodorus, a poet of uncertain date. After an invocation to Calliope for a song of the long war's end and of Athena's ambush, it opens with a review of the closing years of the fighting before Troy and the losses suffered by Trojans and Danaans alike. The narrative then turns to Epeius' divinely aided construction of the Wooden Horse, the concealment of the Greek warriors within it, and the cunning that brings the horse inside the walls. The remaining verses follow the sack of the city, the slaughter and plunder that follow, and the allotment of captives and spoils among the victors.
grc.zenobius_sophista.ἐπιτομὴ_ἐκ_τῶν_ταρραίο: An ancient Greek proverb collection transmitted under the name of Zenobius the sophist, a figure of uncertain date, and bearing the title of an epitome compiled from the proverb collections of Tarrhaeus and Didymus. The entries are arranged in alphabetical order, each headed by a proverb followed by a concise statement of the situations to which it applies. Many entries add an explanatory note or anecdote drawn from myth, history, or social custom, and some cite earlier writers such as Eudoxus, Cratinus, and Aristophanes; among the longer notices are the stories of Admetus and Alcestis and of Demeter's rest on the 'laughterless rock' of Attica.
grc.aelian.epistulae_rusticae: A short set of Greek fictional letters attributed to Aelian, printed by Hercher in his 1866 Teubner volume alongside the De natura animalium, the Varia historia, and the fragments. The correspondence is conducted entirely among rustics, village worthies with comic names, a vine-dresser, a bee-keeper, and a courtesan replying to her rural admirer, and its twenty lines compress vignettes of vintage-time, absconding swarms, pilfering slaves, and disputed harvests. Erotic banter and double entendre run throughout, framed by country cult and lore, from the 'great mysteries' of Pan to an oath by Aristaios and a bee-colony imagined as runaway daughters. For readers of intertexts, the letters offer a compact repository of rural motifs, proverbial sayings, and season-and-beauty conceits within the tradition of the imaginary prose letter.
grc.aelian.ἀποσπασμάτια: The Ἀποσπασμάτια ('Fragments') attributed to Aelian is a collection of excerpted passages and short anecdotes preserving material from the works of the Greek author, much of it drawn from his lost treatise On Providence (Περὶ Προνοίας). The pieces include accounts of the frugal lives of philosophers such as Chrysippus, Cleanthes and Socrates, polemic against Epicurus and his followers, stories of piety, omens, dreams and divine retribution, and episodes from Greek and Roman history involving figures such as Pyrrhus and Mithridates. Many entries carry source headings, notably references to Eustathius's commentaries on the Iliad and on Dionysius, through which much of the material has come down.
grc.aelius_aristides.ars_rhetorica: A Greek rhetorical treatise attributed to Aelius Aristides, preserved in Spengel's collection of the Rhetores Graeci. The work examines the virtues (ideai and aretai) of civic oratory (politikos logos), beginning with solemnity or dignity (semnotes) and analysing how it is produced through the thought content (gnome), the figures (schema), and the wording (lexis) of a discourse. Each category is illustrated with worked examples drawn largely from Demosthenes, including the Philippics and the speech against Aristogeiton, and the discussion treats effects such as asyndeton, amplification, and aetiologia as sources of elevated style.
grc.aelius_herodianus.on_enclitics: A short Greek grammatical treatise by Aelius Herodian on enclisis, the shifting of accent in enclitic words. It opens with definitions of the enclined word, the enclitic particle, and the synenclitic combination, then surveys which of the eight parts of speech undergo enclisis, treating the indefinite pronoun, the verbs phēmi and eimi, and the personal pronouns in detail. The rules are illustrated throughout with verse quotations, drawn chiefly from Homer and occasionally from Hesiod.
grc.aelius_theon.progymnasmata: The Progymnasmata of Aelius Theon is a Greek rhetorical treatise, of uncertain date, on the preliminary exercises that prepare a student for full judicial and deliberative oratory. Its opening argument holds that the successful orators of old approached rhetoric through philosophy, whereas their successors rush into legal and demagogic cases without prior training in the simpler exercises, 'learning pot-making in a wine-jar', as the proverb puts it. The work defines the individual exercises, fable, narrative, chreia, commonplace, ekphrasis, prosopopoeia, comparison, thesis, and encomium, and defends their utility with examples from Homer, Euripides, Thucydides, Demosthenes, Aeschines, and other poets, historians, and orators, before treating reading, paraphrase, elaboration, and counter-argument as further instruments of rhetorical training.
grc.aeschines.against_timarchus: A forensic speech in Attic Greek, the Against Timarchus (Kata Timarchou) presents Aeschines' prosecution in an Athenian court at Timarchus' dokimasia, arguing that a dissolute and shameful life debarred a citizen from speaking in the assembly and that the city's laws demand his exclusion. The orator first surveys, with extensive quotation, the statutes of Solon and earlier lawgivers on the supervision of boys, youths, teachers, gymnasia, and choregoi, before turning to Timarchus' own conduct as the direct violation of those enactments. Readers tracing intertexts will find the speech a dense repository of legal formulas, moralising commonplaces, and civic-constitutional argumentation with close affinities in Demosthenic and other Attic oratory.
grc.aeschylus.libation_bearers: The Libation Bearers (Choephoroi) is a Greek tragedy by Aeschylus. It opens with Orestes, returned in secret from exile, laying a lock of his hair on the tomb of his murdered father Agamemnon, where he soon encounters his sister Electra and a chorus of captive slave women sent by Clytemnestra to appease the dead with libations after alarming dreams. Strengthened by the chorus and by the ghost of Agamemnon, Orestes gains entry to the palace at Argos, kills Aegisthus, and after a moment of hesitation kills his mother Clytemnestra as well. The play ends with Orestes exhibiting the bodies to the Argives and seeing the avenging Furies close around him as he flees.
grc.aeschylus.prometheus_bound: Prometheus Bound (Prometheus Desmotes) is a Greek tragedy attributed to Aeschylus and of uncertain date. Its action centres on the punishment of the Titan Prometheus, who is chained to a remote Scythian crag by Hephaestus at the command of Kratos and Bia for having stolen fire from the gods for mankind. Bound fast, Prometheus receives in turn Oceanus, a chorus of Oceanid maidens, the heifer-maiden Io, and finally Hermes, recounting his gifts to mortals, prophesying their wanderings and woes, and refusing to reveal the secret that threatens Zeus's rule. The drama closes as Prometheus, defying Hermes' warnings, is engulfed by storm and plunges into the abyss beneath the crag.
grc.aesop.fabulae: A Greek prose collection of fables attributed to Aesop, the legendary Greek fabulist, transmitted in compilations of uncertain date. The fables are told as brief narratives, mostly about animals, each closing with an epimythion or moral application drawing a lesson for human conduct, as in the opening tale of Zeus sending goods slowly from heaven while evils stay close to humankind. Individual fables recur in variant versions, the eagle and the fox, for example, is given three times with different wording, since the compiler drew material from more than one source. The collection runs as a single continuous sequence without book divisions, beginning with the fable of the goods and the evils.
grc.aesop.αισώπειων_μύθων_συναγωγή: A Greek prose collection of Aesopic fables attributed to Aesop and of uncertain date, transmitted under the title Αισώπειων Μύθων Συναγωγή. Its 965 lines consist of short fables, largely with animal protagonists, the eagle and the fox, the eagle and the dung beetle, the nightingale and the hawk, most of which close with a moralising epimythion introduced by formulae such as ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ or ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ. For readers hunting intertexts the collection is a primary witness to the traditional fable repertoire, whose plots, animal types, and moralising topoi recur across Greek and Latin literature from Hesiod onward.
grc.agatharchides.ex_agatharchidis_de_maris_: Excerpts in Greek from the De mari Erythraeo of Agatharchides, a prose work on the Red Sea transmitted only in excerpted form. The preserved chapters open with a discussion of Ptolemy's establishment of elephant hunting, then survey rival explanations of the name of the Erythraean Sea, red shores and sunbeams, an eponymous Persian named Erythras, and genealogies traced to Perseus. They close with a long critical dismissal of the mythological tales surrounding Perseus and of the many improbable stories about heroes, gods, and metamorphoses found in Greek poetry and prose.
grc.alcidamas.ὀδυσσεύς: A Greek prosecution speech attributed to Alcidamas and of uncertain date, in which Odysseus accuses Palamedes of treason before the assembled Greeks at Troy. The speaker alleges that Palamedes conspired with Alexander (Paris), citing an arrow bearing an inscribed message and a shield emblem as evidence, and repeatedly dwells on Palamedes' character as a sophist and philosopher. The latter part digresses into the stories of Nauplius, the violation of Auge by Heracles, the birth and upbringing of Telephus, and Alexander's voyage to Greece that ended in the abduction of Helen. The piece belongs to the tradition of rhetorical exercises composed on themes from the Trojan War.
grc.anacharsis.epistulae: A collection of short Greek letters attributed to Anacharsis, the Scythian sage of Greek tradition, composed by an unknown author at an uncertain date. The letters, addressed to recipients such as the Athenians and Solon, defend Scythian simplicity in dress, diet, and speech against Greek mockery, and offer moral reflections on hospitality, wine, envy, tyranny, and the accumulation of wealth. In one letter a vision of a cargo boat on the Danube that sinks under plundered goods serves as a warning against riches addressed to a king.
grc.andocides.against_alcibiades: A Greek speech in the corpus of the Attic orators, transmitted under the name of Andocides and of uncertain date and authorship, framed as an address to the Athenians during a debate on ostracism. The speaker faces exile alongside Alcibiades and Nicias, argues that the law of ostracism contradicts the oath of the demos and council and is practised by no other Greek state, and defends himself against charges of misodemia and factional strife, noting his four earlier acquittals. He then attacks Alcibiades' record, cataloguing his adultery, violence, and lawlessness, and his public acts, above all the doubling of the tribute first assessed by Aristides, which he presents as a betrayal of the allies and a threat to Athens' future.
grc.andocides.on_the_peace: A public address by the Athenian orator Andocides urging his fellow citizens that making a just peace with Sparta is better than continuing the war. The speaker contends that politicians who favor peace in name oppose it in practice, and that the democracy was never overthrown in time of peace. He reviews Athens' earlier agreements with Sparta, including the fifty-year peace, the thirty-year peace, and the peace negotiated by Nicias, listing the ships, fortifications, tribute, and forces each brought the city. He then distinguishes an equal peace from truces imposed by a victor after defeat, and answers the claim that the last peace brought the Thirty and the deaths of citizens by hemlock.
grc.anonymous.geographiae_expositio_compendi: A short anonymous Greek treatise of uncertain date, transmitted under the title Geographiae Expositio Compendiaria among the minor Greek geographers. It opens with the dimensions of the inhabited world in stades, giving an east–west extent measured from the mouth of the Ganges to the Sacred Promontory in Lusitania, a north–south breadth, the uninhabitable belts at the extremes, and the division of the world into the three continents of Europe, Asia, and Libya by the Tanais and the isthmus between the Mediterranean and the Arabian Gulf. The remainder surveys the seas and peoples of each continent in turn, beginning with Europe: the three Spanish provinces, the Gauls, Germany bounded by the Rhine and the Danube, Italy and the Alpine lands, Sarmatia, Dacia, the Moesias and Balkan regions, Macedonia and Greece, and the major offshore islands, including Ireland, Britain with its legionary camps, Thule, Scandia, Sicily, Crete, and Corsica.
grc.antiphon.speeches: A collection of six speeches in Attic Greek attributed to Antiphon, an orator of uncertain date. The corpus consists of forensic orations for prosecution and defence in homicide cases, together with the tetralogies, paired sets of model speeches arguing alternately for and against a single murder charge. The collection opens with a young prosecutor's case against his stepmother, whom he accuses of poisoning his father, while his half-brothers and their mother appear for the defence.
grc.antisthenes.αἴας: A short Greek speech composed in the voice of Ajax, pleading his claim to the arms of Achilles before judges whom he accuses of ignorance of the deeds at issue. Attributed to Antisthenes and of uncertain date. The speaker demands that judgement rest on actions rather than words, contrasts his own openly fought prowess with Odysseus' stealth, reproaching him for the nocturnal theft of the Palladium and his servile habits, and insists that only those who witnessed the deeds, or kings competent in virtue, are fit to decide the contest.
grc.antisthenes.ὀδυσσεύς: A short Greek prose speech transmitted under the name of Antisthenes, in which Odysseus answers Ajax before the assembled Greeks in their dispute over the arms of the dead Achilles. He defends his record at Troy, recovering the stolen image of Athena, entering the city in disguise, scouting by night while Ajax sleeps, arguing that success in war rests on intelligence and endurance rather than open battle or bodily strength, and he ridicules Ajax as a rash and thoughtless fighter unfit to speak of virtue. The speech closes with Odysseus' prediction that a wise poet will one day portray him as the much-enduring, many-witted sacker of Troy.
grc.apollodorus.epitome: The Epitome is a Greek mythographic summary transmitted with the Bibliotheca (Library) attributed to Apollodorus, a prose handbook of mythology; the date and authorship of the Epitome itself are uncertain. It preserves in condensed form the concluding portions of the handbook, opening amid Theseus' exploits on the road to Athens and recounting his recognition by Aegeus, Medea's plot, the slaying of the Minotaur with Ariadne's aid, the stories of Daedalus, Icarus, and Minos' death in Sicily, and the tragedy of Phaedra and Hippolytus. The summary continues through the remaining heroic legends, taking the narrative as far as the Trojan War and its aftermath.
grc.apollonius_dyscolus.περὶ_ἀντωνυμίας: A Greek grammatical treatise by Apollonius Dyscolus, Περὶ Ἀντωνυμίας ('On Pronouns') examines pronouns as a part of speech. The opening announces a concise treatment of the subject and then discusses the name and definition of the word class, weighing rival designations ascribed to Aristarchus, Tyrannion, Dionysiodorus of Troezen, Dionysius Thrax, Apollodorus of Athens and the Stoa, and rejecting the identification of pronouns with articles. Further sections treat the distinction between personal, possessive and reflexive pronouns, the demonstratives οὗτος, ὅδε and αὐτός, and their inflection and grammatical behaviour, with Homeric verses supplying most of the illustrative examples.
grc.appian.civil_wars: Appian's Civil Wars is a Greek prose history in five books dealing with the internal conflicts of the Romans. Its opening survey traces the course of civil strife from early disputes between plebs and senate over laws, debts and land, through the killing of Tiberius Gracchus, the dictatorship of Sulla and the rivalry of Caesar and Pompey, to the triumvirate of Antony, Lepidus and Octavian and the war around Actium. The account closes with Antony's defeat, the taking of Egypt and the elevation of Octavian as Augustus, ruler of Rome and the nations under her.
grc.archimedes.ad_eratosthenem_methodus: A short Greek mathematical treatise by Archimedes, cast as a letter to Eratosthenes and entitled the Ephodos on mechanical theorems. Archimedes explains a procedure for investigating geometrical magnitudes by mechanics, in which figures are imagined suspended and balanced against one another, and records lemmas on the centres of gravity of lines, triangles, parallelograms, circles, cylinders, prisms and cones. The propositions put to mechanical use include the theorem that a segment of a right-angled conic section is equal to four-thirds of the triangle on the same base and of equal height, and the treatise closes with the geometrical demonstrations of the theorems announced at the outset.
grc.archimedes.fragmenta: Greek mathematical fragments attributed to Archimedes. The main surviving passage contrasts the five regular polyhedra associated with Plato with thirteen further solids bounded by equilateral, equiangular polygons of more than one kind, recording for each the number and kind of its faces together with its solid angles and edges. It also sets out rules for calculating the numbers of solid angles and edges from the faces, and describes how several of the solids are generated by truncating a pyramid, a cube, or an octahedron; numbered notes at the end repeat the face, angle, and edge counts for individual figures.
grc.aretaeus.signorum_acutorum_morbum: The Signs of Acute Diseases (De signis acutorum morborum) is a Greek medical treatise belonging to the surviving corpus of Aretaeus the Cappadocian, a physician of uncertain date who wrote in an Ionicising prose; the wording here follows the Greek printed in Francis Adams's edition of 1856. The work catalogues the diagnostic signs of acute conditions: the present section opens with the premonitory aura of epileptic convulsion, from rainbow-like shimmering before the eyes and ringing ears to the fall 'as if struck by a blow', proceeds through a vividly detailed account of the fit itself, and then sets out the signs of tetanic spasms in their three postures (straight, opisthotonos, emprostotonos), their causes in cold, wounds, season, sex and age, and their grim prognosis. For readers hunting intertexts, the treatise offers some of the most striking clinical portraiture in ancient medicine, with symptom vocabulary and phrasing that invite comparison with the Hippocratic corpus and later Greek and Latin medical writers.
grc.aristophanes.acharnians: The Acharnians is a comedy by Aristophanes that turns on the farmer Dicaeopolis, exasperated by an Athenian assembly which will not debate peace, who arranges a private treaty with Sparta through Amphitheus, a figure who claims divine descent and a mandate from the gods to negotiate with the Lacedaemonians. His celebration of the Rural Dionysia draws on him the fury of the chorus of Acharnian charcoal-burners whose lands the enemy has been ravaging; he holds a basket of their charcoal hostage to win a hearing, and, equipped by Euripides with the rags of Telephus, pleads his case in a sustained parody of tragedy. The latter part of the play offers a series of grotesque peacetime dealings, including a starving Megarian selling his daughters as piglets and a Boeotian laden with delicacies, alongside a running rivalry with the braggart general Lamachus. It closes with Dicaeopolis crowned victor at a drinking feast while Lamachus limps back wounded from a night alarm.
grc.aristophanes.birds: A comedy by Aristophanes in which two Athenians, Pisthetairos and Euelpides, weary of their litigious native city, set out to find Tereus, a former king transformed into the hoopoe, in the hope of settling among the birds. They persuade the assembled birds to build a city in the sky, Nephelococcygia, which intercepts the smoke of sacrifices rising from earth to Olympus and forces the gods to send embassies. The dialogue and choral songs follow the founding of the new city, the great parabasis of the bird chorus, and the negotiations with Poseidon, Heracles and the Triballian god that end with Pisthetairos married to Basileia and holding the thunderbolt of Zeus.
grc.aristophanes.thesmophoriazusae: Thesmophoriazusae is a comedy by Aristophanes in which Euripides, menaced by the women of Athens, who intend to condemn him at the festival of the Thesmophoria for his portrayal of them in tragedy, sends a male kinsman disguised as a woman to speak for him at their assembly. The opening scene visits the house of the tragedian Agathon, whose mannered lyrics and effeminate habits are mocked at length, before the kinsman infiltrates the women's gathering and is exposed. The subsequent action burlesques episodes from Euripidean drama, including the Telephus, Palamedes, Helen, and Andromeda, as the kinsman evades capture until Euripides himself appears to negotiate the outcome.
grc.aristotle.categoriae: The Categoriae is a concise Greek treatise on predication, ascribed to Aristotle and of uncertain date. It opens with distinctions among homonyms, synonyms, and paronyms, and with a fourfold classification of what is said of a subject and what is in a subject. It then enumerates the ten categories under which things signified without combination fall, substance, quantity, quality, relation, place, time, position, having, doing, and being acted upon, and proceeds to an extended discussion of primary and secondary substance, arguing that everything else is either said of or present in primary substances.
grc.aristotle.constitution: The Athenaion Politeia is a Greek prose treatise on the constitution of the Athenians, attributed to Aristotle. It opens with the earliest kingship of Attica under Ion and Theseus, recounting the division of the land among his sons and his unification of the people, and then narrates the transition from monarchy to the rule of the Codrid successors. The treatise describes the ancient offices of basileus, polemarch, archon and thesmothetai, the lifetime authority of the Areopagus council, and the oligarchic order in which the poor worked the land of the rich as pelatai and hektemoroi. Solon appears as the first champion of the demos, and the account sets his reforms within a continuous narrative of Athenian political change.
grc.aristotle.de_anima: A Greek philosophical treatise on the soul (peri psychēs) by Aristotle, transmitted under the Latin title De Anima. The opening book establishes the study of the soul as part of natural philosophy, weighs whether its affections such as anger, fear and perception are inseparable from the body, and sets out the methodological difficulties of grasping its essence. It then surveys the doctrines of earlier thinkers, among them Democritus, Leucippus, the Pythagoreans, Anaxagoras and Empedocles, who identified the soul variously as the principle of motion or as the source of knowledge and sensation.
grc.aristotle.de_insomniis: A short Greek philosophical treatise attributed to Aristotle and transmitted among the Parva Naturalia, De Insomniis (On Dreams) continues an inquiry into sleep by asking what dreams are and to which faculty of the soul they belong. It argues that dream appearances are acts neither of opinion nor of plain sensation but of the imaginative faculty (phantasia), a capacity of the sensory soul that remains active in sleep. The argument draws on persistent afterimages, illusions arising in fever, strong emotion, and sickness, and curious observations such as the clouding of clean mirrors, explaining dreams as residual motions left in the sense organs by earlier perception.
grc.aristotle.de_iuventute_et_senectute_de_v: A brief Greek treatise of Aristotle on youth and old age, on life and death, and on respiration. It opens by declaring that an account of breathing must be given alongside life and death, since for some animals the two depend upon it, and then argues that the nutritive and perceptive principles of the soul, whose nature is treated elsewhere, reside in a middle part of the body, the heart in blooded animals. The discussion compares plants and animals with respect to nutrition and generation, observes that insects and other creatures may continue to live when divided, and traces the senses to a common sensorium in the central organ while explaining why the organs of sense are situated in the head.
grc.aristotle.de_longitudine_et_brevitate_vi: De Longitudine et Brevitate Vitae (On the Length and Shortness of Life) is a short Greek treatise by Aristotle. It opens by setting out problems for inquiry concerning why some animals and plants are long-lived and others short-lived, and whether a single cause accounts for both. The discussion then examines what is easily or hardly destroyed in natural substances, surveys which kinds live longest, plants such as the palm, and among animals large, land-dwelling, blooded creatures such as man and the elephant, and explains longevity through the quantity and quality of innate heat and moisture, treating old age as a cooling and drying of the organism.
grc.aristotle.de_partibus_animalium: A philosophical and zoological treatise by Aristotle, De Partibus Animalium (On the Parts of Animals) opens with a methodological discussion of natural science, covering demonstration, the plurality of causes, the priority of the final cause over material necessity, and criticism of earlier natural philosophers such as Empedocles. The remaining portion of the work surveys the constituent parts of animals, describing organs, their material composition, and their functions across blooded and bloodless kinds. The treatise is transmitted in four books of continuous Greek prose.
grc.aristotle.de_sensu_et_sensibilibus: A short treatise by Aristotle on sensation and the objects of sense, forming part of the Parva Naturalia and taking up the inquiry where the De Anima's account of the soul leaves off. It concerns the affections shared by soul and body, reviewing the individual senses and their organs, with detailed discussion of sight and of whether vision operates through fire, light, or a medium, together with criticism of the theories of Empedocles, Democritus, and the Timaeus. Touch and taste, the role of the sense media, and the common sensibles such as shape, magnitude, motion, and number are also examined.
grc.aristotle.de_somno_et_vigilia: A short Greek treatise on natural philosophy attributed to Aristotle, De Somno et Vigilia ('On Sleep and Waking') investigates what sleep and wakefulness are, whether they belong to the soul or the body, and why living creatures possess them. It argues that sleep and waking are affections of the common sense faculty rather than of any single sense, that all perceiving animals sleep while plants do not, and that sleep is a kind of binding or immobility of the primary perceptive organ, with waking as its release. The opening discussion also poses questions about the nature of dreams (enypnia), why sleepers dream at some times and not others, and whether dreams can ever foretell future events.
grc.aristotle.eudemian_ethics: The Eudemian Ethics, a Greek ethical treatise by Aristotle, opens with the story of an inscription set up at Delos before posing its central question: in what living well consists and whether happiness comes by nature, by learning, by habituation, by divine dispensation, or by fortune. It reviews disputed opinions about happiness, distinguishes lives directed toward practical wisdom, virtue, and pleasure, and sets out the political, philosophical, and hedonistic lives as the principal candidates from which a person may choose. The inquiry insists that a life be ordered toward a deliberate end and that the study distinguish what is necessary for noble living from what is merely incidental to it.
grc.aristotle.fragmenta_deperditae_partis_pr: The work gathers the surviving fragments of the lost first portion of the Athenaion Politeia attributed to Aristotle, edited together with the recovered text of the treatise in Kenyon's 1903 Berlin edition. The excerpts, transmitted by later lexicographers such as Harpocration, Suidas, and the Lexicon Bekker, by scholia on Plato and Aristophanes, and by Plutarch, deal with the legendary and constitutional history of early Attica. They cover the early kingship and the name-giving of the Ionians, Theseus' synoecism and his division of the citizens into eupatridai, geomoroi, and demiourgoi, and the pre-Cleisthenic organization of the four Ionian tribes into trittyes and phratries, each subdivided into gene whose members were known as genetai.
grc.aristotle.poetics: A Greek treatise on the poetic art by Aristotle, the work known as the Poetics, opening with an inquiry into poetry itself, its kinds, and the power proper to each kind. Epic, tragedy, comedy, dithyramb, and music for aulos and kithara are treated alike as forms of mimesis, distinguished by their medium, by the objects imitated, and by the manner of imitation. The discussion separates the poet from the mere user of meter in the contrast of Homer with Empedocles, and records the Dorians' claims to tragedy and comedy drawn from the meanings of 'drama' and 'komodia'. A further section derives poetry from two natural causes, the human instinct for imitation and the innate delight in rhythm and harmony, and follows its growth into heroic and iambic verse, with Homer credited as the first to shape the serious and the comic forms of poetry.
grc.aristotle.topica: A Greek treatise on dialectic attributed to Aristotle, the Topica sets out a method by which one may reason syllogistically from reputable opinions (endoxa) about any problem proposed. It defines the syllogism, distinguishes demonstrative, dialectical, and eristic reasoning, and lists three uses of the method: training in argument, everyday encounters, and the examination of first principles in the philosophical sciences. The work then treats the four predicables, definition, property, genus, and accident, and sets out rules and strategies for constructing, defending, and refuting arguments concerning each.
grc.aristotle.μηχανικά: A short Greek treatise on mechanics attributed to Aristotle. Its preface distinguishes effects that occur by nature from those achieved by art, and argues that the circle, being composed of contrary motions, is the principle underlying mechanical marvels in which a small force moves great weights, tracing the behaviour of the balance and the lever back to circular movement. The work then proceeds to a series of mechanical problems, each stating a puzzle about moving bodies and resolving it through proportions of motion and the geometry of the circle.
grc.aristoxenus.elementa_harmonica: A Greek treatise on music theory, the Elementa Harmonica or Harmonics of Aristoxenus, which defines the harmonic science as the first and most elementary branch of the study of melody, concerned with the theory of systems of notes and of intervals. The opening surveys the failings of earlier harmonic writers, who confined themselves to the enharmonic genus and to diagrams of octachord systems, and sets out the questions the inquiry must settle: the motion of the voice, tension and relaxation, acuteness and gravity, the nature of interval and of system, the melodic, and the divisions and differences of the genera. The discussion proceeds through definitions of succession and continuity in systems and of the complete system, together with criticism of predecessors such as Eratocles on the arrangement and enumeration of melodic forms.
grc.arrian.anabasis: Arrian's Anabasis is a Greek prose history of the campaigns of Alexander the Great, arranged in seven books. Its preface names Ptolemy son of Lagus and Aristobulus as the most trustworthy authorities, recording what they agree upon and preferring the more credible account where they diverge. The work opens with Alexander's accession after Philip's death, his settlement of Greece, and his campaigns against the Thracians, Triballi, and Illyrians, before going on to narrate the expedition against the Persians and Alexander's subsequent campaigns through Asia.
grc.artemidorus.onirocriticon: A Greek prose treatise on the interpretation of dreams by Artemidorus of Daldis, of uncertain date. The preface answers those who deny that dreams foretell the future or that the gods exercise providence, censures earlier dream-writers for plagiarizing one another and adding inventions of their own, and recounts the author's travels through Greece, Asia, Italy, and the larger islands to observe dreams and their outcomes. It distinguishes the enypnion, which merely mirrors present conditions such as hunger, thirst, or fear, from the oneiros that signifies things to come, divides the latter into dreams that resemble their fulfillment directly and those that work through allegory, and offers a formal definition of the dream as a movement of the soul signifying future good or evil before turning to the basic elements of interpretation.
grc.aspasius.in_ethica_nicomachea_paraphrasi: A Greek explanatory paraphrase of Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, transmitted under the name of Aspasius, an ancient commentator on Aristotle of uncertain date. The work proceeds lemma by lemma through Aristotle's text, prefaced by a prologue on the relation of ethical and political philosophy to theoretical wisdom and on the necessity of moral virtue for beings united to a body. It then defines art, method, action and choice, and takes up Aristotle's opening argument that every craft, inquiry, action and pursuit aims at some good, culminating in the question of happiness as the end of human life.
grc.athenaeus.deipnosophists: The Deipnosophists ('Dinner-Table Sophists') is a Greek prose dialogue by Athenaeus, of uncertain date, cast as a report to Timocrates of a celebrated banquet given at Rome by the opulent Larensius. Its opening summary praises Athenaeus as 'father of the book' and enumerates the subjects treated: fish and other foods, vegetables, animals, musical instruments, forms of jest, drinking vessels, the wealth of kings, and the deeds of historians, poets and philosophers. The named guests include the jurist Masurius, the grammarians Plutarch, Leonides of Elis and Aemilianus, the philosophers Pontianus and Democritus, the Cynic Cynulcus, the rhetor Ulpian, and the physicians Daphnus and Galen. Athenaeus shapes the whole in conscious imitation of Plato, with the diners pursuing their table-talk in a critical, Socratic manner.
grc.babrius.fabulae_aesopeae: A collection of Aesopic fables in Greek verse by Babrius, a poet of uncertain date, who recasts traditional tales of animals and men in short limping iambics. The prologue, addressed to a boy named Branchus, recalls the mythic ages of mankind, when even beasts had articulate speech and mortals kept company with gods, before announcing that the fables of 'our wise old Aesop' will be set down as broken limbs of bitter iambic verse. The individual fables, a hunter and a lion, a fisherman and his catch, a goatherd and a wounded she-goat, a horse forced to carry a fallen donkey's load, among others, are brief narratives, each furnished with a short moral lesson on prudence, fortune, or human folly.
grc.barnabas.barnabae_epistulae: The Epistle of Barnabas is a Greek Christian letter of uncertain date, attributed to Barnabas and transmitted among the Apostolic Fathers. It opens with a greeting to its recipients, 'sons and daughters', and an expression of joy at their spiritual gifts, before turning to instruction in hope, righteousness, and love. Drawing on the prophetic writings, the author argues that God rejects sacrifices, burnt offerings, and prescribed fasts in favour of a contrite and glorifying heart, and sets forth the new law of Jesus Christ as free from the yoke of necessity. The letter closes with exhortation to shun the works of lawlessness in the present evil days and a warning that the Lord has cut short the times before the coming of the Beloved to his inheritance.
grc.basil_of_caesarea.de_legendis: A prose address in Greek attributed to Basil of Caesarea, transmitted under the title De legendis libris gentilium, 'On Reading the Writings of the Greeks.' Addressed to young men at the outset of their studies, it argues that the goods of the present human life are of little worth beside a life to come, and that profane authors are therefore to be read selectively: whatever serves virtue in the poets and other writers is to be taken up, the rest passed over. Moses trained in Egyptian learning and Daniel among the Chaldaeans are cited as men who turned profane education toward divine ends, and the counsel is reinforced through images of the dyer's preparation of cloth and of a tree whose fruit is set off by its leaves.
grc.callimachus.aetia: Callimachus of Cyrene's Aetia ('Causes'), a Hellenistic elegiac poem in four books, survives only in fragments. The work related the origins of obscure cults, rites, names and customs of the Greek world, framed in a dream vision in which the poet is carried to Helicon and questions the Muses. The remains gathered here open with ancient testimonia and the prologue in which the poet answers the Telchines who mocked his style, and include the exchange with the historian Icarus on poetic taste and the long episode of Acontius and Cydippe. Individual fragments, many only a line or two long, are drawn from quotations in later authors and from papyrus finds.
grc.carmina_delphis_inventa.carmina_delphis_: Ancient Greek collection of the Delphic hymns, songs in honour of Apollo found inscribed at Delphi and transmitted together with the record of the Delphians' decree concerning their composer, the Athenian Cleochares son of Bion. The opening gives the prose inscription from the Athenians' treasury, in which the city orders that the prosodion, paean, and hymn Cleochares wrote for the god be taught each year to the boys who sing at the Theoxenia, grants Cleochares crowns and proxeny, and dates the decree by the archon Patro(n)das. The remainder presents the surviving songs, headed as a hymn and a paean, first with the musical note signs set above the lyric lines and then with the text repeated and underlaid with the notation syllable by syllable, preceded by brief Latin editorial notes on the musical signs and harmony.
grc.chariton.de_chaerea: An extended love romance in Greek prose by Chariton of Aphrodisias, who introduces himself in the opening sentence as secretary to the rhetor Athenagoras, and of uncertain date. The work, commonly known as Chaereas and Callirhoe, narrates the mutual passion of its two young protagonists, beginning in Syracuse with the courtship and marriage of Callirhoe, the famously beautiful daughter of the general Hermocrates, to the handsome Chaereas. It follows the couple through the machinations of disappointed suitors, the turmoil that engulfs the city at their wedding, and the trials and separations that drive the rest of the narrative across the wider Hellenic and eastern world.
grc.clement_of_alexandria.eclogae_prophetica: A short Greek collection of exegetical extracts on prophetic and scriptural passages, attributed to Clement of Alexandria, the Christian teacher of Alexandria. Its sequence of scholia-like notes expounds the hymn of the three young men in the fiery furnace and other verses of Daniel, Hosea and Genesis, drawing doctrinal lessons on the abyss and matter, the Son as the beginning, and baptism 'of water and of spirit' as rebirth and purification. The closing sections treat sickness as chastisement for sin, the beatitudes as provision for the soul's journey, and the soul's emptying and filling by God, sealed against the seven unclean spirits.
grc.clement_of_alexandria.paedagogus: The Paedagogus of Clement of Alexandria is a Greek Christian didactic treatise that opens with a list of chapter headings followed by the text of its first book. It presents the divine Logos as a paedagogus, or tutor, who supervises humanity against sin, trains men and women equally as children of God, and disciplines with both severity and kindness. The argument follows the tutor's instruction through the law and the prophets, his healing of the passions through gentle counsel, and his preparation of the soul for the fuller teaching of the Logos, with frequent citation of Moses and the prophets. The opening remarks that the author's Protrepticus has already dealt with character, while the present work addresses actions and passions.
grc.clement_of_alexandria.quis_dives_salvetu: A Greek homily attributed to Clement of Alexandria, the Christian teacher of Alexandria, on the question 'Which rich man shall be saved?' Of uncertain date, it opens with a denunciation of those who flatter the wealthy and then takes as its principal subject the gospel episode of the rich man who asks Jesus how to inherit eternal life, quoted from Mark and followed by a discussion of the saying about the camel and the needle's eye. Clement argues that the rich are not obliged to renounce all possessions but may attain salvation through rightly ordered use of wealth, almsgiving, and obedience to the commandments, the soul's training being likened to an athlete's preparation for the contest under Christ as judge.
grc.colluthus.rape_of_helen: The Rape of Helen (Harpagē Helenēs) is a Greek epic in hexameters, a single continuous book of 394 lines attributed to Colluthus, a poet of uncertain date. Opening with an invocation to the Trojan nymphs of the Xanthus, the poem recounts the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, the snubbing and vengeance of Eris with the golden apple, the judgement of Paris among Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite, and the ensuing rape of Helen that set the Trojan War in motion. Its compressed reworking of episodes familiar from Homer, Hesiod, and the cyclic tradition of the Cypria makes it a dense site of verbal and thematic allusion, and a rewarding comparand for readers tracing the post-Homeric afterlife of the judgement of Paris and the abduction of Helen.
grc.cratetis_epistulae.epistulae: A short collection of Greek letters attributed to the philosopher Crates and of uncertain date. Most pieces are only a few sentences long and consist of moral exhortation in the Cynic manner, urging the practice of philosophy, endurance of toil, and contempt for wealth, pleasure, and reputation, with repeated appeal to Diogenes of Sinope and Antisthenes. The addressees vary, and include a woman told to adorn herself in virtue like Penelope and Alcestis, and a Lysis reproved for drunkenness and warned against wine with quotations from Homer.
grc.demosthenes.against_androtion: A forensic speech by Demosthenes in Attic Greek, composed for an Athenian court action in which the prosecution supports Euctemon against Androtion. The speaker recalls the wrongs Androtion inflicted on Euctemon and on himself, including a fabricated charge of impiety, and argues chiefly that a decree conferring an honorary crown on the Council of Five Hundred was unlawful because the Council had not built the required triremes and had acted without a probouleuma. Much of the speech anticipates Androtion's defence, rebutting his technical arguments with appeals to the letter of the laws governing public honours.
grc.demosthenes.against_aphobus_1: A forensic oration of the Demosthenic corpus, the first of the speeches delivered in the young Demosthenes' suit against his former guardian Aphobus over the administration of his father's estate. The speaker opens by acknowledging his inexperience in court, then gives a detailed account of the patrimony of nearly fourteen talents left when he was seven years old and entrusted, together with his mother's dowry and his sister's marriage portion, to Aphobus, Demophon, and Therippides. He itemises the assets, two workshops of knife-makers and bed-makers with their slaves, maritime loans deposited with bankers, furniture, plate, and the mother's jewellery, and alleges that ten years of guardianship have reduced the whole to seventy minae. Witness depositions are quoted in support, leading into a fuller inventory of the workshops and their yearly returns.
grc.demosthenes.against_aristocrates: A forensic oration of the Demosthenic corpus, Against Aristocrates (Kata Aristokratous) prosecutes a decree of Aristocrates granting personal immunity (asulia) to the general Charidemus, arguing that it contravenes the laws and endangers Athens' hold on the Chersonese. The speaker, who presents himself as a former trierarch in the Hellespont, rehearses the aftermath of Cotys' death, the rival Thracian kingships of Cersobleptes, Berisades and Amadocus, and the intrigues by which Charidemus and his partisans allegedly sought to steer Athenian policy. Attributed to Demosthenes in the transmitted corpus and printed in Butcher and Rennie's Oxford edition, the speech offers readers of intertexts a dense cluster of Attic legal vocabulary, diplomatic narrative, and the rhetoric of civic danger that recurs across fourth-century oratory.
grc.demosthenes.against_aristogiton_1: A Greek forensic speech attributed to Demosthenes, prosecuting Aristogeiton, a notorious Athenian informer who stands registered in the Acropolis as owing money to the public treasury. The speaker opens by explaining that he was assigned the prosecution by the assembly after Lycurgus' indictment, and argues that the jurors' verdict concerns their own reputation as guardians of the laws as much as the defendant's fate. Invoking personified Eunomia and Dikē, he urges the court to punish such conspicuous wickedness, then turns to Aristogeiton's record of public misconduct and his conduct in the assembly and courts.
grc.demosthenes.against_aristogiton_2: An Athenian forensic speech attributed to Demosthenes and transmitted in his corpus as the second oration Against Aristogiton, of uncertain date; its argument presupposes and discusses the misfortunes that befell the Greeks at Chaeronea. The prosecution contends that Aristogiton, owing money to the public treasury and under atimia, is expressly debarred by the laws from addressing the people and from bringing a graphe paranomon, and that wrongdoing by men in office or engaged in politics damages the whole city and demands swifter punishment than the offences of private citizens. In support the speaker adduces Solon's provision of speedy penalties for officials and demagogues, the fines paid by Aristides, Miltiades and Pericles, and Hyperides' decree restoring the atimoi after Chaeronea, all set against Aristogiton's bid to override the established laws with impunity.
grc.demosthenes.against_boeotus_1: A forensic speech in Ancient Greek, attributed to Demosthenes and of uncertain date, preserved among the private orations of the Demosthenic corpus. It is spoken in a private suit by Mantitheus against his half-brother Boeotus, who has enrolled himself under the same name, and argues that the defendant must not bear the name Mantitheus. The speaker recounts the father's oath before the phratry, the disputed enrolments in the phratry and deme, and the confusion that would follow in liturgies, courts, and civic duties if both men kept the same name.
grc.demosthenes.against_callippus: A forensic oration by Demosthenes, composed for a defendant in an Athenian private action over a bank deposit. The speaker, a son of the banker Pasion, opens by urging the judges not to let an opponent's standing and eloquence outweigh the merits of the case, since a man with reputation and influence can more easily procure false testimony. He then recounts how Lycon of Heraclea left sixteen minae and forty drachmas with his father's bank to be repaid to one Cephisiades, how Lycon died of wounds from a pirate attack off the Argolic gulf, and how Callippus, proxenos of the Heracleots, later challenged the payment. The narrative and supporting depositions are marshalled to show that the money was duly handed over to Cephisiades in the presence of witnesses.
grc.demosthenes.against_dionysodorus: Against Dionysodorus is a forensic speech by the Athenian orator Demosthenes, of uncertain date, written for delivery in a private suit before an Athenian jury. The speaker, a partner in a maritime loan of three thousand drachmae advanced to Dionysodorus and his associate Parmeniscus, accuses them of breaking their written contract, which required the ship to return from Egypt with its grain cargo to Athens, alleging instead that they sold the grain at Rhodes when prices there proved more favourable. The speech includes the reading of the loan agreement and connects the defendants with Cleomenes, the ruler of Egypt, whom the speaker blames for hoarding grain and manipulating prices at the expense of Athens and the Greeks at large.
grc.demosthenes.against_eubulides: A forensic speech in Attic Greek, attributed to Demosthenes and of uncertain date, spoken by a man disenfranchised in a deme scrutiny (diapsephismos) conducted by Eubulides. The speaker alleges that Eubulides, hostile because the speaker had testified against him in a case in which Eubulides had prosecuted the speaker's sister for impiety, deliberately delayed the scrutiny until nightfall, when a diminished body of demesmen cast more ballots than there were voters and the speaker was denied witnesses and an adequate defense. The remainder of the speech defends the speaker's citizenship and his claim to belong to the city, appealing to the jurors to set aside the deme's verdict.
grc.demosthenes.against_lacritus: Against Lacritus is a forensic speech of Demosthenes arising from a dispute under the Athenian commercial laws. The speaker, Androcles of Sphettus, recounts how he and a partner lent three thousand drachmae by maritime contract to the Phaselite merchants Artemon and Apollodorus for a voyage to the Pontus and back to Athens, and how, Artemon having died before repayment, he now sues the deceased's brother Lacritus, who took over the estate while disclaiming liability for the loan. The speech opens with a general attack on the Phaselites' reputation for evading their debts through legal tricks, and its case rests on the reading of the loan agreement and on witness depositions, both of which are quoted in full.
grc.demosthenes.against_leochares: A short forensic speech in Greek transmitted in the Demosthenic corpus and of uncertain date, delivered in an Athenian court in a dispute over the inheritance of the childless Archiades. The speaker, a kinsman of the deceased, attacks the diamarturia (a sworn denial of kinship) lodged by Leochares, who claims to have been legitimately adopted into the family. The speech traces the genealogy of the household from Euthymachus onward to show that the speaker and his father stand closer to the deceased in the male line than Leochares and are therefore entitled to the estate under the law governing anchisteia.
grc.demosthenes.against_macartatus: Against Macartatus is an Attic forensic speech attributed to Demosthenes and transmitted with his private orations; its date is uncertain. The speaker pleads on behalf of a woman who had been adjudged heir to the estate of Hagnias of Oinoe and of her young son, rehearsing earlier hearings in which the rival claimants Glaucon, Glaukos and Theopompus allegedly produced forged wills and were defeated. The present action is directed against Macartatus, son of Theopompus, who challenges the inheritance anew; the speech defends the introduction of the boy, a grandson of Eubulides, into the phratries of the Hagniai by adoption, and argues the family's claim by kinship to the property.
grc.demosthenes.against_nausimachus_and_xeno: A forensic speech in Attic Greek, transmitted in the corpus of Demosthenes' orations, in which a defendant enters a formal plea that a suit brought against himself and his brother by Nausimachus and Xenopeithes is inadmissible. The plaintiffs, sons of Nausicrates, had earlier litigated claims arising from the guardianship of the speaker's father's estate and accepted a settlement with formal release; the speaker cites the relevant statute, depositions and the written charge to argue that a second action over the same matters, pressed for thirty minae, is barred, and rebuts their account of debts allegedly owed in the Bosporus. The oration belongs to fourth-century Athenian courtroom practice and is comparatively brief.
grc.demosthenes.against_olympiodorus: A short forensic speech of Demosthenes, composed for delivery in an Athenian court in a private action against Olympiodorus, a kinsman by marriage. The speaker recounts how, after the death of the childless Comon of Alocale, he brought Olympiodorus into the inheritance, buried the deceased at joint expense, and drew up a written agreement sealed with oaths for dividing the estate, which Olympiodorus is now charged with violating. The speech defends the speaker's earlier concessions, introduces the contract, oaths, and witness testimony in support of his case, and appeals to the jurors to decide between the parties.
grc.demosthenes.against_onetor_31: An Attic forensic oration by Demosthenes, transmitted with his private speeches under the title Against Onetor, in which the speaker prosecutes a dispute over a dowry allegedly paid to Aphobus. Continuing a proof set out in a previous speech, the speaker argues that Onetor's shifting valuations of a house and a country estate show that no dowry was ever given, and he exposes the opposing case as perjury and collusion designed to shield Aphobus. The speech repays readers hunting intertexts with its compact display of Demosthenic reasoning from documents and witness testimony, its legal vocabulary of proofs, valuations and sureties, and its close links to the other orations arising from the same affair.
grc.demosthenes.against_phaenippus: A forensic speech concerning an antidosis, the Athenian procedure by which a citizen assessed for a public liturgy could challenge another man deemed wealthier to assume the burden or exchange properties. Preserved in the corpus of Demosthenes' orations, it belongs to the law courts of classical Athens. The speaker recounts how he challenged Phaenippus to take over a liturgy of three talents, describes the formal inspection and marking of Phaenippus' estate, and alleges that Phaenippus flouted the antidosis law by postponing his sworn valuation, removing goods from his land, and disregarding the speaker's seizures, closing with witness testimony and an appeal to the jurors.
grc.demosthenes.against_stephanus_1: A Greek forensic oration by Demosthenes, prosecuted in an Athenian court against Stephanus on a charge of false witness. The speaker presents himself as having been wrongly condemned through perjured testimony after suffering outrages at the hands of Phormion, and recounts a dispute over an inheritance and household property that underlay the earlier case. The speech quotes the deposition given by Stephanus and his fellow witnesses concerning the will of Pasion, and sets out to demonstrate that their sworn statements were given for gain and are demonstrably false.
grc.demosthenes.against_theocrines: Against Theocrines (Kata Theokrinou) is a short forensic oration preserved in the corpus of Demosthenes' speeches, composed for delivery in an Athenian law court. The speaker, a young man prosecuting on behalf of a father ruined by the defendant, brings an endeixis against Theocrines, alleging that he accepted money to abandon a phasis, a formal information laid against Micon of Cholleidai concerning a ship, rather than proceed with the prosecution as the law required. The speech cites the statutes governing informers, reads out the phasis and supporting witness testimony, and argues that Theocrines has rendered himself liable to the prescribed penalties, including a fine of a thousand drachmae and arrest.
grc.demosthenes.erotic_essay: The Erotic Essay (Erōtikos) is a short Greek prose speech attributed to Demosthenes and of uncertain date. It is framed as a written discourse that the speaker offers to read aloud to Epicrates, a young Athenian distinguished for beauty and ability, arguing that a just lover neither does nor encourages anything shameful. The speech moves from praise of the youth's appearance, natural endowments and upbringing to counsel on education and the choice of a way of life, combining encomium with advice in the manner of epideictic oratory.
grc.demosthenes.for_the_megalopitans: An Athenian deliberative oration of Demosthenes, For the Megalopitans addresses the assembly on whether the city should aid the Arcadian Megalopolitans against Lacedaemonian power. The speaker censures the rival embassies of Arcadians and Lacedaemonians for slandering one another instead of advising on the common interest, and argues that Athens' safety lies in keeping both Sparta and Thebes weak. He invokes the oaths sworn to the Messenians, recalls the Athenians' earlier engagement at Mantinea, and weighs the question of recovering Oropus, concluding that support for Megalopolis accords with the city's policy of preserving a balance among Peloponnesian states.
grc.demosthenes.funeral_speech: A Greek funeral oration (epitaphios logos) attributed to Demosthenes and of uncertain date, composed as the customary eulogy delivered at the public burial of Athenians fallen in war. The speaker, appointed by the city, begins from the difficulty of finding praise adequate to the dead, then praises their autochthonous birth and noble ancestry and recounts the legendary and historical exploits of their forebears: the repulse of the Amazons and of Eumolpus' expedition, the aid given to the Heracleidae, the burial of the Seven against Thebes, and the single-handed defence of Greece against the Asian invasion. The speech culminates in transferring this inherited glory to the fallen themselves, whose valour, noble death, and self-sacrifice for the common freedom of the Greeks it sets above all other achievement.
