grc.demosthenes.letters: A collection of Greek prose letters attributed to Demosthenes and addressed to the council and people of Athens. The first letter, prefaced by a prayer to the gods, presents the writer as an exile offering political counsel, urging concord among the citizens, forbearance toward former opponents, and united action among the Greeks now that Alexander is dead. Combining formal salutation with sustained advice on public affairs, the correspondence also touches on the question of the writer's own return home.
grc.demosthenes.olynthiac_1: Demosthenes' First Olynthiac is a deliberative speech addressed to the Athenian assembly during the war between Philip II of Macedon and Olynthus. The speaker urges the Athenians to send aid to the Olynthians at once, arguing that their present hatred of Philip makes them reliable allies, and warns that if Olynthus falls nothing will hinder Philip from marching where he pleases. Reviewing earlier missed opportunities at Amphipolis, Pydna, Potidaea, Methone, and Pagasae, the speech blames Athenian hesitation for Philip's rise and calls for money, personal service, and vigor in the current crisis. It stands as the first of the three Olynthiac orations.
grc.demosthenes.olynthiac_3: The third of the speeches known as the Olynthiacs, an address to the Athenian assembly attributed to Demosthenes. The speaker argues that delay and mismanagement have allowed Philip of Macedon to grow dangerous, recalling the belated and half-hearted dispatch of the fleet once voted for the Thracian expedition, and urges the Athenians to come to Olynthus' aid promptly and with full force. He further proposes the appointment of nomothetai empowered to suspend the laws governing theoric distributions and certain military exemptions, which he presents as the chief obstacles to mounting an effective campaign.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_halonnesus: A short deliberative oration attributed to Demosthenes, addressed to the Athenian assembly during the dispute with Philip II of Macedon over the island of Halonnesus. The speaker replies to Philip's letter and to the accounts of returning ambassadors, contending that Philip's professed gift of the island is in reality a seizure taken from pirates in name only, and that his offers of arbitration and of joint patrols against piracy would place control of the sea in Macedonian hands. He further rejects Philip's proposal for commercial agreements (symbola), observing that no such agreements existed under earlier Macedonian kings and that the scheme is contrived to make the Athenians ratify Philip's possession of Potidaea and his treatment of its settlers.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_liberty_of_the_rhodia: A deliberative oration of Demosthenes, addressed to the Athenian assembly, urging that the city intervene to restore the liberty of the Rhodians and the rule of the Rhodian demos. The speaker argues that Mausolus of Caria stripped the island of its freedom under pretence of friendship, weighs the position of Artemisia, who now directs its affairs, and warns against the designs of the Persian king after his campaign in Egypt. Earlier Athenian policy is recalled as precedent, including the expedition of Timotheus in aid of Ariobarzanes and the liberation of Samos, and the argument closes by weighing which course will serve the Athenians and all the Greeks.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_navy: An Attic deliberative oration addressed to the Athenian assembly, transmitted among the public speeches of Demosthenes and of uncertain date. The speaker opens by dismissing encomia of the ancestors in favour of practical counsel, arguing that open war against the Persian King would be hazardous because the King's resources in triremes, money and strong places exceed Athens' own. He advises instead that the city keep the peace while making its forces, cavalry, hoplites and three hundred ships, openly ready, so that the other Greeks, seeing both Athenian power and just intentions, will themselves turn to Athens for protection against the common enemy.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_peace: On the Peace is a deliberative oration by Demosthenes, addressed to the Athenian assembly in Attic Greek. The speaker rehearses his earlier public advice, including his opposition to aiding Plutarchus in Euboea and his warnings about the oaths and settlements made with Philip of Macedon, and argues that the existing peace should not be dissolved for new alliances or levies. He urges the Athenians to judge policy on its merits and practical consequences rather than on promises of gain, and to avoid being drawn into a fresh war with Philip through the Amphictyons.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_trierarchic_crown: On the Trierarchic Crown is a short oration in Greek attributed to the Athenian orator Demosthenes and belonging to the corpus of classical Attic oratory. Addressed to the council, it presents the speaker's plea for a crown in recognition of his service as a trierarch, contrasting his own expenditure in fitting out and fully manning a trireme with the conduct of rivals who hired substitutes for the liturgy and failed to equip their ships. Drawing on earlier Athenian practice, including the punishment of trierarchs after a naval defeat, he argues that those who discharge public duties deserve honour, while those who neglect them merit censure rather than reward.
grc.demosthenes.philip: A letter written in the name of Philip of Macedon and addressed to the council and people of Athens, preserved in the corpus of Demosthenes' orations. The writer complains that the Athenians pay no heed to the oaths and agreements between them and sets out a series of grievances: the seizure of his herald Nicias, toleration of pirates, the campaigns of the general Diopeithes in Thrace, an Athenian embassy to the Persian king, and decrees on behalf of the Thracian rulers Teres and Cersobleptes. He contrasts his treatment with earlier grants of citizenship to rulers such as Euagoras and Dionysius, and closes by defending his protection of the Cardians and his seizure of Halonnesus from the pirate Sostratus.
grc.didymus_alexandrinus.mensurae_marmorum_a: A short Greek treatise on practical measurement, attributed to Didymus Alexandrinus and of uncertain date. After distinguishing linear, surface and solid measurement, it sets out worked problems for finding the solid content of marble slabs and of round, square, triangular and half-round timbers, together with the diagonals of square beams. It closes with conversion rules among the cubit, the Ptolemaic foot and the Roman foot, stating their ratios in linear, surface and solid terms and giving sample problems for turning cubits into feet and the reverse.
grc.dinarchus.against_aristogiton: A forensic speech in Ancient Greek attributed to the orator Dinarchus, directed against Aristogiton in the proceedings arising from Harpalus' arrival at Athens. Addressing the Athenians in a case decided on a report of the council of the Areopagus, the speaker accuses Aristogiton of taking bribes, rehearses his earlier convictions, imprisonments and debts to the public treasury, and dismisses appeals for leniency founded on the defendant's supposed moderation and his ancestors' services. The argument dwells on the danger of sparing habitual corruption and cites Aristogiton's neglect of his own father as evidence of his character, urging that the harshest penalty be imposed.
grc.dinarchus.against_demosthenes: Against Demosthenes is a forensic prosecution speech composed by Dinarchus for the trial in which Demosthenes answered charges of taking money from Harpalus. Speaking to the Athenian judges after the Areopagus council had investigated the matter and reported against Demosthenes, the speaker defends that council and its apophasis from Demosthenes' attacks and presses for the death penalty agreed in advance should the charge be proved. He recalls the earlier inquiry into the three hundred talents sent by the Persian king and the alleged betrayal of the Thebans, and rebuts Demosthenes' appeals to his past services, including his claim to have won the Thebans as allies, his command at Chaeronea, and his embassies on the city's behalf.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.ad_ammaeum: A brief Greek treatise cast as a letter from Dionysius of Halicarnassus to Ammaeus, directed against a Peripatetic philosopher who claimed that Demosthenes owed his pre-eminence as an orator to Aristotle's rhetorical technai. Dionysius sets out to show that Demosthenes was already in his prime and had delivered his most celebrated speeches before Aristotle composed his works on rhetoric. Drawing on the common biographical accounts, he dates Demosthenes' birth to the year before the hundredth Olympiad, under the archon Timocrates, and reviews in sequence the public speeches, deliberative and forensic, down to the Against Meidias, numbering twelve then extant. He also announces a fuller discussion of the question in a separate work.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.antiquitates_: The Roman Antiquities of Dionysius of Halicarnassus, a Greek historian and rhetorician who lived and wrote in Rome in the age of Augustus, presents a history of Rome from its earliest, largely legendary beginnings through the early Republic. In the opening preface the author sets out his methods and motives, ranking Roman power above the earlier empires of the Assyrians, Medes, Persians, and Macedonians in extent and duration. The work mingles continuous narrative of the regal period and the early Republic with antiquarian accounts of Roman institutions and customs, and argues that the Roman people were of Greek origin.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_antiquis_o: A Greek treatise on rhetoric by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, introduced by a prefatory address to Ammaeus. The opening praises the return, in the author's own age of Roman supremacy, of the ancient and philosophical Attic manner of oratory after its eclipse by theatrical Asiatic styles in the generations following Alexander's death, and credits the cultured judgment of Rome's governing class with fostering the change. Dionysius then sets out the plan of the work: an examination of six Attic orators, Lysias, Isocrates and Isaeus from the older generation and Demosthenes, Hyperides and Aeschines from the later, treating each man's life, career and the qualities in his speeches to be imitated or avoided, with the first part devoted to the three earlier orators.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_demosthene: A short Greek treatise of rhetorical criticism by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, On Demosthenes examines the style of the great Athenian orator and the prose traditions from which his art arose. The opening chapters characterise the austere, densely wrought manner whose rule and canon is Thucydides and the plain, unforced manner perfected by Lysias, setting out the two poles between which Demosthenes' blended style is to be placed. Dionysius contrasts the effects of the two manners on the hearer, the one able to overawe and concentrate the mind, the other to charm and relax it, and rates both supreme exponents as unmatched yet incomplete. Readers hunting intertexts will find here a dense ancient engagement with Thucydidean and Lysian phrasing, as well as a useful witness to how Demosthenic style was analysed and classified in later Greek criticism.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_dinarcho: A short Greek essay by Dionysius of Halicarnassus devoted to the orator Dinarchus. Dionysius explains why he had passed Dinarchus over in his writings on the ancient Attic rhetoricians, then surveys his life: his Corinthian origins, his association at Athens with Theophrastus and Demetrius of Phalerum, his flourishing after Alexander's death, his exile at Chalcis, and his lawsuit against Proxenus. He characterises Dinarchus's style as ethical and impassioned, lacking little of Demosthenic force and bitterness, and sets out to distinguish the genuine speeches from the spurious ones, drawing on the speech against Proxenus and on Philochorus's Attic History as evidence.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_lysia: A short Greek critical essay by Dionysius of Halicarnassus on the orator Lysias. It opens with a biographical notice of Lysias, covering his Syracusan parentage, his birth and upbringing at Athens, his residence in Thurii, and his later rhetorical career in Athens, where he wrote speeches for courts, councils, assemblies, and other occasions. Dionysius then examines Lysias' style, praising the purity of his Attic diction, his avoidance of poetic and figurative language in favour of plain and ordinary words, and his clarity and brevity, with contrasts drawn against Gorgias and Thucydides and remarks on Isocrates' affinity with him.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_thucydide: A Greek literary-critical treatise by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, addressed to Quintus Aelius Tubero, on the subject matter and style of Thucydides. Framed as a sequel to the author's published notes on imitation, it opens with a defence of the decision to point out failings in a writer conventionally regarded as the greatest of historians, citing Plato and Aristotle as earlier examples of critics who judged their predecessors. The work then examines Thucydides' choice of subject and his qualities as a writer, weighing both the virtues of his composition and the defects that border on them, so as to characterise his manner of writing as a whole.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.epistula_ad_p: A short Greek epistolary treatise by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, written as a reply to a correspondent named Pompeius who had objected to the criticism of Plato in Dionysius' treatises on composition. The author defends the practice of judging a writer's style through explicit comparison, recounting how he selected Isocrates, Plato and Demosthenes as the three most distinguished prose stylists and then weighed Demosthenes' speeches against the best of the other two. He further discusses Plato's strictures on Lysias in the Phaedrus, arguing that Plato's own criticisms of earlier writers, including Homer, license a comparable examination of Plato's own diction.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.libri_secundi: Fragments of the second book of the treatise On the Ancient Orators by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, the Greek rhetorician and literary critic who was active at Rome in the late first century BC. The second book, which was devoted to Demosthenes, is otherwise lost and survives only in quotations transmitted by later scholiasts. The excerpts preserved here concern Demosthenes' diction, noting criticism of the proem of the speech On the Embassy as over-tragic and including remarks on Aeschines' use of words.
grc.dionysius_of_halicarnassus.de_compositio: A Greek epitome of Dionysius of Halicarnassus' treatise on literary composition, addressed in its opening to a young man named Rufus Melitius as a gift marking his entry into manhood. The work treats the arrangement of words (synthesis) as the second division of the study of style, defining it as the ordered placing of words into cola and periods, and maintains that arrangement contributes more to pleasure, persuasion and power in discourse than the mere choice of words. Examples are drawn from Homer's account of Odysseus, Eumaeus and Telemachus and from Herodotus' story of Candaules, together with a deliberately disordered version of Herodotus' sentence about Croesus, to show how the same words yield different effects under different arrangement. The argument closes by likening skilful composition to Athena, who transformed Odysseus' appearance at will.
grc.dionysius_of_halicarnasus.de_imitatione_: Greek fragments of a rhetorical treatise On Imitation by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, surviving only in fragmentary form. The fragments open with definitions of rhetoric, imitation, and the zealous emulation of fine models, and urge close acquaintance with the writings of the ancients, illustrated by the anecdote of the painter Zeuxis. There follow assessments of the characteristic virtues of earlier Greek authors as material for imitation: the poets Hesiod, Antimachus, Panyassis, Pindar, Simonides, Stesichorus, and Alcaeus, the tragedians Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides, comic poetry including Menander, and the historians Herodotus, Thucydides, Philistus, and Xenophon, with judgments on diction, characterization, and arrangement.
grc.epictetus.gnomologium_epicteteum_e_stoba: A gnomologium of moral sayings attributed to Epictetus, transmitted in the anthology of Stobaeus. The collection consists of short numbered maxims on ethical themes, opening with the comparison of a life entangled with fortune to a winter torrent and of a soul companionship with virtue to an ever-flowing spring. The remaining sayings counsel detachment from wealth and luxury, moderation in food and drink, proper conduct at banquets and drinking parties, restraint from quarrels, and the preference of truth over reputation and victory in argument.
grc.epicurus.ratae_sententiae: The Ratae Sententiae (Greek Kyriai Doxai, 'Principal Doctrines') is a short Greek collection of forty numbered maxims setting out the central ethical teachings of Epicurus. The sayings were transmitted by Diogenes Laertius in his life of Epicurus. The maxims treat the blessed and untroubled nature of the gods, death as nothing to us, the measure of pleasure and pain, the need for the study of nature to dispel fear, the classification of desires as natural, necessary, or vain, and the role of friendship and justice in the secure life. Some of the sayings are accompanied by brief explanatory glosses in parentheses.
grc.euripides.heracles: A Greek tragedy by Euripides. The opening scene presents Amphitryon, Megara and the children of Heracles as suppliants at an altar of Zeus Soter in Thebes, where the usurper Lycus, having killed Creon and seized the throne, prepares to slay them in the belief that Heracles has descended to Hades to bring back the three-bodied hound of Taenarus. The drama goes on to follow Heracles' return and killing of Lycus, the madness inflicted on him that drives him to slaughter his own wife and children, and his rescue and consolation by Theseus.
grc.euripides.iphigenia_aulis: Greek tragedy transmitted under the name of Euripides, of uncertain date, printed here in 1,626 lines from Gilbert Murray's Oxford Clarendon Press edition of the Euripidis Fabulae (1913). Set at the Greek camp at Aulis, it dramatises Agamemnon's dilemma when the seer Calchas demands the sacrifice of his daughter Iphigenia to win fair winds for the fleet, moving through his secret letter to Clytemnestra, the deception of Achilles, and the confrontation between father and daughter. Its opening survey of Tyndareus' oath, Helen's wooing, and the muster of the Achaeans condenses much of the prehistory of the Trojan War, making the play a natural comparand for treatments of the house of Atreus, the sacrifice motif, and the mythic prelude to the expedition across Greek and later literature.
grc.eusebius_caesarea.historia_ecclesiastica: The Historia Ecclesiastica of Eusebius of Caesarea is a Greek prose history in ten books, each prefaced by a chapter-by-chapter summary. The preface announces an account running from the economy of Christ down to the author's own day, covering the successions of the holy apostles, the heads of the most prominent churches, those who in each generation passed on the divine word, the heretics who introduced a falsely named knowledge, the war of the Jewish nation that encompassed the plot against the Saviour, the persecutions waged by the nations, and the martyrdoms that followed. The first book treats the preexistence and theology of Christ, the antiquity of his name among the prophets, the chronology of his manifestation under Herod and Pilate, the genealogies in the Gospels, the high priests of the period, John the Baptist, the disciples, and the story of the ruler of the Edessenes.
grc.flavius_josephus.contra_apionem: Contra Apionem is a two-book apologetic treatise in Greek by the Jewish historian Flavius Josephus, addressed to a certain Epaphroditus and written in reply to detractors of the Jewish nation, notably Apion. The first book argues for the extreme antiquity of the Jews, rebuts the claim that the nation lacks witnesses among the Greeks, and appeals to Egyptian, Chaldaean, Phoenician, and Greek authors, whose records Josephus depicts as far more recent and mutually inconsistent. The second book continues the refutation of hostile writers and presents an account of the Mosaic law and constitution as a divinely ordained polity, together with a catalogue of nations among whom the Jews are attested.
grc.flavius_josephus.de_bello_judaico_libri_: The Bellum Judaicum is a historical narrative in seven books by Flavius Josephus, who introduces himself in the preface as Josephus son of Matthias, a priest from Jerusalem who first fought against the Romans and later accompanied them. It recounts the great war between the Jews and the Romans, from the turmoil that followed Nero through the outbreak of the revolt and the Roman campaigns to the siege of Jerusalem and its destruction under Titus. Josephus presents the work as a Greek rendering of an account he had earlier composed in his ancestral language for the peoples beyond the Euphrates, and defends its accuracy against writers whom he accuses of flattering the Romans or slandering the Jews. The narrative stresses the part played by internal tyrants and factions in the city's fall, and joins the historian's account of events to the author's lament for the misfortunes of his homeland.
grc.galen.ad_glauconem_de_methodo_medendi: A Greek medical treatise by Galen, addressed to a correspondent named Glaucon, setting out a general method of healing. The opening argues that a physician must know not only the common nature of all people, as Hippocrates taught, but also the individual constitution of each patient, and dwells on the proper division of diseases into genera, species, and differences, citing Hippocrates and Mnesitheus of Athens. The remaining portion treats fevers, beginning with the simplest 'ephemeral' fevers of Hippocratic classification, describing their causes, the diagnostic signs drawn from pulse, urine, complexion, and other symptoms, and their management by bathing and regimen.
grc.galen.an_in_arteriis_sanguis_contineatur: A Greek medical treatise by Galen, transmitted under the Latin title An in arteriis sanguis contineatur ('Whether blood is contained in the arteries'). Opening from the observation that blood flows at once from a wounded artery, Galen argues that the arteries must already have held blood before the injury, against the doctrine of Erasistratus and his followers that they naturally contain only pneuma. The work then answers the Erasistratean objection that pneuma escapes unseen because of its fineness and lightness, examines whether it moves of its own accord or is driven out by the heart, and draws on the views of Praxagoras and Erasistratus, together with the analogy of inflated reeds, to show that neither account can dispense with blood in the arteries.
grc.galen.de_anatomicis_administrationibus: De Anatomicis Administrationibus ('On Anatomical Procedures') is a Greek instructional treatise on dissection by the physician Galen, composed during the reign of the emperor Antoninus. Its autobiographical opening explains why the author reworks the anatomical manual he had earlier written for the Roman consul Flavius Boethus, whose copies were lost, promising a fuller and more accurate treatment informed by his subsequent anatomical studies. The surviving portion lays out the order in which a student should learn anatomy, beginning with the skeleton, observed directly on human bones or, failing that, on apes chosen for their resemblance to humans, and proceeding through muscles, arteries, veins, nerves, and viscera, with advice on demonstration and dissection technique.
grc.galen.de_antidotis: A Greek medical treatise by Galen, On Antidotes (De Antidotis), defines antidotes as remedial agents taken into the body rather than applied from outside and divides them into three kinds: those against deadly poisons, those against the bites of venomous creatures, and those easing disorders arising from faulty regimen. It recounts the Mithridatium composed by Mithridates and the theriac of Andromachus, physician to Nero, and describes the emperor Marcus Aurelius taking theriac daily, with Galen himself charged with preparing it. The remainder gives instructions for the best preparation of theriac, along with guidance on testing the strength and quality of simple drugs, their places of origin, and the detection of adulterated ingredients.
grc.galen.de_causis_morborum: De Causis Morborum (On the Causes of Diseases) is a Greek medical treatise by Galen. Building on an earlier work that classified diseases by species and genus as simple and compound, it takes up the causes of each kind, beginning with the affections of the so-called homoeomerous parts, conceived as dyscrasias or divisions of bodily continuity, and passing on to the composite and organic diseases. Its opening exposition attributes the simple hot diseases to immoderate heat, tracing its origins in exercise, putrefaction, contact with warmer bodies, confinement of vapors, and warming foods, wines, and sharp drugs, and arguing that such causes kindle fever only where the magnitude of the cause, the lapse of time, and the condition of the body allow. Causes arising within the animal itself, whether dispositions or movements contrary to nature, are styled preceding causes, while those impinging from outside and greatly altering the body are called antecedent causes.
grc.galen.de_constitutione_artis_medicae_ad_: A short Greek treatise by Galen, addressed to Patrophilus, on how medicine is constituted as an art. After a preface recalling Patrophilus's demand for a demonstrative method, it classifies the arts as theoretical, practical, productive and acquisitive, and argues that medicine belongs among the productive arts, one that restores a natural state rather than creating something that did not exist before. From the end of the art, health, Galen derives the physician's need to know the parts of the body, both the simple homogeneous parts and the organic composites, together with their functions, a knowledge reached through anatomy. The work presents itself as the second of two companion treatises Galen composed for Patrophilus, the first having shown how every art arises from the conception of its end.
grc.galen.de_consuetudinibus: A short Greek medical treatise by Galen, De consuetudinibus argues that habit ranks among the chief therapeutic indications in medicine. It maintains that customary foods, drinks, exercises, and other practices are tolerated better than unfamiliar ones, so that sudden departures from habit cause harm, and supports the claim with passages from Hippocrates and Erasistratus and with an anecdote about a Peripatetic philosopher of Mytilene who died after refusing cold drink to which he was unaccustomed. Galen adds his own experience of giving cold water to patients in acute fever once long practice had proved the remedy safe.
grc.galen.de_crisibus: On Crises (Greek Peri kriseōn) is a Greek medical treatise by the physician Galen of the second century CE on the critical phases of disease. It surveys competing definitions of crisis, sets out the four periods of illness, onset, increase, acme, and decline, and teaches how to prognosticate whether a disease is worsening, at its height, or resolving from the timing, duration, severity, and symptomatic character of paroxysms and the intervals between them. Tertian and quartan fevers and pleurisy supply examples, and the method rests on Hippocratic instructions for comparing successive paroxysms.
grc.galen.de_curandi_ratione_per_venae_secti: A Greek medical treatise by Galen, preserved in Karl Gottlob Kühn's Opera Omnia (Leipzig, 1826), the De Curandi Ratione per Venae Sectionem ('On the Method of Cure by Venesection') organises the practice of bloodletting as a sequence of questions: which bodily conditions require evacuation, which patients can tolerate it, which veins should be opened, and how much blood should be withdrawn. Galen defends the remedy against the school of Erasistratus, Chrysippus of Cnidus, Medius, and Aristogenes in particular, while appealing to Hippocrates and the most reputable physicians for the view that the choice of vein matters greatly. The treatise also points repeatedly to Galen's own earlier writings, such as the Therapeutic Method and his two books against Erasistratus and the Erasistraleans of Rome, so that a reader hunting intertexts finds a dense web of allusions to Hippocratic doctrine and to the rest of Galen's corpus.
grc.galen.de_diebus_decretoriis: De diebus decretoriis (On Critical Days) is a Greek medical treatise by Galen concerning the days on which crises in disease occur and how far they can be trusted. The opening argues that a sudden resolution of illness counts as a genuine crisis only when accompanied by visible evacuations such as sweats, abundant urine, haemorrhages, or discharges, and that convalescents must accordingly be kept under strict regimen. Crises are then classified as complete or incomplete, trustworthy or unreliable, dangerous, clear, obscure, or plainly foreshadowed, with the seventh day presented as the most reliable crisis day and those on the sixth, twelfth, and sixteenth as rare, incomplete, or generally unfavourable. In support of this scheme the treatise appeals to Hippocrates and to the accumulated experience of earlier physicians including Archigenes, Heracleides of Tarentum, Philotimus, and Diocles.
grc.galen.de_difficultate_respirationis: A Greek treatise by Galen on difficult breathing, arguing that dyspnoea is a form of disturbance affecting respiration just as disturbances affect sensation and movement. It examines the natural components of breathing, inspiration, expiration, and the pauses between them, and classifies forms of dyspnoea as simple or compound, arising in the speed, size, or spacing of the breath. Galen further criticises newer physicians who departed from the names for breathing defects customary among Hippocrates and the older medical writers.
grc.galen.de_elementis_ex_hippocrate: A Greek treatise by Galen, 'On the Elements according to Hippocrates', which investigates the ultimate constituents of the human body and of natural things. Galen argues that sense-perception cannot be the criterion of the elements, since many things escape notice by their smallness while not being truly simple, and that the real elements are the primary and simplest parts by nature, incapable of further resolution. Expounding Hippocrates' dictum that if man were one he would never suffer, he defends a plurality of elements against monist positions and against the atomist theories of Democritus, Leucippus and Epicurus, as well as against the doctrine of homoiomerous parts, illustrating the argument with examples such as the needle piercing flesh.
grc.galen.de_foetuum_formatione: A short Greek medical treatise by Galen on the formation of the embryo, known by the Latin title De Foetuum Formatione. It opens by censuring philosophers who wrote about embryonic development without anatomical experience and credits Hippocrates with first grounding the inquiry in observation, quoting the Hippocratic account of the six-day embryo. The remaining portion describes the membranes surrounding the foetus (the chorion, amnion and allantois), the growth and convergence of the umbilical vessels and the urachus, and the successive formation of the foetal parts, beginning with the liver.
grc.galen.de_hirudinibus_revulsione_cucurbit: A brief Greek therapeutic manual attributed to Galen, comprising four chapters on methods of drawing off blood and humour: the use of leeches, revulsion, the cupping glass, and incision with scarification. The opening chapter gives practical directions for catching and keeping leeches, preparing the skin so they bite, curbing the bleeding they cause, and dressing the wounds afterwards. The later chapters explain how revulsion redirects humoral flows from one region of the body to another, when cupping is beneficial and when it must be avoided, and why scarifying the legs is often preferable to frequent venesection.
grc.galen.de_inaequali_intemperie: De Inaequali Intemperie is a short Greek treatise in which Galen examines anomalous or uneven dyscrasia, an imbalance of bodily qualities that afflicts one part of the body differently from another. The opening chapters distinguish such irregular imbalances, whether affecting the whole body or a single member, from uniform ones, illustrating them with conditions such as erysipelas, phagedaena, herpes, and elephantiasis, and then survey the body's structures from the largest visible parts down to the homogeneous tissues. The remainder follows the course of a hot flux invading a muscle, explaining how inflammation and pain arise as the parts are heated and compressed, and how recovery proceeds either by dispersion of the flux or by its concoction into pus, together with an account of which cavities offer the safer sites for suppuration. Hippocratic sayings on pain arising during alteration of nature are invoked along the way.
grc.galen.de_instrumento_odoratus: A short Greek treatise by Galen on the organ of smell, transmitted under the Latin title De instrumento odoratus. The opening distinguishes smell (osphrēsis) as both a faculty and its exercise, and surveys the anatomy of the nasal passages, the ethmoid bones, the membranes lining them, and the nerves rising from the brain. The argument holds that neither the nasal bone nor its enveloping membrane is the true organ of smell, adducing demonstrations with stopped nostrils and incense-filled rooms to show that odours are perceived only during inhalation, and concludes that the sensorium lies deeper within the head. Throughout, each sense organ is compared with the nature of its proper object, smell being assigned an intermediate substance between air and moisture.
grc.galen.de_locis_affectis: A Greek medical treatise by the physician Galen, De Locis Affectis (On the Affected Parts) sets out methods for determining which part of the body is affected by disease, on the premise that treatment must vary with the affected region. Galen argues that diagnosis of hidden lesions requires knowledge of each organ's substance, position, activity and function, and illustrates the method with anatomical observations and case histories, including wounds, ulcers of the lung and kidneys, and cases of urinary retention managed with the catheter. The opening portion also contains criticism of rival physicians such as Archigenes and Asclepiades and dismisses several theoretical disputes as useless for medical practice.
grc.galen.de_marcore: De Marcore ('On Marasmus') is a brief Greek medical treatise by Galen. It defines marasmus as the destruction of a living body through dryness, distinguishing a simple form arising from starvation from compound forms accompanied by excessive heat or cold, as in certain fevers and in old age. An opening digression recalls a philosopher who promised to rear infants immune to aging, an anecdote Galen uses to illustrate how plausible but unproved arguments persuade. The discussion then investigates the cause of aging, rejecting the doctrine that innate heat consumes the body as a flame consumes its fuel, and engages with a Hippocratic saying on the killing power of the heat that shaped the body.
grc.galen.de_morborum_differentiis: De Morborum Differentiis (On the Differences of Diseases) is a Greek medical treatise by Galen that opens by defining what a disease is and proposing to enumerate the simple, primary diseases that serve as the elements from which all others are compounded. Health is located in the due proportion, or crasis, of the body's constituents, and disease in their disproportion, whether in the breadth of the pores or in the mixture of hot, cold, dry and wet. The argument goes on to distinguish disorders of the homoiomerous parts, such as flesh and bone, from those of the organic parts and of the body as a whole, and to classify deviations from natural symmetry as excess or deficiency.
grc.galen.de_motu_musculorum: A Greek medical treatise by Galen on the movement of muscles, which identifies the muscles as the organs of voluntary motion and surveys their great number, varied shapes, and points of attachment to bone. It distinguishes tendons, ligaments, and nerves, describing the tendon as a mixed nature between ligament and nerve, and traces the powers of motion and sensation from the brain and spinal cord through the nerves into the body of the muscle, which is also nourished by artery and vein. It sets the psychic, voluntary movements of the muscles apart from the natural movements of arteries and veins, and closes with a physiological account of how the tendon, formed from both nerve and ligament, binds the muscle to the bone and draws it in movement.
grc.galen.de_nervorum_dissectione: A short Greek anatomical treatise by Galen, transmitted under the Latin title De Nervorum Dissectione ('On the Dissection of the Nerves'). It opens by stating that no part of the animal body has voluntary motion or sensation without a nerve, and that the origin of all nerves lies in the brain and spinal cord. The account then proceeds pair by pair through the cranial nerves, tracing the optic, oculomotor, and successive pairs from their roots through the skull to their distributions among the eyes, the muscles of the face and jaw, the teeth, and the tongue, the last being named by some the gustatory pair because taste operates through it. The fourth and fifth pairs are treated with reference to the anatomist Marinus, and the description throughout appeals to what dissection makes visible.
grc.galen.de_parvae_pilae_exercitio: A short Greek treatise by Galen, known by the Latin title De parvae pilae exercitio ('On Exercise with the Small Ball'), takes the form of a direct address to Epigenes. It argues that exercise with a small ball surpasses all other kinds of exercise: it requires nothing but a ball and so is within reach of the poorest, it moves every part of the body in turn, and its pace and intensity can be varied at will. Galen holds that the game benefits the soul as well as the body, training the attention and foresight that generals need, and he contrasts it with hunting, running, and wrestling, which he criticises as expensive, one-sided, or harmful through excess.
grc.galen.de_placitis_hippocratis_et_platoni: A Greek medical-philosophical treatise by the physician Galen, De Placitis Hippocratis et Platonis sets out the agreement of Hippocratic medicine with Platonic teaching on the soul. The work opens in the midst of an extended anatomical argument, appealing to dissection and vivisection to show that the left ventricle of the heart holds blood rather than pneuma and that the psychic pneuma resides in the ventricles of the brain. Galen presses the case against Chrysippus, Erasistratus, Aristotle, and Praxagoras, whom he charges with placing the ruling part of the soul or the origin of the nerves in the heart contrary to what observation of the body reveals.
grc.galen.de_plenitudine: De Plenitudine ('On Fullness') is a short Greek treatise by the physician Galen on the medical term plēthos, the excessive accumulation of matter in the body. Galen opens by surveying the confusion among contemporary doctors, including the Empiric and Methodist sects, over whether 'much' and 'little' are to be understood relative to the capacity of the containing organs or relative to an innate faculty (dynamis). Through examples such as distended stomachs and bladders, overstretched vessels, and spontaneous ruptures with haemorrhage, he argues that partisans of either definition must concede the other sense, so that fullness is acknowledged in both ways.
grc.galen.de_praenotione_ad_epigenem: A Greek medical treatise by Galen on prognosis, addressed to Epigenes. It opens with a denunciation of physicians who pursue favour through flattery, display, and attendance on the wealthy, and who persecute those claiming foreknowledge of the course of disease. The main part is a narrative account of the quartan fever of Eudemus, a Peripatetic philosopher whom Galen attended in Rome, recording his pulse-based predictions of the fever's critical days and his disagreements with rival physicians over treatment, notably their administration of theriac. The account also refers to anatomical demonstrations on voice and respiration given before distinguished Romans, including men of consular rank.
grc.galen.de_praesagitione_ex_pulsibus: A Greek medical treatise by Galen, De Praesagitione ex Pulsibus ('On Prognosis from the Pulse') teaches how to draw prognostic signs from the pulse, taking prognosis to cover present and past conditions as well as things to come. Its discussion centers on the pulse conventionally called 'great,' examining how changes in size, speed, and density arise from causes such as bodily constitution, thinness, exercise, bathing, food and wine, anger, warming drugs, and the onset of fever. It also treats the examination of patients who conceal their condition, including an anecdote in which Galen detects that a wealthy man has secretly taken medicine despite his denials. Throughout, the argument presupposes Galen's earlier treatises on the diagnosis, differences, and causes of pulses.
grc.galen.de_propriorum_animi_cuiuslibet_aff: A short Greek ethical treatise by Galen, cast as a reply to an interlocutor who asked for a summary of the book Galen had written for Antonius the Epicurean on watchfulness over one's own passions. It distinguishes errors, which arise from false opinion, from the passions, which arise from an irrational power in the soul that disobeys reason, and argues that self-love blinds everyone to his own failings. Following the fable of Aesop's two sacks and sayings of Plato, it prescribes entrusting self-knowledge to an impartial observer, neither loved nor hated, who will report one's faults, and counsels patience under criticism. Practical directions follow for testing such a companion's honesty and for treating able critics, in Zeno's phrase, as paedagogues.
grc.galen.de_ptisana: A short Greek medical treatise by Galen on the ptisan, a decoction made from hulled barley and water, written after he found physicians giving it to the sick without defining when it helps or harms, or in what manner, quantity, and season it should be administered. Following Hippocrates as his model, he sets out the proper selection of water and barley, the correct method of boiling, and the appropriate occasion, dose, and mode of giving the drink. The work then enumerates the properties of well-cooked ptisan, smooth, even, moist, mildly slippery, cleansing, and easily digested, and the kinds of bodies for which it is fitting, especially patients suffering acute and continued fevers, as well as the harm it does when given unseasonably.
grc.galen.de_pulsibus_ad_tirones: A brief Greek treatise by the physician Galen introducing the study of the pulse to beginners, addressed in its opening to a pupil named Teuthras. It identifies the arteries accessible to touch, the wrist pulse above all, and classifies differences among pulses according to the size of the arterial dilation, the speed and force of the beat, the texture of the vessel wall, and the interval between beats. Later sections treat uniformity and irregularity in the pulse, including irregularities that recur in ordered cycles and others arising within a single beat.
grc.galen.de_purgantium_medicamentorum_facul: A Greek medical treatise by Galen on the action of purgative drugs, De Purgantium Medicamentorum Facultate ('On the Faculties of Purging Medicines'). Galen argues that cathartics possess an attractive power proper to each humour, drawing out that humour alone from the veins, and directs the argument against Erasistratus, who allowed no such faculty, and against the followers of Asclepiades, who held that purgatives transform all the humours indiscriminately rather than evacuating one. The treatise invokes Hippocratic authority for the doctrine of attraction and repeatedly challenges its opponents to public demonstrations of treatment on patients suffering from jaundice and dropsy, to be decided by deeds rather than long speeches.
grc.galen.de_sanitate_tuenda: A Greek medical treatise by Galen, De Sanitate Tuenda ('On the Preservation of Health') sets out the hygienic half of the art concerned with the human body, arguing that the preservation of health must be examined before the treatment of disease. It defines health as a due proportion of the elementary qualities in the body's parts and surveys the harms to which the body is subject, both those innate from conception, such as the progressive drying that constitutes old age, and those arising from outside. The discussion then turns to the replenishment of lost substance through food, drink, respiration and the pulse, the digestion of nutriment into matter resembling the body, and the formation and evacuation of residues as the chief means of keeping the body free of corruption.
grc.galen.de_sectis_ad_eos_qui_introducuntur: Galen's De Sectis ad Eos Qui Introducuntur ('On the Sects for Beginners') is a short Greek treatise setting out the two chief schools of medicine, the Empiric and the Rationalist or Dogmatic. Opening with the definition of medicine as the science of things healthy and diseased, whose goal is the attainment of health, it presents the Empiric account of the art as built up from experience, through observation of oft-repeated cases, records handed on to learners, and trial by transition to the similar, against the Rationalist demand for knowledge of the natures and causes of the body and of airs, waters, places, foods, and customs. The treatise goes on to set out the Rationalist doctrine of indications, whereby treatment is reasoned from the cause of the disease together with the patient's strength, age, season, region, occupations, and habits.
grc.galen.de_sophismatis_seu_captionibus_pen: A short Greek treatise by Galen on fallacies arising from wording, preserved under the Latin title De Sophismatis seu Captionibus penes dictionem. It sets out Aristotle's six modes of verbal sophism, homonymy, amphiboly, accent, combination, division, and figure of speech, judging Aristotle's own supporting argument entirely obscure and the explanations of earlier interpreters unsuccessful. Galen then argues that diction has a single virtue, clear signification, and a single vice, ambiguity, so that every fallacy dependent on language ultimately arises from a word's double meaning.
grc.galen.de_substantia_facultatum_naturaliu: A Greek fragment of On the Substance of Natural Faculties by Galen, the second-century CE Greek physician. The fragment takes up the apparent discrepancy in claims that animals are hot and plants cold, defending Plato against the charge of inconsistency between his ordinary statements and the doctrine of the Timaeus that the world's soul extends through the whole cosmos. It then distinguishes the natural faculties of attraction, retention, alteration, and expulsion from psychic powers, maintains that bodies arise from a thorough mixture of the four elements, and argues that questions about the substance and immortality of the soul need not be settled by the physician, since such knowledge is unnecessary for curing disease, preserving health, or the practical part of moral philosophy.
grc.galen.de_symptomatum_differentiis: Galen's De Symptomatum Differentiis (On the Differences between Symptoms) is a Greek medical treatise that takes up symptoms as the remaining part of a larger account of abnormal bodily conditions, after diseases and their causes, which the author says were treated in other works. It distinguishes the terms nosos (disease), pathos and pathēma (affection), and symptōma, defining disease as an unnatural disposition that primarily impairs a natural activity and symptom as whatever befalls the body contrary to nature. The discussion further separates antecedent causes of disease from diseases themselves, contrasts primary with incidental causation, and comments on the conventions of Greek medical terminology.
grc.galen.de_temperamentis: Galen's De Temperamentis is a Greek treatise on temperaments (kraseis), the mixtures of the hot, the cold, the dry and the wet of which the bodies of animals are compounded. Galen states that his earlier work on the elements according to Hippocrates established that fourfold composition, and announces that the present work will set out all the differences of temperament, how many they are and of what kind, dividing them by species and genus and beginning with an explanation of the terms. It then rehearses the views of the most celebrated physicians and philosophers before him on which pairings of the four elementary qualities can occur together, whether a hot-and-moist mixture is possible, and how many kinds of mixture there are, before turning to his own account.
grc.galen.de_theriaca_ad_pisonem: A Greek prose treatise on the theriac, the compound antidote against venomous bites and poisons, in which Galen addresses a friend named Piso. The opening praises Andromachus, a Cretan physician esteemed by the emperors of his time and credited with a treatise on the antidote, and recounts Galen's observation of Piso tending his own son's injury. Later sections celebrate the drug's reputation and power, explain how a batch of theriac may be tested for adulteration using cockerels and purgatives, and condemn vendors who trade on its name. The closing portion credits the emperor Marcus with habitual use of the remedy, praises the liberality with which the reigning emperors dispense medicines, and recounts cures such as those of Antipater and of Arrhia.
grc.galen.de_totius_morbi_temporibus: A short Greek medical treatise by Galen on the 'times' (kairoi) of the whole disease, distinguishing four phases analogous to the ages of living creatures: genesis or onset, ascent, acme, and decline. The discussion rehearses disputes among physicians over how these phases are to be defined and whether some diseases lack one or another of them, then applies the scheme to inflammation, fever, ulcers, ophthalmia, and discharges from the head, holding that the stage reached is recognized through signs of defective or completed digestion in the evacuations, urine, and sputum. Hippocratic sayings on the timing of remedies such as venesection, clysters, and purging are cited in the course of the argument about treatment at each phase.
grc.galen.de_tremore_palpitatione_convulsion: A short Greek medical treatise by Galen on tremor, palpitation, spasm, and rigidity, treated as faulty movements of the parts that, in health, carry out voluntary motion through the nerves and muscles. The preface notes that pulse has been dealt with in a separate work on that subject and takes issue with Praxagoras, son of Nicarchus, for classifying all these affections as disorders of the arteries, a view that Herophilus, who became his pupil, had already refuted. Tremor is defined as arising from weakness of the power that moves and bears up the body, as in old age, fear, or excessive burden, and is then distinguished from palpitation by place, cause, and accompanying symptoms. Along the way the argument holds that apparently motionless bodies may still be in compound motion, and Hippocratic sayings, such as that standing is least beneficial for sufferers from ulcers, are cited in support.
grc.galen.de_tumoribus_praeter_naturam: A short Greek prose treatise by the physician Galen, On Tumors Contrary to Nature (De Tumoribus Praeter Naturam) examines abnormal swellings of the body. After defining onkos, or swelling, and distinguishing states that are according to nature, beyond nature, and contrary to nature, it takes up inflammation as the first of the contrary-to-nature swellings. Its main argument holds that the bulk, heat, and redness of an inflamed part arise from an accumulation of blood in the flesh and vessels rather than from heat alone or trapped pneuma, a claim supported by clinical signs such as the behavior of wounds, the emergence of previously invisible veins, and the effects of cooling, together with remarks on treatment.
grc.galen.de_uteri_dissectione: A short anatomical treatise in Greek by Galen, transmitted under the title De uteri dissectione, which announces as its subject the womb's position, size and shape, its attachments, nourishment and interwoven vessels, and the membranes enclosing the embryo. The discussion places the uterus between the bladder and the rectum, distinguishes its size in the virgin, the mature woman and the pregnant, and describes its horn-like lateral outgrowths, for which it records the divergent accounts of Herophilus, Diocles, Eudemus, Praxagoras and Philotimus. Galen then sets out the ligaments, veins, arteries and nerves by which the organ is attached, interwoven and fed, its unions with the cervix, vagina and genitalia, and the curvature of the lower spine, citing Hippocrates on the latter point.
grc.galen.de_utilitate_respirationis: De Utilitate Respirationis ('On the Use of Breathing') is a short Greek medical treatise by Galen on why respiration is necessary for life. Opening with the question of what use breathing serves, it surveys rival doctrines, the generation of the soul (Asclepiades), strengthening (Nicarchus after Praxagoras), the cooling of innate heat (Philistion and Diocles), nourishment (Hippocrates) and the filling of the arteries (Erasistratus), and divides these into theories concerned with the substance and with the quality of inhaled air. The bulk of the argument refutes Erasistratus, drawing on breath-holding, the heart's capacity to draw air from lung and artery, arterial motion and the relief of suffocation by exhalation to show that animals perish not from want of the air's substance but because the heart requires its quality, in keeping with the view that breathing preserves the innate heat.
grc.galen.de_venarum_arteriarumque_dissectio: A short Greek anatomical treatise by Galen, transmitted under the Latin title De Venarum Arteriarumque Dissectione, On the Dissection of Veins and Arteries. It takes the form of a synopsis written for a friend named Antisthenes, recalling what he had seen demonstrated in the dissected body of an ape, and traces the branching of the veins from the portal vein and the hollow vein down into the roots supplying the abdomen and upward through the vena cava to the head and limbs, then the arteries growing from the heart. The exposition works throughout with an analogy between the vascular system and a tree dividing below into roots and above into branches, an image the author ascribes to Hippocrates and the most reputable anatomists after him, and it records variant nomenclature such as Herophilus' term for the duodenum and the alternatives aorta and great artery for the largest arterial vessel.
grc.galen.de_victu_attenuante: De Victu Attenuante ('On the Thinning Regimen') is a short Greek dietetic treatise by Galen on the regimen held necessary for the treatment of most chronic illnesses. The opening section credits this diet with curing or easing conditions such as nephritis, arthritis, breathlessness, enlarged spleen and epilepsy, and explains that foods able to thin the body's humours declare their power through pungent taste and smell. The treatise then catalogues such foods, including garlic, onions, cress, leeks, mustard, capers, celery, radishes, cabbage and numerous wild greens, and discusses how preparation with vinegar, oxymel, oil or salt modifies their effect.
grc.galen.institutio_logica: Galen's Institutio Logica is a compact Greek introduction to logic, opening from the distinction between things known through sense perception, things grasped by intellect alone, and things established by demonstration. It sets out the basic apparatus of the discipline, defining propositions, terms, axioms, syllogisms, and conclusions, and classifying propositions as categorical or hypothetical and as universal, particular, conditional, or disjunctive. Definitions are illustrated with simple examples, notably an argument in which Theon, equal to Dion, who is equal to Philon, is shown to be equal to Philon.
grc.galen.quod_optimus_medicus_sit_quoque_ph: A short Greek treatise by Galen arguing that the best physician must also be a philosopher. It opens by comparing most physicians to athletes who desire Olympic victory without training, and faults contemporary doctors for praising Hippocrates while neglecting the logical study, knowledge of the body, and diagnostic and prognostic care that he demanded. The argument concludes that the practice of medicine requires all three parts of philosophy, the logical, the physical, and the ethical, so that the physician, practising temperance and holding wealth in contempt, may pursue the art for the good of patients rather than for gain.
grc.gorgias_of_leontini.ἑλένης_ἐγκώμιον: An encomium attributed to Gorgias of Leontini, of uncertain date, written in defense of Helen of Troy against the blame attached to her departure with Paris. The speaker examines four possible causes of her voyage, the decrees of Fortune and the gods, abduction by force, persuasion by speech, and the power of eros and sight, arguing that under each she merits acquittal rather than censure. In the course of the argument the speech dwells on the power of logos, which can calm fear, remove grief, and work upon the soul as drugs work upon the body, illustrating its force through poetry, incantation, and philosophical disputation.
grc.hermogenes.progymnasmata_dub: A short Greek treatise on the preliminary rhetorical exercises (progymnasmata), of uncertain date and transmitted under the name of Hermogenes, printed among the dubia in Rabe's Teubner edition of his Opera (1913). Across some fifty-seven lines it defines and classifies the fable, the narrative, and the chreia, treating their subdivisions (Aesopic, Cyprian, Libyan, and Sybaritic fables; mythical, dramatic, historical, and political narratives) and demonstrating the elaboration (ergasia) of a chreia with stock examples from Plato, Isocrates, and Demosthenes. Readers of intertexts will find here the schoolroom vocabulary and exemplary phrasings, from Hesiod's nightingale and Archilochus' fox to Medea's betrayal of the golden fleece, through which fable and narrative were processed in ancient rhetorical education and passed into later literary use.
grc.hermogenes.περὶ_τῶν_στάσεων: A Greek treatise on rhetorical staseis, or issues, attributed to Hermogenes, concerned with how civic and forensic questions are to be divided and argued. It defines the political question, ranks the kinds of persons and acts that may be brought under examination, and catalogues both the classes of wholly untenable issues and those nearly untenable types still practised in declamation. Its hypothetical cases invoke figures from classical history and oratory, among them Pericles, Demosthenes, Alexander, Socrates, Critias and Cleon, and its framework for classifying arguments is of value to readers tracing the technical rhetoric and commonplaces that lie behind ancient speeches.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.belopoeica: A short Greek treatise by Hero of Alexandria on the construction of artillery engines. It opens with a preface presenting mechanics as the means by which cities remain at peace and free from alarm, then defines belopoeica as the art of casting a missile far and forcefully upon a given target, dividing engines into straight-spring (euthytona, also called scorpions) and bent-spring (palintona, also called stone-throwers) types. The author criticises earlier writers for recording measurements without setting out constructions or uses, and proceeds to trace these machines' origin from the hand bow, describing a bow-operated engine in detail: the names and functions of its parts and the procedure for spanning and releasing it.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.de_automatis: A Greek treatise on the construction of automata by Hero of Alexandria. The proem distinguishes two kinds of device: movable automata, such as shrines and altars that process under their own power with figures moving in accordance with a chosen story, and stationary automata, plinths with doors that open repeatedly to reveal successive animated tableaux. The exposition sets out the practical requirements for such machines, including level ground, light dry timber, axles, wheels and cords, and a timing mechanism in which a weight descends slowly through grain or sand to regulate the movements. The first book is devoted to the movable kind, with a following book on the stationary kind announced.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.de_mensuris: A short Greek treatise on practical mensuration attributed to Hero of Alexandria and transmitted with the Sterometrica in the corpus of works circulating under his name. It opens by distinguishing three kinds of measurement, linear, plane, and solid, and then works through a series of numerical examples: lime pits, wells, square and round stones, timber of square, round, tapered and equilateral cross-section, a raft, a column, a wall, a tympanum, a round shield, a tower, and a vault. Further problems compute the grain capacity of ships in Italian modii and artabas, the load a diver's bell holds in metretai, choes and xestai, and the time two conduits together take to fill a cistern. The arithmetic is carried out in feet, cubits, palms, digits and dry measures, set out step by step after the model of each problem.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.mechanicorum_fragment: A short collection of Greek prose fragments on mechanics transmitted under the name of Hero of Alexandria, an author better known for his treatises on mechanics, optics, and automata. The fragments describe how to move a given weight with a given force by mounting toothed drums on parallel axles inside a frame, as in the machine called the Baroulkos, and work through numerical examples in which a pulling force of a few talents shifts loads of a thousand. They also invoke Archimedes' remark about moving the earth with a lever and refer to the five powers, the wedge, lever, screw, pulley, and wheel-and-axle, whose proofs the text assigns to Hero's Mechanica.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.metrica: A Greek treatise on mensuration by Hero of Alexandria, of uncertain date. The Metrica opens with an account of geometry's origins in the measurement and division of land, recalling the demonstrations of Eudoxus and Archimedes on the sphere, cylinder and cone, and sets out the author's aim of gathering what earlier writers found useful together with his own additions. The opening sections then treat plane measurement, giving methods and worked examples for the areas of rectangles and of right, isosceles and scalene triangles, including a test of whether a triangle's angles are right, acute or obtuse, with results expressed in abstract units rather than in feet or cubits.
grc.heronis_alexandrini.liber_geeponicus_sp: A Greek geometrical manual attributed to Hero of Alexandria, preserved among the remains of his geometrical and stereometrical writings. It opens as a question-and-answer sequence of definitions of plane figures, circle, triangle, quadrilateral, parallelogram, trapezium, together with their parts, such as base, diagonal, perpendicular and parallel lines, before turning to solid figures including the pyramid. The longer second part treats practical mensuration: after deriving measures from parts of the human body (finger, palm, span, foot, cubit, pace, fathom), it works through calculations of areas and diagonals of squares, rectangles and right-angled triangles, with numerical examples in alphabetic Greek notation.
grc.hesiod.works_and_days: The Works and Days is a didactic epic in dactylic hexameters attributed to Hesiod and of uncertain date. Addressed in part to Perses over the division of an inheritance, it argues that Zeus ordains prosperity for the just and hardship for the wicked, and weaves moral instruction with myth, notably the two Strifes, the theft of fire by Prometheus, and the fashioning of Pandora. Later passages supply counsel on farming through the agricultural year, on seafaring and household management, and on days of good and bad omen.
grc.hippocrates.coa_praesagia: Coa Praesagia is a Greek medical treatise of uncertain date, attributed to Hippocrates and transmitted in the Hippocratic Corpus. It consists of short, numbered prognostic judgements arranged in two books, assessing the signs of acute disease, rigors, chills, fevers, sweats, delirium, phrenitis and lethargy among them, and declaring whether the patient will live or die. The pronouncements are compressed and aphoristic in form, often a single clause, and attend closely to the timing of crises, critical days and changes in symptoms such as urine, stools and breathing.
grc.hippocrates.de_alimento: De Alimento ('On Nutriment') is a brief Greek medical treatise of uncertain date, transmitted in the Hippocratic Corpus under Hippocrates' name. Composed in a terse, aphoristic Ionic style, it sets out a general account of nourishment: how food, once assimilated, sustains and alters every part of the body, from flesh, bone, vein, artery, and nerve to marrow, brain, and spinal cord, and how its powers act for harm or benefit according to dose, mixture, and the body's nature. The treatise ranges over growth and wasting, the unity and common sympathy of the body's parts, natural and unnatural discharges, signs of disease, and the channels by which nutriment and pneuma reach the whole frame, ending with the liver and heart as the roots of the veins and arteries.
grc.hippocrates.de_arte: De Arte ('On the Art') is a Greek prose treatise of the Hippocratic corpus, transmitted under the name of Hippocrates and of uncertain date. It is an argumentative defence of medicine against detractors who disparage the arts, contending that medicine is a genuine technē whose workings are evident even in recoveries achieved without a physician, and that success cannot be ascribed to mere chance. The author defines medicine as the relief of the sick from the weariness of disease and the dulling of its violence, together with the refusal to treat those already overpowered by their illness, and closes by arguing that dietetic and other measures as much as drugs bear witness to the art's ordered method.
grc.hippocrates.de_genitura: De Genitura (On Generation) is a short Greek medical treatise of the Hippocratic Corpus, transmitted under Hippocrates' name and of uncertain date. It sets out the pangenesis doctrine that seed is secreted from the strongest portion of all the body's moisture and travels through the veins and spinal marrow, using this account to explain nocturnal emissions, the infertility of eunuchs, and the absence of seed in children and virgins. Further sections treat female pleasure and emission during intercourse, the mingling of male and female seed in the womb at conception, and the determination of the child's sex by the relative strength of the two kinds of seed, each parent containing both male and female. The treatise also names the four humours, blood, bile, water, and phlegm, as the forms of moisture in the body from which diseases arise.
grc.hippocrates.de_humoribus: De Humoribus (On Humours) is a very short Greek medical treatise attributed to Hippocrates and of uncertain date. Written in dense, list-like prose, it sets out the colours and movements of the humours, the directions in which evacuations and purgings should be guided, and the signs by which disease, crisis, and the settling of humours in the body are to be judged. Later sections catalogue symptoms, discharges, dreams, foods, and drugs in relation to critical days and the timing of treatment, closing with brief remarks on where humours deposit themselves in fevers, including a passing reference to coughing patients at Perinthus.
grc.hippocrates.de_liquidorum_usu: De Liquidorum Usu ('On the Use of Liquids') is a brief Greek medical treatise of uncertain date transmitted in the Hippocratic Corpus under Hippocrates' name. In four short chapters it takes up the therapeutic employment of liquids, distinguishing potable water, sea water and vinegar and setting out the effects of hot and cold applications on the body. It discusses the proper degree of heat in washing and pouring over wounds, the parts of the body that tolerate heat and cold, and the uses of sea water and vinegar for sores, burns, skin conditions and disorders of the ears, nails and eyes. The prose is the terse Ionic Greek characteristic of the collection.
grc.hippocrates.de_natura_hominis: De Natura Hominis ('On the Nature of Man') is a Greek medical treatise attributed to Hippocrates. Its opening chapters reject monist accounts of human nature, whether those identifying man with a single element such as air, fire, water or earth, or physicians who hold that man is blood, phlegm or bile alone. The author instead maintains that the body contains four humours, blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile, whose balanced mixture in quantity and power constitutes health, while the separation or excess of any one of them produces disease. Drawing on human generation, the variety of illnesses and the effects of drugs and wounds, the treatise argues that these humours are distinct, permanent components of the human constitution.
grc.hippocrates.de_salubri_diaeta: De Salubri Diaeta ('On a Salubrious Diet') is a brief Greek dietetic treatise attributed to Hippocrates and transmitted in the Hippocratic Corpus, of uncertain date. It opens with seasonal prescriptions for laypersons, enjoining heavier eating and unmixed wine in winter, softer foods and diluted drink in summer, and gradual transitions between the seasons. Further sections adjust regimen to bodily type and age, prescribe walking, bathing and clothing, and give programmes for losing or gaining weight. The treatise then regulates the seasonal use of emetics and enemas and closes with directions for the bathing and diet of infants and of women.
grc.hippocrates.praeceptiones: Praeceptiones (Precepts) is a short Greek medical treatise attributed to Hippocrates and of uncertain date. It opens with reflections on time (chronos) and opportunity (kairos) in treatment and on the relation of reason to perception, memory, and accumulated experience, arguing that medicine rests on trained practice and observation rather than on plausible argument alone. The remaining sections offer practical counsel to the physician: to learn even from laypersons and from colleagues called in consultation, to behave with tact and humanity in matters of fees and toward poor or foreign patients, and to shun rivalry and boastfulness, with censure of ignorant practitioners who exploit the sick.
grc.hippocrates.prognosticon: A Greek medical treatise of the Hippocratic Corpus, attributed to Hippocrates and of uncertain date, commonly cited under its Latin title Prognosticon ('Prognostic'). Its opening argues that the best physician is one who practices prognosis, foretelling from the patient's present condition the past, present, and future course of a disease, so that the sick will entrust themselves to the physician, who, knowing in advance who will die and who will survive, can treat without blame. The remainder sets out the observable signs in acute diseases by which recovery or death may be predicted: the facial appearance and the eyes, the patient's posture and involuntary habits such as grinding the teeth or picking at the bedclothes, the character of the breathing, and the different kinds of sweat, both favorable and fatal.
grc.hippocrates.vectiarius: A brief Greek surgical treatise of the Hippocratic Corpus, transmitted under Hippocrates' name and of uncertain date, known by the Latinized title Vectiarius. It opens with an anatomical account of the bones and their articulations, covering the digits, hand, foot, leg, thigh, spine, ribs, sternum, clavicles, shoulder blade, and upper arm. The remainder treats injuries in sequence: the setting of a broken rib, a fractured ear, dislocation of the jaw, and dislocation of the shoulder, giving diagnostic signs and a range of reduction manoeuvres involving leverage, traction, and positioning, together with bandaging and aftercare.
grc.isidore_of_charax.mansiones_parthicae: The Mansiones Parthicae (Stathmoi Parthikoi, 'Parthian Stages') is a brief Greek itinerary of uncertain date attributed to Isidore of Charax. It sets out the overland route across the Parthian empire stage by stage, from the crossing of the Euphrates at Zeugma through Mesopotamia and Babylonia, Media, and the Caspian Gates to Hyrcania, Parthia, Aria, and Arachosia, giving distances in schoinoi and naming the cities, villages, fortresses, royal residences, temples, and treasuries encountered along the way. Several stations are identified as Greek or Macedonian foundations, among them Niciphorion, Doura Nicanoros, and Alexandreia, the metropolis of Arachosia. A fragment quoted from Athenaeus, in which Isidore's Periegētikē of Parthia describes a pearl-bearing island in the Persian Sea, is appended after the itinerary.
grc.isocrates.letters: A collection of nine short letters in classical Attic prose attributed to Isocrates. Most are cast as epistles of counsel addressed to rulers and dynasts: the opening letter urges a powerful addressee, at war with Carthage while Spartan supremacy recedes, to weigh the safety of the Greeks and the perils of rash boldness against the pursuit of martial glory. The letters reflect on the limits of advising in writing rather than in person, on the difference between flatterers and honest counsellors, and on the conditions under which a death in battle brings honour rather than disgrace.
grc.libanius.declamations: Greek prose declamations by Libanius, consisting of fictional speeches composed for rhetorical display and training. The opening speech is a defence of Socrates, delivered by an imagined friend who pleads before the Athenian jury against the charges of Meletus, Anytus, and Lycon and urges an acquittal grounded in justice and the jurors' oath. The collection follows the conventions of sophistic declamation, casting invented personae in courtroom crises drawn from classical Athenian history.
grc.libanius.orations: Orations by Libanius, the Greek rhetorician who styles himself a citizen of great and famous Antioch, collected here as a corpus of prose speeches. The collection opens with an autobiographical oration in which the author sets out to correct both those who pronounce him the most fortunate and those who pronounce him the most wretched of men, recounting his family's wealth and losses, his upbringing by a widowed mother, his early love of letters, and the recurring headaches that marked his youth. In the course of the narrative he describes his training under successive sophists, his devotion to rhetoric, and the fortunes of his life as a teacher and man of letters.
grc.libanius.orations_1-11: Orations 1-11 gathers the opening speeches of Libanius, a Greek rhetorician of Antioch, printed here from Richard Foerster's Teubner edition. The first oration is his autobiography, in which he corrects those who call him either the most fortunate or the most wretched of men by narrating his family history at Antioch, his orphaned childhood, and his ardour for the study of rhetoric. Because Libanius frames his life through allusion to earlier Greek literature, citing Aristophanes' Acharnians outright and recalling his memorization of the ancient orators, the autobiography offers rich pickings for readers tracing intertextual parallels.
grc.lucian.abdicatus: The Abdicatus is a short Greek speech by Lucian, cast as a defence delivered before judges by a young man whom his father has disowned for a second time. The speaker, a physician, recounts how his father first cast him off, how he then went abroad and studied medicine, and how on his return he alone recognised and cured the parent's madness; publicly restored and forgiven, he now faces renewed expulsion for refusing to obey the recovered father in matters his art cannot comply with. The speech rehearses the earlier quarrels, the details of the cure, the father's formal revocation of the disinheritance, and the resentment the reconciliation aroused among certain onlookers.
grc.lucian.adversus_indoctum_et_libros_multo: A short Greek satire by Lucian of Samosata, transmitted under the Latin title Adversus Indoctum et Libros Multos Ementem ('Against an Uneducated Man Who Buys Many Books'). A speaker rebukes a wealthy ignoramus who amasses fine old volumes, buying whatever booksellers praise, and argues that mere ownership of books is no proof of education. The argument proceeds through a series of analogies, an unskilled possessor of Timotheus' auloi or of Heracles' bow, a pilot without seamanship, a rider with a splendid horse, and closes with the proverbs of the ape with golden coin, the ass listening to the lyre, and the dog in the bath-house. The comic effect is heightened by the interlocutor, who answers the interrogation only with nods.
grc.lucian.anacharsis: The Anacharsis is a short Greek dialogue by Lucian of Samosata in which the Scythian sage Anacharsis questions the Athenian lawgiver Solon about the athletic training he has witnessed in the gymnasium of Apollo Lyceus. Perplexed by youths who strangle, kick and roll one another in mud and dust, Anacharsis asks what good such exercises do, and Solon replies by describing the disciplines of wrestling, boxing and the pankration, the great festivals of Olympia, Isthmia, Nemea, Delphi and the Panathenaia with their prizes of crowns, sheep and olive oil, and the glory that awaits the victor. The exchange proceeds entirely between the two speakers, closing with Solon's invitation to Anacharsis to attend the festivals and see the vast crowds and the near-divine honours accorded to successful athletes.
grc.lucian.bacchus: A short Greek prose piece by Lucian of Samosata, the Bacchus presents a speaker's retelling of Dionysus' mythic campaign against the Indians. It dwells on the grotesque appearance of the Bacchic host, a beardless commander drawn by leopards, drunken Silenus on his donkey, goat-legged dancing soldiers, and maenads with thyrsi, the Indians' initial contempt for such a force, and their panic-stricken rout once the god sets their land ablaze. The speaker then turns the episode into an analogy for the reception of his own new kind of discourse, which hearers expect to be merely comic, and closes with an account of a walled Dionysiac grove among the Machlian Indians, where three springs named for Silenus, Pan, and the Satyrs are drunk each year by celebrants according to their age.
grc.lucian.calumniae_non_temere_credundum: A short Greek prose essay by Lucian of Samosata, transmitted under the Latin title Calumniae non temere credendum ('On Slander, or That It Should Not Be Readily Believed').
