The work opens with reflections on the havoc wrought by ignorance and hearsay, illustrated through the story of the painter Apelles, falsely accused of conspiracy before Ptolemy, who afterwards depicted Calumny in an allegorical painting peopled with figures such as Ignorance, Suspicion, Envy, Fraud, Repentance, and Truth. The remainder defines slander as an accusation made in the absence of the accused and examines in turn the three parties to it, the slanderer, the slandered, and the listener, showing how belief in it may be guarded against.
grc.lucian.cataplus: A short Greek comic dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, of uncertain date, whose title denotes the voyage down to Hades; it runs to only twenty-eight lines and is presented here from Karl Jacobitz's Teubner edition of 1896. The scene is set at the edge of the underworld, where Clotho and Charon chafe at delays while Hermes drives down a flock of the newly dead, including a tyrant who has tried to slip away from his allotted fate. With its cast of Clotho, Charon, Hermes, and Aeacus, the piece turns the traditional furniture of the descent to Hades, the ferryman's obol, the counting of souls, the thread of the Fates, into farce at the expense of the reluctant dead. Its compact parody of underworld convention makes it a useful touchstone for readers tracing Charon scenes and katabasis motifs across ancient and later literature.
grc.lucian.de_domo: A short Greek prose piece attributed to Lucian, transmitted under the title De Domo ('On a House'), is a rhetorical exercise defending the delivery of formal speeches in praise of a splendid building. The speaker holds that a cultivated viewer who meets a beautiful hall with silence is a philistine, and that settings of great beauty naturally call forth eloquence, adducing Alexander's longing to bathe in the Cydnus and Socrates' conversation by the Ilissus as instances. The argument proceeds to praise the proportions, light, and judicious use of gold in the house, contrasting them with the ostentatious but artless luxury of the Persian kings, and closes with the figure of the modest woman who wears gold only in measured ornament.
grc.lucian.de_luctu: De Luctu ('On Mourning') is a short Greek satirical piece by Lucian of Samosata. Its speaker surveys the picture of the underworld held by the many on the authority of Homer, Hesiod and the other mythmakers, the realm of Pluto and Persephone, its rivers and the Acherusian lake, Cerberus, the judgements of Minos and Rhadamanthus, Elysium and the punishments of the wicked, and then turns to the funeral customs practised in consequence, from placing an obol in the dead man's mouth to the washing, anointing, crowning and noisy lamentation of the corpse. The piece argues throughout that such beliefs and rites rest on mere custom and inherited opinion rather than on any sure knowledge of what befalls the dead.
grc.lucian.de_mercede: De Mercede, a short Greek satirical dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, is an admonition addressed to Timocles against accepting paid posts as companion to wealthy patrons. The speaker catalogues the indignities of such salaried friendships, likening the patron's favour to a baited hook and the dependent's situation to that of a shipwrecked sailor; recipients of pay, he says, are bound to endure whatever the rich may inflict. The argument extends beyond philosophers to grammarians, rhetoricians, and musicians who live by paid attendance, holding that such dependence is most shameful for the cultivated.
grc.lucian.de_sacrificiis: A brief satirical essay in Greek by Lucian of Samosata, the second-century CE rhetorician and satirist. It mocks the anthropomorphic piety of traditional cult, arguing that a religion in which gods need offerings, sulk when slighted, and sell their favours for hecatombs makes them less than noble. To make the point it rehearses mythic exempla drawn largely from Homer and the poets: Artemis's vengeance on Oeneus, Chryses' bargaining with Apollo, Apollo's servitude to Admetus and Laomedon, Zeus's overthrow of Cronus and his many amours, the births of Athena and Dionysus, the lameness of Hephaestus, and Prometheus chained on the Caucasus.
grc.lucian.de_saltatione: A Greek dialogue by Lucian of Samosata in which Lycinus answers Crato's attack on theatrical dancing as an effeminate and frivolous spectacle. Lycinus defends the art by tracing dance back to the primal harmony of the cosmos, arguing for its high antiquity and for its power, through music, rhythm and mime, to delight and instruct its audiences. The exchange combines comic banter at Crato's expense with an encomiastic account of dancing and the dancer's craft.
grc.lucian.de_syria_dea: De Syria Dea is a short Greek prose work by Lucian, composed in the Ionic dialect and cast as the first-person report of an Assyrian narrator recounting what he has seen himself and learned from priests. It describes the holy city of Hierapolis near the Euphrates and its temple of the Syrian goddess, covering the origin of the city's name, the cult statues that sweat, move, and utter prophecies, the rites, festivals, and sacrifices performed there, and the offerings and revenues that flow in from Arabia, Phoenicia, Babylonia, Cappadocia, and Cilicia. The account also ranges over the older sanctuaries of Syria and Phoenicia, taking in the Heracles at Tyre, the temple of Astarte at Sidon, the mourning and rites of Adonis at Byblos, the annual reddening of the river Adonis, and the ancient foundation of Aphrodite on Lebanon.
grc.lucian.deorum_consilium: A short satirical dialogue in Greek by Lucian of Samosata, in which Zeus convenes an assembly of the gods to hear complaints that unworthy mortals are being admitted to divine honours. Hermes acts as herald, and Momus, styling himself a free-speaking public accuser, denounces the apotheosis of Dionysus together with his retinue of Pan, Silenus and the Satyrs, and enumerates further cases including Ariadne, Erigone and her dog. Zeus forbids mention of Asclepius and Heracles, but Momus ends by attacking Zeus himself, charging the king of the gods with peopling heaven through his amours with mortal women.
grc.lucian.dialogi_marini: The Dialogi Marini ('Dialogues of the Sea') is a group of short dramatic dialogues in Greek by Lucian, cast as conversations among sea gods, Nereids, and other figures of myth. The opening pieces present Doris mocking Galatea over her monstrous suitor the Cyclops Polyphemus, the blinded Polyphemus complaining to his father Poseidon about Odysseus' escape from his cave, and Poseidon questioning the river-god Alpheus about his love for the Sicilian spring Arethusa. Familiar mythological episodes are retold in colloquial spoken exchanges with a light satirical touch.
grc.lucian.dialogi_mortuorum: A collection of brief comic dialogues set among the dead, written in Greek by Lucian. Its scenes stage conversations between underworld figures, Diogenes and Menippus among the Cynics, Pluto, the wealthy kings Croesus, Midas and Sardanapallus, the seers Trophonius and Amphilochus, and assorted plutocrats and philosophers, as they mock the riches, beauty and wisdom that death has stripped from them and ridicule those who still cling to such things. In the opening dialogue Diogenes dispatches Polydeuces to the upper world to summon Menippus and to carry messages of derision to the rich, the powerful, the beautiful and the quarrelsome wise.
grc.lucian.dipsades: The Dipsades is a short prose piece in Greek by Lucian of Samosata, cast as a speaker's descriptive address to an audience. It surveys the scorched sands of southern Libya and the tent-dwelling Garamantes who hunt there, then catalogues the region's serpents and scorpions, dwelling at length on the dipsas, whose bite inflicts a thirst no quantity of drink can quench. A funerary epigram likening the sufferer to Tantalus and the Danaids is quoted, and the piece closes by comparing the audience's appetite for the speaker's own words to the victim's unslakable thirst, with a nod to Plato's dictum that there is no satiety of the good.
grc.lucian.electrum: A short Greek prose dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, preserved under the title Electrum. The speaker recounts how, having believed the poets' tale that the poplars on the river Eridanus still weep drops of amber in mourning for Phaethon, he sailed there hoping to gather the gem, only to be laughed at by local boatmen who know nothing of Phaethon, weeping poplars, or the melodious swans he also expects to find. The closing lines reflect on the deceptions of poets who magnify everything, and the speaker disclaims any such promise of treasures in his own plain, myth-free discourse, warning his listeners against hoping for more than it contains.
grc.lucian.eunuchus: A short Greek dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, cast as a conversation in which Lycinus recounts to Pamphilus a lawsuit he witnessed between rival philosophers. The case concerned succession to a yearly stipend paid by the king to philosophers of the Stoic, Platonic, Epicurean, and Peripatetic schools, and was contested between Diocles the elder, a disputatious older philosopher, and Bagoas, a eunuch who styled himself a philosopher. Diocles sought to disqualify Bagoas from philosophy and from sacred and civic honors altogether, arguing that a eunuch was neither man nor woman but a mixed and monstrous creature, and the exchange dwells on the defenders Bagoas musters and the judges' debate over whether a eunuch may deserve philosophical office.
grc.lucian.gallus: A short comic dialogue in Greek by Lucian of Samosata, in which the poor cobbler Micyllus curses his rooster for crowing before dawn and rousing him from a dream of wealth, only to have the bird answer him in human speech. The cock explains that a keeper of Ares was changed into a rooster for failing to announce the sun's rising during the god's liaison with Aphrodite, and then reveals that he is the reincarnated soul of Pythagoras. Their conversation touches on metempsychosis and the claims of philosophical wisdom, with running jokes against Pythagorean taboos such as silence and abstinence from beans.
grc.lucian.harmonides: The Harmonides is a short Greek dialogue by Lucian of Samosata. The aulos-player Harmonides asks his teacher Timotheus how he may win glory through his art, and Timotheus answers that the praise of a few expert judges, rather than the acclamation of the crowd, secures an artist's fame, illustrating the point with the death of Harmonides himself, who expired uncrowned at his first contest in the Dionysia. A closing section, spoken by a first-person narrator, generalises the lesson to all who seek public renown and applies it to the speaker's own ambition for literary reputation, ending with an appeal for the favourable verdict of a single authoritative judge.
grc.lucian.hercules: A short Greek prose piece by Lucian of Samosata in the form of an ecphrasis, describing a painting among the Celts in which Hercules, called Ogmios in the native tongue, appears as a decrepit old man drawing a crowd of willing followers by fine chains of gold and amber that run from their ears to his pierced tongue. A cultivated Celt in the narrative explains the image as an allegory of eloquence, identifying the god with the power of persuasive speech, which alone displays its full strength in old age. The closing section turns personal, as the speaker invokes the aged Hercules to justify his resumption of public lecturing and rhetorical display despite his own advanced years.
grc.lucian.hermotimus: A short Greek satirical dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, in which Lycinus gently quizzes his friend Hermotimus about the twenty years of study and toil he has devoted to following his philosophical teacher up the long, steep road towards virtue and happiness. Beneath the banter lies an ironic assault on the philosophical schools, whose professors promise an ascent to blessedness that no pupil can ever be sure of completing within a lifetime. Readers hunting parallels will find the exchange thick with allusion, reworking Hesiod's rough uphill path to Virtue, Homer's golden chain let down by Zeus, and the Coan physician's maxim that life is short while art is long.
grc.lucian.hippias: A short Greek prose piece attributed to Lucian of Samosata, cast as an encomium. It opens by praising sages whose deeds matched their verbal undertakings, citing physicians, musicians, and generals such as Agamemnon and Achilles, together with engineers and thinkers, Archimedes, Sosistratus of Cnidus, Thales, and Epeius, who left lasting memorials of their skill. The argument then turns to a contemporary figure, Hippias, presented as preeminent alike in mechanics, geometry, optics, harmonics, and music. The bulk of the work describes the public bathhouse Hippias designed, from the levelling of the sloping site and its foundations through the propylaeum, changing rooms, and successive cold, warm, and hot chambers, noting the stones, statues of Hygieia and Asclepius, lighting, and orientation of each room to sun and wind.
grc.lucian.iudicium_vocalium: A short comic piece in Greek by Lucian of Samosata, cast as a case heard under the archon Aristarchus of Phalerum. The letter Sigma prosecutes the letter Tau before the seven vowels sitting as judges, charging it with forcibly usurping the sounds that belong to Sigma and wronging the other letters besides. The mock-forensic speech turns on Attic spellings in which tt supplants ss, kitta for kissa, Thettalia for Thessalia, basilitta for basilissa, and closes with brief laments from Delta, Theta and Zeta over losses to the same defendant. The prose parodies the diction of Athenian courtroom oratory throughout.
grc.lucian.iuppiter_confuatus: A short Greek dialogue attributed to Lucian of Samosata, in which Zeus is cross-examined by the Cynic Cyniscus about fate and the gods' power over it. Drawing on Homer and Hesiod, the interlocutor asks whether all things are fixed by the Moirai, Heimarmene, and Tyche, whether anything can escape the thread of Clotho, and why humans sacrifice and pray if the gods themselves are bound by necessity. Zeus's increasingly uneasy answers lead to the closing suggestion that gods and men are alike slaves of the Fates, spinning eternally on their spindle.
grc.lucian.iuppiter_tragoedus: Iuppiter Tragoedus (Zeus the Tragedian) is a short comic dialogue in Greek by Lucian of Samosata. Zeus, pale and distracted, confides to Hermes and the other gods that the Stoic Timocles and the Epicurean Damis have been publicly disputing over providence, leaving the gods' honours and even their existence at stake, and the divinities resolve to hold an assembly to decide what should be done. In a style that mixes comic and tragic diction, Hermes is coached to summon the gods with a grand Homeric proclamation, and the assembled deities, seated by the material and craftsmanship of their statues, debate the threat posed by the philosophers' arguments.
grc.lucian.marcrobii: A short Greek prose piece attributed to Lucian, framed as a gift of 'long-lived men' offered to a Quintillus in obedience to a dream. After collecting proverbial examples of great age from Homer and tragedy, together with long-lived peoples and sages such as the Egyptian priests, the Indian Brahmans and the Magi, it proceeds to a catalogue of individuals famed for extreme longevity, arranged by occupations and beginning with kings and generals. Named examples include Numa Pompilius and other Roman kings, Arganthonius of Tartessus, Agathocles, Hiero of Syracuse and the Scythian Ateas, each with his reported lifespan and the source of the report. The piece breaks off unfinished in the middle of a list of Balkan rulers.
grc.lucian.muscae_encomium: The Muscae Encomium, or praise of the fly, is a brief Greek prose piece attributed to Lucian of Samosata and of uncertain date, in the tradition of mock encomia that celebrate trivial subjects as if they were worthy of high praise. The speaker catalogues the fly's anatomy, its delicate wings, and its bloodsucking proboscis, traces its growth from worm to winged insect, and praises its boldness, citing Homer's likening of heroic courage and of Athena to a fly. It goes on to treat the fly's revival from its own ashes when dust is sprinkled upon them as proof that the soul is immortal, a proof said to have been overlooked by Plato, and closes with an account of the fly's idle life, feeding at tables prepared by others.
grc.lucian.navigium: Navigium (The Ship) is a brief Greek dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, cast as a conversation between Timolaus, Lycinus and Samippus after they have viewed an enormous Alexandrian grain ship moored at the Piraeus. The speakers recall the vessel's colossal dimensions, its gilded goose ornament, Isis figureheads and crowded crew, together with an elderly helmsman of famed skill. Adeimantus of Myrrhinous, lost among the spectators, frames the opening exchange, and the dialogue closes with the shipmaster's account of storms off Chelidoniae and a nearly fatal voyage.
grc.lucian.necyomantia: A short Greek comic dialogue attributed to the satirist Lucian of Samosata, in which Menippus is met on his return from the lower world and questioned about his unexpected journey to Hades. He explains that the contradictory lessons of Homer, Hesiod and the philosophers, who preached one way of life and lived another, drove him to descend and consult the Theban seer Teiresias for a plain rule of living. In answer he recounts the motive for his descent, what he saw and heard below, and the oracle and decrees issued against the rich. Menippus speaks largely in rhapsodised hexameter verse, having lately consorted with Homer and Euripides, while his friend replies in iambic trimeters and repeatedly calls him back to plain prose.
grc.lucian.philopseudes: Philopseudes ('The Lover of Lies') is a comic dialogue in Greek by Lucian, framed as a conversation between Tychiades and Philocles on why people delight in lying for its own sake. After discussing the falsehoods of poets, historians, and cities' foundation stories, Tychiades recounts a visit to the ailing philosopher Eucrates, where a company of philosophers, a physician, and other acquaintances exchange tales of ghosts, sorcerers, and other marvels. The dialogue contrasts the speaker's exasperated rationalism with the credulous storytelling of the men gathered around Eucrates' sickbed.
grc.lucian.pro_imaginibus: A short Greek dialogue by Lucian, in which a woman addressing Lycinus takes issue with the flattery of an earlier written portrait of her, objecting above all to having been likened to Hera and Aphrodite. She recounts anecdotes of extravagant praise, a poet celebrating a bald woman's hair, sitters who commission painters to beautify their features, and argues that such comparisons with goddesses border on impiety, citing the fate of Cassiopeia. Lycinus is accordingly instructed to recast the offending passages, and the piece closes with the story of Alexander, who refused an architect's promise to reshape Mount Athos into his image.
grc.lucian.prometheus: A short Greek comic dialogue by Lucian of Samosata in which Hephaestus and Hermes escort the Titan Prometheus to Mount Caucasus to fasten him to a crag as punishment for cheating Zeus in the division of sacrificial meat, fashioning humankind, and stealing fire. Prometheus protests his innocence, and the scene turns into a parody of courtroom procedure, with the pair cataloguing his offenses while he answers them in the manner of a professional sophist. The exchange ends before the eagle that is to feed on Prometheus's liver makes its appearance.
grc.lucian.prometheus_es_in_verbis: A short Greek piece by Lucian of Samosata, transmitted under the Latin title Prometheus Es in Verbis ('Prometheus in Words'), cast as a speech of self-defence. The speaker, charged with being a second Prometheus because he has moulded works of his own, answers that his clay is humbler than the Titan's and that praise of their cleverness may be only Attic irony. An anecdote about Ptolemy son of Lagus exhibiting a black Bactrian camel and a half-black, half-white man in Egypt illustrates that novelty alone fails to please, since audiences judge by harmony and beauty. The piece ends by weighing whether the speaker's fusion of dialogue and comedy has produced something deformed, like the centaur, or agreeable, like wine mixed with honey.
grc.lucian.saturnalia: A short comic Greek dialogue by Lucian in which Cronos is questioned about the Saturnalia. The interlocutor first asks the god for wealth, and Cronos explains that his kingship lasts only seven days, granting licence for feasting, dice-playing, mockery, and the temporary equality of slaves and masters, while riches remain in Zeus's gift. Cronos then rebuts the stories, ascribed to Hesiod and Homer, that he devoured his children and was deposed and bound in Tartarus, insisting that he surrendered the throne voluntarily in old age and recalling the spontaneous abundance of his own reign.
grc.lucian.soleocista: A short comic Greek dialogue of uncertain date, attributed to Lucian, on the catching of solecisms. Two interlocutors test one another's ability to spot grammatical errors, with one speaker slipping a series of solecisms past the other unnoticed and the exchange turning on the difficulty of recognizing faulty Greek in practice. It closes with recollections of a Socrates of Mopsus whom the speaker met in Egypt, whose unfailingly witty and unoffensive corrections of solecisms and Atticisms are illustrated through a long string of examples.
grc.lucian.symposium: A Greek satirical dialogue by Lucian, cast as a conversation in which Lycinus describes to Philo a wedding banquet hosted by Aristaenetus, at which philosophers of the Stoic, Epicurean, Peripatetic, and Platonic schools drink, boast, and dispute until the party ends in a brawl. The frame dialogue gives way to Lycinus' extended narrative of the guests, their seating, their drunken speeches and toasts, and the escalating disorder of the evening. Named figures include the Stoic Zenothemis, the Epicurean Hermon, the Peripatetic Cleodemus, and the Platonist Ion, whose conduct at the feast supplies the comedy.
grc.lucian.zeuxis: A brief Greek prose piece by Lucian of Samosata, here spanning only a dozen lines in Jacobitz's Teubner text, in which the speaker answers admirers who praise nothing in his writing but its novelty. To make his case he recalls the painter Zeuxis, who scorned conventional subjects such as gods, heroes, and battles and instead dared to depict a female centaur nursing twin infants, and offers a lively description of a copy of that picture then in Athens, the original having been lost at sea while being shipped to Italy by Sulla. The paired defence of artistic and literary originality, together with allusions such as Homer's 'new song', makes the piece a compact witness both to Lucian's self-fashioning as a stylist and to the ancient anecdotal tradition surrounding Zeuxis' lost art.
grc.nicomachus_of_gerasa.excerpta: A brief Greek collection of excerpts on music theory attributed to Nicomachus of Gerasa and of uncertain date. It opens with the mythical history of the lyre, recounting its invention by Hermes and its transmission through Orpheus, Linus, Amphion, and Terpander. Subsequent sections give numerical demonstrations of the intervals of the fourth and fifth, computing them through epogdoic and other ratios, and conclude with a discussion assigning the string names hypate, mese, and nete, together with the remaining strings, to the planets and other celestial bodies.
grc.nicomachus_of_gerasa.ἐγχειρίδιον_ἁρμονικ: A brief Greek treatise on harmonics by Nicomachus of Gerasa, composed as a compact epistolary summary that the author promises to follow with a larger and more exact introduction. It opens with a set of twelve chapter headings and then discusses, chapter by chapter, the continuous and intervallic kinds of the voice and their ranges, the derivation of the names of the notes from the seven planets, the numerical ratios governing the notes, Pythagoras' addition of the eighth string to the seven-stringed lyre to complete the octave harmony, the diatonic division of the octave, the harmonic teaching of Plato's Timaeus, and a proof drawn from Philolaus. The closing chapters treat the fitting of the notes by arithmetic ratios across the double octave and its progression through the three genera of notes.
grc.nonnus_of_panopolis.dionysiaca: The Dionysiaca is a lengthy Greek epic in dactylic hexameters attributed to Nonnus of Panopolis and of uncertain date, recounting the birth and career of the god Dionysus. The opening invocation calls for song of the god's double birth, rescued from the fire and sewn into Zeus's thigh after the death of Semele, before turning to the tale of Cadmus and the carrying-off of Europa by Zeus in the form of a bull. Across its books the poem follows Dionysus's wanderings and conquests, including his war against the Indians, told in an ornate manner dense with mythological episode and elaborate compound diction.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_galatas: The Epistle to the Galatians is a Greek prose letter of the New Testament, composed at some point in the Roman imperial era and attributed to Paul the Apostle, who writes to the Christian communities of Galatia. Alarmed that the Galatians are turning to a different gospel, Paul opens with a rebuke followed by an autobiographical defense of his apostolic calling, recounting his former persecution of the church, his commissioning through revelation, and his confrontation with Peter at Antioch. The letter's central argument maintains that Gentiles are justified by faith in Christ rather than by works of the law, supported by the example of Abraham and the promise made to his seed. Its later chapters include the allegory of Hagar and Sarah, exhortations to walk by the Spirit rather than gratify the flesh, a catalogue of ethical duties, and closing personal greetings.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_philippenses: The Epistle to the Philippians is a Greek prose letter preserved in the New Testament, opening in the names of Paul and Timothy and addressed to the Christian community at Philippi together with its bishops and deacons; its date of composition is uncertain. Written from the standpoint of imprisonment, the letter combines thanksgiving and news of the writer's circumstances with exhortations to unity, humility, and steadfastness. Notable passages include a hymnic account of Christ's self-emptying and exaltation, an autobiographical review of the writer's Jewish credentials, warnings against rival teachers, and commendations of Timothy and Epaphroditus, closing with calls to rejoice in the Lord.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_thessalonicenses_ii: The Second Letter to the Thessalonians is a New Testament epistle in Greek, written in prose during the Imperial era and attributed in its opening to Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, who address the church of the Thessalonians. The letter gives thanks for the recipients' growing faith and endurance amid persecution and teaches that the day of the Lord will not come until the apostasy and the revelation of the 'man of lawlessness,' a figure whose coming works through Satan and whom the Lord will destroy at his appearing. It then urges the addressees to stand firm in the traditions they were taught, commands that anyone living in idleness and disorder be shunned so as to be put to shame, and closes with a greeting in Paul's own hand and a blessing of peace and grace.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_titum: The Epistle to Titus is a book of the New Testament, a Greek prose letter of the Imperial era presented as from Paul the Apostle to Titus, whom the writer says he has left in Crete to put matters in order there. The letter directs Titus to appoint elders and bishops of blameless character, sets out how older men and women, younger people, and slaves should conduct themselves, and urges rejection of foolish controversies, genealogies, and divisive heretics after repeated warnings. It also reflects on salvation through God's grace rather than righteous deeds and closes with plans to send Artemas or Tychicus, a request that Titus join the writer at Nicopolis, arrangements for Zenas and Apollos, and final greetings.
grc.novum_testamentum.lucas: The Gospel according to Luke (κατὰ Λουκᾶν εὐαγγέλιον) is a Greek prose narrative of the life and ministry of Jesus that forms part of the New Testament, written in the Imperial period and attributed to Luke. It opens with a preface dedicated to one Theophilus, followed by accounts of the announcements and births of John the Baptist and Jesus, including the annunciations to Zechariah and Mary, the Magnificat, and the birth and naming of John. The work proceeds through Jesus's teaching and activity in Galilee and Judea to his passion, death, and resurrection.
grc.novum_testamentum.petri_ii: The Second Epistle of Peter is a New Testament epistle in koine Greek prose, ascribed in its opening verse to Simeon Peter and of uncertain date within the Roman imperial period. The first chapter urges its recipients to cultivate faith, virtue, and knowledge, appeals to the apostle's eyewitness of the Transfiguration, and affirms the divine origin of prophecy. The second chapter denounces false teachers, illustrating coming judgment with the fallen angels, the flood, Sodom and Gomorrah, and Balaam, while the third answers scoffers who doubt the return of Christ, insisting that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years.
grc.orphica.fragmenta: A short collection of Greek fragments and testimonia attributed to Orpheus and the Orphic poets, preserved as quotations in Plato, Aristotle, Aelian, Tatian and other ancient authors. The excerpts concern theogonic matters such as the marriage of Oceanus and Tethys and the rule of Night, together with the origin and wanderings of the soul, the body as tomb or prison, Orphic books used in rites of purification and initiation, and the hymns of Orpheus and Thamyris. Their date and authorship are uncertain, and ancient witnesses themselves dispute whether the verses were Orpheus' own work or were later compiled, for instance by Onomacritus.
grc.paradoxographus_florentinus.mirabilia_de: A brief Greek collection in the paradoxographical tradition, the work of an anonymous compiler conventionally designated the Florentine Paradoxographer, of uncertain date. Its entries catalogue springs, lakes and rivers, from Greece, Italy and Sicily to Persia, Ethiopia and Arabia, credited with extraordinary properties, among them waters that drive horses mad, cure wounds, petrify the drinker, induce loathing of wine or make hair and teeth fall out, together with floating islands and springs that fill spontaneously with oil. The notices are mostly a sentence or two long, frequently close with an appeal to a named source such as Isigonus, Ctesias, Aristotle, Theopompus or Hellanicus, and a few quote epigrams said to be inscribed at the waters themselves.
grc.phalaridis_epistulae.epistulae: A collection of Greek prose letters attributed to Phalaris, the tyrant of Acragas, of uncertain date. Written in the tyrant's own voice, the letters address civic communities such as the Leontines and Tauromenitans as well as private correspondents, and take up matters of war, ransom, diplomacy, and personal conduct. Their tone mixes menace, reproach, and gruff magnanimity: Phalaris threatens adversaries, spares a captive, consoles a bereaved father, and sends horses and gifts to friends.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_abrahamo: De Abrahamo, a Greek treatise by the Hellenistic Jewish writer Philo Judaeus, belongs to his sequence of works expounding the Mosaic law. After a preface on the five books of the holy laws and the pre-eminence of Genesis, it presents the patriarchs as 'living laws' whose biographies embody the virtues, treating Enos as a figure of hope and Enoch of repentance. The work then takes up Abraham himself, retelling the Genesis narrative of his migration from Chaldea, his faith and obedience, and his covenant with God through philosophical and allegorical exegesis.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_aeternitate_mundi: A Greek philosophical treatise by Philo Judaeus on the question of whether the cosmos is ungenerated and imperishable or generated and corruptible. The author distinguishes the various senses of 'world' and 'destruction' and then surveys the doctrines of Democritus, Epicurus, the Stoics with their doctrine of ekpyrosis, Aristotle, and the Pythagorean Ocellus Lucanus. Turning to Plato's speech in the Timaeus, in which the world, though generated, is declared indissoluble, the work follows the Platonic position that the cosmos had a beginning but will never be destroyed, since the will of its maker binds it more firmly than nature.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_agricultura: De Agricultura is a Greek treatise by Philo Judaeus that takes as its starting point Genesis 9:20–21, the passage in which Noah, a tiller of the ground, plants a vineyard and drinks of the wine. It first distinguishes the farmer's skilled cultivation from mere hired earth-working and then develops agriculture as an image of the tending of the soul, in which the mind cuts away the growths of folly, passion, and vice and plants virtue instead. Along the way it assigns the encyclical arts the role of preliminary nourishment for the young and likens the threefold division of philosophy, physical, ethical, and logical, to field, fruit, and the hedge that guards them, citing Deuteronomy 20:20 in support.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_cherubim: De Cherubim is a short Greek treatise by Philo Judaeus, the Jewish exegete and philosopher, expounding Genesis 3:24, the expulsion of Adam and the stationing of the cherubim and the flaming sword to guard the way to the tree of life. Philo distinguishes between being 'sent out' and being 'cast out', and reads Hagar, Ishmael, Sara and Isaac as symbols of intermediate encyclical education on the one hand and of general, incorruptible virtue and its fruits on the other. The cherubim and the flaming sword are then interpreted allegorically, with collateral discussions of the senses of 'opposite' (antikrys), of Cain's settlement in Naïd opposite Eden, and of the ordeal of the suspected wife in Numbers 5.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_confusione_linguarum: A Greek treatise by Philo Judaeus presenting an allegorical exposition of the story of the tower of Babel and the confusion of tongues in Genesis 11. Opening with a remark that earlier matters have been sufficiently treated, it quotes Genesis 11:1–9 in full and surveys alternative accounts of the episode, including a comparison with Homer's myth of the giants who piled mountains to reach heaven and a fable in which all animals once spoke a single language. Philo asks whether the division of languages was a punishment meant to hinder concerted wrongdoing and argues instead that a common tongue would not have curbed wickedness, so that linguistic diversity is more useful than harmful; the discussion serves as a defense of the Mosaic legislation against detractors who mock the sacred books as myths.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_congressu_eruditionis_g: A Greek allegorical treatise by Philo Judaeus, De Congressu Eruditionis Gratia ('On Mating with Preliminary Studies') takes as its starting point Genesis 16:1-2, the account of Sarai's barrenness and her giving of the Egyptian handmaid Hagar to Abraham. Sarai is interpreted as virtue and Hagar as enkyklios paideia, the encyclical or intermediate education in grammar, geometry, music, rhetoric, and dialectic, through which the soul must pass before it can bear the offspring of wisdom. The work unfolds as continuous philosophical exegesis, quoting the biblical verses and elaborating their symbolic meaning, including discussion of why virtue is figured as barren yet prolific, and of the individual disciplines that prepare the mind for philosophy.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_decalogo: A Greek treatise by Philo Judaeus on the Ten Commandments, forming part of a larger exposition of the Mosaic law. The opening section asks why the law was given in the wilderness rather than in cities, citing the corruption and idolatry of urban life, the need to purify the soul before receiving sacred legislation, the preparation of the people before settlement, and the miracles in the desert that attested the laws' divine origin. It then distinguishes between the commandments that God promulgated directly and those delivered through the prophet Moses, and dwells on the completeness of the number ten as embracing all numbers, ratios, and harmonies. Subsequent sections examine each of the ten commandments in turn as the summary heads of the particular laws.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_fuga_et_inventione: De Fuga et Inventione ('On Flight and Finding') is a Greek allegorical treatise by the Jewish exegete Philo Judaeus, written as a sequel to a preceding book in his allegorical exposition of Genesis. Taking its starting point from Hagar's flight from Sarai (Genesis 16), it distinguishes three causes of flight, hatred, fear, and shame, and examines biblical fugitives such as Jacob, who flees Laban and Esau, and Hagar herself. Around these figures Philo builds philosophical interpretations of the ignorant and the educated soul, of virtue, wealth, and true glory, and of the divine reason that meets and redirects the fugitive.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_gigantibus: De Gigantibus ('On the Giants') is a Greek allegorical treatise by Philo Judaeus, taking as its starting point Genesis 6:1–4 and the multiplication of mankind, the daughters of men, and the angels who took wives for themselves. Philo asks why the human race flourished after the birth of Noah and his sons, identifies the 'angels of God' with souls moving through the air, and distinguishes souls that descended into bodies from those that remain in the service of the creator. The wicked angels are interpreted as pursuers of the mortal pleasures figured by the daughters of men, and the treatise closes with an exposition of Genesis 6:3 on God's spirit refusing to abide for ever in flesh.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_josepho: De Josepho ('On Joseph') is a Greek biographical treatise by Philo Judaeus presenting the biblical Joseph as an exemplar of the political life. The opening situates the work as the fourth in a series of lives of the patriarchs linked to Moses, following lives that illustrate virtue acquired through learning, through nature, and through practice. The narrative retells the Genesis story of Joseph's dreams of dominion, his brothers' jealousy and attempted murder, his sale to traders bound for Egypt, and the grief of his father at the false report of his death. Philo expands the scriptural account in the manner of Greek moral biography, weaving speeches and ethical reflection into the retelling.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_migratione_abrahami: De Migratione Abrahami ('On the Migration of Abraham') is a Greek allegorical treatise by Philo Judaeus, a Jewish author writing in Greek, which opens from Genesis 12:1–3, the divine command that Abraham depart from his land, his kindred, and his father's house. The command is interpreted symbolically as the soul's migration away from the body, from sense perception, and from spoken reason, the land standing for the body, the kindred for the senses, and the father's house for the word. Other Genesis and Exodus passages receive the same allegorical treatment: Egypt figures the body and its pleasures, the Exodus the mind's deliverance from passion, and Lot the soul's inclination toward the sensible, while the discernment of true from false impressions and the preservation of Joseph's bones are likewise expounded. The discussion ranges over the nature of mind and its indwelling word, the discipline of the soul's ruling faculty, and the contrast between the life devoted to incorporeal goods and the life bound to the senses.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_opificio_mundi: De Opificio Mundi is a Greek philosophical treatise by Philo Judaeus that takes the creation account in the Mosaic law as its subject, opening with a contrast between Moses and other lawgivers, who either set out their ordinances without adornment or veil the truth in mythical fictions. The work argues that the world must be generated, since the visible and sensible belongs to becoming, while the active cause of all things is the purest mind shaping passive matter into the perfect work of the cosmos. It defends divine providence against those who pronounce the world ungenerated and God idle, explains the six-day schema through the perfection of the number six, and distinguishes the intelligible cosmos, conceived beforehand as a paradigm like the plan of an architect founding a city, from the sensible world fashioned after it, before proceeding through the works of the successive days.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_plantatione: De Plantatione is a Greek allegorical treatise by Philo Judaeus, the Hellenistic Jewish philosopher of Alexandria who wrote in the first century CE. It belongs to his allegorical commentary on Genesis and takes its departure from the verse describing Noah, the just man, as a tiller of the ground who plants a vineyard (Genesis 9:20). Continuing the discussion of agriculture in general from the preceding book, the work moves from viticulture to an account of God as the great planter and the cosmos as the perfected plant rooted in the divine Logos, and goes on to treat the ordering of the elements, plants, animals, angels, and man, whose upright form and rational soul, formed from the divine breath and made in God's image, distinguish him from the rest of creation.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_praemiis_et_poenis_et_d: A Greek treatise by Philo Judaeus on the rewards and punishments set out in the Mosaic law, with a concluding section on the curses. The opening divides the sayings delivered through Moses into cosmogony, history and legislation, and the argument then sets out the prizes held before the virtuous, beginning with hope and repentance, and the penalties appointed for the wicked, graded by individuals, households, cities and nations. As the title indicates, the work ends with an exposition of the cursings pronounced against transgressors.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_sacrificiis_abelis_et_c: De Sacrificiis Abelis et Caini is a Greek exegetical treatise by Philo Judaeus, an allegorical reading of the Genesis story of Cain and Abel. It identifies Cain with the self-loving mind that claims to possess everything and Abel with the God-loving disposition that refers all things to the divine, presenting the two as warring opinions borne by a single soul and illustrating the conflict through Rebekah's twins. Interwoven with quotations from Genesis in Greek, the discussion also takes up the brothers' offerings, the seniority of vice in time against the seniority of virtue in worth, and the figures of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Moses as stages in the soul's progress toward God.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_somniis_lib_iii: De Somniis Book III is a Greek prose treatise by Philo Judaeus offering a philosophical and allegorical interpretation of divinely sent dreams recorded in Genesis. It opens by distinguishing two classes of God-sent dreams and takes as its subject the second kind, in which the human mind, set in motion by the mind of the whole, appears to be god-possessed and to foresee the future. Its principal example is Jacob's dream of the ladder reaching from earth to heaven (Genesis 28:12–15), expounded through symbolic readings of details such as the well called 'of the oath' as an image of knowledge, together with discussions of the four elements of the cosmos and the boundless nature of learning.
grc.philo_judaeus.quis_rerum_divinarum_heres: Quis rerum divinarum heres sit ('Who Is the Heir of Divine Things?') is a Greek prose treatise by Philo Judaeus, the Greek-writing Jewish exegete. Opening with a reference to a preceding treatise on rewards, it takes its subject from Genesis 15:1–15, where the childless Abraham asks who will inherit him and receives the oracle 'your reward shall be very great.' In a running allegorical exposition of the passage, the work asks who truly inherits the things of God, treating the heir as the soul that possesses virtue and wisdom, and dwelling on themes such as silence and hearing, the sage's freedom of speech toward God, and the service owed to him. Alongside the Abraham material it repeatedly cites passages about Moses in Exodus and Numbers as illustrations of the wise man's boldness before God.
grc.philo_judaeus.quod_deterius_potiori_insi: Quod Deterius Potiori Insidiari Soleat ('That the Worse Attacks the Better') is a Greek allegorical treatise on Genesis by the Jewish exegete Philo Judaeus. Taking its start from Cain's luring of Abel to the plain and his murder of him there (Genesis 4:8), it interprets the plain as the arena of contest and strife, and reads further patriarchal episodes, Jacob's calling of Leah and Rachel to the flock, and Joseph's being sent to his brothers at Shechem, as figures for the governance of the soul's irrational powers. The argument also treats the three classes of goods, the many-colored and labyrinthine doctrine attributed to Joseph, and the discipline required of the soul that advances toward knowledge.
grc.philostratus_the_athenian.de_gymnastica: De Gymnastica is a Greek treatise by Philostratus the Athenian on the art of physical training. The opening ranks gymnastike among forms of wisdom rather than among banausic crafts, laments the decline of present-day athletes from the standard of Heracles, Theseus, Peleus and the champions of earlier ages, and promises counsel to those who train and are trained. The work then sets out the causes and origins of the contests, the stadion, dolichos, diaulos, hoplite race, jumping, javelin and discus, wrestling, boxing and the pankration, together with the pentathlon drawn from both light and heavy events, with accounts of Olympic origins at Elis and stories of legendary competitors throughout.
grc.philostratus_the_athenian.epistulae_et_d: A collection of short Greek prose pieces attributed to Philostratus the Athenian, comprising letters (epistulae) and brief rhetorical discourses (dialexeis). The opening letters are erotic compositions in epistolary form, several devoted to roses sent to a beloved and to the flower's associations with Aphrodite and Adonis. Later pieces take up such themes as a beloved's unrelenting refusal of love, the superiority of a poor lover to a rich one, and the attractions of a foreign beloved. The pieces are written in a compressed, epigrammatic rhetorical style.
grc.philostratus_the_athenian.vita_apollonii: The Vita Apollonii of Philostratus the Athenian is a Greek prose life of Apollonius of Tyana, the Pythagorean sage and wonder-worker, presented in eight books after Carl Ludwig Kayser's Teubner edition of 1870 and of uncertain date. The narrator frames the work as a reworking of the travel-notes kept by Damis of Nineveh, which he says he revised for the empress Julia, and he sets his hero beside Pythagoras, Empedocles, Democritus, Plato, and Socrates as a figure of divine wisdom whose contact with the magi of Babylon, the Brahmans of India, and the gymnosophists of Egypt drew mistaken charges of sorcery. The narrative follows Apollonius through his journeys, sayings, acts of foreknowledge, and letters to kings, cities, temples, and philosophers, gathered from urban traditions, sanctuaries, earlier accounts, and his own correspondence. Readers of intertexts will find in it a dense web of echoes of Homer, Plato, Herodotus, and the Pythagorean biographical tradition, and one of the fullest ancient portraits of a philosopher credited with superhuman knowledge.
grc.philostratus_the_lemnian.imagines: The Imagines (Eikones) attributed to Philostratus the Lemnian is a Greek prose collection of ekphraseis, that is, rhetorical descriptions of individual paintings. A prologue sets the scene at a gallery in a seaside suburb of Naples, where the speaker, a guest of Aristodemus of Caria, expounds the pictures to his host's young son and a circle of studious youths. The descriptions take mythological and Homeric subjects, beginning with the contest of fire and water at the Scamander from Iliad 21 and continuing with figures such as the personified Comus, and discuss in detail how each painting renders its story, its figures, and its effects of colour and light.
grc.phlegon.de_mirabilibus: A short Greek prose work, the De Mirabilibus ('On Marvels') attributed to Phlegon, preserved as a single narrative episode. It recounts the story of Philinnion, a young woman who returned from the dead to visit Machates, a guest lodging in her family's house, told as a report addressed to a king. The account follows the alarm of her parents Charito and Demostratus, Machates' production of the ring and breastband she had left with him, the opening of her tomb, and the chthonic purifications ordered after her final disappearance. It closes with the narrator's offer to send further witnesses and particulars to the king.
grc.plato.alcibiades_2: Attributed to Plato and printed among his works in Burnet's Oxford edition of 1903, the Second Alcibiades is a short Socratic dialogue in Attic prose in which Socrates meets Alcibiades on his way to pray and questions whether it is safe to ask the gods for anything, since they sometimes grant requests that prove disastrous, as Oedipus' prayer for the division of his paternal inheritance showed. The ensuing discussion treats foolishness and madness as fundamentally the same, grades its milder forms under flattering names, and suggests that most citizens are thus 'mad', so that prayer requires knowledge of what is truly beneficial. Readers of intertexts may value the dialogue's close kinship with the first Alcibiades and its handling of madness, prayer, and Socratic ignorance, themes that echo elsewhere in the Platonic corpus.
grc.plato.apologia: Plato's Apologia presents the defence speech of Socrates before an Athenian jury, delivered in his own voice. Socrates first answers the long-standing slander of older accusers who have spread the image of a man busied with things beneath the earth and in the heavens and making the weaker argument the stronger, a caricature he connects with Aristophanes' comedy; he then turns to the formal indictment brought by Meletus, disclaims expertise in such speculation, and calls his hearers as witnesses that he has never taught such things. He asks leave to speak in his accustomed plain manner, without rhetorical polish, as befits a man of seventy standing in court for the first time.
grc.plato.charmides: A dialogue in ancient Greek by Plato, cast as a conversation between Socrates, Critias, and the young Charmides. The scene is set in the palaestra of Taureas at Athens immediately after Socrates' return from the fighting at Potidaea, where Critias presents his nephew Charmides, famed for both beauty and philosophical promise, under the pretext of a headache remedy. The ensuing discussion pursues the question of what sophrosyne, temperance or sound-mindedness, is, examining a succession of candidate definitions, including modesty, quietness, doing one's own things, self-knowledge, and knowledge of knowledge itself.
grc.plato.euthyphro: Plato's Euthyphro is a short Greek prose dialogue set at Athens outside the stoa of the king archon, shortly before the trial of Socrates. Socrates and Euthyphro compare their legal business, the indictment for impiety brought against Socrates by Meletus, and Euthyphro's prosecution of his own father for the death of a hired labourer, before turning to the question of what piety is. Euthyphro offers a series of definitions, from 'doing what I am now doing' to 'what is loved by all the gods', each of which Socrates subjects to examination and refutation.
grc.plato.hipparchus: Hipparchus, a short Socratic dialogue attributed to Plato and printed in Burnet's Oxford text, opens with Socrates and an unnamed friend attempting to define the lover of gain (philokerdes) and to settle whether gain itself is good. A string of elenctic exchanges, built on analogies with the farmer, horseman, helmsman, and other experts who know the worth of their equipment, dismantles the friend's successive accounts, until the two concede that everyone loves gain and that the reproached philokerdes is the one who profits from things from which the good do not dare to profit. A later digression praises Hipparchus, son of Pisistratus, as a benefactor who brought the poems of Homer to Athens, giving the dialogue its title. Its aporetic handling of value, profit, and the appetite for more affords close parallels with the definitional dialogues of the Platonic corpus and with later Greek discussions of pleonexia and acquisition.
grc.plato.hippias_maior: The Greater Hippias is a Socratic dialogue in which Plato stages a conversation between Socrates and the celebrated sophist Hippias of Elis, newly returned to Athens after serving as ambassador for his city. The two seek a definition of the beautiful itself (to kalon), considering and rejecting in turn the claims that the beautiful is a beautiful maiden, gold, appropriate wealth and honor, the profitable, and the pleasant in sight and hearing. The inquiry ends without resolution, Socrates professing bewilderment at the elusive character of the fine. The dialogue also presents Hippias as a wealthy traveling teacher and diplomat, with references to Gorgias, Prodicus and Protagoras.
grc.plato.ion: The Ion is a short Socratic dialogue in which Plato stages a conversation between Socrates and Ion of Ephesus, a professional rhapsode fresh from a victory in a recitation contest at the Asclepieion of Epidaurus. Socrates elicits Ion's admission that he can interpret Homer alone among the poets, and then tests whether rhapsody rests on any art or knowledge, arguing by analogy with arithmetic, medicine, divination, and other crafts that no genuine expertise could be confined to a single poet. The dialogue ends by attributing both poetry and its performance not to technical knowledge but to a divine inspiration, passing to the poet and rhapsode like the power of a magnet through the rings of iron.
grc.plato.lovers: A short Socratic dialogue attributed to Plato and transmitted with his works, of uncertain date. Socrates recounts how he entered the school of the grammarian Dionysius and found two young men quarrelling over what appear to be astronomical questions, one of whom had dismissed philosophy as an ugly thing. He questions each in turn about whether philosophy is fine and good and what it consists in, drawing a comparison between the love of wisdom, defined as a love of many learnings, and the love of physical training, and probing whether moderate rather than excessive exertion produces good condition of body.
grc.plato.philebus: Plato's Philebus is a prose dialogue in Attic Greek, cast as a conversation between Socrates, Protarchus, and Philebus. Philebus maintains that pleasure, enjoyment, and delight are the good for all living creatures, while Socrates argues that thought, understanding, memory, true opinion, and correct reasoning yield a better and more useful life. The speakers set out to determine which of the two states of soul can render human existence happy, examining the nature of pleasure, approached through the goddess called Aphrodite, whose truest name is pleasure, and asking whether its many kinds, and the sciences likewise, are one or many, alike or unlike one another.
grc.plato.symposium: Plato's Symposium is a Greek philosophical dialogue of the fourth century BCE, framed as a retelling by Apollodorus, on the authority of Aristodemus, of a banquet held at the house of the tragedian Agathon to celebrate his victory in the dramatic competitions. At the dinner the guests, Phaedrus, Pausanias, Eryximachus, Aristophanes, Agathon, and Socrates, each deliver a speech in praise of love, Socrates recasting the subject through his account of the priestess Diotima's teaching. The dialogue closes with the drunken arrival of Alcibiades, who offers his own encomium of Socrates.
grc.plato.theaetetus: Plato's Theaetetus is a dialogue on the definition of knowledge, in which Socrates questions the young Theaetetus in the presence of the geometer Theodorus of Cyrene and successively tests the claims that knowledge is perception, that it is true judgement, and that it is true judgement accompanied by an account, refuting each in turn and closing without a settled answer. The main conversation is framed by a discussion between Euclides of Megara and Terpsion about the wounded and dying Theaetetus and about the written record Euclides has made of Socrates' exchange, which is set shortly before Socrates' trial and death. In the course of the dialogue Socrates compares his philosophical practice to midwifery, and the argument ranges over perception, memory, false judgement, and the notion of logos as an account that renders belief true.
grc.plutarch.ad_principem_ineruditum: Ad Principem Ineruditum ('To an Uneducated Ruler') is a short Greek moral essay by Plutarch arguing that philosophy and education, rather than outward severity or display, are a ruler's true safeguard. It opens with Plato's refusal to legislate for the Cyrenaeans, cites Pindar's saying that law is king of all, mortal and immortal, and depicts the law as an ensouled reason seated within the ruler's soul. Anecdotes about Theopompus of Sparta, Alexander, Epaminondas, Cato of Utica, and the tyrants Clearchus and Aristodemus illustrate the difference between kings who fear wrongdoing on their subjects' behalf and tyrants who fear their subjects themselves. The essay closes by counselling the ruler to govern his own soul first, after the manner of the cosmic order, so as to stand as an image of God among men.
grc.plutarch.adversus_colotem: A polemical treatise in Greek by Plutarch, handed down among the Moralia, directed against the Epicurean Colotes of Lampsacus, whose book argued that it is impossible even to live according to the doctrines of the other philosophers. The dialogue is framed as a conversation in which Aristodemus of Aegium and other companions consider how to answer Colotes, whose compilation of quotations torn from context they compare to a shop of monsters. Plutarch then takes up Colotes' attacks in turn, defending Democritus, Protagoras, Empedocles, Parmenides, Melissus, Stilpo, and Plato, and showing that Epicurus owed his principal doctrines to Democritus.
grc.plutarch.agesilaus: Plutarch's Agesilaus is a Greek prose biography of Agesilaus II, king of Sparta in the early fourth century BC, composed by the biographer and essayist of the early Roman imperial period. Opening with the king's genealogy and his schooling in the Spartan agoge, the narrative follows his disputed accession over Leotychides, secured through Lysander's influence, his studied deference to the ephors, and his campaigns in Asia Minor and the Corinthian War, down to his death in Egypt at an advanced age. Anecdotes, quotations from earlier writers, and moral commentary throughout delineate a character marked by cheerfulness, endurance of his lameness, piety, and obedience to Spartan law.
grc.plutarch.agis: Plutarch's Life of Agis is a Greek biographical narrative of Agis son of Eudamidas, the Eurypontid king of Sparta who sought to restore the city's ancient civic order and encountered the opposition of the wealthy and of his fellow king Leonidas. The work opens with a general discussion of demagogy and the force of popular opinion, illustrating it from myth and from the careers of Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus, to whom Agis and Cleomenes are explicitly paired as a Laconian counterpart. It then sets out the genealogies of the two Spartan royal houses, tracing Agis' descent from Agesilaus and Leonidas' from Pausanias the victor of Plataea, before proceeding to Agis' own reign and reforming activity.
grc.plutarch.alcibiades: Plutarch's Life of Alcibiades is a Greek prose biography from his Lives, opening with its subject's lineage, descent from Eurysaces son of Ajax through his father Cleinias and from the Alcmaeonids through his mother Deinomache, and with the guardianship of the boy by Pericles and Ariphron. It recounts his celebrated beauty, his lisp, the devoted attention of Socrates, and a series of childhood anecdotes illustrating his fiercely competitive and ambitious character. The narrative then follows him into public life, where, as Plutarch notes, his temperament displayed many inconsistencies and changes amid great affairs and shifting fortunes.
grc.plutarch.alexander: A Greek biographical account of Alexander the Great by Plutarch, opening with remarks on method: the author writes lives rather than histories, holding that a small deed, a saying, or some jest often reveals character more plainly than great battles and sieges. The work recounts Alexander's descent from Heracles through Caranus and from Aeacus through Neoptolemus, the omens surrounding the marriage of Philip and Olympias and the birth of their son, and traditions about the king's appearance and temperament, before following the course of his life. Sayings and reports drawn from named earlier writers are cited throughout the narrative.
grc.plutarch.amatoriae_narrationes: A short collection of Greek prose love stories transmitted with Plutarch's Moralia and attributed to Plutarch. It comprises three tales of disastrous courtship: the Boeotian maiden Aristocleia, killed in a scuffle when a spurned suitor abducts her during her wedding rites; the Corinthian youth Aktaion, whose death at the hands of his would-be lover Archias brings divine vengeance on the city and leads to the founding of Syracuse; and the daughters of the poor Leuctrian Scedasus, violated and slain by two Spartans, whose violated tomb and the father's curses are linked with the Theban victory at Leuctra. Each story is told briefly and plainly, ending in violent death and framed by local cult, omen, and divine retribution.
grc.plutarch.an_recte_dictum_sit_latenter_es: A short Greek essay by Plutarch, preserved in the Moralia, directed against the Epicurean precept 'live unnoticed' (lathe biosas). The argument holds that concealment renders virtue useless both to its possessor and to others, contrasting the injunction with the public careers of figures such as Epaminondas, Themistocles, Camillus, and Dion, and observing that Epicurus himself contravened the maxim through his letters, friendships, and teaching. Obscure retirement is likened to stagnant water and to the drowsiness of night, while recognition is said to give virtue its operative force in action.
grc.plutarch.an_virtus_doceri_possit: A Greek moral essay by Plutarch, transmitted among the Moralia, arguing that virtue is teachable. The opening poses the question whether sound judgement, just conduct, and the good life can be learned, and presses the objection that while the skills of orators, pilots, musicians, builders, and farmers are all acquired by instruction, good men seem to exist in name only. Against the view that only minor, childish matters admit of teaching, the argument ranges over examples drawn from music, seamanship, cookery, household management, and military command, with citations of Plato, Heraclitus, Herodotus, Diogenes, Aristippus, and Iphicrates.
grc.plutarch.an_vitiositas_ad_infelicitatem_: A short Greek moral essay by Plutarch, transmitted among the Moralia under the Latin title An Vitiositas ad Infelicitatem Sufficia ('Whether Vice Is Sufficient to Cause Unhappiness'). The speakers set out to show that vice by itself, without instruments or assistants, is enough to make a person wretched, filling the soul with grief, regret, and distress. Fortune, the essay argues, can work ruin only upon those whom vice has already softened, and examples such as Socrates, Diogenes, and the Roman general Decius demonstrate that poverty, slavery, poison, and even death cannot afflict the courageous. Unhappiness is therefore traced to characters that are untrained and unreasoning, clinging to opinions formed in childhood.
grc.plutarch.aratus: Plutarch's Life of Aratus is a Greek prose biography of the Sicyonian statesman Aratus, preceded by a prefatory letter addressed to Polycrates that defends the commemoration of noble ancestors through a discussion of a proverb cited by Chrysippus and countered by Dionysodorus of Troezen. The narrative follows Aratus from his father Cleinias's murder by the tyrant Abantidas and his own childhood flight to Argos, through his daring recovery of Sicyon from tyranny, to his long leadership in the Achaean League and his death. Throughout, the work presents his career as a domestic example for Polycrates's sons, Polycrates and Pythocles, to imitate.
grc.plutarch.brutus: Plutarch's Life of Brutus is a Greek prose biography of Marcus Junius Brutus, the assassin of Julius Caesar. It opens with Brutus's claimed descent from Junius Brutus, who expelled the Tarquins, and with the conflicting ancient reports about his ancestry through his mother Servilia. The narrative follows his upbringing under his uncle Cato, his attachment to the Old Academy of Plato, his terse Laconic manner in Greek letters, his mission to Cyprus on Cato's behalf, and his choice to join Pompey in the civil war against Caesar.
grc.plutarch.caius_marcius_coriolanus: A Greek biographical essay by Plutarch on the early Roman patrician Caius Marcius Coriolanus, forming part of his Lives of Greek and Roman figures. The work opens with the genealogy of the Marcian house in Rome and Coriolanus's fatherless upbringing by his widowed mother, before depicting his austere temperament and his appetite for deeds of arms. It then recounts his first campaigns in the war against the expelled king Tarquinius, the oak crown he earned for shielding a fallen citizen, and his constant striving to surpass his own earlier exploits, animated above all by his longing for his mother's approval.
grc.plutarch.caius_marius: A Greek biographical Life of the Roman general and statesman Caius Marius, composed by Plutarch as part of his Parallel Lives and printed here in Bernadotte Perrin's 1920 Harvard edition. The Life opens with a digression on Roman naming customs before following Marius from his poor upbringing near Arpinum through early service under Scipio Aemilianus at Numantia, his tribunate, his rise through the cursus honorum and successive consulships amid military crisis, and on to the savagery of his last years and his rivalry with Sulla. The opening's explicit engagement with Posidonius on the tria nomina, together with the dense web of anecdotes and phrasing shared with Roman historiography, makes the work a productive hunting ground for textual parallels, both to lost Hellenistic and Roman sources and to Plutarch's other biographies.
grc.plutarch.cato_minor: Plutarch's Cato Minor, written in Greek, is a biography of Cato the Younger, the Roman republican famed for Stoic incorruptibility. It opens with his lineage as great-grandson of Cato the Censor and his orphaned upbringing in the house of Livius Drusus, then builds a portrait of unbending character from childhood anecdotes, his defiance of Pompeius Silo, his demand for a sword against Sulla's proscriptions, before following his public career through the civil strife of the late Republic to his death at Utica. For readers of intertexts, the life offers a Greek window on late Republican Rome and a store of moral exempla, constancy under tyranny, austere virtue, patriotic suicide, that echo throughout later Greek, Latin, and European literature.
grc.plutarch.cimon: A Greek biographical composition by Plutarch, the Life of Cimon belongs to the Parallel Lives and is paired with the life of Lucullus. It opens with the story of Damon of Chaeronea and the fortunes of the author's own ancestors, followed by remarks on the biographer's duty to truthfulness, and then sets out the grounds for treating Cimon and Lucullus together as soldiers and civic leaders. The main narrative recounts the career of the Athenian general Cimon, his campaigns against the Persians, and his conduct in political life, including the partiality and generosity for which the pairing with Lucullus is drawn.
grc.plutarch.comparison_aegisalius_pompey: Plutarch's formal comparison (synkrisis) of the Spartan king Agesilaus and the Roman general Pompey, written in Greek as the epilogue to their paired biographies. Opening with the words 'now that the Lives have been set forth,' it weighs the two men under successive numbered heads, contrasting their access to power, their treatment of patrons such as Sulla and Lysander, their breaches of civic justice, and their relations with fortune. The closing sections compare their records as commanders, from Agesilaus's defense of Sparta after the defeat at Leuctra to Pompey's abandonment of Rome to Caesar.
grc.plutarch.comparison_agis_cleomenes_gracc: A brief Greek comparison (synkrisis) by Plutarch, concluding the paired Lives of Agis and Cleomenes and of Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus. It sets the Spartan kings and the Roman brothers against each other in a point-by-point appraisal covering natural endowment and education, incorruptibility with money, the scale and boldness of their political innovations, military exploits, the manner of their deaths, and the chief accusations each pair faced. Agis and Cleomenes are judged stronger in nature despite a corrupt upbringing and customs, while Cleomenes' lawless killing of the ephors and his restoration of Spartan power are weighed against the Gracchi's more moderate, though equally fatal, careers.
grc.plutarch.comparison_alcibiades_coriolanu: The Comparison of Alcibiades and Coriolanus is a short closing essay (synkrisis) in Greek by Plutarch, weighing the two subjects of his paired biographies against one another. It reviews their military records, contrasting Alcibiades' victories by land and sea with Marcius' campaigns for Rome and later against it, and then compares their political conduct, with the Athenian's brilliant but unscrupulous demagogy set beside the Roman's harsh, oligarchic manner. Plutarch further contrasts their tempers, their honesty over money, their dealings with Sparta, Rome and the Volscians, and the ways each man's relations with his fellow citizens broke down, finding neither wholly without fault.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_demosthenes_with_: A short Greek synkrisis by Plutarch, forming the formal comparison that concludes his paired Lives of Demosthenes and Cicero. It weighs the two orators' rhetorical powers and styles, then turns to their characters as these appear in their speeches, treating their humour, gravity, and self-display. Further sections contrast the authority each held and how he used it, their conduct toward money and royal gifts, and the differing circumstances of their flights and downfalls.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_dion_and_brutus: Plutarch's Comparison of Dion and Brutus is the brief Greek synkrisis that closes the paired lives of Dion of Syracuse and Marcus Junius Brutus. In point-by-point contrasts it weighs the two men's circumstances, resources, and conduct as generals, their motives for taking up arms against a tyrant, and the differing characters of Dionysius of Syracuse and Julius Caesar, asking in each case whether the champion acted for himself or for his citizens. The closing sections consider the justice of each man's cause, the risks each undertook, and the esteem or blame each earned from his contemporaries.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_lucullus_and_cimo: A short Greek comparison (synkrisis) from Plutarch's Lives, weighing the Roman general Lucullus against the Athenian Cimon. It opens by contrasting their ends, Lucullus having died before the civil wars he foresaw while Cimon fell still on campaign, and then considers their lavishness and use of wealth, their victories by land and by sea, their relations with soldiers and allies, and the hostility each met from his own citizens. It closes by crediting Lucullus with the greater military reach, citing his capture of Tigranocerta, Sinope, and Nisibis and his crossings of the Taurus and the Tigris against Tigranes and Mithridates.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_lycurgus_and_numa: The Comparison of Lycurgus and Numa is the formal concluding comparison (synkrisis) to the paired Lives of the Spartan lawgiver Lycurgus and the Roman king Numa in Plutarch's Parallel Lives, a Greek work of uncertain date. Starting from the points the two men held in common, moderation, piety, political and educational concern, and divine sanction for their legislation, it weighs their differences, contrasting Numa's acceptance of kingship with Lycurgus's voluntary laying of it down, and the harsh Spartan discipline, including the treatment of the Helots, with Numa's milder and more peaceable regime at Rome. Later sections take up the regulation of wealth, the redistribution of land, and the two founders' distinctive customs concerning marriage and childbearing, judging Lycurgus's arrangements the more austere and Numa's the more permissive.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_philopoemen_and_t: The Comparison of Philopoemen and Titus is Plutarch's formal synkrisis concluding his paired lives of the Achaean general Philopoemen and the Roman commander Titus Quinctius Flamininus. Written in Greek, it weighs the two men's benefactions toward the Greeks, their failings of ambition and hot temper, their military experience and innovation in arms and tactics, and their effectiveness both as private citizens and as holders of office. The verdict is carefully balanced: Philopoemen is credited with more numerous victories won amid Greece's decline, Titus with justice and benevolence exercised at the height of Roman power, and the judgement proposes awarding the crown of generalship to the Greek and of righteousness to the Roman.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_theseus_and_romul: A short Greek prose composition by Plutarch, forming the formal comparison that concludes his paired biographies of Theseus and Romulus. It weighs the two founders against each other, contrasting Theseus's voluntary exploits against brigands with Romulus's actions under compulsion, and assesses their courage, Theseus's voyage with the tribute youths and Ariadne, and their contrasting political tendencies, one toward democracy and the other toward tyranny. Further sections compare their lapses of anger toward a brother and a son, their differing achievements as founders, and the circumstances of Aegeus's death, awarding the vote to each figure on separate points.
grc.plutarch.consolatio_ad_apollonium: A Greek prose consolation addressed to Apollonius on the premature death of his son, written by Plutarch. The speaker opens with sympathy for the bereaved father and argues that grief, though natural, must be kept within rational measure, rejecting both unfeeling insensibility and unbridled lamentation in favour of a moderated response to loss. The argument is reinforced with quotations from poets and philosophers, including Euripides, Menander, and the Academic Crantor.
grc.plutarch.consolatio_ad_uxorem: The Consolatio ad Uxorem is a short Greek prose letter in which Plutarch consoles his wife on the death of their young daughter. Writing as her husband, he urges restraint in grief, praises her self-command at the funeral and in the household's mourning, and recalls the child's affectionate and gentle nature. The letter argues that excessive lamentation, neglect of the body, and ostentatious funerary display feed rather than relieve sorrow, and that memory of the dead should be a source of more gladness than pain.
grc.plutarch.crassus: A Greek biography by Plutarch of Marcus Licinius Crassus, the Roman triumvir, forming one of his parallel lives of Greek and Roman statesmen. The narrative opens with Crassus's upbringing and the avarice that contemporaries judged his dominant fault, recounts his escape from the persecutions of Cinna and Marius into Spain, and describes the vast fortune he amassed from Sulla's confiscations, the frequent fires of Rome, and a household of hundreds of skilled slaves. Later portions treat his hospitality, his standing as an orator beside Pompey, Caesar, and Cicero, and his public career down to the Parthian expedition in which he died.
grc.plutarch.de_alexandri_magni_fortuna_aut_: A Greek prose oration by Plutarch, preserved among the Moralia, debating whether Alexander the Great owed his conquests to Fortune or to his own virtue. The work opens with an imagined speech in which Alexander answers Fortune directly, enumerating the wounds he received at Granicus, Issus, Gaza, Maracanda and elsewhere as proof that his empire was won through endurance and courage rather than luck. It goes on to argue that philosophy, more than Homer, was Alexander's true provision for his campaign, crediting the teachings of Aristotle and comparing his civilising of Asia through the founding of cities and the spread of Greek religion with the instruction offered by Socrates and Plato.
grc.plutarch.de_amore_prolis: De Amore Prolis (On Affection for Offspring) is a Greek prose treatise by Plutarch, transmitted among the Moralia. The work argues that parental love is natural and freely given, contrasting the laws, honours, and incentives by which human beings are induced to marry and rear children with the untutored devotion of animals to their mates and young. Its case rests on copious natural observation, describing the kingfisher's woven nest, the viviparous sharks, the bear's licking of her formless cubs, the partridge's diversion of hunters, and the care shown by hens, dogs, and horses, and it closes by setting the beasts up as witnesses against a human nature that alone appears to love for a price.
grc.plutarch.de_capienda_ex_inimicis_utilita: A short Greek moral essay by Plutarch, part of the Moralia, addressed to Cornelius Pulcher, who is credited with choosing the gentlest mode of political life. Taking its cue from Xenophon's remark that sensible men are benefited by their enemies, the work argues that enmity, though a fertile source of passion, can be turned to advantage: the enemy keeps constant watch over a man's affairs, exposes his faults, and drives him toward vigilance and blameless conduct. The argument is illustrated with examples and comparisons drawn from Chilon, the musicians of Dionysus, Diogenes, Crates, Zeno, and the Roman Nasica, alongside observations on animals, fire, seafaring, and agriculture.
grc.plutarch.de_communibus_notitiis_adversus: Plutarch's De communibus notitiis adversus Stoicos ('On Common Conceptions, Against the Stoics') is a short Greek dialogue, preserved among the Moralia, spoken by Lamprias and Diadumenus. The two speakers attack the Stoic appeal to common conceptions and preconceptions, arguing that Stoic doctrines, among them the paradoxes that only the sage is king, rich, and blessed, and the ranking of health, beauty, and strength as indifferent things, contradict notions shared by all humanity. The argument turns repeatedly on Chrysippus, his dialectic, and his quarrels with the Academics Arcesilaus and Carneades, and moves toward a point-by-point examination of Stoic teaching against the common conceptions.
grc.plutarch.de_cupiditate_divitiarum: A short Greek moral essay by Plutarch on the love of wealth, preserved among the Moralia.
