It argues that money cannot cure the desire for money: greed is a disease of the soul calling not for satisfaction but for purgation, since no one who has what suffices is poor, and the man who always wants more is beset not by poverty but by insatiability. The argument proceeds through anecdotes about figures such as the trainer Hippomachus and Aristippus, comparisons between wealth and bodily appetite, and quotations from poets including Hipponax, Menander and Solon.
grc.plutarch.de_curiositate: A short Greek moral essay by Plutarch, transmitted with the Moralia, on polypragmosynē, the itch to pry into other people's affairs. The author likens the meddling disposition to a disease of the soul and to a dweller in a dark, unhealthy house who could open doors and windows to let in light and clean air. Examples drawn from myth, history, and everyday domestic life, Odysseus questioning the shades in Hades, Aristippus pursuing Socrates' conversation, knocks and doorkeepers at a neighbor's house, show the busybody scrutinizing others' faults while neglecting his own, and the essay urges turning that scrutiny inward upon one's own life.
grc.plutarch.de_defectu_oraculorum: A Greek philosophical dialogue by Plutarch, handed down among the Moralia, on the question of why oracles have fallen silent. The conversation is set at Delphi and conducted by a company of speakers that includes Terentius Priscus, the grammarian Demetrius of Britain, Cleombrotus the Lacedaemonian, and the philosopher Ammonius. It opens with the myth of eagles and swans converging on the earth's omphalos and turns on a report that the inextinguishable lamp in the temple of Ammon consumes less oil each year, a sign taken to point to change in the cosmos. The speakers' explanations range over travellers' tales from distant lands, astronomical argument, and the role of intermediary daimones between gods and men.
grc.plutarch.de_e_delphos: A Greek philosophical dialogue by Plutarch, set at Delphi and framed as a conversation among Ammonius, Lamprias, and other speakers gathered by the temple. The work takes as its puzzle the letter E dedicated at Apollo's sanctuary, and the speakers weigh rival explanations, including Pythagorean numerology, readings based on the seven vowels and planets, and stories about the Five and Seven Sages. Along the way it discusses the Pythian epithets of the god, the oracular inscriptions 'know thyself' and 'nothing in excess', and the view of Apollo as a god who prompts philosophical inquiry into truth.
grc.plutarch.de_esu_carnium: A short Greek prose tractate attributed to Plutarch and transmitted with the Moralia, the De esu carnium ('On the Eating of Flesh') argues against the slaughter and consumption of animals. Cast as a reply to an interlocutor's question about Pythagorean abstinence from meat, it contrasts humanity's first recourse to flesh-eating amid primeval scarcity with the abundance enjoyed in the present age, and denounces the killing, preparation and serving of animals in sustained rhetorical invective. The argument survives only in fragmentary form, breaking off in mid-course.
grc.plutarch.de_esu_carnium_2: A short Greek philosophical essay by Plutarch, the second book of On the Eating of Flesh (De esu carnium), argues for abstaining from animal flesh. The speaker urges his audience to cut out gluttony and blood-guilt as the Egyptians cut out the stomachs of their dead, catalogues the cruelties inflicted on beasts at slaughter and in luxury cookery, and traces the appetite for meat to excess beyond natural need. Pythagoras and Empedocles appear as authorities for justice toward animals and for the belief that souls transmigrate among bodies, and the essay ends by asking whether such rebirth can be demonstrated, while insisting that a diet steeped in blood trains the soul toward war and murder.
grc.plutarch.de_exilio: A Greek prose essay attributed to Plutarch, preserved among the Moralia, written as a consolation to a friend in exile. It argues that exile, like other misfortunes, weighs upon the sufferer through opinion rather than nature, and that a homeland arises from dwelling and use, so that the philosopher may count himself a citizen of the cosmos. The argument is illustrated with quotations and examples drawn from lyric and epic poetry, from Plato and Socrates, and from an image of the whole world ordered under a single divine lawgiver.
grc.plutarch.de_fato: A very brief Greek treatise attributed to Plutarch and preserved among the Moralia, framed as a letter to one Piso. It distinguishes two senses of fate, as activity and as substance, and supports the distinction with interpretations of Platonic passages from the Phaedrus, the Timaeus and the Republic, including the law of Adrasteia and the parts assigned to Lachesis, Clotho and Atropos. The argument then considers whether fate is finite or infinite, likening it to the recurrent cosmic cycle of the Timaeus and comparing it with a civic law that ordains universals rather than particular cases.
grc.plutarch.de_fortuna_romanorum: Plutarch's De Fortuna Romanorum ('On the Fortune of the Romans') is a Greek rhetorical essay that stages a contest between personified Fortune and Virtue over which of them brought Rome to hegemony. After arguing that the two must have joined forces rather than contended, the speaker musters Roman heroes such as Camillus, Mucius Scaevola, Horatius, Marcellus, Marius, and the Scipiones under Virtue's banner, while Fortune claims beneficiaries from Numa Pompilius and Tarquinius Priscus to Aemilius Paullus, Caecilius Metellus, and Sulla. The piece survives in the collection of Plutarch's Moralia.
grc.plutarch.de_fraterno_amore: De Fraterno Amore ('On Brotherly Love') is a Greek moral essay by Plutarch, one of the treatises of the Moralia, framed as a dedication to the brothers Nigrinus and Quinctus and introduced through the image of the Spartan 'dokana,' the paired beam consecrated to the Dioscuri. The argument holds that concord among siblings is rooted in nature rather than mere convention, supported by analogies with the body's paired and duplicated organs, by reflections on brothers who quarrel over property and status, and by warnings against the flatterers and slanderers who breed domestic discord. Quotations from poetry and comedy, together with the author's account of arbitrating between two estranged brothers at Rome, illustrate its case for fraternal goodwill and for honoring siblings as one honors parents.
grc.plutarch.de_garrulitate: De Garrulitate (Peri adoleschias), 'On Talkativeness', is a Greek moral essay by Plutarch preserved among the Moralia. It treats garrulity as a disease of the soul that philosophy must attempt to cure, since the talkative man speaks continually and listens to no one, and it examines the social nuisance such people cause at dinners, assemblies, and on journeys. The argument is illustrated with anecdotes about figures such as Aristotle, Bias, and Zeno, and with quotations from Homer, Euripides, Archilochus, and Sophocles. Drunken loquacity is discussed as an aggravated form of the vice, and the essay closes by observing that ill-timed speech destroys even the good deed.
grc.plutarch.de_genio_socratis: A Greek prose dialogue by Plutarch, preserved in the Moralia and printed here from Bernardakis's Teubner edition of 1891. Set at Thebes, it opens with Caphisias and Archidamus arranging a full account of the conspiracy that liberated the city from its Spartan-backed oligarchy, gathering figures such as Epameinondas, Pelopidas, Simmias and the seer Theocritus, and moving towards the celebrated question of the daimonion of Socrates that gives the work its title. An explicit quotation of Pindar in the opening exchange, Socratic characters inherited from the Platonic corpus, and the layered narration of an episode central to Greek historical memory offer readers of intertexts abundant points of verbal and thematic contact.
grc.plutarch.de_gloria_atheniensium: A brief Greek essay by Plutarch, known by its Latin title De Gloria Atheniensium ('On the Glory of the Athenians'). It argues that the glory of Athens rests chiefly on its generals and statesmen rather than on its poets and artists, and it surveys Athenian achievements in war and politics from the Persian Wars to the age of Epameinondas. A substantial portion of the essay compares painting with historical writing, taking up Simonides' dictum that painting is silent poetry and poetry speaking painting; Plutarch discusses painters such as Apollodorus, Euphranor, and Parrhasius, and praises the vividness of Thucydides' battle narratives, with examples drawn from Pylos and the Sicilian expedition. The closing argument holds that historians are messengers of deeds performed by others, deriving their fame only secondhand from the doers of the actions they record.
grc.plutarch.de_invidia_et_odio: A brief Greek moral treatise by Plutarch, transmitted with the Moralia, comparing the passions of envy (phthonos) and hatred (misos). It argues that the two differ in origin and scope: hatred is directed at those deemed wicked and can extend even to animals, whereas envy is felt only toward human good fortune and is never held justly. Drawing on figures from Themistocles and Charillus to Socrates' accusers and Alexander, it traces how each passion arises, grows with the virtue or vice of its object, and responds differently to success and misfortune.
grc.plutarch.de_iside_et_osiride: A Greek philosophical dialogue addressed to Clea, forming part of the Moralia of Plutarch. The work treats the Egyptian deities Isis and Osiris, giving an allegorical account of Isis as knowledge of what truly is, of Typhon as ignorance that tears apart the sacred discourse, and of the myth of the dismemberment and recovery of Osiris in terms of reason and the divine. It also examines the rationale behind Egyptian priestly observances, including abstention from wool and certain foods, linen clothing, ritual shaving, and the special watering of the Apis bull.
grc.plutarch.de_primo_frigido: De Primo Frigido ('On the Primary Cold') is a short Greek philosophical dialogue by Plutarch, one of the treatises of the Moralia, opening with a question put to Favorinus: whether cold is a primary power and substance, as fire is of heat, or merely the privation of heat. The speaker argues against the privation view, maintaining that cold is a positive force with its own principle, which contracts, congeals, and transforms bodies and admits degrees of intensity. The argument draws on the mixture of contraries in art and nature, disputes the Stoic claim that embryos become soul through condensation of breath, and describes the divine harmonizer of the cosmos balancing heat and cold, with winter and the north winds cited as positive powers rather than mere absences.
grc.plutarch.de_pythiae_oraculis: De Pythiae oraculis ('On the Oracles of the Pythia') is a Greek dialogue by Plutarch, preserved among the Moralia. Set at Delphi, it opens with Basilocles and Philinus awaiting Theon and their guest Diogenianus, and its conversation moves from the bluish colour of Delphic bronze, explained through theories of air, moisture, and patination, to wider questions about the oracle, including the nature of the Pythia's inspiration and why she no longer delivers oracles in verse. The work combines antiquarian observation of the sanctuary with philosophical argument about prophecy.
grc.plutarch.de_recta_ratione_audiendi: A short Greek moral essay by Plutarch, addressed to one Nicander, on the art of listening properly to lectures and philosophical instruction. It observes that young men who have just passed from the authority of teachers and tutors are prone to mistake licence for freedom, and argues that correct listening must be learned before speaking, since the ears are the chief channel through which reason and virtue enter the soul. The argument is supported with anecdotes and sayings concerning figures such as Xenocrates, Bias, and Epaminondas, and the work belongs among the minor treatises of Plutarch gathered in the Moralia.
grc.plutarch.de_se_ipsum_citra_invidiam_laud: A Greek moral essay by Plutarch, cast as a dialogue with Herclanus, on the question of when it is permissible for a statesman to praise himself. Beginning from the received view that speaking about oneself is burdensome and illiberal, the argument distinguishes empty boasting and envious rivalry from self-commendation offered in self-defence against slander or in the course of action that requires it. Historical and literary examples, among them Pericles, Epaminondas, Homer's Sthenelus, Cicero and Scipio, illustrate both the offences of indiscriminate self-praise and the occasions on which it may be justified.
grc.plutarch.de_sollertia_animalium: A Greek dialogue transmitted among the Moralia of Plutarch, De Sollertia Animalium is framed as a conversation between Autobulus and Soclarus on the eve of judging a contest in which Aristotimus defends the cleverness of land animals and Phaedimus that of sea creatures. The speakers maintain that animals share in reason, memory, foresight and emotion, supporting the claim with anecdotes of animal behaviour and arguing against the Stoic doctrine that beasts are wholly irrational. The opening portion also touches on the praise of hunting and its supposed effects on the young, before turning to preparatory discussion of perception, judgement and the capacities of the soul.
grc.plutarch.de_tranquilitate_animi: A Greek moral essay by Plutarch on euthymia, or tranquillity of mind, cast as a letter to his friend Paccius. The opening explains that, lacking time for a fresh composition, the author has assembled remarks on the subject from the notebooks he kept for himself. The essay then examines whether withdrawal from affairs secures peace of mind, rejecting the view that doing little makes one cheerful and arguing instead that tranquillity depends on reason's habitual command of the passions rather than on any particular manner of life. Quotations from Homer, Hesiod and Menander and references to Xenophon and Epicurus illustrate the discussion.
grc.plutarch.lycurgus: Plutarch's Lycurgus is one of his Lives, a biographical account of the Spartan lawgiver Lycurgus. It opens by observing that almost nothing about him, his lineage, travels, death, laws, or dates, can be affirmed without dispute, and surveys the conflicting testimonies of earlier historians before beginning its narrative. The Life recounts his Heracleid descent, his regency at Sparta for the infant Charilaus, his self-imposed exile, and his return to frame the Spartan constitution, with its division of land, common messes, council of elders, ephorate, and training of the young. It concludes with his death and the enduring observance of his ordinances at Sparta.
grc.plutarch.marcellus: The Marcellus is a Greek biographical account by Plutarch of Marcus Claudius Marcellus, the Roman general and statesman who held the consulship five times. It opens with Marcellus' ancestry and the origin of his name, then recounts his youthful exploits in single combat, his early magistracies and priesthood, the trial of his colleague Capitolinus, and the Roman campaigns against the Gallic Insubres and their mercenaries during the wars with Carthage. The narrative also records the religious measures, drawn from the Sibylline books, by which the Romans sought to avert the Gallic threat, and follows Marcellus' rise through public honours won in war and civic life.
grc.plutarch.marcus_cato: A Greek biography of the Roman statesman Marcus Porcius Cato, one of the biographies in Plutarch's Lives. Opening with Cato's Tusculan descent and upbringing in the Sabine countryside, the narrative follows his enlistment at seventeen during Hannibal's campaigns in Italy, his service under Fabius Maximus at the capture of Tarentum, and his rise as a pleader and orator at Rome. It dwells on his austerity in food, dress, and bodily training, his admiration for Manius Curius' frugality, his late study of Greek letters through the Pythagorean Nearchus and his reading of Thucydides and Demosthenes, and the encouragement he received from Valerius Flaccus.
grc.plutarch.numa: Plutarch's Life of Numa is a Greek biography of Numa Pompilius, the Sabine who succeeded Romulus as king of Rome, preserved among the author's Lives. The work opens by weighing the chronological difficulties surrounding Numa's lifetime and the ancient debate over whether he was ever a companion of Pythagoras. It then recounts Romulus's sudden disappearance and deification, the interregnum governed by patricians in rotation, the dispute between Romans and Sabines over the succession, and the election of the Sabine Numa, whose virtue marked him out and who is summoned by envoys to accept the kingship.
grc.plutarch.pelopidas: A Greek biographical work by Plutarch, one of his Parallel Lives, pairing the Theban general Pelopidas with the Roman commander Marcellus. It opens with an essayistic preface on the dangers commanders ought to run in person, drawing on examples from Homer, Iphicrates, Callicratidas, Antigonus, Chares, and Timotheus, before turning to Pelopidas himself, son of Hippocles, a wealthy Theban who shared with Epaminondas a life of deliberate frugality. The narrative continues with his career in fourth-century BC Theban politics and war, his devotion to his friends, and his death while fighting Alexander of Pherae.
grc.plutarch.phocion: A Greek biographical treatise by Plutarch, the Life of Phocion narrates the career of the Athenian statesman and general Phocion, whose austere and largely uncelebrated virtue is set against the shipwreck of the city's fortunes under Macedonian dominance. A prologue considers how character fares in prosperous and in ruined cities, illustrated through Demades and through Cato the Younger, whose life serves as the companion piece against which Phocion's is measured. The work then follows Phocion's conduct of public affairs, including his dealings with Antipater, in a manner interweaving narrative with ethical and political reflection.
grc.plutarch.pompey: A Greek prose biography by Plutarch, composed under the Roman Empire as one of the paired Greek and Roman lives of his Parallel Lives. The work follows the career of the Roman general Pompey the Great from his youth as son of the unpopular commander Strabo and his rise in the civil wars of the late Republic, through his military commands and political prominence, to his rivalry with Julius Caesar and his final defeat and death. The opening chapters contrast popular hatred of the father with the affection won by the son, note Pompey's supposed resemblance to Alexander the Great, and recount early anecdotes, including the foiled assassination plot of Terentius and a charge of theft arising from his father's handling of public funds.
grc.plutarch.pyrrhus: Plutarch's Life of Pyrrhus is a Greek biographical account of the king of Epirus, one of the bioi collected in Plutarch's Lives. It opens with the legendary genealogy of the Molossian rulers, tracing Pyrrhus's descent from Achilles through Neoptolemus, and then recounts the perils of his infancy: the flight from rebellious Molossians, the escape of the child across a flooded river with his message conveyed on a strip of bark, and his reception at the court of Glaukias, who restored him to the throne. The narrative blends antiquarian and genealogical material with vivid anecdote and continues through Pyrrhus's later loss of power and his entanglement with Demetrius, in the manner characteristic of Plutarch's biographical writing.
grc.plutarch.quaestiones_graecae: A series of short questions and answers on antiquarian matters, preserved among the Greek essays of Plutarch's Moralia. The entries explain obscure local terms, civic institutions, cult practices, and festivals of various Greek communities, including Epidauros, Kyme, Soloi, Knidos, Opous, Boeotia, Corcyra, and Delphi. Typical items are the councilors called 'artynoi' at Epidauros, the punishment of adulterous women at Kyme, and the nine-yearly festival of Charila at Delphi, with explanations drawn from earlier historians, poets, and local tradition.
grc.plutarch.quaestiones_naturales: The Quaestiones Naturales is a short Greek treatise by Plutarch, preserved among the Moralia, posed as a sequence of questions each beginning 'why' (dia ti). It seeks explanations of natural phenomena: why seawater fails to nourish trees and land animals, why rainwater accompanied by thunder and lightning benefits seeds, why herdsmen give salt to their cattle, and similar problems of weather, plant growth, and animal husbandry. Each question is followed by one or more candidate answers, often framed as alternatives and frequently attributed to earlier philosophers such as Plato, Aristotle, and Empedocles.
grc.plutarch.quaestiones_romanae: A Greek prose treatise in question-and-answer form, attributed to Plutarch and transmitted with the Moralia. It consists of a series of questions about Roman customs and rituals, including wedding rites, temple restrictions, funerary purification, and rules governing kinship and marriage, each followed by one or more proposed explanations, sometimes offered as alternatives. The answers draw on antiquarian learning and cite named authorities such as Varro, weighing mythological, religious, and rationalizing accounts of the practices under discussion.
grc.plutarch.quomodo_adolescens_poetas_audir: A Greek prose essay by Plutarch, transmitted with the Moralia and addressed to Marcus Sedatus concerning the poetic studies of Sedatus's son Cleander. It argues that the young should not be barred from the poets, since poetry mixes profitable and pleasing matter with falsehood, but should instead be trained in judgement so that pleasure in myth does not carry the mind toward what is harmful. Treating the poets partly as deliberate fabricators and partly as sincere but mistaken reporters, it draws its illustrations chiefly from Homer and from philosophical and didactic verse such as that of Empedocles, Parmenides, Nicander, Theognis, and Xenophanes, and closes with the counsel to temper the young reader's encounter with the poems by the introduction of philosophy.
grc.plutarch.quomodo_quis_suos_in_virtute_se: A Greek moral essay by Plutarch, addressed to Sossius Senecio, on how a person may become aware of his own progress toward virtue. The opening discusses the difficulty of perceiving moral improvement while vice still presses on the soul with equal weight, and criticises the doctrine that virtue arrives all at once, leaving everyone except the perfect sage equally wicked. Plutarch then argues that progress in philosophy is gradual and continuous rather than sudden, and begins to set out the signs by which such advance may be recognised, such as steady and unbroken effort in the daily struggle against vice.
grc.plutarch.romulus: A Greek prose biography of Rome's legendary founder by Plutarch, forming part of his collection of lives of notable figures. The opening chapters survey the conflicting ancient accounts of how the city received its name, from Pelasgian settlers and Trojan refugees to eponymous heroes such as Romus and Rhomus, and rehearse the genealogies and marvel-tales attached to the founder's conception. Plutarch then sets out the story of the Alban kings Numitor and Amulius, the violated Vestal's twin sons, and the exposure of the infants on the Tiber, where they are rescued and suckled by a she-wolf, citing Diocles of Peparethus and Fabius Pictor among his sources.
grc.plutarch.septem_sapientium_convivium: The Septem Sapientium Convivium ('Dinner of the Seven Sages'), a Greek dialogue by Plutarch preserved in the Moralia, recounts the banquet that Periander hosts at Lechaeum beside the sanctuary of Aphrodite, attended by the renowned wise men of Greece. The opening narrative follows the guests on their way to the feast, taking in Neiloxenus of Naucratis with his riddling commission from Bias, the celebrated story of the sacrificial animal whose best and worst portion is the tongue, and Thales's measurement of the Egyptian pyramid by its shadow. At table the company ranges over tyranny, flattery, and the art of agreeable dinner conversation, and the dialogue's accumulation of sententiae, exemplary anecdotes, and sympotic staging makes it a productive hunting ground for readers tracing gnomic wisdom and the literary tradition of the philosophical banquet.
grc.plutarch.sertorius: A Greek prose biography from Plutarch's Lives, the Sertorius pairs the Roman general Quintus Sertorius with Eumenes of Cardia. The opening chapter reflects on chance and on coincidental repetitions in myth and history, figures of the same name meeting like fates, Troy taken through horses, commanders alike in the loss of an eye, before drawing the comparison between the two subjects. The narrative then follows Sertorius from his Sabine upbringing and early service under Caepio and Marius against the Cimbri and Teutones, through his campaigns in Spain, the Marsic war, and the loss of an eye, portraying a commander distinguished by cunning, endurance, and hard fortune.
grc.plutarch.sulla: A Greek biography of the Roman general and dictator Lucius Cornelius Sulla, forming part of Plutarch's Lives. The work opens with Sulla's patrician but impoverished family background, his harsh complexion and famously convivial temperament, and his early rise through service under Marius in the war against Jugurtha, before going on to his later commands, his rivalry with Marius, the civil war, and his dictatorship. As elsewhere in the Lives, political and military narrative is interspersed with anecdote and reflection on character and fortune.
grc.plutarch.timoleon: Plutarch's Timoleon is a Greek prose biography of the Corinthian general and statesman Timoleon, written as one of the author's Lives and paired with that of Aemilius Paulus. After a preface on the moral benefit of dwelling on the deeds and virtues of great men, it recounts the disorders at Syracuse following the assassination of Dion and the restoration of Dionysius to power, the Syracusan appeal for aid to Corinth, and Timoleon's unexpected appointment to the command. The narrative then follows his expedition to Sicily, his liberation of Syracuse and other Greek cities from tyrants and Carthaginian domination, his temperate conduct in public life, and his final years and death.
grc.plutarch.παροιμίαι_αἷς_ἀλεξανδρεῖς_ἐχρῶν: A collection of Greek proverbs attributed to Plutarch and of uncertain date, presented as sayings in use among the Alexandrians. Each entry cites a proverb, states the circumstances or the class of persons in connection with whom it was employed, and often appends a short explanatory anecdote, mythological tale, or etymology. The material ranges from historical episodes, such as Aristagoras of Miletus before the Spartan ephors, to legends concerning figures like Tydeus, Heracles, Dionysus, and the Amazons.
grc.plutarch_pseudo.de_musica: A Greek dialogue on music transmitted under Plutarch's name but pseudonymous, and of uncertain date. It opens by ranking education above military achievement, then sets a symposium at which the host Onesicrates asks guests expert in music who first used the art, how time improved it, and to what uses it may be put. The speakers Lysias and Sotericus of Alexandria answer with accounts of mythical and early musicians such as Amphion, Linus, Thamyris, Demodocus and Phemius, and of early citharodic and aulodic composers such as Terpander, Clonas and Polymnestus, together with the musical nomoi ascribed to them. Lysias also observes that Platonic and Peripatetic philosophers, grammarians and harmonic theorists had all written on ancient music and on its corruption.
grc.polybius.histories: Polybius' Histories is a Greek prose universal history of how, in not quite fifty-three years, nearly the whole inhabited world came under the power of Rome. Opening with the 140th Olympiad, it takes in the Social War in Greece, the war over Coele-Syria between Antiochus and Ptolemy Philopator, and the Hannibalic war between Romans and Carthaginians, treating Italian, Libyan, Asian, and Greek affairs as strands of a single connected narrative and continuing the account of Aratus of Sicyon. Its programmatic preface contrasts Rome's rise with the earlier empires of the Persians, Spartans, and Macedonians and presents the study of history as training for political life and for bearing the reversals of fortune. Of the work's forty books, the first five survive complete, while the remainder is preserved in fragments of varying extent.
grc.pseudo_dicaearchus_messeniushe.dicaearch: A short Greek periegetic description transmitted under the name of Dicaearchus of Messene but assigned by its own title rather to an Athenaeus, of uncertain date. Composed in prose, it traces a journey that begins at Athens and proceeds through Attica and Boeotia by way of Oropus, Tanagra and Plataeae to Thebes. Its notices record road distances in stades and describe the appearance, fertility and monuments of each city, including the Odeon, the Parthenon, the unfinished Olympieion and the gymnasia of the Academy, Lyceum and Cynosarges at Athens, while sketching the manners of their inhabitants in a sharp, often satirical vein and quoting verses of Lysippus and Xenon. The preserved portion covers only Attica and Boeotia, breaking off amid the account of Thebes.
grc.pseudoarrianus.anonymi_arriani_ut_fertur: A Greek periplus, or coastal sailing guide, transmitted under the name of Arrian and ascribed to a Pseudo-Arrian, with both its author and its date uncertain. It moves station by station along the shores of the Erythraean Sea, describing the 'Barbarian country' south of Berenice with its fish-eating and cattle-eating peoples, Ptolemais of the Hunts, the emporium of Adulis and the Axumite hinterland under its ruler Zoskales, and the trans-Berbaric emporia of Avalites, Malao, Mundu and Mosylon. At each station it records distances in stades, the character of the anchorage, the local inhabitants, and the goods traded there, listing exports such as ivory, tortoiseshell, frankincense, myrrh and cassia and imports from Egypt such as textiles, metalware, wine, oil and coinage.
grc.pseudogalen.de_fasciis: De Fasciis ('On Bandages') is a short Greek medical treatise transmitted under the name of Galen; its actual author and date of composition are unknown. The work opens with an appeal to Hippocratic precepts on cleanliness, speed, and rhythm in the medical art, and defends the use of variegated, ornamental bandages against critics who cite Hippocratic passages to condemn such dressings as harmful. The remainder classifies bandages by material, woolen, linen, or leather, by configuration as rolled, split, or sewn, and by length, width, and manner of construction, naming specialized forms employed for fractures, head wounds, chest support, and other conditions.
grc.pseudogalen.de_remediis_parabilibus: De remediis parabilibus is a Greek medical handbook transmitted under Galen's name and classed as pseudo-Galenic, of uncertain date. Its preface states that it is written for people dwelling in the countryside, on the roads, or in remote places, who lack access to physicians and expensive drugs, and it therefore gathers treatments made from commonly available materials. The body of the work moves from the head downwards, offering remedies for complaints such as headaches arising from heat, cold, vapours, wine, and injuries, and occasionally reproducing prescriptions attributed to earlier physicians such as Archigenes.
grc.pseudogalen.introductio_seu_medicus: The Introduction, or Physician (Introductio seu Medicus) is a brief Greek treatise on medicine transmitted under Galen's name and of uncertain date. It opens with an account of how the art was discovered, tracing medicine from Asclepius' instruction by Apollo through early empirical use of drugs and herbs among Greeks and Egyptians, and noting findings credited to chance or to the dissection of corpses in Egyptian embalming. A second section distinguishes three principles of the art, discovery, the reduction of medicine to a system, and its teaching, before the longest part characterises the three schools of medicine, rationalist, empiricist, and methodist, setting out the doctrines, identifying marks, and therapeutic methods of each, including the methodist theory of commonalities.
grc.pseudolucian.δημοσθένους_ἐγκώμιον: A brief Greek dialogue preserved in the manuscripts of Lucian and ascribed to a pseudo-Lucianic author, of uncertain date. The narrator, walking through a stoa, falls in with the poet Thersagoras, who has risen before dawn to offer first-fruits of poetry to Homer on the poet's birthday, and the two begin debating whether Homer or Demosthenes merits the greater encomium. Their exchange weighs poetic inspiration against rhetorical power, sets phrases from Demosthenes' speeches beside Homeric verses, and remarks on the obscurity surrounding Homer's birthplace, parentage, and era, before Thersagoras concedes that the orator supplies a panegyrist with far richer material.
grc.pseudolucian.κυνικός: Κυνικός (The Cynic) is a short Greek dialogue in which the interlocutor Lycinus questions a Cynic philosopher about his barefoot, cloakless, and itinerant manner of life, and the Cynic defends his way of living against the charge of destitution. The exchange defines the sufficient as whatever meets each person's need, argues that the body and feet of the Cynic are no worse off than other men's, and contends that the gods and nature supply what is necessary while luxury breeds toil, expense, strife, and bloodshed. The work is transmitted under the name of Lucian but is attributed to pseudo-Lucian, and its date is uncertain.
grc.pseudolucian.λούκιος_ἢ_ὄνος: A short Greek comic narrative, transmitted under the name of Lucian, of uncertain authorship and date. The first-person narrator, Lucius, travels to Thessaly and lodges at Hypata with the miser Hipparchus, where his eagerness to witness magic brings him into contact with a supposed sorceress and her circle. After an affair with his host's maid Palaestra, he pursues the promised wonders of witchcraft, and the tale moves toward the transformation into an ass announced by its title, told in a colloquial and racy style.
grc.pseudolucian.φιλόπατρις_ἢ_διδασκόμενος: A brief Greek dialogue transmitted under Lucian's name and attributed to Pseudo-Lucian, the Philopatris, or The Disciple (Φιλόπατρις Ἢ Διδασκόμενος), of uncertain date. It stages a comic exchange between Triephon and Critias, in which Critias arrives distraught and nauseated by a 'great and bewildering discourse' he has heard from certain sophists, while Triephon teases and questions him. The pair then turn to ridicule the traditional gods, Zeus, Apollo, Poseidon, Hermes, Ares and Athena, enumerating their amours, deceits and quarrels, and the dialogue closes with a question about the purpose of Athena's Gorgon aegis.
grc.pseudolucian.ἀλκυών: The Ἀλκυών (Alcyon) is a short Greek dialogue bearing the name of Lucian but transmitted as a pseudo-Lucianic work, of uncertain date and written in the manner of a Platonic conversation between Socrates and Chaerephon. Walking by the shore at Phalerum, the two hear the mournful cry of the halcyon, and Socrates recounts the story of Alcyon, daughter of Aeolus, transformed into a kingfisher as she wandered the seas seeking her dead husband Ceyx, together with the legend of the halcyon days of midwinter calm granted to the bird's nesting. The dialogue then widens into a reflection on human ignorance and impotence, arguing that mortals, who cannot judge the great works of nature, should not dismiss as impossible the transformations wrought by divine power, before the pair turn back toward the city.
grc.rufus_of_ephesus.de_renum_et_vesicae_aff: A Greek medical treatise by Rufus of Ephesus, of uncertain date, on diseases of the kidneys and bladder. It opens by announcing that each ailment of those organs will be set out with its diagnosis and treatment, and observes that renal complaints are generally less acute but no less deadly than those of the bladder, which tend to strike children while kidney diseases belong mostly to the elderly. The body of the work describes the signs of renal inflammation, flank pain, inability to stand or walk, pains radiating toward the liver, bladder, hips and thighs, cold extremities, and changes in the urine, and then gives treatments in detail: rest and regimen, warm enemas, poultices including the plaster of Chrysippus, cupping, draughts of pain-relieving drugs, diuretic herbs and foods, and the reading of the urine as a diagnostic sign.
grc.rufus_soph.ars_rhetorica: A brief Greek rhetorical manual attributed to the sophist Rufus, of uncertain date. It defines rhetoric as the ability to frame any argument well and persuasively, divides rhetoric into four kinds, judicial, deliberative, encomiastic, and historical, and describes the parts of the speech, namely prooemium, narration, proof, and epilogue, together with the modes of narration and the sources of arguments. Each definition is illustrated with short specimen passages drawn from Attic oratory.
grc.scylax_of_caranda.periplus_scylacis: A Greek periplus of uncertain date attributed to Scylax of Caranda, presenting itself as a coastal survey running from the Pillars of Heracles in Europe to the Pillars of Heracles in Libya and the land of the great Ethiopians. The work proceeds people by people along the shoreline, listing the tribes, cities, and harbours of Iberia, Liguria, Etruria, Italy, Sicily, and the Adriatic coast as far as Illyria, and distinguishing Greek settlements from barbarian populations. Sailing distances between landmarks are given throughout in days and nights, alongside notes on islands, rivers, and notable features such as tombs and sanctuaries.
grc.septuaginta.abdias: Abdias, the book of Obadiah in the Septuagint, is the Greek version of a prophetic oracle attributed to the prophet Obadiah and counted among the Twelve Minor Prophets. Composed in Hellenistic prose, it reports the word of the Lord against Idumaea, reproaching Edom for its pride in its mountain strongholds, its violence against its brother Jacob, and its conduct in the day of Jerusalem's plunder by strangers. The oracle proclaims a day of the Lord upon all nations, retribution falling upon Edom's own head, deliverance on Mount Zion, and the house of Jacob consuming the house of Esau as fire consumes stubble, concluding that the kingdom shall be the Lord's. The Greek translation is anonymous, and its date within the Hellenistic period is uncertain.
grc.septuaginta.baruch: The Book of Baruch, transmitted in Greek within the Septuagint, is a prose biblical work of the Hellenistic period attributed in its opening verse to Baruch, son of Neriah, scribe to the prophet Jeremiah. Set in Babylon in the fifth year after the Chaldaeans captured and burned Jerusalem, it opens with the exiles by the river Sud gathering money to send to Jerusalem for sacrifices, incense, and prayers on behalf of Nebuchadnezzar and Baltasar, and directing that the accompanying book be read aloud in the house of the Lord at the feast. What follows is a lengthy communal confession of Israel's disobedience since the exodus from Egypt, with petitionary prayer asking God to turn aside his wrath, hear the suppliants, and deliver those scattered among the nations.
grc.septuaginta.bel_et_draco_translatio_grae: Bel and the Dragon survives in Greek as one of the additions to Daniel in the Septuagint, an anonymous prose biblical narrative of Hellenistic date. It recounts Daniel's exposure of the cult of Bel in Babylon, showing that the idol's offerings are eaten by its priests through secret passages, and his killing of the sacred dragon by feeding it a mixture of pitch, fat, and hair. Daniel is then cast into the lions' den, where the prophet Habakkuk, carried from Judaea by an angel, brings him food, and the story ends with Daniel's deliverance and the king's confession that the Lord alone is God.
grc.septuaginta.esdras_b: Esdras B is the second of the books of Esdras in the Septuagint, preserving in Greek the scriptural narrative of Ezra and Nehemiah. It opens with the decree of Cyrus of Persia permitting the exiles to return from Babylon to Jerusalem and to rebuild the temple, followed by long lists of returning households, priests, Levites, temple servants and contributions to the work. The narrative then recounts the rebuilding and dedication of the temple, the public reading of the law under Ezra, and Nehemiah's account of the refortification of Jerusalem's walls and of religious and social reforms. The translation is of Hellenistic date and its translator is anonymous.
grc.septuaginta.esther: The Greek Book of Esther preserved in the Septuagint is a Hellenistic prose version of the biblical Esther narrative, the work of an anonymous translator of uncertain date. It opens with Mordecai's dream of two dragons and of nations stirred to war against the righteous, then recounts his discovery of a conspiracy against King Artaxerxes, the great banquets at Susa, Queen Astin's refusal to appear before the king and her consequent deposition, and the search throughout the empire for a new queen. Esther, the daughter of Mordecai's uncle, whom he had brought up after the death of her parents, is taken into the royal household, and the narrative moves toward the hostility of Haman, who seeks to injure Mordecai and his people, whose deliverance the opening dream has foretold.
grc.septuaginta.habacuc: The Greek version of the biblical book of Habakkuk as it stands in the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures produced in the Hellenistic period by anonymous translators. The book records the prophet's laments and dialogues with God over the prospering of the wicked and the coming of the Chaldeans, followed by a series of woes against oppression and idolatry. It closes with a prayer attributed to Habakkuk, cast as a hymn with liturgical refrains.
grc.septuaginta.job: Job in its ancient Greek version as preserved in the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament translated from Hebrew during the Hellenistic period, the date of this particular translation being uncertain. The work opens with a prose narrative in which Job, a blameless and wealthy man of the land of Ausitis, loses his herds, his children, and his health after the devil questions the sincerity of his piety before the Lord. The arrival of the three royal friends Eliphaz, Baldad, and Sophar leads into the dialogues that occupy the rest of the book, beginning with Job's curse on the day of his birth.
grc.septuaginta.michaeas: Michaeas is the Book of Micah as it stands in the Septuagint, the Greek version of the Hebrew scriptures produced in the Hellenistic period and transmitted without named translators. The book presents itself as the word of the Lord addressed to Micah of Moresheth in the days of Joatham, Achaz, and Ezekias, kings of Judah, concerning Samaria and Jerusalem. Its oracles announce the Lord's descent in judgement upon the sins of Jacob and the house of Israel, denounce rapacious rulers, corrupt priests, and false prophets, and turn towards promises of gathering and restoration, culminating in the vision of the mountain of the Lord raised above the hills with law going forth from Zion.
grc.septuaginta.osee: Osee (Hosea) is the book of Hosea in the Hellenistic-era Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible known as the Septuagint, the first of the books of the Twelve Prophets. The book presents Hosea son of Beeri as prophesying in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel. It opens with the prophet's marriage to Gomer and the symbolic naming of his children, Jezreel, 'Not Pitied', and 'Not My People', before moving into oracles that denounce Israel's harlotry, idolatry, and faithlessness, alternating judgments with promises of healing, renewal of the covenant, and restoration.
grc.septuaginta.sapientia_salomonis: The Wisdom of Solomon (Sapientia Salomonis) is a Greek prose book of the Septuagint, a Hellenistic work of uncertain date and authorship that bears Solomon's name in its title. Its opening chapters exhort rulers and judges to love righteousness and seek God in uprightness of heart, contrasting the specious reasoning of the wicked with the immortality and vindication of the souls of the just. Later sections present Solomon's pursuit and praise of wisdom and recount Wisdom's activity in sacred history from creation through the exodus.
grc.septuaginta.sophonias: The Septuagint version of the biblical book of Zephaniah (Sophonias), a Greek prose translation of a Hebrew prophetic text made in the Hellenistic period and transmitted among the Twelve Minor Prophets. The book opens as the word of the Lord delivered to Zephaniah in the days of Josiah king of Judah, and comprises oracles of judgment on Judah and Jerusalem, warnings of the approaching day of the Lord, pronouncements against the Philistine cities, Moab, Ammon, Cush and Assyria, and closing promises of restoration for the humble remnant.
grc.sextus_empiricus.adversus_mathematicos: A Greek prose work of uncertain date by Sextus Empiricus, running to some 2,800 lines and comprising a sustained Pyrrhonian attack on the learned disciplines. After surveying Epicurean and Pyrrhonian hostility to formal education, including Epicurus' disparagement of his teacher Nausiphanes, it argues at length that nothing can be taught and then brings particular refutations against individual arts and sciences such as grammar, geometry and music. Rich in quotation, anecdote and doxographical material about earlier philosophers and schools, it serves as a central point of reference for tracing sceptical formulae and shared commonplaces across ancient literature.
grc.sophocles.electra: A Greek tragedy by Sophocles, of uncertain date, the Electra dramatizes Orestes' covert return to Mycenae and the revenge he takes with his sister Electra on Clytemnestra and Aegisthus for the murder of Agamemnon. The opening scene, set at dawn before the palace, shows Orestes with Pylades and an old attendant arranging a false report of his own death at the Pythian games, on which the plot turns; Electra's laments at Agamemnon's tomb, the recognition of the siblings, and the ensuing killings form the main action. The play alternates spoken dialogue with choral lyric and closes with the usurpers defeated within the royal house.
grc.soranus.vita_hippocratis_secundum_soranu: A Greek biography of Hippocrates attributed to Soranus, a physician whom the work itself identifies as a Coan, of otherwise uncertain date. It traces Hippocrates' descent from Heracles and Asclepius, places his birth on Cos in the time of the Peloponnesian War, and names his teachers, including Heracleides, Herodicus, Gorgias, and Democritus, citing earlier authorities such as Eratosthenes, Apollodorus, and Areius of Tarsus. The narrative recounts his travels and celebrated cures, at the courts of Perdiccas of Macedon and Artaxerxes, and at Abdera and in Illyria, along with the honors paid him by Greek states, his death and burial near Larissa, and traditions about his portrait. A concluding section discusses his sons Thessalus and Draco and the disputed authorship of the writings handed down under his name.
grc.strabo.geography: The Geography of Strabo is a prose treatise in Greek, transmitted in seventeen books, presenting a regional description of the inhabited world. The opening books set out the principles and usefulness of geography as a branch of philosophy, defend Homer as the founder of the discipline, and review earlier practitioners from Anaximander and Hecataeus through Eratosthenes, Polybius, and Posidonius. The remaining books proceed region by region across Europe, Asia, and Africa, recording rivers, mountains, cities, peoples, and political arrangements, with frequent criticism of earlier writers' accounts.
grc.strabo.strabonis_geographiae_chrestomath: A Greek chrestomathy attributed to Strabo, which presents the Geography in a sequence of short propositions each beginning with 'hoti' ('that...'). The entries open by presenting Homer as the first to undertake geography, explaining his encircling Ocean, its tides and currents, and the coastlines he names, and then set out the geometric, astronomical, and meteorological knowledge a geographer requires. Later propositions distinguish geography from chorography, discuss Eratosthenes and the place of poetry and myth in geographic writing, and weigh the respective ends of history, poetry, and fable in Homeric interpretation.
grc.theophrastus.concerning_odours: A short Greek treatise by Theophrastus examining odours as products of mixture, distinguishing pleasant from unpleasant smells and classifying them as watery, sweet, pungent, heavy, and the like. The work considers how smell accompanies taste and nourishment, the weakness of the human sense of smell compared with that of other animals, and the odours of plants, animals, and inanimate substances. Later portions describe the perfumer's craft of compounding unguents and aromatics, explain why perfume sweetens wine yet spoils food, and ask why flowers give off scent from a distance while roots and dry aromatics such as iris, nard, myrrh, and frankincense yield their odour only when crushed or burned.
grc.theophrastus.de_lapidibus: A short Greek prose treatise on stones, transmitted under the name of Theophrastus and of uncertain date. It distinguishes stones formed from earth from water-formed substances such as mined metals and classifies stones by color, smoothness, density, transparency, hardness, and similar qualities. Further chapters treat the behavior of stones in fire, whether they melt, burn, or resist both, and describe individual stones, including the Lydian and Heraclean touchstones used to assay gold and silver, gems such as the emerald, sapphire, and carbuncle, and celebrated building stones including Parian, Pentelic, Chian, and Theban marbles and Egyptian alabaster.
grc.theophrastus.de_sensu_et_sensibilibus: A short Greek treatise attributed to Theophrastus, De Sensu et Sensibilibus surveys ancient doctrines of sense perception, opposing the theory that like is known by like, held by Parmenides, Empedocles, and Plato, to the view that perception arises through opposites, associated with Anaxagoras and Heraclitus. The work then reviews the individual senses and subjects Empedocles' accounts of vision, hearing, smell, taste, and thought to sustained criticism. For readers of intertexts it is valuable chiefly as a doxographical repository that paraphrases and at times quotes earlier philosophers, supplying numerous verbal parallels to Presocratic and Platonic passages on cognition and the senses.
grc.theophrastus.fragmenta_varia_13190: A collection of fragmentary remains of Theophrastus of Eresus, the associate of Aristotle, transmitted as quotations embedded in the works of later ancient authors, among them Clement of Alexandria, Simplicius, and Themistius. The excerpts, drawn mostly from Theophrastus' physical and logical writings, treat sensation as the starting point of conviction, the principles of natural bodies, the division of things that come into being, the definition and kinds of motion, and the nature of place. Several preserve longer continuous passages, including the account of motion as an incomplete actuality of what exists in potentiality and the puzzle over whether motion has an end but no beginning.
grc.theophrastus.περί_ὀσμών: A short Greek treatise by Theophrastus, On Odours examines the nature, causes, and varieties of smell. It argues that odours arise from mixture, distinguishes pleasant from unpleasant scents and their qualitative kinds, and surveys smells in plants, animals, and inanimate substances, noting how weak the human sense of smell is compared with that of animals. Later sections discuss the artificial blending of perfumes and unguents, why wine takes scent while foods do not, and why flowers give off odour from afar whereas roots and dry aromatics such as myrrh and frankincense require crushing or burning to release theirs.
grc.theophrastus.περὶ_φυτῶν_αἰτιῶν: A Greek prose treatise by Theophrastus, the Περὶ Φυτῶν Αἰτιῶν examines the causes behind the ways plants come into being, grow and propagate. It opens from general principles, generation from seed, spontaneous growth, and the interplay of moisture, heat and dryness, and then takes up the particular modes of propagation of individual trees, including the palm, pine, fir, cypress, olive, vine and fig, explaining why each species admits some methods, such as slips, cuttings, branches or trunks, and not others. The work refers back to earlier inquiries into plants, presenting its account as a causal treatment of the phenomena there described.
grc.thucydides.peleponnesian_war: The Peloponnesian War is an ancient Greek prose history in eight books by the Athenian Thucydides, recounting the conflict between Athens and the Peloponnesian alliance. The opening announces the author's intention to record a war greater than any before it, and is followed by the so-called Archaeology, a survey of early Greek settlement and power, and by methodological remarks on evidence and causation. The narrative then traces the origins and course of the war, incorporating set speeches, the plague at Athens, and the Sicilian expedition, and it breaks off abruptly toward the close of the eighth book.
grc.aelius_herodianus.περι_καθολικης_προσῳδι: Περὶ Καθολικῆς Προσῳδίας (On General Prosody) is a Greek grammatical treatise on accentuation attributed to Aelius Herodianus, transmitted in an epitome that presents itself as an abridgement of Herodian's fuller treatment. A prefatory summary describes twenty books arranged by the terminations of accented words: nouns ending in various letters and syllables, verbs in -ω and -μι and their compounds, pronouns, articles, prepositions, adverbs and conjunctions, with a closing book on vowel quantities and breathings. The surviving exposition defines prosody and sets out rules for placing the acute and circumflex accents, treating enclitics, diacritics, word length and dialectal forms, and illustrating the rules chiefly from Homeric verses.
grc.aeschines_sp.ἐπιστολαί: Pseudepigraphic correspondence transmitted under the name of the Athenian orator Aeschines, the letters being of uncertain date. The collection presents itself as the exiled orator's writing from abroad: one letter to Philokrates recounts a storm-driven voyage by way of Ceos, Delos, and Rhodes; another rebukes Ctesiphon for taunting Aeschines over his downfall; another defends that downfall before the Athenian council and people; and a lengthy letter to Cleocrates answers his inquiries with an elaborate genealogical narrative reaching back to Pindar and culminating in the tale of the aged woman who entered the stadium at Olympia. The prose imitates the manner of Attic oratory.
grc.alcidamas.περὶ_σοφιστῶν: Περὶ Σοφιστῶν (On the Sophists) is a short Greek rhetorical treatise by Alcidamas, a sustained attack on written speeches composed in praise of extemporaneous speaking. It opens by deploring those called sophists who neglect general education and the ability to speak like ordinary men, boasting instead of rehearsed written discourses; the argument then runs that writing speeches is easy, requires leisure, and rarely meets the occasions of life, whereas skill in improvisation serves assemblies, lawcourts and private dealings alike. Examples drawn from weight-lifting, running and javelin-throwing illustrate the claim that one trained in the harder art of spontaneous eloquence can also compose well, while practice in writing leaves a speaker helpless without his notes.
grc.andocides.on_his_return: A short Attic oration by Andocides, in which the speaker addresses the Athenians in support of a proposal concerning his return from exile. He protests against opponents who make his past misfortunes a reproach, recounts how he was forced to choose between denouncing those who had wronged the city and the death of his innocent father, and argues that his ruin coincided with the city's recovery. He then sets out the services rendered to Athens since his exile, including the rowers, grain, and bronze he furnished while the Four Hundred held power, and asks to be judged humanely for what befell him.
grc.appian.foreign_wars: A Greek prose work transmitted under the name of Appian, the Foreign Wars presents a series of compressed summary accounts, many introduced by the excerpt-marker 'that' (ὅτι). It opens with Aeneas' flight from Troy and settlement on the Italian coast, follows the succession of the seven kings from Romulus to Tarquinius, and carries the narrative into the early Republic, with notices on figures such as Coriolanus and on Rome's wars with the Sabines, Latins, and Volscians. The material is arranged in thirteen book divisions in the corpus.
grc.aratus.phaenomena: A didactic poem in ancient Greek hexameters attributed to Aratus, the Phaenomena opens with an invocation of Zeus as the source of the signs by which human affairs are steered. Its first and longest part describes the constellations of the night sky, the two Bears, the Dragon coiled between them, the Crown, the Serpent-Bearer and many others, figure by figure, together with their positions relative to one another, to the poles and to the great circles of the heavens. The closing section treats weather signs, reading the sun, moon and stars for indications of rain, wind and fair sailing weather.
grc.archimedes.de_conoidibus_et_sphaeroidibu: A Greek mathematical treatise by Archimedes, composed as a letter and written in the Doric dialect, on solids of revolution generated by rotating conic sections: the right-angled and obtuse-angled conoids and the oblong and flat spheroids. After a preface explaining how the proofs were delayed and later rediscovered, it sets out definitions of the solids, their axes, vertices, bases and segments, and states the theorems to be established. The subsequent propositions determine the ratios between the volumes of segments cut from these solids by planes and the volumes of cones and other figures sharing the same bases and axes, results fundamental to Archimedes' method of measuring curvilinear volumes.
grc.archimedes.de_sphaera_et_cylindro: De Sphaera et Cylindro (On the Sphere and Cylinder) is a Greek geometrical treatise by Archimedes devoted to the surface and volume of the sphere and related solids. It opens with a prefatory letter announcing the principal results: that the surface of any sphere is four times its greatest circle, that the surface of a spherical segment equals a circle whose radius is the line from the segment's apex to the circumference of its base, and that a cylinder with base equal to the sphere's great circle and height equal to its diameter is one and a half times the sphere in both volume and surface; the letter also cites the earlier theorems of Eudoxus on the pyramid and cone. The body of the work states the axioms and assumptions on which the proofs rest, then proceeds through lemmas and propositions on curved lines and surfaces and on the measurement of spherical segments, cones, and cylinders.
grc.archimedes.liber_assumptorum: A short collection of geometrical propositions attributed to Archimedes, transmitted in Greek and written in the Doric forms typical of ancient mathematical prose. The propositions, each with enunciation and proof in the Euclidean manner, treat tangent circles, semicircles described on segments of a diameter, inscribed circles, and the curvilinear figure called the arbelos, establishing equalities of lengths, areas, and circles. The work closes with a problem set in the same style, to find the ratio between the diameter of a given semicircle and that of a circle inscribed in the arbelos.
grc.archytas_of_tarentum.fragmenta: Short fragments, in the Doric dialect, ascribed to the Pythagorean philosopher Archytas of Tarentum and preserved in quotations by Porphyry, Nicomachus, Iamblichus, Stobaeus and Theon of Smyrna. The largest piece, from a work on mathematical learning, ranks astronomy, geometry, arithmetic and music as kindred sciences and argues that swift motion produces high pitch and slow motion low. A further excerpt, from a work on music, sets out the arithmetic, geometric and harmonic means, while other passages present calculation as the discovery that ended strife and secured equality, and one notice refers to a treatment of the decad.
grc.aristophanes.plutus: Plutus is a Greek comedy by Aristophanes in which the god of wealth, Plutus, appears as a blind figure whom the oracle of Apollo directs the poor but honest Athenian Chremylus to follow. The opening exchange between Chremylus and his slave Cario establishes the central comic premise, that the god's blindness explains why riches go to rogues and sycophants rather than to the just. The play then follows the god's restoration of sight at the shrine of Asclepius and the comic consequences of the attempt to redistribute wealth among men.
grc.aristotle.de_memoria_et_reminiscentia: De Memoria et Reminiscentia is a short Greek treatise by Aristotle on memory and recollection. It opens by asking what memory is, through what cause it arises, and in which part of the soul it occurs, arguing that memory belongs neither to perception nor to opinion but is a lasting state or affection tied to imagination and to the perception of time, so that only the past is remembered while the present is perceived and the future hoped for. The treatise then distinguishes good rememberers from those skilled at recollecting, accounts for forgetfulness in the very young and the very old, and goes on to examine reminiscence and how what has been forgotten comes to be recovered.
grc.aristotle.economics: A brief Greek treatise on household management (oikonomia) attributed to Aristotle and of uncertain date. It opens by distinguishing economics from politics, since the household rather than the city is its subject, and argues that economics is prior to politics in point of origin. The surviving discussion covers the proper conduct of husband and wife, the bearing and rearing of children, the acquisition of property with agriculture ranked first among natural means, and the keeping and treatment of slaves, with quotations from Hesiod and a Pythagorean saying along the way.
grc.aristotle.metaphysics: Aristotle's Metaphysics is a Greek prose treatise on first philosophy, concerned with being, substance, and the causes and principles of things. Its opening book begins from the claim that all humans by nature desire to know and traces the growth of knowledge from sensation through memory and experience to art and science. Wisdom is there characterized as the knowledge of first causes and principles, more exact and more instructive than the other sciences and pursued for its own sake rather than for practical ends.
grc.aristotle.res_publica_atheniensium: The Res Publica Atheniensium, known in Greek as the Athenaion Politeia, is a treatise on the constitution of Athens attributed to Aristotle. Its text opens with the Cylonian affair and Epimenides' purification of the city, then surveys the aristocratic constitution that preceded Draco, the offices of king, polemarch and archon, and Draco's written laws with their property qualifications for office. It goes on to describe the strife between the nobles and the common people that led to Solon's appointment as arbitrator, and records Solon's measures, including the cancellation of debts on the person, the seisachtheia, together with the accusations of profiteering levelled against him and his associates.
grc.aristotle.rhetoric: A Greek prose treatise by Aristotle on the art of persuasion, opening with the declaration that rhetoric is the counterpart of dialectic and that both concern matters which lie within the grasp of all people without any specialised science. The work criticises earlier handbooks for attending to matters outside the case at hand, arousing pity, anger and prejudice in the judges, while neglecting the technical proofs, and argues that the core of the art is the enthymeme, a form of rhetorical syllogism. Rhetoric is defended as useful because truth and justice naturally prevail over their opposites, and because a speaker must be able to argue either side of a question in order to refute unsound argument. The treatise goes on to survey the kinds of oratory, the sources of proof in character, emotion and reasoning, and questions of style and arrangement.
grc.aristotle.virtues_and_vices: A short Greek ethical treatise attributed to Aristotle and transmitted in the Aristotelian corpus, of uncertain date. Dividing the soul into rational, spirited, and appetitive parts in the Platonic manner, it assigns a virtue to each, practical wisdom to the rational, gentleness and courage to the spirited, temperance and self-control to the appetitive, and a matching vice, adding justice, liberality, and magnanimity as virtues of the soul as a whole. The work then defines each virtue in turn, cataloguing its characteristic activities, accompanying states, and effects, with parallel definitions of the corresponding vices. Its manner is compressed and handbook-like, built from brief definitions rather than extended argument.
grc.aristotle.περί_χρωμάτων: A short Greek treatise on colour attributed to Aristotle and of uncertain date. It defines the simple colours as those accompanying the four elements, air and water white by nature, fire and the sun yellow, earth white but appearing multicoloured through dyeing, and treats black as arising when the elements change into one another, with darkness a privation of light rather than a colour in itself. Other hues, such as the purplish and the wine-dark, are explained as products of mixture, with the varying strength of sunlight accounting for phenomena like shadows, the sea's purple sheen, and the sky's colours at dawn and dusk. The account closes by insisting that colours be analysed from the interplay of reflected rays rather than by the painter's method of mixing pigments.
grc.aristotle.ἐκ_τοῦ_περὶ_ἀκουστῶν: A short Greek treatise on voice and hearing, of uncertain date, transmitted under the title 'From the work On Things Heard' and attributed to Aristotle. It argues that voices and sounds arise from the impact of breath and of air striking against bodies, and explains how the size, shape, and condition of the lungs, windpipe, and mouth account for differences among the voices of humans, birds, and other animals. The closing portion treats the propagation of sound through the air and the perception of near and distant sounds, illustrated by examples drawn from trumpets, tubes, and drawing.
grc.arius_didymus.liber_de_philosophorum_sec: An ancient Greek epitome of the doctrines of the philosophical sects, preserved in the anthology of Stobaeus and transmitted under the name of Arius Didymus. The epitome sets out definitions and doctrines concerning happiness, character, and passion as held by successive thinkers, among them Xenophanes, the followers of Plato, the Stoic Zeno, Aristotle and the Peripatetics, and the Academic Philo of Larissa. One section reproduces the division of philosophy attributed to Philo, treating the exhortation to philosophy, the parts concerned with goods and evils and with the end, and the discussion of ways of life.
grc.callistratus.statuarum_descriptiones: A collection of ekphraseis, rhetorical prose descriptions of individual statues, attributed to Callistratus and of uncertain date, transmitted with the works of Philostratus. The pieces treat celebrated sculptures, including a stone Satyr in a cave near Egyptian Thebes, a Bacchante by Scopas, and the bronze Eros of Praxiteles, dwelling on the pose, material, and lifelike quality of each figure. Each description pairs formal account of the artwork with reflection on the artist's divine inspiration and on art's power to endow inert stone or metal with movement, breath, and feeling.
grc.chionis_epistulae.epistulae: A short collection of Greek letters attributed to Chion and of uncertain date, composed in the persona of a son writing to his father from stops on his travels around Byzantium and the Pontus. The letters contain paternal exhortation to virtue, an introduction of the merchant Thrason, and an extended narrative of an encounter with Xenophon and the Greek mercenaries who had marched with Cyrus against Artaxerxes. The writer repeatedly reflects on the compatibility of philosophy with military valour and announces his intention to sail to Athens and devote himself to philosophy.
grc.claudius_ptolemaeus.musica: A short Greek treatise on music attributed to Claudius Ptolemaeus. It opens with the numerical ratios of the cosmic system, assigning interval numbers to the spheres of the seven planets and the fixed stars, and then gives definitions of music, melody, harmony, and rhythm, classifies the rhythmic feet into dactylic, iambic, and paeonic genera with their magnitudes, and recounts the qualities proper and common to fire, air, water, and earth. Further passages divide the tone into twelve parts after the values of Eratosthenes, discuss the rhythmizing of word, melody, and bodily movement, and credit Hermes with the invention of the seven-stringed lyre. The work closes with a list of the standing notes of the world system, each set down with its number, its position in the tetrachords, and its planetary sphere.
grc.clement_of_alexandria.excerpta_ex_theodo: A short Greek compilation of excerpts and notes preserving the scriptural exegesis of the Valentinian teacher Theodotus, of uncertain date and attributed to Clement of Alexandria as excerptor. The excerpts expound gospel passages, the Saviour's last words from the cross, the vision on the mountain, and the Prologue of John, in Valentinian terms, treating the spiritual seed of the elect, the Saviour's descent through the flesh, and the distinction between the called and the chosen. Interspersed among the Valentinian readings are brief notes in which the compiler states his own dissenting view.
grc.cleonides.εἰσαγωγὴ_ἁρμονική: The Eisagōgē Harmonikē ('Introduction to Harmonics') is a short Greek treatise on music theory attributed to Cleonides and of uncertain date. It defines harmonics as the theoretical and practical science of the nature of the harmonised and divides the subject into seven parts: notes, intervals, genera, systems, tone, modulation, and melopoeia. The work defines each of these in turn, distinguishing the three genera (diatonic, chromatic, and enharmonic), enumerating the notes of the perfect system under their traditional names, and classifying notes as fixed or movable and intervals as consonant or dissonant, simple or compound, and rational or irrational.
grc.demades.on_the_twelve_years: A Greek forensic speech bearing the title On the Twelve Years and attributed to the Athenian orator Demades, of uncertain date. The speaker, standing trial at Athens, defends his political career against charges of slander and of bribery by the Macedonians, appealing to the jurors for an impartial verdict and recounting his humble birth and his conduct in public life. He claims credit for negotiating the peace with Philip of Macedon, which he says recovered two thousand prisoners and a thousand Athenian citizens without ransom or embassy, denies that he proposed Philip's honours from corruption, and closes by describing the exhaustion of Athens and Sparta after Leuctra amid the rise of Alexander.
grc.demosthenes.against_apatourius: A forensic speech from the corpus of Demosthenes' private orations, of uncertain date, written for an Athenian merchant answering a charge brought by Apatourius in a maritime commercial suit. The speaker enters a paragraphē, or preliminary objection, arguing that all transactions between himself and Apatourius had been fully discharged: he had guaranteed a loan raised through the banker Heracleides for the Byzantine exile Parmenon, secured the debt by the sale of a ship and its slave children, and settled all accounts before witnesses. The opening sets out the laws governing commercial litigation and contracts of paragraphē, and the narrative of the dealings is supported by witness testimony.
grc.demosthenes.against_aphobus_2: A forensic speech in Attic Greek, the second of Demosthenes' orations against Aphobus, one of the guardians appointed over the estate left by the speaker's father. The speaker undertakes to refute Aphobus' claim that the grandfather had owed a debt to the public treasury and that the father had refused to let out the house for fear of it, arguing from the family's liturgies, the symmoria assessment, and the openly declared fortune that the estate was large and exposed to no such risk. He accuses the guardians of plundering the inheritance, suppressing the will, and acting each in his own interest, and closes by summoning witness testimonies concerning the workshop leased to Therippides, the slaves, and other property said to have been withheld.
grc.demosthenes.against_callicles: 'Against Callicles' is a short Athenian forensic speech transmitted among the private orations of Demosthenes, of uncertain date. The speaker, a litigant in a private suit, answers his neighbour Callicles' charge that a retaining wall built by the speaker's father along a ravine diverted rainwater onto Callicles' land; he contends that the plot belonged to his family from before his birth, that it is planted with vines and figs and holds ancestral tombs rather than being a watercourse, and that Callicles and his kinsmen raised no protest for more than fifteen years after the wall was built. The plea closes by appealing to the opposing party's own past inaction and to witness depositions confirming the nature of the property.
grc.demosthenes.against_evergus_and_mnesibul: A short forensic speech of Demosthenes, addressed to a panel of dicasts, in which the speaker prosecutes Evergus and Mnesibulus for false witness. The disputed testimony was given in an earlier suit between the speaker and Theophemus over an assault, and concerned a challenge to hand over a slave woman for examination under torture before the arbitrator Pythodorus. The speaker argues that the defendants' repeated refusal to produce the woman exposes their evidence as false, and he recounts the challenges, proceedings, and depositions bearing on the case.
grc.demosthenes.against_nicostratus: An Athenian forensic oration in Greek, transmitted among the private speeches of the Demosthenic corpus and attributed to Demosthenes, of uncertain date. The speech is delivered in court by a plaintiff who has made a formal inventory (apographē) of enslaved persons belonging to Nicostratus of Arethusa, and who presents the registration as redress for injury rather than malicious prosecution. It recounts the former friendship and neighbourly dealings between the two men, the speaker's trierarchy, Nicostratus's capture and ransoming at Aegina, and the loans and gifts surrounding that ransom, which now form the substance of the quarrel.
grc.demosthenes.against_spudias: A forensic speech of the Demosthenic corpus, attributed to the Athenian orator Demosthenes and of uncertain date, composed in Attic Greek and addressed to Athenian judges. The speaker, husband of the elder daughter of Polyeuctus, prosecutes Spudias, who married the younger daughter, over an unpaid thousand drachmae of a forty-mina dowry secured by a mortgage on Polyeuctus' house. The speech recounts the marriage settlements and subsequent family quarrels, cites witnesses, laws, and documents left by Polyeuctus, and answers the defendant's counter-charges concerning a slave, a phiale, and other appraised property.
grc.demosthenes.against_zenothemis: Against Zenothemis is an Athenian courtroom speech preserved in the corpus of Demosthenes, of uncertain date, arising from a dispute over maritime commerce. The speaker answers Zenothemis's preliminary challenge (paragraphē) that the case is inadmissible, invoking the laws governing suits between shipowners and merchants, and rejects the claim that he has seized freight on the strength of a loan Zenothemis allegedly made to the shipowner Hegestratos. He recounts how Hegestratos of Massalia, who had borrowed money at Syracuse against grain aboard his vessel, plotted with Zenothemis to scuttle the ship and defraud the lenders, and how Hegestratos drowned when caught in the act. The speech closes with denunciations of Zenothemis and of a clique of unscrupulous men in the Piraeus, naming Aristophon, an envoy engaged by the speaker, as a party to the alleged intrigue.
grc.demosthenes.philippic_2: A short deliberative oration in Attic Greek against Philip II of Macedon, addressed to the Athenians and attributed to Demosthenes, the fourth-century BC Athenian statesman and orator; it is the second of the so-called Philippics. The speaker complains that repeated denunciations of Philip have produced words but no action, surveys the gains Philip has made since the peace, including control of Phocis and favour with Thebes, Argos and Messene, and argues that only deeds rather than speeches can check his ambitions. In support of the appeal, the speech contrasts Athenian steadfastness against the Persian invader with the conduct of the ancestors of Thebes and Argos, and closes by anticipating and rebutting the claim that Philip's earlier choices rested on grounds of justice.
grc.demosthenes.reply_to_philip: A short deliberative oration addressed to the Athenian assembly, transmitted under Demosthenes' name with the title Reply to Philip. The speaker contends that Philip of Macedon has not made peace with Athens but merely postponed the war, and that the Athenians should neither dread his power nor shrink from opposing him, since his perjured breach of the settlement has forfeited divine support. The speech goes on to survey Philip's strained relations with the Thessalians, Thebans, and his Greek allies, the prospect of Persian money and military aid for Athens, and the internal weakness of the Macedonian regime, whose subjects serve unwillingly and whose companions live in fear of the king.
grc.dinarchus.against_philocles: A Greek courtroom oration by Dinarchus, prosecuting Philocles for bribery and treachery in connection with the money Harpalus brought into Attica. The speaker recalls that Philocles, though repeatedly condemned by the council of the Areopagus and sworn to keep Harpalus out of the Peiraeus, took bribes while holding the generalship over Mounichia and the ship-sheds, and now stands trial only for the assessment of his penalty. Treating the charges as admitted rather than disputed, the speech weighs fine, death, and confiscation, and presses for the harshest sentence, warning that a commander who sells his trust would as readily betray the fleet, the harbors, and the city itself.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_compositio: A Greek rhetorical treatise by Dionysius of Halicarnassus on the arrangement (synthesis) of words, addressed as a gift to the young Rufus Metilius.
