The prefatory letter contrasts word choice with word arrangement as the two branches of stylistic training, presents the work as the first adequate treatment of its subject, and defines composition as the placement of the parts of speech beside one another, sketching how philosophers and Stoics counted those parts from three up to many. The treatise then undertakes to explain the nature and power of composition, what it aims at, its principal varieties and the character of each, and the agreeable, honey-flavoured quality in prose that imitates poetic construction.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_isaeo: A short rhetorical treatise in Greek by Dionysius of Halicarnassus on the Attic orator Isaeus, a pupil of Isocrates and teacher of Demosthenes. The essay reviews what ancient writers record of Isaeus's life and then characterises his style as forensic and largely modelled on that of Lysias, setting out the similarities and differences between the two in diction, argumentation, and arrangement. To illustrate the comparison it quotes the opening of Isaeus's speech on behalf of Eumathus, a metic banker in Athens who was being claimed as a slave.
grc.dionysius_of_halicarnasus.ars_rhetorica: The Ars Rhetorica (Art of Rhetoric) of Dionysius of Halicarnassus is a Greek prose treatise on rhetoric. The opening section takes the form of counsel addressed to one Echecrates on composing the panegyric speech delivered at a festival, proceeding from praise of the presiding god through praise of the city, the contest, the victor's crown, and the presiding patron, and ending with advice on diction that blends plain narration with the antithetical manner of Isocrates. A personal conclusion offers the whole to the addressee as a gift on the occasion of his approaching marriage.
grc.epictetus.fragments: A collection of short Greek philosophical fragments attributed to Epictetus, presented under headings naming Arrian and Rufus as sources and drawn from contexts such as Arrian's hortatory conversations, the Encheiridion, and records of Epictetus' sayings. The items are mostly brief discourses, anecdotes, and maxims on themes including the distinction between what is and is not within one's control, the right use of impressions, friendship, and acceptance of the order of the cosmos. Socrates, Lycurgus, Agrippinus, Nero, and the Delphic precept 'know thyself' number among the figures and topics invoked, and several entries are single-line sayings. The fragments are of uncertain date.
grc.euripides.medea: Medea is a Greek tragedy by Euripides, composed for the Athenian stage in the later fifth century BC and written mainly in iambic trimeters interspersed with lyric choral odes. The play takes up the myth of the Colchian princess who betrayed her father's house to help Jason win the Golden Fleece and, after he abandons her for the daughter of Creon, king of Corinth, takes revenge by destroying his new bride, Creon himself, and the two sons she bore him. The action occupies a single day in Corinth, opening with a nurse's report of Medea's distress and closing with the heroine aloft in the chariot of the Sun bearing her children's bodies; the speaking parts belong to Medea, Jason, Creon, Aegeus of Athens, a nurse and tutor, and a chorus of Corinthian women.
grc.euripides.suppliants: A Greek tragedy by Euripides. The Suppliants stages the appeal of the Argive mothers of the Seven against Thebes, who with Adrastus take refuge as suppliants at the altar of Demeter and Persephone at Eleusis, begging that their sons' unburied bodies be recovered from Thebes; Aethra persuades her son Theseus to demand the corpses, and after his victory over the Thebans the dead receive their funeral rites. The action includes laments over the fallen, a formal debate between Theseus and a Theban herald on kingship and democracy, the suicide of Evadne on her husband Capaneus's pyre, and a closing appearance by Athena.
grc.galen.de_comate_secundum_hippocratem: A brief Greek treatise by Galen on the sense of the term kōma in Hippocrates. It surveys the explanations offered by earlier interpreters, a sinking into sleep, sleep itself, a drowsy heaviness, or a lethargic state, and then tests each against Hippocrates' own wording, citing case histories and outbreak descriptions, especially from the third book of the Epidemics, where kōma appears together with sleeplessness. Galen argues that Hippocrates uses kōma for a heavy drooping (kataphora) of two kinds, one accompanied by sleep and one not, so that the word cannot simply denote sleep or drowsiness.
grc.galen.de_compositione_medicamentorum_sec: An Ancient Greek pharmacological treatise by the physician Galen, belonging to his work on the composition of remedies according to the affected parts of the body, the De Compositione Medicamentorum Secundum Locos. The book opens a survey of drug treatment running from head to foot, taking up the scalp and hair first: it discusses the causes and naming of conditions such as alopecia, ophiasis, depigmentation and baldness, prescribes purgative and depletive regimens, and lists simple drugs, including thapsia, euphorbium, laurel oil and aged olive oil, with their heating and drawing powers, dosages and methods of preparation. Earlier medical writers are cited alongside accounts of Galen's own clinical cases and observations on the failures of remedies applied without method.
grc.galen.de_experientia_medica: De Experientia Medica is a Greek polemic by the physician Galen directed against the Empiric school of medicine and its claim that expertise arises from the repeated observation of similar cases. Cast largely as a dialogue, the work argues that the medical art is secured by evident phenomena rather than by accumulated experience, and presses its opponents to state how many observations would suffice to establish a technical theorem. In the course of the argument the speaker adduces Democritus on the testimony of the senses and Plato's dictum that what is without reason is mere practice and experience, not art.
grc.galen.de_simplicium_medicamentorum_tempe: A Greek pharmacological treatise by Galen, De Simplicium Medicamentorum Temperamentis ac Facultatibus sets out how single, uncompounded drugs act on the body through the primary qualities of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. The opening argument defines the terms pharmakon and dynamis, distinguishes simple from compound medicines, and rejects the position of the Sceptic philosophers and the Empiric doctors that such powers are unknowable, holding instead that they arise from the four elemental qualities. Galen lays down a method of testing each drug by its observed effect on the body to which it is administered, insisting that judgement rest on the substance itself rather than on colour, texture, or incidental properties. Examples drawn from substances such as pepper, hellebore, henbane, and mandrake illustrate the classification of simple drugs by their degrees of heating, cooling, drying, and moistening.
grc.galen.de_venae_sectione_adversus_erasist: A short Greek polemical treatise by Galen against Erasistratus on the subject of venesection. Galen asks why Erasistratus, otherwise so meticulous as to record recipes for vegetables and poultices, nowhere discussed phlebotomy, a remedy he shows to have been practised and praised by Hippocrates, Diocles, Euryphon and the other ancient physicians. After reviewing and dismissing the conjectures of the pupils of Chrysippus of Cnidus about Erasistratus' reasons for avoiding the procedure, Galen sets out Erasistratus' doctrines that the arteries contain pneuma and the veins blood, that fever and inflammation arise when blood is driven from the veins into the arteries, and that depletion is required in their treatment. Quoting Erasistratus' own prescriptions from his work on fevers, Galen argues that they tacitly concede the value of emptying the veins, the remaining dispute being only over the manner in which this should be done.
grc.galen.natural_faculties: A Greek medical treatise by Galen on the natural faculties, the powers by which living things grow, are nourished, and perform their other natural works. The opening distinguishes the psychical functions of sensation and voluntary movement from the natural functions of growth and nutrition, defines terms such as rest, motion, alteration, change of place, and increase and decay, and sets out an inquiry into by what faculties the works of nature are produced. The argument separates an activity from its completed product, with digestion, the transport of nutriment, and the conversion of food into blood as examples, and argues against those who dismiss the transformation of food into blood as mere deception of the senses.
grc.galen.protrepticus: Galen's Protrepticus is a hortatory treatise in Greek prose on the superiority of a life devoted to reason and the arts. It opens by asking whether reason belongs to the so-called irrational animals, concludes that humans alone possess logos and are receptive to every craft, and condemns entrusting one's life to Fortune, depicted by the ancients as blind and unstable, holding a rudder and standing on a rolling sphere. Against her it sets Hermes, lord of speech and discoverer of every art, whose followers form an ordered chorus of geometers, astronomers, physicians, philosophers, and other craftsmen, exemplified by Socrates, Homer, Hippocrates, and Plato and illustrated by the tale of Aristippus shipwrecked on the Syracusan shore.
grc.galen.synopsis_librorum_suorum_de_pulsib: A short Greek synopsis by the physician Galen of his own four treatises on the pulse, which together ran to sixteen books. Galen explains in the preface that inaccurate epitomes of his writings made by others compelled him to compose the summary himself, beginning with the treatise on the differences of pulses. The portion preserved here defines the pulse as the perceptible dilatation and contraction of an artery and classifies its differences by size, speed, tone, and the hardness or softness of the vessel, enumerating twenty-seven kinds in respect of dimension alone.
grc.hanno.periplus_hannonis: A short Greek narrative of a Carthaginian sea voyage, attributed to Hanno and of uncertain date. Opening with the Carthaginians' decree that Hanno should sail beyond the Pillars of Heracles to found cities of the Libyphoenicians, the account follows a fleet of sixty penteconters along the African coast: colonies such as Thymiaterion and Kerne are established, and the voyagers meet the Lixitae, Troglodytes and other peoples, pass burning lands and fiery torrents, and sight a great mountain called the Chariot of the Gods. The narrative closes with the capture of three hairy wild women whom the interpreters call 'gorillas', after which shortage of provisions turns the expedition back to Carthage.
grc.hippocrates.de_articulis: A Greek medical treatise on the joints, attributed to Hippocrates and of uncertain date. The work concerns dislocations and their reduction, opening with the shoulder: it distinguishes genuine dislocation from the forward prominence of the head of the humerus caused by wasting of the flesh around the joint, a condition by which physicians are easily misled. Successive chapters set out methods of replacing a dislocated shoulder, among them reduction with the physician's hands, head and knees, reduction by the heel with a ball fitted into the armpit, hoisting the patient over the operator's shoulder, the use of a lever, and reduction by means of a ladder. Throughout, rival techniques are weighed for safety and conformity to nature, with indication of the circumstances in which each is to be employed.
grc.hippocrates.de_morbis_popularibus: The De Morbis Popularibus is a Greek prose medical treatise attributed to Hippocrates and of uncertain date. It records the seasonal weather conditions at Thasos, winds, rains, snows, and droughts, together with the outbreaks of disease that attended them, describing symptoms such as fevers, coughs, throat inflammations, dysentery, and wasting illnesses, with notes on crises, critical days, and the deaths or recoveries of patients. Written in the Ionic dialect, the work combines general observations on the character of successive epidemics with detailed case histories in the manner of the Hippocratic corpus.
grc.hippocrates.de_officina_medici: De Officina Medici (Greek Peri iētreiou) is a short Greek surgical treatise attributed to Hippocrates and of uncertain date. In a compressed, note-like style it sets out the conduct of surgery in the physician's workshop, covering the operator's posture relative to the patient and the light, the training and use of both hands, the fingernails, instruments, and the roles of assistants. A substantial closing portion deals with bandaging, specifying the shapes of bandage, the direction of turns, and the padding and support suited to different parts of the body.
grc.hippocrates.epidemiarum: The Epidemics is a Greek medical treatise of uncertain date, attributed to Hippocrates and transmitted as part of the Hippocratic Corpus. It records the seasonal weather and prevailing disease 'constitutions' of particular years and places, most famously on Thasos, describing the symptoms, courses, and outcomes of fevers, phthisis, and other affections. Interspersed with these general accounts are individual case histories, noted day by day, which follow patients from the onset of illness through crisis to death or recovery.
grc.hippocrates.prorrheticon_i: Prorrheticon I, the first of the Prorrhetic treatises in the Hippocratic Corpus, is a Greek work of prognostic medicine transmitted under Hippocrates' name, though its date and authorship are uncertain. It consists of a long series of very brief aphoristic entries, most of a single clause, setting out symptoms of acute disease, phrenitic delirium, sleeplessness, a dry or darkened tongue, abnormal urine, sweats, loss or change of voice, and assigning each an outcome, usually a fatal one. Several entries cite individual patients by name, some identified as from Cos, and the collection as a whole is concerned with the signs and crises of acute fevers.
grc.libanius.declamations_1-12: A collection of the first twelve declamations in Greek by the sophist Libanius, presented in a single book. Declamations of this kind are imagined courtroom speeches composed for rhetorical display, in which the speaker assumes an assigned historical persona. The opening speech casts an unnamed friend of Socrates as defense advocate before the Athenian jurors, answering the prosecution of Anytus, Meletus, and Lycon and arguing that to condemn the philosopher would bring shame on the city. The speeches that follow continue the same practice of fictitious pleading in dramatic situations drawn from the past.
grc.lucian.de_astrologia: De Astrologia is a very short Greek prose treatise by Lucian of Samosata, written throughout in an archaizing Doric (Laconian) dialect. The speaker defends astrology against learned detractors and recounts the art's legendary descent: the Ethiopians first observed the moon and the wandering stars and handed on an incomplete lore to the Egyptians, who fixed the measures of months and years, divided the heavens among twelve animal-shaped signs, and drew from it their sacred animal cults, while the Libyans with the oracle of Ammon and the Babylonians likewise took up the discipline. The closing section brings the art to the Greeks through Orpheus, whose seven-stringed lyre was thought to mirror the harmony of the planets and survives in a constellation, through the teaching of Tiresias on male and female stars, and through the astronomical rivalry of Atreus and Thyestes that set the golden ram in the sky.
grc.lucian.de_parasito_sive_artem_esse_paras: A short Greek comic dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, transmitted under the title De Parasito sive Artem Esse Parasiticam ('The Parasite, or That Parasitism Is an Art'). Tychiades questions his acquaintance Simon, who defends his life of sponging on dinner invitations as a genuine technē, offering a formal definition of the art and boasting that it surpasses music, geometry, rhetoric, even the sculptor's craft in difficulty and skill. The mock-technical argument cites Euripides and Plato as authorities while parodying the manner of philosophical treatises on the parts of an art.
grc.lucian.dialogi_deorum: Dialogi Deorum (Dialogues of the Gods) is a collection of short comic dialogues in Greek prose by Lucian of Samosata. The pieces stage conversations among Olympian deities, Zeus, Hermes, Hephaestus, Eros, Prometheus, in colloquial language, reworking mythological episodes such as Prometheus' release from the Caucasus, Zeus' quarrels with Eros over his love affairs, the rescue of Io from Argus, and the abduction of Ganymede. Most dialogues pair Zeus with a single interlocutor, compressing the myths into brief exchanges that deflate divine dignity and expose the gods' petty motives.
grc.lucian.herodotus: A short Greek prose piece by Lucian of Samosata, a rhetorician and satirist writing in Greek in the second century CE. The work opens with a wish to rival Herodotus and recounts how Herodotus recited his Histories at the Olympic festival, thereby winning a panhellenic reputation, and how other sophists and orators likewise used the games to become known. An extended passage describes the painting of the marriage of Alexander and Roxane by the painter Aetion, whose art so pleased the Hellanodic judge Proxenidas that he made Aetion his son-in-law. The piece closes with Lucian explaining that he, like Herodotus, chose a great gathering at which to display his own works, in his case before an audience in Macedonia.
grc.lucian.hesiod: A short comic dialogue in Greek attributed to Lucian, in which an unnamed interlocutor reproaches Hesiod for claiming inspiration from the Muses while offering little real foreknowledge of the future in his poetry. Hesiod answers that the divine gift was spent on the origins of the gods and on practical farming precepts rather than prophecy, and defends the poet's freedom against captious demands for exactness. The exchange closes with the questioner mockingly observing that farmers can predict the obvious consequences of rain, drought, and carelessness at least as well as any prophet.
grc.lucian.imagines: The Imagines is a brief Greek dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, cast as a conversation between Lycinus and Polystratus. Opening with jests about a beholder petrified as by the Gorgon, it has Lycinus undertake to describe an unnamed woman of Ionia whose beauty has left him speechless. At Polystratus' prompting he summons the great sculptors of the past, Praxiteles, Alcamenes, Phidias, Calamis, and builds up an encomiastic portrait from head to foot, taking from each famous statue, such as the Cnidian Aphrodite, the Lemnian Athena, and Calamis' Sosandra, its finest feature as the model for a part of her person. The work unfolds as a sustained rhetorical description (ekphrasis) that moves part by part through the ideal beauty it constructs in words.
grc.lucian.phalaris: A short Greek prose piece by Lucian of Samosata, cast as the address of envoys sent by Phalaris, tyrant of Acragas, to the Delphians concerning the dedication of the bronze bull. Speaking in the tyrant's voice, the speaker recounts how he took power to save a faction-torn city, describes his mild and public-spirited rule, and defends his punishments of conspirators as necessary rather than cruel, seeking to overturn the reputation handed down by his enemies. The work belongs among Lucian's rhetorical pieces on historical themes, an apologia composed for a figure proverbial for savagery.
grc.lucian.pro_lapsu_inter_salutandum: A brief Greek piece by Lucian, written as a mock apology in which the speaker, having embarrassed himself by greeting an acquaintance in the morning with the wrong formula, resolves to compose a consolation for his slip of the tongue. The work surveys Greek salutations, principally chairein, eu prattein, and hygiainein, tracing their occurrence from Homeric epic, tragedy, and comedy through historical letters and the sayings of figures such as Phidippides, Cleon, and Nicias. It then sets out the prescriptions of philosophers, comparing Plato's preference for eu prattein, the Pythagorean practice of opening letters with hygiainein, and Epicurus's usage, before citing greeting formulas from old comedy and lyric verse in support of the primacy of health.
grc.lucian.pseudologista: The Pseudologista is a short Greek invective by Lucian of Samosata, in which a speaker denounces a malicious critic who has taunted him as a barbarian and jeered at his declamations. Threatening repayment in the biting iambs associated with Archilochus, the speaker appeals to the prologue-figure of a Menandrian comedy as an ally in frank speech and rehearses the man's notorious conduct. The closing portion recounts an anecdote from Olympia, where a sophist passed off as his own improvisation a written speech about Pythagoras that had been patched together from borrowed material, while the audience recognised each stolen passage.
grc.lucian.quomodo_historia_conscribenda_sit: Quomodo Historia Conscribenda Sit ('How to Write History') is a Greek satirical essay by Lucian of Samosata, cast as an address to one Philo. It opens with the tale of the Abderites driven into tragic delirium by a performance of Euripides' Andromeda and with the anecdote of Diogenes rolling his barrel while the Corinthians hurried to arm themselves against Philip, which Lucian offers as his excuse for adding a word of counsel amid the crowd of self-appointed historians. The work goes on to mock the pretensions of contemporary writers of history and to set out precepts on what to avoid and how to select, arrange, and narrate material, taking its occasion from a recent war against the barbarians and a campaign in Armenia.
grc.lucian.scytha: A very short Greek prose piece by Lucian of Samosata, the Scytha recounts how Toxaris, a Scythian who had come to Athens in pursuit of Greek learning before Anacharsis, died there and received heroic honours under the name of a healer. It tells how the hero ended a great plague by instructing the Athenians, through the wife of the Areopagite Architelus, to sprinkle their narrow streets with wine, and how a white horse is still sacrificed at his tomb near the Dipylon in payment for the cure. The narrative then turns to Anacharsis, newly landed at Athens and bewildered as a barbarian stranger, whom Toxaris greets in Scythian in the Ceramicus and consoles, promising to guide him through the finest sights of Athens and Greece and to introduce him to a wise and poor Athenian who serves as lawgiver to the city.
grc.lucian.tyrannicida: A short Greek composition by Lucian of Samosata, cast as a courtroom speech in which a self-styled tyrannicide demands a reward from the judges. The speaker recounts how he freed his city from two tyrants, a father and son who ruled together, killing the son with his sword and bringing about the father's death through his grief over the son's corpse, and he boasts that no one before him ended two despots at a single stroke. He answers an opponent who champions the dead men, reviews the double misrule the city endured and its despair of ever being free, and closes by pleading that the recompense owed by the laws should not pass him by.
grc.lucian.vitarum_auctio: A short Greek dialogue by Lucian, the Vitarum Auctio stages an auction of philosophical lives. Zeus instructs Hermes to herald the sale and arrange the wares, and prospective buyers examine the goods on offer: a Pythagorean expounds reincarnation, number symbolism and his diet of beans, and a Cynic who calls himself a citizen of the world and a physician of the passions is appraised like a watch-dog. The closing exchange presents the Cynic's self-description as a liberator of mankind and a prophet of truth and frank speech.
grc.maximus_of_tyre.dialexeis: The Dialexeis of Maximus of Tyre, also transmitted under the title Philosophumena, is a collection of philosophical lectures composed in Greek. It consists of orations on ethical and philosophical subjects, the first of which contrasts the actors of Dionysus with the philosopher, who plays many roles in a civic drama directed by god. That opening oration argues that the philosopher's logos must adapt to every occasion of human life, illustrating the point with Homeric quotations and analogies drawn from musical harmonies, rivers, and athletic contests.
grc.niciae_epistula.epistula: A Greek prose letter attributed to the Athenian general Nicias and addressed to the Athenians, presenting itself as a dispatch from the force besieging Syracuse in Sicily. The speaker recalls victories already reported in earlier letters, the arrival of the Lacedaemonian Gylippus with troops from the Peloponnese and certain Sicilian cities, and the counter-wall by which the enemy have checked the Athenian circumvallation. He goes on to describe the attrition of the fleet through waterlogged hulls and crews wasted by desertion and losses to enemy cavalry, and closes by urging the Athenians to send fresh land and naval forces, ample money, and a successor commander, pleading ill health and the need for swift action once spring arrives.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_timotheum_ii: The Second Epistle to Timothy is a Greek New Testament letter of the Roman imperial period, attributed in its opening to the apostle Paul writing to his associate Timothy. Presented as a final charge from prison, it urges Timothy to rekindle his gift, guard the sound teaching entrusted to him, and endure hardship for the gospel, using the figures of the soldier, the athlete and the farmer. The letter warns against teachers such as Hymenaeus and Philetus and against the conduct of the last days, and closes with instructions to preach the word alongside final personal instructions and remarks.
grc.philip_ii_king_of_macedonia.epistulae: The Epistulae is a short Greek collection of letters transmitted under the name of Philip II of Macedon and preserved among the collected Greek epistolographers. The letters are addressed to the council and people of Athens: the first reports Philip's operations in Phocis and warns against Athenian aid to the Phocians, while the longer second letter sets out a catalogue of grievances over Athenian conduct of the peace, including the seizure of heralds and envoys, the harbouring of pirates, and support for the Thracian rulers Teres and Cersobleptes. The collection comprises at least two letters; both are of uncertain date, and the attribution to Philip II is conventional.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_ebrietate: De Ebrietate (On Drunkenness) is a Greek treatise by the Jewish philosopher and scriptural exegete Philo Judaeus. Continuing a discussion begun in the preceding book, it surveys the passages of Mosaic legislation that mention wine and the vine, which permit drink to some and forbid it to others, such as priests and those under the vow of Numbers 6, and asks what the lawgiver intends by these provisions. Drunkenness serves as a symbol of a range of failings, including raving, insensibility, insatiable desire, false cheer, and spiritual nakedness, each traced to causes such as want of education, ignorance, and uncontrolled passion. Biblical episodes, among them Noah's drunkenness, Jacob's departure and Esau's return, and the stoning of the rebellious son in Deuteronomy, are expounded allegorically in support of these interpretations.
grc.philo_judaeus.in_flaccum: In Flaccum is a Greek prose treatise by Philo Judaeus concerning Aulus Avilius Flaccus, the Roman prefect of Egypt and Alexandria. It casts Flaccus as the successor of Sejanus in the campaign of hostility toward the Jews and relates the harm he brought upon the nation as far as his power allowed. The narrative sketches his energetic and upright administration over five years under Tiberius, then follows his decline after the accession of Gaius, as ambition and fear displaced his earlier judgment. The opening anticipates the charge of inconsistency, explaining that the prefect is praised first so that his later wickedness may appear the more plainly.
grc.plato.alcibiades_1: A Socratic dialogue by Plato, set in Athens at the moment when the young Alcibiades, son of Cleinias, is about to enter public life. Socrates, who has long kept his distance, explains that a daimonic sign opposing him has only now ceased, and proceeds to probe the grounds of Alcibiades' self-assurance: his beauty, noble birth, wealth, and the guardianship of Pericles. He sets against these Alcibiades' ambition to display himself before the Athenian demos and to extend his power over the other Greeks and beyond, arguing that success in politics requires prior knowledge of oneself and care of one's own soul.
grc.plato.critias: A Platonic dialogue of uncertain date, the Critias continues the conversation of the Timaeus among Socrates, Timaeus, Critias and Hermocrates. Critias undertakes to tell, from an account Solon brought from Egypt, the war waged nine thousand years before between ancient Athens and the inhabitants of Atlantis, an island greater than Libya and Asia that later sank beneath the sea in earthquakes and mud. The surviving portion consists largely of introductory remarks on the greater difficulty of imitating human than divine affairs, a request for indulgence, and an invocation of Memory, before turning to the prehistoric Athenians and their adversaries. The narrative then breaks off, leaving the work unfinished.
grc.plato.epinomis: The Epinomis is a short Greek philosophical dialogue transmitted under Plato's name and read as an appendix to the Laws. It resumes the conversation of the Athenian Stranger with Cleinias and Megillus after their long examination of the founding of laws, now asking what a mortal must learn in order to become truly wise. The speakers pass in review the arts bound up with necessity, farming, the preparation of food, building and toolmaking, hunting, divination, painting and music, and generalship, and find that none of them yields wisdom, leaving open what knowledge might deserve that name and make human life blessed.
grc.plato.minos: The Minos is a short prose dialogue attributed to Plato, in which Socrates questions an unnamed companion about what law is in itself. After testing definitions such as what is legally recognised and the decree of the city, the discussion arrives at law as a kind of right opinion that aims at the discovery of what truly is, and then asks why laws differ among peoples and change over time, with examples drawn from Greek and barbarian customs. The closing section turns to Minos of Crete, examining his reputation and presenting him as the most ancient of lawgivers.
grc.plutarch.apophthegmata_laconica: A Greek collection of pithy sayings (apophthegms) ascribed to Spartan kings, generals, and citizens, transmitted among the Moralia of Plutarch. The sayings are arranged in alphabetical order by speaker, opening with Agesicles and Agesilaus, and each remark is prefaced by a short anecdote indicating the occasion on which it was uttered. The material ranges over war, kingship, discipline, lawcourt conduct, and domestic matters, exemplifying the celebrated terseness of Laconic speech.
grc.plutarch.aquane_an_ignis_sit_utilior: A short Greek prose comparison by Plutarch, preserved in the Moralia and known by its Latin title 'Aquane an ignis sit utilior', which argues that water is more useful to humankind than fire. The case rests on citations of Pindar and Hesiod, on water's constant and universal necessity, its role in the growth of plants and animals, its harmlessness, cheapness and capacity to combine with fire, and on the sea's power to join distant peoples through trade and exchange. A closing argument from cosmology assigns earth and water the role of matter, with fire and breath as formative principles, while still granting fire a governing place among the elements.
grc.plutarch.aristides: The Aristides, a Greek biographical narrative from Plutarch's Lives, treats the Athenian statesman Aristides son of Lysimachus of the deme Alopecē. The work opens by weighing conflicting traditions about the extent of Aristides' poverty, setting Demetrius of Phalerum's case against the rejoinder of Panaetius concerning the choregic tripod dedications, and takes his ostracism as further evidence in the discussion. It then presents his austere and justice-minded character, his association with Cleisthenes and admiration for Lycurgus, and his prolonged political rivalry with Themistocles.
grc.plutarch.comparationis_aristophanes_et_m: A brief Greek comparison of the comic poets Aristophanes and Menander, transmitted among the Moralia attributed to Plutarch. The piece contrasts the harsh, coarse and often ill-fitted diction of Aristophanes with the blended and graceful style of Menander, whose language suits every character, age and circumstance alike. It observes that Aristophanes satisfied neither the many nor the discerning, whereas Menander's comedies offered enjoyment in the theatre, at symposia and in private reading, and it likens the biting salt of Aristophanes' wit to the abundant, sweet harvest brought by Menander's plays.
grc.plutarch.comparison_aristides_cato: A short Greek prose work by Plutarch, the formal comparison (synkrisis) that closes his paired lives of Aristides of Athens and Cato the Elder. It weighs the two statesmen point by point, noting their rise from modest means, their contrasting political circumstances in Athens and Rome, and their military records at Marathon and Plataea and in the war against Antiochus. Further passages contrast Aristides' ostracism by Themistocles with Cato's endurance of many prosecutions, discuss household economy and frugality with digressions on Lycurgus at Sparta and quotations from Hesiod and Homer, and conclude with the divergent fortunes of the two men's descendants.
grc.plutarch.comparison_demetrius_antony: A brief Greek prose piece, the formal comparison (synkrisis) that concludes the paired lives of Demetrius and Antony in Plutarch's Parallel Lives. Plutarch weighs the two men point by point: the origin and extent of each man's power, conduct in office, military achievements, liberality, indulgence in pleasure, marriages, religious offences, treatment of parents and kinsmen, and breaches of oaths and treaties. Throughout, Demetrius is judged the less culpable of the two, while Antony's greatest victories are ascribed to his generals rather than to his own doing.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_lysander_sulla: A short Greek composition of uncertain date attributed to Plutarch, serving as the formal comparison (synkrisis) that closes his paired biographies of Lysander and Sulla. Weighing the Spartan against the Roman, it contrasts their paths to power, Lysander's rise in an orderly Sparta, Sulla's amid civil disorder at Rome, and reviews their conduct in matters of wealth, pleasure, friends, and their native cities, judging Sulla the greater general but the more tyrannical character. The closing section touches on Sulla's two naval victories, the siege of Athens, and the misadventure at Haliartus.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_nicias_and_crassu: A short formal comparison (synkrisis) in Greek by Plutarch, concluding his paired biographies of the Athenian Nicias and the Roman Crassus. The passage weighs the two men point by point: Nicias's wealth is judged more blameless in its acquisition than Crassus's, and his public spending on festivals and dedications is set against Crassus's lavish feasting, political violence, and ambition, including his rivalry with Pompey and Caesar and his command against Spartacus. It then contrasts Nicias's cautious, peace-loving conduct and his forced generalship, notably in the Sicilian expedition, with Crassus's aggressiveness and hunger for command, closing with reflections on courage, safety, and service to the state.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_pelopidas_and_mar: A short Greek essay by Plutarch, forming the formal comparison that closes his paired Lives of Pelopidas and Marcellus. It weighs the shared qualities of the two generals, courage, toil, and greatness of spirit, while contrasting Marcellus's victories over the Celts, his capture of Syracuse, and his contests with Hannibal against Pelopidas's triumphs at Tegyra and Leuctra and his part in overthrowing the tyrants at Thebes. The later passages take up the deaths of both men, Pelopidas falling in battle against a tyrant and Marcellus in a reckless scouting exploit, and reflect on the reputation, mourning, and burial each received.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_timoleon_and_aemi: A short Greek prose comparison (synkrisis) that Plutarch appends to the paired biographies of Timoleon and Aemilius Paulus. It weighs the two commanders point by point: both waged wars against distinguished antagonists, Macedonians in Aemilius's case and Carthaginians and tyrants in Timoleon's, and the comparison covers the justice of their conduct, their disinterestedness toward wealth, and their bearing under fortune, judging Aemilius the more steadfast in calamity. Timoleon's twenty-year withdrawal from the assembly and marketplace after the deed done to his brother is noted as a failure of firmness in an otherwise gentle character.
grc.plutarch.de_amicorum_multitudine: A short Greek ethical essay from Plutarch's Moralia, De Amicorum Multitudine ('On Having Many Friends') argues that genuine friendship cannot be extended to a crowd, since affection divided among many, like a river split into channels, runs thin and weak. Opening from Socrates' cross-examination of Menon the Thessalian about virtue, the essay warns against a heedless love of many friends, who are gathered from dinner parties, gymnasia and market-places, and contrasts with them the celebrated pairs of legend, Theseus and Peirithous, Achilles and Patroclus, Orestes and Pylades, Damon and Phintias, Epaminondas and Pelopidas. Citing Homer, Menander and Empedocles and closing with the painter Zeuxis' remark that he works slowly because he works for a long time, it holds that a friend must be chosen by judgment and kept through long familiarity and usefulness rather than taken up casually.
grc.plutarch.de_faciae_quae_in_orbe_lunae_ap: A Greek philosophical dialogue by Plutarch, preserved in the Moralia, in which the speakers investigate the cause of the face-like figure seen on the moon. The discussion, framed as a conversation among friends, examines a series of rival explanations, including optical weakness of the eye, reflections of the outer sea from the lunar surface, and the theories of earlier natural philosophers such as Empedocles, Epicurus, and Clearchus, and it goes on to consider the physical nature and composition of the moon itself. The work is of uncertain date, belonging to the period of Plutarch's writing in Greek under Roman rule.
grc.plutarch.de_fortuna: A short Greek prose essay by Plutarch, De Fortuna ('On Fortune') argues that human affairs are governed not by chance but by good counsel (euboulia) and prudence (phronesis). Historical exempla, including Aristides' endurance of poverty, Scipio's refusal of spoil after taking Carthage, Alexander's restraint, and Priam's ruin, serve to show that virtue and vice alike arise from reasoned choice rather than luck. Quoting Sophocles, Plato, Heraclitus, Empedocles, Aeschylus, and Anaxagoras, the essay credits the Promethean gift of reason with human mastery over the animals and with the success of the crafts, which it describes as scattered fragments of prudence apportioned to the needs of life.
grc.plutarch.de_sera_numinis_vindicta: A Greek philosophical dialogue by Plutarch, handed down among the Moralia, on the question of why divine punishment of the wicked is so often long delayed. In the frame conversation, Patrocleas, Timon and Olympichus, walking together in a stoa, take up the Epicurean objection that deferred vengeance undermines belief in providence, illustrated from Euripides' image of Justice advancing on slow feet. The work defends divine providence by likening divine justice to the physician's art, which administers punishment as a remedy with due regard to the timing, measure and condition of each offender.
grc.plutarch.de_superstitione: A short Greek treatise by Plutarch, the biographer and moral essayist who flourished around the turn of the first and second centuries CE, preserved among his Moralia. It opens by dividing false opinion about the gods into atheism and superstition, and argues that superstition is the worse condition, a passion rooted in fear rather than a mere false judgement. The essay describes how the superstitious man is robbed of sleep, tormented by terrifying dreams, and driven to degrading purifications, bathings, and obeisances at the hands of charlatans and soothsayers. Contrasting such bondage with the calm of proper piety, it urges prayer to the gods in plain and rightful speech, ending with the observation that the superstitious find no rest in waking or in sleeping.
grc.plutarch.demetrius: Plutarch's Life of Demetrius is a Greek biographical work, paired with the Life of Antony, as its opening prologue announces. The prologue argues by analogy with the senses and the arts that good and bad must alike be brought before the judgment, citing the Spartan custom of forcing helots to drink unmixed wine before the young as a precedent for exhibiting bad lives alongside good ones, and declares that Demetrius Poliorcetes and Antony exemplify how great natures produce great vices as well as great virtues. The narrative then turns to Demetrius, son of Antigonus, treating the question of his parentage, his remarkable appearance, his resemblance to Dionysus in his alternation of warfare and luxury, his devotion to his father, and a career marked by great successes, great failures, and dramatic reversals of fortune.
grc.plutarch.galba: The Galba is a Greek prose biography by Plutarch, one of the Lives devoted to Roman statesmen and emperors. It opens with reflections on the relation between commanders and their armies, citing the sayings of Iphicrates, Paulus Aemilius, and Plato, and describes the turmoil after Nero's death, when the Palatine received four emperors in rapid succession. The narrative recounts Nymphidius Sabinus's proclamation of Galba amid promised donatives to the troops, then turns to Galba's lineage, wealth, kinship with Livia, consulship, frugal manner of life, and appointment by Nero as governor of Hispania. It follows his conduct in that province, his popularity amid the prosecutions under Nero's procurators, and the revolt of Julius Vindex, whose letters urged him to assume imperial power.
grc.plutarch.mulierum_virtutes: Mulierum Virtutes ('The Virtues of Women') is a Greek essay by Plutarch, transmitted as part of the Moralia, addressed to a woman named Clea. The preface rejects Thucydides' notion that the best woman is the one of whom least is said, and argues, with appeals to Gorgias, Roman funerary custom, and pairings such as Semiramis with Sesostris and Porcia with Brutus, that virtue is one and the same in men and women, differing only in the color it takes from each subject's nature and habits. The work then assembles reports of women's courage and resolve, beginning with the Trojan women who burned the ships on the Italian coast and the Phocian women who bound themselves to share their men's decision to face the Thessalians, an episode commemorated in the festival of the Elaphebolia at Hyampolis.
grc.plutarch.parallela_minora: A short Greek work of uncertain date transmitted under the name of Plutarch and printed among the Moralia. Its preface defends apparently incredible stories of the past against charges of invention, and the body assembles a series of brief paired anecdotes in which an episode from early Greek history is matched with a similar episode from early Roman history, each entry closing with a citation of the historian from whom the story is drawn. The episodes include battlefield deeds and acts of self-sacrifice at Marathon, Thermopylae, and the Caudine Forks, together with marvels such as the chasm at Celaenae and the leap of Curtius into the Tiber.
grc.plutarch.pericles: A Greek life of the Athenian statesman Pericles by Plutarch, written during the Roman imperial period as part of his series of paired biographies. The work opens with a preface defending the study of the deeds of virtuous men, citing Caesar's remarks on pampered pets and contrasting fine artwork with the character of its makers, and announces its pairing of Pericles with Fabius Maximus. The narrative then treats Pericles' distinguished lineage through Xanthippus and Agariste, his distinctive appearance as mocked by comic poets such as Cratinus, Telecleides and Eupolis, and his teachers in music and statesmanship, including Damon.
grc.plutarch.praecepta_gerendae_reipublicae: An essay in Greek by Plutarch, transmitted with the Moralia and framed as advice to Menemachus, a young citizen embarking on a public career. The speaker declines purely theoretical instruction and sets out practical precepts for political life: entering public affairs from settled judgment rather than vanity, accident, or appetite, gauging the character of one's fellow citizens before attempting to guide it, and avoiding the snares of flattery, reputation, and power once taken up. Historical exempla drawn from Greek and Roman affairs, including Stratocles, Caius Gracchus, Alcibiades, and Hanno, illustrate the argument throughout.
grc.plutarch.themistocles: A Greek biography of the Athenian statesman Themistocles, composed by Plutarch during the Roman imperial period as one of his Parallel Lives. It opens with the obscurity of Themistocles' origins, his father Neocles of the deme Phrearrhioi and a mother variously named as the Thracian Abrotonon or the Carian Euterpe, and with stories of his ambitious, restless youth. The narrative then follows his rivalry with Aristides, his championing of naval power and leadership at Salamis against the Persians, and his eventual ostracism and reception at the Persian court. It closes with the conflicting traditions surrounding his death in exile.
grc.plutarch.titus_flamininus: Plutarch's Life of Titus Quinctius Flamininus, composed in Greek, is one of the paired Greek and Roman biographies in his series of Lives. It opens by describing the Roman commander's appearance as shown in a bronze statue in Rome and his temperament, said to have been quick to anger and quick to gratitude, before recounting his service under Marcellus in the war against Hannibal, his part in the second capture of Tarentum and appointment as its governor, and his election to the consulship before he was thirty. The narrative follows his conduct of the war against Philip V of Macedon, his preference for persuasion and diplomacy with the Greeks, his crossing into Epirus with three thousand picked veterans from Scipio's campaigns, and the hard fighting needed to force a passage through the defiles of the Apsus river.
grc.polyaenus.excerpta_polyaeni: The Excerpta Polyaeni is a short Greek compilation of excerpts on military command transmitted under the name of Polyaenus of Macedonia, of uncertain date. Its opening item catalogues the virtues of an ideal general, from tirelessness and prudence to the management of soldiers' morale and fears, and the remaining items, each introduced by 'that' (ὅτι), recount anecdotes and stratagems of commanders such as Iphicrates, Philip and Alexander of Macedon, Brasidas, Timotheus, Pisistratus, Mucius Scaevola, Caesar, and Cassander. The entries illustrate training under false alarms, endurance of hardship, secrecy and deception, clemency toward captives, and the staging of appearances on campaign.
grc.pseudoaristotle.de_spiritu: De Spiritu (On Spirit) is a short Greek treatise attributed to Aristotle but transmitted under the name of pseudo-Aristotle, and of uncertain date. Composed in prose, it takes the form of an aporetic inquiry into the innate pneuma or spirit, asking how it is maintained and increased within the body. The discussion weighs whether the spirit is nourished through respiration or through the digestion of food, raises objections against the view of Aristogenes that breath itself is concocted as nutriment, and criticises accounts of breathing associated with Empedocles and Democritus. It closes by distinguishing three movements of the pneuma in the artery, respiration, the pulse, and the processing of nourishment, and examining their order and causes.
grc.pseudogalen.ad_gaurum_quomodo_animetur_f: A short Greek treatise transmitted under Galen's name but Neoplatonic in character and of uncertain date, addressed to one Gaurus and asking how embryos come to be ensouled. It debates whether the embryo is an animal in actuality or only in potentiality, or rather lives in the manner of a plant, and when the soul enters the body. The author surveys and rejects answers that place ensoulment at conception, at the first formation of the seed, or at the embryo's first movement, including Pythagorean and Numenian speculations and a fanciful account of the womb drawing in a soul through breath, while appealing to Hippocrates on the timing of formation. It concludes that ensoulment comes from outside and follows birth, presenting this as the position that saves Plato's account of the entry of souls.
grc.septuaginta.bel_et_draco_theodotionis: The Greek episode of Bel and the Dragon, transmitted in the Septuagint corpus in the version attributed to Theodotion, forms one of the additions to the book of Daniel and is written in biblical prose of Hellenistic date. Beginning with the death of Astyages and the accession of Cyrus the Persian, it recounts how Daniel exposes the idol Bel as mere clay and bronze, its offerings being consumed nightly by the priests and their households through a hidden entrance, and how he slays the great dragon worshipped by the Babylonians with cakes of pitch, fat, and hair. Cast into the lions' pit by the enraged Babylonians, Daniel survives there six days, until the prophet Habakkuk, carried by an angel from Judaea by the hair of his head, brings him food in the den.
grc.septuaginta.machabaeorum_g: Third Maccabees, a Hellenistic Jewish narrative in Greek prose preserved in the Septuagint, is anonymous and of uncertain date. The book opens with Ptolemy IV Philopator's campaign against Antiochus III and the battle of Raphia, then recounts the king's attempt to force his way into the Jerusalem temple, the panicked prayers of the priests and populace, and the divine intervention that thwarts him. It continues with his persecution of the Jews of Egypt, the humiliating registration of the community, the condemnation of two thousand captives in the hippodrome, their deliverance through two heavenly agents, and the closing thanksgiving that establishes an annual festival.
grc.septuaginta.malachias: Malachias is the Septuagint's Greek rendering of the book of Malachi, the concluding book of the Twelve Prophets, translated from the Hebrew in the Hellenistic period. The work unfolds as a sequence of disputations between the Lord and Israel, reproaching the priests for blemished offerings and unfaithful teaching, recalling the covenant with Levi, condemning faithlessness in marriage and in tithes, and announcing a coming messenger and a day of judgement. Its prose keeps the dialogue form of the original, in which the people repeatedly question the Lord and receive answers delivered through the prophet.
grc.septuaginta.paralipomenon_i_sive_chronic: Paralipomenon I sive Chronicon I is the first book of Chronicles in its Septuagint Greek version, the Hellenistic translation of the Hebrew scriptures, rendered by an anonymous translator. The book consists chiefly of prose genealogical lists running from Adam through Noah, Abraham, Esau, and the twelve tribes of Israel to the house of David, followed by an account of David's reign, including the removal of the ark to Jerusalem and the preparations for building the temple. Greek-speaking readers transmitted it under the title Paralipomenon, 'things passed over', reflecting its supplementary relation to the narratives of Samuel and Kings.
grc.septuaginta.psalmi_salomonis: A Hellenistic Greek collection of psalms transmitted with the Old Testament in Greek and attributed in its title to Solomon. The poems lament the desecration and captivity of Jerusalem at the hands of foreign invaders and sinners within the city, denounce an arrogant ruler who blasphemed against God and met a shameful end, and proclaim divine justice that repays the wicked while showing mercy to the faithful. Several pieces take the form of first-person prayers or admonitions on righteousness, discipline, and trust in the Lord, and one promises that the righteous will rise to eternal life in the light of the Lord.
grc.soranus.de_fasciis: A short Greek treatise on surgical bandaging transmitted under the name of Soranus and of uncertain date. It consists of numbered instructions for applying bandages to the head and face: each entry states where to set the beginning of the bandage, how to lead the windings, straight, oblique, or circular, across the scalp, forehead, brows, eyes, nose, cheeks, or jaws, and for which part the binding is intended. The sections bear traditional bandage names, among them mitra, basiliskos, hierax, charax, and phalaron, and refer to numbered tables of diagrams, one of which is recorded as corrupted.
grc.tryphon_i_grammaticus.περὶ_τρόπων: A short Greek grammatical treatise attributed to Tryphon the grammarian and of uncertain date, on tropes (tropoi), the departures from literal expression characteristic of poetic diction. After defining phrasis and distinguishing kyriologia, the plain use of words, from trope, it enumerates fourteen kinds, metaphor, catachresis, allegory, riddle, metalepsis, metonymy, synecdoche, onomatopoeia, periphrasis, anastrophe, hyperbaton, pleonasm, ellipsis and parapleroma, and defines each in turn. The definitions are illustrated chiefly with examples from Homer and other poets, and neighbouring figures such as metaphor and catachresis, or allegory and riddle, are carefully distinguished from one another.
grc.xenophon.anabasis: A Greek prose narrative by Xenophon, the Anabasis opens with the rivalry between Cyrus the Younger and his elder brother Artaxerxes and recounts Cyrus' secret assembly of a Greek mercenary force under cover of campaigns against the Pisidians and Tissaphernes. The work takes its name from the army's march up-country from Sardis into the interior of the Persian empire, and goes on to follow the fortunes of the Greek soldiers after Cyrus' death in battle. Xenophon himself appears in the narrative among those who lead the retreat.
grc.archimedes.dimensio_circuli: A short Greek mathematical treatise by Archimedes, transmitted under the Latin title Dimensio Circuli ('Measurement of a Circle'). It sets out and proves three propositions: that the area of any circle equals that of a right-angled triangle whose legs correspond to the radius and the circumference; that the circle is to the square on its diameter in the ratio of 11 to 14; and that the circumference exceeds three times the diameter by less than a seventh and more than ten seventy-firsts, a result established by approximating the circle with inscribed and circumscribed ninety-six-sided polygons.
grc.aristotle.de_divinatione_per_somnum: A short Greek philosophical treatise, transmitted under Aristotle's name as part of the Parva Naturalia and of uncertain date, on the divination said to occur through dreams. It rejects the view that dreams are sent by a god, since they come indiscriminately to animals and to ordinary and melancholic people rather than to the best and wisest, and classifies them instead as causes, signs, or coincidences of the events they appear to foreshadow. A naturalistic explanation follows, in which small movements and perceptions registered in sleep account for apparent foresight, with discussion of Democritus' theory of images and effluences, of physicians' attention to dreams as bodily symptoms, and of the claim that the ablest judge of dreams is the one who can quickly discern their resemblances.
grc.artaxerxis_epistulae.epistulae: Two royal letters in Greek attributed to the Persian king Artaxerxes and preserved among the Greek epistolographers. The first purports to be the decree ordering the extermination of the Jews throughout the empire at Haman's instigation, the second the revocation of that decree, the crucifixion of Haman at Susa, and the granting of peace and honour to Mordecai and Esther on the thirteenth of Adar. Together they retell the story of the Book of Esther in the king's own voice, in the elevated prose of an imperial rescript. The composition is of uncertain date.
grc.critias.fragmenta: A collection of fragments of Critias of Athens, son of Callaeschrus and one of the Thirty, preserved as quotations in later authors including Athenaeus, Plutarch, Stobaeus, Hephaestion and Diogenes Laertius. The verse is chiefly elegiac and lyric: a tribute to Anacreon, lines on the Sicilian invention of the kottabos, an account of Spartan drinking customs, an elegy in praise of Alcibiades that recalls Critias' motion for his recall, a prayer for the wealth of Skopas and the victories of Arcesilas, and gnomic sayings such as the 'nothing in excess' ascribed to Chilon, together with a note crediting Orpheus with the invention of the hexameter. The collection closes with lines from the tragedies Tennes, Rhadamanthys and Peirithous, transmitted under Euripides' name but placed here among the fragments attributed to Critias.
grc.demosthenes.against_pantaenetus: An Attic forensic speech preserved among the orations of Demosthenes, composed for delivery in an Athenian private suit in the fourth century BCE. The speaker answers a claim for damages brought by Pantaenetus by entering a paragraphē, or demurrer, arguing that the suit is inadmissible because Pantaenetus has already obtained a judgment against Euergetus, his partner in a loan of a hundred and five minas secured on a workshop and thirty slaves at Maroneia. The speech sets out the making of the loan, the leasing of the workshop and slaves to Mnesicles, the speaker's absence on a voyage to the Black Sea, and the subsequent disputes and confrontations with the claimants.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_accession_of_alexande: A short deliberative speech of Demosthenes, addressed to the Athenian assembly at the time of Alexander's accession to the Macedonian throne. The speaker argues that exhortations to abide by the oaths and clauses of the Common Peace are justified only where the settlement is genuinely honoured, and contends that Alexander has himself broken it by installing tyrants at Messene, the sons of Philiadas, and at Pellene, where Chaeron was set over a demos stripped of its property, in defiance of the treaty's guarantee of Greek freedom and autonomy. Since the treaty declares such violators common enemies against whom all signatories are to campaign, the speaker urges the Athenians to treat the breaches as grounds for war, and assails those who preach obedience to the oaths while enriching themselves in Macedonian pay.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_thucydidis: A short Greek treatise by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, framed as a letter to Aelius Tubero, on the language and style of the historian Thucydides. It surveys the distinctive features of Thucydides' diction, including archaisms, poetic and rare vocabulary, and unconventional grammatical constructions such as inversions of case, number and voice, and characterises his style through its concision, harshness and rapidity of expression. Passages from Thucydides' history are cited and analysed to illustrate each usage, and the work presents itself as a fuller treatment of points already discussed in the author's other writings on Thucydides and the early orators.
grc.epicharmus.fragmenta: The Fragmenta of Epicharmus gathers the surviving remains of the Greek poet's verse, composed in Doric dialect. The pieces are short and largely gnomic or dialectical, treating subjects such as the usefulness of maxims, the ceaseless change of all things, the difference between perceiving through the senses and understanding, and the presence of intelligence in living creatures. The fragments stand embedded in excerpts from the later ancient writers who quote them, and the collection closes with a passage in which Epicharmus foretells that his sayings will one day be recast in new dress.
grc.euripides.ion: The Ion is a Greek tragedy by the Athenian dramatist Euripides, whose career fell in the later fifth century BC; the date of its first production is uncertain. The prologue, spoken by Hermes, recounts how Apollo fathered Ion on Creusa, daughter of Erechtheus of Athens, and how the exposed infant was reared as a temple servant at Delphi, ignorant of his parents. The drama that follows centres on the childless Creusa and her husband Xuthus consulting Apollo's oracle about offspring, and on the recognition of the youth, who is destined to give his name to the Ionians.
grc.eutropius.breviarium_historiae_romanae: A Greek version of the Breviarium Historiae Romanae, the compressed history of Rome from the foundation of the city composed by Eutropius. The work recounts how Roman power grew from the humblest beginnings to a dominion without equal in memory, opening with the birth of Romulus to Rhea Silvia and Mars and his founding of the settlement on the Palatine hill. The narrative proceeds reign by reign through the seven kings, Romulus, Numa Pompilius, Tullus Hostilius, Ancus Marcius, Tarquinius Priscus, Servius Tullius and Tarquinius Superbus, down to the rape of Lucretia, the expulsion of the Tarquins and the end of the monarchy.
grc.galen.de_bono_habitu: A short Greek medical treatise by Galen, known by the Latin title De Bono Habitu. The work begins from the ordinary use of the term hexis for a stable disposition of the body and distinguishes euexia, or good condition, from kakexia, defining true good condition as the perfection of health found in the best-constituted bodies. The greater part of the discussion contrasts this with the condition of athletes, which Hippocrates, Plato, and other ancient authorities are cited as condemning as precarious and useless for the natural activities of the body, since it depends on immoderate bulk and overfullness of the veins. The treatise closes with an account of how excess nourishment suppresses the innate heat, bursts the vessels of the lungs, liver, and thorax, and produces the sudden paralyses described in Hippocratic writings.
grc.galen.de_humero_iis_modis_prolapso_quos_: A brief Greek medical treatise by Galen on dislocations of the shoulder occurring in ways that Hippocrates had not described. Galen contrasts the single mode of dislocation recorded by Hippocrates with the additional modes known to later physicians and recounts five cases he himself witnessed, one in Smyrna during his student years and four in Rome, arguing that their frequency reflects the size of those cities and the unskilful practices of doctors and wrestling trainers. The work then describes reduction techniques, including countertraction, a broad strap around the chest, slings, and the Hippocratic bench, and closes with a discussion of how muscle tension or laxity and bodily condition, whether lean or fleshy, make dislocation and reduction easier or harder, with remarks on the interpretation of Hippocratic wording.
grc.galen.de_usu_partium_corporis_humani_ixi: A Greek prose treatise on teleological anatomy by the second-century physician Galen, On the Usefulness of the Parts of the Body argues that each bodily part exists for the sake of the soul's activities. The portion here contains the work's opening argument, which defines a part as something with its own outline yet joined to other parts, presents the body as the soul's instrument, and surveys how the endowments of different animals, horns, tusks, speed, strength, match their several natures. Humans, alone naked and unarmed yet rational, receive hands in place of natural weapons, and Galen follows Aristotle in holding that man possesses hands because he is wisest, the hand serving as an organ before all organs as reason is an art before all arts. Hippocrates, Plato, and Aristotle are invoked by name throughout the argument.
grc.gregory_of_nazianzus.theological_oration: The Theological Orations are a set of five Greek discourses by Gregory of Nazianzus, a fourth-century Cappadocian church father, composed to defend the Nicene doctrine of the Trinity against Eunomian and kindred opponents who disputed the full divinity of the Son and the Holy Spirit. The first oration attacks the fashion for treating theology as a display of clever dialectic and lays down the principle that philosophising about God is not for everyone, nor at every time, nor on every subject, but only for those purified in soul and body, within the limits of human capacity. The remaining speeches apply these cautions to the divine nature itself, setting out Gregory's teaching on the generation of the Son and the godhead of the Spirit and showing why technical syllogistic argument cannot circumscribe the divine essence.
grc.herodian.ab_excessu_divi_marci: Herodian's Greek history, conventionally titled Ab excessu divi Marci ('From the death of the deified Marcus'), narrates the fortunes of the Roman empire from the reign and death of Marcus Aurelius through the succession of his son Commodus. The preface criticises earlier historians for preferring style and flattery to truth and announces a programme of careful, firsthand record of the era since Augustus, and especially of the period after Marcus, described as crowded with rapid successions of rulers, civil and foreign wars, revolts, plagues, earthquakes, and extraordinary imperial careers. The opening narrative treats Marcus's final illness while on campaign, his anxious provision for the young Commodus's education and conduct, and his address to his friends before his death. The author presents himself as a contemporary who saw, heard, and in some cases personally experienced the events he recounts, arranging the material by reigns and dynasties.
grc.hyperides.speeches: Forensic speeches and fragments by the Athenian orator Hyperides, active in the fourth century BC. The remains consist of excerpts of speeches addressed to Athenian jurors, including a defence against a public indictment (eisangelia) and material from private causes touching marriage, adoption, and inheritance, while the public charges alleged range from the betrayal of the dockyards to the seizure of a stronghold. Much of the wording survives only in passages quoted by later grammarians, notably Pollux, so the speeches are preserved discontinuously.
grc.lucian.bis_accusatus_sive_tribunalia: A Greek dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, bearing the Latin title Bis Accusatus sive Tribunalia ('Double Indictment, or Tribunals'). In the opening scene Zeus complains to Hermes of the endless toil of divine rule and of the suits long lodged by the arts and sciences against mortals who have abandoned them, which have lain untouched through the gods' supposed idleness. Hermes is sent to proclaim a day of court, and Justice (Dikē) is appointed to sit in judgment on the Areopagus over the accumulated cases.
grc.lucian.demonax: A short biographical encomium in Ancient Greek by Lucian, celebrating the philosopher Demonax, a Cypriot who settled in Athens. The narrative traces Demonax's self-directed turn to philosophy in youth, his eclectic adherence that mixed many schools while recalling Socrates and Diogenes of Sinope, and his practice of correcting others with wit and gentleness rather than anger. It records the esteem he won among the Athenians, his fearless defence against accusers who charged him, as Anytus and Meletus once charged Socrates, with never sacrificing to Athena or undergoing initiation in the Eleusinian Mysteries, and his willing departure from life after a long career of friendship and public service.
grc.lucian.fugitivi: A short satirical dialogue in Greek by Lucian of Samosata, transmitted under the Latin title Fugitivi ('The Runaways'). The speakers, Zeus and Philosophy, open by discussing the self-immolation of an elderly wonder-worker at the Olympic games, and Philosophy then laments the impostors who borrow her garb, gait, and name, occupying a middle ground between the general public and genuine philosophers. In her complaint she recounts how she set out to reform mankind, instructing Indian Brahmans and gymnosophists, Egyptian priests, Chaldaeans and Magi, and finally the Thracians, where Orpheus and Eumolpus received her teaching.
grc.lucian.lexiphanes: Lexiphanes is a satirical dialogue in Greek by Lucian of Samosata. Its title character offers Lycinus a reading from a newly composed work of his own, styled as an anti-Symposium after Plato's, written in extravagantly rare and bombastic Attic vocabulary. The recited passage, which recounts everyday episodes, a walk in the country, a visit to the baths and gymnasium, and an elaborate dinner, entirely in far-fetched jargon, allows Lycinus to mock the obscure and inflated diction at which Lucian's satire is directed.
grc.lucian.nigrinus: A short Greek dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, framed as a letter addressed to Nigrinus. It opens with a jest on the proverb about owls to Athens, after which a narrator recounts a visit to Nigrinus, a Platonic philosopher, whose conversation praised philosophy and the freedom it brings while deriding wealth, fame, rule, and other goods conventionally esteemed. The account dwells on the transforming effect of Nigrinus's words upon his listener and ends with the narrator memorising and rehearsing them in his absence.
grc.lycophron.alexandra: The Alexandra is a Greek dramatic monologue attributed to Lycophron and of uncertain date, spoken almost entirely by the Trojan prophetess Cassandra, whom the poem calls Alexandra, in the presence of her father Priam. The opening lines give the word to an attendant who explains that the maiden, seized by prophetic frenzy, now pours forth her oracles in dark, riddling speech like the voice of the Sphinx, before undertaking to recount the whole story from the beginning. The prophecy that follows foretells, in densely obscure diction thick with rare compounds and periphrastic mythological reference, the ruin of Troy, the griefs of Priam's house, and the varied fates of the Greek heroes on their homeward returns.
grc.marcus_aurelius.m._antonius_imperator_ad: Written in Greek by the Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius in the second century CE, the work transmitted under the title M. Antonius Imperator ad Se Ipsum and conventionally known as the Meditations (Ta eis heauton, 'To Himself') is a collection of private philosophical notes. It comprises twelve books of short, aphoristic entries: the first records the moral debts the author owes to relatives and teachers, while the remaining books set out Stoic reflections on self-control, impermanence, duty to others, and the rational order of the cosmos.
grc.nicomachus_of_gerasa.problemata_arithmet: A short collection of arithmetical problems in Greek, attributed to Nicomachus of Gerasa and transmitted with his Introductio Arithmetica. The problems show how to sum any run of consecutive numbers starting from a unit, offer rapid methods for computing such totals, and give a rule for summing numbers placed in arithmetical progression. One problem records a puzzle ascribed to a king Leo, requiring ten given numbers to be divided into two groups of five with equal sums, and the closing section explains a procedure for discovering a number someone holds secretly in mind through successive subtractions of three, five, and seven.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_thessalonicenses_i: First Thessalonians (Ad Thessalonicenses I) is a koine Greek prose epistle of the New Testament, composed in the Imperial period and addressed to the church of the Thessalonians in Macedonia. It opens in the names of Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, who give thanks for the recipients' faith, love, and endurance, recall the missionaries' hardships and labors at Thessalonica, and recount the sending of Timothy and the encouraging report he brought back. The letter then proceeds to exhortations on sanctification, sexual purity, and brotherly love, and teaches concerning the dead in Christ, the sudden coming of the day of the Lord, and the conduct expected of the community, closing with charges, prayer, and greetings.
grc.novum_testamentum.ioannis_i: The First Epistle of John is an anonymous Greek prose work of the New Testament, composed during the Imperial era and attributed by tradition to John, though neither its author nor its precise date is certain. It lacks the opening address and closing greetings of a normal letter, and in form stands closer to a circular homily or treatise addressed to Christian communities. The prologue bears witness to the word of life that was from the beginning and was manifested in Jesus Christ, after which the epistle proceeds through antitheses of light and darkness, love and hatred, and truth and falsehood, urging confession of sins and keeping the commandments. Recurring themes include divine sonship, the command to love one another, and warnings against antichrists who deny that Jesus is the Christ.
grc.plato.epistles: The Epistles is a collection of thirteen letters attributed to Plato, of uncertain date, most of them addressed to Dionysius of Syracuse or to Dion and the circle around him. They present themselves as correspondence arising from Plato's entanglement in Syracusan politics, combining reproach and counsel to the tyrant with reflections on friendship, reputation, and the philosophical life. The longest letter, conventionally numbered seventh, gives an autobiographical account of Plato's visits to Sicily and of the events surrounding Dion's death.
grc.plutarch.epitome_argumenti_stoicos: A short Greek epitome of an argument by Plutarch against the Stoics, condensing the polemic into a handful of compact illustrative sections. Each pairs a mythological or poetic exemplum, Pindar's Kaineus, Euripides' rejuvenated Iolaus, Athena's beautifying of Odysseus, the poetic Heracles, with the figure of the Stoic sage, mocking the paradoxes of apatheia, the sage's overnight passage from utter vice to perfect virtue, and his professed wealth and kingship alongside actual beggary. The recurring contrast runs between the invulnerability granted to mythical heroes and the Stoics' claim that their sage remains fearless, painless, and unbeaten amid wounds, torture, shipwreck, and want.
grc.pseudogalen.de_optima_secta_ad_thrasybul: A short Greek treatise on medical method, transmitted under the name of Galen and addressed to Thrasybulus, of uncertain date. It lays down three criteria by which any medical doctrine must be judged, truth, usefulness, and consistency with assumed principles, and then examines how doctrines are formed and tested, distinguishing appearances graspable by the senses from hidden things known through observation or demonstration. The author rejects the view that medicine rests on appearances alone or that its doctrines are merely conjectural, and the discussion closes by turning to the end of the medical art, by reference to which the usefulness of each doctrine is to be assessed.
grc.pseudolucian.ἔρωτες: A Greek dialogue transmitted under the name of pseudo-Lucian, the Erotes stages a conversation between Lycinus and Theomnestus on a festival day of sacrifice to Heracles and Aphrodite, turning on the question whether love of boys or of women is preferable. Lycinus answers with an account of a sea voyage toward Italy during which two men, one devoted to boys and the other to women, argued their respective causes, and he proceeds to report their speeches in detail. Authorship and date are uncertain, the work being ascribed to pseudo-Lucian in the Lucianic corpus.
grc.septuaginta.paralipomenon_b: Paralipomenon B is the second of the two Books of Paralipomena in the Septuagint, the Greek rendering of the Hebrew book known in English as 2 Chronicles, translated by an anonymous hand in the Hellenistic period. In biblical prose it narrates the reign of Solomon, the building and dedication of the temple at Jerusalem, and the subsequent history of the kings of Judah down to the Babylonian destruction of the city and the decree of Cyrus. The precise date and place of the translation are uncertain.
grc.septuaginta.susanna_translatio_graeca: The Susanna of the Septuagint is a Hellenistic prose narrative preserved in Greek among the additions to the book of Daniel. It recounts how Susanna, the pious wife of Joakim in Babylon, is lusted after by two elders appointed as judges, falsely accused of adultery when she refuses them, and condemned on their testimony; the young Daniel intervenes, questions the elders separately, exposes their contradictory accounts, and secures their execution while Susanna is vindicated. A brief closing coda praises the younger generation of Jacob and prays for a spirit of knowledge and understanding among the young.
grc.sextus_empiricus.pyrrhoniae_hypotyposes: The Pyrrhoniae Hypotyposes, a Greek prose treatise by the sceptical philosopher Sextus Empiricus of uncertain date, offers a systematic account of Pyrrhonian scepticism. The first book opens with a list of its chapters and then treats the division of philosophy into dogmatic, Academic and sceptical tendencies, the concept, principles, criterion and end of scepticism, the ten, five and two modes that lead to suspension of judgement (epochē) and tranquillity (ataraxia), and the characteristic sceptical phrases such as 'no more' and 'I suspend judgement'. Its remaining chapters distinguish scepticism from the Heraclitean, Democritean, Cyrenaic and Protagorean philosophies, from the Academy, and from empirical medicine.
grc.theophrastus.enquiry_into_plants: A Greek prose treatise on weather signs (De signis) by Theophrastus, transmitted alongside his botanical writings. It catalogues observable signs foretelling rain, wind, storms, and spells of fair weather, drawing on the risings and settings of stars such as the Pleiades, Arcturus, and Orion, on solar and lunar appearances, on the behaviour of birds and other animals, and on the conditions of mountains, coasts, and other localities. It also records named observers of the heavens, including Matricetas of Methymna, Cleostratus of Tenedos, Phaeinus of Athens, and Meton.

it.dante.inferno: The first cantica of Dante's Commedia, thirty-four cantos in which the poet, lost in a dark wood in 1300, is led by Virgil down through the nine circles of Hell. Each circle punishes a class of sin by a penalty that mirrors it, and the damned tell their stories as the travellers descend to the frozen centre of the earth.
it.dante.purgatorio: The second cantica, thirty-three cantos on the mountain of Purgatory, where souls are cleansed of the seven capital vices on ascending terraces. Virgil guides Dante to the summit and the earthly paradise, where he departs and Beatrice takes his place.
